paragraphs: The stone was not the end of the story. It was the opening sentence, and like all opening sentences it raised a question it could not answer: what happens when the hand that throws the stone meets a hand that throws a better one? The answer, repeated across ten thousand years and every continent, is the engine of this history. Weapons do not develop in a vacuum, nor on their own schedule. They develop in the space between two armed forces, each watching the other, each measuring the gap, each racing to close it. The stone gave way to the spear because the spear outranged the stone. The spear gave way to the bow because the bow outranged the spear. The bow gave way to the firearm because the firearm outranged the bow and asked less of the body that wielded it. Each step was not a leap of genius but a response to a problem posed by an adversary. The history of weapons is a conversation, and the conversation is mostly conducted in the imperative: *you must not be able to reach me.*

To see how that imperative works, it helps to begin not with the famous inventions but with the humble, stubborn constraints that shaped them. Consider the human body. A thrown stone travels as far as the shoulder can torque it—perhaps thirty or forty meters for a trained arm—and it arrives with energy that falls off sharply with distance. A spear extends the arm by two meters and concentrates its force on a point, but it can be thrown only once before the thrower must retrieve it or draw a knife. A bow stores energy in bent wood and sinew and releases it in a fraction of a second, sending an arrow two hundred meters or more with enough force to pierce hide and, at close range, bronze. The bow is the first weapon that lets a human being strike beyond the reach of the arm, and that single fact reorganizes everything around it: how battles are fought, who fights them, what armor is worth, and how much training a soldier needs. The bow is not a better stone. It is a different theory of the stone.

The earliest bows are lost to us, because wood and sinew rot. What survives are arrowheads: flint and chert points, some unmistakably projectile points, from sites in Africa and Europe dating back tens of thousands of years. The bowstring leaves no fossil. But the arrowhead is a confession. A point designed to be shot is a point designed for a weapon that throws it, and the bow is the only weapon that throws a point with that economy. By the time the first cities rise in Mesopotamia, the bow is already ancient, already refined, already the subject of myth. The Assyrians carve archers into their palace walls, and the archers wear conical helmets and draw composite bows from chariots. The composite bow—wood, horn, and sinew laminated under tension—is a technological achievement of a high order, and it exists because the simple wooden bow has a limit: the further you draw it, the more it wants to break. Lamination distributes the stress. The horn resists compression on the belly of the bow; the sinew resists tension on the back; the wood is the core that holds them together. The result is a bow shorter than a longbow yet storing more energy, which makes it a cavalry weapon, which makes it a weapon of the steppe.

Here the argument takes a concrete turn. The composite bow did not spread because it was elegant. It spread because it was useful to people on horseback, and people on horseback were useful to empires that needed to move fast across grass. The Scythians, the Huns, the Mongols—each built a way of war around the horse and the bow, and each posed a problem that settled empires could not solve with infantry alone. The settled empires answered with walls, fortifications, crossbows, and eventually gunpowder. The steppe answered with mobility and the recurve. For more than a thousand years the argument between the steppe and the sown was conducted in these terms, and the terms were set by the range and rate of fire of a bow.

The counterargument was the crossbow, and it is worth pausing on because it illustrates a principle that recurs throughout this history: a weapon that is easier to learn can beat a weapon that is harder to master, even if the harder weapon is better in the hands of an expert. A crossbow stores its energy in a stiff prod held by a catch, and the shooter releases it with a trigger. The draw weight can be enormous—far beyond what a hand-held bow can bear—because the shooter does not hold the string at full draw. The consequence is that a peasant can be trained to use a crossbow in weeks, while a longbowman takes years. The crossbow is the first weapon of mass infantry, the first weapon that says: the state does not need a caste of archers; it needs a supply of bolts and a levy of men. The Chinese deployed crossbows in enormous numbers, and the Song dynasty fielded crossbowmen as a core of its armies. In Europe the crossbow became the weapon of the town militia and the mercenary, and the Church famously tried to restrict its use against Christians—itself a sign of how effective it was. The longbow, by contrast, was a weapon of a particular society—the English yeomanry—and its power depended on a whole culture of archery practice, of Sunday butts and royal statutes, of a class of men whose bodies were shaped by the bow from boyhood.

The *Mary Rose* gives us the numbers. When Henry VIII's flagship sank in 1545 and was raised in 1982, the wreck yielded 137 longbows, and the surviving bows have estimated draw weights of 100 to 185 pounds. A modern archer drawing a 50-pound bow is considered strong. A 150-pound bow, drawn to the ear and held, then loosed, is a different order of physical fact, and it explains why the English longbowman was a product of lifelong training and why the weapon could not simply be copied by anyone who wanted it. The arrow from such a bow could pierce mail at close range and could kill a horse. At Agincourt in 1415 the longbowmen were the deciding arm, and the mud, the stakes, and the narrow field were the conditions that let them be decisive. The bow was not magic. It was a system: the bow, the arrow, the archer, the ground, the supply of goose feathers and yew staves. Take away any part and the system fails. This is the first great lesson of weapons history, and it will recur: *a weapon is never just an object; it is an object plus the society that can make it, feed it, and wield it.*

And then, in the space of a few centuries, the bow was overtaken. Not because it stopped working—longbows still killed men at Waterloo in the hands of a few diehards—but because a new system arrived that asked less of the body and more of the chemist. That system was gunpowder, and its history begins not with a bang but with a recipe.

The earliest extant gunpowder formulas appear in the Chinese military treatise *Wujing Zongyao*, compiled in 1044. The recipes combine saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal, and they are not yet explosives in the modern sense: the nitrate content is relatively low, and the mixtures were used for incendiaries, smoke, and fire weapons before they were used to throw projectiles. This is a crucial point that popular history often skips. Gunpowder did not arrive as a bomb. It arrived as a chemical that burned fiercely and produced smoke, and its first military uses were in fire arrows and fire lances—weapons that spat flame and noxious smoke at close range. The fire lance is the ancestor of the gun: a tube packed with powder and projectiles, ignited to spew fire and fragments. It is not a firearm in the sense of a barrel that directs a single projectile with accuracy, but it is the beginning of the idea that a chemical reaction can be aimed.

The transition from incendiary to projector is marked by a single artifact: the Heilongjiang hand cannon, dated by inscription to 1288. It is a bronze barrel, short and thick, with a touch hole, and it is among the earliest dated metal-barreled firearms. Its significance is not that it was powerful—it was not, by later standards—but that it represents a conceptual shift. A fire lance burns; a hand cannon *throws*. The powder is confined in a metal tube, and the gas it produces drives a projectile out of the muzzle. The barrel is the key. The barrel is what turns a chemical reaction into a directed force, and once you have a barrel you have a parameter to optimize: the strength of the metal, the fit of the projectile, the ratio of powder to charge, the length of the tube. From 1288 onward, the history of the gun is a history of metallurgy and chemistry, and the men who advanced it were as often founders and assayers as generals.

The spread of gunpowder weapons from China across Asia and into Europe is a story of transmission, and transmission is never simple. The Mongols carried gunpowder weapons westward in the thirteenth century, and the battles of the Mongol conquests introduced the idea to the Islamic world and to Europe. But the Europeans did not simply receive the idea; they transformed it, because they had something the Chinese did not prioritize in the same way: a competitive system of warring states with a hunger for artillery that could knock down castle walls. The Chinese had gunpowder first, but the Europeans had the social conditions to make it central. This is a recurring pattern in the history of weapons: the inventor is not always the innovator, and the innovator is not always the victor. The question is never who thought of it first; the question is who built a system around it.

The European answer was the cannon. By the early fourteenth century, European foundries were casting bronze guns, and by the fifteenth century the great bombards were throwing stone balls at castle walls with enough force to make the medieval fortress obsolete. The Ottoman Turks, meanwhile, built the largest bombards in the world and used them to breach the walls of Constantinople in 1453. The fall of Constantinople is often told as the end of the Middle Ages, and in weapons terms it is the moment when the wall—the defining technology of the settled empire—met its match. A wall is a promise: you cannot reach me. A cannon is a reply: I can reach your wall, and I can reach through it. The promise and the reply are the grammar of the whole subsequent history.

The castle did not disappear. It changed. The trace italienne—the low, star-shaped fortification with angled bastions—was the answer to the cannon, designed to present sloped surfaces that absorbed shot and to allow defenders to sweep the approaches with interlocking fire. The trace italienne was expensive, and its expense centralized power: only a state with deep pockets could build and garrison a modern fortress, and only a state with a standing army could hold the field around it. Here the argument about weapons and society becomes concrete in stone and earth. The cannon did not just kill people; it changed who could afford to defend themselves, and therefore who could govern. The military revolution of the early modern period—the growth of standing armies, the rise of the fiscal state, the professionalization of the officer corps—was driven in large part by the cost of gunpowder artillery and the fortifications needed to resist it.

The handgun followed a similar path. The matchlock, the wheel lock, the flintlock—each was an attempt to solve the problem of ignition, which is the problem of making a chemical reaction happen at the right moment and not before. The matchlock used a burning cord; it was cheap and reliable but required the shooter to keep a smoldering match away from the powder, which made it awkward in rain and dangerous in a line. The wheel lock used a spring-wound wheel to strike sparks; it was expensive and delicate but could be carried loaded and ready, which made it a cavalry and hunting weapon. The flintlock used a flint striking steel; it was the synthesis, cheap enough for mass infantry and reliable enough for the field, and it dominated for two centuries. Each is a small engineering problem with large social consequences. The matchlock musket required the shooter to stand in ranks and fire by volley, because it was too inaccurate to aim individually and too slow to reload under pressure. The volley was a social technology as much as a mechanical one: it turned a crowd of men into a machine that could deliver a wall of lead at a fixed range. The drill, the discipline, the command—these were the software that made the hardware work.

The bayonet is a small invention with an outsized effect. For most of the gunpowder era, the musketeer was protected by pikemen, because a man reloading a musket could not defend himself against cavalry. The plug bayonet, shoved into the muzzle, turned the musket into a spear but prevented firing. The socket bayonet, which fit around the barrel, allowed the musket to fire and to receive a charge. With the socket bayonet, the pikeman became redundant, and the infantry line became a single arm that could shoot and stab. The bayonet is the kind of weapon historians of technology call a "domestication"—it does not add a new capability so much as remove a dependency. The musket with a socket bayonet is a self-sufficient infantry weapon, and the armies that adopted it first could shed a whole branch of their organization. The lesson generalizes: some of the most consequential weapons are the ones that let you *stop* doing something.

The rifle is the next step, and it took centuries to complete because the technology of the barrel had to catch up with the theory. A rifle barrel has spiral grooves that spin the projectile, and the spin stabilizes it in flight, making it far more accurate than a smoothbore. Rifles existed in the sixteenth century, but they were slow to load because the ball had to be forced into the grooves, and a slow-loading weapon is a weapon for skirmishers and hunters, not for line infantry. The Minié ball changed that. Invented by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, the hollow-base bullet expanded when the powder charge drove it, so it gripped the rifling even though it could be dropped down the barrel quickly. The Minié ball made the rifled musket practical, and the rifled musket made the line infantryman accurate at ranges unthinkable a generation earlier. The British Pattern 1853 Enfield and the U.S. Springfield Model 1861 were both rifled muskets firing Minié-type bullets, and their effective range was several times that of the smoothbore musket they replaced.

The consequence was written in blood. In the American Civil War, infantry could hit targets at ranges where the old smoothbore would have been useless, and the tactics of the era—massed lines, frontal assaults, close-order formations—had not yet adapted. The result was slaughter on a scale that shocked observers. The Minié ball is a case study in the lag between a weapon's capability and the doctrine that governs its use. A new weapon does not automatically produce new tactics; the tactics have to be learned, and the learning is often paid for in casualties. The generals who ordered the charges at Fredericksburg and Gettysburg were not stupid men; they were men whose mental model of the battlefield had been formed by an earlier technology. The weapon had changed, and the model had not.

The same lag appears, with even greater force, in the machine gun. Hiram Maxim demonstrated a recoil-operated automatic machine gun in 1884, and the British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891. The Maxim was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun: it used the recoil of the previous shot to load and fire the next, so a single gunner could deliver sustained fire without cranking a handle or working a lever. The earlier Gatling gun was hand-cranked; the Maxim was automatic. The distinction is the difference between a weapon that a crew operates and a weapon that operates itself, and it changed the calculus of the infantry assault. A Maxim gun in a defensive position could sweep a field and cut down a battalion before it crossed a hundred meters. The European armies knew this in theory—they had the guns—but the doctrine of the offensive, the cult of the bayonet, and the belief that morale could overcome firepower all persisted into 1914. The result was the trenches.

The First World War is the great case study in the collision between industrial production and military doctrine, and its central weapon was not the machine gun but the artillery piece. The French 75mm field gun, the Canon de 75 modèle 1897, is the emblem. It used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady, so the gun did not have to be re-aimed after every shot. The result was rapid fire—often cited at roughly fifteen rounds per minute—with the sights staying on target. The 75 was a triumph of mechanical design, and it was also a weapon that consumed ammunition at a rate no prewar logistics system had anticipated. The artillery of 1914 was designed to support a war of movement; the war of 1914 became a war of position, and the guns fired for four years.

Verdun is the purest expression of what artillery had become. The battle ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916 and produced roughly 700,000 casualties. It was fought over a few square miles of ground, and the ground was churned into a moonscape by millions of shells. The infantry fought and died, but the battle was decided by the guns, and the guns were decided by the factories. The phrase "industrial war" is often used loosely, but at Verdun it is exact: the battle was a contest of production, of shell output, of rail capacity, of the ability to replace worn barrels and exhausted crews. The weapon had become a system that reached back from the trench to the mine and the steel mill. The soldier at the front was the tip of a supply chain, and the supply chain was the real battlefield.

The First World War also produced the answer to the machine gun and the artillery: the tank. The tank exists to solve a specific problem—how to cross a fire-swept zone and reach the enemy's line—and its development is a case study in the way a weapon is shaped by the problem it is built to solve. The early tanks were slow, unreliable, and mechanically fragile, but they carried armor that could stop machine-gun bullets and a gun that could silence a nest. The tank is not a cavalry charge; it is a mobile bunker, and its logic is the logic of the siege engine applied to the open field. The interwar years were spent working out what the tank was for, and the answers differed: the British saw it as an infantry support weapon, the Germans as the core of a combined-arms team that could break through and exploit, the French as a defensive tool distributed along the line. The German answer, worked out in the 1930s and tested in 1940, was the one that mattered, and it was less a matter of better tanks than of better organization. The panzer division was a weapons system in which the tank, the motorized infantry, the artillery, and the close air support were designed to work together. The lesson is that the decisive innovation is often organizational, not mechanical.

The Second World War is the hinge of this history, because it is the war in which the weapon became a system of systems and in which the ultimate weapon was not a better gun but a new kind of physics. The war began with the tank and the dive bomber and ended with the atomic bomb, and the distance between those two is the distance between the industrial and the nuclear ages. Along the way, the war produced radar, the proximity fuse, the jet engine, the ballistic missile, and the computer, and each was a weapon or a weapon's handmaiden. The proximity fuse, which detonated an artillery shell when it came near a target, was a miniature radar set inside a shell, and it multiplied the effectiveness of anti-aircraft fire. The jet engine was a propulsion revolution that arrived too late to change the outcome but early enough to set the terms of the postwar air war. The ballistic missile was the V-2, a weapon that killed more people in its production than in its use, but which pointed the way to the future.

And then, on 16 July 1945, at Trinity in New Mexico, the plutonium implosion device called "Gadget" detonated with a yield of about 21 kilotons. The first nuclear explosion was not a bigger bomb; it was a different order of energy. The fission of a few kilograms of plutonium released the energy of tens of thousands of tons of TNT, and the weapon that did it was small enough to be carried by an aircraft. The Trinity test opened the nuclear age, and the nuclear age changed the logic of war in a way no previous weapon had. For the first time, a single weapon could destroy a city, and a war between great powers could destroy civilization. The consequence was deterrence: the strategy of preventing war by the threat of unacceptable retaliation. The bomb did not make war impossible, but it made general war between nuclear powers irrational, and that irrationality has held, more or less, for nearly eighty years.

The nuclear age is the point at which the history of weapons becomes a history of restraint. The Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and in force since 1970, is the institutional expression of that restraint. It has 191 states parties; India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The NPT is not a disarmament treaty in any complete sense—the nuclear powers kept their arsenals—but it made the spread of nuclear weapons a matter of international law and inspection rather than a free-for-all. The treaty is a weapon in its own right: a tool of statecraft that shapes what states can build and what they can be seen to build. The history of weapons is not only the history of things; it is the history of the rules that surround them, and the rules are often as decisive as the things.

The postwar period also produced the precision revolution, the slowest and most consequential change in the history of air power. The bombing of the Second World War was area bombing: a formation of bombers dropped a pattern of bombs on a city and hoped to hit the factories. The accuracy was measured in hundreds of meters, and the casualties were measured in tens of thousands. The precision-guided munition changed that. A PGM is a bomb or missile that can be steered to a target, using laser designation, television guidance, satellite navigation, or radar. The first PGMs were used in Vietnam, and they matured in the 1991 Gulf War. In Desert Storm, coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, and about 6,520 tons were precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent. The percentage was small, but the effect was disproportionate because the PGMs were used against the targets that mattered: bridges, command bunkers, air defenses, and leadership facilities. The images of laser-guided bombs going down ventilation shafts in Baghdad reshaped public expectations of air power. The military learned a lesson it has been relearning ever since: precision is not about the tonnage dropped; it is about the target destroyed.

The precision revolution is the hinge between the industrial and the information ages of war. An industrial bomb is a dumb object that falls; an information bomb is a guided object that thinks, or at least corrects. The guidance system is a computer, and the computer is the weapon. The same logic runs through the drone, the most recent major development in the history of weapons and the one still unfolding. A drone is an aircraft without a pilot, controlled by a remote operator or, increasingly, by onboard autonomy. The armed drone combines the sensor, the communications link, and the munition into a single system, and it allows a state to strike a target without risking a pilot. The United States used armed drones extensively in the post-9/11 wars, and the drone became the signature weapon of the "forever war" in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia.

The drone's coming-of-age as a weapon of state-on-state war came in 2020, in the 44-day Nagorno-Karabakh war between Azerbaijan and Armenia. Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses, and the effect was devastating. The Royal United Services Institute's 2021 study treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense. The drones were not invincible—they were shot down in numbers—but they demonstrated that a relatively cheap, relatively small state could use armed drones to destroy a conventional armored force. The lesson was not that tanks are obsolete; it was that tanks without air cover and without counter-drone defenses are targets. The drone is the first weapon since the airplane that has fundamentally changed the relationship between the air and the ground, and it has done so by being cheap, persistent, and expendable.

The next step, and the most contested, is autonomy. A loitering munition is a weapon that flies to a target and explodes; an autonomous loitering munition is one that selects its target without a human in the loop. The UN Security Council's Panel of Experts on Libya reported in 2021 that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The claim is contested and has not been independently confirmed, and it should be treated with caution. But the fact that the claim was made at all is significant, because it marks the point at which the question of autonomous weapons moved from speculation to allegation. The history of weapons has always been a history of removing the human from the point of impact: the spear extends the arm, the bow extends the arm further, the gun removes the arm entirely, the missile removes the eye, and the autonomous weapon removes the decision. Each removal is a transfer of responsibility, and each transfer raises the question of who is accountable when the weapon does what it was built to do.

The history of weapons is not a story of progress in any simple sense. It is a story of problems and solutions, and of the new problems that solutions create. The stone solved the problem of the unarmed hand and created the problem of the armed enemy. The bow solved the problem of the distant enemy and created the problem of the unprotected body. The gun solved the problem of the trained archer and created the problem of the mass army. The bomb solved the problem of the fortified city and created the problem of the destroyed city. The nuclear weapon solved the problem of the decisive victory and created the problem of the unwinnable war. The drone solves the problem of the risky strike and creates the problem of the unaccountable strike. Each weapon is a sentence in the conversation, and the conversation has no last word.

There is a temptation, in a history of this kind, to organize the story around the great inventions and the great battles, and there is a reason for that: the inventions and the battles are the visible events, the places where the current of change breaks the surface. But the deeper argument of this book is that the visible events are the froth on a deeper current, and the deeper current is the interaction between technology and society. A weapon is never just a weapon. It is a way of organizing labor, a way of raising money, a way of training bodies, a way of imagining the enemy. The longbow was a weapon of a particular kind of village, and it died when that village died. The musket was a weapon of a particular kind of state, and it spread when that state spread. The drone is a weapon of a particular kind of information society, and its future will be shaped by the kind of society that makes it.

Consider the economics. The cost of a weapon is not the price of the object; it is the price of the system that supports it. A longbow costs a few shillings and a lifetime of practice. A crossbow costs more and a few weeks of training. A musket costs more still and requires a supply of powder and ball and a drill that can be taught in months. A rifle costs more and requires a factory that can cut grooves in a barrel. A machine gun costs more and requires a factory that can make interchangeable parts and a logistics system that can feed it ammunition. A tank costs more and requires a factory that can make armor plate and engines and a supply chain that can move fuel. A fighter aircraft costs more and requires a factory that can make jet engines and avionics and a training system that can produce pilots. A nuclear weapon costs more and requires a scientific establishment, an industrial base, and a system of secrecy. Each step up the ladder of cost is a step up the ladder of social organization, and the states that could climb the ladder were the states that could tax, borrow, and mobilize. The history of weapons is a history of state capacity, and the states that won the wars were usually the states that could pay for them.

Consider the geography. The composite bow was a weapon of the steppe because the steppe had the horses and the grass. The longbow was a weapon of England because England had the yew and the yeomanry. The cannon was a weapon of the European monarchies because Europe had the foundries and the competition. The drone is a weapon of the information age because the information age has the satellites and the semiconductors. Geography is not destiny, but it is a constraint, and the constraints shape the choices. A state that lacks the resources for one kind of weapon will find another, and the another is often the innovation that changes the game. The English could not field the massed cavalry of the continent, so they perfected the infantry bow. The Americans could not match the Soviet tank numbers in Europe, so they invested in precision and air power. The weak find a way, and the way is often a new weapon.

Consider the culture. A weapon is adopted when the culture that uses it can imagine it. The Japanese adopted the gun enthusiastically in the sixteenth century and then, in the Tokugawa period, deliberately restricted it, because the sword was the symbol of the samurai and the gun was the weapon of the peasant. The restriction was not a failure of technology; it was a choice about what kind of society Japan wanted to be. The Chinese invented gunpowder and then, in some periods, underinvested in firearms relative to their potential, because the threats they faced were different and the costs of a gun-centered army were different. The Europeans invested heavily because the competition was intense and the returns were high. Culture is not a fog; it is a set of incentives, and the incentives shape the adoption.

Consider the law. The laws of war are an attempt to limit what weapons can do, and they have a history that runs alongside the history of the weapons themselves. The medieval Church tried to restrict the crossbow. The nineteenth century produced the Declaration of St. Petersburg, which banned explosive bullets, and the Hague Conventions, which restricted dum-dum bullets and poison gas. The twentieth century produced the Geneva Conventions and the Chemical Weapons Convention and the Biological Weapons Convention and the NPT. The laws are not always obeyed, and they are often violated, but they matter because they set the terms of legitimacy. A weapon that is banned is a weapon that carries a cost, and the cost shapes the decisions of states. The law is a weapon in the conversation, and it is one of the few that can be used by the weak against the strong.

The history of weapons is also a history of the body. Every weapon is designed for a body, and the body's limits are the weapon's limits. The arm can throw a stone; the shoulder can draw a bow; the eye can aim a gun; the hand can pull a trigger; the finger can press a button. Each step removes the body further from the point of impact, and each step changes the moral relationship between the killer and the killed. The man who stabs another man with a spear feels the resistance of the body. The archer who looses an arrow at two hundred meters sees a distant figure fall. The bombardier who drops a bomb from five miles up sees a city burn through a bombsight. The drone operator who fires a missile from a console in Nevada sees a grainy image on a screen and a puff of smoke. The distance is not just physical; it is psychological, and the psychology of distance is one of the deepest themes in the history of weapons. The further the killer is from the killed, the easier it is to kill, and the easier it is to kill, the more the weapon spreads. This is not a moral judgment; it is an observation about human nature, and it explains why the history of weapons has moved steadily in the direction of distance.

But distance has a cost. The weapon that kills at a distance is a weapon that can be used without the restraint that comes from seeing the enemy's face. The drone operator who kills from a console is not a coward; he is a man doing a job, and the job is designed to make the killing easy. The ease is the point, and the ease is the problem. The history of weapons is a history of making killing easier, and the moral question that runs through it is whether the ease is a good thing or a bad thing. The answer depends on what the killing is for, and that is a question that weapons cannot answer.

The history of weapons is also a history of the wounded. The weapon that kills is only half the story; the weapon that wounds is the other half, and the wounded are often more numerous than the dead. The arrow that lodges in a thigh, the bullet that shatters a bone, the shell fragment that tears a belly—these are the ordinary products of war, and the history of medicine is intertwined with the history of weapons. The Minié ball produced wounds that shattered bone and required amputation, and the surgeons of the Civil War learned to operate at a speed that seems incredible today. The machine gun produced wounds that were multiple and massive, and the surgeons of the First World War learned to treat shock and infection. The nuclear weapon produced wounds that were burns and radiation sickness, and the doctors of Hiroshima learned a new pathology. The weapon and the wound are a pair, and the history of one is incomplete without the other.

The history of weapons is also a history of the dead. The dead are the silent majority of this history, and their silence is the reason the history is often told as a story of inventions. But the inventions are the surface, and the dead are the depth. The dead at Verdun were killed by artillery, and the artillery was made possible by the factories, and the factories were made possible by the coal and the iron and the railroads, and the railroads were made possible by the capital and the state. The chain of causation runs from the dead man in the trench back to the mine and the mill and the bank, and the history of weapons is the history of that chain. To tell the history of weapons without the dead is to tell the history of the tools without the work.

And so the argument returns to the stone. The stone was the first weapon because it was the first object that extended the body's power beyond the body's reach. Every weapon since has been a variation on that theme: an extension of the reach, an increase of the power, a reduction of the risk. The spear extended the arm; the bow extended the arm further; the gun extended the arm further still; the missile extended the arm to the horizon; the drone extended the arm to the other side of the world. The reach has grown, the power has grown, and the risk has shrunk, and the history of weapons is the history of that triple movement. The movement is not linear, it is not inevitable, and it is not always progressive in any moral sense. But it is the shape of the story, and the shape is the argument.

The stone was also the first weapon because it was the first object that could be made in quantity. A hand axe is a stone shaped by another stone, and the shaping is a technology. The technology of making weapons is the technology of making things, and the history of weapons is the history of manufacturing. The knapper who struck a flint blade was the first engineer, the foundry that cast a bronze sword was the first factory, the mill that rolled armor plate was the first heavy industry, and the fab that etched a silicon chip was the first of a new kind. Each step in the history of weapons is a step in the history of making, and the making is the material base of the war.

The stone was also the first weapon because it was the first object that could be traded. A good flint is not found everywhere, and the trade in flint and obsidian runs back into the Neolithic. The trade in weapons is as old as the weapons themselves, and the trade shapes the politics. The embargo on strategic goods is an ancient instrument, and the effort to control the supply of copper and tin was a driver of the first empires. The history of weapons is a history of supply chains, and the supply chains were global long before the word global was invented.

The stone was also the first weapon because it was the first object that could be buried with the dead. The grave goods of the Neolithic include axes and arrowheads, and the inclusion is a statement about the value of the weapon. The weapon is not just a tool; it is a symbol, and the symbol is a form of power. The sword of the Bronze Age was a symbol as much as a weapon, and the sword was buried with kings. The gun of the modern age is a symbol of the state, and the state monopolizes the gun. The history of weapons is a history of symbols, and the symbols are the way the weapons enter the imagination.

The stone was also the first weapon because it was the first object that could be used against a person. The distinction between a tool and a weapon is the distinction between a use and a target, and the target is the human body. The history of weapons is a history of the body as a target, and the body has not changed much in ten thousand years. The body is soft and vulnerable and slow, and the weapons have become hard and precise and fast. The asymmetry between the body and the weapon is the engine of the history, and the engine has not stopped.
The stone was also the first weapon because it was the first

chapters.title: Part 3
chapters.preview: The first arms race did not begin with a weapon. It began with a wall.
paragraphs: The first arms race did not begin with a weapon. It began with a wall.

Once people learned to throw a stone with intent, they learned almost immediately to hide from a thrown stone. The Neolithic archaeological record tells not of steadily improving projectiles but of a sudden, widespread investment in barriers: ditches, palisades, earthen ramparts, and eventually walls of mudbrick and stone. Jericho, in the Jordan Valley, is the oldest and most instructive case. By roughly 8000 BCE, the settlement had raised a stone wall nearly four meters high and a meter and a half thick, fronted by a rock-cut ditch more than eight meters wide and three deep, and dominated by a circular stone tower about eight meters tall. For a community of perhaps a few thousand people working with flint and bone, this was an enormous expenditure of labor—thousands of person-days dragged out of the agricultural surplus. The tower at Jericho is one of the earliest monumental structures in the world, and it was built not to honor a god or a king but to watch an approach.

That is the first lesson in the history of weapons, and it repeats in every era: the shape of a weapon is legible in the shape of the defenses built against it. A wall tells you what people feared. A ditch tells you how they expected the attack to come. The height of a tower tells you the range of the threat. The history of fortification is therefore a shadow history of the projectile, and the two move together, each dragging the other forward. The wall is the weapon's mirror. When you study the wall, you are studying the weapon from behind.

Jericho's wall did not appear in a vacuum. It appeared when people stopped moving and started storing. Agriculture created the granary, and the granary created the raid. A mobile band of hunter-gatherers has little to defend and can always walk away from a threat; a village with a season's grain in a silo has something worth killing for and nowhere to flee. The domestication of plants created the first strategic assets, and strategic assets created the first strategy. The wall is the physical form of the phrase "we have something you want." Every fortification in history, from Jericho to the Maginot Line, is a sentence in that same language.

So the story of early weapons is not a story of clever inventions arriving one after another. It is a story of a feedback loop. A new projectile appears; a new defense is built against it; the defense forces the projectile to change; the changed projectile forces the defense to thicken. The loop runs through the entire history of war, and it is still running. The drone that loiters over a trench in Ukraine is the descendant of the slingstone at Jericho, the trench of the ditch, and the electronic jammer of the tower. The names change; the loop does not.

Consider the sling. It is one of the oldest and most underrated weapons in the human repertoire, and it deserves more attention than it usually gets because it is the first weapon that separated stored energy from the arm. A thrown stone draws its energy from the thrower's muscles in a single motion. A sling multiplies that energy by extending the lever arm and allowing the thrower to build speed through a circular whirl before release. A skilled slinger could hurl a fist-sized stone at speeds modern experiments place at sixty to one hundred miles per hour, with ranges exceeding a hundred meters and, in trained hands, considerably more. The stone was not a toy. In the hands of a Balearic slinger or a Rhodian or an Assyrian, it was a lethal weapon of war, and it was cheap. A sling is a length of cord and a pouch. The ammunition is the ground itself.

The sling's great advantage was logistical. An archer needs a supply of arrows, each requiring a shaft, a head, and fletching, and each lost when shot. A slinger needs a supply of stones, which are everywhere and can be gathered by anyone. A sling-armed force could therefore be raised quickly and supplied almost for free, which made the sling the weapon of the poor, the shepherd, and the irregular. The biblical image of David and Goliath is not a fable about the weak defeating the strong through divine favor alone; it is a precise description of a real tactical matchup. A heavily armored infantryman with a spear and a shield is a slow, short-range system. A slinger is a fast, long-range system. If the slinger can keep his distance and aim for the exposed head, the armored man is in serious trouble. The story encodes a genuine military truth every armored soldier has had to reckon with: armor is a solution to a specific threat, and it creates a vulnerability to every threat it was not designed for.

The bow is the other great early projectile, and it is a more demanding technology. A bow is a spring. It stores energy in the bent limbs and releases it into the arrow, and the efficiency of that transfer depends on the quality of the wood, the geometry of the limbs, and the skill of the bowyer. The earliest bows we know of are the Holmegaard bows from Denmark, made of elm around 7000 BCE, and they are already sophisticated objects—tillered so the limbs bend evenly, with a stiff handle section, a design a modern bowyer would recognize as sound. The bow did not evolve slowly from a crude beginning. It arrived in the archaeological record already well made, which suggests a long prior development we have not found. Wood rots; stone and bone do not. The earliest weapons we can see are those made of durable materials, and those made of wood and cord and hide have vanished, taking their history with them.

The composite bow was the next great leap, and it was a leap in materials science. A simple wooden bow is limited by the properties of a single piece of wood. A composite bow is built from layers of wood, horn, and sinew, glued together with animal glue, and the layers work together: the horn resists compression on the belly of the bow, the sinew resists tension on the back, and the wood core holds them apart. The result stores far more energy per unit of length than a wooden bow, which means it can be shorter and still powerful—short enough to shoot from horseback, from a chariot, or from a cramped position on a wall. The composite bow is the first great example of a weapon that is also a piece of engineering, where the designer thinks about the properties of materials and how to combine them. It appeared in the steppe and in the river valleys of the Near East, and it became the signature weapon of the horse archer, the chariot archer, and the nomadic warrior. The Scythians, the Parthians, the Huns, the Mongols—all rode behind the composite bow, and it is why they could do what they did.

The chariot deserves its own paragraph, because it is the first weapon system that was also a vehicle, and the first that required a substantial industrial base. A chariot is not a cart with a horse in front of it. It is a carefully engineered platform: a light frame of bent wood, a spoked wheel that is a marvel of joinery and tension, an axle designed to turn, a pole and yoke designed to transmit the pull of the horses without breaking. The spoked wheel alone is a significant invention; a solid disc wheel is heavy and slow, a spoked wheel light and fast, and making one requires a wheelwright who understands how to pre-stress the spokes so the wheel carries the load in tension rather than compression. The chariot appeared in the Near East around 2000 BCE, and within a few centuries it had transformed warfare from the Euphrates to the Nile. The Battle of Megiddo, fought around 1457 BCE between the Egyptian forces of Thutmose III and a coalition of Canaanite princes, is the first battle we can reconstruct in any detail, and it is a chariot battle. The Egyptians deployed their chariots in a coordinated attack, broke the enemy line, and then—in a detail the scribe records with evident disgust—stopped to loot the enemy camp, allowing the enemy commanders to escape. The scribe's complaint is the first recorded instance of a military failure caused by indiscipline in victory, and it is a reminder that the history of weapons is always also a history of the people who use them.

The chariot was expensive. It required horses, which were rare and costly; a trained charioteer and a warrior; a crew to maintain it; and a workshop to build it. This made it the weapon of a caste, and the chariot-using elites of the Bronze Age—the Maryannu of the Mitanni, the knights of the Shang, the chariot aristocracy of Mycenaean Greece—were among the first groups in history to define themselves by their weapons. The chariot was not just a tool of war; it was a marker of status, a way of saying you belonged to the small group of people who could afford to ride into battle. The connection between weapons and social class, which will run through the entire history, begins here, with the chariot and the horse.

And the chariot created the first arms race in the modern sense, because the chariot demanded a counter. If your enemy has chariots and you do not, you lose. So everyone who could afford chariots bought them, and the number of chariots a kingdom could field became a measure of its power. The Hittites and the Egyptians, the two great powers of the Late Bronze Age, both built chariot forces in the thousands, and the Battle of Kadesh, around 1274 BCE, is the largest chariot battle we know of, with thousands of chariots on each side. The battle was a draw, or perhaps a narrow Egyptian victory, and Ramesses II commemorated it in inscriptions and reliefs that exaggerated his own role and minimized the Hittite achievement—the first great example of a ruler using a battle as propaganda. Within a few centuries of its invention, the chariot had become a strategic asset so important that kings lied about it.

The chariot's dominance was broken by a combination of new weapons and new tactics. The first was the horse archer, who could do everything a chariot archer could do without the chariot, and who was far cheaper and more mobile. The second was the massed infantryman with a long spear and a shield, fighting in formation, who could stop a chariot charge by presenting a wall of points. The third was the development of iron, which we will come to. But the deepest reason for the chariot's decline is the same reason any weapon system declines: it became too expensive relative to its effectiveness, and a cheaper system that did most of the same job replaced it. The horse archer is the chariot's successor, and the horse archer's dominance would last more than a thousand years.

Before we leave the ancient world, we should look at the fortifications its weapons produced, because they are the most visible record of the arms race. The walls of the ancient Near East grew steadily thicker and taller as siege technology improved. The walls of Uruk, the great Sumerian city, were legendary; the Epic of Gilgamesh opens with an invitation to inspect them. The walls of Babylon were one of the wonders of the ancient world. The Assyrians, the great siege engineers of the ancient Near East, developed a systematic approach to taking cities: they built ramps, used battering rams, undermined walls, blockaded and starved. The reliefs from the palaces of Assyrian kings show sieges in detail—rams with articulated heads, sappers working under shields, defenders pouring fire and stones from the walls. These reliefs are propaganda, but they are also technical documents, and they show a mature siege craft that had developed in tandem with the walls it was designed to overcome.

The Assyrian war machine is worth a closer look because it is the first fully documented example of a state built around war. The Assyrian army was a standing force, paid and equipped by the state, organized into units of chariots, cavalry, infantry, and siege engineers. It had a logistics system, a supply train, and a corps of scribes who recorded the campaigns. The Assyrian kings campaigned almost every year, and they treated war as a form of statecraft: the army was the instrument by which tribute was extracted, rebellion punished, and the king's power displayed. The Assyrian practice of deporting conquered populations—moving entire communities to new lands—was a weapon in itself, a way of breaking the social ties that made resistance possible. The Assyrians understood something every great military power has understood since: that war is not only a matter of killing, but of organizing, supplying, and administering. The weapon is only the sharp end of a much larger system, and the system is what wins wars.

The Assyrian army also gives us the first clear evidence of a combined-arms approach. The Assyrians did not rely on a single weapon; they coordinated chariots, cavalry, archers, spearmen, and siege engines, each covering the weakness of the others. The chariot was vulnerable to infantry in rough terrain; the cavalry could pursue; the archers could soften a line before the spearmen closed; the siege engines could break a wall the infantry could not climb. This coordination is the beginning of tactical thinking as we understand it, and it is why the Assyrians dominated the Near East for centuries. A single weapon, no matter how good, can always be countered. A system of weapons, each covering the others, is much harder to beat.

The Greeks took a different path, and their path would shape the Western tradition of war. The Greek innovation was not a weapon but a formation: the phalanx. A phalanx is a dense line of heavily armored infantry, each man carrying a large round shield and a long spear, standing shoulder to shoulder so the shields overlap and the spears project forward in a bristling hedge. The phalanx's strength is not in the individual soldier but in the cohesion of the line. A single hoplite is vulnerable; a phalanx is a wall of bronze and wood that moves forward together, and the men in the front rank are protected by the men behind them, who push forward and steady the line. The phalanx required a new kind of soldier: a man who could afford the armor, who had been trained to hold his place, and who was willing to trust the men beside him. The Greek city-state was, in a real sense, built around the phalanx, because the phalanx required the participation of the citizen body, and the citizen body demanded a share of political power in return. The connection between military service and political rights, one of the foundations of Western political thought, begins with the hoplite and his shield.

The hoplite's equipment is worth describing in detail, because it shows how a weapon system is really a set of interlocking solutions. The shield, the aspis, was about a meter in diameter, made of wood covered with bronze, and held by a central grip and a forearm band rather than a single handle at the edge. This double grip let the hoplite hold the shield more securely and use it more actively, and it also let him use the shield to push. The spear, the dory, was about two to three meters long, held in one hand and used overhand or underhand. The helmet, the Corinthian type, covered the whole head and face, which protected the hoplite but limited his vision and hearing—a trade-off every armor designer has had to make. The greaves protected the shins; the breastplate, initially bronze and later linen, protected the torso. The total weight was perhaps thirty kilograms, and the hoplite fought in it in the Mediterranean summer. The phalanx was not a comfortable place to be.

The phalanx's weakness was its rigidity. A phalanx could only move forward on level ground; it could not turn easily, could not pursue a broken enemy, and was vulnerable on its flanks. The Thebans, under Epaminondas, exploited this weakness at the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE by refusing their left wing and massing their best troops on the left, opposite the Spartan elite, and breaking the Spartan line before the rest of the Spartan army could engage. This was a tactical revolution: instead of meeting the enemy line strength against strength, Epaminondas concentrated his force at one point and broke through. The principle of concentration, one of the most basic principles of war, was demonstrated at Leuctra, and it would be rediscovered by every generation of commanders.

The Macedonians, under Philip II and his son Alexander, took the phalanx and made it part of a larger system. The Macedonian phalanx used a longer spear, the sarissa, perhaps four to six meters long and requiring two hands to hold, with the shield slung on the forearm. The sarissa gave the phalanx greater reach, but it made the phalanx even less flexible. So Philip paired the phalanx with cavalry, which could strike the flanks and rear while the phalanx held the enemy's front. He paired it with light infantry, which could skirmish and screen. He paired it with siege engines, which could take cities. The Macedonian army was a combined-arms force in the fullest sense, and it was the most effective military system in the world for a century. Alexander used it to conquer the Persian Empire, and the speed of his conquest is a testament to the power of a well-designed system.

Alexander's campaigns also illustrate a deeper point about the history of weapons: the decisive factor is often not the weapon but the organization that wields it. The Persians had more men, more money, and more territory than the Macedonians. They had chariots, cavalry, and archers. What they lacked was a coherent system that could bring these elements together under a single commander who could make decisions quickly. Alexander's army was smaller but more cohesive, and its commander was willing to take risks the Persian king was not. The weapon is a tool, and the tool is only as good as the hand that holds it and the mind that directs it. The history of weapons is full of superior weapons that lost to better-organized opponents, and the reason is always the same: a weapon is a component of a system, and the system is what fights.

The Roman army is the greatest example of this principle in the ancient world. The Romans did not invent many weapons. Their gladius, a short sword, was adapted from the Spanish; their pilum, a heavy javelin, may have had Italian or Celtic origins; their scutum, a large curved shield, was influenced by the Samnites. What the Romans did invent was a military organization that could absorb losses, adapt to new enemies, and maintain discipline over centuries. The Roman legion was a flexible formation of maniples or cohorts that could maneuver on the battlefield, independent of the rigid phalanx. The legionary carried a pilum, which he threw to disrupt the enemy line, and then closed with the gladius, a short, fast weapon suited to the close-quarters stabbing that the legionary's large shield made possible. The shield and the short sword are a system: the shield protects the body and creates a space in which the sword can work, and the sword is short enough to be used in that space. The legionary's equipment is not impressive in isolation, but it is superbly adapted to the way the legionary fights.

The Roman army's real weapon was its engineering. The Romans built roads, bridges, camps, and fortifications with a speed and consistency no other ancient power could match. A Roman army on the march built a fortified camp every night, with a ditch and a rampart, so that it could never be surprised. The Romans built siege works—ramps, towers, walls—that were engineering projects as much as military ones. They built roads that allowed them to move troops quickly across their empire, and a system of frontier fortifications, the limes, that defined the edge of the Roman world. The Roman soldier was as much a builder as a fighter, and the Roman army as much a construction corps as a combat force. This is a crucial point in the history of weapons: the most important weapon of an empire is often not a weapon at all, but the infrastructure that allows the empire to project force.

The Romans also give us the first great example of a weapon designed to counter a specific enemy and rendered obsolete when that enemy was gone. The gladius was designed for close combat against the kind of enemies the Romans faced in the Mediterranean world—infantry with shields and spears, fighting in formation. When the Romans faced the cavalry of the Parthians and the Scythians, the gladius was inadequate, and the Romans had to develop new weapons and tactics to cope. The Parthian horse archers, who shot their bows while retreating, drew the Roman legions into a trap at Carrhae in 53 BCE and destroyed them. The Romans never solved the problem of the horse archer, and the problem would return to haunt them, and their successors, for centuries.

The horse archer is the great weapon system of the Eurasian steppe, and it deserves full treatment because it dominated a huge part of the world for a very long time. The steppe is a vast grassland stretching from the Hungarian plain to Manchuria, a hard environment for agriculture but an excellent one for herding. The peoples of the steppe lived by their herds, and they lived on horseback. A steppe nomad learned to ride before he learned to walk, and he learned to shoot a bow from horseback as a child. The composite bow was the perfect weapon for him: short enough to use from the saddle, powerful enough to kill at range, and made from the materials the steppe provided—wood, horn, sinew, and glue. The horse archer could ride circles around a slower enemy, shoot from a distance, and retreat before the enemy could close. He could live off the land, moving with his herds and his family, and he could concentrate his forces quickly when he needed to. The steppe nomad was, in military terms, a self-contained weapon system: the horse, the bow, the rider, and the mobility were all one thing.

The horse archer's tactics were simple and effective. He would approach the enemy, shoot a volley, and retreat, drawing the enemy into pursuit. If the enemy pursued, the horse archers would scatter and reform, shooting as they went, and the enemy's formation would break up. Then the horse archers would concentrate and attack the broken formation. This is the tactic that destroyed the Roman legions at Carrhae, and the tactic the Mongols used to conquer half the known world. The horse archer's weakness was that he could not take fortified cities; he could raid and ravage, but he could not hold territory. The solution was to acquire siege engineers, which the Mongols did by recruiting them from the peoples they conquered. The Mongol army that conquered China and Persia was a combined-arms force: horse archers, heavy cavalry, Chinese siege engineers, Persian administrators. The Mongols were not just a horde of horsemen; they were a sophisticated military organization that absorbed the technology of the peoples it defeated. This is another recurring theme: the most successful military powers are the ones that can learn from their enemies and adopt their weapons.

The Mongol conquests are also a case study in the relationship between weapons and terror. The Mongols understood that a reputation for ruthlessness was itself a weapon, because a city that surrendered without a fight was spared, and a city that resisted was destroyed. This policy was not merely cruelty; it was a rational strategy for a small army trying to control a vast territory. The terror weapon is as old as war, and it is one of the most effective weapons ever devised, because it attacks the enemy's will rather than his body. The history of weapons is not only the history of killing; it is the history of the threat of killing, and the threat is often more powerful than the act.

The other great weapon system of the ancient and medieval world was the fortification, and the medieval castle is its most elaborate expression. A castle is a machine for holding territory, designed around the weapons it expects to face. The early medieval castle was a motte and bailey: a wooden tower on an artificial mound, surrounded by a ditch and a palisade. This was cheap and fast to build, and effective against the kind of raiding that characterized the early medieval period. As siege technology improved, castles became more elaborate: stone walls replaced wood, towers were added, and the walls were designed to let defenders shoot at attackers while being protected themselves. The castle's design is a record of the weapons of its time. Arrow slits are narrow because the archer inside needs protection from arrows outside. The height of the walls is a response to the range of siege engines. The moat is a response to the battering ram and the mine. The castle is the weapon's mirror, and the mirror shows us what the people of the time feared.

The siege, in turn, developed into a science. The medieval siege engineer had a repertoire of techniques: the battering ram, the siege tower, the trebuchet, the mine, and the blockade. Each technique was a response to a specific defense, and each defense a response to a specific technique. The trebuchet, which appeared in the Mediterranean world in the twelfth century and in Europe shortly after, was a counterweighted catapult that could throw a heavy stone with great accuracy and force. It was a machine of pulleys and levers, and it could be built on site from local materials. The trebuchet made walls obsolete, or at least made them much taller and thicker, and the response was the concentric castle, with multiple rings of walls and towers, designed to make the attacker fight for every foot of ground. The arms race between the siege engine and the castle is one of the clearest examples of the feedback loop in the history of weapons, and it ran for centuries.

The trebuchet also illustrates a point about the relationship between weapons and mathematics. A trebuchet is a physics problem: the counterweight's mass, the length of the arm, the length of the sling, the angle of release, and the mass of the projectile all interact to determine range and accuracy. The medieval engineers who built trebuchets did not have Newton's laws, but they had a practical understanding of the principles, and they built machines that worked. The history of weapons is full of this kind of practical science, where the knowledge is embedded in the craft rather than in a theory. The bowyer who tillers a bow, the wheelwright who builds a chariot wheel, the trebuchet builder who tunes the sling—all are doing applied physics, and their knowledge is as real as any written in a book.

The crossbow is another weapon that deserves attention, because it changed the social structure of war. A bow requires years of training; a crossbow requires a few weeks. A crossbowman can be recruited from the general population, given a weapon, and taught to shoot in a few days. The crossbow stores its energy in a steel or composite prod, held by a mechanical catch and released by a trigger. The crossbowman does not need the strength or skill of a longbowman; he needs only the ability to aim and pull a trigger. This made the crossbow a weapon of the masses, and it made it a threat to the mounted knight, because a crossbow bolt could punch through armor at close range. The Church tried to ban the crossbow, or at least its use against Christians, in the twelfth century, but the ban was ineffective, and the crossbow spread across Europe. The crossbow is the first weapon seen as a threat to the social order, because it allowed a commoner to kill a nobleman. The history of weapons is full of this anxiety: the fear that a new weapon will upset the social hierarchy by giving power to people who were not supposed to have it. The crossbow provoked it, the gun provoked it, and the drone provokes it today.

The longbow is the counterexample, and it is worth examining because it shows the other path: a weapon that requires so much training that it becomes a way of life. The English longbow was a yew bow, roughly the height of a man, with a draw weight of one hundred to one hundred and eighty pounds. Drawing such a bow requires a lifetime of practice, and the English kings encouraged archery by law, requiring men to practice on Sundays and holidays. The result was a corps of archers who could shoot accurately at long range and at a high rate of fire. The longbow's effectiveness is a matter of some debate among historians, but the evidence from the Mary Rose, the English warship that sank in 1545 and was raised in 1982, is instructive. The wreck yielded 137 longbows, and the surviving bows have estimated draw weights of one hundred to one hundred and eighty-five pounds. These are not hunting bows; they are weapons designed to kill armored men at range, and they required archers who had trained from childhood. The longbow is inseparable from the society that produced it, and it is a reminder that a weapon's effectiveness is not just a matter of its design but of the skill of the people who use it.

The longbow's great moment was the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, where an English army of perhaps six thousand men, mostly archers, defeated a French army of perhaps twenty thousand, mostly knights. The battle is famous for the mud, which bogged down the French cavalry and made the French knights easy targets for the archers. But the deeper reason for the English victory was the longbow's rate of fire and range, which allowed the English to break up the French charges before they reached the English line. The longbow did not make the knight obsolete—the knight remained a dominant force on the battlefield for another century—but it showed that a well-trained infantry force armed with a cheap projectile weapon could defeat a much larger force of heavily armored cavalry. This is a lesson that would be repeated, with different weapons, in every era.

The development of gunpowder is the great discontinuity in the history of weapons, and it is worth treating carefully because it is often misunderstood. Gunpowder was not invented in Europe. It was invented in China, and the earliest extant formulas are found in the Chinese military treatise Wujing Zongyao, compiled in 1044. These early formulas combined saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal, but the nitrate content was relatively low, and the early mixtures were used for incendiaries, smoke, and fire weapons rather than true explosives. The Chinese used gunpowder in bombs, in fire lances, and in rockets, and they developed a sophisticated pyrotechnic technology long before the Europeans did. The crucial step was a mixture with a high enough nitrate content to explode rather than simply burn, and this seems to have happened in China in the twelfth or thirteenth century. The first metal-barreled firearms appear in China in the late thirteenth century; the Heilongjiang hand cannon, dated by inscription to 1288, is among the earliest dated metal-barreled firearms. This is the moment when gunpowder shifts from an incendiary to a projectile weapon, and it is the beginning of the end of the medieval battlefield.

The hand cannon is a crude weapon: a metal tube, closed at one end, with a touch hole for igniting the powder. It was fired by holding a burning match to the touch hole, which meant the gunner had to hold the weapon with one hand and ignite it with the other, and it was aimed by pointing the tube in the general direction of the enemy. It was inaccurate, slow to reload, and dangerous to the user. But it had one great advantage: it could penetrate armor. A lead ball fired from a hand cannon could punch through a knight's breastplate at close range, and this made it a threat to the mounted knight, who had dominated the battlefield for centuries. The hand cannon was the first weapon that made armor obsolete, and the process of making armor obsolete would take centuries, but it had begun.

The development of the firearm is a story of incremental improvements, each solving a problem created by the previous one. The matchlock solved the problem of holding the match while aiming by using a mechanical lever to bring the match to the powder. The wheellock solved the problem of the match going out in wet weather by using a spinning wheel to generate sparks. The flintlock solved the problem of the wheellock's complexity and expense by using a flint striking a steel plate to generate sparks. Each of these mechanisms was a response to a specific problem, and each made the firearm more reliable, faster to fire, and easier to use. The flintlock, which appeared in the early seventeenth century, was the dominant firearm mechanism for two hundred years, and it armed the armies of the eighteenth century.

The development of the firearm also changed the relationship between the soldier and his weapon. A bowman is a craftsman; his weapon is an extension of his body, and his skill is a personal achievement. A musketeer is a component of a machine; his weapon is a standardized tool, and his skill is a matter of drill. The musket can be mass-produced, and the musketeer can be mass-trained. This is the beginning of the industrial army, and of a new kind of war in which the decisive factor is not individual skill but the ability to produce and supply large numbers of standardized weapons. The history of weapons is the history of the shift from the craftsman's weapon to the industrial weapon, and the musket is the hinge on which that shift turns.

The musket also changed the tactics of war. A formation of musketeers is not a phalanx; it is a machine for delivering volleys of fire. The musketeers stand in ranks, fire together on command, and then reload while the next rank fires. This is volley fire, designed to maximize the volume of fire rather than the accuracy of individual shots. The musket is inaccurate at long range, so the volley is aimed at a formation rather than a person, and the effect is achieved by the sheer number of balls in the air. This is a new kind of warfare: war by arithmetic, where the side that can deliver more fire wins. The musket made war a matter of numbers, and the numbers would grow larger and larger as the centuries passed.

The bayonet is a small invention with large consequences. A musket with a bayonet is a musket that can also be a spear, which means the musketeer does not need a separate bodyguard of pikemen to protect him from cavalry. The bayonet, which appeared in the seventeenth century, allowed the musketeer to defend himself, and it allowed the army to dispense with the pike. The result was a simpler, cheaper army, and the result of that was a larger army. The bayonet is a good example of a small technological change with a large organizational effect, and the history of weapons is full of these. The weapon is not just a tool for killing; it is a tool for organizing, and the organization is often the more important effect.

The socket bayonet, which fits around the barrel rather than plugging into it, was the final step, because it allowed the musket to be fired with the bayonet fixed. This seems a small thing, but it meant the musketeer could shoot and then charge without changing weapons, and it made the bayonet charge a standard tactic. The bayonet charge is a psychological weapon as much as a physical one; it is a threat the enemy must respond to, and the response is often to break and run. The history of weapons is full of weapons whose main effect is psychological, and the bayonet is one of them.

The cannon is the other great gunpowder weapon, and it changed the nature of fortification. The medieval castle was designed to resist the siege engines of its time, but not cannon. A cannonball could knock down a stone wall, and the tall, thin walls of the medieval castle were especially vulnerable. The response was the trace italienne, the low, thick, angled fortification designed to absorb cannon fire and to let defenders sweep the approach with flanking fire. The trace italienne is a fortification designed around the cannon, and it is the weapon's mirror again: the shape of the fort tells you what the weapon can do. The trace italienne was expensive to build, and it changed the geography of war, because only rich states could afford to fortify their cities in this way. The cannon, in other words, favored the large state over the small one, and it is one of the reasons for the consolidation of political power in the early modern period.

The cannon also changed the nature of siege warfare. A medieval siege was a slow affair, a matter of blockade and starvation, with occasional assaults. A cannon siege was faster, because the cannon could breach the wall and allow an assault. This made sieges more decisive, and it made the siege train a key asset of any army. The cannon was expensive, and it required a specialized corps of gunners, engineers, and suppliers. The cannon, in other words, was a weapon that required a state to support it, and the states that could support it became the great powers of the early modern world. The history of weapons is the history of the state, and the cannon is one of the clearest examples.

The development of the cannon also illustrates the relationship between weapons and metallurgy. A cannon is a pressure vessel, and it must contain the explosion of the powder without bursting. This requires a metal with the right properties, and a manufacturing process that can produce a consistent product. The early cannons were made of iron bars bound with hoops, and they were prone to bursting. The development of cast bronze and later cast iron cannons made the weapon safer and more powerful, and it required a foundry industry that could produce large, consistent castings.
