paragraphs: The foundry that produced a cannon was a place where several distinct crafts met and had to be reconciled. The gun founder needed copper and tin in reliable supply, and tin was the harder problem: Europe's principal sources lay in Cornwall and the Erzgebirge, and the tin trade ran through few hands. He needed charcoal in quantity, because a furnace that could melt a ton of bronze consumed wood at a rate that stripped the surrounding countryside. He needed a bell-founder's knowledge of large castings, since cannon techniques were adapted directly from bell casting, and the men who made the first great guns often cast the bells of the parish church. He needed a boring mill to true the bore, because a cast cannon emerges from the mold with its interior slightly eccentric, and an eccentric bore throws the ball wide. And he needed a proofing ground where the finished piece could be fired with a heavy charge to see whether it would burst—a test that killed a certain number of the men who conducted it.

The organization of this work shaped the weapon. In the fifteenth century the great bombard was cast in place or near the siege, because a piece weighing several tons could not easily be moved over roads not built for it. The Ottoman bombards that battered the walls of Constantinople in 1453 were cast by a Hungarian founder, Orban, who had offered his services first to the Byzantines and been turned away for want of money. The largest threw a stone ball of formidable size and had to be loaded with a great charge of powder, and the chroniclers describe it being hauled by teams of oxen and men and fired only a few times a day. The weapon was less a machine than a construction project, and its value lay in the fact that no wall then standing could resist it for long. The Byzantines had relied for a thousand years on the walls of Theodosius, which had turned back every besieger for a millennium. They could not turn back the bombard, and the fall of the city in 1453 is one of the moments at which a change in the technology of weapons becomes a change in the political order.

The casting of bronze cannon required a mold of clay and loam around a core, and the core had to be positioned precisely so the bore would run true. The founder built up the mold in layers, drying each before adding the next, and bound the whole assembly with iron hoops to keep it from splitting when the molten metal was poured. The pour itself was dangerous: the metal had to be hot enough to flow into every part of the mold and not so hot that it burned the loam, and a single flaw could produce a gun that would burst on the first discharge. The bronze was an alloy of copper and tin, usually about nine or ten parts copper to one of tin, and the founder judged the alloy by the color of the molten metal and the sound it made when poured. The craft was empirical, passed from master to apprentice, and the knowledge was held in the hands rather than in books.

The development of the iron cannon followed a different path. Iron could be cast in a furnace that produced liquid metal hot enough to flow into a mold, and the blast furnace that made this possible was itself a development of the late medieval period. The first blast furnaces in Europe appear in the fifteenth century, in the Low Countries and the Rhineland, and they were built to make iron for many purposes, of which cannon was one. Cast iron is brittle, and an iron gun was more likely to burst than a bronze one, so early iron cannon were made with thick walls and were heavier for their power than bronze pieces. But iron was cheaper than bronze, and countries lacking access to copper and tin could arm themselves with iron guns. Sweden, with abundant iron ore and charcoal, became a major producer of iron cannon in the seventeenth century, and the export of Swedish guns shaped the balance of power in the Baltic and beyond.

The boring of cannon was a separate craft, and it was one of the first operations in which a machine tool was used to produce a precise cylindrical surface. The boring mill turned a cutting tool against the interior of the bore while the gun was rotated or held stationary, and the machine had to be rigid enough to cut iron or bronze without chattering. The water-powered boring mill appears in the fifteenth century, and it allowed the founder to produce a gun whose bore was true to a degree that hand work could not achieve. The improvement in the bore improved accuracy, and accuracy mattered more for the smaller pieces—the field guns that accompanied an army—than for the great siege bombards fired at a wall from close range.

The field gun was a different problem from the siege bombard, and its development followed a different logic. A siege gun could be heavy, because it was fired from a fixed position and moved only when the siege was over. A field gun had to accompany an army on the march, and it had to be light enough to be hauled by horses over roads that were often no more than tracks. The sixteenth-century field gun was a bronze piece of modest size, firing an iron ball of a few pounds, mounted on a carriage with two large wheels and a trail that rested on the ground. The carriage absorbed the recoil, and the gun had to be re-laid after each shot, because the recoil moved it out of position. The rate of fire was slow, and the gun was a supporting weapon rather than a decisive one. The infantry and the cavalry decided battles, and the artillery supported them.

The tactical use of artillery in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries was shaped by these limitations. Gustavus Adolphus, the Swedish king who campaigned in Germany during the Thirty Years' War, is often credited with developing a lighter field gun that could be moved quickly and used in close support of infantry. The Swedish guns were made of thinner bronze and fired a smaller charge, and they were designed to be hauled by a small team of horses or even by men. The king's artillery was organized into batteries that could be moved to a threatened point, and the guns were used to break up the dense infantry formations of the day. The innovation was as much organizational as technical: the Swedes integrated the guns into the tactical scheme of the army rather than treating them as a separate arm that arrived before the battle and left after it.

The seventeenth century also saw the development of the science of gunnery, part of the broader scientific revolution of the period. The trajectory of a projectile was a problem in mechanics, and Galileo's work on falling bodies and projectiles was directly relevant to the gunner's craft. Galileo showed that a projectile follows a parabolic path when air resistance is neglected, and he derived the relationship between the angle of elevation and the range. The gunner's rule that maximum range is obtained at an elevation of forty-five degrees followed from this analysis, and it was one of the first practical applications of mathematical physics to the art of war. The science of gunnery was taught in the military academies founded in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and the gunner became a professional who calculated his aim rather than guessing it.

The calculation of range required instruments, and the development of instruments was part of the same movement. The gunner's quadrant measured the elevation of the piece, and calipers measured the diameter of the bore and the ball. The ballistic pendulum, invented by Benjamin Robins in the eighteenth century, allowed the velocity of a projectile to be measured, and Robins's work on the resistance of the air was one of the foundations of external ballistics. The eighteenth-century gunner could measure the velocity of his shot and the elevation of his piece, and he could consult a table of ranges worked out by experiment. The gun was becoming a scientific instrument as well as a weapon, and the men who served it were becoming technicians.

The improvement of the gun was accompanied by the improvement of the powder, and the two were linked. Early gunpowder was a mixture of saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal, and the proportions varied widely. Saltpeter was the critical ingredient, because it supplied the oxygen that allowed the sulfur and charcoal to burn, and its quality determined the strength of the powder. The saltpeter of the early period was often impure, contaminated with common salt and other materials, and the powder made from it was weak and unreliable. The development of the process of refining saltpeter, by dissolving it in water and allowing it to crystallize, produced a purer product and a stronger powder. The proportion of saltpeter in the mixture was increased over time, from about fifty percent in the early recipes to about seventy-five percent in the powder of the eighteenth century, and the increase raised the energy released by the explosion.

The manufacture of gunpowder was a dangerous and specialized trade, organized in powder mills often located near a supply of water power for the stamping mills that ground the ingredients together. The ingredients were mixed in a mill and then pressed into a cake, which was broken into grains of a uniform size. The graining of the powder was important because the size of the grains determined the rate at which the powder burned: a fine powder burned quickly and was suitable for small arms, while a coarse powder burned more slowly and was suitable for cannon. The development of corned powder, in which the ingredients were moistened and pressed into grains, was a significant improvement over the earlier serpentine powder, a dry mixture that tended to separate during transport and to burn unevenly.

The chemistry of gunpowder was not understood until the nineteenth century, but the empirical knowledge of the powder makers was considerable. They knew that the powder had to be kept dry, that it deteriorated with age, and that the quality of the ingredients determined the quality of the product. The testing of powder was a practical matter: a sample was burned on a sheet of paper, and the residue was examined to judge the purity of the saltpeter. The powder maker's craft was one of the many technical trades that fed the development of weapons, and it was one of the most dangerous, because a powder mill could explode and kill everyone in it.

The eighteenth century saw the development of the artillery arm into a distinct branch of the army, with its own organization, uniforms, and schools. The French artillery, under the direction of Jean-Baptiste Vaquette de Gribeauval, was reorganized in the 1760s and 1770s into a system of standardized guns, carriages, and ammunition. The Gribeauval system reduced the number of calibers from a bewildering variety to a few standard sizes, and it standardized the carriages and limbers so that the guns could be moved and supplied more efficiently. The system was adopted by the French army and was used by Napoleon, and it was one of the reasons for the effectiveness of French artillery in the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars.

The Gribeauval system was a product of the eighteenth-century faith in standardization and system, and it was one of the first examples of a systematic approach to the design of military equipment. The guns were designed to be interchangeable, and the carriages to be repaired with standard parts. The system included a range of guns from a four-pounder to a twelve-pounder, designed to be as light as possible consistent with the strength needed to fire the charge. The carriages were made of seasoned wood and iron fittings, and they were designed to be repaired in the field. The system was a considerable improvement over the ad hoc arrangements that had preceded it, and it was copied by other armies.

The Napoleonic wars demonstrated the value of massed artillery, and they also demonstrated the limits of the smoothbore gun. The guns of the period were accurate enough at close range but inaccurate at long range, because the ball did not fit the bore tightly and rattled down the barrel, and because the smoothbore could not impart a spin that would stabilize the projectile. The effective range of a field gun was a few hundred yards, and the gun was used to batter a position at close range rather than to strike a distant target. The development of the rifled gun, which would extend the range and the accuracy of artillery, was still in the future.

The rifle was a separate development, and it followed a different path from the cannon. The rifle was a small arm with a barrel cut with spiral grooves, which imparted a spin to the bullet and stabilized it in flight. The spin made the rifle far more accurate than the smoothbore musket, but the early rifle was slow to load, because the bullet had to be forced down the barrel against the resistance of the rifling. The rifle was therefore a specialist's weapon, used by hunters and by skirmishers, and it was not suitable for the massed infantry fire that decided battles. The musket, which could be loaded quickly and fired in volleys, remained the standard infantry weapon, and the rifle was a supplement to it.

The American long rifle, developed by German and Swiss gunsmiths in Pennsylvania in the eighteenth century, was one of the finest examples of the rifle maker's craft. The long rifle had a barrel of great length, sometimes forty-four inches or more, and it fired a small ball of about half an ounce with a carefully measured charge of powder. The rifle was accurate to a range of two hundred yards or more, and it was used to great effect by American riflemen in the Revolutionary War. The riflemen were skirmishers, and their marksmanship supplemented the volley fire of the line infantry rather than substituting for it. The long rifle was slow to load and delicate to maintain, and it was not a weapon for the mass army.

The development of the rifle was held back by the problem of loading, and the problem was solved in the nineteenth century by a series of inventions that transformed the small arm. The first was the percussion cap, invented in the 1820s, which replaced the flintlock with a small copper cap containing a fulminate that ignited the charge when struck by the hammer. The percussion cap was more reliable than the flintlock, because it was not affected by wind or rain, and it fired more quickly. The second was the Minié ball, developed by the French officer Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, a hollow-based bullet that expanded into the rifling when the charge was fired. The Minié ball could be loaded quickly, because it was small enough to slide down the barrel, and it expanded to engage the rifling when fired. The combination of the percussion cap and the Minié ball made the rifled musket a practical infantry weapon, and it was adopted by the British as the Pattern 1853 Enfield and by the Americans as the Springfield Model 1861.

The rifled musket changed the character of infantry combat. The smoothbore musket was accurate to about fifty yards and could be fired at a mass of men at a hundred yards with some chance of hitting. The rifled musket was accurate to several hundred yards, and it could strike an individual man at a range at which the smoothbore could not reach. The effect on tactics was profound: the dense formations that had been necessary to deliver volley fire became suicidal when they came within range of the rifled musket. The attackers had to cross a beaten zone of several hundred yards under fire from defenders who were themselves dispersed and protected, and the cost of the attack rose sharply.

The American Civil War was the first great conflict in which the rifled musket was the standard infantry weapon, and the casualties were enormous. The battles of 1862 and 1863, at Shiloh, Antietam, and Gettysburg, produced casualty figures that shocked contemporaries and that are explained in part by the range and accuracy of the rifled musket. The attackers at Gettysburg, in Pickett's Charge, crossed a mile of open ground under artillery and rifle fire, and they were broken before they reached the Union line. The defensive power of the rifled musket was demonstrated, and the tactics of the war were slow to adapt. The generals on both sides had been trained in the tactics of the smoothbore era, and they continued to order frontal attacks against entrenched positions, with the results that the casualty lists recorded.

The rifled musket was not the only development of the mid-nineteenth century, and the others were equally consequential. The breech-loading rifle, in which the cartridge was inserted at the rear of the barrel rather than rammed down from the muzzle, allowed the soldier to reload while lying prone and to fire at a much higher rate. The Prussian needle gun, adopted in the 1840s, was a breech-loader that used a paper cartridge with the primer inside the cartridge, and it could be fired at a rate of several rounds a minute. The Prussian army used the needle gun to great effect in the wars of German unification, and the Austrian army, which still used muzzle-loading rifles, was defeated at Königgrätz in 1866 in part because of the superiority of the Prussian firearm.

The development of the breech-loader was followed by the development of the metallic cartridge, in which the primer, the powder, and the bullet were combined in a single unit with a brass case. The metallic cartridge made the breech-loader reliable and allowed the development of the repeating rifle, in which a magazine held several cartridges and the action was worked by a lever or a bolt. The repeating rifle was adopted by the armies of the later nineteenth century, and it increased the rate of fire of the infantryman from a few rounds a minute to a dozen or more. The increase in the rate of fire was accompanied by a decrease in the caliber of the bullet, as the small-bore high-velocity bullet was found to be more effective than the large, slow bullet of the earlier period.

The development of the small-bore rifle was driven by the discovery that a small, fast bullet could inflict a severe wound, because the energy of the bullet was transferred to the tissue and caused a cavity larger than the bullet itself. The wound ballistics of the late nineteenth century were studied by military surgeons, and the results were used to design bullets that would incapacitate an enemy without requiring a large caliber. The bullet of the late nineteenth-century rifle was typically of about .30 caliber, and it was fired at a velocity of two thousand feet per second or more. The range of the rifle was extended to a thousand yards or more, and the infantryman could engage a target at a distance at which the earlier musket could not reach.

The development of the machine gun was the logical extension of the trend toward rapid fire. The first practical machine gun was the invention of Hiram Maxim, an American who had settled in England, and it was demonstrated in 1884. The Maxim gun used the recoil of the cartridge to operate the mechanism, so that the gun loaded and fired itself as long as the trigger was held and the ammunition lasted. The gun was cooled by a water jacket around the barrel and fed by a belt of cartridges. The Maxim gun could fire several hundred rounds a minute, and it was adopted by the British Army in 1891 as the .303-caliber Maxim.

The machine gun changed the tactical problem of the infantry attack. A single machine gun could deliver the fire of a company of riflemen, and it could do so continuously. The gun was heavy and had to be mounted on a tripod or a carriage, and it was a defensive weapon used to hold a position against attack. The combination of the machine gun and the rifled musket made the frontal attack against a prepared position almost impossible, and the armies of the early twentieth century were slow to recognize the implications. The doctrine of the offensive, which held that the attacker had the advantage and that the spirit of the attack would carry the day, was still dominant, and it led to the slaughter of the First World War.

The development of artillery in the late nineteenth century followed a similar path. The introduction of the rifled breech-loading gun, with a steel barrel and a copper driving band on the shell that engaged the rifling, extended the range and the accuracy of the field gun. The recoil system was the critical problem: a gun that was not held in place by its carriage would move out of position after each shot, and the gunner had to re-lay the piece before firing again. The French solved the problem in 1897 with the Canon de 75 modèle 1897, which used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that absorbed the recoil and returned the barrel to its original position. The gun could be fired at a rate of about fifteen rounds a minute without re-laying, and it was the most advanced field gun in the world at the time of its introduction.

The French 75 was a product of the French artillery tradition, shaped by the Gribeauval reforms and by the experience of the Napoleonic wars. The gun was designed to fire a high-explosive shell at a high velocity, and it was intended for close support of the infantry. The recoil system was a complex mechanism of cylinders and pistons filled with oil and compressed air, and it required a high level of manufacturing precision. The gun was a symbol of French military prowess, and it was used to great effect in the battles of 1914, when the French artillery broke up the German attacks and contributed to the failure of the Schlieffen Plan.

The First World War was the first conflict in which the industrial production of weapons became the decisive factor. The war began with the armies of 1914 equipped with the weapons of the prewar period, and the consumption of ammunition in the first months of the war exceeded all expectations. The French army fired its reserves of 75mm ammunition in a few weeks, and the factories of France, Britain, and Germany were strained to produce the shells that the guns required. The shell shortage of 1915 was a political crisis in Britain, and it led to the creation of a Ministry of Munitions under David Lloyd George that organized the industrial production of the war.

The artillery of the First World War became the dominant weapon of the battlefield, and the development of artillery tactics and technology was driven by the demands of the trench war. The guns were used to cut the barbed wire in front of an attack, to destroy the enemy's trenches and machine-gun posts, and to counter the enemy's artillery. The barrage, in which a line of exploding shells moved across the battlefield ahead of the advancing infantry, was developed to protect the attackers from the enemy's defenders. The creeping barrage required precise timing and coordination between the artillery and the infantry, and it was one of the tactical innovations of the war.

The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916, was the greatest artillery battle of the war and one of the greatest in history. The German attack was preceded by a bombardment of unprecedented intensity, and the French defense was organized around the fire of the guns. The battle produced roughly 700,000 casualties, and the landscape of the battlefield was so thoroughly churned by shellfire that it became a symbol of the destructiveness of industrial war. The artillery at Verdun was supplied by a vast logistical organization that brought shells to the guns by rail and by truck, and the battle was as much a contest of industrial production as of military skill.

The development of the tank was a response to the deadlock of the trench war. The tank was an armored vehicle that could cross the broken ground of the battlefield and crush the barbed wire, and it was armed with guns and machine guns. The first tanks were used by the British at the Battle of the Somme in September 1916, and they were slow, unreliable, and mechanically primitive. The tank of the First World War was a beginning rather than a decisive weapon, but it pointed the way to the future of armored warfare.

The development of the tank was a product of the combination of several technologies: the internal combustion engine, the continuous track, and the armor plate. The track allowed the vehicle to cross soft ground and obstacles, and the armor protected it from small-arms fire. The engine was the critical component, because the tank had to be powerful enough to move its own weight and to cross the broken ground of the battlefield. The early tanks were underpowered and prone to breakdown, and they required a crew of several men to drive and fight the vehicle. The development of the tank was slow, and it was not until the Second World War that the tank became the decisive weapon of the ground battle.

The First World War also saw the development of the submarine as a weapon of war, and the submarine changed the character of naval warfare. The submarine could attack a surface ship without warning, and it could operate in waters that were controlled by the enemy. The German U-boat campaign against the shipping of the Allies was an attempt to starve Britain into submission, and it brought the United States into the war in 1917. The submarine was a weapon of the weak against the strong, and it was the first weapon that could threaten the command of the sea without a fleet.

The submarine was a product of the combination of the internal combustion engine, the electric battery, and the torpedo. The submarine of the First World War was a surface vessel that could submerge, and it was powered by diesel engines on the surface and by electric motors underwater. The torpedo was a self-propelled underwater missile that could be launched from a tube and that would explode on contact with a ship's hull. The development of the torpedo was a separate line of technological development, and it was one of the most important naval weapons of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

The First World War was a war of attrition, and the weapons that were developed during the war were designed to inflict casualties on the enemy and to protect the attacker. The flamethrower, the gas shell, and the trench mortar were all weapons of the trench war, and they were used to attack the enemy's positions and to break the deadlock. The development of chemical weapons was one of the most controversial episodes of the war, and it was a breach of the existing conventions on the conduct of war. The use of chlorine gas at Ypres in 1915 was followed by the development of phosgene and mustard gas, and the gas shell became a standard weapon of the artillery. The chemical weapons of the First World War were not decisive, but they added a new dimension of horror to the war and they shaped the later attempts to control the development of weapons.

The Second World War was the greatest war of industrial production in history, and the development of weapons during the war was driven by the mobilization of the industrial resources of the combatant nations. The United States, which had the largest industrial base in the world, produced an enormous quantity of weapons of every kind, and the Soviet Union, after the evacuation of its industry to the east, produced tanks and aircraft in numbers that exceeded the German production. The war was won by the side that could out-produce the other, and the development of weapons was shaped by the demands of mass production.

The development of the tank during the Second World War was rapid, and the tank became the core of the armored division. The German Panzer divisions, which combined tanks with motorized infantry and artillery, were the instrument of the blitzkrieg, and they demonstrated the power of the combined-arms formation. The Soviet T-34, which was introduced in 1940, was one of the best tanks of the war, with a combination of armor, firepower, and mobility that was superior to the German tanks of the period. The development of the tank was a contest between armor and anti-tank weapons, and the guns of the tanks grew larger and the armor grew thicker as the war went on.

The development of the aircraft was one of the most significant technological developments of the war. The aircraft of the First World War had been fragile machines of wood and fabric, and they had been used for reconnaissance and for limited ground attack. The aircraft of the Second World War were all-metal monoplanes with powerful engines, and they could carry heavy loads of bombs and fire heavy cannon. The strategic bombing campaign against Germany and Japan was an attempt to destroy the enemy's industrial capacity and to break the will of the population, and it was one of the most destructive campaigns of the war.

The development of the bomber was accompanied by the development of the fighter, and the two were locked in a contest of speed and firepower. The fighter of the Second World War was a high-performance aircraft with a powerful engine and a battery of machine guns or cannon, and it was used to protect the bombers and to establish air superiority. The Battle of Britain, fought in the summer and autumn of 1940, was a contest between the German bomber force and the British fighter force, and it was one of the first battles in history to be decided by air power alone.

The development of radar was one of the technological developments that shaped the air war. Radar allowed the defenders to detect the approach of enemy aircraft and to direct their fighters to intercept them. The British chain of radar stations, which was built in the late 1930s, was a key factor in the success of the RAF in the Battle of Britain, and it was one of the first applications of electronics to the conduct of war. The development of radar was a product of the combination of the cavity magnetron, which was invented in Britain in 1940, and the electronics industry that could produce the equipment in quantity.

The development of the atomic bomb was the most significant technological development of the war, and it changed the character of war and of international relations. The Manhattan Project, which was organized in the United States with the participation of Britain and Canada, produced the first nuclear weapons. The first test, code-named Trinity, was conducted on 16 July 1945 at the Alamogordo Bombing Range in New Mexico, and it detonated a plutonium implosion device with a yield of about 21 kilotons. The test was the culmination of a scientific and industrial effort of unprecedented scale, and it opened the nuclear age.

The development of the atomic bomb was a product of the discovery of nuclear fission in 1938 and of the recognition by the scientists who made the discovery that a chain reaction could release enormous energy. The physicists who worked on the project, including Enrico Fermi, J. Robert Oppenheimer, and Niels Bohr, were among the most distinguished scientists of the age, and they were organized into a laboratory at Los Alamos under military direction. The project required the production of fissile material in quantity, and the plants at Oak Ridge and Hanford were built to produce enriched uranium and plutonium. The industrial effort was enormous, and it was one of the largest construction projects in history.

The atomic bomb was used against Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, and the bombs destroyed the two cities and killed tens of thousands of people. The use of the bomb was the subject of intense debate at the time and has remained so since. The official justification was that the bomb shortened the war and avoided the casualties that an invasion of Japan would have cost. The critics argued that Japan was already defeated and that the use of the bomb was unnecessary and morally indefensible. The debate is unresolved, but the fact of the bomb's use shaped the postwar world and the development of weapons in the decades that followed.

The development of the atomic bomb was followed by the development of the hydrogen bomb, which used the fusion of hydrogen isotopes to release energy on a far greater scale than fission. The first hydrogen bomb was tested by the United States in 1952, and the Soviet Union tested its own hydrogen bomb in 1953. The development of the hydrogen bomb was a step in the arms race that characterized the Cold War, and it led to the accumulation of arsenals of nuclear weapons that could destroy the world many times over.

The Cold War was a period of intense technological competition between the United States and the Soviet Union, and the development of weapons was driven by the logic of the arms race. The two superpowers competed in the development of nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, and the systems that were designed to detect and intercept them. The development of the intercontinental ballistic missile, which could deliver a nuclear warhead to a target on the other side of the world in a matter of minutes, changed the strategic calculus. The missile made the bomber vulnerable, and it made the warning time for a nuclear attack a matter of minutes rather than hours.

The development of the ballistic missile was a product of the combination of the rocket technology developed in Germany during the Second World War and the nuclear weapons developed in the United States. The German V-2 rocket, which was used against London in 1944 and 1945, was a ballistic missile of limited range and accuracy, but it demonstrated the potential of the rocket as a weapon. The engineers who had worked on the V-2, including Wernher von Braun, were brought to the United States after the war, and they contributed to the development of the American missile program. The Soviet Union also captured German rocket technology and engineers, and it developed its own missiles.

The development of the ballistic missile was accompanied by the development of the submarine-launched ballistic missile, which gave the nuclear powers a survivable second-strike capability. The submarine could hide in the ocean and could launch its missiles from a position that was difficult to detect. The development of the submarine-launched missile was a key element of the strategy of deterrence, because it ensured that a nuclear attack on one power would be answered by a retaliatory strike from the submarines at sea.

The strategy of deterrence was the organizing principle of the nuclear arms race. The theory of deterrence held that the possession of a secure second-strike capability would deter an adversary from launching a first strike, because the adversary would know that it would suffer a devastating retaliation. The theory was codified in the doctrine of mutual assured destruction, which held that the two superpowers were deterred from attacking each other by the certainty of their mutual destruction. The doctrine was a product of the nuclear age, and it was one of the most important developments in the history of strategy.

The nuclear arms race was accompanied by attempts to control the proliferation of nuclear weapons. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, was the cornerstone of the international effort to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons. The treaty committed the nuclear powers to pursue negotiations on disarmament and committed the non-nuclear states to forgo the development of nuclear weapons. The treaty has 191 states parties, but India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The treaty has been a partial success, but it has not prevented the spread of nuclear weapons to all the states that sought them.

The development of conventional weapons during the Cold War followed the logic of the competition between the two alliances. The armies of NATO and the Warsaw Pact were equipped with tanks, artillery, and aircraft that were designed to fight a war in Europe, and the development of these weapons was driven by the perception of the threat from the other side. The development of the tank continued, and the tanks of the Cold War were equipped with more powerful guns, thicker armor, and better fire-control systems than the tanks of the Second World War.

The development of the aircraft during the Cold War was dominated by the jet engine, which was invented in Britain and Germany during the Second World War and which transformed the performance of the aircraft. The jet fighter of the Cold War was faster and more heavily armed than the propeller-driven fighter of the Second World War, and it was equipped with radar and missiles. The development of the jet engine was one of the most significant technological developments of the twentieth century, and it shaped the development of both military and civil aviation.

The development of the helicopter gave the army a new kind of mobility. The helicopter could carry troops and supplies over terrain that was impassable to ground vehicles, and it could be armed with rockets and machine guns to support the troops that it carried. The helicopter was used extensively in the Vietnam War, and it changed the character of the war in the jungle. The development of the helicopter was a product of the combination of the jet engine and the rotor technology, and it was one of the most significant developments in the history of military mobility.

The Vietnam War was a conflict in which the technological superiority of the United States was not sufficient to win. The United States had the most advanced weapons in the world, but it was fighting an enemy that was willing to accept heavy casualties and that was supported by the terrain and by the political situation. The war demonstrated the limits of technology in a conflict that was as much political as military, and it shaped the American approach to war in the decades that followed.

The development of precision-guided munitions was one of the most significant developments in the history of air power. The first precision-guided munitions were developed during the Vietnam War, when the United States used laser-guided bombs to destroy bridges and other targets that had resisted conventional bombing. The precision-guided munition was a bomb or missile that could be guided to its target by a laser or a television camera, and it could strike a target with a high degree of accuracy. The development of the precision-guided munition changed the character of air power, because it allowed a single aircraft to destroy a target that would previously have required a large formation of bombers.

The development of precision-guided munitions was a product of the combination of the laser, the television camera, and the computer, and it was one of the first applications of information technology to the conduct of war. The guided bomb of the Vietnam War was a crude device compared with the weapons that followed, but it demonstrated the potential of the technology. The development of the precision-guided munition was slow during the Cold War, because the weapons were expensive and the military was committed to the doctrine of mass bombing. The Gulf War of 1991 was the first conflict in which precision-guided munitions were used on a large scale.

The Gulf War of 1991 was a demonstration of the power of precision-guided munitions and of the information technology that supported them. The coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs during the war, of which about 6,520 tons were precision-guided, roughly 7.4 percent of the total. The precision-guided munitions were used against high-value targets such as bridges, command centers, and air-defense systems, and they struck these targets with a high degree of accuracy. The small share of precision-guided munitions in the total bomb tonnage was disproportionate to their effect, and the war reshaped the expectations of air power.

The Gulf War was also a demonstration of the power of the information technology that supported the precision-guided munitions. The coalition forces used satellites, radar, and computers to locate and identify targets and to direct the aircraft to them. The information technology was the key to the precision of the weapons, and it was one of the most significant developments in the history of war. The Gulf War was called the first information war, and it was a preview of the conflicts of the twenty-first century.
The development of the drone was a continuation of the trend toward precision and information. The drone was an unmanned aircraft that could be controlled from a distance and that could carry cameras

paragraphs: The Predator’s flight over the desert culminated a lineage stretching back to the first time a human killed another from beyond the reach of an arm. To understand the drone—its promise, its limits, and the strange moral weather it would bring—one had to follow the thread backward through a century of remote warfare: the unmanned balloons of the nineteenth century, the radio-controlled boats of the First World War, the crude television-guided glide bombs of the Second, and the reconnaissance drones that flew over Vietnam and, decades later, became the ancestors of the armed aircraft now circling above the battlespace at twenty thousand feet. The drone did not appear from nowhere. It was the product of a long, patient, often obscure history of efforts to separate the weapon from the warrior, extend the human hand across distance, and substitute the machine for the man.

The impulse to strike from afar is ancient. The sling, the bow, the javelin, the crossbow—each allowed a combatant to harm an enemy who could not reach him in return. The English longbow, with its draw weight of one hundred to one hundred and eighty-five pounds, as the surviving bows from the *Mary Rose* attest, could send an arrow more than two hundred yards, and the archer who loosed it stood well behind the line of battle. The crossbow, which the medieval church once tried to ban as too murderous for Christians to use against one another, was a machine for the same purpose: it stored the energy of a windlass or lever and released it in a single, unanswerable blow. The musket extended the reach further still, and the rifle beyond that. The Minié ball, with its hollow base that expanded into the rifling, made the rifled musket a weapon that could kill at five hundred yards—without the soldier who fired it ever seeing the face of the man who fell. The history of weapons is in large part the history of this extension of range, and the drone was simply its most recent and most radical expression.

But the drone was different in kind, not only in degree. The bow and the rifle extended the reach of the human body; the drone extended the reach of the human mind while removing the body from the scene altogether. The pilot of a Predator sat in a ground-control station in Nevada or the Persian Gulf, thousands of miles from the aircraft, and watched the world through a camera lens. He fired a missile at a target he could see only as a smudge of heat on a screen, and the missile killed men he would never meet, in a country he might never visit, on a day recorded in a log file and a news release but not in any personal memory of the act. The drone was the culmination of the long trend toward precision and information, and it was also a rupture. It made killing abstract in a way no previous weapon had, and it raised questions about responsibility, distance, and the moral character of war that would preoccupy soldiers, lawyers, and philosophers for decades.

The prehistory of the drone began in the nineteenth century, with the balloon. The Montgolfier brothers had demonstrated the hot-air balloon in 1783, and within a decade the French revolutionary armies were using captive balloons for observation. The balloon was the first platform that lifted a human being above the battlefield to see what could not be seen from the ground, and the first weapon system that separated the observer from the danger of the line of battle. At the Battle of Fleurus in 1794, a French balloon named *l'Entreprenant* hovered above the Austrian lines and sent down messages that helped the French commander, Jourdan, direct his troops. The balloon was not a weapon in the sense of a device that killed, but it was a weapon system in that it gathered the information on which killing depended. The observation balloon became a standard feature of nineteenth-century warfare and reached its apotheosis in the First World War, when thousands of balloons, tethered behind the lines, watched the enemy trenches and directed the artillery that killed millions.

The balloon was captive, its range limited by its tether. The next step was to make the platform free-flying and unmanned. The first unmanned aerial vehicles were developed during and after the First World War, and they were, in essence, flying bombs. The Sopwith Camel was a piloted fighter, but the Sopwith Salamander was an armored ground-attack aircraft, and the Kettering Bug, developed by the American inventor Charles Kettering in 1918, was an unmanned biplane that carried a warhead and was designed to fly a preset course to a target. The Bug was guided by a gyroscope and a barometer, and it was intended to be launched from a rail and to dive onto its target when its engine cut out after a predetermined number of revolutions. It was never used in combat—the war ended before it could be deployed—but it was the first true cruise missile, and it established the principle that an aircraft could be flown without a pilot to deliver a weapon at a distance.

The First World War also produced the first remote-controlled boat, the FL-boats the German navy used to attack Allied shipping, and the first radio-controlled aircraft, tested by the British and Americans in the years after the war. The technology of remote control was in its infancy, and the reliability of the early systems was poor, but the idea was established: a vehicle could be controlled from a distance by a human operator who was not aboard. The Second World War accelerated these technologies. The German *Fritz X* was a radio-controlled glide bomb used with devastating effect against the Italian battleship *Roma* in 1943, and the *Henschel Hs 293* was a similar weapon that sank several Allied ships. The Japanese *Ohka* was a rocket-powered suicide aircraft guided by a pilot, but the American *Azon* was a radio-controlled bomb guided by an operator in a following aircraft, and the *Bat* was a radar-guided glide bomb used against Japanese shipping in the Pacific. The Second World War also produced the first mass-produced unmanned aircraft, the German *V-1* flying bomb, guided by a simple autopilot and a preset fuel cutoff, which killed thousands of civilians in London and Antwerp. The V-1 was a terror weapon, but it also demonstrated that an unmanned aircraft could be produced in large numbers and deliver a warhead at a distance of hundreds of miles.

The Second World War also produced the first reconnaissance drones, used by the United States Navy to photograph Japanese-held islands in the Pacific. These were modified radio-controlled aircraft that carried cameras, and they were the direct ancestors of the reconnaissance drones developed during the Cold War. The Cold War was the great age of the unmanned aircraft, because the superpowers needed to see what the other was doing without risking pilots' lives. The American *Ryan Firebee* was a jet-powered target drone modified to carry cameras and electronic sensors, and it was used extensively over North Vietnam and China in the 1960s and 1970s. The Firebee was launched from a transport aircraft or from the ground, flew a preset course taking photographs and gathering electronic intelligence, and was recovered by parachute or helicopter. It was not armed, but it was a crucial step toward the armed drone, because it demonstrated that an unmanned aircraft could fly deep into hostile territory, survive, and return with the information commanders needed.

The Israeli experience was decisive in the development of the armed drone. Israel had been at war with its neighbors since its founding in 1948 and had learned the value of aerial reconnaissance in the wars of 1967 and 1973. In 1982, during the war in Lebanon, Israel used a combination of unmanned and manned aircraft to destroy the Syrian air-defense system in the Bekaa Valley. The Israelis sent small, inexpensive drones over the Syrian positions to provoke the Syrians into turning on their radars, then used the emissions from the radars to locate and destroy the missile batteries. The operation was a stunning success, demonstrating that drones could be used not only for reconnaissance but as part of a coordinated strike package. The Israelis also developed the *Pioneer* drone, sold to the United States Navy and used in the Gulf War of 1991, and the *Hunter* drone, developed jointly with the United States.

American development of the armed drone was driven by the experience of the Gulf War and the wars that followed. The Predator was originally developed by General Atomics as a reconnaissance drone and used in the Balkans in the 1990s to monitor the conflict in Bosnia and Kosovo. It was a slow, propeller-driven aircraft that could loiter over a target for hours, carrying a suite of cameras and sensors that could see in the visible and infrared spectrum. The decision to arm the Predator was made in the aftermath of the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the United States found itself at war with a diffuse enemy operating in countries where American troops could not easily go. The first armed Predator flight was in February 2001, and the first lethal strike was in October 2001, in Afghanistan. The target was Mullah Omar, the leader of the Taliban, but the strike missed him and killed several other people. The Predator was armed with the AGM-114 Hellfire missile, a laser-guided weapon developed for anti-tank use, and the combination of the drone's persistent surveillance and the missile's precision made it a weapon of extraordinary lethality.

The Predator and its larger successor, the Reaper, became the signature weapons of the American wars in Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, Somalia, and Pakistan. The drones flew thousands of sorties and killed thousands of people, including many civilians. The strikes were conducted by the Central Intelligence Agency and by the military, often directed at individuals identified as militants by intelligence analysis that was sometimes reliable and sometimes not. The drone made it possible to kill a single individual in a remote village without putting a single American soldier at risk, and to do so on the basis of intelligence that might be hours or days old. The drone was a weapon of precision, but it was also a weapon of surveillance, and the two functions were inseparable. It could watch a house for days, noting who came and went, then strike at the moment when the target was most vulnerable. The drone was a weapon of patience, and a weapon of information.

The information technology that supported the drone was as important as the aircraft itself. The Predator was controlled by a satellite link that allowed the pilot in Nevada to see what the aircraft saw and to fly it in real time. The video was transmitted to commanders around the world and often used to support troops on the ground engaged in combat. The drone was a node in a network that included satellites, ground stations, intelligence analysts, and commanders, and the network was what made it effective. It was the first weapon system that was fundamentally an information system, and a preview of the way information technology would transform warfare in the twenty-first century. The Gulf War had been called the first information war, but the drone was the first weapon that was itself an information system, and the first weapon that could be controlled by a human being who was not in the same country as the target.

The drone also raised profound questions about the ethics of war. The just-war tradition had long held that the use of force must be proportionate, discriminate between combatants and civilians, and be undertaken with a reasonable chance of success. The drone made it possible to strike at a single individual with a missile guided to within a few feet of its target, without risking the pilot's life. The precision of the drone was a moral advantage, because it reduced the risk of collateral damage, but its distance was a moral problem, because it removed the pilot from the consequences of his actions. The pilot of a drone could kill a man and then go home to his family, without ever seeing the body of the man he had killed. The drone made killing easy, and the ease of killing was a moral danger. The philosopher Michael Walzer had argued that moral restraint in war depended on the proximity of the combatants, on the fact that the soldier who killed had to face the possibility of being killed in return. The drone removed that reciprocity, and it raised the question of whether a war fought by drones could be a just war at all.

The drone also raised questions about sovereignty and international law. The United States conducted drone strikes in countries with which it was not at war, without the consent of their governments. The strikes in Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia were conducted by the CIA and by the military, and they killed people accused of being members of al-Qaeda or its affiliates. The United States justified them as acts of self-defense against a non-state enemy that had attacked the United States and continued to pose a threat. The governments of the countries where the strikes took place sometimes protested and sometimes acquiesced, and the legal basis was contested by international lawyers and human-rights organizations. The drone blurred the line between war and peace, because it could be used at any time, in any place, without a declaration of war and without a visible battlefield. It made war permanent and invisible, and it made the whole world a potential battlefield.

The drone was also increasingly available to non-state actors and to states that were not great powers. The technology was cheap and widely available, and the proliferation of small, inexpensive drones transformed the battlefield in ways the developers of the Predator had not anticipated. The small drone—the quadcopter that could be bought in a toy store and modified to carry a grenade—became a weapon of the insurgent and the terrorist. The Islamic State used drones to drop small bombs on Iraqi and Syrian forces, and the Houthis in Yemen used drones to attack Saudi Arabia. The small drone was a weapon of asymmetry, allowing a weak actor to strike at a strong actor without the cost of a conventional air force. It democratized air power, and it did so in a way that was deeply destabilizing.

The war in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 was a landmark in the history of the drone. The conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed territory was fought over forty-four days and decided in large part by drones. Azerbaijan used Turkish-made Bayraktar TB2 drones and Israeli-made loitering munitions to destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, and air-defense systems. The TB2 was a medium-altitude drone that could carry laser-guided missiles, and it was used to devastating effect against Armenian armor that was not protected by effective air defense. The loitering munitions, small drones that could circle over a target and then dive onto it, were used to destroy air-defense radars and missile launchers. The Armenian air-defense system, based on Soviet-era equipment, was unable to cope with the small, slow, numerous drones, and the Armenian army suffered heavy losses. The war demonstrated that drones could be decisive in a conventional conflict, and it warned armies around the world that the age of the tank and the artillery piece might be coming to an end.

The RUSI study of the Nagorno-Karabakh war, published in 2021, treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense. The study noted that the drones were effective because they were part of a system that included electronic warfare, precision-guided munitions, and a sophisticated command-and-control network. The drones were not a wonder weapon that could win a war on their own, but they could change the balance of power between offense and defense. The study also noted that the drones were effective against armies that were not prepared for them, and that the development of counter-drone technologies would be a major task for the armies of the future. The drone was a weapon still in its infancy, and its full implications were not yet understood.

The loitering munition was a particularly significant development, because it combined the functions of the drone and the missile. It was a small aircraft that could be launched from a tube or a rail, fly to a target area, and circle over it for minutes or hours, waiting for a target to appear. When the target appeared, the munition would dive onto it and explode. The loitering munition could be used against tanks, radar, and even individual soldiers, and it could be used by small units without the support of an air force. It was a weapon of the infantry, and a weapon that could be used by the insurgent as well as by the state. The technology was spreading rapidly, and it was likely to be a feature of the battlefields of the twenty-first century.

The question of autonomy was the most difficult question raised by the drone. The Predator and the Reaper were remotely piloted, which meant that a human being was always in the loop. The human being decided when to fire and was responsible for the consequences of the shot. But the loitering munition could be programmed to attack a target without human intervention, and the development of artificial intelligence was making it possible for machines to identify and engage targets on their own. Whether a machine could be trusted to make the decision to kill went to the heart of the ethics of war. The United Nations had debated the question of lethal autonomous weapons systems for years, and a group of experts had been convened to discuss the issue, but no agreement had been reached. The United States and other countries argued that existing international humanitarian law was sufficient to regulate autonomous weapons, while human-rights organizations and a number of states called for a treaty that would ban them. The debate was unresolved, and the technology was advancing faster than the law.

The claim that a loitering munition had been used in autonomous mode in Libya in 2021 was a case in point. A United Nations Panel of Experts report on Libya stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces, but the claim remained contested and was not independently confirmed. The report was based on information that was not fully verified, and the manufacturer of the munition denied that it had been used in autonomous mode. The claim was important because it was the first time a United Nations report had suggested that an autonomous weapon might have been used in combat, and it was a warning that the age of autonomous warfare might be closer than many people thought. But the claim was also a reminder that the evidence for autonomous warfare was often ambiguous, and that the line between remote control and autonomy was not always clear. The drone was a weapon surrounded by uncertainty, and the uncertainty was part of its nature.

The history of the drone was also a history of the way technology shaped strategy. The drone made it possible for the United States to conduct a war against al-Qaeda and its affiliates that was fought largely by special-operations forces and by aircraft, with a small number of troops on the ground. It made it possible to kill individual militants without invading their countries, and to do so at a cost measured in millions of dollars rather than billions. The drone was a weapon of the small war, fought by a few hundred operators and a few dozen aircraft against an enemy that was dispersed and elusive. It was suited to the wars of the twenty-first century—wars against non-state actors, wars fought in the shadows, wars fought without a clear front line. The drone was a weapon of the age of terrorism, and it was shaped by the age of terrorism.

But the drone was also shaped by the age of information. It was a sensor platform as much as a weapon, and the information it gathered was often more important than the missiles it fired. The video from a Predator could track a target for days, identify the people who came and went from a house, and build a picture of a network of militants that could not be seen from the ground. The drone was a tool of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, used by the CIA and by the military to build the picture of the enemy necessary for the conduct of the war. It was a weapon of the information age, and it was shaped by the information age.

The development of the drone was also a development in the history of the relationship between the soldier and the machine. The pilot of a drone was a soldier who sat in a chair in a container in the Nevada desert and fought a war thousands of miles away—a soldier who was not in danger, and who could go home to his family at the end of his shift. He was exposed to the stress of combat without the camaraderie of the unit and without the physical danger that had always been part of the soldier's experience. The psychological toll on drone pilots was a subject of study, and the studies found that they suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder at rates comparable to those of pilots who flew manned aircraft. The drone pilot saw the consequences of his actions in high-definition video, and he saw them again and again, because the video was recorded and could be replayed. He was a soldier both present and absent, and the ambiguity of his position was a source of psychological strain.

The drone also changed the relationship between the soldier and the civilian. It could see into the windows of houses and follow a single person through a crowded market. It was a weapon of surveillance that could be used against anyone, and the distinction between combatant and civilian was blurred by the ability of the drone to watch and kill at a distance. It made it possible to kill a man in his home, in his car, or in his field, without warning and without trial. The drone was a weapon of assassination, and its use for targeted killing raised the question of whether the United States was conducting a program of extrajudicial execution that violated the laws of war and of human rights. The drone was both precise and indiscriminate, because it could kill the intended target with great accuracy but could also kill the people who happened to be near the target. It was a weapon surrounded by moral ambiguity, and the ambiguity was not resolved by the precision of the weapon.

The drone also changed the relationship between the state and the citizen. It made it possible for the state to kill without the consent of the people who were killed, and without the consent of the people who were doing the killing. It was a weapon used by a small number of people, in secret, in countries far away, and the public was often not informed of the strikes until they were reported by the media. The drone was a weapon of the secret war, used by the CIA, an intelligence agency not subject to the same rules of transparency and accountability as the military. It raised questions about the accountability of the state, and it was used in a way that made those questions difficult to answer.

The drone was also used by other countries. The United Kingdom used drones in Afghanistan and Iraq and conducted its own drone strikes in Syria. Israel used drones to kill militants in Gaza and the West Bank and was one of the pioneers of the armed drone. Turkey used drones in Syria, Libya, and Nagorno-Karabakh and became one of the leading exporters of drones. China developed its own drones, including the CH-4 and the Wing Loong, and sold them to countries in the Middle East and Africa. Iran developed drones and used them to attack Saudi Arabia and to support its allies in Syria and Iraq. The drone was proliferating rapidly, and it was changing the balance of power in the Middle East and beyond.

The proliferation of the drone was a problem for the United States, because the drone had been one of its most important military advantages. The United States had used the drone to kill its enemies without risking its soldiers and to gather intelligence that no other country could gather. But the drone was no longer a technology unique to the United States, and the countries that had acquired it were using it in ways the United States could not control. It was spreading around the world and changing the character of war in ways not yet understood.

The drone was also changing the character of the battlefield. It made it possible to see the battlefield from above, in real time, and to direct fire onto targets that could not be seen from the ground. It made it possible to track the movement of enemy forces, identify their positions, and destroy them with precision. It allowed a small unit to call in fire from a distance, and a commander to see the battle as it unfolded. The drone was a tool of command and control, and it was changing the way battles were fought.

The drone was also changing the character of the soldier's experience. The soldier who fought with the support of a drone was never alone, because the drone was always overhead, watching and ready to strike. He could call in fire on a target a few hundred yards away without the delay that had always been part of calling for artillery or air support. The drone made the battlefield more lethal, because it made it possible to kill more quickly and more accurately, and more transparent, because it made it possible to see what the enemy was doing. It was changing the way soldiers fought, and the way they thought about war.

The drone was also changing the way wars were ended. It made it possible to kill the leaders of an enemy organization without invading its territory, and without the cost of a conventional military campaign. The drone was used to decapitate an enemy, remove its leaders, and disrupt its operations. It was a weapon of counterinsurgency, used to kill the people responsible for the violence. But it could also create new enemies, because the people killed by drones had families and friends who might seek revenge. The drone was both a solution and a problem, and it was changing the way wars were fought and ended.

The drone was also changing the way the public thought about war. It made it possible for a country to fight a war without the casualties that had always been part of war, and for the public to support a war without the sacrifice that had always been part of war. The drone was used by the United States in Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, Somalia, and Pakistan, and the public was largely unaware of the strikes conducted in its name. It made war invisible, and the cost of war invisible, and it made it possible for a country to fight a war without the public debate that had always been part of the decision to go to war. It was changing the relationship between the public and the war, and the way the public thought about the use of force.

The drone was also changing the way the law thought about war. It was used in countries that were not at war with the United States, and to kill people who were not on a battlefield. It challenged the traditional categories of the laws of war, which had been developed for a world of armies and battlefields and declarations of war. It was used in a world of non-state actors and failed states and permanent emergencies, and the law had not yet caught up with the technology. The drone was surrounded by legal uncertainty, and the uncertainty was a source of controversy and of danger.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the United States. It was used by the United States more than by any other country, and it was associated with the United States in the minds of people around the world. It killed people in countries that were poor and weak, and it was seen by many as a symbol of American arrogance and American power. It was used to kill Muslims in Muslim countries, by a country that was not Muslim, and the strikes were seen by many as a new kind of crusade. The drone was creating resentment and anger, and it was creating new enemies for the United States.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about technology. It had been developed for war and used to kill people, but it also had civilian applications. It was used for photography, agriculture, delivery, and inspection, and it was becoming part of everyday life. It was both a weapon and a tool, and the line between the two was not always clear. It was changing the way people thought about the sky, because the sky was no longer empty, and the way people thought about privacy, because the drone could see into places that had once been private. It was changing the world, and the way the world thought about technology.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the future. It was becoming more autonomous, more lethal, and more numerous, and it was likely to be a feature of every future conflict. It was being developed by many countries and used by non-state actors, and it was likely to be used in ways not yet imagined. It was changing the character of war, and the character of peace, because it made it possible to kill without war and to fight without a battlefield. It was changing the world, and the way the world thought about the future.

The history of the drone was a history of the way technology shaped strategy, and of the way strategy shaped technology. The drone had been developed to meet the needs of the wars the United States was fighting, and it had been shaped by those wars. It had been used to kill the leaders of al-Qaeda and the Taliban, and to support the troops fighting in Afghanistan and Iraq. It had been used to gather intelligence, track the enemy, and direct fire onto the enemy, in ways that had changed the character of the wars the United States was fighting. The drone was both a cause and a consequence of the wars of the twenty-first century, and it was changing the way wars were fought.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the human and the machine. It was a machine controlled by a human being, but also a machine capable of acting on its own. It could see and hear and sense, and it could be programmed to make decisions. It was becoming more intelligent and more autonomous, and the question of how much autonomy to give the machine went to the heart of the ethics of war. It was changing the way the world thought about the human, because it could do things that only humans had done before, and it raised the question of what it meant to be human in a world of intelligent machines.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the state and the individual. It was a weapon used by the state to kill individuals, without the consent of the individuals who were killed. It was used by the state to protect its citizens, and to kill people seen as a threat to the state. It was used in the name of security, in a way that raised questions about the balance between security and liberty. It was changing the way the world thought about the state, because it gave the state a power it had never had before, and it was being used in ways not yet fully understood.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the rich and the poor. It was developed by rich countries and used against poor countries, and it was seen by many as a tool of the strong against the weak. It was cheap enough to be acquired by poor countries and by non-state actors, and it was being used by the weak against the strong. It was changing the balance of power between the rich and the poor, and the way the world thought about that relationship.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the present and the future. It was being developed now, and it would be used in the future, and it raised questions that would have to be answered in the future. It was changing the world, and the way the world thought about the future, because it made the future seem both more dangerous and more uncertain.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the visible and the invisible. It could see things that could not be seen, and kill things that could not be seen. It was invisible to the people it was watching, and invisible to the people it was killing. It made war invisible, and it made the invisible visible, because it could see into places that had once been hidden. It was changing the way the world thought about the visible and the invisible, and the way the world thought about war.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the past and the present. It had been developed over a century, and it was the product of a long history of technological development. It was the culmination of the history of the extension of range, and of the separation of the weapon from the warrior. It was the product of the past, changing the present, and shaping the future. It was part of a long history, and it was changing the way the world thought about that history.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the human and the natural. It was a machine that flew in the sky, made of metal and plastic and silicon, and it was changing the sky. It was changing the way the world thought about the sky, because the sky was no longer empty, and the way the world thought about the natural world, because the natural world was now a place where machines could fly and watch and kill. It was changing the world, and the way the world thought about the natural world.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the relationship between the human and the divine. It was a machine that could see everything and kill anywhere, and it was seen by some people as a kind of god. It was omniscient and omnipotent, and it was changing the way the world thought about the divine, because it had attributes that had once been reserved for the gods. It was changing the world, and the way the world thought about the divine.
