paragraphs: The drone was also a weapon that was changing how the world thought about the relationship between human and machine. The drone was a machine controlled by a human being, but it was also a machine capable of acting on its own, and it was becoming more autonomous with every passing year. The pilot sat in a container in Nevada, the aircraft flew over Kandahar, and the signal traveled up to a satellite and down to the aircraft and back again; the whole loop took about 1.2 seconds. In that 1.2 seconds the machine was doing things no human being was doing, and the human being was doing things no machine was doing, and the question of where the human ended and the machine began was becoming one nobody could answer cleanly.

But to understand how that question became urgent, it helps to go back. Way back. The drone did not appear out of nowhere in the twenty-first century. It was the latest link in a chain that stretched back to the first time a human being picked up a rock and threw it at another human being, and the chain had a logic: every weapon humans have ever built has been an attempt to put distance between the person who kills and the person who is killed. The rock was the first distance. The spear was more distance. The arrow was more distance still. The bullet was more distance than the arrow. The artillery shell was more distance than the bullet. The bomber was more distance than the artillery shell. The drone was more distance than the bomber. And the autonomous weapon, if it ever truly arrived, would be the final distance—the distance of zero, the distance of no human being at all.

That is the argument of this book, and this part is where it starts to become concrete, where the abstractions of the previous parts begin to resolve into specific machines, specific decisions, specific people. Because the history of weapons is not a history of objects. It is a history of relationships. The relationship between the hand and the tool. Between the eye and the target. Between the person who gives the order and the person who carries it out. And, increasingly, between the human being and the machine that is doing the killing.

Consider the longbow. This is not a digression. The longbow is the perfect place to start, because the longbow proves the point. In 1545, Henry VIII's flagship *Mary Rose* sank in the Solent, and when she was raised in 1982, she gave up 137 longbows, and those bows told a story no chronicle could tell. The surviving bows have estimated draw weights of 100 to 185 pounds. That is not a weapon a casual user can pick up. That is a weapon that requires a lifetime of training, a lifetime of pulling a string that pulls back with the force of a grown man's body weight, and the skeletons of the archers who pulled those strings show the evidence in their bones. The shoulder joints are deformed. The left arm is thicker than the right. The fingers of the drawing hand are grooved. These were not soldiers who picked up a bow when the war started. These were men shaped by the bow from childhood, whose bodies had been remade by the weapon—remade in a way no other weapon had remade any other soldier before or since.

The longbow proves that a weapon is not just a tool. A weapon is a training regime. A weapon is a social system. A weapon is a way of organizing a society around the production of a certain kind of body. England could field longbowmen because England had organized its villages around the production of longbowmen, because the crown had passed statutes requiring archery practice, because the churchyards had butts where men practiced on Sundays, because the whole society had been bent toward creating a human being who could pull a 150-pound bow. The weapon was not the bow. The weapon was the society that made the bow possible.

And that is the first concrete lesson of this part. A weapon is never just a weapon. A weapon is always a system, and the system includes the people who make it, the people who use it, the people who train to use it, and the society that supports the whole arrangement. When we talk about the development of weapons, we are talking about the development of societies. When we talk about a new weapon changing the course of a war, we are talking about a new system changing the course of a society.

The longbow also proves something else, something that will matter more and more as this book goes on. The longbow was a weapon that could not be improved. It had reached the limit of what a bow could do. The wood could only be so strong. The arm could only pull so hard. The arrow could only fly so fast. There was no next step for the longbow, no way to make it better, and so the longbow was eventually replaced, not improved, by a weapon that came from a completely different direction. The gun.

And the gun came from China, and its arrival in Europe is one of the great hinge points of world history—a hinge point usually told badly, as a story of a single invention that changed everything overnight. The truth is slower and stranger and more interesting. The first gunpowder formulas appear in the Chinese military treatise *Wujing Zongyao*, compiled in 1044, and those formulas are not the formulas of a modern explosive. The nitrate content is low. The mixtures are designed to burn, to smoke, to frighten, to set things on fire, not to shatter walls. The earliest gunpowder weapons were incendiaries and smoke machines and fire-lances; they were weapons of psychology as much as physics, and they were used for centuries before anyone figured out how to make them go bang.

The shift from burning to exploding was slow, and it happened in stages, and each stage was a small revolution. The first stage was the discovery that a tighter mixture, with more saltpeter, would not just burn but detonate. The second was the discovery that a tube could contain the detonation and direct it. The third was the discovery that a projectile could be placed in the tube and driven out by the detonation. And the fourth stage—the one that matters most for this book—was the discovery that the whole thing could be made small enough and light enough for a single person to carry and fire.

The Heilongjiang hand cannon, dated by inscription to 1288, is one of the earliest surviving metal-barreled firearms. It is a small thing, a bronze tube a foot long, and it would not have been much use against a castle wall, but it changed the relationship between the person who held it and the person who was hit by it. Before the hand cannon, a soldier's reach was the length of his arm plus the length of his spear. After the hand cannon, a soldier's reach was the length of his arm plus the length of his weapon plus the distance the projectile could fly. The distance had grown. The distance would keep growing.

And here is the thing the longbow tells us, the thing the hand cannon confirms, the thing that will be true of every weapon in this book. When the distance grows, the relationship changes. The person who kills is further away from the person who is killed, and the further away the killer is, the easier it is to kill. This is not a moral observation. It is a mechanical one. It is a fact about human beings, and the history of weapons has been exploiting it for ten thousand years.

There is a famous experiment in psychology, usually told as a story about obedience, but it is also a story about distance. In the 1960s, Stanley Milgram brought ordinary people into a laboratory and asked them to administer electric shocks to a stranger. He found that most of them would do it, and that the ones who would do it most readily were the ones who could not see the person they were shocking. The ones who had to hold the person's hand down on the plate were the ones who refused. The distance made the difference. The distance is always what makes the difference.

The history of weapons is the history of increasing that distance. The club was zero distance. The spear was a few feet. The bow was a hundred yards. The musket was a few hundred yards. The rifle was a thousand yards. The artillery piece was miles. The bomber was thousands of miles. The drone was anywhere on Earth. And at each step, the same thing happened. The killer became more efficient, because the killer was less troubled, because the killer was further away. This is not a comfortable thing to say. But it is true, and it is the engine of the whole story.

Now consider the Minié ball, and consider what it did to the American Civil War, and what it tells us about the relationship between a weapon and the war it makes. Claude-Étienne Minié was a French army officer, and in 1849 he solved a problem that had bedeviled gunners for centuries. A round ball fired from a smoothbore musket was inaccurate and short-ranged, but it could be loaded quickly. A ball fired from a rifled barrel was accurate and long-ranged, but it had to be hammered down the barrel, which took time, which meant rifled muskets could not be used by infantry in the field. Minié's solution was a bullet with a hollow base. The bullet was small enough to slide down the barrel easily, but when the powder exploded, the base expanded and gripped the rifling, and the bullet spun, and the spin made it accurate, and the accuracy made it deadly.

The Minié ball was used in the British Pattern 1853 Enfield and the U.S. Springfield Model 1861, and it changed the calculus of the battlefield. A soldier with a rifled musket could hit a man at 500 yards, where a soldier with a smoothbore could barely hit a man at 100. The effective range of the infantryman had multiplied by five, and the tactics of the age had not caught up. The generals of the Civil War had learned their trade in the age of the smoothbore, and they still believed in the massed charge, in the close-order line, in the idea that men could be marched into the open and expected to survive. The Minié ball made those ideas obsolete, and the generals did not know it, and the men paid the price.

The casualty figures of the Civil War are usually explained by the size of the armies, by the length of the war, by the disease that killed more men than the bullets did. But the Minié ball deserves its share. At Antietam, at Gettysburg, at Cold Harbor, men were ordered to charge across open ground into the fire of rifled muskets, and the rifled muskets reached them long before they reached the enemy line, and the result was slaughter on a scale the American continent had never seen. The weapon had changed, and the tactics had not, and the gap between them was filled with bodies.

This is a pattern that will repeat. It is one of the great patterns of military history, and it is worth naming clearly here, because it will recur in every part of this book. A new weapon arrives, and the tactics do not change, and the men die, and then the tactics change, and the men die less, and then a new weapon arrives, and the cycle begins again. The lag between the weapon and the tactics is where the killing happens. The lag is the thing the generals never see, because the generals are trained in the last war, and the last war was fought with the last weapon.

The machine gun is the next step in the chain, and the machine gun is the weapon that made the lag unbearable. Hiram Maxim was an American inventor who had moved to England, and in 1884 he demonstrated a gun that used the recoil of the cartridge to reload itself. The gun could fire six hundred rounds a minute; it was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun and a template for everything that came after. The British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891, and the gun went to Africa and to India and to the Sudan, and it did its work with a terrible efficiency, and the men who saw it called it the devil's paintbrush, and the name was not entirely a joke.

The Maxim was not the first machine gun. There had been hand-cranked guns before—the Gatling, the Gardner, the Nordenfelt—and they had been used in the American Civil War and the Franco-Prussian War, but they were cranky and unreliable and required a crew to turn the crank, and they were never quite decisive. The Maxim was different. The Maxim was self-powered. It did not need a man to turn a crank. It needed only a man to hold the trigger, and the trigger was light, and the gun did the rest. It was the first weapon that could kill without a human being doing the work of killing, and the men who faced it understood this, and they feared it in a way they did not fear the rifle.

The Maxim was used at Omdurman in 1898, where Kitchener's army faced the Mahdist forces outside Khartoum, and the result was not a battle but a massacre. The Mahdists charged, and the Maxims fired, and the Maxims fired, and the Maxims fired, and when it was over, the Mahdists had lost ten thousand men and the British had lost less than fifty. The battle was a demonstration, and the demonstration was not lost on the military men of Europe. They took note, and the note they took was this: the machine gun is the weapon of the future, and the future will be a place where the men who have machine guns will kill the men who do not, and the killing will be quick and it will be total.

And yet. And yet when the First World War began in 1914, the armies of Europe went to war with tactics designed for the rifle and the bayonet, and they went to war against machine guns, and the result was the trenches. The trenches were the answer to the machine gun, and the trenches were not a strategy, they were a reflex, they were what happened when men discovered they could not cross the open ground, and so they dug in, and the war became a war of position, and the position was held by the machine gun.

The First World War is the war where the lag between weapon and tactics became visible to everyone, where the gap was measured in millions of bodies. It is the central event of the modern history of weapons and deserves the care such an event deserves. But before we get to the war, we need to understand the weapon that made the war what it was, and the weapon was not the machine gun alone. The weapon was the artillery piece, and the artillery piece dominated the battlefield, and the artillery piece turned the war into a war of production.

The Canon de 75 modèle 1897 is the artillery piece that changed everything, and it changed everything because of a single innovation: the recoil system. Before the French 75, an artillery piece had to be re-aimed after every shot, because the recoil threw the carriage back, and the crew had to push the gun back into position and re-lay it on the target, and the whole process took time. The French 75 used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady, so the gun did not move when it fired, did not have to be re-aimed, and could fire as fast as the crew could feed it—about fifteen rounds a minute. Fifteen rounds a minute. The gun was a machine that could throw a high-explosive shell three miles, fifteen times a minute, and the shell was fused to burst on contact or in the air, and the shell was filled with shrapnel that could kill a man at a hundred yards. It was the most lethal weapon that had ever been fielded, and the French knew it, and the French built thousands of them.

The French 75 was a secret weapon, and the secret was the recoil system, and the secret did not stay secret for long. By 1914 every army in Europe had a quick-firing field gun, and the quick-firing field gun made the battlefield a place where men could not stand in the open. The field gun could fire over the horizon, at a rate no infantryman could match, and kill from a distance no infantryman could see. It was the weapon that made the trenches necessary, because the trenches were the only place a man could be safe from the field gun—and even the trenches were not safe, because the field gun could be elevated and the shell dropped into the trench, and the trench became a place where men lived and died in the mud.

And then there was Verdun. The Battle of Verdun ran from the 21st of February to the 18th of December 1916, and it produced roughly seven hundred thousand casualties. It was a battle fought not for territory but for the sake of killing, and the killing was done by artillery. The German plan was to bleed the French army white, to attack a place the French would have to defend, and to destroy the French army with artillery. The plan was the plan of a man named Erich von Falkenhayn, and it was almost successful, and the almost is the thing that matters, because the French did defend Verdun, and the French did not break, and the battle became a battle of attrition, and the attrition was measured in shells.

At Verdun, the artillery fired more than twenty million shells, and the shells were made in factories, and the factories were the real battlefield, and the war became a war of production, and the nation that could make the most shells would win. The shell production of France and Germany and Britain and Russia and Austria-Hungary became the central fact of the war, and the governments of Europe took control of their economies, and they built factories, and they hired women, and they ran the factories day and night, and the shells came out of the factories and went to the front and were fired at the enemy, and the enemy fired back, and the shells fell, and the men died, and the war went on.

This is the moment in the history of weapons when the weapon becomes an industrial product, and the industrial product becomes the thing that decides the war, and the soldier becomes a small part of a vast machine. The soldier at Verdun was not a warrior in the old sense. He was a component in a system—a system of production and logistics and transportation and communication—and the soldier's job was to hold a piece of ground while the system did its work, and the system did its work with shells, and the shells were the real weapon of the war.

And here is the thing that connects Verdun to the drone, the thing that makes the whole history a single story. The system at Verdun was a system of distance. The gunner who fired the shell at Verdun never saw the man he killed. The gunner was miles away, and the shell was fired at a map coordinate, and the man who died was a dot on a map, and the distance between the gunner and the man was the thing that made the killing possible. The drone is the same thing, pushed further. The drone pilot never sees the man he kills either, or sees him only as a shape on a screen, and the distance is the thing that makes the killing possible, and the distance is the thing the history of weapons has been increasing for ten thousand years.

But the First World War also produced the weapon that would make the distance absolute: the airplane. The airplane could fly over the trenches and drop bombs on the factories and the cities behind them, and the airplane would eventually become the bomber, and the bomber would eventually become the drone. The airplane was not a very effective weapon in 1914. The airplanes of 1914 were fragile things of wood and canvas, and they carried a few small bombs, and they were used mostly for reconnaissance, and the reconnaissance was valuable, and the reconnaissance was the thing the airplanes did best. But the airplanes of 1914 were the ancestors of the bombers of 1945, and the bombers of 1945 were the ancestors of the drones of 2001, and the line is straight, and the line is the line of distance.

The airplane made the third dimension of war, and the third dimension changed everything, because the third dimension was a place where the enemy could not reach, and a place from which the enemy could be reached, and the place where the war would be decided. The airplane made the home front a battlefield, and the home front was where the factories were, and the factories were the thing that decided the war, and so the airplane made the factories a target, and the bombing of factories became the strategy of the Second World War.

And the Second World War is the war where the bomber became the weapon of terror, and the bombing of cities became a strategy, and the strategy was called strategic bombing, and the strategic bombing of Germany and Japan killed hundreds of thousands of civilians, and the killing was done from a distance of thousands of miles, and the men who did the killing were young men in bombers, and they were not monsters, they were boys from farms and cities, and they did what they were told, and the distance made it possible.

The bomber also made the Holocaust possible, in a way, because the Holocaust was an industrial killing, and the industrial killing was done in factories, and the factories were the death camps, and the death camps were the logical extension of the industrial system the war had created. The gas chamber was a machine, and the machine was designed by engineers, and the engineers were the same kind of men who designed the bombers, and the distance between the designer and the victim was the thing that made the design possible. This is a hard thing to say, but it is true, and it is part of the history of weapons, and it cannot be left out.

And then there was the bomb. On the 16th of July 1945, at a place called Trinity in the New Mexico desert, a plutonium implosion device called Gadget was detonated, and the yield was about twenty-one kilotons, and the bomb was the most powerful weapon that had ever been built, and the bomb was the weapon that ended the Second World War and began the Cold War, and the bomb changed the relationship between the human being and the weapon forever. The bomb was a weapon that could not be used without killing everyone, and the bomb was therefore not used, and the not-using became the strategy, and the strategy was called deterrence, and deterrence was the idea that the weapon was so terrible it would never be used, and the idea worked, mostly, and the world lived under the shadow of the bomb for forty years, and the shadow is still there.

The bomb is the weapon that proves the history of weapons is not a history of progress. The bomb made the world more dangerous, not less; it made the great powers cautious, not bold; it changed the relationship between the weapon and the war in a way no weapon had ever changed it before. Before the bomb, a weapon was a thing you used to win a war. After the bomb, a weapon was a thing you did not use, because using it would mean losing everything. The bomb made the weapon obsolete, and the bomb made the weapon permanent, and the paradox is the thing the nuclear age has never resolved.

The NPT is the treaty that tried to resolve the paradox. The NPT opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, and it has 191 states parties, and it is the most widely adhered-to arms control agreement in history, and it is also a treaty India and Israel and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. It has not stopped the spread of nuclear weapons, but it has slowed it, and the slowing is the thing that matters, because the slowing is the difference between a world with nine nuclear powers and a world with ninety.

But the bomb is not the end of the story, and the bomb is not the weapon this part is about. The bomb is the background against which the weapons of the late twentieth century were developed, and the weapons of the late twentieth century were the weapons of precision, and the weapons of precision made the distance precise, and the precision was the thing that changed the war.

The precision-guided munition is the weapon that made the distance smart. The PGM is a bomb or a missile that can be steered to a target, by laser or satellite or camera, and the steering means the weapon hits what it is aimed at, and the hitting-what-it-is-aimed-at changes everything, because a weapon that hits what it is aimed at can be used in places where a weapon that hits whatever it happens to hit cannot. The PGM made it possible to bomb a city and kill only the people in one building, and that possibility made the bombing of cities acceptable again, and that acceptability made the wars of the twenty-first century possible.

In 1991, in the war the Americans called Desert Storm, the coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, and about 6,520 tons of those bombs were precision-guided, and 6,520 tons is about 7.4 percent of the total, and 7.4 percent is a small share, and the small share is the thing that matters, because the small share did most of the work. The PGMs struck the high-value targets—the command bunkers and the bridges and the air defense sites and the tanks—and the strikes were shown on television, and the television showed the bombs going down the chimneys and through the doors, and the pictures changed the way the world thought about air power, and the pictures changed the way the world thought about war.

The pictures from Desert Storm were the pictures of a clean war, a war where the bombs hit only the bad things, a war where the good guys won and the bad guys lost and the civilians were not hurt. The pictures were not the whole truth, and the whole truth was messier, and the messiness would become visible in the years that followed, but the pictures were the thing the world remembered, and the pictures were the thing the militaries of the world tried to reproduce, and the reproduction became the goal of a generation of weapons development.

The PGM is the weapon that made the distance moral, or at least made it seem moral, and the seeming is the thing that matters, because the seeming is the thing the publics of the democratic world demanded. Those publics would not tolerate a war that killed civilians by the thousands, and they would tolerate a war that killed civilians by the dozens, and the difference between the thousands and the dozens was the difference between the dumb bomb and the smart bomb, and the smart bomb became the weapon that made the war tolerable, and the tolerability was the thing that made the war possible.

And the drone is the smart bomb's child. The drone combines the precision of the PGM with the persistence of the airplane and the distance of the missile. It can loiter over a target for hours, and the loitering is what makes the drone different, because the loitering means the drone can wait for the right moment, and the waiting means the drone can strike when the target is alone, when the target is in a car, when the target is walking across a courtyard, and the striking-when-the-target-is-alone keeps civilian casualties low, and the low civilian casualties are what make the drone war politically sustainable.

The drone war is the war the United States fought in Pakistan and Yemen and Somalia and Afghanistan and Iraq and Syria and Libya, and the drone war was fought largely in secret, and the secrecy made the war possible, because the publics of the democratic world would not have tolerated a war fought openly in countries the United States was not at war with, and the secrecy allowed the war to go on, and the war went on for years, and the war killed thousands of people, and the killing was done by machines flown by pilots who sat in air-conditioned containers in Nevada and California and North Dakota.

The drone pilots are the soldiers of the new war, and they are the soldiers who go home to their families every night, and the going-home is what makes the drone war different from every war that came before, because the soldiers of the drone war are not in danger, and the not-being-in-danger changes the psychology of the soldier, and the psychology of the soldier changes the war. The drone pilot fights a war and then drives home and has dinner with his children; he kills a man in the morning and coaches a soccer game in the afternoon; he is not a soldier in the old sense, and he is the soldier of the future.

And the drone pilots have their own kind of trauma, which the military did not expect. It is called moral injury, and it is what happens when a person kills and is not in danger, when a person kills and then goes home, when a person kills and cannot stop thinking about the killing. The drone pilots have higher rates of certain kinds of psychological problems than pilots who fly manned aircraft, and the higher rates are what the military has had to learn to deal with, and the dealing-with has changed the way the military thinks about the drone war.

The drone is the weapon that made the distance psychological, and the psychological distance is what the history of weapons has been building toward, and the psychological distance is what the autonomous weapon would complete. The autonomous weapon would remove the human being from the loop entirely, and the removal would be the final distance, and the final distance is what the world is arguing about now.

The argument about autonomous weapons is the argument about whether a machine can be trusted to kill, and it is not a new argument; it is as old as the first trap, the first snare, the first pit with spikes at the bottom. A trap is an autonomous weapon. A trap is a machine that kills without a human being present, and the trap is the weapon the hunter sets and leaves, and the trap is the weapon that kills whoever walks into it, and the trap is the weapon the history of weapons has been trying to build better for ten thousand years.

The landmine is the trap's descendant, and the landmine is the autonomous weapon the world has already banned, and the ban is the Ottawa Treaty, and the Ottawa Treaty was signed in 1997 and has been signed by more than 160 countries, and the United States has not signed it, and the United States has not signed it because the United States believes landmines are necessary for the defense of South Korea, and the necessity is what the argument about autonomous weapons will have to confront, because the necessity is always what the argument about weapons has to confront.

The loitering munition is the landmine's smart descendant, and the loitering munition is a drone that carries a warhead and can circle over a target and then dive into it, and the loitering munition is the weapon the Azerbaijanis used in the Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020, and the war of 2020 is the war that showed the world what the drone can do. In the forty-four-day war, Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor and artillery and air defenses, and the drones destroyed the Armenian tanks and the Armenian guns and the Armenian air defense systems, and the destruction won the war, and the war changed the way the world thought about drones.

The RUSI study of the Nagorno-Karabakh war, published in 2021, treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and suppression of air defense, and the study was right, and the landmark is what the militaries of the world have been studying ever since. The war showed that a country with a modest air force and a lot of drones could defeat a country with a larger army and a lot of tanks, and the showing made every army in the world rethink its procurement, and the rethinking is still going on.

And the war also showed the limits of the drone, because the drones in Nagorno-Karabakh were effective against a poorly prepared enemy, and they would have been less effective against an enemy with modern air defenses, and the lesson of the war is not that the drone wins wars but that the drone changes the terms of the war, and the changing of the terms is the thing that matters.

And then there is the autonomous weapon, the weapon that would decide for itself, and the autonomous weapon is what the world is arguing about, and the argument is the argument about the Kargu-2, and the Kargu-2 is a Turkish loitering munition, and the Kargu-2 was the subject of a report by the United Nations Panel of Experts on Libya, issued in 2021, and the report said that the Kargu-2 "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces, and the "may have been" is the thing that matters, because it is not a confirmation, and the claim remains contested, and the claim has not been independently confirmed, and the claim should be treated with caution.

But the claim is the thing the world has been waiting for, the thing the world has been fearing, the thing the world has been arguing about for years, and the claim is what makes the argument about autonomous weapons urgent, because if the claim is true, then the world has already crossed the line, and the line was crossed in Libya, in 2020, in a war most people did not notice, and the crossing was done by a machine that decided for itself.

The autonomous weapon would complete the history of distance, and the completion is what the world is trying to prevent, and the prevention is what the campaign to stop killer robots is about, and the campaign is a campaign of nongovernmental organizations and academics and diplomats, and the campaign has been going on since 2013, and the campaign has not stopped the development of autonomous weapons, and the development has continued, and the weapons have been deployed, and the deployment has been quiet, and the quiet is what the campaign is trying to break.

The argument against autonomous weapons is the argument about accountability, and accountability is what the laws of war require, and the laws of war require that a human being be responsible for every killing, and the autonomous weapon would remove the human being, and the removal would remove the accountability, and the removal of accountability is what the campaign is fighting against. The argument is a good argument, and a strong argument, and it has not yet won, and the not-yet-winning is what the history of weapons would predict, because the history of weapons is the history of arguments that were lost.

But the argument about autonomous weapons is not the end of the story, and the story is not over, and the story is the story of the relationship between the human being and the weapon, and the relationship is changing, and the change is what this book is about. The change is what the drone represents, and the drone is the weapon that made the change visible, and the change is the change from the weapon as a tool to the weapon as a system to the weapon as an agent.

The weapon as a tool is the club and the spear and the bow. The weapon as a tool is an extension of the human body, and the human being is in control, and the human being is responsible, and the human being is present. The weapon as a system is the artillery piece and the bomber and the aircraft carrier. The weapon as a system is a machine that requires a vast organization to build and maintain and use, and the human being is a component of the system, and the human being is responsible but the responsibility is diffuse, and the human being is present but the presence is distant. The weapon as an agent is the drone and the autonomous weapon and the algorithm. The weapon as an agent is a machine that makes decisions, and the human being is a supervisor, and the human being is responsible but the responsibility is unclear, and the human being is present but the presence is optional.

The shift from tool to system to agent is the shift this part has been tracing, and the shift is what the history of weapons has been building toward, and the shift is not finished, and the shift is what the future will be about. The drone is the weapon that made the shift visible, and the drone is the weapon the world is still learning to live with, and the learning is what the twenty-first century is about.

And the learning is hard, because the drone is a weapon that is easy to use, and the ease is what makes it dangerous. A weapon that is easy to use is a weapon that will be used, and the drone is easy to use, and the drone is cheap, and the drone is

paragraphs: The ease began with the price. In 2020, a Bayraktar TB2 cost roughly one to two million dollars, depending on configuration and buyer. A modern main battle tank cost five to ten million. A fourth-generation fighter cost sixty to a hundred million, and a single hour of flying one could cost tens of thousands of dollars in fuel and maintenance. The arithmetic was not subtle. A nation that could not afford an air force could afford a drone fleet, and a nation that could not afford a tank could afford the thing that killed tanks. The arithmetic began the shift and made it irreversible.

In the autumn of 2020, the arithmetic was tested in the South Caucasus, in a war that lasted forty-four days and that much of the world watched on social media. The war was fought over Nagorno-Karabakh, a mountainous enclave that had been the subject of a frozen conflict since the early 1990s, by Azerbaijan against Armenia and the self-declared Republic of Artsakh. It was not a great-power war, nor a war between advanced industrial states, but a war between two small nations with limited industrial bases and limited access to the most advanced weapons. And it was arguably the first war in which the drone was the defining weapon—arguably, because the criterion is decisive effect on the outcome of a conventional interstate campaign, and on that criterion the claim holds; on broader criteria, the American drone campaigns of the 2000s have a prior claim. It was a war the rest of the world studied, and is still studying.

The Azerbaijani armed forces had spent the years before the war building a drone capability that was, by regional standards, substantial. Its core was the Turkish Bayraktar TB2, a medium-altitude, long-endurance unmanned combat aerial vehicle developed by the Turkish company Baykar and in service with the Turkish armed forces since the mid-2010s. The TB2 was not stealthy, not fast, and—by the standards of the American and Israeli drones that had dominated the previous two decades—not particularly sophisticated. It had a maximum speed of about 220 kilometers per hour, a service ceiling of about 8,200 meters, an endurance of about twenty-seven hours, and a payload of about 150 kilograms. The payload was the point. The TB2 could carry four MAM-L precision-guided munitions, each weighing about twenty-two kilograms, each with a range of about fourteen kilometers, each capable of being guided to a target by a laser designator the drone itself carried. It could loiter above a battlefield, find a target, designate it, and destroy it—without exposing a pilot to risk and without the infrastructure a manned aircraft required.

The TB2 was not the only drone in the Azerbaijani inventory. Azerbaijani forces also used Israeli loitering munitions, including the IAI Harop and the SkyStriker, Turkish loitering munitions, and a range of smaller reconnaissance drones that fed targeting information to artillery and to the larger armed drones. This was not the inventory of a great power, nor of a nation that had spent decades building a military-industrial complex. It was the inventory of a nation that had identified a gap in the market and filled it—the gap between the cost of a modern air force and the cost a middle-income nation could bear.

The Armenian forces had a different inventory. The Armenian military had invested heavily in air defense, armor, artillery, and the fortifications that had defined the previous war in the region. Its air defense inventory included the S-300PS, a long-range surface-to-air missile system developed in the Soviet Union in the 1980s and, by 2020, capable but aging. It also included shorter-range systems, including the Tor-M2KM and the Osa-AKM, a range of man-portable air-defense systems, and electronic warfare equipment meant to degrade the guidance of precision munitions. On paper, this was a credible air defense network—the kind that would make a drone campaign expensive.

The war began on 27 September 2020 with a barrage of artillery and rocket fire that, in its intensity, departed from the skirmishes of previous decades. Azerbaijani forces advanced along multiple axes, using drones to suppress Armenian air defenses, destroy Armenian armor, and break the Armenian fortifications built over the previous quarter-century. The drones did not do everything, and they were not invincible, but they were the thing that made the other things possible.

The suppression of enemy air defenses came first, and it worked by attacking the parts of the network rather than the network itself. The Armenian S-300 systems were the most capable air defense systems in the Armenian inventory and would have made Azerbaijani drone operations expensive if they could have engaged the drones effectively. Azerbaijani forces used a combination of tactics against them: loitering munitions to attack the radars the S-300s depended on, decoys to draw them into firing, and electronic warfare to degrade the command-and-control links connecting them to the rest of the Armenian air defense network. They also used TB2s to attack S-300 launchers and associated radar vehicles when located, and to attack the shorter-range systems that filled gaps in S-300 coverage.

The destruction of the Armenian air defenses was not complete, not quick, and the result of a campaign that lasted for days and required the coordination of multiple systems. But it was sufficient to allow Azerbaijani drones to operate over the battlefield with a degree of freedom the Armenian forces had not anticipated—and it was the precondition for everything that followed.

Against armor, the mechanism was geometry. The Armenian forces had, by regional standards, a substantial armored force, deployed in fortified positions built over the previous decades. Many Armenian tanks were dug in, protected by earthworks and terrain—the product of a century of development in which the tank had been optimized for a battlefield where the primary threats were other tanks and anti-tank guns. A TB2 could loiter above the battlefield at an altitude above the effective range of many Armenian short-range air defense systems, use its electro-optical and infrared sensors to find a dug-in tank, and guide a MAM-L onto the top of the tank, where the armor was thinnest. The MAM-L was not a large munition and did not always destroy a tank with a single hit, but it was a precision-guided munition small enough to be carried in numbers and cheap enough to be used in numbers. It was accurate, it was fired from a platform the tank could not see or hit, and it made the dug-in tank a liability rather than an asset.

The videos the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense released in the weeks after the war began showed the pattern. A tank would be visible in the center of the frame, stationary, in a revetment or behind a berm. The crosshairs of the drone's camera would settle on it. The tank would explode. The camera would linger on the wreckage, then move on to the next target. The videos were propaganda—edited to emphasize the effectiveness of the drones and released to shape the perceptions of the international audience watching the war on social media. But they were also a record of a real change in the character of the battlefield, a change the Armenian forces could not counter, and one the rest of the world would have to reckon with.

Against artillery, the mechanism was time. The Armenian forces had, by regional standards, a substantial artillery force, deployed in the fortified positions built over the previous decades—the product of a century of development in which artillery had been optimized for a battlefield where the primary threats were counter-battery fire and air attack. A TB2 could find an artillery piece concealed in a revetment or under camouflage and guide a MAM-L onto it in minutes rather than the hours a counter-battery campaign would have required. Artillery, king of the battlefield in the First World War and queen in the decades that followed, became in the face of the drone a target that could be found and destroyed with a speed it could not match.

Against supply lines, the mechanism was accumulation. Azerbaijani forces used drones to attack the trucks, fuel tankers, and ammunition carriers moving along the roads connecting Armenian positions to the rear; to attack the bridges and culverts those supply lines depended on; and to attack convoys moving at night. No single strike was decisive. In cumulative effect, these attacks were as important as those on armor and artillery, because they made it impossible for the Armenian forces to sustain the defense, to replace the equipment the drones had destroyed, and to feed, fuel, and resupply the soldiers holding the line.

The Armenian response was shaped by the assumptions of the previous era. The Armenian forces had invested in air defense systems designed to engage aircraft that flew at high altitude and high speed, aircraft large enough to be detected by radar at long range, aircraft expensive enough to make the exchange ratio favorable. The TB2s were none of these things. They flew low and slow, were small enough to be difficult to detect, and were cheap enough that the exchange ratio favored the attacker. Armenian air defense systems could, in principle, engage the TB2s; in some cases they did, and in some cases they shot them down. But they were not designed for the threat the TB2s represented, were not deployed in the numbers required to cover the entire battlefield, and were not connected by a command-and-control network that could have coordinated the defense against the drones.

The Armenian forces also attempted to use electronic warfare. They had, by regional standards, a substantial capability and had invested in systems designed to jam the GPS signals the drones used for navigation and the command links they used for control. The Azerbaijani TB2s were in some respects vulnerable: they used a line-of-sight data link that could be jammed and GPS navigation that could be spoofed, and—by the standards of the American and Israeli drones that had dominated the previous two decades—they were not hardened against electronic attack. But the Azerbaijani forces had anticipated the threat, developed tactics to mitigate it, and used the drones in ways that minimized exposure to jamming. They also used loitering munitions, autonomous in their terminal phase and not dependent on a command link once launched, to attack the electronic warfare systems themselves, and used TB2s to attack those systems when located.

The Armenian forces also attempted to use their own drones to counter Azerbaijani drones, attack Azerbaijani forces, and provide reconnaissance for their artillery. The Armenian drone capability was, by regional standards, smaller than the Azerbaijani one—the capability of a nation that had not invested in the drone revolution to the same degree as its adversary. The Armenian forces did use drones, did achieve some successes with them, and did shoot down some Azerbaijani drones. But their drone capability was not sufficient to change the character of the war, to counter the Azerbaijani drone campaign, or to give the Armenian forces the situational awareness the Azerbaijani forces had.

The war ended on 10 November 2020 with a ceasefire agreement brokered by Russia that was, in its terms, a victory for Azerbaijan. It required Armenia to withdraw from the districts around Nagorno-Karabakh under Armenian control since the early 1990s, accept a Russian peacekeeping presence in the region, and accept a corridor connecting Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenia controlled by Russian peacekeepers. The agreement was a humiliation for Armenia, a demonstration of the limits of the Armenian military, and a demonstration of the effectiveness of the Azerbaijani drone campaign.

The war was not the first in which drones had been used, in which they had been effective, or in which they had changed the character of a battlefield. The American drone campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban in Afghanistan and Pakistan, begun in the early 2000s, had demonstrated that a drone could find and kill a target with a precision impossible in the previous era, and do so without exposing a pilot to risk. Israeli drone campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon had demonstrated that a drone could be integrated into a combined-arms campaign—used to suppress air defenses, destroy armor, and provide real-time intelligence to ground forces. British and French drone campaigns in Libya, Mali, Iraq, and Syria had demonstrated that a drone could be used across a range of environments and operated by a nation without the resources of the United States.

But the Nagorno-Karabakh war was different. It was arguably the first war in which drones were the decisive weapon in a conflict between two nations with substantial military forces, arguably the first in which drones were used at scale against a modern air defense network, and arguably the first in which their effectiveness was visible to the entire world in near real time. The criterion is decisive effect on the outcome of a conventional interstate campaign; by that criterion the claims hold, though scholars continue to debate how much of the Azerbaijani victory to attribute to the drones themselves. The war was a demonstration—one the rest of the world studied, and is still studying.

The most detailed public study appeared in 2021: "The Air and Missile War in Nagorno-Karabakh: Lessons for the Future of Strike and Defense," published by the Royal United Services Institute, based on interviews with participants and on analysis of the videos and data the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense had released. Its central finding was that Azerbaijani forces had used drones to achieve a degree of battlefield awareness the Armenian forces could not match, and that the combination of drones, loitering munitions, and electronic warfare had suppressed Armenian air defenses and destroyed Armenian armor, artillery, and supply lines faster than the Armenian forces could adapt or replace their losses. The drones had not made the tank, the artillery, or the air defense obsolete. They had made all three more expensive to use, more vulnerable to attack, and more dependent on the systems that could counter the drones.

The shift the study described was from the weapon as an object to the weapon as a system, from the weapon as a thing a soldier carried to a thing a network controlled, from the weapon as a tool to the weapon as an agent. The drone made the shift visible, and the world is still learning to live with it.

The learning was not confined to analysts. The militaries of the world were doing it, the defense budgets of the world were reflecting it, and the procurement decisions of the world were shaped by it. In the years after the Nagorno-Karabakh war, nations began to invest in drones and counter-drone systems at a scale not seen before, develop doctrines for the use of drones and defense against them, and reorganize their forces to accommodate the drone.

The United States, pioneer of the armed drone, found itself in an awkward position. The American drone fleet was, by world standards, the most capable in existence, including the MQ-9 Reaper, the RQ-4 Global Hawk, the MQ-1C Gray Eagle, and a range of smaller systems. But it was also expensive, optimized for the counterinsurgency campaigns of the previous two decades rather than the kind of high-intensity conflict the Nagorno-Karabakh war had demonstrated. The MQ-9 Reaper cost about thirty million dollars per aircraft, was vulnerable to the kind of air defense systems a peer adversary would deploy, and was not the kind of system that could be lost in large numbers. The American military began to invest in cheaper, more attritable systems, develop concepts for operating in an environment where the air was contested, and study the lessons of the Nagorno-Karabakh war with an intensity that reflected the stakes.

The Chinese military, which had been investing in drones for two decades, found itself in a stronger position. The Chinese drone industry had produced a range of systems that were, by world standards, capable and affordable, exported them to a range of nations, and developed the kind of loitering munitions used in the Nagorno-Karabakh war. The Chinese military had also invested in counter-drone systems, developed the kind of integrated air defense networks required to defend against a drone campaign, and studied the Nagorno-Karabakh war as a preview of the kind of conflict it might face in a confrontation with the United States and its allies.

The Turkish defense industry, which had produced the TB2, found itself in a position it had not occupied before. The TB2 had been exported to a range of nations, including Azerbaijan, Ukraine, Libya, Qatar, and Morocco; used in conflicts in Libya, Ukraine, and Nagorno-Karabakh; and acquired a reputation disproportionate to its capabilities. The Turkish defense industry had also developed other systems, including the Akinci, a larger and more capable drone that entered service in 2021, and the kind of loitering munitions used in the Nagorno-Karabakh war. It had become a significant player in the global arms market—and a demonstration that the drone revolution was not confined to the great powers.

The Russian military, which had supplied the Armenian air defense systems that failed in the Nagorno-Karabakh war, found itself in an uncomfortable position. It had invested heavily in air defense, developed some of the most capable air defense systems in the world, and exported them to a range of nations, including Armenia. The failure of the Armenian air defense systems was a failure of the Russian systems—a blow to the reputation of the Russian defense industry that the Russian military had to reckon with. It began to invest in counter-drone systems, develop electronic warfare systems that could degrade the guidance of drones, and study the lessons of the Nagorno-Karabakh war with an intensity that reflected the stakes.

The lessons were not confined to the great powers. The smaller nations of the world were learning them, applying them, and shaping the conflicts that followed. In the years after the war, nations began to acquire drones at a scale not seen before and to use them in conflicts ranging from Ukraine to Ethiopia to Yemen to Gaza. The drone had become a commodity in the global arms market—and the commodity made the shift irreversible, and dangerous.

The war in Ukraine, which began with the Russian invasion in February 2022, was arguably the first war in which the drone became the defining weapon of a large-scale conventional conflict—again by the criterion of decisive effect, and again with the caveat that artillery and infantry decided far more of the outcome than any single system. Ukrainian forces used Turkish TB2s to attack the Russian columns advancing on Kyiv in the first weeks of the war, destroying Russian armor, artillery, and supply trucks and slowing the Russian advance. Russian forces used their own drones, including the Orlan-10 reconnaissance drone and the Lancet loitering munition, to find and destroy Ukrainian armor and artillery and to direct artillery fire. The war became a laboratory for the drone—one the rest of the world studied, and is still studying.

Ukrainian forces also used small, commercial drones not designed for military use, providing reconnaissance and dropping small munitions on Russian positions in numbers not seen before. These drones were cheap, easy to acquire, and easy to operate—the thing that made the drone revolution accessible to a nation without a large defense industry. Ukrainian forces also used the kind of loitering munitions used in the Nagorno-Karabakh war, attacking Russian air defenses, armor, and command posts.

Russian forces also used loitering munitions, including the Lancet, to attack Ukrainian artillery, air defenses, and command posts. The Lancet was small, cheap, and the kind of system that could be produced in large numbers and used in the attritional campaign the war had become. Russian forces also used the Shahed-136, an Iranian-designed loitering munition, to attack Ukrainian infrastructure and cities; it was cheap, simple, and the kind of system that could be produced in large numbers and used in the kind of campaign the war had become.

The war in Ukraine demonstrated the limits of the drone. Drones were not invincible, not a substitute for the other systems of war, and not a thing that could win a war on their own. Russian forces developed counter-drone tactics, deployed electronic warfare systems that degraded the guidance of Ukrainian drones, deployed air defense systems that shot them down, and deployed jamming that made them ineffective. Ukrainian forces developed their own counter-drone tactics, deployed air defense systems that could shoot down Russian drones, and deployed electronic warfare systems that could degrade their guidance. The war became a contest between the drone and the counter-drone—one the rest of the world studied, and is still studying.

The contest was also the thing the defense industry was responding to. It began to develop counter-drone systems that could detect, track, and destroy the kind of drones used in the Nagorno-Karabakh war and in Ukraine, and that could be deployed at scale and at a cost a nation could bear. These included radar that could detect small drones, jammers that could degrade the command links the drones depended on, lasers that could destroy drones in flight, and guns that could shoot them down at close range. The counter-drone systems were a new frontier in the history of weapons.

The counter-drone systems were also the thing the smaller nations of the world were acquiring, deploying, and using to defend against the kind of drone campaigns seen in the Nagorno-Karabakh war and in Ukraine. They were not cheap, not simple, and required the kind of industrial base only a few nations possessed. They were a demonstration that the drone revolution did not favor the weak—that it favored the nations that could afford to develop and deploy the kind of systems that could counter the drone.

The drone revolution was also a revolution in the kind of war the world was fighting. Drones made it possible for a nation to attack another without exposing its own soldiers to risk, without the kind of mobilization a conventional war required, and without the kind of declaration of war the previous era had required. Drones made war easier, and the ease made them dangerous—and the ease is what the twenty-first century will have to reckon with.

The ease was also what the drone had in common with the other weapons this book has traced. The longbow was easy to use, in the sense that a trained archer could loose a dozen arrows in a minute, and it made the English army a force the French could not ignore. The musket was easy to use, in the sense that a soldier could load and fire it in a fraction of the time a crossbow required, and it made the infantry the dominant arm of the battlefield. The machine gun was easy to use, in the sense that a single gunner could fire hundreds of rounds in a minute, and it made the frontal assault a thing of the past. The drone is easy to use, in the sense that a single operator can find and destroy a target from hundreds of kilometers away, and it is making the battlefield transparent and lethal in a way it has not been before.

The ease is not the only thing the drone has in common with the other weapons this book has traced. The drone has also made the weapon more precise, and precision has made the weapon more discriminate and more dependent on the kind of information it needs to function. The precision-guided munitions this book has traced were the first step in this direction, drones are the second, and the autonomous weapons the next part will trace are the third. Precision is what the history of weapons has been building toward, and precision is what the future will be about.

Precision has also made the weapon more dependent on the kind of systems it needs to function. The drone depends on the satellite that provides navigation, the data link that provides control, the sensor that provides targeting, and the kind of network that connects the sensor to the shooter. The drone is not a weapon a soldier carries; it is a weapon a system controls, and the system is what makes the drone function. The system is also what makes the drone vulnerable, because it can be jammed, spoofed, and attacked—and attacking the system is what the counter-drone systems are designed to do.

The system has also made the drone a weapon not confined to the battlefield. The drone can attack a pipeline, a power plant, a refinery, a city. It can be used by a state, a non-state actor, a criminal, a terrorist. It is easy to acquire, easy to use, and easy to hide—and it has made the kind of asymmetric warfare the twenty-first century has seen possible in a way it was not before.

The drone has also made the kind of surveillance the twenty-first century has seen possible in a way it was not before. It can loiter above a city for hours, watch a house, follow a car, and record the kind of data the previous era could only have imagined. It has made the kind of surveillance state George Orwell imagined possible in a way Orwell did not anticipate, and it has made the kind of privacy the previous era took for granted a thing of the past.

The drone has also made the kind of targeted killing the twenty-first century has seen possible in a way it was not before. It can find a target and kill it without the kind of ground operation the previous era would have required. It has made the kind of assassination the previous era would have called murder a thing a state can do openly, and the kind of killing the previous era would have called war a thing a state can do without the kind of declaration the previous era would have required.

The drone has also made the kind of war the twenty-first century has seen possible in a way it was not before. It has made the kind of war fought by a few operators in a room in Nevada a thing a state can do, and a thing the world has had to reckon with. It has made the kind of war the previous era would have called war a thing the previous era would not recognize, and the kind of war the previous era would have called peace a thing the previous era would not recognize.

The drone has also made the kind of ethics the twenty-first century has seen possible in a way it was not before. It has made the kind of killing the previous era would have called murder a thing a state can do without the kind of accountability the previous era would have required, and the kind of killing the previous era would have called war a thing a state can do without the kind of responsibility the previous era would have required. The drone has made the kind of ethics the twenty-first century has seen a thing the twenty-first century has had to reckon with, and the reckoning is what the twenty-first century is about.
