chapters.title: Part 8
chapters.preview: The reckoning is what the previous parts of this book have been tracing. The tracing has been the argument: weapons are not neutral instruments but crystallized decisions—each a settlement of some prior dispute
paragraphs: The reckoning is what the previous parts of this book have been tracing. The tracing has been the argument: weapons are not neutral instruments but crystallized decisions—each a settlement of some prior dispute about who may kill whom, at what distance, under whose authority, and at what cost. A sword settles the dispute in favor of the strong arm and the trained wrist. A wall favors the defender who can wait. A rifle favors the man who can see farther than his enemy and hit what he sees. A machine gun favors the side that can afford the ammunition and the factory. A nuclear warhead favors the side that got there first and can prove it. A drone favors the side that can watch and strike without exposing a pilot's body to the consequences. Each settlement is provisional, contested by the next weapon, which is contested by the next; the history of war is the history of these settlements being made, broken, and remade. Part 8 takes up one of the longest and most consequential: the settlement of the gunpowder age, and the long, uneven, often misunderstood transition from the world of the bow and blade to the world of the firearm. Historians once told this transition as a clean story—the gun arrives, the knight dies, the modern world begins—and the evidence has made it much messier, and much more interesting, than the clean story allowed.

The clean story has a shape anyone schooled in the twentieth century would recognize. In the Middle Ages, war was fought by armored knights on horseback, and the knight dominated the battlefield because nothing could penetrate his armor. Then gunpowder arrived from the East; cannon and handgun made armor useless, the knight became obsolete, chivalry ended, and the modern age of gunpowder, standing armies, and the state began. The story has the appeal of any single cause explaining a large effect. It is also, in almost every particular, wrong or misleading—and the way it is wrong is instructive, because the errors are not random. They come from reading the history of weapons backward from the present: from assuming that because the firearm eventually won, it won quickly, obviously, and for reasons that seem obvious in retrospect.

The first thing the evidence shows is that gunpowder did not arrive in Europe as a finished technology with a clear military purpose. It arrived as a substance with a confusing reputation and a long list of possible uses, most of them not military. The Chinese had known gunpowder since at least the ninth century, and the earliest surviving formulas, recorded in the *Wujing Zongyao* of 1044, were mixtures of saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal with relatively low nitrate content—mixtures that burned, smoked, and made noise but did not reliably explode. Early Chinese gunpowder weapons were incendiaries, smoke generators, and fire-lances: devices that spat flame, frightened horses, and set things alight, not devices that threw projectiles with the force of a cannon. The transition from incendiary to propellant was gradual and depended on a chemical insight that took centuries to refine: the more saltpeter in the mixture, the more powerful the explosion, and the more powerful the explosion, the more useful the substance became for throwing things. The Chinese got there first, the Mongols carried the knowledge westward, and by the thirteenth century it had reached the Islamic world and Europe, where it was received not as a revelation but as one more item in a crowded marketplace of military and alchemical ideas.

The second thing the evidence shows is that the earliest European firearms were not obviously superior to the weapons they competed with. The Heilongjiang hand cannon, dated by inscription to 1288, is among the earliest dated metal-barreled firearms: a small, crude, heavy object, difficult to aim, slow to reload, and dangerous to the user as well as the target. The earliest European depictions of firearms, from the fourteenth century, show devices like small pots or bottles mounted on sticks, fired by touching a match to a touchhole, capable of throwing a stone or lead ball a short distance with indifferent accuracy. A longbowman could shoot farther, faster, and more accurately than the first generation of hand-gunners, without risking his weapon exploding in his face. The fourteenth-century commander's question was not "should I adopt the firearm?" but "why would I adopt the firearm?"—and for a long time the answer was not obvious.

The answer, when it came, was not about the weapon's performance in a single duel but in a system. The longbow was superb in the hands of a longbowman, and the longbowman was a product of a particular social and economic system: one that trained boys from childhood, required weekly practice, rewarded them with status and pay, and could produce, in England at the height of the longbow's dominance, tens of thousands of men who could draw a bow of a hundred pounds or more and loose a shaft that would punch through mail at two hundred yards. The Mary Rose, sunk in 1545 and raised in 1982, yielded 137 longbows, with estimated draw weights of 100 to 185 pounds—evidence of a lifetime of training the modern archer can barely imagine, let alone replicate. The longbow was not just a weapon. It was an institution, expensive to maintain and fragile, because it depended on a continuous supply of trained men and a culture that valued the training.

The firearm was a different kind of institution. It was cheap to make, at least relative to a good bow, and cheap to train, at least relative to a longbowman, because the gunner's skill lay in the weapon rather than the body. A peasant could be taught to load and fire a matchlock in a few weeks. He could not be taught to draw a war bow in a few weeks, or months, or years. The firearm transferred skill from the man to the machine, and in doing so transferred power from the class of men who had spent their lives acquiring the skill to the class of men who could afford to equip and pay the men who had not. This is the deep argument of the gunpowder age, and it is about social organization as much as chemistry. The gun did not defeat the bow because it was a better weapon. It defeated the bow because it was a weapon that could be produced and used by a different kind of society—one that could mass-produce the weapon, mass-train the user, and mass-supply the ammunition on a scale the bow could never match.

The knight is the test case for this argument, and the knight is where the clean story goes most wrong. The clean story says gunpowder made armor useless and the knight obsolete. The evidence says something more complicated. Armor did not become useless in the face of firearms; it adapted. Late medieval and early modern armorers thickened the breastplate, added a central ridge to deflect shot, and produced the "proof" marks testifying that a cuirass had been tested against a pistol or musket. The knight did not vanish from the battlefield when the gun appeared; he fought alongside the gunner for centuries, and in some theaters outlasted the gunner's first generation by a wide margin. What killed the knight was not the gun alone but a combination of changes—the rise of the infantry phalanx, the pike and shot formation, the increasing cost of cavalry, the centralization of military power in the state—of which the gun was one element and not always the decisive one. The knight's decline was a long, uneven, contested process, and the gun was a participant in it, not the cause.

The pike and shot formation is the emblem of the transition, and it deserves to be understood as a system rather than a slogan. The Spanish *tercio*, perfected in the sixteenth century, combined a block of pikemen with a screen of arquebusiers or musketeers. The pikemen protected the gunners from cavalry, the gunners protected the pikemen from the enemy's gunners, and the two arms together were more effective than either alone. No single weapon could defeat the *tercio*; it had to be defeated by a better system, and the better system, when it came, was not a better gun but a better combination of guns, pikes, cavalry, artillery, and above all discipline. The military revolution historians have debated for half a century was not a revolution in weapons. It was a revolution in organization, and the gun was one of the technologies that made the new organization possible.

The artillery tells a parallel story, and it connects the gunpowder age to the industrial age that followed. The first cannon were small, crude, and dangerous, used as much for siege as for battle, because a cannon that could throw a stone ball at a wall could do something no other weapon could: bring down a fortification without waiting for starvation or treachery. The development of the cannon drove the development of the fortification, and the development of the fortification drove the development of the cannon, in a dialectic that would become familiar in the history of weapons—offense and defense chasing each other, each advance provoking an advance in the other, the cost of the chase rising with every round. The *trace italienne*, the low, thick-walled, angled fortification that replaced the high medieval castle, was a response to the cannon, and the cannon that could breach the *trace italienne* was a response to the *trace italienne*, and the whole cycle was expensive in a way that favored the state over the lord. A nobleman could build a castle. Only a state could build a fortress system, and only a state could afford the artillery train that could reduce it.

This is the point at which the history of weapons becomes indistinguishable from the history of the state, and the indistinguishability is not an accident. The gunpowder age is the age in which the state acquired a monopoly on the means of large-scale violence, and it acquired the monopoly because those means became too expensive for anyone but the state to afford. The cannon, the fortress, the magazine, the foundry, the powder mill, the standing army—these were not weapons in the narrow sense. They were institutions, and the institutions required capital, and the capital required taxation, and the taxation required bureaucracy, and the bureaucracy required a state. The gun did not create the state, but the gun made the state the only organization that could compete in the new kind of war, and the states that failed to make the transition were conquered by the states that did.

The naval dimension of the gunpowder age is often treated as a footnote, and it should not be, because it is where the gunpowder age produced its most decisive strategic result. The cannon at sea changed the relationship between ships and between nations in a way the cannon on land did not, because the sea is a medium with no terrain to hide behind and no wall to shelter behind, and the ship that can throw more iron farther and faster than the other ship wins. The development of the broadside, the gunport, and the purpose-built warship—the galleon, the ship of the line—was a development in the technology of the gun as much as in the technology of the ship, and it gave the states that mastered it a reach no land power could match. The Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, and English built their empires on the cannon at sea, not because the Europeans were braver or smarter than the peoples they conquered but because they had a weapon system those peoples did not have and could not easily acquire. The gunpowder age is the age of European expansion, and the expansion is not separable from the gun.

The handgun's own development is a story of small improvements compounding into a large change. The matchlock, which used a burning cord to ignite the powder, was replaced by the wheellock, which used a spring-driven wheel to strike a spark, and the wheellock was replaced by the flintlock, which used a flint striking steel to make the spark. Each was a modest improvement in reliability, and each made the gun a little more useful, a little more dependable, a little more capable of being used by a soldier who was not a specialist. The flintlock, perfected in the seventeenth century, was the first firearm reliable enough to be the standard weapon of an army, and the armies that adopted it were the armies that could fire in volleys, and the volleys were what made the gun a battlefield weapon rather than a curiosity. The bayonet, which allowed a gunner to defend himself without a separate pike, was the final piece of the system—not a weapon in its own right so much as a way of making the gun a complete weapon, one that could shoot and could also stand in a line and receive a charge.

The eighteenth-century musket is the weapon the gunpowder age produced, and it is worth pausing on because the clean story treats it as the culmination of the gun's development while the evidence treats it as a compromise. The musket was accurate to perhaps fifty yards and could kill at a hundred, took a trained soldier perhaps twenty seconds to load and fire, was unreliable in wet weather, and was prone to misfire. By any measure, it was a poor weapon. Yet the armies of the eighteenth century were built around it, because the musket was not designed to be a good weapon in the hands of an individual. It was designed to be a good weapon in the hands of a formation, and a formation of musketeers firing in volleys could produce a volume of fire no formation of archers or pikemen could match, and the volume of fire was what mattered. The musket was a weapon of the line, the line was the institution, and the institution was the thing the gun had made possible.

The American Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars are the testing ground for the musket, and the testing ground is where the limitations of the system become visible. American riflemen, with their slow-loading but accurate long rifles, could pick off British officers at ranges the muskets could not match, and the British response was not to adopt the rifle wholesale but to supplement the musket with rifle-armed skirmishers. The Napoleonic *tirailleurs* and the British Rifle Brigade were the acknowledgment that the musket's volume of fire was not enough, that accuracy mattered, and that the future lay in a weapon combining the volume of the musket with the accuracy of the rifle. The weapon that combined them was the rifled musket, made possible by a technological change that is one of the hinges of the history of weapons: the Minié ball.

The Minié ball, developed by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, was a hollow-base bullet that expanded into the rifling when the powder charge drove it forward. The expansion meant a soldier could load a rifled musket as quickly as a smoothbore, because the bullet did not have to be forced down the barrel against the rifling. The Minié ball allowed the rifled musket to become the standard infantry weapon, and the rifled musket extended the infantryman's effective range from fifty yards to several hundred, and the extension of range changed the shape of the battlefield. The British Pattern 1853 Enfield and the U.S. Springfield Model 1861 carried the Minié ball into the hands of hundreds of thousands of soldiers, and the American Civil War was the war in which the rifled musket was used on a scale no previous war had seen. The casualties of the Civil War were not caused by the rifled musket alone, but it was one of the reasons the war was so costly, because it allowed the defender to kill the attacker at a range where the attacker's own weapons were useless, and the tactical formations of the previous century—the close-order line, the frontal assault—became suicidal in a way the generals of 1861 did not fully understand.

The Civil War is the war in which the gunpowder age's long accumulation of small improvements produced a sudden, visible change in the character of battle, and the change was not in any single weapon but in the relationship between weapons. The rifled musket, the rifled cannon, the railroad, the telegraph, the ironclad, the repeating rifle—each had been foreshadowed in previous decades, each arrived in the Civil War in a form mature enough to be used, and the combination made the Civil War the first modern war. The generals who fought it had been trained in the tactics of the musket age, and those tactics did not work against the rifled musket, and the result was a war of attrition that the previous age would have regarded as barbaric and the next age would regard as normal.

The repeating rifle is the weapon the Civil War foreshadowed and the next generation of wars made standard, and its development is a case study in how a weapon's social meaning can change faster than its technical performance. The Henry rifle, with its sixteen-round magazine and lever action, was available during the Civil War and used by some Union units, and conservative officers of the day regarded it as a waste of ammunition, because they had been trained in a doctrine that emphasized aimed fire and disciplined volleys and regarded rapid fire as a sign of panic. The doctrine was not stupid. It had been developed for a weapon that could not fire rapidly, and it had become a habit of mind that outlasted the weapon that produced it. The repeating rifle did not become standard until the armies of the late nineteenth century had learned, through colonial warfare and the wars of German unification, that rapid fire was not a waste of ammunition but a source of power. The lesson was learned slowly, and at the cost of lives.

The machine gun is the weapon that made the lesson unavoidable, and its history is the history of the gunpowder age reaching its logical conclusion. Hiram Maxim demonstrated a recoil-operated automatic machine gun in 1884, and the British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891. The Maxim was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun—a weapon that used the energy of its own recoil to load and fire the next round, and could therefore fire continuously as long as the ammunition held out. It was not the first weapon that could fire rapidly; the Gatling gun, the mitrailleuse, and the volley gun had all preceded it. But the Maxim was the first rapid-fire weapon reliable enough to be a standard weapon of war, and its reliability was what made it a revolution. The Maxim and its descendants—the Vickers, the Maxim-Nordenfelt, the German MG 08—were the weapons that made the trench a necessity, because a single machine gun could sweep a field of advance and kill an entire battalion, and the only defense against the machine gun was to dig in and wait.

The French 75mm field gun, adopted in 1897, is the other half of the revolution, and its story is how a single technological insight can transform an entire arm of service. The Canon de 75 modèle 1897 used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady when the gun fired; the steadiness meant the gun did not have to be re-aimed after every shot, and the absence of re-aiming meant it could fire at a rate previous artillery could not approach—often cited at roughly fifteen rounds per minute. The French 75 was not a bigger gun than its predecessors. It was a faster gun, and the speed was what mattered, because speed of fire allowed the artillery to support the infantry in a way the slow-firing guns of the previous generation could not. The French 75 became an icon of the First World War, and the icon was deserved, because the gun was one of the weapons that made the war the war that it was.

The First World War is the war in which the gunpowder age's long accumulation of improvements produced a battlefield no previous generation had imagined, and that battlefield was a battlefield of artillery. The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916, produced roughly 700,000 casualties, overwhelmingly by artillery, and the artillery was produced by factories, and the factories were supplied by railroads, and the railroads were the arteries of the war. The infantryman at Verdun was not primarily a killer. He was primarily a target; the artillery was the killer, and the artillery's dominance meant the war was a war of production as much as a war of tactics. The generals who fought the First World War have been criticized for their tactics, and the criticism is often fair, but it misses the point that the tactics were constrained by the weapons. The weapons had made the frontal assault suicidal, and no general had yet found a way to break the trench line that did not involve the frontal assault, and the search for a way to break the trench line produced the tank, the airplane, and the storm-troop tactics of the war's last year.

The tank is the weapon the First World War produced in response to the machine gun, and its history is a case study in how a new weapon can be misread by the institution that adopts it. The first tanks were slow, unreliable, and mechanically fragile, used in small numbers and in conditions that did not favor them, and conservative officers who saw them regarded them as a curiosity. The officers who understood them—who saw that the tank was not a mobile machine gun but a mobile fortress, a weapon that could cross the trench line and survive the machine-gun fire that killed the infantry—were a minority, and the minority had to fight the institution as much as the enemy. The tank's development between the wars was a story of doctrinal argument as much as technical improvement, and the argument was about whether the tank was a support weapon for the infantry or a weapon in its own right, and it was not settled until the Second World War demonstrated, at the cost of enormous casualties, that the tank was a weapon in its own right and that the doctrines treating it as a support weapon were doctrines that lost battles.

The airplane is the other weapon the First World War produced, and its history is the history of a weapon that began as a reconnaissance tool and became a weapon of mass destruction in a single generation. The first military airplanes were used to see over the trench line, and the seeing was so valuable that the other side had to stop it, and the stopping produced the fighter, and the fighter produced the bomber, and the bomber produced the doctrine of strategic bombing, and the doctrine of strategic bombing produced the firestorms of the Second World War and the nuclear weapons of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The airplane's trajectory is the trajectory of the gunpowder age itself: a technology that begins as a tool, becomes a weapon, and ends as a system that shapes the entire society that uses it.

The Second World War is the war in which the gunpowder age's logic reached its extreme, and the extreme is the point at which the logic breaks. The war was a war of production on a scale no previous war had approached, organized by states that had made the mobilization of their entire societies the object of their policy, and the weapons those mobilized societies produced were weapons the previous age would have regarded as science fiction. The bomber, the aircraft carrier, the submarine, the rocket, the radar, the proximity fuse, the computer—each was a weapon or a weapon-support technology that the war produced or perfected, each changed the balance of power between offense and defense, and the changes were so rapid that the doctrines of 1939 were obsolete by 1943. The Second World War is the war in which the gunpowder age's long accumulation of improvements produced a change in the character of war that was not a change in degree but a change in kind, and the change in kind was the atomic bomb.

The atomic bomb is the weapon the gunpowder age produced and could not contain, and its history is the history of the point at which the logic of the gunpowder age—the logic of the weapon that settles the dispute—produced a weapon that settled the dispute so completely that it made the dispute itself obsolete. The Trinity test of 16 July 1945, which detonated a plutonium implosion device with a yield of about twenty-one kilotons, was the first nuclear detonation, and it opened the nuclear age, and the nuclear age is the age in which the settlement the gunpowder age had been making and breaking for six centuries was replaced by a settlement that could not be broken without breaking the world. The bomb did not end war. It ended the kind of war the gunpowder age had made, and it inaugurated a kind of war the gunpowder age had not imagined—a war of deterrence, of proxy, of precision, of the drone and the algorithm—and the war the twenty-first century is fighting is the war the bomb made possible by making the previous kind of war impossible.

The bomb is also the weapon that makes the argument of this book most visible, because no one can pretend it is a neutral instrument. The bomb is a settlement, and the settlement is explicit: the state that possesses the bomb may kill on a scale no previous state could imagine, and the possession is the authority, and the authority is the thing the bomb was built to establish. The bomb is the purest case of the weapon as crystallized decision, and the purity is what makes it useful as a limit case, because the bomb shows what all weapons are doing in a lesser way. Every weapon is a claim about who may kill whom, and the bomb is the claim stated in its most extreme form, and the history of the gunpowder age is the history of the claim being made, contested, and remade in forms that were less extreme but no less consequential.

The gunpowder age's settlement was not only a settlement about who may kill whom. It was a settlement about who may pay for the killing, and the settlement about payment is the one the clean story ignores, and it is the one that matters most for the history that follows. The gunpowder age made war expensive, and the expense was the thing that made the state, and the state was the thing that made the gunpowder age's wars possible. The cost of a cannon, a fortress, a magazine, a standing army was a cost only a state could bear, and the states that could bear it were the states that could tax, and the states that could tax were the states that could borrow, and the states that could borrow were the states that could make war on a scale the previous age had not imagined. The financial revolution of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries—the Bank of England, the national debt, the stock market—was a revolution in the technology of war as much as in the technology of finance, and the two technologies were the same technology seen from different angles. The gunpowder age is the age in which war became a financial instrument, and the instrument was as important as the weapon, and the two were inseparable.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about who may know, and the settlement about knowledge is the one the twenty-first century is now contesting. The gunpowder age made war a matter of science—the science of ballistics, metallurgy, chemistry, and eventually nuclear physics—and the scientists who made the science were the scientists who made the weapons, and the weapons were the things the scientists could not unmake. The Manhattan Project is the emblem of the scientist's entanglement with the weapon, and the emblem is not a happy one, because the scientists who built the bomb discovered that the knowledge they had produced could not be recalled, and the discovery was the discovery the gunpowder age had been making for six centuries: knowledge, once weaponized, becomes a permanent feature of the world, and the world that has the knowledge is not the world that did not have it, and there is no going back.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about distance, and the settlement about distance is the one that connects the gunpowder age to the drone age. The gun was a weapon that killed at a distance, and the distance made the gun a moral problem as well as a military one, because the man who kills at a distance does not see the face of the man he kills, and the not-seeing makes the killing easier, and the easier killing is what the gun made possible. The longbowman saw the faces of the men he killed, or at least saw them at a distance short enough to make them visible as men. The musketeer saw them as a line of colored coats. The artilleryman saw them as a grid reference. The bomber crew saw them as a city. The drone operator sees them as a screen, and the screen is the latest stage in a long process of distancing the gun began, and the process is what the twenty-first century is now trying to reckon with, and the reckoning is what the drone has made unavoidable.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about time, and the settlement about time is the one the industrial age made explicit. The gun was a weapon that could be produced in advance and stored, and the storage made the standing army possible, and the standing army made the state possible, and the state made the gunpowder age's wars possible. The pre-gunpowder warrior had to be fed and paid and sent home, and the sending home limited the length of the campaign, and the limitation made pre-gunpowder war a seasonal activity. The gunpowder age's soldier could be kept in the field for years, and the keeping made the siege the dominant form of war, and the siege made the gunpowder age's wars slow, expensive, and devastating to the civilian population. The gunpowder age is the age in which war became a permanent condition rather than an episodic one, and the permanence is what the state was built to sustain.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the body, and the settlement about the body is the one the history of weapons has been tracing since the first stone was thrown. The gun was a weapon that could kill a man without touching him, and the not-touching made the gun a weapon that could be used by a man who was not a warrior, and by a man who was afraid, and the fear was what the gun was designed to overcome. The pre-gunpowder warrior had to close with his enemy, and the closing required courage, and the courage was what the warrior culture celebrated, and the celebration was what the gun made obsolete. The gun did not make courage obsolete, but it made courage less decisive, and the making-less-decisive changed the culture of war, and the change of culture is what the history of weapons is really about.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the enemy, and the settlement about the enemy is the one the gun made most visible. The pre-gunpowder enemy could be seen and named and fought, and the seeing and naming and fighting made the enemy a person, and the personhood of the enemy made the war a human activity, however terrible. The gun made the enemy a target, and the target is not a person, and the not-person is what the gun made possible, and the possibility is what the gunpowder age's wars made actual on a scale the previous age had not approached. The gunpowder age is the age in which the enemy became a statistic, and the statistic is what the twenty-first century's drones have perfected, and the perfection is what the twenty-first century is now trying to reckon with.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the civilian, and the settlement about the civilian is the one the gunpowder age made most ambiguous. Pre-gunpowder war was a war of warriors, and the civilian was a bystander, and the bystander was often a victim, but the victim was not the target. The gunpowder age's war was a war of states, and the state's war mobilized the entire society, and the mobilization made the civilian a participant, and the participation made the civilian a target, and the targeting of the civilian is what the gunpowder age's wars made normal. The siege, the blockade, the strategic bombing, the nuclear strike—each is a weapon that targets the civilian, each is a weapon the gunpowder age produced, and the production is what the gunpowder age's ethics had to reckon with, and the reckoning is what the gunpowder age never fully accomplished.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the law, and the settlement about the law is the one the gunpowder age's lawyers, theologians, and generals argued about for centuries. The pre-gunpowder just war tradition, from Augustine to Aquinas to the Spanish scholastics, tried to limit war by limiting the authority to wage it, the cause that justified it, and the means permitted in it. The gunpowder age made the tradition harder to apply, because the gun made the means more destructive and the state made the authority more absolute, and the harder application produced the modern law of war, and the modern law of war is what the gunpowder age's lawyers built to contain the gunpowder age's weapons. The law of war is not a thing the gunpowder age produced by accident. It is a thing the gunpowder age produced because its weapons made the law necessary, and the necessity is what the twenty-first century's drones are now testing.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the future, and the settlement about the future is the one the gunpowder age's philosophers, prophets, and poets argued about, and the argument is the argument the twenty-first century is still having. The gunpowder age's prophets predicted that the gun would end war by making it too terrible to fight, and the prediction was wrong, and the wrongness is what the gunpowder age's history teaches. The gun did not end war. It changed war, and the change was what the gunpowder age's societies had to adapt to, and the adaptation is what the gunpowder age's history is about. The twenty-first century's prophets predict that the drone and the algorithm and the autonomous weapon will end war by making it too easy to fight, and the prediction may be wrong in the same way, and the wrongness may be what the twenty-first century's history teaches. The gunpowder age is the mirror in which the twenty-first century can see its own predicament, and the mirror is what the history of weapons is for.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the past, and the settlement about the past is the one the gunpowder age's historians made and the twenty-first century's historians are now revising. The gunpowder age's historians told the clean story, and the clean story served the gunpowder age's purposes, because it made the gun the hero of the story and the gun's heroes the ancestors of the present. The revision is what the evidence has forced, and the evidence is what the twenty-first century's historians have, and the evidence shows that the gunpowder age was not a clean story but a messy one, and the messiness is what makes the gunpowder age interesting. The gunpowder age's settlement was made by people who did not know they were making it, and the not-knowing is what the history of weapons has to recover, because the not-knowing is what makes the history of weapons a human history rather than a technological one.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the world, and the settlement about the world is the one the gunpowder age's empires made and the twenty-first century's nations are still living with. The gunpowder age's empires were built on the gun, and the gun allowed a small number of Europeans to conquer a large part of the world, and the conquest was not a conquest of superior people over inferior people but of a superior weapon system over an inferior one, and the superiority of the weapon system was what the gunpowder age's empires could not afford to lose. The gunpowder age's empires are gone, but the world they made is not gone, and the world they made is the world the twenty-first century is trying to reckon with, and the reckoning is what the gunpowder age's history is for.

The gunpowder age's settlement was also a settlement about the self, and the settlement about the self is the one the gunpowder age's soldiers made and the twenty-first century's soldiers are still making

paragraphs: The soldier of the gunpowder age was made, not born, and the making was done by drill. Histories of weapons tend to bury this fact under the histories of the weapons themselves, because the weapon is the visible thing and the drill is the invisible thing, and the invisible thing decided the battles. A musket in the hands of a man who has never loaded one is a club with a complicated lock. A musket in the hands of a man who has loaded one ten thousand times is a machine for killing at a hundred paces. The difference is not in the iron but in the man, and the man was made by the drill.

The drill was the great invention of the gunpowder age, of the same order as the gun itself, and made in the same place at the same time. The Dutch, in the last years of the sixteenth century, under Maurice of Nassau and his cousin William Louis, took the Roman drill out of the texts of Aelian and Vegetius and made it a living thing, and the living thing was the countermarch: the rotation of ranks so that a line of musketeers could keep up continuous fire without breaking. The countermarch required every man in the line to know exactly what he was to do and exactly when, and the knowing was not a matter of courage or intelligence but of repetition. The men who did it were not heroes. They were cogs, and the cogs were the point. Maurice's army was small and poor and fought the greatest empire in Europe to a standstill because its men could do a thing together that the Spanish tercios could not: load and fire and step and load again in a rhythm that never broke. The rhythm was the weapon.

The rhythm spread. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden took the Dutch drill and added the salvo, the volley fired by three ranks at once, along with the Swedish brigade, the lighter musket, and the cartridge, and the Swedish army became the model every army in Europe copied for a century. The copying was the important part. The drill was not a secret. It was published in manuals, in woodcuts, in the little books officers carried in their coats, and it was published because it could not be kept secret: the drill was a way of moving men, and a way of moving men can be seen and copied and improved, and the improvement was the whole of the military history of the seventeenth century. The men who improved it were not usually the men who fought with it. They were the theorists, the drillmasters, the colonels who had never held a pike, and the gunpowder age was the first age in which the theorist of war mattered as much as the warrior, because the theory was the thing that could be taught and the teaching multiplied the weapon.

The drill did something to the men that the drillmasters did not entirely intend and did not entirely understand, and what it did was the foundation of the gunpowder age's settlement about the self. A man who has been drilled has been given a second body, a body that moves without his willing it, and the second body carries him through the battle when his first body wants to run. The drill is not courage. It is a substitute for courage, and a better substitute, because courage is unevenly distributed and runs out, and the drill is evenly distributed and does not. The drilled man does not have to decide to load and fire. He loads and fires because his hands know how, and the knowing is in his hands and not his mind, and his mind is free to be terrified, and the terror does not stop the hands. This is what the gunpowder age discovered, and every army since has built on it, and the twenty-first century's soldier, sitting in a container in Nevada with a joystick in his hand, is still its heir, because the joystick is a drill too, and the man who flies a drone has been drilled until his hands know the thing his mind is afraid of.

The drill made the standing army possible, the standing army made the state possible, and the state made the drill possible; the circle is the circle of the gunpowder age. Before the gunpowder age, armies were raised for a campaign and disbanded after it, and the men went back to the fields, and the skills of war decayed between wars, and the decay was why wars were short and small and seasonal. The gunpowder age's armies could not be disbanded, because a musketeer drilled for a year is worth ten who have not been, and if you disband him you lose the year, and the year is what your enemy is spending. So you keep him, and keeping him costs money, and the money comes from taxes, and the taxes come from a bureaucracy, and the bureaucracy comes from a state, and the state is the standing army's shadow. The standing army and the state grew up together and neither could have grown without the other, and the growth was the great political fact of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and the drill was the small technical fact at the bottom of it, and the small technical fact is the one the histories of politics leave out.

The drill was also a school, and the school taught more than loading and firing. It taught obedience, in a particular form: the form that does not require the man to understand the order, only to execute it, and the form was new. The medieval soldier obeyed his lord because he was the lord's man, bound by a personal tie between two people who knew each other. The drilled soldier obeyed an officer he had never met, in a language of command the same in every regiment, and the obedience was not personal and did not need to be, and the anonymity of the obedience made the army a machine. The machine could be aimed. It could be aimed by a general who had never seen a single man in it, and the aiming was the art of war, and the art of war became the art of moving the machine, and the moving of the machine could be done on a map, and the map was the general's instrument, and the general's instrument replaced the general's eye, and the general's eye had been the thing that won the medieval battle. The replacement was the gunpowder age's deepest change in the nature of command.

The map and the drill and the musket made the line, and the line was the formation of the gunpowder age, and the line was the thing the age's soldiers died in. The line was not a thing any soldier would have chosen. It was a thing the weapon chose, because the musket was slow to load and inaccurate and needed to be fired in mass to be effective, and the mass had to be arranged so that every man could fire and every man could be seen and every man could be ordered. The arrangement was a line two or three ranks deep and as long as the field allowed, and the line was a target that could not miss, and the men in it knew they were a target and stood in it anyway, and the standing was what the age asked of its soldiers and what the age's drill was for. The line was a machine for converting men into fire, and the conversion was efficient, and the efficiency was measured in the only currency the age cared about: the number of men who could be brought to fire on a given front in a given time. The number went up and up as the drill improved and the musket improved, and the up and up was the whole of the tactical history of the age.

The line had a cost the age did not count, and the cost was what the age's soldiers carried home in their bodies if they came home at all. A man who has stood in a line and watched the men on either side of him fall has learned something about the world that cannot be unlearned: that the world is a place where men are arranged in lines and killed, and the arrangement is not his and the killing is not his and the only thing that is his is the standing, and the standing is the whole of his dignity and the whole of his terror at once. The literature of the gunpowder age is full of this, and it is not the literature of heroes. It is the literature of men who did a thing that was asked of them and were broken by it, and the breaking was not a failure of courage but a success of the drill, because the drill had made them into a machine and the machine had done its work and the man inside the machine had watched the work being done and could not stop it. The gunpowder age's settlement about the self was a settlement in which the self was split, and the split was the price of the line, and the price was paid by every soldier who ever stood in one.

The great battle of the gunpowder age's line was Blenheim, fought on the thirteenth of August 1704, and Blenheim shows what the drill could do when it was done well and what it cost when it was done at all. The Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy commanded an allied army of some fifty-two thousand men against a French and Bavarian army of some fifty-six thousand under the Duc de Tallard, and the battle was fought for control of the Danube and the rescue of Vienna, and it was won by the drill. Marlborough's infantry attacked the village of Blenheim itself, and the attack was a feint that became a slaughter, and the French infantry in the village were packed so densely that they could not use their muskets, and the allied infantry that attacked them were cut down in ranks, and the ranks closed and attacked again, and the closing of the ranks was the drill, and the drill was what made the attack possible. The French cavalry in the center was broken by the allied cavalry, and the French infantry in the village was surrounded, and some eleven thousand Frenchmen surrendered there, the largest surrender of the war, and the battle was a decisive allied victory, bought with some twelve thousand allied casualties and some twenty thousand French and Bavarian, and the numbers are the numbers of the line.

Blenheim shows the line's logic in its purest form. The French infantry in the village were not worse soldiers than the allied infantry. They were the same kind of soldiers, drilled the same way, armed the same way, and they lost because they were in a place where their drill could not work, and the place was chosen by the enemy, and the choosing of the place was the general's art, and the general's art was what the drill could not supply. The drill made the soldier a machine, and the machine was the same on both sides, and the difference between victory and defeat was not in the machines but in the man who aimed them, and the man who aimed them was the general, and the general was the one man in the army who was not drilled. The gunpowder age's settlement about the self was a settlement in which the many were machines and the one was an artist, and the one was what the many were for.

The one was Frederick the Great, and Frederick is the gunpowder age's soldier in the way that Marlborough was its general, and the difference is that Frederick was both, and the both made him the age's model. Frederick inherited an army from his father, Frederick William I, the Soldier King, who had spent his reign building the drill into a religion. The religion was the Potsdam drill, the most exact in Europe, and the exactness was what Frederick William loved more than anything, and he loved it so much that he drilled his grenadiers until they could march in step and fire in step and wheel in step, and he drilled them until the drilling was the point and the war was the excuse. The army he left his son was the most drilled army in Europe and the smallest of the great powers' armies, and the smallness was what Frederick had to solve.

Frederick solved it by using the drill better than anyone had used it, and the using was what the drill was for, and the using was what Frederick William had not understood. Frederick's army moved faster than any army in Europe, and it moved faster because it was drilled, and the drill was not a parade-ground thing but a road thing, and the road thing was the column, and the column was the drill applied to movement. Frederick's columns arrived where the enemy did not expect them and deployed from column into line faster than the enemy could deploy, and the deployment was the drill, and the drill was the advantage, and the advantage was used at Rossbach and at Leuthen and at Hohenfriedberg, and the using of it was the art of war. At Leuthen, on the fifth of December 1757, Frederick attacked an Austrian army nearly twice his size, marching his army in column across the front of the Austrian line, hidden by a ridge, then wheeling into line and falling on the Austrian left flank. The wheeling was the drill, and the drill was done in the presence of the enemy and under fire and did not break, and the Austrian army was rolled up and destroyed, and the destruction was the most complete victory of the age, and the victory was the drill's masterpiece.

Leuthen is also the battle that shows the drill's limit, and the limit is what the gunpowder age's soldiers learned and what the twenty-first century's soldiers are still learning. The drill worked at Leuthen because the ground allowed it and the enemy allowed it and the weather allowed it, and the drill did not work at Kunersdorf, two years later, when Frederick attacked a fortified Russian and Austrian position and his infantry was shot to pieces in front of the entrenchments, and the army was destroyed, and Frederick wrote that evening that he had lost the war and had nothing left, and the letter is one of the age's great documents of the self, and the self in it is a self broken by the machine it built. The drill had made Frederick's army the best in Europe, and the drill had made Frederick's army unable to do anything but what it was drilled to do, and what it was drilled to do was attack in line, and the attack in line against entrenchments was suicide, and the army did it anyway because it was drilled to, and the doing of it was the drill's failure, and the failure was what the age's soldiers could not escape, because the drill was the only thing they had and the only thing they knew and the only thing that made them what they were.

The drill's failure at Kunersdorf was the failure of the line, and the line was what the gunpowder age's enemies learned to defeat, and the learning was done by the men who fought the line and by the men who thought about the line, and the thinking produced the next great change in the gunpowder age's way of war, and the change was the skirmisher. The skirmisher was not a new thing. The skirmisher was the old thing, the thing the line had replaced: the man who fought on his own and aimed his own weapon and chose his own ground. The skirmisher came back because the line had become too costly, and the coming back was the gunpowder age's great dialectic, and the dialectic was what the age's soldiers lived through and what the twenty-first century's soldiers are still living through, because the line and the skirmisher are the two poles of the gunpowder age's settlement about the self, and the settlement was never stable, and the instability was the age's condition.

The skirmisher came back in the American Revolution, and the coming back was what the British army could not understand, and the not understanding was what lost the war. The British fought in line, and the line was the best thing in the world at what it did, and what it did was break other lines, and the Americans did not have lines to break. The Americans fought from behind walls and trees and rocks, and they fired at officers and at the flanks of the line, and they ran when the line advanced and came back when the line halted, and the running and coming back was not cowardice but a way of war, and the way of war was the way of the frontier, and the frontier was the place where the line had never worked, because there was no enemy line to break and no ground that could be held by a line and no supply that could feed a line. The Americans won because they did not fight the way the British were drilled to fight, and the British lost because they could not learn to fight any other way, and the learning was what the gunpowder age's armies had to do and what they did not want to do, because the learning meant unlearning the drill, and the drill was what made them what they were.

The lesson was learned in Europe, slowly and bloodily, and the learning was what the French Revolution and Napoleon did to the gunpowder age's way of war. The French Revolution gave the gunpowder age's armies something they had never had: the nation in arms, which was not a drill and could not be drilled, and was a mass of men who fought because they believed in the thing they were fighting for, and the belief was what the drill could not supply, and the belief was what made the French armies of the 1790s able to do what the drilled armies of Europe could not: absorb losses and keep coming and attack in masses the line could not stop. The French attacked in columns of men who were not fully drilled and did not need to be, because the column could be moved by enthusiasm and not by drill, and the enthusiasm was what the Revolution supplied, and the supply was what the old armies could not match, and the old armies were beaten by the enthusiasm until they learned to supply it themselves.

Napoleon learned it, and Napoleon's learning was what made him the age's greatest soldier, and the greatness was not in the drill but in the combination. Napoleon's armies were drilled, and they were also enthusiastic, and they were also numerous, and they were also fast, and the combination was what the age had been building toward and what the age's soldiers had been made for. Napoleon's corps were self-contained armies of all arms that could march separately and concentrate suddenly, and the concentration was what the drill made possible, because the drill was what let a corps march and deploy and fight as a unit, and the unit was what Napoleon aimed, and the aiming was what won Austerlitz and Jena and Wagram, and the winning was the drill's triumph and the enthusiasm's triumph at once, and the two were what the gunpowder age's settlement about the self had been trying to reconcile, and the reconciliation was what Napoleon was, and what Napoleon was is what the age's soldiers wanted to be.

Austerlitz, fought on the second of December 1805, shows the reconciliation at its height. Napoleon had some sixty-eight thousand men and the allied Russians and Austrians had some eighty-five thousand, and the allies attacked Napoleon's right, and Napoleon had deliberately weakened his right to invite the attack, and the weakening was what the drill made possible, because a drilled army can be trusted to hold with a thin line and a drilled general can be trusted to know it. The allies took the bait and marched off the Pratzen Heights, and Napoleon attacked the heights and took them, and the taking of the heights split the allied army in two, and the splitting was what won the battle, and the winning was the drill's and the general's and the enthusiasm's all at once. The allied army was destroyed, and some twenty-seven thousand allied soldiers were killed or captured, and the French lost some nine thousand, and the numbers are the numbers of the age's way of war at its most efficient, and the efficiency was what the age's soldiers had been drilled for, and the drill was what made the efficiency possible.

The drill's cost was what the age's soldiers carried and what the age's literature recorded, and the record is how the gunpowder age's settlement about the self is known. The memoirs of the age's soldiers are full of the drill, and the drill in the memoirs is not a proud thing but a numb thing, and the numbness is what the soldiers remember, and the numbness is what the drill was for. A soldier who has been drilled remembers the drill as a kind of death, a death of the self that made the self able to do what the self could not do, and the remembering is what the age's soldiers did and what the twenty-first century's soldiers do, and the doing is what the gunpowder age's settlement about the self was, and the settlement was a bargain, and the bargain was the self for the machine, and the machine was what won the battles, and the self was what paid.

The bargain was made in the eighteenth century and made again in the nineteenth, and the remaking was what the industrial revolution did to the gunpowder age's way of war, and the remaking was what the age's soldiers had to live through, and the living through was what broke them. The industrial revolution gave the gunpowder age's armies new weapons, and the new weapons were what the drill had to be rebuilt around, and the rebuilding was what the nineteenth century's soldiers did, and the rebuilding was what the twentieth century's soldiers inherited, and the inheritance was what made the twentieth century's war what it was. The first of the new weapons was the percussion cap, a small thing that made a large difference, because the percussion cap replaced the flintlock's spark with a chemical detonation that worked in the rain and the wind and did not misfire, and the misfire had been the flintlock's great flaw, and the flaw was what the drill had to allow for, and the allowance slowed the fire and complicated the drill, and the percussion cap removed the allowance and simplified the drill and sped the fire, and the speeding was what the nineteenth century's armies were made of.

The second of the new weapons was the rifled musket, and the rifled musket was what changed the line, and the change was what the line could not survive. The smoothbore musket was accurate to perhaps fifty yards and could be fired at a hundred and hit a formation but not a man, and the inaccuracy was what the line was for, because the line was a way of putting enough balls in the air that some would hit something, and the something was a mass and not an individual, and the mass was what the smoothbore could hit. The rifled musket was accurate to three hundred yards and could be fired at a man and hit him, and the accuracy was made possible by the Minié ball, which Claude-Étienne Minié perfected in 1849, and the Minié ball was a hollow-based bullet that expanded into the rifling when the powder exploded behind it, and the expansion let the bullet be loaded easily and still take the rifling, and the easy loading was what made the rifled musket a military weapon, because before the Minié ball a rifle had to be loaded with a mallet and a patch and was too slow to use in line. The Minié ball let the rifled musket be loaded as fast as a smoothbore and fire four times as far, and the four times as far was what killed the line, because a line that could be hit at three hundred yards could not stand in the open and fire at a hundred, and the standing in the open was what the line was, and the line was what the drill was for, and the drill was what the age's soldiers had been made by, and the making was undone by a bullet.

The undoing was done in the American Civil War, and the Civil War is the war that shows the gunpowder age's soldiers being broken by the gunpowder age's weapons. The Civil War's infantry were armed with rifled muskets, the Springfield Model 1861 and the Enfield Pattern 1853, and the rifled muskets were accurate to three hundred yards and more, and the generals who commanded the infantry had been drilled in the old way and did not know what the new weapons could do, and the not knowing was what killed them. The generals attacked in line and in column, and the attacks were the attacks of the gunpowder age, and the attacks were met by fire the gunpowder age had never seen, and the fire was what made the attacks suicide, and the suicide was what the war was, and the war was what the age's soldiers died in.

The numbers of the Civil War are the numbers of the line's death. At Antietam, on the seventeenth of September 1862, some twenty-three thousand men were killed or wounded in a single day, the bloodiest day in American history, and the blood was the blood of the line, because the line was the formation both armies used and the line was the formation the rifled musket destroyed. At Fredericksburg, on the thirteenth of December 1862, the Union army attacked the Confederate line on Marye's Heights, in column and in line, and the attackers were shot down in ranks, and some twelve thousand Union soldiers were killed or wounded, and the Confederate losses were some five thousand, and the disproportion was the disproportion of the new weapon against the old drill, and the disproportion was what the generals could not see, and the not seeing was what the age's soldiers paid for.

What the generals could not see was that the drill had to change, and the change was what the Civil War's soldiers made without the generals, and the making was what the age's settlement about the self was becoming, and the becoming was what the twentieth century inherited. The Civil War's soldiers learned to dig, and the digging was what the line could not do and what the soldiers did anyway, and the entrenchments at Petersburg and at Cold Harbor were what the soldiers built because the line could not stand in the open, and the building was what the soldiers did without orders, and the doing without orders was what the drill had not taught, and the not teaching was where the drill's limit lay. The soldiers who dug were the soldiers who had been drilled, and the digging was what the drill could not supply, and the supplying of it was what the soldiers did for themselves, and the doing for themselves was what the gunpowder age's settlement about the self was turning into, and the turning was what the twentieth century's soldiers inherited, and the inheritance was what made the twentieth century's war what it was.

The Civil War also showed what the industrial revolution had done to the gunpowder age's way of war, and the showing was what the war's numbers were made of. The war was the first in which the railroad moved armies and the telegraph moved orders and the factory moved weapons, and the moving was what made the war big, and the bigness was what the age had never seen, and the bigness was what the age's soldiers could not understand, and the not understanding was what the war's casualties were made of. The Union produced some two million rifles in the war, and the production was what the industrial revolution had made possible, and the production was what the war was fought with, and the fighting was what the production fed, and the feeding was what made the war last four years and kill some six hundred and twenty thousand men, and the number is the number of the gunpowder age's settlement about the self being paid for, and the payment was what the age's soldiers made, and the making was what the age's soldiers were.

The payment was made again in Europe, and the making was what the Crimean War and the Franco-Prussian War and the wars of German unification were, and the making was what the age's soldiers did not learn from, and the not learning was what the twentieth century's soldiers paid for. The Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71 was the war that showed what the new weapons and the new railroads and the new staff work could do, and the showing was what the German army made and the French army did not, and the making was what the war was decided by. The German army had a general staff that planned the war on maps and moved the armies by rail and concentrated them faster than the French could concentrate, and the concentration was what won the war, and the winning was what the age's soldiers had been building toward, and the building was what the drill and the map and the railroad and the telegraph had made, and the making was what the twentieth century inherited, and the inheritance was what the twentieth century's war was made of.

The Franco-Prussian War also showed what the rifled musket and the breech-loading rifle had done to the line, and the showing was what the age's soldiers did not learn, and the not learning was what the First World War was made of. The German needle gun and the French chassepot were breech-loaders that could be fired from prone and reloaded in cover, and the firing from prone and reloading in cover was what the line could not do, and the not doing was the line's death, and the death was what the age's soldiers did not see, and the not seeing was what the age's soldiers paid for. The Franco-Prussian War's battles were fought at ranges the age's drill had never allowed for, and the ranges were what the artillery and the rifles made, and the making was what the age's soldiers did not understand, and the not understanding was what the age's soldiers carried into the twentieth century, and the carrying was what the twentieth century's war was made of.

The carrying was done by the staffs and the schools and the manuals, and the manuals were what the gunpowder age's settlement about the self was written in, and the writing was what the age's soldiers obeyed, and the obeying was what killed them. The manuals of the late nineteenth century were manuals of the line, and the line was what the manuals had been written for, and the writing was what the age's soldiers could not escape, because the manuals were what the drill was, and the drill was what the age's soldiers were, and the being was what the age's soldiers could not see past. The manuals said that the attack was what won battles, and the attack was what the age's soldiers believed in, and the belief was what the age's soldiers carried into the twentieth century, and the carrying was what the twentieth century's war was made of, and the making was what the age's soldiers paid for with their bodies, and the payment was what the age's settlement about the self was, and the settlement was a bargain, and the bargain was the self for the machine, and the machine was what the age's soldiers had made, and the making was what the age's soldiers could not undo.

The machine was the machine gun, and the machine gun was what the industrial revolution did to the gunpowder age's way of war, and the doing was what the age's soldiers could not understand, and the not understanding was what the First World War was made of. Hiram Maxim demonstrated his recoil-operated automatic machine gun in 1884, and the demonstration was what the age's soldiers should have learned from, and the learning was what the age's soldiers did not do, and the not doing was what the age's soldiers paid for. The Maxim gun was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun, and the self-powered was what made it different, because the self-powered gun used the recoil of the fired cartridge to load and fire the next, and the using made the gun automatic, and the automatic made the gun a machine, and the machine was what the age's soldiers had never faced, because the age's soldiers had faced weapons powered by men, and the men could be killed and the weapons silenced, and the machine was powered by itself and could not be silenced until it was destroyed or ran out of ammunition, and the running out was what the machine's enemies could not cause, and the not causing was what the machine was.

The Maxim gun was adopted by the British Army in 1891, and the adoption was what the age's soldiers did, and the doing was what the age's soldiers did not think about, and the not thinking was what the age's soldiers paid for. The Maxim gun was used in the colonial wars, and the using was what the age's soldiers saw, and the seeing was what the age's soldiers did not learn from, because the colonial wars were wars against men who did not have machine guns, and the using was what the age's soldiers thought was the machine gun's only use, and the thinking was what the age's soldiers were wrong about, and the wrongness was what the First World War was made of. The Maxim gun was used at Omdurman in 1898, where Kitchener's army of some twenty-five thousand men with Maxim guns and artillery defeated the Mahdist army of some fifty thousand, and the Mahdists lost some ten thousand killed and the British lost some forty-eight, and the disproportion was the disproportion the machine gun made, and the making was what the age's soldiers saw, and the seeing was what the age's soldiers did not apply to Europe, and the not applying was what the age's soldiers paid for.

The not applying was what the age's soldiers could not help, because the applying would have meant unlearning the drill, and the drill was what the age's soldiers were, and the being was what the age's soldiers could not escape. The drill said that the attack was what won battles, and the attack was what the age's soldiers believed in, and the belief was what the age's soldiers carried into the twentieth century, and the carrying was what the twentieth century's war was made of. The drill said that the line was what the attack was made of, and the line was what the age's soldiers had been drilled in, and the drilling was what the age's soldiers could not undo, and the undoing was what the age's soldiers did not do, and the not doing was what the age's soldiers paid for with their bodies, and the payment was what the age's settlement about the self was, and the settlement was a bargain, and the bargain was the self for the machine, and the machine was what the age's soldiers had made, and the making was what the age's soldiers could not undo.

The First World War was what the age's settlement about the self was broken by, and the breaking was what the twentieth century's soldiers inherited, and the inheritance is what the twenty-first century's soldiers are still living with. The First World War was the war in which the gunpowder age's drill and the gunpowder age's weapons and the gunpowder age's settlement about the self were all brought to the test at once, and the test was what the age's soldiers failed, and the failure was what the age's soldiers paid for with their bodies, and the payment was what the age's settlement about the self was, and the settlement was a bargain, and the bargain was the self for the machine, and the machine was what the age's soldiers had made, and the making was what the age's soldiers could not undo.

The First World War's opening was what the drill had made, and the making was what the drill's failure was. The German army attacked through Belgium in August 1914 with the drill the age had made, and the drill was what the German army was, and the German army was the best-drilled army in Europe, and the drilling was what the German army's victories were made of, and the victories were what the German army expected, and the expectation was what the German army did not survive. The German army's infantry attacked in line and in column, and the attacks were the attacks of the gunpowder age, and the attacks were met by the fire of the French 75 and the British rifle and the machine gun, and the fire was what the attacks could not survive, and the not surviving was what the war was, and the war was what the age's soldiers died in.
