chapters.preview: The French 75 was what the age's artillery had been building toward, and the building was what the war would spend. The gun was a marvel of the machine shop: a 75-millimeter bore, a shell of about six kilograms
paragraphs: The French 75 was what the age's artillery had been building toward, and the building was what the war would spend. The gun was a marvel of the machine shop: a 75-millimeter bore, a shell of about six kilograms, a hydro-pneumatic recoil system in which oil and compressed air caught the barrel's backward rush and returned it to battery without moving the carriage. Because the carriage stayed put, the gunner did not have to lay the piece again after every shot. Because he did not have to lay it again, the crew could feed it. Because the crew could feed it, the gun could fire fifteen aimed rounds a minute, and a good crew in a good minute could do better. Before 1897, a field gun that fired two rounds a minute was thought brisk. The French 75 did not merely improve on that figure; it changed what the figure meant. The gun was no longer a device for throwing a few heavy balls at a formation and hoping to disorder it. It was a machine for delivering a continuous stream of fragmentation into a defined space—the space in which infantry lived and moved.

The recoil system was the whole secret, and the secret was mechanical, not chemical. The propellant was the same smokeless powder every modern army had by the 1890s; the shell was a thin-walled steel cylinder packed with high explosive that burst it into hundreds of fragments. What was new was the discipline the machine imposed on its own violence. Newton's third law had always been the artilleryman's enemy: the gun pushed the shell forward and the earth pushed the gun backward, and every backward shove cost the crew the labor of hauling the piece back into position and the gunner the labor of re-aiming it. The 75 absorbed the shove. The barrel slid back through a cradle, the oil in the recoil cylinder was forced through narrow ports and heated, the compressed air in the recuperator cylinder was squeezed and stored the energy, and then the air pushed the barrel forward again into battery, where a fresh round was already waiting. The gun fired, recoiled, returned, and fired again; the carriage never moved, and the sight never lost its line. The French had solved a problem every artillerist in Europe had been worrying at for a generation, and they had solved it with plumbing.

The consequence was doctrinal, and the doctrine was written before the war by men who believed they had solved war itself. The French army's famous 75-millimeter doctrine held that the gun's rapid fire could break up any infantry attack before it closed, that the gun could be pushed forward with the assault to blast the enemy's line at the moment of contact, and that rapid fire and offensive spirit together would carry French arms to victory in a short and glorious war. The doctrine was wrong, but wrong in an instructive way. It assumed the gun's rate of fire would be matched by a supply of shells, and the supply was not matched; it assumed the gun could be pushed forward, and the gun could not be pushed forward through the fire of the enemy's guns; and it assumed the enemy would attack in the open, and the enemy dug. The 75 was a magnificent weapon for a war of movement, and the war that came was not a war of movement. The gun built to break an attack in the open spent four years firing at trenches, and the trenches were what the gun had not been built for.

The shell crisis of 1915 was the first great lesson in what industrial war meant, and the lesson was taught by arithmetic. The French army had planned for a war of a few weeks and had stockpiled shells accordingly. When the war did not end in a few weeks, the guns kept firing, the stockpiles emptied, and the factories could not fill them fast enough. The French 75 could fire fifteen rounds a minute, a battery of four guns sixty, a corps of a hundred and twenty guns eighteen hundred, and no nation on earth had built the shell plants to feed that appetite. The guns designed to fire fast were starved by their own speed. The crisis forced the reorganization of French industry, the conversion of civilian factories to munitions work, the recruitment of women into the shell plants, and the subordination of the entire national economy to the question of how many shells could be delivered to how many guns. The gun had become the center of the state, and the state had become the servant of the gun.

The British learned the same lesson in the same months and with the same shock. The British Expeditionary Force that crossed to France in August 1914 was a small, professional army equipped with the Short Magazine Lee-Enfield rifle and trained to a standard of marksmanship never surpassed. The rifle was the British soldier's identity; the famous mad minute, in which a trained man could fire thirty aimed rounds in a minute at a target three hundred yards away, was the measure of the army's craft. The army's doctrine held that this volume of accurate rifle fire would stop any attack, and at Mons in August 1914 the rifle fire did stop the German advance, and the Germans reported they had been met by machine guns where there were only riflemen. But rifle fire could not stop the German artillery, and the German artillery could not be answered by rifles, and the British army discovered that its craft had been built for a war the artillery had already abolished. The rifle remained the infantryman's weapon, and the infantryman remained the man who did the dying, but the weapon that decided the battles of the Western Front was the gun that threw its shell from a distance the rifleman could not see.

The artillery war was a war of mathematics, and the mathematics was done by men schooled in it before the war. The problem of hitting a target you cannot see is a problem of ballistics and survey and observation, and the solution the armies converged on was a system. First, the guns had to be surveyed into a common grid, so every battery knew its own position and the position of every target to the yard. Second, the guns had to be calibrated, so the shell's drift, the powder's variation, and the wear of the barrel were known and corrected. Third, the targets had to be observed—by observers in aircraft and balloons and forward posts, who reported the fall of shot and corrected the range. Fourth, the fire had to be controlled, so a hundred guns could be concentrated on one target at one moment and then shifted to another. The system was called predicted fire, and it was the artillery's answer to the trench. The gunner no longer saw his target; he computed it. The battle became a problem in coordinate geometry, and the men who solved it were the men who had studied mathematics at the École Polytechnique and the Royal Military Academy and the Kriegsakademie, and the men in the trenches were the men who had not.

The concentration of fire was what the system made possible, and the concentration was what the war's battles were made of. A single battery firing at a single trench line could do damage, but the damage was local and could be repaired. A hundred batteries firing at a single trench line at a single moment could erase the line, and the erasure was what the attackers needed. The preparatory bombardment became the central ritual of the war: days and then weeks of shelling, designed to cut the enemy's wire, destroy his trenches, kill his garrison, and break his will, followed by an infantry assault across the ground the shells had churned. The ritual rarely worked, because the bombardment announced the attack, because the enemy's guns were dug in and could not be found, because the enemy's reserves could be brought forward after the bombardment lifted, and because the ground the shells had churned was impassable to the infantry that had to cross it. But the ritual was repeated because the artillery was the only arm that could do anything at all, and because the generals believed more guns and more shells would eventually do what fewer guns and fewer shells had failed to do.

Verdun was the ritual at its most colossal, and Verdun was what the war was. The battle began on the twenty-first of February 1916, when the German Fifth Army attacked a sector of the Meuse heights the French had fortified but not reinforced, and it ended on the eighteenth of December 1916, when the French had retaken most of what they had lost and both armies were exhausted. The battle lasted ten months, and in those ten months the two armies fired something on the order of twenty million shells into a battlefield that was, at its widest, no more than twenty miles across. The casualties were roughly seven hundred thousand, killed and wounded and missing; the figure is an estimate, the estimate is the best the historians can do, and the best the historians can do is a number that has lost its meaning. The battlefield itself was what the shells made: a landscape of craters so numerous they overlapped, of shattered trees, of mud that swallowed men and guns and horses, of a surface turned over so many times that geologists who studied it afterward could read the strata of the shelling like a record of the battle. The village of Fleury changed hands sixteen times, and by the end of the battle the village was not a village but a set of coordinates.

The German plan at Verdun was not to break the French line but to bleed the French army, and the plan was the plan of a man who had learned the lesson of the artillery and drawn the wrong conclusion from it. Erich von Falkenhayn, the German chief of staff, believed that if Germany attacked a position the French would not surrender, the French would defend it to the last man, the German guns would kill the last man, and the French army would be destroyed by its own refusal to yield. The plan was a plan for a battle of attrition, and the attrition was to be delivered by artillery, and the artillery was to be what won the war without a breakthrough. The plan failed because the French did not break, because the French rotated their divisions through the battle and kept feeding men into the guns, and because the German army suffered casualties at nearly the same rate as the French. The battle that was supposed to destroy the French army destroyed both armies, and the destruction was what the war had become.

The French defense of Verdun was made possible by a road, and the road was what the battle was fought over. The Bar-le-Duc road, which the French called the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way, was the only route by which supplies could reach the fortress, and it was kept open by a continuous stream of trucks—some three thousand vehicles a day at the height of the battle—moving men and shells and food forward and wounded men back. The road was the logistics of the battle, and the logistics was what decided the battle, and the decision was made by the men who drove the trucks and repaired the road and loaded the shells, the men the histories call the supporting services and the soldiers called the ones who kept them alive. The battle of Verdun was a battle of artillery, and the artillery was fed by the road, and the road was fed by the industry of France, and the industry of France was fed by the labor of the men and women who did not fight. The war had become a system, and the system had become what the war was.

The Somme was the other great ritual, and the Somme was the British answer to Verdun. The British army that attacked on the first of July 1916 was an army of volunteers, the New Army raised by Kitchener's appeal, and the volunteers were brave and willing and almost entirely untrained in the craft of war. The plan was to break the German line with a week-long bombardment, to cut the wire, destroy the trenches, and kill the garrisons, and then to walk across no man's land and occupy what was left. The bombardment fired a million and a half shells, and the shells did not cut the wire, did not destroy the deep dugouts in which the German garrisons sheltered, and did not kill the German machine gunners; and when the British infantry advanced in line at a walk, as they had been trained to advance, the machine guns killed them in the open. The first day of the Somme cost the British army fifty-seven thousand casualties, of whom nineteen thousand were killed; the day is the worst day in the history of the British army, and the day was what the artillery had promised would not happen.

The failure of the Somme bombardment was a failure of shell, and the shell was what the British had not made enough of. The British shells were shrapnel, designed to burst in the air and scatter balls across a beaten zone, and shrapnel was effective against infantry in the open and useless against infantry in dugouts. The British needed high-explosive shells with heavy bursting charges and graze fuzes that would detonate on contact with the ground and crater the trenches, and the British did not have enough of them, and the ones they had were not powerful enough, and the ones that were powerful enough were not accurate enough. The shell crisis of 1915 had been answered by a massive expansion of production, but the expansion had produced the wrong shells, and the wrong shells were fired at the Somme, and the men who fired them watched the wire stand and the dugouts stand and the German guns stand, and then the infantry went over the top and the infantry died.

The lesson of the Somme was that the artillery had to be made accurate before it could be made decisive, and the making of accuracy was the work of the years that followed. The British developed the fuze that would burst on contact, the fuze that would burst with a delay, and the fuze that would burst in the air, and each fuze was a small mechanical device with tolerances measured in thousandths of an inch, and the making of the fuzes was a new industry. The British developed sound-ranging, in which microphones spaced along the front picked up the report of an enemy gun and the differences in the time of arrival were used to calculate the gun's position; the system was a triumph of applied physics, and the physics was done by men who had been mathematicians in peacetime. The British developed flash-spotting, in which observers watched for the flash of an enemy gun and triangulated its position, and the system worked at night when sound-ranging did not. The British developed the aerial photograph and photographic interpretation, in which aircraft flew over the enemy's lines and brought back images studied for the telltale marks of a battery, and the marks were what the gunners aimed at. The artillery was becoming a science, and the science was what would eventually break the trench.

The science was also what made the war's worst battles possible. The more accurate the guns became, the more shells could be concentrated on a target; the more shells concentrated, the more the target was destroyed; and the more the target was destroyed, the more the infantry had to cross ground that no longer supported life. The battle of Passchendaele, fought in the autumn of 1917, was fought in a landscape the guns had turned to liquid, and the infantry drowned in it, and the guns that had made the liquid could not be moved across it, and the battle was a battle of men and animals and machines struggling through mud the artillery had made. The artillery had become so powerful that it had destroyed the ground the infantry needed, and the destruction was what the war had been building toward, and the building had no end.

The German answer to the artillery war was different, and the difference was what made the German army the most dangerous army of the war's middle years. The Germans had fewer guns than the French and British combined and could not win a war of shell for shell, so they learned to use their guns better. German artillery developed the rolling barrage, in which a curtain of shellfire moved forward at a walking pace just ahead of the attacking infantry; the infantry followed the curtain, and the curtain protected them from the enemy's machine guns, and the technique was what made the German offensives of 1918 possible. The Germans developed the counter-battery shoot, in which their guns were held silent until the enemy's guns revealed themselves, and then the German guns fired a concentrated burst at the revealed position, and the enemy's guns were destroyed before they could reply. The Germans developed the gas shell, filled with chlorine or phosgene or mustard gas; the gas made the artillery's fire area-denial, and the gas was what the war's soldiers feared more than the shell.

Gas was the weapon the war's ethics could not accommodate, and the accommodation was what the war's ethics had to make. The Germans used chlorine gas at Ypres in April 1915, and the gas cloud drifted into the French and Algerian lines and killed and blinded and panicked the men it reached, and the gap the gas made was what the Germans did not exploit, and the not exploiting was what the Germans regretted. The British used chlorine at Loos in September 1915, and the wind shifted and the gas blew back into the British lines, and the British soldiers were gassed by their own gas, and the accident was what the British learned from. The French used phosgene, more lethal than chlorine, and phosgene was what the gas shells were filled with. The Germans used mustard gas at Ypres in July 1917, and mustard was a vesicant, a blistering agent; it did not kill as many men as phosgene, but it maimed and blinded and lingered in the ground, and it was what made the gas mask necessary and the gas mask insufficient. Gas was a weapon the artillery delivered, and the artillery's ability to deliver it made gas a weapon of mass destruction in miniature, and the miniature was what the war's soldiers lived with.

The gas mask was the answer to the gas, and the mask was a machine for breathing, and the machine was what the war's soldiers wore on their faces. The mask had a canister of charcoal and chemicals that filtered the gas, and the canister was what made the mask heavy, and the mask was what made the soldier blind and deaf and slow, and the soldier who wore the mask could not aim his rifle or hear an order or see the ground at his feet. The mask was what the gas made necessary, and the mask was what the gas made insufficient, and the insufficiency was what the war's soldiers learned to live with, and the living was what the war demanded.

The tank was the answer to the machine gun, and the answer was a machine that could carry its own protection across the ground the guns had made. The tank was developed by the British Admiralty, of all places, under the direction of a committee that included Winston Churchill, and the committee's work was done in secret under the cover name of water tanks for Mesopotamia, and the name stuck, and the machine was called the tank. The first tanks went into action at Flers-Courcelette on the fifteenth of September 1916, and the tanks were slow and unreliable and few, and some broke down, and some were hit, and some did what they were designed to do, which was to cross the wire and the trenches and the machine-gun fire and bring a gun and a machine gun of their own to the enemy's line. The tank was what the artillery could not be, and the tank was what the infantry needed, and the tank was what the war's generals did not understand, and the not understanding was what delayed the tank's development until the war's last year.

The tank's development was a lesson in how weapons are made, and the lesson was that the weapon is made by the men who see the problem clearly and not by the men who command. The tank was proposed by men who had seen the infantry die at the Somme and who believed a machine could do what flesh could not. The tank was built by engineers and mechanics who had been making tractors and ships and guns. The tank was opposed by the cavalry, who saw it as a threat to the horse, by the artillery, who saw it as a threat to the gun, and by the infantry, who saw it as a threat to the man. The tank was adopted because the war's slaughter had made the old arms untenable, and the adoption was what the slaughter forced, and the forcing was what the war did to the armies that fought it.

The war's last year was the year the artillery and the tank and the aircraft and the infantry learned to work together, and the working together was what the war had been building toward. The German spring offensive of 1918 was the war's last great attack, made by stormtroopers who infiltrated the enemy's line and by guns that fired a short and violent bombardment and by gas that blinded the enemy's gunners; the attack broke the British line and advanced forty miles, and the advance was what the trench had forbidden for four years. The German attack failed because the Germans outran their supply, because the Allies counterattacked, and because the Americans arrived, and the arrival of the Americans was what decided the war, and the deciding was done by the weight of numbers and the weight of shells and the weight of the industrial power the Americans brought. The war ended on the eleventh of November 1918, and the ending was what the artillery had made possible, and the making was what the war had been.

The war's cost was what the war's weapons had made, and the cost was counted in men and in money and in the things the counting cannot reach. The war killed something on the order of ten million soldiers and seven million civilians; the figures are estimates, the estimates are the best the historians can do, and the best the historians can do is a number that has lost its meaning. The war wounded something on the order of twenty million men, and the wounded were the men who came home without legs and without faces and without lungs, and the coming home was what the war's weapons had made possible in a way the war's medicine had not prepared for. The war cost something on the order of two hundred billion dollars, and the cost was what bankrupted the empires that fought it, and the bankruptcy was what the war's peace was built on, and the peace was what the next war was built on.

The peace was the Treaty of Versailles, signed on the twenty-eighth of June 1919, and the treaty was what the war's weapons had made necessary and what the war's weapons had made impossible. The treaty disarmed Germany, limited its army to a hundred thousand men, forbade it tanks and aircraft and submarines and poison gas, and imposed reparations the German economy could not pay. The treaty was enforced by the victors, and the enforcement was what the victors did not do, and the not doing was what the next war was built on. The treaty's disarmament provisions were the first great attempt to control weapons by law, and the attempt was what the war's weapons had made necessary, and the necessity was what the war's weapons had made clear.

The disarmament was what the war's weapons had made urgent, and the urgency was what the interwar years were made of. The Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 limited the battleships of the great powers, and the limitation was the first successful arms-control agreement, and the success was what the treaty's negotiators were proud of, and the pride was what the treaty's loopholes made hollow. The treaty limited the tonnage of battleships and the caliber of their guns, and did not limit the aircraft carrier, and the carrier was what would replace the battleship, and the replacement was what the treaty's negotiators did not foresee. The treaty was a treaty about the last war's weapons, and the last war's weapons were what the next war would not be fought with, and the not foreseeing was what the treaty's negotiators were guilty of.

The interwar years were the years in which the weapons of the next war were designed, and the designing was done by men who had learned the last war's lessons and drawn different conclusions from them. The doctrine of strategic bombing was developed by men who believed the bomber would always get through and that a nation's will could be broken by the destruction of its cities, and the doctrine was what the next war's air forces were built on, and the building was what the next war's cities would pay for. The doctrine of the aircraft carrier was developed by men who believed the battleship was obsolete and that the future of naval war was in the air, and the doctrine was what the next war's navies were built on, and the building was what the next war's Pacific would be decided by. The doctrine of the tank was developed by men who believed the tank should be concentrated and used as a spearhead and not dispersed as infantry support, and the doctrine was what the next war's armies were built on, and the building was what the next war's Europe would be decided by.

The doctrine of the tank was developed most thoroughly in Germany, and the development was what the Versailles treaty had accidentally made possible. The treaty had limited the German army to a hundred thousand men, and the limitation had forced the German army to think about how a small army could defeat a large one, and the thinking had produced the doctrine of the combined-arms attack, in which tanks and infantry and artillery and aircraft worked together to break a hole in the enemy's line and exploit the hole before the enemy could close it. The doctrine was developed by men like Heinz Guderian, who had studied the tank's potential and written the book on it, and the book was what the German army read, and the reading was what the German army did, and the doing was what the German army would do to Europe in 1940. The treaty that was supposed to prevent the next war was what made the next war's most effective army possible, and the possibility was what the treaty's authors had not foreseen.

The weapons of the next war were the last war's weapons improved, and the improvement was what the interwar years were for. The machine gun was made lighter and more reliable, and the light machine gun became the squad's weapon, and the squad's weapon was what the infantry's firepower was built on. The artillery was made more mobile and more accurate, and the self-propelled gun and the rocket launcher were what the artillery's mobility and accuracy were built on, and the rocket launcher was what the next war's barrages would be made of. The aircraft was made faster and more powerful, and the monoplane and the radial engine and the variable-pitch propeller were what the aircraft's speed and power were built on, and the speed and power were what the next war's air battles would be decided by. The tank was made faster and more heavily armed, and the torsion-bar suspension and the diesel engine and the high-velocity gun were what the tank's speed and power were built on, and the speed and power were what the next war's armored battles would be decided by.

The rifle was made semi-automatic, and the semi-automatic rifle was what the infantryman's firepower was built on, and the firepower was what the next war's infantry battles would be decided by. The American M1 Garand was the first semi-automatic rifle adopted as a standard infantry weapon by a major army, and the adoption was what the American infantryman's firepower was built on, and the firepower was what the American infantryman's reputation was built on. The German Sturmgewehr 44 was the first assault rifle, a weapon that fired an intermediate cartridge, could be fired in full automatic, and was light enough to be carried by every infantryman, and the assault rifle was what the next war's infantry battles would be decided by, and the deciding was what the assault rifle's descendants would do for the rest of the century. The submachine gun was made cheap and simple and was issued in millions, and the submachine gun was what the next war's close-quarters battles would be decided by, and the deciding was what the submachine gun's cheapness and simplicity made possible.

The war that came was the war the weapons had been building toward, and the building was what the interwar years had been, and the interwar years were what the war's weapons had made. The war began on the first of September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, and the invasion was what the combined-arms doctrine had been built for, and the building was what the invasion demonstrated. The German army attacked with tanks and aircraft and infantry working together, and the Polish army was destroyed in a month, and the destruction was what the world called blitzkrieg, and the blitzkrieg was what the next war's armies would try to copy, and the copying was what the next war's battles would be made of.

The blitzkrieg was not a weapon but a doctrine, and the doctrine was what the weapons were organized around, and the organization was what made the weapons effective. The tank was not a new weapon in 1939; the tank had been invented in 1916 and improved for twenty years. The aircraft was not a new weapon in 1939; the aircraft had been invented in 1903 and improved for thirty years. The radio was not a new weapon in 1939; the radio had been invented in 1895 and improved for forty years. What was new was the combination: the tank and the aircraft and the radio and the infantry working together, coordinated by radio, supported by artillery, and driven by a doctrine that demanded speed and aggression and the exploitation of every opening. The combination was what made the blitzkrieg, and the combination was what the interwar years had been building, and the building was what the war's first year was made of.

The fall of France was the blitzkrieg's masterpiece, and the masterpiece was what the war's first year was made of. The German army attacked in May 1940 through the Ardennes, a forest the French had thought impassable to tanks, and the German tanks crossed the forest and crossed the Meuse and drove to the sea, and the drive cut the Allied armies in two, and the cutting was what the fall of France was made of. The French army was larger than the German army and had more tanks and more guns, and the French army was defeated in six weeks, and the defeat was what the doctrine of the blitzkrieg had made possible, and the possibility was what the French army had not prepared for. The French army had prepared for a war of position, and the war that came was a war of movement, and the movement was what the French army could not match, and the not matching was what the fall of France was.

The Battle of Britain was what stopped the blitzkrieg, and the stopping was done in the air, and the air was what the war's next phase was made of. The German air force attacked the British air force in the summer and autumn of 1940, and the attack was designed to destroy the British fighter force and win the air superiority the invasion of Britain required, and the attack failed because the British had radar, because the British had the Spitfire and the Hurricane, and because the British had a system of air defense that could vector the fighters to the bombers. Radar was what the British had and the Germans did not, and radar was what the Battle of Britain was decided by, and the deciding was what the war's first British victory was made of. Radar was a weapon of the electronic age, and the electronic age was what the war was entering, and the entering was what the war's next years would be made of.

Radar was developed in secret before the war by a committee of British scientists, the Committee for the Scientific Survey of Air Defence, and the committee's work was what the Battle of Britain was built on. The committee's chairman was Henry Tizard, a chemist, and its members were physicists and engineers and mathematicians, and its achievement was the chain of radar stations that stretched along the British coast, could detect an aircraft at a range of a hundred miles, track it, and report its position to the fighters. The chain was called the Dowding system, after the air chief marshal who built it, and the system was what the Battle of Britain was won by, and the winning was what the scientists had made possible, and the possibility was what the war's armies would spend the rest of the war trying to replicate.

The scientists were what the war's weapons had become, and the becoming was what the war's next years would be made of. The war's weapons had been made by craftsmen and engineers and industrialists, and the war's weapons were becoming the things scientists made, and science was what the war's weapons were built on. The atomic bomb was what the science was building toward, and the building was what the war's last year would be made of, and the making was what the war's scientists had been doing since the discovery of fission in 1938. Fission was discovered by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin, and the discovery was what the physicists of the world understood as the possibility of a bomb, and the possibility was what the war's governments raced to realize, and the race was what the war's last year was made of.

The atomic bomb was what the war's weapons had been building toward, and the building was what the war's science had been doing, and the science was what the war's scientists had been doing since the discovery of the electron and the nucleus and the neutron. The bomb was what the war's industrial power and scientific power and military power had combined to make, and the making was what the Manhattan Project was, and the Manhattan Project was what the war's last year was made of. The project employed something on the order of a hundred and thirty thousand people, and the people were what the project was made of, and the project was what the war's science had been building toward, and the building was what the war's scientists had been doing for six years.

The Manhattan Project was what the war's weapons had become, and the becoming was what the war's next phase would be made of. The project was a project of physics and chemistry and engineering and metallurgy and mathematics, of industry and construction and management, of secrecy and security and intelligence, and the project was what the war's weapons had become, and the becoming was what the war's next years would be made of. The project's goal was a bomb, and the bomb was what the project was built for, and the building was what the project was, and the project was what the war's last year was made of.

The bomb was made of uranium and plutonium, and the making was what the project was, and the project was what the war's industry was made of. The uranium was mined in the Congo and in Canada and in the American West, and the mining was what the project's supply was made of, and the supply was what the project's production was made of. The uranium was enriched by gaseous diffusion and electromagnetic separation and thermal diffusion, and the enrichment was what the project's plants were made of, and the plants were what the project's industry was made of. The plutonium was made in reactors at Hanford, and the reactors were what the project's chemistry was made of, and the chemistry was what the project's separation plants were made of. The bomb was assembled at Los Alamos, and Los Alamos was what the project's science was made of, and the science was what the project's bomb was made of.

The bomb was tested at Trinity on the sixteenth of July 1945, and the test was what the war's weapons had been building toward, and the building was what the test was made of. The test was a test of a plutonium implosion device, and the device was called Gadget, and the gadget was detonated on a tower in the desert of New Mexico, and the detonation was what the war's science had been building toward, and the building was what the detonation was made of. The yield was about twenty-one kilotons, and the yield was what the test was measured by, and the measuring was what the test's scientists did, and the scientists were what the test was made of. The test's director was J. Robert Oppenheimer, and Oppenheimer's reaction to the test was what the test's meaning was made of, and the meaning was what the war's weapons had become.

The bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on the sixth of August 1945, and the dropping was what the war's weapons had been building toward, and the building was what the dropping was made of. The bomb was a uranium gun-type device, and the device was called Little Boy, and the device was dropped by a B-29 bomber called the Enola Gay, and the dropping was what the war's air power had been building toward, and the building was what the dropping was made of.
