paragraphs: The plutonium implosion bomb designated Fat Man was dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, three days after Little Boy, a gun-type uranium device, was dropped on Hiroshima. The gun-type design had never been tested as a complete weapon; its mechanism was considered so certain that Los Alamos did not assemble a full unit for a proof test. The implosion design, by contrast, had been validated at Trinity on 16 July 1945. That asymmetry—one bomb tested, one not—shaped how each was fielded: the untested weapon was released without a rehearsal, the tested one with confidence in its physics but not in its delivery.

The three-day interval was an accident of weather rather than a decision of the war's leadership. The second mission had been scheduled for 11 August; a forecast of poor conditions over the target moved it forward to 9 August. The primary target was Kokura, but smoke obscured the city, and the B-29 Bockscar diverted to the secondary, Nagasaki. Cloud there ruled out visual bombing, so the crew dropped by radar. The bomb detonated roughly a mile and a half from the aim point, and the miss—together with the city's hilly topography—confined the blast in ways that shaped the casualty toll.

Estimates of the dead remain contested. At Nagasaki, roughly 40,000 to 70,000 people had died by the end of 1945; at Hiroshima, roughly 70,000 to 140,000. The ranges reflect disagreement over the treatment of missing persons, radiation deaths, and the reliability of Japanese census data, and historians continue to debate the figures. Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on 15 August 1945, and the instrument of surrender was signed aboard the battleship Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September. The war was over.

The war's end did not halt weapons development. The Manhattan Project had employed roughly 130,000 people at its peak and cost roughly two billion dollars—an industrial and scientific mobilization that continued into the postwar period, when the laboratories, production plants, and scientific cadres built during the war were redirected to new designs. The scientists who had built the bomb did not decide its use. A group led by James Franck petitioned against a demonstration-free attack on a populated city, and Leo Szilard circulated a further petition; neither altered the decision, which rested with President Truman and his advisers. The same scientists were then recruited into the next program, and some of those who had petitioned against the use of the first bomb petitioned against the development of the next. The petitions again did not determine policy; the hydrogen bomb was authorized by Truman on 31 January 1950.

The Soviet Union tested its first atomic device, First Lightning (RDS-1), on 29 August 1949 at Semipalatinsk. It was a plutonium implosion weapon closely resembling the American Fat Man, a resemblance that owed much to espionage. Soviet intelligence, through sources including Klaus Fuchs at Los Alamos and the Rosenberg network, obtained design information that shortened the Soviet program's path; historians debate how much of the Soviet success should be attributed to the stolen designs and how much to independent Soviet physics, but the similarity of RDS-1 to Fat Man is not in dispute. The American response was the hydrogen bomb. Fusion, rather than the fission of the earlier weapons, was its mechanism, and the arms race now ran on thermonuclear yields.

The first American thermonuclear test, Ivy Mike, was conducted on 1 November 1952 at Eniwetok Atoll in the Marshall Islands. Its yield was roughly 10 megatons, some five hundred times that of Trinity. Ivy Mike was a stationary device, not a deliverable weapon; the subsequent task was to shrink the design to a bomb that an aircraft could carry. The Soviet Union tested its first thermonuclear device in 1953, and the British tested their first atomic bomb in 1952—Operation Hurricane, in the Monte Bello Islands off Australia—followed by a hydrogen bomb in 1957. The British program drew on the wartime Quebec Agreement and postwar cooperation with the United States, though cooperation lapsed after the war and resumed only in 1958. France tested its first atomic bomb in 1960—Gerboise Bleue, in the Algerian Sahara—and its first hydrogen bomb in 1968; the French program was shaped by American wartime assistance and by the postwar alliance, though France developed its weapons largely independently after the war. China tested its first atomic bomb in 1964—Project 596, at Lop Nur in Xinjiang—and its first hydrogen bomb in 1967; the Chinese program was shaped by early Soviet technical assistance, which ended with the Sino-Soviet split of 1960.

Proliferation was not halted by the war's end. The arms race drove the development of delivery systems: bombers first, then missiles. The intercontinental ballistic missile, defined by range, became the centerpiece of the competition. The Soviet Union tested the first ICBM, the R-7, in 1957, and the same rocket launched Sputnik on 4 October 1957. Sputnik's launch drove the American response, and the perception of a "missile gap"—the belief, later shown to be exaggerated, that the Soviets held a decisive lead in ICBMs—shaped the funding and urgency of the American program. Minuteman, a solid-fueled missile, was developed for rapid launch and deployed in hardened silos for survivability; the silo, in turn, was a response to the vulnerability of earlier liquid-fueled missiles. The submarine-launched ballistic missile added a mobile leg to the deterrent, and the nuclear submarine—the USS Nautilus, commissioned in 1954, was the first—gave the missile endurance and concealment. Together these formed the triad of bombers, land-based missiles, and ballistic missile submarines, which became the structure of deterrence.

The bomber leg rested on intercontinental range, and the B-52, powered by jet engines, provided it. The jet engine had been developed during the war, and the German jet fighter program produced the Messerschmitt Me 262, the first operational jet fighter, which entered service in 1944. The Me 262's development was constrained by German industry's shortages and by Hitler's insistence that it be used as a bomber, and its effect on the war was limited; its significance for the postwar lay in the jet technology it demonstrated, which shaped aircraft development in both the United States and the Soviet Union.

Strategic bombing was the war's most extensive use of air power. The Royal Air Force bombed German cities by night, the United States Army Air Forces by day, and the B-29 bombed Japan from bases in the Marianas. The B-29's range made the Marianas campaign possible, and the same aircraft carried the atomic bombs: the Enola Gay, a B-29, dropped Little Boy on Hiroshima. The strategic bombing campaigns shaped the war's end, and the atomic bombings were their culmination. This is the section's central thesis: the atomic bombings fulfilled the trajectory of wartime weapons development—the pursuit of decisive aerial destruction of cities and industry—rather than diverging from it. The bombing campaigns against Germany and Japan had already made civilian populations and urban industry the targets of air power; the atomic bombings continued that logic with a single weapon. Where the bombings diverged was not in their target but in their scale and in the political shock they produced, which shaped the postwar order. Historians debate the causation of the surrender—whether the atomic bombings, the Soviet declaration of war on 8 August, or the cumulative pressure of blockade and conventional bombing was decisive—and the casualty estimates remain contested; the bombings' place in the trajectory of wartime weapons development, however, is clear.

chapters.title: Part 12
chapters.preview: The development of weapons cannot be told in a straight line, because the things themselves do not travel in straight lines. They loop, they stall, they get reinvented on the far side of a mountain range by peo
paragraphs: The development of weapons cannot be told in a straight line, because the things themselves do not travel in straight lines. They loop, they stall, they get reinvented on the far side of a mountain range by people who have never heard of the first invention, and then the branches meet again and one turns out to have been the dead end all along. Part 12 takes up one of those loops and follows it through the whole of the ancient world, because the loop is the argument: the weapons that decided the great battles of the classical Mediterranean were not the products of a smooth ascent from stone to iron to steel, but of a long, grinding, often interrupted negotiation between what a society could make, what it could feed, and what it could persuade its men to do while other men were trying to kill them.

Begin with the simplest thing a soldier can carry: a stick with a point. The spear is so old that it has no inventor, and so persistent that it outlasted nearly every weapon invented to replace it. The Egyptian infantry of the New Kingdom carried spears with leaf-shaped bronze heads and wooden shafts; the Greek hoplite carried the dory, eight to nine feet of ash or cornel wood with an iron head at one end and a bronze butt-spike at the other. The butt-spike was not decoration. It let the hoplite plant the spear against a cavalry charge, finish a fallen enemy without turning around, and balance the weapon so it could be held steady through the long minutes before the lines closed. A weapon is always more than its killing part. The dory was a system: a shaft of a particular wood, a head of a particular iron, a spike of a particular bronze, a grip bound in a particular way, and a man trained from boyhood to hold the whole assembly at the right height and angle while other men screamed at him. Take away any piece and the system fails.

The Greeks did not invent the phalanx, but they made it into an argument about citizenship. A hoplite furnished his own equipment, which meant the men in the front ranks were men of property, and the depth of the formation was a statement about who counted. At Marathon in 490 BCE the Athenian line was thin in the center and thick on the wings—a deliberate arrangement that let the wings envelop the Persian flanks while the center gave ground. The Persians had archers, cavalry, and far more money, and they lost. The lesson the Greeks took from Marathon was not that spears beat bows but that disciplined heavy infantry, standing together, could beat a larger force in looser order. It was a lesson about organization as much as metal, and it was repeated at Plataea the next year, where the Spartans and their allies broke the Persian army in a long, ugly, confused fight in which the decisive weapon was probably not the spear at all but the willingness of the line to hold while it was being killed.

The Persians had their own answer, worth pausing on because it shows how a weapon's development is shaped by the kind of empire that fields it. The Achaemenid army was a coalition army. It drew contingents from satrapies across Anatolia, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Iranian plateau, and each fought in its own way with its own equipment. The Persians contributed cavalry, the Medes cavalry and infantry, the Egyptians heavy infantry with great rectangular shields, the Bactrians archers, the Indians elephants. This was a system built for an empire that ruled many peoples and needed each to fight as it knew how. It was flexible and enormous, and also slow to concentrate and hard to coordinate, and against a compact, homogeneous, highly trained phalanx it could be beaten in detail. The Persian answer to the phalanx, when they finally got a good one, was not a better spear but a different kind of soldier: the Cardaces, young men trained to fight as hoplites, and later the Greek mercenaries the satraps hired in numbers. When a weapon system is embedded in a social order, the way to beat it is often to import the social order—or at least the training—and the Persians understood this.

Then comes Philip of Macedon, the sarissa, and what happens when a military reformer decides the phalanx has been built too short. The sarissa was a pike of perhaps fifteen to eighteen feet, held in both hands, with the first five or six ranks projecting their points beyond the front of the formation. Holding a sarissa takes both hands, so you cannot carry a big round shield on your arm; you carry a smaller shield slung from shoulder or neck, which means the man in front of you is your protection. The sarissa phalanx was therefore more collective than the hoplite phalanx, and also more fragile, because a formation of men holding eighteen-foot pikes cannot easily turn, break, or fight on broken ground. Philip and Alexander used it as one part of a combined-arms system: the phalanx fixed the enemy, the Companion cavalry delivered the decisive blow, light troops and archers and slingers screened and harassed, and a commander who rode with the cavalry could see the battle and coordinate the whole. At Gaugamela in 331 BCE Alexander drew up his line to refuse his left and drive his right into a gap that opened in the Persian line—a gap that opened because the Persian cavalry had been drawn off to the left. The sarissa made the Persian center immovable, the cavalry made the Persian flank movable, and the combination broke Darius.

The Romans watched all of this and then did something that looks, from a distance, like a step backward. They abandoned the phalanx for the manipular legion: small units, the maniples, drawn up in three lines—hastati in front, principes behind them, triarii behind them—each maniple with gaps between it and its neighbors, the whole line able to open and close like a set of teeth. The Roman soldier carried a sword, the gladius, two javelins, the pila, and a large curved shield, the scutum. The gladius was short, about two feet, designed for stabbing rather than cutting, and used at close quarters after the pila had been thrown. The pilum was clever: a wooden shaft with a long iron shank and a small pyramidal point, the shank soft enough to bend on impact, so the pilum stuck in a shield and could not be thrown back, and the man carrying the shield had to drop it or drag it. The legionary's equipment was a system for getting close to an enemy and killing him at a distance of two feet, and the manipular formation was a system for getting him close without being broken by a phalanx or a cavalry charge.

Why did the Romans abandon the phalanx? Polybius, who was in a position to know, says the phalanx could not fight on rough ground, and the legion was more flexible, could be reinforced, could fight in small groups. True as far as it goes, but it misses the deeper point: the legion was a weapon system that matched the kind of army Rome could raise. Rome's army was a militia of citizen farmers, and the manipular system let a line of citizen soldiers, each fighting with his own equipment and initiative, hold together against a more rigid enemy. The phalanx required one kind of training and social discipline; the legion required another, one that rewarded individual aggression within a collective frame. The Romans did not choose the legion because it was better in the abstract. They chose it because it was better for them, and then spent three centuries proving it against the phalanx—at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE and at Pydna in 168 BCE, where the Macedonian phalanx actually broke the Roman line at first and then lost because it could not keep formation on broken ground and the Romans got in among the pikes.

The Roman case is worth dwelling on because it shows how a weapon system becomes an institution. The gladius, the scutum, and the pilum were not just tools; they were the material expression of a way of organizing men. The legion had a standard, the eagle, a religion of discipline, and a system of rewards and punishments that made the individual soldier's courage a public matter. When Marius reformed the army at the end of the second century BCE and allowed the landless poor to enlist, the weapon system did not change much, but the relationship between soldier and state did, and the legions became a political instrument that could march on Rome. The weapons were the same; the thing they were embedded in had changed, and the change was decisive. This is a pattern that will recur: the decisive development is often not the weapon but the institution that holds it.

Now move east, and follow the loop. The Chinese had been developing a different kind of weapon system, based on the crossbow and the mass infantry army, shaped by a different set of problems: the steppe frontier, the great river valleys, the need to mobilize enormous numbers of men for sieges and campaigns against nomad cavalry. The crossbow stores energy in a bent bow and releases it through a trigger, and it has one great advantage over the ordinary bow: it can be held at full draw indefinitely, so a line of crossbowmen can wait for the order to shoot, and it can be taught in a few weeks rather than a lifetime. The Qin and Han armies used crossbows in enormous numbers, and the trigger mechanisms were precision bronze castings made to interchangeable specifications—a fact worth sitting with: the Chinese were mass-producing precision components for weapons more than two thousand years before the industrial revolution.

The crossbow's weakness is its rate of fire. A good archer can loose ten or twelve arrows a minute; a crossbowman with a windlass or belt-hook might manage two or three. The Chinese answer was to put crossbowmen in ranks that fired in sequence, so a continuous stream of bolts came off the line, and to protect them with spearmen and shields. This is the same problem the English would solve with the longbow and the musketeers with volley fire, and it is worth noticing that the solution is almost always organizational rather than mechanical. You do not need a better bow to get a continuous stream of missiles; you need a better drill.

The Chinese also developed the weapon that would eventually become the thing this book is about, and it is important to be precise about when and how. Gunpowder was not invented as an explosive. The earliest recipes, in the Wujing Zongyao of 1044, combine saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal in proportions relatively low in nitrate, and the resulting mixture burns rather than detonates. It was used for incendiaries, smoke, and fire-arrows, and the military problem it solved was setting things on fire at a distance. The shift to a true explosive required a higher proportion of saltpeter, and that shift happened gradually over the twelfth and thirteenth centuries; the first metal-barreled firearms appear in the archaeological record in the late thirteenth century. The Heilongjiang hand cannon, dated by inscription to 1288, is a bronze tube with a touch-hole—a projectile weapon, not an incendiary. The loop from the fire-lance to the hand cannon took roughly two hundred years, driven by trial and error by people who did not know they were inventing explosives. They were trying to make a better fire weapon, and they made a gun.

This matters for the argument because it shows that the development of weapons is not a process of realizing a predetermined end. Nobody in 1044 was trying to invent the cannon. They were trying to solve a tactical problem, and the solution they found had consequences they could not have imagined. The same is true of the crossbow, the stirrup, the longbow, and every other weapon in this book. The weapon is a solution to a problem, the problem is always local, and the consequences are always global.

Now go back west, to the thing the Romans could not solve, which was the horse. The Roman army was an infantry army, its cavalry auxiliary and second-rate, and this was a structural weakness the Romans knew about and could not fix, because the kind of cavalry that could break an infantry line required a kind of social organization Rome did not have. The Parthians had it. At Carrhae in 53 BCE, a Roman army under Crassus was destroyed by a Parthian force that was almost entirely cavalry, and the destruction was accomplished by a weapon system the Romans had never seen: the horse archer, supported by the cataphract. The horse archer could ride up to a Roman line, loose arrows, and ride away before the legionaries could close, and the legionaries could not catch him because they were on foot and he was on a horse. The cataphract was a cavalryman in scale armor on a horse in scale armor, and his job was to charge home once the horse archers had disordered the enemy. The combination was deadly because it was a system: the horse archers wore the enemy down, the cataphracts broke him, and the whole thing was possible because the Parthian nobility had the horses, the pasture, and the leisure to train for a lifetime.

The Romans never solved the Parthian problem, and neither did the Byzantines, and neither did anyone else until the invention of gunpowder. The steppe cavalryman was the dominant military system of Eurasia for more than a thousand years, and he was dominant because he combined mobility, firepower, and shock in a way no infantry army could match. The Huns, the Avars, the Magyars, the Mongols, and the Turks all used variants of the same system, and they all beat infantry armies that were larger and better equipped. The reason is not that the horse archer was a better soldier. The reason is that the horse archer was a better system, embedded in a way of life no settled society could copy. You cannot train a peasant to be a horse archer in a few months. You have to start him as a child, give him horses and pasture and the leisure to hunt, and make him part of a society that values the skills he is learning. The weapon is not the bow. The weapon is the whole steppe.

This is the point Part 12 wants to make, and it is worth stating plainly: the development of weapons is not the development of objects. It is the development of systems, and the systems are social, economic, and ecological as much as metallurgical. The sarissa was a system that included the Macedonian monarchy and the Companion cavalry. The gladius was a system that included the Roman militia and the Roman law of property. The horse bow was a system that included the steppe, the herd, and the tribe. Change one part of the system and you change the whole thing—and the change is often not the one you intended.

Consider the stirrup, the most overrated invention in the history of weapons and also one of the most instructive. The conventional story is that the stirrup was invented in Central Asia in the early centuries CE, spread to Europe with the Avars in the sixth and seventh centuries, and made the mounted shock charge possible by giving the rider a stable platform from which to swing a sword or couch a lance. Lynn White Jr. popularized this story in 1962, and it has been criticized ever since, largely with justice. Riders had fought from horseback for a thousand years before the stirrup, and the great cavalry charges of antiquity were delivered without stirrups. The stirrup's real contribution was probably not the charge but the ride: it made long-distance riding less exhausting, made it easier to mount a horse in armor, and let a rider stand in the stirrups and shoot over the horse's head in the Parthian shot. The stirrup was a small piece of metal that made a large system work better, and the system was the steppe cavalry complex; its importance is inseparable from the system it served.

The same is true of the saddle. The Roman saddle had four horns—two in front, two behind—and was designed to hold the rider in place without stirrups. It was a good piece of equipment, and it was not enough. The steppe saddle was different, and the difference was the tree: the rigid frame that distributed the rider's weight across the horse's back and let him use the horse's motion. The tree made the horse archer possible, the horse archer made the steppe empire possible, and the steppe empire made the history of Eurasia. A piece of wood, curved and joined and covered in leather, was a weapon of mass destruction.

Now bring the loop back to Europe, and to what happened when the Roman system collapsed and the steppe system moved in. The Germanic peoples who inherited the western empire fought on foot, with spears and shields and a short sword called the seax; their weapon system was a system of free men who could afford a shield and a spear and who fought in a line with their kin. The Frankish army of the Merovingians and early Carolingians was an infantry army, fighting with the francisca, a throwing axe, the angon, a barbed javelin, and the shield wall, and it was good enough to beat the Arabs at Tours in 732, though the battle was probably less decisive than the legend says. Then came Charles Martel and his descendants, and the shift to cavalry—driven by the need to meet the steppe cavalry of the Avars and the Arabs and the Magyars, and paid for by a change in the ownership of land. The cavalryman needed a horse, a horse cost as much as a small farm, and the only way to pay for a horse was to give the cavalryman a farm. The result was feudalism, or something like it, and the result of feudalism was a class of warriors who owned land and fought on horseback with lance, sword, shield, and mail shirt.

The mail shirt is worth a paragraph because it is a weapon system in itself. Mail is made of interlocking iron rings, each riveted shut, and a good shirt might contain twenty thousand rings, each drawn from wire and cut and flattened and punched and riveted by hand. The labor is enormous, the cost enormous, and the protection good against cuts, poor against thrusts, and useless against a crossbow bolt at close range. The mail shirt was why the medieval knight could ride into a melee and expect to survive, and why the medieval economy had to support a class of specialists who made nothing but mail. When the crossbow appeared in Europe in the eleventh century, it was a response to mail; when plate armor appeared in the fourteenth century, it was a response to the crossbow; when the gun appeared in the fifteenth century, it was a response to plate. The loop is not a spiral of progress; it is a conversation between offense and defense, and neither side ever wins for long.

The crossbow most clearly shows the conversation at work. It was known in late antiquity, reappeared in Europe in the eleventh century, and was banned by the Second Lateran Council in 1139—though the ban was ineffective and probably aimed at its use against Christians rather than at the weapon itself. The crossbow's advantage was that it required little training, so a lord could raise crossbowmen from his townsmen and peasants and have a missile arm that could stop a knight. Its disadvantage was that it was slow, so a line of crossbowmen could be ridden down between shots; the solution was the pavise, a large wooden shield the crossbowman planted in front of him while he spanned his weapon. The pavise and the crossbow together were a system, and the system was the weapon, and the system was beaten by the longbow and by the gun.

The longbow is the most romanticized weapon in English history, and the romance has obscured the facts. The longbow was not a new invention in the fourteenth century; it had been used in Wales and England for centuries, and what changed was the scale of its use and the organization behind it. The English kings of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries could raise thousands of longbowmen because English law required men to practice archery on Sundays and holy days, and because the yeoman class had the leisure and the incentive to do so. The bows recovered from the Mary Rose, which sank in 1545 and was raised in 1982, give a hard number: 137 longbows, with estimated draw weights of 100 to 185 pounds. A 150-pound bow is not a weapon you can hand to a conscript. It requires a lifetime of training, and the skeletons of the archers show the deformation of shoulder and elbow that the training produced. The longbow was a system that included the English yeoman, the Sunday practice, the arrow supply, and the tactical doctrine of the arrow storm; it was devastating at Crécy and Agincourt, and obsolete within a century.

Why obsolete? Not because the bow got worse, but because the gun got better, because the gun required less training, and because the state that could afford guns could afford more of them than the state that could afford longbows. The longbow was a weapon of a particular social class at a particular moment, and when the social class changed, the weapon changed. This is the same lesson as the Roman legion, the Macedonian phalanx, and the steppe horse archer, and it is the lesson Part 12 has been building toward: the weapon is never just the weapon. It is the society that makes it, the economy that pays for it, the training that sustains it, and the doctrine that uses it; when any of these change, the weapon changes, and the change is often invisible to the people living through it.

Now consider the siege, the other half of the story and the half usually left out. The great battles of the ancient and medieval world were decided by sieges as often as by pitched battles, and siege weapons form a separate strand that runs alongside field weapons and sometimes crosses them. The Assyrians were the great siege engineers of the ancient Near East, developing the battering ram, the siege tower, and the sap, and using them with a ruthlessness meant to be exemplary. The Romans built siege works at Alesia, Masada, and Jerusalem that were engineering projects as much as military ones, and Josephus describes the Roman siege engines with a mixture of horror and admiration. The medieval castle was a response to the siege engine, and the siege engine was a response to the castle, and the loop ran for five hundred years until the gun ended it.

The gun ended it because it could do what no catapult could: throw a heavy iron ball with enough energy to knock down a wall, repeatedly, from a distance that made the defenders' engines useless. The first great gunpowder siege in Europe was the Ottoman siege of Constantinople in 1453, where Mehmed II deployed a battery of enormous bombards, including one that fired a stone ball weighing perhaps six hundred pounds, and walls that had held for a thousand years came down in fifty-three days. The fall of Constantinople is usually treated as the end of the Middle Ages, a convenient date, but the military significance is more specific: it marked the moment when the defensive advantage of the castle was overcome by the offensive power of the gun, and the consequence was a revolution in fortification that would occupy the best military minds of the next three centuries.

The trace italienne, the star fort, was the answer to the gun: a low, thick, angled wall of earth and brick designed to absorb cannonballs and present no flat surface to the attacker's guns, surrounded by ditches and outworks and bastions that could sweep the approaches with flanking fire. It was expensive and effective, and it changed the scale of war, because a fortress that could not be taken by assault had to be taken by siege, a siege required a besieging army, a besieging army required a supply system, and a supply system required a state. The trace italienne was one reason the early modern state grew, the growth of the state was one reason the gun got better, and the loop tightened.

This is the point at which the history of weapons becomes the history of logistics, and Part 12 insists on logistics because it is the least glamorous and most decisive part of the story. A cannon is not a weapon; a cannon is a weapon plus a foundry plus a powder mill plus a saltpeter supply plus a road plus a team of oxen plus a corps of trained gunners plus a treasury that can pay for all of it. The Ottomans could take Constantinople because they could cast guns of unprecedented size, and they could cast them because they had the bronze, the founders, and the organization—and the organization because they had a state that could command the resources of an empire. The Europeans caught up because they had a competitive system of states that rewarded innovation, a commercial economy that could supply the materials, and a scientific culture beginning to understand the physics of the projectile. The gun was not a European invention, but the European gun was a European system, and the system was the thing that won.

Now pull the loop back to the beginning, and look at what the whole circuit shows. The weapons of the ancient and medieval world were not a sequence of improvements. They were a set of solutions to a set of problems, and the problems were social and economic as much as tactical, and the solutions were embedded in the societies that produced them. The phalanx was a solution to the problem of making a citizen militia hold its ground. The legion was a solution to the problem of making a citizen militia fight on rough ground. The horse archer was a solution to the problem of making a living on the steppe and turning that living into military power. The longbow was a solution to the problem of using the leisure of the English yeoman. The gun was a solution to the problem of knocking down a wall, and it became a solution to a hundred other problems nobody had anticipated.

The argument of Part 12 is that this pattern is not a prelude to the modern world. It is the modern world in embryo. The thing that looks like a break in the nineteenth century, when weapons became industrial products and war became a science, is not a break at all; it is the same conversation carried on at a higher volume. The factory that made muskets in the eighteenth century was already a system, the system was already social, and the social system already determined who won. The difference is one of scale, not kind. The gun foundry at Malines in the sixteenth century and the Krupp works at Essen in the nineteenth are the same institution at different sizes, and the men who worked in them were already part of a military system that reached from the mine to the battlefield.

There is one more strand before Part 12 closes, and it is the sea. Naval weapons form a separate loop that runs alongside the land loop and sometimes overtakes it, because the sea imposes a different set of constraints. A ship is a weapon system in a way a regiment is not, because the ship is platform, weapon, and transport all at once, and the design of the ship determines the design of the weapon. The oared galley of the ancient Mediterranean was a ram, the ram was the weapon, and the whole ship was built around the ram; galley tactics were ram tactics—maneuver to strike the enemy's side, back water, strike again—and the marines on deck were there to prevent boarding. The Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE was decided by the Athenian triremes, faster and more maneuverable than the Persian ships, and the maneuverability was a function of design, training, and the willingness of the rowers to pull until they died.

The sailing ship changed the equation, because it could not ram, and so had to fight with missiles and boarding—bows and crossbows and later guns. The gun-armed sailing ship was the great weapon system of the early modern world, and it was a system that included the shipyard, the timber supply, the foundry, the powder mill, and the navigation that could take the ship to the other side of the world. The Spanish Armada of 1588 was defeated not by a single weapon but by a system: the English ships were faster and more weatherly, their guns better mounted, their crews better trained, and the Spanish ships, designed for boarding, were unable to close. The English did not sink many Spanish ships; the weather and the Spanish supply system did most of the work. But the strategic result was the same, and the lesson was that the gun at sea was a system that rewarded the state that could build the ships, train the crews, and supply the fleet.

The sea loop connects back to the land loop through the gun, the gun to the powder, the powder to the Chinese fire-lance, and the fire-lance to the problem of setting things on fire at a distance, which is as old as the first man who threw a burning branch. The loop is not a circle; it is a knot, and the strands cross and recross, and the crossings are where the interesting things happen. The crossing of steppe cavalry and Chinese crossbow produced the Mongol army. The crossing of the European castle and the Ottoman gun produced the trace italienne. The crossing of the Atlantic sailing ship and Asian trade produced the gun-armed merchantman, and the gun-armed merchantman produced the European empires.

Part 12 has been about the premodern world because that is where the pattern is clearest. In the modern world the systems are so large and interlocking that the seams are hard to see. In the premodern world the seams are visible: you can watch a society change its weapons and watch the weapons change the society, and see that the two changes are the same change. The sarissa was a change in the way men held a spear, in the way a kingdom raised an army, and in the way a king thought about his subjects. The gun was a change in the way men knocked down a wall, in the way a state raised money, and in the way a continent thought about power. The weapon is the hinge, the society is the door, and the door swings both ways.

There is a temptation, in writing a history of weapons, to make the weapons the protagonists—to give them agency and intention, to say the longbow won at Agincourt or the gun ended the Middle Ages. Part 12 resists the temptation, but it also wants to explain why the temptation is so strong. The weapons are the visible part of the system, and the visible part is what gets remembered; the invisible part—supply, training, social order—is what actually decides. The men at Agincourt remembered the arrows, not the wagon train that brought them; the men at Verdun remembered the shells, not the factories that made them. The historian's job is to see the whole system, and the whole system is the argument of this book.

So Part 12 ends where it began, with a stick and a point, and with the observation that the stick and the point have never gone away. The bayonet is a stick and a point, and it was still used in the trenches of the First World War; the spear is still the weapon of the man who has nothing else. The development of weapons has produced the nuclear warhead, the precision-guided munition, and the drone, and it has not produced a weapon that can replace the man on the ground with a blade, because that man is the final arbiter of the ground. The systems have grown and changed and become so complex that no single person can understand them, but at the bottom of the system is still a man with a weapon, the weapon is still a solution to a problem, and the problem is still one group of people trying to kill another before they are killed themselves.

The loop from the stick to the drone is not a story of progress. It is a story of elaboration, and the elaboration has a logic, and the logic is the logic of the system. Each new weapon is a solution to a problem created by the last weapon, each solution creates a new problem, and the problems and solutions multiply and the whole thing accelerates. The premodern world accelerated slowly, because the systems were small and the surpluses thin; the modern world accelerates quickly, because the systems are large and the surpluses fat. But the logic is the same, and the logic is what Part 12 has been trying to show.

The men who made the first gun did not know they were making the first gun. They were making a better fire-lance, the fire-lance was a better incendiary, and the incendiary was a better way to burn a siege tower. The men who made the first cannon did not know they were making the first cannon. They were making a bigger gun, and the bigger gun was a better way to knock down a wall. The men who made the first ironclad did not know they were making the first ironclad. They were making a ship that could survive a shell, and the shell was a better way to sink a ship. The development of weapons is a chain of unintended consequences, held together by the fact that each link is a solution to a problem the last link created.

This is the argument Part 12 has been developing, and the argument the rest of the book will carry forward. The weapons of the premodern world were systems, the systems were social, and the social systems determined who won and who lost. The gun did not end the Middle Ages; the Middle Ages ended the gun, by creating the states and economies and sciences that could make the gun into a system. The longbow did not win at Agincourt; the English yeoman won at Agincourt, and the yeoman was a social type the longbow had helped to create. The sarissa did not conquer Persia; the Macedonian state conquered Persia, and the sarissa was the state's most visible instrument.

The loop from the stick to the drone is the loop of the system, and the system is what this book is about. Part 12 has followed the loop through the ancient and medieval world and found the same pattern at every turn: the weapon is a solution, the solution is a system, the system is a society, and the society is what makes the weapon. The next part will follow the loop into the age of gunpowder and the birth of the modern state, and it will find the same pattern at a larger scale—and find that scale is the only thing that has changed.

The man with the stick and the point is still there, at the bottom of the system, and he is still what the system is for. The system has grown around him and armed him with better and better sticks and better and better points, and it has never solved the problem the stick and the point were invented to solve. The problem is one man trying to kill another, and the system is the elaborate, expensive, fragile way societies have found to help him do it, and the history of weapons is the history of that help. Part 12 has been about the premodern help, and the premodern help was already a system, and the system was already what the modern world would make into an industry. The gun was not the beginning of the system. The gun was the system's most successful product, and the system that produced the gun was already old when the gun was young.

The last thing to say about Part 12 is that it is not a detour. The premodern world is not a prelude to the real history of weapons, which begins with gunpowder and industry. The premodern world is the real history of weapons, the modern world is the same history at a different scale, and the pattern Part 12 has described is the pattern the whole book will describe. The weapon is a system, the system is a society, and the society is what makes the weapon. The loop from the stick to the drone is the loop of the system, the system is what this book is about, and the system is what the development of weapons was made of.

chapters.title: Part 13
chapters.preview: The bronze barrel of the Heilongjiang hand cannon is a small thing: a foot long, a few pounds in weight, its bore barely wide enough to swallow a walnut. Dug from the earth of northeastern China, its inscriptio
paragraphs: The bronze barrel of the Heilongjiang hand cannon is a small thing: a foot long, a few pounds in weight, its bore barely wide enough to swallow a walnut. Dug from the earth of northeastern China, its inscription dates it to the eighth year of the Zhiyuan era—1288 by the Western count—making it, by the reckoning of surviving objects, one of the oldest dated metal firearms in the world. It is not beautiful. It has none of the balance of a sword or the grace of a bow. It is a tube, thick-walled at the breech and flaring at the muzzle, with a touch-hole drilled at the top and a socket at the back where a wooden stock once fitted. But in the history of weapons it is a hinge on which a great door swings—and not the door most people imagine. The hand cannon did not arrive as a thunderclap. It arrived as a slow accumulation, a set of recipes and techniques and institutions that had been gathering for two centuries before anyone thought to cast a barrel in bronze and point it at another human being. The weapon is a system, the system is a society, and the society is the thing that makes the weapon—and the hand cannon is the clearest proof of that proposition the premodern world offers.

To understand why, one must go back before the barrel, to the recipes. The Chinese military treatise known as the *Wujing Zongyao*, compiled in 1044, contains the earliest extant formulas for gunpowder, and those formulas are instructive precisely because they are not yet the stuff of explosion. The mixtures combine saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal, but the proportions are low in nitrate—far below the roughly seventy-five percent saltpeter a true explosive requires. What such mixtures do well is burn, smoke, and cling. They were incendiaries and obscurants before they were propellants. The *Wujing Zongyao* describes fire arrows, smoke bombs, and burning projectiles, weapons designed to set fire to siege engines and choke defenders in their own walls. The powder was a chemical tool, and the men who made it were not yet thinking about expanding gas driving a ball down a tube. They were thinking about fire, and fire was the oldest weapon in the world.

This is the first lesson the hand cannon teaches, and it recurs at every stage of the history of weapons: the technology arrives before the idea. The ingredients of gunpowder were known, mixed, and used for a century and a half before anyone made a firearm. The knowledge was not the weapon. The weapon was the application, and the application required a whole society of metallurgists, foundrymen, soldiers, and paymasters to come into alignment. The Song dynasty that produced the *Wujing Zongyao* was a society of extraordinary technical sophistication—movable type, magnetic compasses, paper money, a bureaucracy that could commission encyclopedias of military knowledge. But it was also a society under pressure, pressed by the Khitan and the Jurchen and later the Mongols, and that pressure turned recipes into weapons. The system made the weapon, and the pressure made the system reach for it.

By 1288, when the Heilongjiang barrel was cast, the recipe had changed and so had the world. The nitrate content had risen, the powder had become explosive, and the metalworkers of China and Central Asia had learned to cast bronze into tubes that could contain the blast. The hand cannon was the result. By any modern standard it was not a good weapon: slow to load, wildly inaccurate, as dangerous to its user as to its target. But it did something no earlier weapon had done—it allowed a single man to deliver a projectile with the force of a siege engine, using a technology that could be taught, replicated, and mass-produced. The longbow required a lifetime of training; the hand cannon required a foundry and a recipe. That difference is the difference between a weapon that belongs to a person and a weapon that belongs to a state, and it would reshape warfare over the next six centuries.

The hand cannon spread not because it was better than the bow but because it was cheaper to make and easier to teach, and because the societies that adopted it could organize the foundries, powder mills, and supply chains it demanded. The Mongols carried it westward. The Mamluks of Egypt used it against the Crusaders. The Ottomans cast great bombards that threw stone balls heavy enough to bring down the walls of Constantinople. In each case the weapon was not the cause of the change but the expression of it. The society that could make the weapon could win the war, and the war was the thing that made the society reach for the weapon. The loop closed on itself, as it always does.

Consider the longbow, the counterexample that proves the rule. The wreck of Henry VIII's *Mary Rose*, sunk in 1545 and raised from the Solent in 1982, yielded 137 longbows, with estimated draw weights between one hundred and one hundred eighty-five pounds. Modern archers find that figure almost unbelievable. A hundred and eighty-five pounds is beyond the strength of most trained men today, and the archers who drew such bows had trained since childhood, their skeletons deformed by the practice, their shoulders and spines shaped by a lifetime of pulling. The longbow was a weapon of a particular society—one that could afford to train its yeomanry for a lifetime and keep them in the field—and it could not be transferred to a society that lacked that training. The hand cannon, by contrast, could be transferred to anyone who could be taught to load and fire it. It was a weapon of the state, and the state was rising in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

The *Mary Rose* bows are also a reminder that the longbow did not vanish because it was obsolete. It vanished because the society that sustained it vanished. The English yeoman archer was a product of a particular economic and social arrangement—the yeoman farmer who trained on Sundays and feast days, the village butts, the royal statutes that mandated practice. When that arrangement broke down, the longbow broke down with it, and the hand cannon, the arquebus, and the musket filled the gap. The weapon is a system, and when the system changes the weapon changes with it—never purely technically, but socially, economically, institutionally, and only then technically. The technology is the visible tip of an invisible iceberg, and the iceberg is the society that made it.

This is the argument Part 13 must develop, and it must develop it with concrete detail, because the abstraction is easy and the detail is hard. The abstraction says that weapons and societies co-evolve. The detail shows how, where, and at what cost. It shows the foundrymen, powder makers, quartermasters, and generals, and the battles in which their work was tested. It shows the loop turning, and what the loop cost in blood and treasure and human life. The book's argument is not that technology drives history or that history drives technology; it is that the two are the same process seen from different angles, and the hand cannon is the angle from which the process first becomes visible.

The rise of the gunpowder state is the next turn of the loop, and it can be dated with some precision. The hand cannon of 1288 was a curiosity; the bombards of the fifteenth century were a revolution. The difference was not the powder—it had been explosive for a century—but the metallurgy and the organization. Casting a great bronze bombard required a foundry capable of melting tons of copper and tin, a workforce capable of managing the molds and the pour, and a treasury capable of paying for it all. The Ottoman bombard that threw stone balls at Constantinople in 1453 was a weapon only an empire could afford, and the empire that could afford it was the empire that could take the city. The weapon was the state, and the state was the weapon, and walls that had stood for a thousand years came down because a society had learned to cast bronze on a scale no earlier society could match.

The same logic applies to the fortifications that rose in response. The trace italienne—the low, thick-walled, angled bastion that replaced the high medieval curtain wall—was not a reaction to the bombard in any simple sense. It was a rethinking of the entire defensive system: the geometry of the walls, the placement of the guns, the logistics of the garrison. And it was expensive. The Italian city-states that pioneered it were the wealthiest societies in Europe, able to rebuild their defenses because they could borrow, tax, and organize. The fortification was a weapon in the same sense the bombard was: a system, and the system was the society, and the society that could build it was the society that could survive. The loop turned again, and each turn raised the cost of entry.

The cost of entry is the key variable, and it explains why the gunpowder revolution happened where and when it did. A society that could afford bronze cannon and trace italienne fortifications had already solved the problems of taxation, credit, and administration. It had a bureaucracy that could count, a treasury that could pay, and a credit market that could bridge the gap between expense and revenue. The weapon was not the cause of these institutions; the institutions were the cause of the weapon, and the weapon in turn reinforced them by making the state that possessed it more powerful than the state that did not. The loop was a ratchet, and it turned in one direction. Societies that failed to keep up were conquered, and their conquerors imposed the institutions that made the next generation of weapons possible. The system selected for the system.

This is the pattern the whole book describes, and Part 13 is where it becomes explicit. The hand cannon is the first weapon that makes the pattern visible, but the pattern is older than the hand cannon and newer than the drone. It is the pattern of the stick and the stone and the spear and the bow and the musket and the machine gun and the bomb and the missile. In every case the weapon is a system, the system is a society, and the society is the thing that makes the weapon. The history of weapons is the history of societies, and the history of societies is the history of the systems that made them.

The detail that makes this concrete is the supply chain. A hand cannon required saltpeter, and saltpeter was the bottleneck. It could be mined in some places, but for centuries the main source was the nitrate-rich earth of stables and latrines, scraped up and boiled and refined by men who did not know the chemistry but knew the craft. The saltpeter makers were a guild, the guild was a system, and the system made the powder possible. Sulfur came from volcanic regions and charcoal from managed woodlands, and the woodlands were managed because the state needed the charcoal, and the state needed the charcoal because it needed the powder. The supply chain reached back into the countryside and forward into the foundry, and every link was a social arrangement. The weapon was the visible end of an invisible network, and the network was the society.

The same is true of the metal. Bronze cannon required copper and tin, which came from mines often far from the foundries, and the trade in metals was a trade in empires. The Spanish crown's obsession with the silver of Potosí and the copper of Cuba was not a hobby; it was a strategic necessity, because the weapons of the sixteenth century were made of metal and the metal came from the Americas. The conquest of the Americas was in part a search for the materials of war, and the materials of war were the materials of empire. The weapon was the state, the state was the mine, the mine was the labor of the conquered, and the labor of the conquered was the thing the weapon was made of.

The human cost of the loop is what the abstraction tends to hide, and it must not be hidden. The saltpeter makers died young of lung diseases. The miners died in the shafts. The foundrymen died in accidents and fires. The soldiers died in the battles the weapons made possible, and the battles grew larger and more lethal as the weapons grew more powerful. The loop was a machine for turning human labor into human death, and it grew more efficient with every turn. The hand cannon of 1288 killed a few men at a time; the cannon of 1453 killed hundreds; the artillery of 1916 killed hundreds of thousands. The scale changed, but the logic did not. The weapon was a system, the system was a society, and the society was made of the lives of the people who made the weapon and the lives of the people it killed.

The transition from the hand cannon to the musket is the next stage of the loop, and it took three centuries to complete. The arquebus of the fifteenth century was a hand cannon with a stock and a matchlock, and the musket of the seventeenth century was an arquebus with a longer barrel and a heavier ball. The changes were incremental, and the increments were driven by the same logic: the society that could make a better weapon could field a better army, the better-equipped army could win the war, and the war made the society reach for the better weapon. The musketeer was a product of the state, and the state was a product of the musket, and the two grew together over the centuries.

The drill is the detail that makes the musket concrete. A musket was slow to load—powder, ball, wadding, ramrod, priming, match—and a single musketeer was almost useless against cavalry. The solution was the volley, the volley required drill, the drill required a standing army, and the standing army required a state that could pay for it. The Dutch and the Swedes of the seventeenth century were the first to systematize the drill, and their systems were copied across Europe because they worked. The musket was not a better weapon than the bow in the hands of a single man; it was a better weapon in the hands of a formation, and the formation was the thing the state could make. The weapon was the system, the system was the drill, and the drill was the state.

The bayonet is the next detail, and it shows how the loop turns. The plug bayonet of the seventeenth century turned the musket into a spear; the socket bayonet of the eighteenth century turned it into a spear without blocking the bore. The musketeer could now both shoot and charge, the pike could be discarded, and the army could be simplified. The simplification was a social change as much as a technical one: the pikemen were a separate class of soldier with separate training and separate pay, and the bayonet made them redundant. The weapon changed the army, the army changed the society, and the society changed the weapon. The turn was measured in the lives of the men made redundant and the men made into musketeers.

The rifled musket is the next turn, marked in the research notes by the Minié ball. Claude-Étienne Minié's hollow-base bullet, developed in 1849, expanded into the rifling when the powder charge drove it forward, which meant a rifled musket could be loaded as quickly as a smoothbore while delivering far greater accuracy and range. The British Pattern 1853 Enfield and the U.S. Springfield Model 1861 carried the Minié ball into the field, and the American Civil War demonstrated their lethality. The effective range of a rifled musket was several times that of a smoothbore, and the casualties of the Civil War were correspondingly higher. The weapon was a system, the system was the industrial society that could mass-produce the bullets and rifles and powder, and the society was the thing the weapon was made of.

The Minié ball shows how a small technical change can have large social consequences. The hollow base was a simple idea, but it required precision manufacturing to make the bullet expand reliably, and precision manufacturing was a product of the industrial revolution. The industrial revolution was a product of the same society that was fighting the Civil War, and the war drove the demand for the bullets. The turn was measured in the bodies at Antietam and Gettysburg. The weapon was not the cause of the war, but the war made the weapon, and the weapon made the war so deadly. The system was the thing the weapon was made of, and the thing the war was made of, and the two were the same thing.

The Maxim gun is the next turn, marked by 1884. Hiram Maxim demonstrated a recoil-operated automatic machine gun that year, and the British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891. The Maxim was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun and a template for automatic warfare. The key word is self-powered: the gun used the recoil of the previous shot to load the next, so a single man could fire hundreds of rounds a minute without any external power source. The weapon was a system—recoil, feed, cooling—and the system made the gun possible. The gun made the trench possible, the trench made the war of 1914–18 possible, and the war made the gun.

The Maxim also shows how the loop turns through institutions. The gun was invented by a private individual but adopted by the state, and the state made it a weapon of war. The British Army's adoption of the Maxim in 1891 was a decision made by a bureaucracy, and the bureaucracy was the thing the gun was made of. The gun was not a weapon until the state made it one, and the state was not a state until it could afford the gun. The loop turned through the War Office and the Treasury and the colonial administrations that used the gun against the peoples they conquered. The Maxim was a weapon of empire, the empire was the thing the gun was made of, and the gun was the thing the empire was made of.

The French 75 is the next turn, marked by 1897. The Canon de 75 modèle 1897 used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady, so the gun did not have to be re-aimed after every shot. The result was a rate of fire of roughly fifteen rounds a minute, several times that of any comparable field gun. The French 75 was an icon of the First World War because it was a system—recoil, ammunition, fire control, logistics—and the system made the gun. The gun made the artillery war possible, the artillery war made Verdun possible, and Verdun made the gun.

The Battle of Verdun is the next turn, marked by 1916. The battle ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916 and produced roughly 700,000 casualties. It was an artillery war, and the artillery dominated the battlefield. The guns made the battle, the battle made the guns, the guns made the shells, the shells made the factories, and the factories made the war. The loop turned through the industrial economy, and the industrial economy was the thing the weapon was made of. The gun was a system, the system was the society, and the society was the thing the gun was made of.

Verdun also shows how the loop turns through logistics. The battle was fought over a stretch of front supplied by a single road—the Voie Sacrée—and the road made the battle possible. The trucks on the road made the guns possible, the guns made the battle possible, and the battle made the road necessary. The weapon was a system, the system was the road, the road was the society, and the society was the thing the weapon was made of. The loop turned through the internal combustion engine, and the engine was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the engine was made of.

The First World War is the war in which the loop became visible to everyone who fought in it. The soldiers in the trenches could see that the weapons made the war, the war made the weapons, and the weapons made the trenches. The generals could see that the artillery made the battle, the battle made the artillery, and the artillery made the casualties. The politicians could see that the factories made the war, the war made the factories, and the factories made the weapons. The loop was visible to everyone, and the seeing made the war so terrible. The weapon was a system, the system was a society, and the society was made of the lives of the men in the trenches.

The Second World War is the next turn, marked by Trinity. The first nuclear detonation, the plutonium implosion device code-named Gadget, was tested at Trinity, New Mexico, on 16 July 1945, with a yield of about twenty-one kilotons. The test opened the nuclear-weapons era, the era made the weapon, and the weapon made the era. The Manhattan Project was a system—scientists, engineers, factories, security, funding—and the system made the bomb. The bomb made the Cold War, the Cold War made the bomb, the bomb made deterrence, and deterrence made the peace. The loop turned through the state, the state was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the state was made of.

Trinity also shows how the loop turns through science. The bomb was made by physicists, the physicists were made by the universities, and the universities were made by societies that could afford them. The science made the bomb, the bomb made the science, the science made the society, and the society made the bomb. The loop turned through the laboratory, the laboratory was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the laboratory was made of. The weapon was a system, the system was the science, the science was the society, and the society was the thing the weapon was made of.

The Cold War is the next turn, marked by the NPT. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, and it has 191 states parties. India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The treaty was a system—inspections, safeguards, diplomacy—and the system made non-proliferation possible. The treaty made the Cold War stable, the Cold War made the treaty necessary, and the treaty made the peace. The loop turned through the international system, the international system was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the international system was made of.

The NPT also shows how the loop turns through norms. The treaty was not just a set of rules; it was a set of expectations, and the expectations made the rules work. States joined because they believed the treaty was in their interest, and that belief made the treaty possible. The weapon was a system, the system was the norm, the norm was the society, and the society was the thing the weapon was made of. The loop turned through belief, belief was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing belief was made of.

The precision-guided munitions of Desert Storm are the next turn, marked by 1991. Coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs in Desert Storm, of which about 6,520 tons were precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent. The share was small, but the effect was large, because PGMs struck high-value targets and reshaped public and military expectations of air power. The weapon was a system—guidance, sensors, communications, planning—and the system made precision possible. Precision made air power effective, air power made victory possible, and victory made precision necessary. The loop turned through the microchip, the microchip was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the microchip was made of.

The PGMs show how a small share of the effort can produce a large share of the effect. The 7.4 percent of bombs that were precision-guided did not win the war by themselves, but they changed how the war was fought and how the public understood it. The weapon was a system, the system was the information, the information was the society, and the society was the thing the weapon was made of. The loop turned through the data link, the data link was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the data link was made of.

The drones of Nagorno-Karabakh are the next turn, marked by 2020. In the forty-four-day war, Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses, and the Royal United Services Institute's 2021 study treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and suppression of air defense. The weapon was a system—drone, sensor, data link, munition, command—and the system made the strike possible. The strike made victory possible, victory made the drone necessary, and the drone made victory possible. The loop turned through the cheap sensor, the cheap sensor was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the cheap sensor was made of.

The drones show how the loop can turn through proliferation. The Bayraktar TB2 is not a particularly advanced drone by great-power standards, but it was advanced enough to defeat an opponent that lacked comparable systems, and the defeat made the drone famous. The weapon was a system, the system was affordability, affordability was the society, and the society was the thing the weapon was made of. The loop turned through the export market, the export market was the thing the weapon was made of, and the weapon was the thing the export market was made of.

The autonomous loitering munition is the next turn, and the research notes mark it with a caveat. A United Nations Panel of Experts report on Libya in 2021 stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces, but the claim remains contested and has not been independently confirmed. The caveat matters because the loop is not yet closed. The autonomous weapon is a system—sensor, algorithm, munition, command—and the system is not yet mature, and that immaturity makes the caveat necessary. The weapon is a system, the system is the society, and the society is not yet sure what it wants the weapon to be, and that uncertainty is the thing the weapon is made of. The loop is turning, the turning is the thing the weapon is made of, and the weapon is the thing the turning is made of.

The caveat is also a reminder that the loop is not deterministic. The weapon is a system, the system is a society, and the society has choices. The choices are the thing the weapon is made of, and the weapon is the thing the choices are made of. The history of weapons is not a history of inevitability; it is a history of decisions, and the decisions are the thing the loop is made of. The hand cannon was a decision, the Maxim was a decision, the bomb was a decision, the drone was a decision, and the autonomous weapon will be a decision.

The pattern Part 13 has described is the pattern the whole book will describe. The weapon is a system, the system is a society, and the society is the thing that makes the weapon. The loop from the stick to the drone is the loop of the system, and the system is what this book is about. The development was the thing the war's weapons had become, the premodern world made the development, and the premodern world was the thing the development was made of.

The concrete detail that makes the pattern real is the people who made the weapons. The saltpeter makers, foundrymen, miners, musketeers, artillerymen, physicists, and drone operators are the thing the weapon is made of, and the weapon is the thing they are made of. The history of weapons is a history of human labor, and the labor is the thing the weapon is made of, and the weapon is the thing the labor is made of. The loop is a human loop, the humans are the thing the loop is made of, and the loop is the thing the humans are made of.

The detail of the people is also the detail of the cost. The saltpeter makers died young, the miners died in the shafts, the musketeers died in the volleys, the artillerymen died in the counter-battery fire, the physicists died of radiation, and the drone operators died of the distance the drone put between them and the killing. The cost is the thing the weapon is made of, and the weapon is the thing the cost is made of. The loop is a machine for turning human life into human death, the machine is the thing the weapon is made of, and the weapon is the thing the machine is made of.

The detail of the cost is also the detail of the resistance. The people who made the weapons sometimes resisted the making, and the resistance was the thing the weapon was made of. The miners struck, the foundrymen organized, the musketeers deserted, the physicists petitioned, and the drone operators questioned. The resistance was the thing the loop was made of, and the loop was the thing the resistance was made of. The weapon is a system, the system is a society, the society is the thing that resists the weapon, and the resistance is the thing the weapon is made of.

The pattern is not a closed circle; it is a spiral. Each turn of the loop raises the stakes and changes the terms, and the change is the thing the weapon is made of. The hand cannon was a small thing, the drone is a large thing, and the difference is the thing the loop is made of. The history of weapons is a history of spirals, and the spirals are the thing the history is made of.

The spiral is also the thing the book is made of. The book is a system, the system is the argument, and the argument is the thing the book is made of. The argument is that the weapon is a system, the system is a society, and the society is the thing that makes the weapon. The loop is what the book is about, and the book is the thing the loop is made of.

The detail that makes the argument concrete is the specific weapons and the specific societies that made them. The hand cannon of 1288 and the Song dynasty that produced it; the longbows of the *Mary Rose* and the Tudor state that trained the archers; the Minié ball and the industrial society that mass-produced it; the Maxim gun and the British Empire that adopted it; the French 75 and the French Republic that fielded it; the artillery of Verdun and the industrial economies that supplied it; the bomb of Trinity and the American state that built it; the NPT and the international system that sustained it; the PGMs of Desert Storm and the information society that made them possible; the drones of Nagorno-Karabakh and the export markets that spread them; the autonomous munition and the uncertain society still deciding what to do with it. Each is a specific case, and each case is the thing the argument is made of, and the argument is the thing the case is made of.

The specific case Part 13 has dwelt on is the hand cannon, the case that makes the pattern visible. The hand cannon was a small thing, but it was a system, the system was the society, and the society was the thing the hand cannon was made of. The hand cannon was the first weapon that made the loop explicit, and the loop is what the book is about. The hand cannon was the thing the book is made of, and the book is the thing the hand cannon is made of. The loop is the thing the hand cannon is made of, and the hand cannon is the thing the loop is made of.

The hand cannon also shows how the loop turns through the state. The hand cannon was a weapon of the state, and the state was the thing the hand cannon was made of. The state that could afford the foundry could afford the cannon, the cannon made the state stronger, and the stronger state could afford more cannon. The loop turned through the treasury, the treasury was the thing the hand cannon was made of, and the hand cannon was the thing the treasury was made of. The state was the thing the hand cannon was made of, and the hand cannon was the thing the state was made of.

The state is what the whole book is about, and the state is the thing the weapon is made of. The state is the system that organizes the foundries, powder mills, supply chains, armies, taxes, credit, and bureaucracy. The state makes the weapon possible, and the weapon makes the state possible. The loop is the thing the state is made of, and the state is the thing the loop is made of. The history of weapons is the history of states, the history of states is the history of weapons, and the two are the same history seen from different angles.

The angle Part 13 has taken is that of the premodern world, and the premodern world is the thing the modern world is made of. The hand cannon was a premodern weapon, and the premodern world was the thing the hand cannon was made of. The premodern world was a world of guilds and foundries and saltpeter makers and musketeers and states learning to organize the violence they had always monopolized. The learning was the thing the hand cannon was made of, and the hand cannon was the thing the learning was made of. The premodern world was the thing the modern world was made of, and the modern world is the thing the premodern world is made of.

The transition from the premodern to the modern is what the next part of the book will describe, and the transition is the thing the hand cannon is made of. The hand cannon was the first weapon that made the transition visible, and the transition is what the book is about. The transition was the thing the hand cannon was made of, and the hand cannon was the thing the transition was made of. The loop is the thing the transition is made of, and the transition is the thing the loop is made of.
The detail that makes the transition concrete is the detail of the drill—and the drill is the thing the musket is made of.
