chapters.preview: The drill was the thing that made the musket into a weapon of state, and the drill was made of paper.
paragraphs: The drill was the thing that made the musket into a weapon of state, and the drill was made of paper.

That is not a metaphor. In the first half of the seventeenth century, the armies of the Dutch Republic and the Swedish Empire fought and won with muskets whose decisive component was a printed booklet—a numbered sequence of movements, illustrated with small woodcuts, that told a soldier exactly where to put his feet, his hands, his match, and his powder. The booklet was cheap. It was reproducible. It could be carried by a sergeant who could not read it but who could count to forty-three. And because it could be counted to forty-three, the musket became something the premodern world had never possessed: a weapon whose performance depended less on the strength and skill of the individual holding it than on the coordination of the many individuals standing beside him.

The musket itself was a mediocre device. It was heavy, slow, inaccurate, and prone to misfire in wet weather. A longbow in the hands of a trained archer could loose ten arrows in the time a musketeer fired once, and could do so with better accuracy at a hundred yards. Yet by 1700 the longbow was a museum piece and the musket ruled every battlefield in Europe. The reason was not metallurgy or chemistry. The reason was the drill—the thing that the musket was made of, and the state was made of, and the transition from premodern to modern was made of.

To understand why, it helps to look at what the drill actually did, movement by movement, and to see how a sequence of printed commands turned a crowd of hired men into a machine that could deliver volleys of lead at a rate no individual could match.
**The problem the musket posed.**

A crossbowman could be trained in a few weeks. A longbowman took a lifetime—the skeletons of English archers recovered from the *Mary Rose*, sunk in 1545 and raised in 1982, show the deformed shoulder joints and thickened arm bones of men who had drawn bows of 100 to 185 pounds since boyhood. The longbow was a weapon of a society organized around archery, with statutes requiring practice on Sundays and holidays, and a rural population whose leisure was spent loosing arrows at butts. When that society changed—when enclosure and wage labor broke the rural archery culture—the longbow could not be replaced by decree. It could only be replaced by a weapon that did not require a lifetime to master.

The musket was that weapon, but only in principle. In practice, the early musket was dangerous and unreliable. The matchlock mechanism—a smoldering cord of treated hemp, called the match, held in a serpentine lever that dropped it into a priming pan of fine powder—required the musketeer to manage a live ember while handling loose gunpowder. A man who spilled powder on his hand and then touched the match to it lost the hand. A man who loaded too much powder burst the barrel. A man who loaded too little watched his ball dribble out of the muzzle and fall to the ground ten paces away. The rate of fire was perhaps one shot every two minutes for a well-drilled soldier, the effective range perhaps fifty to a hundred yards, and the accuracy such that a volley was aimed not at a man but at a formation.

And yet the musket had one advantage no bow could match: it did not require a lifetime of training, and it could be taught from a book. The bow was a craft. The musket was a procedure. And procedures could be standardized, printed, distributed, and enforced.
**Maurice of Nassau and the invention of the count.**

The man usually credited with turning the musket into a system was Maurice of Nassau, Prince of Orange, who commanded the armies of the Dutch Republic from 1585 until his death in 1625. Maurice was not a great battlefield commander in the mold of Alexander or Caesar. He fought a long, grinding war of sieges against Spain—the Eighty Years' War—and won most of his victories by avoiding battle and taking fortified towns. But he was a student of antiquity, of mathematics, and above all of the problem of making soldiers do the same thing at the same time.

Maurice's insight was that the Roman legion had been effective not because Roman soldiers were braver or stronger than their enemies but because they were drilled. He read the Roman military writers—Vegetius, Aelian, Polybius—and noticed that the Romans had broken every movement into a sequence of numbered steps, taught by repetition until it became automatic. The Roman soldier did not think about how to draw his sword. He drew it. He did not think about how to form a testudo. He formed it. The thinking had been done in advance, by the drillmaster, and the soldier's job was to execute.

Maurice applied this insight to the musket. He broke the loading and firing sequence into a fixed number of steps—by some accounts forty-two, by others forty-three, depending on the manual and the weapon—and gave each step a name and a command. *Open your pan. Prime your pan. Shut your pan. Cast about your musket. Blow your pan. Charge your musket with powder. Ram your powder. Charge your musket with ball. Ram your ball. Prime your pan. Blow your pan. Cock your match. Guard your pan. Present your musket. Give fire.* The commands were not suggestions. They were orders. A soldier who skipped a step was punished. A company that fell out of sequence was drilled until it did not.

The effect was transformative. A company of musketeers drilled to Maurice's count could fire in ranks—one rank firing while the ranks behind it loaded—and sustain a rate of fire no undisciplined formation could match. The front rank fired, stepped back, and loaded while the second rank stepped forward and fired, and the third rank stepped forward and fired, and by the time the first rank had reloaded, it was its turn again. The volley became continuous. The formation became a machine for delivering lead at a steady rate, determined not by the skill of any individual but by the precision of the drill.

Maurice's system was published, copied, and improved. His cousin William Louis of Nassau wrote a letter in 1594 describing the countermarch—the technique of ranks advancing and retiring through each other—and the letter circulated among military men across Europe. Jacob de Gheyn, a Dutch engraver, produced a series of forty-two plates illustrating the musket drill, published in 1607 as *The Exercise of Arms*. The plates showed a soldier in a plumed hat and knee breeches, step by step, from the moment he took his musket from his shoulder to the moment he returned it. The book was printed in multiple languages, carried by officers, copied by drillmasters. It was, in effect, the first widely distributed technical manual for a firearm, and it made the musket into a standardized weapon in a way no previous weapon had been standardized.

De Gheyn's plates are worth looking at closely, because they show something the text alone cannot. Each plate shows the same soldier, in the same posture, with the same musket, and the only thing that changes is the position of his hands and the angle of his body. The sequence is not a description of how a skilled man loads a gun. It is a description of how a soldier is to be made to load a gun, step by step, so that the loading can be supervised, corrected, and timed. The plates are instructions for the manufacture of a human machine.
**Gustavus Adolphus and the drill as tactics.**

The drill became tactics in the hands of Gustavus Adolphus, King of Sweden from 1611 to 1632. Gustavus was a military innovator of the first rank, and his innovations lay not so much in the weapons themselves as in how they were organized. He reduced the size of the infantry formation—from the deep, square *tercio* of the Spanish, which packed men twenty or thirty deep, to a shallower line six deep—so that every musket in the formation could fire. He mixed cavalry with infantry in combined-arms formations. He used light artillery that could be moved with the infantry. And he drilled his men relentlessly, so that they could perform the countermarch and the volley and the advance under fire without breaking.

At Breitenfeld, in 1631, Gustavus's Swedish and Saxon army met the army of the Catholic League under Tilly, and the battle was decided not by numbers but by the rate at which the Swedish infantry could fire. The Swedish brigades, six ranks deep, delivered volleys the deeper Spanish formations could not match, and the Swedish cavalry, drilled to charge home rather than to caracole—to ride up to the enemy and fire pistols rather than to close with the sword—broke the Imperial horse. The battle was a demonstration of what the drill could do. It was also a demonstration of what the drill cost. The Swedish army was a national army, raised by conscription, and the conscription was possible because the drill made it possible to turn a farm boy into a soldier in a few months rather than a few years. The state that could drill could conscript. The state that could conscript could field armies larger than any mercenary captain could afford.

The drill and the state grew together. The Dutch Republic, a confederation of merchant cities with a small population, could not field large armies, so it drilled its soldiers to make each one count for more. Sweden, a poor and sparsely populated kingdom, could not afford mercenaries, so it conscripted and drilled. The drill was a way of turning men into a resource, and the state that could turn men into a resource was the state that could survive in the new kind of war the musket had made.

The drill also changed the relationship between the soldier and the state. A mercenary fought for pay, and his loyalty was to his captain, and his captain's loyalty was to whoever paid him. A drilled soldier fought for a state, and his loyalty was to the state, and the state could call on him again and again. The drill was a form of discipline that did not depend on personal loyalty. It depended on habit, and habit could be instilled by repetition, and repetition could be enforced by officers who were themselves drilled. The drill created a hierarchy of drill, with the sergeant drilling the company and the colonel drilling the regiment and the general drilling the army, and the hierarchy was the state in miniature.
**The paper war: manuals, orders, and the standardization of violence.**

The drill was made of paper in a more literal sense as well. The seventeenth century was the century of the printed manual, and the military manual was one of its most successful genres. De Gheyn's *Exercise of Arms* was followed by dozens of others—English, French, Spanish, German, Swedish—each with its own numbered sequence, its own commands, its own illustrations. The manuals were not identical. A soldier trained to the English manual might use forty-two steps, a soldier trained to the Dutch manual forty-three, and the difference could matter when the two were called upon to fight side by side. But the manuals were close enough to be mutually intelligible, and the process of standardization was driven by the need for armies to fight together.

The standardization was not just a matter of aesthetics. It was a matter of logistics. A musket made to a standard pattern could be repaired with standard parts. A cartridge made to a standard size could be used in any musket of that pattern. A soldier trained to a standard drill could be moved from one company to another without retraining. The standardization of the musket and the standardization of the drill went together, and both depended on the standardization of the printed page.

The paper war was also a war of orders. The seventeenth-century army ran on written orders—orders for the march, orders for the camp, orders for the battle—and the orders were written down and copied and distributed because the army was too large to be commanded by voice. A general could not shout at ten thousand men. He could write an order, and the order could be carried by a rider, and the rider could deliver it to a colonel, and the colonel could read it to his officers, and the officers could pass it down. The written order was the nervous system of the army, and the drill was the muscle that the nervous system controlled.

The paper war had a dark side, and the dark side was that the drill made it possible to do things that had not been possible before. A drilled army could be marched into a killing zone and made to stand there. A drilled army could be ordered to fire into a crowd. A drilled army could be sacrificed—held in place while the artillery tore it apart—because the drill made it possible to hold men in place. The drill was a technology of obedience, and obedience is a virtue only when the thing being obeyed is virtuous. The seventeenth century did not worry much about this. The eighteenth century worried about it more, and the nineteenth century worried about it a great deal, and the twentieth century discovered what a drilled army could do when the drill was combined with the machine gun and the artillery and the ideology of the nation-state.
**The flintlock and the bayonet: the drill's two children.**

The matchlock was a drill weapon, but it was an awkward one. The match had to be kept lit, which meant that a musketeer on night duty had to tend his match and a musketeer in the rain had to keep his powder dry. The match was visible at night, which meant that a sentry with a matchlock was a target. The match was smelly, which meant that a formation of musketeers was a cloud of sulfurous smoke. And the match was dangerous, which meant that the drill had to include elaborate precautions against accidental discharge.

The flintlock solved these problems. The flintlock mechanism—a piece of flint held in a cock that struck a steel frizzen, which scraped sparks into a priming pan—was self-igniting. It did not require a match. It could be carried loaded and ready. It could be fired in the rain, if the pan was kept covered. It was, in short, a weapon that could be carried by a soldier who was not also a pyrotechnician, and it became the standard infantry weapon of the eighteenth century.

The flintlock did not change the drill in its essentials. The loading sequence was still a numbered series of steps, still taught by repetition, still enforced by officers. But the flintlock made the drill faster and safer and more reliable, and it made the volley more effective, and it made the line infantry the dominant arm of every European army.

The bayonet changed the drill more fundamentally. The early bayonet was a plug bayonet—a blade with a wooden handle that was inserted into the muzzle of the musket. A soldier with a plug bayonet could not fire his musket, because the bayonet blocked the barrel. The plug bayonet turned a musket into a pike, which was useful when the cavalry charged, but it meant that the soldier had to choose between firing and defending himself. The socket bayonet, developed in France in the late seventeenth century, fitted over the muzzle and locked in place with a ring, so that the musket could be fired with the bayonet attached. The socket bayonet turned the musket into a weapon that could both shoot and stab, and it made the pike obsolete.

The socket bayonet was a small piece of metal, but it had large consequences. It meant that the infantry no longer needed a separate arm of pikemen to protect the musketeers from cavalry. It meant that every infantryman was both a shooter and a spearman. It meant that the drill could be simplified—no more coordination between musketeers and pikemen—and that the line infantry could be made more uniform. The bayonet was the drill's child in the sense that it was a weapon designed for a drilled army, and the drill's child in the sense that it made the drill more important, because a soldier with a bayonet had to be drilled to use it without getting in the way of the man beside him.
**The Prussian drill and the invention of the modern army.**

The drill reached its eighteenth-century apogee in Prussia. The Prussian army of Frederick William I and his son Frederick the Great was the most drilled army in Europe, and its drill was the most elaborate. The Prussian manual specified not only the loading sequence but the marching step, the cadence, the angle of the foot, the position of the hands, the distance between files, the distance between ranks, and the exact words of every command. The Prussian drill was a total system, enforced with a brutality that shocked even eighteenth-century observers. Prussian soldiers were flogged for minor errors. Prussian officers were expected to know the drill by heart and to be able to perform it themselves. The Prussian army was a machine, and the machine was the state.

The Prussian drill was designed for a specific tactical problem: how to deliver volleys of musketry at the closest possible range without the formation breaking. The Prussian infantry advanced in line, in step, to within fifty paces of the enemy, and then fired a volley timed to be simultaneous. The volley was not aimed at individuals. It was aimed at the formation, and the formation was a dense mass of men, and a volley fired at fifty paces into a dense mass of men would kill or wound a significant fraction of them. The Prussian advance was a calculated risk: the formation was exposed to enemy fire for the time it took to close the distance, and the drill was designed to minimize that time by keeping the men moving at a steady pace and keeping the formation intact.

The Prussian drill was also a system of social control. The Prussian army was recruited from the peasantry and the urban poor, and the drill was a way of turning them into something the state could use. The drill taught obedience, and obedience was the virtue the Prussian state most valued. The drill also taught literacy, in a limited sense—a soldier who could read the manual could be promoted—and it taught numeracy, because a soldier who could count the steps could be trusted to perform them. The Prussian drill was an education, and the education was designed to produce soldiers.

The Prussian system was copied across Europe, and the copying was not always successful. The Austrian army tried to copy the Prussian drill and found that its multinational recruits could not be made to perform it with the same precision. The French army copied the Prussian drill and added its own innovations, including the use of skirmishers—light infantry who fought in open order and aimed at individual targets—and the skirmishers were a response to the rigidity of the Prussian line. The British army copied the Prussian drill and added the volley fire it had learned in America, where the terrain favored loose formations and aimed fire. The drill was not a single thing. It was a family of things, and each army adapted it to its own circumstances.
**The drill and the soldier's body.**

The drill was a technology of the body, and it is worth pausing to consider what it did to the bodies of the men who performed it. A drilled soldier stood in a specific posture—back straight, shoulders back, head up, feet at a specific angle—and he held his musket in a specific way, and he moved in a specific cadence. The posture was not natural. It was imposed, and the imposition was painful. Soldiers who were not used to standing for hours in a rigid posture developed back problems. Soldiers who were not used to marching in step developed knee and hip problems. Soldiers who were not used to carrying a heavy musket developed shoulder and arm problems. The drill was a form of labor, and like all forms of labor it left marks on the body.

The drill also changed the soldier's relationship to his weapon. A musket that was carried in a specific way, loaded in a specific sequence, and fired in a specific posture became an extension of the soldier's body. The soldier did not think about the musket. He thought through it. The musket was a tool that had been incorporated into his motor cortex, and the incorporation was the result of thousands of repetitions. The drill was a technology of embodiment, and the embodiment was the point. A soldier who had to think about how to load his musket was a soldier who would be slow. A soldier who did not have to think was a soldier who would be fast.

The embodiment had a cost. A soldier who had been drilled to perform a sequence of movements automatically could not easily unlearn them. A soldier who had been drilled to stand in line and fire volleys could not easily be taught to fight in open order. A soldier who had been drilled to obey could not easily be taught to think for himself. The drill produced a specific kind of soldier, well suited to a specific kind of war, and the specific kind of war was the war of the eighteenth century. When the nature of war changed—when the French Revolution produced mass armies and the Industrial Revolution produced rifled muskets and the railroad produced rapid mobilization—the drilled soldier had to be retrained, and the retraining was difficult, and the difficulty was one of the reasons the nineteenth century was so bloody.
**The drill and the state: the fiscal-military connection.**

The drill was expensive. A drilled army required officers who could read and write, sergeants who could count, and a bureaucracy that could produce and distribute manuals and orders. It required a treasury that could pay soldiers regularly, because a soldier who was not paid would desert, and a soldier who deserted took his drill with him. It required a state that could enforce conscription, because the drill was most effective when applied to a large number of men, and a large number of men could only be obtained by conscription. The drill was, in short, a state-building technology, and the states that built it were the states that survived.

The connection between the drill and the state is visible in the fiscal history of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The Dutch Republic, which pioneered the drill, also pioneered the modern system of public debt, because a state that could borrow could pay its soldiers, and a state that could pay its soldiers could keep them drilled. Sweden, which perfected the drill under Gustavus Adolphus, also perfected the system of conscription, because a state that could conscript could field a large army, and a large army could be drilled. Prussia, which made the drill into a total system, also made the army into the central institution of the state, and the Prussian state was, in a real sense, an army with a country attached.

The connection between the drill and the state is also visible in the history of taxation. The drill required a standing army, and a standing army required a permanent revenue, and a permanent revenue required a bureaucracy that could assess and collect taxes. The English Parliament, which had fought a civil war over whether the king could tax without consent, resolved the question by giving the Crown a permanent revenue in exchange for parliamentary control of the army. The settlement of 1689—the Bill of Rights and the Mutiny Act—created a standing army paid by Parliament and drilled by the Crown, and the arrangement was the foundation of the British fiscal-military state, the most successful state of the eighteenth century.

The drill was not the only thing that made the fiscal-military state possible. It was one of the things, and it was a thing that made the others possible. A state that could drill could field an army that could win battles, and a state that could win battles could acquire colonies, and colonies produced revenue, and revenue paid for more drill. The loop was the thing that the state was made of, and the state was the thing that the drill was made of, and the drill was the thing that the musket was made of.
**The drill and the American Revolution: the limits of the system.**

The American Revolution was a test of the drill, and the test was inconclusive in a way that is instructive. The British army was the most drilled army in the world in 1775, and it won most of the battles it fought in the open field. The American army was initially undrilled, and it lost most of the battles it fought in the open field. But the Americans won the war, and they won it by not fighting the kind of war the drill was designed for.

The American victory was not a victory of the undrilled over the drilled. It was a victory of a drilled army—the Continental Army, drilled at Valley Forge by Baron von Steuben, a Prussian officer who wrote a manual that became the basis of the American drill—over a drilled army fighting at the end of a long supply line in a hostile country. Von Steuben's drill was a simplified version of the Prussian drill, adapted to American circumstances, and it made the Continental Army into a force that could stand in line against the British and win. The Americans also used militia, who were not drilled to the same standard, and the militia were useful for skirmishing and for harassing British columns, but not for standing in line.

The American Revolution also demonstrated the limits of the drill. A drilled army could win battles, but it could not win a war against a population determined to resist. The British army could march wherever it wanted, but it could not hold the countryside, and the countryside was where the war was decided. The drill was a technology of battlefield dominance, and battlefield dominance was not enough to win a war of insurgency. The lesson was learned by the British, and learned again by the French in Spain, and learned again by the Americans in Vietnam, and is being learned again in the twenty-first century. The drill is a thing that the musket is made of, and the musket is a thing that the battlefield is made of, and the battlefield is not the thing that the war is made of.
**The drill and the French Revolution: the levee en masse.**

The French Revolution transformed the drill by transforming the army that performed it. The revolutionary armies were mass armies—the *levée en masse* of 1793 conscripted hundreds of thousands of men—and mass armies could not be drilled to the Prussian standard, because the Prussian standard required years of training and a professional officer corps. The revolutionary armies were drilled to a lower standard, but to a different purpose. They were drilled to attack, not to stand and fire. They were drilled to advance in columns, not to deploy in lines. They were drilled to overwhelm the enemy with numbers and enthusiasm, not to outmaneuver him with precision.

The French column was a formation designed for a mass army. It was a dense block of men, and it could move quickly, and it could break through a line that was not prepared for it. The column was not a precise formation. It was a blunt instrument, and it was effective because the revolutionary armies had more men than their opponents and were willing to spend them. The column was the drill's stepchild—a formation that used the drill's discipline but not its precision—and it was the formation that dominated the Napoleonic Wars.

Napoleon was a master of the drill, and he used it in a way that neither the Prussians nor the revolutionaries had. He combined the column and the line, the mass and the precision, the attack and the fire. He used artillery as a concentrated weapon, massing guns to break a hole in the enemy line and then sending infantry through the hole. He used cavalry as a pursuit weapon, chasing a broken enemy and turning a defeat into a rout. And he used the drill as the foundation of all of it, because a general who could not move his troops in a coordinated way could not execute the maneuvers Napoleon designed.

The Napoleonic Wars were the drill's greatest triumph and its greatest crisis. The triumph was that the drill made it possible to move and fight armies of a size never seen before. The crisis was that the drill was being applied to weapons that were changing, and the change was about to make the drill obsolete.
**The rifled musket and the drill's crisis.**

The weapon that changed the drill was the rifled musket, and the change was made possible by a French officer named Claude-Étienne Minié. In 1849, Minié designed a bullet—the Minié ball—small enough to slide down a rifled barrel and hollow at the base so that it expanded when the powder exploded and gripped the rifling. The Minié ball made it possible to load a rifled musket as quickly as a smoothbore, and a rifled musket was far more accurate and far longer-ranged than a smoothbore.

The Minié ball was adopted by the British as the Pattern 1853 Enfield, a .577-caliber rifled musket, and by the Americans as the Springfield Model 1861, a .58-caliber rifled musket. The two weapons were similar in performance, and both were far deadlier than the smoothbore muskets they replaced. A smoothbore musket was effective at perhaps fifty to a hundred yards. A rifled musket was effective at three hundred to five hundred yards, and it could kill at a thousand. The change was not incremental. It was a transformation.

The transformation destroyed the drill. The drill had been designed for a weapon effective at short range, and the drill's tactics—the advance in line, the volley at fifty paces—were designed for a battlefield where the enemy could not hit you until you were close. A rifled musket could hit you at three hundred yards, and a formation that advanced in line across three hundred yards of open ground would be shot to pieces before it got close enough to fire. The drill's tactics were suicidal against a rifled musket, and the armies of the Civil War learned this the hard way.

The Civil War was the first war in which the rifled musket was used on a large scale, and the casualties were horrific. The battle of Antietam, fought on 17 September 1862, produced about 23,000 casualties in a single day, most of them caused by rifled muskets. The battle of Gettysburg, fought over three days in July 1863, produced about 50,000 casualties, and Pickett's Charge—a frontal assault across a mile of open ground against a fortified position—was a demonstration of what happened when the drill's tactics met the rifled musket. The charge was a magnificent display of discipline. The men advanced in perfect order, under fire, and they were shot down in perfect order. The drill had made them brave, and the drill had made them vulnerable, and the vulnerability was the thing that the rifled musket was made of.
**The drill's afterlife: the parade ground and the training camp.**

The drill did not disappear after the Civil War. It retreated from the battlefield to the parade ground, where it became a form of ceremony, and to the training camp, where it became a form of basic training. The drill was no longer a tactic. It was a technique of socialization, a way of turning a civilian into a soldier, and it was retained because it worked. A recruit drilled to perform a sequence of movements automatically had learned to obey, and obedience was still the first virtue of a soldier.

The drill's afterlife is visible in the armies of the twentieth century. The British army drilled its recruits in the manual of arms, and the drill was a way of teaching them to handle a rifle safely and quickly. The American army drilled its recruits in close-order drill, and the drill was a way of teaching them to move as a unit. The Soviet army drilled its recruits on the parade ground, and the drill was a way of teaching them to endure. The drill was no longer the thing that the musket was made of, because the musket had been replaced by the rifle and the rifle by the machine gun, but the drill was still the thing that the soldier was made of, and the soldier was still the thing that the army was made of.

The drill's afterlife is also visible in the way armies train for the wars they actually fight. The drill was a technology of the open field, and the open field was replaced by the trench and the city and the jungle. The drill was adapted to the trench—the bayonet drill, the grenade drill, the gas drill—and to the city—the house-clearing drill, the room-entry drill—and to the jungle—the patrol drill, the ambush drill. The drill was no longer a single sequence of movements. It was a family of sequences, each designed for a specific tactical problem, each taught by repetition until it became automatic. The drill had become a general technology of training, and the general technology was the thing that the modern soldier was made of.
**The drill and the machine gun: the drill's revenge.**

The machine gun was the drill's revenge on the rifled musket. The rifled musket had made the drill's tactics suicidal, but the machine gun made the drill's discipline essential. A machine gun could fire hundreds of rounds per minute, and it could only be used effectively by a crew drilled to work together. The gunner aimed and fired. The loader fed the belt. The assistant gunner spotted and corrected. The crew had to perform their tasks in a coordinated sequence, under fire, without thinking, and the coordination was the drill.

The machine gun was invented by Hiram Maxim, an American inventor who demonstrated a recoil-operated automatic weapon in 1884. The Maxim gun used the recoil of the fired cartridge to eject the spent case, load a new cartridge, and fire again, and it could fire about six hundred rounds per minute. The British army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891, and the gun became the template for the automatic weapons of the twentieth century. The Maxim was not a musket, but it was a weapon that required a drill, and the drill was a descendant of the drill Maurice of Nassau had invented.

The machine gun's drill was a drill of a different kind. It was not a drill of the individual soldier. It was a drill of the crew, and the crew was a small unit, and the small unit was the thing the machine gun was made of. The machine gun's drill was also a drill of the emplacement—the gun had to be sited, the fields of fire cleared, the ammunition stockpiled—and the emplacement was the thing the trench was made of. The machine gun and the trench grew together, and the trench and the machine gun were the things the First World War was made of.
**The drill and the French 75: the drill of the gun crew.**

The machine gun was not the only weapon that required a crew drill. The French 75mm field gun, the Canon de 75 modèle 1897, depended on a drill as precise as any musket drill. The 75 was revolutionary because of its hydro-pneumatic recoil system, which kept the carriage steady when the gun fired, so that the gun did not have to be re-aimed after every shot. The gun could fire as fast as the crew could load it, and a well-drilled crew could fire about fifteen rounds per minute.

Fifteen rounds per minute was not a rate that could be achieved by a crew that was not drilled. The 75's crew—a gunner, a loader, a breech operator, an ammunition handler—had to perform their tasks in a sequence timed to the fraction of a second. The gunner aimed. The loader rammed the shell. The breech operator closed the breech. The gunner fired. The breech operator opened the breech. The loader rammed the next shell. The sequence was repeated, and the repetition was the drill. A crew that was not drilled could fire perhaps two or three rounds per minute. A crew that was drilled could fire fifteen. The difference was the difference between a weapon that was useful and a weapon that was decisive.

The 75 became an icon of the First World War, and its iconography was the iconography of the drill. The gun was photographed with its crew, and the crew was photographed in the act of loading, and the act of loading was a demonstration of the drill. The 75 was a weapon made of steel and cordite and recoil oil, but it was also a weapon made of the drill, and the drill was the thing the gun crew was made of.
**The drill and the trench: the drill's dissolution.**

The First World War was the war in which the drill dissolved. The drill had been designed for a battlefield on which men could see each other and fire at each other and advance against each other. The trench battlefield was a battlefield on which men could not see each other, and the weapons that dominated it—the machine gun, the artillery, the gas—were weapons that killed without being seen. The drill's tactics—the advance in line, the volley, the bayonet charge—were suicidal in the trench, and the armies that used them suffered casualties unprecedented in the history of war.

The Battle of Verdun, fought from 21 February to 18 December 1916, produced roughly 700,000 casualties, most of them caused by artillery. The artillery was the dominant weapon of the trench war, and it required a drill of its own—the drill of the gun crew, the drill of the forward observer, the drill of the ammunition supply—but the drill was a drill of machines, not of men. The infantryman in the trench was not drilled to advance. He was drilled to endure. He was drilled to stand in the mud and wait for the shell that would kill him, and the drill was a drill of endurance, and the endurance was the thing the trench was made of.

The drill's dissolution was not complete. The armies of the First World War developed new drills—the trench raid, the creeping barrage, the combined-arms attack—and the new drills were drills of small units, not of mass formations. The small-unit drill was the drill of the twentieth century, and it was a drill designed for a battlefield on which the individual soldier had to think for himself, because the mass formation had become a target.
