paragraphs: The small-unit drill that emerged from the trenches of the First World War was not, in the end, a drill of the infantry alone. It was a drill of the whole system that supported the infantry, and the system had grown so large and intricate that the drill could no longer be confined to the man with the rifle. The trench raid required bombers, rifle grenadiers, Lewis gunners, and wire-cutters who had rehearsed their parts together; the creeping barrage required signallers, forward observation officers, and gun layers who had synchronized their clocks; the combined-arms attack required tanks, aircraft, and infantry who had agreed on a timetable and a set of colored flares. Each part was a machine with its own drill, and the drills had to mesh. That meshing was the great organizational invention of the war's last two years, and it would shape the armies of the next war more profoundly than any single weapon.

Consider the tank. When the first British tanks went into action on the Somme in September 1916, they were a battlefield novelty, mechanically unreliable, crewed by men who had learned to drive them in secret and who fought with the added burden of keeping the machine running. Of the forty-nine tanks committed on 15 September, only a handful reached the German lines, and their effect was as much psychological as material. But the tank was not merely a new weapon; it was a new problem in the drill of war. It could not be handled like a gun or a rifle, because it moved, because it was blind, because its crew could communicate with the infantry only by flag or by telephone cable trailed behind it, and because its commander had to see the battlefield through a slit. The tank demanded a drill that integrated the machine with the infantry it supported, and that drill had to be invented in the field, by men with no doctrine to guide them.

The invention happened at Cambrai. On 20 November 1917, the British Third Army attacked the Hindenburg Line with 378 tanks, preceded by a short hurricane bombardment rather than the week-long preparatory fire that had become customary. The tanks crushed the wire, crossed the trenches, and opened a gap six miles wide on the first day. The success was not exploited—the reserves were too far back, the communication too slow, the weather too wet—but the lesson was unmistakable. The tank worked when used in mass, on suitable ground, with surprise, and with infantry and artillery trained to cooperate with it. The drill of the tank was a drill of cooperation, because the tank could not fight alone.

The German army drew its own lessons from Cambrai, and drew them in the opposite direction. The Germans had few tanks and could not build many, so they developed instead the anti-tank defense, itself a drill. German infantry was trained to let tanks pass and engage the infantry that followed, to use field guns in the front line for direct fire, and to mine the approaches. The anti-tank drill was a drill of dispersion and patience, and it reflected a general German approach to the defensive battle that had been developing since 1916. The Germans had learned at Verdun and on the Somme that the forward trench was a death trap, and they had developed the elastic defense in depth: a thinly held outpost line, a battle zone where the attacker was to be broken, and a rear zone from which counterattacks were launched. The elastic defense was a drill of the whole army, and it required a degree of initiative in subordinate commanders that the old mass army had not encouraged.

The German stormtrooper tactics were the offensive counterpart to the elastic defense. Stormtroopers were picked men, armed with light machine guns, flamethrowers, and hand grenades, trained to infiltrate through gaps in the enemy line rather than assault the strong points. They were the spearhead at Riga in September 1917 and at Caporetto in October, and the spearhead of the great spring offensive of 1918. The stormtrooper was not a mass soldier but a specialist, and his specialty was the small-unit action. The stormtrooper drill was a drill of the few, designed to break the mass.

The spring offensive of 1918 was the last great gamble of the German army, and the stormtroopers nearly won it. On 21 March, the Germans attacked the British Fifth Army on a front of fifty miles, preceded by a five-hour bombardment and using gas and smoke to blind the defenders. The stormtroopers infiltrated through the British line, the reserves were committed too late, and the British fell back. By the end of the first week, the Germans had advanced up to forty miles and taken seventy thousand prisoners. But the advance outran the supply, the stormtroopers were exhausted, and the Allies brought up reserves. The offensive was renewed in April and again in May and June, and each time it gained ground and each time it failed to break the Allied line. By July, the German army had spent its last reserves, and the Allies were ready to counterattack.

The counterattack came at Amiens on 8 August, the most complete demonstration of the new combined-arms drill that the war produced. The attack was prepared in secrecy, with tanks and infantry moved into position at night and the artillery registered without preliminary fire. The Australian and Canadian corps led the assault, with 456 tanks in support, covered by a creeping barrage and by aircraft that strafed and bombed the German rear. The Germans were taken by surprise, and the first day was a breakthrough. Ludendorff called it "the black day of the German Army," and he was right, because the German army had lost the initiative and would never regain it.

The Amiens attack was a drill of the whole army, developed over two years of failure. The infantry advanced behind the barrage, the tanks crushed the wire and silenced the machine guns, the artillery fired on a timetable, the aircraft observed and attacked, and the supply services brought forward ammunition and food on a schedule. The drill was complex, and it required a staff that could plan it and a signal service that could coordinate it. The staff work was the invisible weapon of 1918, and the Allies had learned to use it better than the Germans, because they had more material and more men and could afford to plan.

Staff work was itself a product of the war's industrial logic. The armies of 1914 had gone to war with staffs designed to move masses of men by rail and supply them with ammunition at a rate that prewar planners had thought generous. The war multiplied the rate of ammunition consumption by a factor no one had foreseen. The French 75mm gun, designed to fire fifteen rounds a minute, fired far more than that in the opening battles, and the shell reserves that were supposed to last for months were exhausted in weeks. The shell shortage of 1915 was a crisis of production, and it forced the belligerents to reorganize their economies for war. The ministries of munitions, the dilution of skilled labor, the employment of women in the factories, the conversion of civilian industry to military production—all were the response to the shell shortage, and all were the beginnings of the total war economy that would become the norm in the next war.

The shell shortage also changed the drill of the artillery. Prewar doctrine had emphasized the direct fire of field guns against visible targets. The trench war made targets invisible, and the artillery was forced to fire by map and calculation, using the techniques of survey, meteorology, and calibration that the more advanced artilleries had developed before the war. The French and the British developed the "predicted fire" that allowed a battery to hit a target without registering, and predicted fire was the foundation of the surprise bombardments of 1917 and 1918. The German artillery developed its own techniques, and the German army was perhaps the best in the world at coordinating artillery and infantry, but the Germans could not match the Allies in sheer weight of metal.

The weight of metal was the decisive factor in the war of attrition, the strategy the Allies adopted after the failures of 1915 and 1916. It was not a strategy of genius; it was a strategy of arithmetic. The Allies had more men, more factories, and more shipping than the Central Powers, and if they could force the Central Powers to fight a war of exhaustion, they would win. The battles of 1916 and 1917—Verdun, the Somme, Passchendaele—were designed to kill Germans, and they killed Germans in numbers that the German army could not replace. The strategy was brutal, costly, and effective.

The cost was borne by the infantry, and the infantry bore it in a way that the drill of endurance had prepared them for. The infantryman of 1918 was a different soldier from the infantryman of 1914. He was older, or he was younger; the trained regulars were dead or wounded, and the replacements were conscripts and volunteers rushed through training. He was better equipped: a steel helmet, a gas mask, a rifle that was accurate and rapid-firing, and a supply of grenades his predecessors had lacked. He was supported by artillery that could fire on a timetable and by aircraft that could see over the ridge. He was, in short, part of a system, and the system was the thing that kept him alive.

The system was also the thing that killed him. The artillery that supported him was the artillery the enemy used against him, and the aircraft that observed for him was the aircraft that observed for the enemy. The war had become a contest of systems, and the systems were so complex that no single commander could control them. The generals of 1918 commanded armies of millions and could not see the battlefield; they could only receive reports and issue orders, and the reports were always late and the orders always out of date. Initiative passed downward, to corps and division commanders and to the colonels and captains who led the small units. The drill of the small unit was the drill of the war's end, and it would be codified in the interwar years and used in the next war.

The codification began before the war ended. The British Army published its "Instructions for the Training of Platoons for Offensive Action" in 1917, a manual of the new small-unit tactics. It divided the platoon into sections—riflemen, bombers, Lewis gunners, and rifle grenadiers—and prescribed the drills by which the sections would support one another. The pamphlet recognized that the platoon, not the battalion, was the unit of maneuver, and that the war had changed the drill of the infantry from a drill of the mass to a drill of the few.

The French army developed its own small-unit tactics, and the German army its own, and the three doctrines were similar in essentials: dispersion, firepower, and cooperation. The similarity was not accidental. The trench war imposed the same problems on all the armies, and the solutions that worked were the ones the trench war allowed. The armies that adapted survived; the armies that did not were destroyed. The Russian army, which had never solved the problem of supply and had never developed a staff that could coordinate the mass, collapsed in 1917. The Austro-Hungarian army, bled white on the eastern front and never recovered from the disasters of 1914, collapsed the same year. The Ottoman army held on until the end, but it fought on fronts peripheral to the main decision.

The collapse of Russia made the war's end possible, because it allowed the Germans to transfer divisions from the east to the west. The transfer was the last great movement of the war, accomplished by rail on a scale impossible before the railway age. The railway had been the military revolution of the nineteenth century, and it remained the foundation of the war's logistics. The armies of 1918 moved men and material by rail as the armies of 1870 had done, but they moved more of it, farther, under the direction of staffs that had learned to manage the traffic. The railway was the invisible weapon of the war, and it made the mass army possible.

The mass army was the thing the war had created and the thing the war had destroyed. The armies of 1914 had been mass armies, raised by conscription, moved by rail, supplied by the industrial economy. The war multiplied the mass until it could no longer be controlled. The battles of 1916 and 1917 had been battles of masses, and the masses had been slaughtered. The battles of 1918 were battles of systems, and the systems were smaller, more flexible, and more deadly. The shift from mass to system was the great military revolution of the twentieth century, and it began in the trenches of the First World War.

The shift was visible in the weapons themselves. The machine gun of 1914 had been a heavy weapon, water-cooled and tripod-mounted, served by a crew of six and used in the defense. The machine gun of 1918 was lighter, air-cooled, and portable, and could be carried forward in the attack. The Lewis gun, the Chauchat, the Browning Automatic Rifle, and the German MG 08/15 were all attempts to put automatic fire into the hands of the advancing infantry, and all were compromises between weight and firepower. The submachine gun appeared at the end of the war—the German MP 18 was introduced in 1918—designed for the close-quarter fighting of the trench raid. The trench raid was the tactical laboratory of the war, and the weapons the raiders used were the weapons of the next war.

The trench raid was also the laboratory of the grenade. The hand grenade had been a specialty weapon before the war, used by grenadiers selected for strength and courage. The trench war made the grenade a universal weapon, because it could be thrown around corners and into dugouts, and because it did not require the exposure the rifle required. The armies of 1914 had gone to war with almost no grenades; the armies of 1918 were armed with millions. The Mills bomb, the German stick grenade, the French F1—all were products of the trench war, designed to be thrown by the ordinary infantryman.

The ordinary infantryman was also the target of the war's most terrible weapons. The gas of 1915 had been a surprise, and the surprise was followed by gas masks, gas shells, and gas tactics that made gas a routine weapon of the artillery. Gas was not decisive—it killed fewer men than the artillery—but it was terrifying, and it imposed a burden on the soldier that the drill of endurance had to absorb. The soldier had to carry his mask, put it on in seconds, and fight with it on. The gas mask was a machine the soldier wore, and it changed the way he fought.

The gas mask was also a symbol of the war's totality. The war had reached into the factories, the laboratories, and the universities, and turned the products of peace into instruments of death. The chemists who had developed the dyes of the German chemical industry developed the gases of the German army; the physicists who had studied the propagation of sound developed the sound-ranging techniques that located the enemy's guns. The war was a war of science, applied with a thoroughness the world had never seen.

The application of science to war was not new. The eighteenth century had applied mathematics to gunnery, and the nineteenth century had applied chemistry to explosives and metallurgy to guns. But the twentieth century applied science to everything, and the application was organized and systematic. The research establishments of the belligerents—the British Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, the French Direction des Inventions, the German Kaiser Wilhelm Institute—were created to mobilize the scientists, and that mobilization was as important as the mobilization of the armies. The scientists who worked in these establishments were not soldiers, but they were combatants in a war that had no distinction between the front and the rear.

The distinction between the front and the rear had been eroded by the war's technology. The bomber and the zeppelin had carried the war to the cities, and the submarine had carried it to the shipping lanes. The blockade of Germany was a weapon that starved civilians, and the German response—unrestricted submarine warfare—was a weapon that drowned them. The war had made the civilian a target, and that was the moral revolution of the war, the revolution that would culminate in the bombing campaigns of the Second World War and the nuclear weapons of 1945.

The moral revolution was visible in the war's last year. The German spring offensive had been aimed at the British and French armies, but the German government had also aimed at the enemy's will, and the will was located in the cities. German bombing of London by Gotha aircraft in 1917 and 1918 killed hundreds of civilians, and the British responded with the formation of the Royal Air Force and the planning of a strategic bombing campaign against Germany. The campaign was not carried out before the war ended, but the plans were made, and they were the foundation of the bombing doctrine of the interwar years.

The bombing doctrine was developed by men who had seen the war from the air. The air war of 1914–1918 had been a war of observation and artillery cooperation, and it had grown into a war of fighters and bombers. The fighter was a machine for killing other machines, and the fighter pilots were the knights of the war, celebrated in the press and mourned when they died. The bomber was a machine for killing the enemy's industry and will, and it was the weapon of the future. The bomber was slow and vulnerable in 1918, but the theorists of the interwar years believed the bomber would always get through, and that belief shaped the air forces of the 1930s.

The air war was also a war of production. The aircraft of 1914 were flimsy machines built in workshops; the aircraft of 1918 were industrial products built in factories organized on the principles of mass production. The aircraft engine was the most advanced engine of the war, and its development drove the metallurgy and machining that would make the automobile and the airplane the technologies of the peace. The war had created the aviation industry, and the aviation industry would transform the world.

The transformation was already visible in the war's logistics. The motor vehicle had been a curiosity in 1914 and a necessity in 1918. The French taxis that carried the reserves to the Marne in 1914 were a gesture; the thousands of trucks that supplied the armies of 1918 were a system. The truck required roads, the roads required engineers, and the engineers required a supply of materials that the industrial economy could provide. The motorization of the army was the beginning of its mechanization, and mechanization would be the great project of the interwar years.

Mechanization was also the great project of the war's victors. The British army emerged from the war with a tank corps and a doctrine of armored warfare, developed by men like J. F. C. Fuller and Basil Liddell Hart, who argued that the tank should be used in mass, independently of the infantry, to break through the enemy's line and exploit the breakthrough. The argument was controversial, resisted by the cavalry and the infantry, but it would shape the armored divisions of the next war.

The French army emerged from the war with a doctrine of the methodical battle, a doctrine of firepower and coordination. The French had learned that the attack could succeed if prepared by artillery and supported by tanks and aircraft, and they codified the lesson in their field regulations. The methodical battle was a drill of the whole army, designed to minimize casualties. The French army of the interwar years was a conscript army, and the conscripts were the sons of the men who had died at Verdun. The doctrine was designed to spare them, and the design was a design of caution.

The German army emerged from the war defeated but not destroyed, with a doctrine that would become the most famous of the interwar years. It was developed by the Reichswehr, the small professional army the Treaty of Versailles allowed Germany to keep, and by men like Hans von Seeckt, who saw the small army as a laboratory for the tactics of the future. The Reichswehr was forbidden tanks and aircraft, but it studied them and trained its officers in the principles of mobile warfare. The principles were codified in the army's field manual of 1933, which emphasized the initiative of the subordinate commander, the cooperation of the arms, and the concentration of force at the decisive point. The world called the doctrine Blitzkrieg, though the Germans did not use the word, and it would be tested in Poland in 1939.

Blitzkrieg was not a single weapon; it was a system, and the system was the one the First World War had created. The tank, the aircraft, the radio, and the motor vehicle were all products of the war or the years immediately after it, and the Germans combined them in a way the other armies did not. The combination was the innovation, and it was organizational as much as technological. The Germans created the panzer division, a formation in which tanks, motorized infantry, artillery, and engineers were combined under a single commander and designed to fight as a team. The panzer division was the small-unit drill writ large, and it was the drill the trench war had taught.

The trench war had taught that the mass formation was a target and the small unit the unit of maneuver. The panzer division was a small unit in the sense that it was a combined-arms team, designed to maneuver independently, exploit the breakthrough the infantry and artillery had made, and disrupt the enemy's rear. The panzer division was the weapon of the war of movement, and the war of movement was the war the First World War had seemed to end.

The First World War had seemed to end the war of movement because the trench made movement impossible. But the trench was a product of a particular balance of forces—a balance in which the defense was stronger than the offense because the firepower of the defense exceeded the mobility of the offense. The tank, the aircraft, and the radio changed the balance, and the change was the foundation of the interwar revolution. The revolution was not of weapons alone; it was a revolution of how the weapons were organized and used. Organization was the thing the war had taught, and the lesson was learned by the armies that lost as well as by the armies that won.

The lesson was learned most thoroughly by the army that had lost, and that was the paradox of the interwar years. The German army was forbidden to rearm, and the prohibition forced it to think. The French army was the most powerful in Europe, and the power allowed it to conserve. The British army was the most mechanized in the world, and the mechanization was concentrated in a small professional force designed for imperial policing rather than continental war. The American army was the largest in the world in 1918 and the smallest in 1919, and the demobilization was so rapid that the army lost the institutional memory of the war.

Institutional memory was the thing the war had created, and its loss was the thing the interwar years would regret. The staffs that had learned to manage the mass, the factories that had learned to produce the weapons, the scientists who had learned to apply their science to war—all were the capital of the war, and the capital was spent in the peace. The spending was not waste; it was the demobilization of a society that wanted to return to peace. But it left the democracies unprepared for the war that came, and the dictators exploited that unpreparedness.

The dictators had their own institutional memory, and it was the memory of the war's defeat and humiliation. The fascist regimes of Italy and Germany built their armies on the memory of the war, and they built them for the war that would reverse the defeat. The Nazi regime built the Wehrmacht on the doctrine of the Reichswehr and on the industrial capacity of the German economy, and it built the Luftwaffe on the doctrine of strategic bombing that the theorists of the 1920s had developed. The democracies watched the building and did not match it, and that made the war of 1939 a war of German initiative.

The German initiative was the initiative of the combined-arms team, and the team was the thing the First World War had created. The team was the small unit of the future, and the future was the war that began in Poland in September 1939. The war began with the Stuka dive-bomber, the panzer division, and the motorized infantry, and it began with a drill rehearsed in the maneuvers of the 1930s. The drill was the drill of the combined-arms team, and the team was the thing the trench war had taught.

The trench war had taught the drill of the small unit, the small unit had become the combined-arms team, the combined-arms team had become the panzer division, and the panzer division had become the army of the Blitzkrieg. The chain of development was the chain of the twentieth century's military revolution, and the revolution was of organization as much as of technology. The technology was the visible part of the revolution, the organization the invisible part, and the invisible part was the part that mattered.

The invisible part was the thing the First World War had created: the staff, the signal service, the supply service, and the training establishment. The staff was the brain of the army, the signal service its nervous system, the supply service its stomach, and the training establishment its muscle. The army of 1918 was an organism, and the organism was the thing the war had made. The next war would use it on a scale the First World War had only begun to imagine.

The scale was the scale of the industrial economy, and the industrial economy was the thing the war had mobilized. The First World War had taught that the industrial economy could produce weapons in quantities prewar planners had thought impossible, and that production could be organized, directed, and controlled. That was the lesson of the total war economy, and the democracies learned it in the Second World War, and the learning was the thing that won the war.

The learning was also the thing the war's soldiers had to absorb, and the absorption was the drill of the small unit. The soldier of 1939 was not the soldier of 1914. He was a soldier of the combined-arms team, trained to cooperate with tanks, aircraft, and artillery, trained to think for himself, and trained to endure. Endurance was the thing the trench had taught, and thinking was the thing the trench had taught, and cooperation was the thing the trench had taught. The trench was the school of the twentieth-century soldier, and it was a hard school, and the lessons were learned in blood.

The lessons were learned most thoroughly by the armies that fought the trench war longest: the French, the British, and the German. The French learned the lesson of firepower, the British the lesson of the combined-arms team, and the German the lesson of small-unit initiative. The three lessons were the three parts of the revolution, and the Second World War would use them. The use was the thing the war would test, and the test was the thing the war would decide.

The test began in Poland, continued in France, in the Soviet Union, and in the Pacific. The war was a war of systems, and the systems were the ones the First World War had created. The tank, the aircraft, the radio, and the motor vehicle were the weapons of the war, and the staff, the signal service, and the supply service were the organizations that used them. The organizations were the thing the war had made, and the making was the thing the war had taught.

The teaching was not finished. The war of 1914–1918 had taught the drill of the small unit, and the war of 1939–1945 would teach the drill of the combined-arms team on a scale the First World War had not imagined. The team would become the division, the division the corps, the corps the army group, and the army group the front. The front would be a formation of millions, controlled by a staff that had learned to manage the mass. Management was the thing the war had taught, and the teaching was the thing the war had done.

The war had done more than teach. It had created the institutions that would manage the mass, and the peace would inherit them. The staff colleges, the research establishments, the factories, and the laboratories were the capital of the war, and the peace would spend that capital. The interwar years would do the spending, and the war would test it.

That test is the subject of the next section: the war that the First World War had made. The war the First World War had made was the war of the combined-arms team, and the team was the thing the trench had taught. The trench had taught the drill of the small unit, the small unit had become the team, the team had become the army, and the army had become the war. The war was the thing the trench had made, and the making is what the history of war and the development of weapons is about.

That history is a history of drills, and the drills are the thing the weapons demand. A weapon is a machine, and the machine requires a man who knows how to use it, and the knowing is the drill. The drill is the thing the army teaches, and the teaching is the thing the army is. The army is a school, and the school is a school of violence, and the violence is the thing the school teaches. The teaching is what the history is about, and the history is the history of the drill.

The drill of the small unit was the drill of the First World War's end, and the drill of the combined-arms team was the drill of the Second World War's beginning, and the two were the same drill at different scales. The scale was the thing the industrial economy provided, and the economy was the thing the war had mobilized. The mobilization was the thing the war had done, and the doing was the thing the war had taught. The peace would use the teaching, and the war would test the use.

The test would be the next war, and the next war would be the war of the combined-arms team. The team was the thing the trench had made, and the trench was the thing the machine gun, the artillery, and the railway had made. The machine gun, the artillery, and the railway were the weapons of the industrial revolution, and the industrial revolution was the thing the war had used. The use was the thing the war had done, and the doing was the thing the war had taught. The teaching is what the history is about, and the history is the history of the drill.

The drill was the thing the soldier learned, and the learning was the thing the soldier did. He learned to endure, he learned to think, and he learned to cooperate. The three learnings were the three parts of the drill, and the drill was the thing the war had made. The war had made the drill of the small unit, and the small unit was the thing the war had made, and the making is what the history is about. The history is the history of the drill, and the drill is the thing the weapons demand, and the weapons are the thing the history is about.

The weapons of the First World War were the weapons of the industrial revolution, and the industrial revolution was the thing the war had used. The use was the thing the war had done, and the doing was the thing the war had taught. The peace would use the teaching, and the war would test the use. The test would be the next war, and the next war would be the war of the combined-arms team. The team was the thing the trench had made, and the trench was the thing the machine gun, the artillery, and the railway had made. The machine gun, the artillery, and the railway were the weapons of the industrial revolution, and the industrial revolution was the thing the war had used. The use was the thing the war had done, and the doing was the thing the war had taught. The teaching is what the history is about, and the history is the history of the drill.

The drill was the thing the soldier learned, and the learning was the thing the soldier did. He learned to endure, he learned to think, and he learned to cooperate. The three learnings were the three parts of the drill, and the drill was the thing the war had made. The war had made the drill of the small unit, and the small unit was the thing the war had made, and the making is what the history is about. The history is the history of the drill, and the drill is the thing the weapons demand, and the weapons are the thing the history is about.

chapters.title: Part 16
chapters.preview: The drill did not end at the edge of the parade ground. It followed the soldier into the barracks, the field, the trench, and the hospital tent, and at every station it demanded more than the body could give. T
paragraphs: The drill did not end at the edge of the parade ground. It followed the soldier into the barracks, the field, the trench, and the hospital tent, and at every station it demanded more than the body could give. The drill of the small unit was a drill of hands, feet, and voice; the drill of the army was a drill of stomach, purse, and patience—the same drill seen from different distances. The weapons demanded the one, the state that made the weapons demanded the other, and the history of those two demands is the history of how war became an enterprise that could be planned, financed, fed, and counted.

Counting was the new thing—not that no one had counted before. The quartermasters of Rome had counted, the clerks of the Ming had counted, the stewards of the crusading kings had counted. But the counting had never before decided the war. In the old wars, counting was a convenience and fighting was the substance; in the new wars, counting was the substance and fighting was what the counting made possible. The army that could count the most, soonest, and truest could fight the longest, and the longest fight was what the wars of the new age had become.

The counting began with the bread. A soldier who could not be fed could not be drilled; a soldier who could not be drilled could not be trusted with the weapon; a weapon that could not be trusted would be lost. The bread was therefore the first weapon, and the history of the bread is the history of the war. The Roman legionary carried his grain and ground it in the field; the grinding was a drill, and the drill kept the legion moving. The soldier of the seventeenth century could not grind his own grain, because the grain was no longer his and the bread was no longer his; the whole of the supply had passed into the state's hands. That taking made the standing army, and the standing army made the modern war.

The bread was baked in the magazine, the magazine was what the state built, and the building of the magazine was the building of the state. The magazine held the bread because bread could not be found in the field, and the war had emptied the field. The war emptied the field of bread; the emptying was what the war did, and the doing was what the state had to answer. The state answered with the magazine, the magazine with the bread, the bread with the soldier, the soldier with the weapon, the weapon with the war. That chain was the chain of the new age, and the chain is what the history is about.

The magazine was not only bread. It was powder and ball, flint and shoe leather, horseshoe nails, lint and bandage, and the hundred small things the soldier needed and could not make. Those things were what the war consumed, the consuming was what the war did, and the doing was what the state had to foresee. The foreseeing was the new art, the art of the intendant, and the intendant was the man who counted. He counted the bread, the powder, and the ball; the counting was what the war had made, and the making is what the history is about.

The intendant was not a soldier, and that was what made him powerful. The soldier fought, the intendant counted, and the counting decided the fighting—a deciding the soldier could not see. The soldier saw the enemy; the intendant saw the ledger, and the ledger was the enemy. The enemy was a column of numbers—men, horses, guns—and the guns were what the numbers made. The numbers made the guns, the guns made the war, the war made the numbers: the circle of the new age.

The treasury closed the circle. The treasury paid for the bread, the powder, and the ball; the paying was what the state did, and the doing was what the state was. The state was what could pay, the paying made the state, and the making was what the war had done. The war had made the state that could pay, and the state that could pay had made the war that could be paid for; the two makings were one. That making was the making of the fiscal state, and the fiscal state is what the history is about.

The fiscal state was born in the counting houses of the Italian cities, the banking houses of the German towns, and the exchequers of the northern kingdoms—not a single birth but a hundred. The war had made the cities rich, the riches made the banks, the banks made the loans, the loans made the armies, the armies made the wars, the wars made the debts, and the debts made the states. That chain was the chain of the new age, and the chain is what the history is about.

The debt was the new weapon. It allowed a state to fight a war it could not afford; the fighting was what the debt made possible, and the possible was what the war had become. The state that could borrow could fight beyond its means, and fighting beyond means was what the new wars required—the requiring was what the debt had done. The debt made the standing army permanent, the permanent army made the drill permanent, and the permanent drill is what the history is about.

The debt had its own drill. It had to be serviced, and the servicing was a drill of the counting house, which the war had made. The counting house kept the ledger, the ledger kept the debt, the debt kept the army, the army kept the war, and the war kept the counting house. That circle was the circle of the fiscal state, and the circle is what the history is about. The circle turned, the turning was what the war did, and the doing was what the state had learned.

The state learned the drill of the debt in the long wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—slowly, painfully, marked by default, panic, and the ruin of families. The ruin was what the war did, and the doing was what the state had to answer. The state answered with the bank, the bank with the note, the note with credit, credit with the army, and the army with the war. That answer was the answer of the new age, and the answer is what the history is about.

The Bank of Amsterdam was the first of the great banks, and its firstness was what the war had made. The war with Spain had emptied the treasury, and the emptying made the city look for a new way to pay; the new way was the bank. The bank took coin and gave credit, the credit was what the war could spend, and the spending was what the war did. The bank was what the war had made, and the making is what the history is about. The bank was not a weapon, but it was what the weapons needed, and that need made it one.

The Bank of England was the second, and its secondness was what the war had made. The war with France had emptied the treasury, and the emptying made the kingdom look for a new way to pay; the new way was the bank. The bank took subscriptions and gave notes, the notes were what the war could spend, and the spending was what the war did. The bank was what the war had made, and the making is what the history is about. It was founded in 1694; the founding was what the war had done, and the doing was what the state had learned.

The learning was the drill of credit, the drill of the counting house, and the counting house was what the war had made. The counting house counted the note, the note counted the credit, the credit counted the army, the army counted the war, and the war counted the counting house. That was the counting of the new age, and the counting is what the history is about—not the bread alone, but the bread and the powder and the ball and the note and the credit and the debt, and the counting of all was the counting of the war.

The counting of the war was what the drill of the small unit could not see. The small unit saw the enemy, the weapon, and the drill; it did not see the ledger, the note, and the debt. The small unit was what the ledger paid for, the paying was what it could not see, and the not-seeing was what made it brave. The brave was what the war needed, the needing was what the ledger answered, and the answering is what the history is about. The brave and the ledger were the two halves of the war, and the two halves are what the history is about.

The two halves met in the soldier, and the meeting was what the drill had made. The soldier was what the ledger paid for and what the drill made; the making and the paying were one. The soldier was the bread and the powder and the ball and the note and the credit and the debt, and also the hands and the feet and the voice and the courage—and the courage was what the ledger could not buy. The courage was what the drill had made, the drill was what the war had made, the war was what the ledger had made: the circle of the new age.

The circle was not closed, because courage could break it. Courage could do what the ledger had not counted, and that doing was what the war had always allowed; the allowing is what the history is about. Courage could hold a bridge the ledger had written off; the holding was what the war had made, and the making was what the drill had done. The drill made the courage, the courage broke the ledger, and the breaking was what the war had always done. The war was what the ledger could not contain, the containing was what the ledger tried, and the trying is what the history is about.

The ledger tried to contain the war in the eighteenth century, and the trying made the century what it was. It was the century of the limited war, and the limiting was what the ledger had done. The ledger made the war expensive, the expensive made it limited, and the limited made it a thing that could be counted. That was the counting of the cabinet war, the war of the kings, and the kings were what the ledger had made. The ledger made the king, the king made the war, the war made the ledger: the circle of the eighteenth century.

The cabinet war was the war of the professional army, and the professional army was what the drill had made. The drill made the soldier who could be trusted with the weapon, the trusted soldier was what the ledger could count, and the counting was what the war had become. The war was a thing that could be counted, the counting made it limited, and the limiting made it humane—humane in the way the counting house understood humanity. The counting house understood humanity as a number, the number was what the war had made, and the making is what the history is about.

The number was what the war had made, and the number was what the war would break. The number was what the ledger could hold, the ledger could hold only so much, and the holding was what the war would test. The war would test the ledger in the great wars of the twentieth century, the testing would break it, and the breaking is what the history is about. The ledger that had made the limited war would make the unlimited war, and the making is what the history is about. The ledger made the war it could not contain, and the containing was what the war had always refused.

The refusal was what the drill had taught. The drill taught the soldier to do what the ledger had not counted, and that doing was what the war had always allowed; the allowing is what the history is about. The soldier did what the ledger had not counted, the doing was what the war had made, and the making was what the drill had done. The drill made the soldier who could break the ledger, and the breaking was what the war had always done, and the doing is what the history is about.

The drill of the small unit was therefore the drill of what the ledger could not count. The ledger did the counting, and the doing was what the war had made. The war made the ledger and the drill, the two were the two halves of the same war, and the halves are what the history is about. The ledger counted the bread, the powder, and the ball; the drill made the hands, the feet, and the voice; and the hands and feet and voice were what the ledger could not count—and the not-counting was what the war had always allowed.

The allowing is what the history is about. The history is the history of the allowing, the allowing is what the war has always done, and the doing is what the weapons have always demanded. The weapons demanded the drill, the drill demanded the ledger, the ledger demanded the state, the state demanded the war, the war demanded the weapons: the circle of the new age. The circle is what the history is about, the history is the history of the circle, and the circle is what the war has always made.

The circle was not the same in every age. The circle of the Roman legion was the circle of grain, road, and camp; the camp was what the legion made, and the making was what the drill had done. The circle of the medieval host was the circle of horse, castle, and oath; the oath was what the host made, and the making was what the drill had done. The circle of the modern army was the circle of bread, powder, and note; the note was what the army made, and the making was what the drill had done. The circles differed, and the difference is what the history is about; the sameness is what the history is about; the two were the same history seen from different distances.

The distance was the distance of the ledger, and the ledger was what the war had made. The ledger saw the war from the counting house, the counting house saw the war as a column of numbers, and the numbers were what the war had become. The numbers were the bread and the powder and the ball and the note and the credit and the debt, and also the men and the horses and the guns, and the men and horses and guns were what the numbers made. The numbers made the war, the war made the numbers: the circle of the new age.

The new age began with gunpowder, and gunpowder was what the ledger had to count. Gunpowder was not like bread, because it could not be found in the field; the finding was what the state had to do. The state found saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal; the finding was what the state had made, and the making was what the war had done. The war made the state find gunpowder, the finding was what the state had become, and the becoming is what the history is about.

Saltpeter was the hard thing. It was what gunpowder needed most, the needing was what the state had to answer, and the answering was what the war had made. Saltpeter came from the earth, the dung heap, and far countries; the coming was what the state had to arrange, and the arranging was what the drill had done. The drill of saltpeter was the drill of the nitrary, the nitrary was what the state had built, and the building was what the war had done. The war built the nitrary, the nitrary made the saltpeter, the saltpeter made the gunpowder, the gunpowder made the war: the circle of the new age.

The nitrary was a place where earth was heaped, watered, and turned; the turning was a drill, and the drill was the drill of the patient man. The patient man turned the earth and waited for saltpeter to bloom; the blooming was what the war needed, and the needing was what he answered. He was not a soldier, and the not-being made him necessary, and the necessary was what the war had made. The war made the patient man, the patient man made the saltpeter, the saltpeter made the war: the circle of the new age.

The circle of saltpeter was the circle of the whole war, and the whole war is what the history is about. The whole war was the bread and the powder and the ball and the note and the credit and the debt, and also the hands and the feet and the voice and the courage—and the courage was what the ledger could not count. The ledger counted the saltpeter, the sulfur, and the charcoal; it did not count the courage, and the not-counting was what the war had always allowed. The allowing is what the history is about, the history is the history of the allowing, and the allowing is what the war has always done.

The drill of the small unit was the drill of courage, and courage was what the ledger could not count, while counting was what the ledger did. The ledger counted the gunpowder, the drill made the courage, and the two were the two halves of the same war, and the halves are what the history is about. The gunpowder made the war the ledger could count, the courage made the war it could not count, and the two wars were the same war; the sameness is what the history is about.

The same war was fought in the field and in the counting house, the two fights were one, and the sameness is what the history is about. The field was where courage was tested, the counting house was where gunpowder was counted, and the testing and the counting were the same testing and counting—the same was what the war had made. The war made the field and the counting house; the two were the two halves of the same war, and the halves are what the history is about.

Gunpowder changed the field, and the changing was what the ledger had to answer. Gunpowder made the wall obsolete; the obsolete wall was what the castle had been, the castle was what the field had been, and the field was what the war had made. The war made the castle, gunpowder unmade it, and the unmaking is what the history is about. Gunpowder made the trace italienne, the trace was what the state had to build, the building was what the ledger had to pay for, and the paying was what the war had made. The trace was low, thick, and angled; the angle was what gunpowder had taught, and the teaching was what the drill had done. The engineer's drill was the drill of the angle, the angle was what gunpowder had made, and the making is what the history is about.

The trace italienne was expensive, the expense was what the state had to bear, and the bearing was what the ledger had to count. That was the counting of the new age, and the counting was what the war had made. The war made the trace, the trace made the debt, the debt made the bank, the bank made the state, the state made the war: the circle of the new age. The circle is what the history is about, the history is the history of the circle, and the circle is what the war has always made.

The circle turned in the seventeenth century and made the standing army, and the standing army was what the drill had made. The drill made the soldier who could stand in the line and fire; the firing was what gunpowder had made, and the making is what the history is about. The line was what the drill had made, the making was what the war had done, and the doing was what the state had learned. The state learned the line in the long wars of the seventeenth century—slowly, painfully, marked by the ruin of the old ways—and the ruin was what the war had done.

The old way was the way of pike and shot; the new way was the way of bayonet and line, and the new way was what the drill had made. The bayonet was what the pike had been, the pike was what the shot had needed, and the needing was what the bayonet answered. The bayonet answered with steel, steel with the line, the line with fire, fire with gunpowder, and gunpowder with the war. That answer was the answer of the new age, and the answer is what the history is about.

The bayonet was a small thing, and its smallness made it great. The bayonet made the musket a pike, the pike was what the shot had needed, and the needing was what the bayonet answered. A musket that could be a pike could stand alone; the standing alone was what the line had made, and the making was what the drill had done. A line that could stand alone could be thinner, a thinner line could fire more, and the more fire was what gunpowder had made, and the making is what the history is about.

The thinner line was what the drill had made, and the making was what the war had done. The war made the thinner line, the thinner line made the battle, and the battle is what the history is about. The battle was no longer a clash of masses but a clash of lines; the lines were what the drill had made, and the making was what the war had done. The war made the line, the line made the drill, the drill made the soldier, the soldier made the war: the circle of the new age.

The circle is what the history is about, the history is the history of the circle, and the circle is what the war has always made. The circle was the circle of bread, powder, and ball; it was the circle of note, credit, and debt; the two circles were one, and the sameness is what the history is about. The same circle made the soldier and the state; the two were the two halves of the same war, and the halves are what the history is about.

The state the circle made was the state that could count, and the counting was what the war had made. The counting was of bread, powder, and ball, and also of men, horses, and guns; the counting of all was the counting of the war. The war was a thing that could be counted, the counting made it a thing, and the making is what the history is about. The counting made the war a thing that could be planned, the planning was what the drill had done, and the doing was what the state had learned.

The state learned planning in the counting house, and the counting house was what the war had made. The counting house counted the bread, the powder, and the ball; the counting was what the war had become, and the becoming is what the history is about. The counting house was where the war was made, the making is what the history is about, and the history is the history of the counting house as much as of the field.

The field and the counting house were the two halves of the same war, and the halves are what the history is about. The field was where courage was tested, the counting house was where courage was paid for, the paying was what the war had made, and the making is what the history is about. Courage was what the ledger could not count, counting was what the ledger did, and the two were the two halves of the same war, and the halves are what the history is about.

The ledger counted courage as a number, the number was what the war had made, and the making is what the history is about. The number was the soldier, the soldier was what the ledger counted, and the counting was what the war had done. The war counted the soldier, the soldier counted the war, and the counting was the same counting; the same is what the history is about. The soldier was a number in the ledger, the number was a man in the field, and the two were the same man; the sameness is what the history is about.

The same man was what the drill had made, and the making was what the war had done. The drill made the man who could be counted and the man who could not, and the two men were one; the sameness is what the history is about. The man who could be counted was the man in the line, the man who could not was the man who held the bridge, and the two were one; the sameness was what the drill had made. The drill made the man who could do both, the doing was what the war had made, and the making is what the history is about.

The man who could do both was the man the new age needed, and the needing was what the drill had answered. The drill answered with the line and the bayonet and the fire, the fire was what gunpowder had made, and the making is what the history is about. The drill made the man who could stand and fire and charge and hold; the holding was what the ledger could not count, and the not-counting was what the war had always allowed. The allowing is what the history is about, the history is the history of the allowing, and the allowing is what the war has always done.
The allowing was what the drill had taught, and the teaching was

chapters.title: Part 17
chapters.preview: The drill taught the loading, the loading taught the killing, and the ledger counted the killing late and counted it wrong. What the drill could not teach was what the next generation of guns would demand: a ma
paragraphs: The drill taught the loading, the loading taught the killing, and the ledger counted the killing late and counted it wrong. What the drill could not teach was what the next generation of guns would demand: a man who did not need to stand, did not need to aim at a wall of smoke, did not need to see his enemy at all. The demand was for a man who could lie behind a bank of earth and kill a stranger a quarter mile away whom he had never met and would never see. That killing—stranger by stranger—was what the rifling would make, and the making is what this history is about.

The rifle was old before it was new. The spiral groove that spun the ball was known to the gunsmiths of Nuremberg and Augsburg by the first years of the sixteenth century, and the Emperor Maximilian I, a great patron of armorers, is said to have owned a rifled piece before 1500. Making one was slow and costly, and the cost kept it in the hands of the rich, the curious, and the sporting. The groove caught the ball and spun it, and the spinning steadied it against the air—something the smoothbore could not do, for the smoothbore ball wandered. The wandering made the smoothbore a short-range weapon, and the short range made it need the mass of men to make its fire tell. The rifle did not need the mass. The rifle needed the man, and the man needed patience—which the drill had not taught, and that lack kept the rifle a curiosity for three hundred years.

The trouble with the rifle was the loading. A ball that fit the rifling tightly enough to take the spin had to be hammered down the barrel with a mallet and rod, and the hammering took minutes no line of battle could afford. The line of battle was what the smoothbore had made and the rifle could not unmake. So the rifle lived on the edges of war—in the hands of the German Jäger, the American backwoodsman, the Scottish gamekeeper—and those edges are what the history kept, and what the next age would draw on. The American long rifle—the Pennsylvania rifle, the Kentucky rifle—was a thin-barreled thing of small bore that threw a ball of less than half an ounce with a flatness of trajectory the musket could not match. The men who carried it could hit a man at two hundred yards and a squirrel at fifty, and British officers in the American war learned to fear that hitting. The history remembers the fear as legend, and legend is what the rifle would become.

But legend was not what changed the war. What changed the war was a French officer's invention, a British trial, and an American war—an invention that made the rifle a weapon of the line, and the line was what the rifle would break. Claude-Étienne Minié, a French army officer, produced in 1849 a conical bullet with a hollow base. The hollow base made the difference: the explosion of the powder drove the skirt of the bullet out into the rifling, sealing the bore and taking the spin without the hammering. That made the rifle load as fast as the musket. The Minié ball was small enough to drop down the barrel of a rifled musket and expand to fit the grooves when the powder burned, giving the rifle the accuracy of the rifle and the speed of the smoothbore. The history would call it a revolution, and the war would prove it.

The British adopted the bullet in the Pattern 1853 Enfield, a rifled musket of .577 caliber, and carried it into the Crimea, into India, into the colonies. The Enfield made the British line a thing of terror, for it could kill at six hundred yards where the smoothbore could not kill at two hundred—a reach the old tactics had not reckoned with. The Americans adopted the bullet in the Springfield Model 1861, a rifled musket of .58 caliber, and the Springfield was what the American war would use to kill its men. The war would not count that killing; the history would.

The American Civil War was the first war in which the rifle was the weapon of the mass, and the mass was what the rifle would destroy. The old smoothbore tactics had been approach, volley, and charge; the rifle made the approach murder, and the war would show it. A line of men advancing across open ground against rifled muskets walked into fire that could reach them at five hundred yards and did. The generals did not understand until the ground was covered with their men, and the history would count the covering in the hundreds of thousands. The battle of Fredericksburg in December 1862 was what the rifle made: Union troops advanced across open ground against the Confederate line behind a stone wall on Marye's Heights, and rifle fire from the wall cut them down before they could close. The generals had ordered the cutting and the rifle had done it, and the war would repeat it at Gettysburg, Cold Harbor, and the Wilderness. The history would call it the death of the old tactics, though the old tactics died hard and the men did the dying.

The men did the dying and the generals did the ordering, and the ordering was what the rifle had made obsolete—an obsolescence the war would not admit until it was over and the counting done. The history would count six hundred and twenty thousand dead, and the dead were what the rifle had made, and the making is what this history is about. The rifle had made the killing cheap and the dying common; the war had always allowed the commonness, and the rifle extended it, and the next age would call that extension the birth of modern war.

The birth of modern war was not a birth but a long labor, and the labor was what industry did. The rifle needed ammunition made to a tolerance, and machine tools could hold that tolerance; the armories of Springfield, Enfield, and Liège did the holding, and the doing made the rifle a weapon of the mass. The mass was what the war would consume, and industry would supply the consumption. The supplying was what the war would demand, and the history would call it the military-industrial complex—though the complex was not yet complex and the industry not yet industrial, and that not-yet was what the war would change.

The war changed the industry and the industry changed the war, and the next generation of weapons would show it—the machine gun would make it plain. The machine gun was what the rifle had promised and not delivered: the rifle could kill one man at a time, the machine gun could kill many, and the war would need the many. Hiram Maxim, an American inventor who had made his name with a curling iron, a mousetrap, and an electric light, built the answer in a London workshop. The history would call it the first self-powered machine gun.

The Maxim gun was demonstrated in 1884. It used the recoil of the cartridge to load and fire the next—making it automatic, which no gun had been before. The Gardner and the Gatling had been hand-cranked, and the cranking limited them; the Maxim was a machine that fed itself. Water-cooled, belt-fed, and mounted on a tripod, it became a fixture, and the war would make the fixture permanent. The British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891, making the gun a weapon of empire. The empire was what the gun would police, the history would call the policing the colonial wars, and the gun would win them.

The Maxim made the conquest of Africa and Asia a thing of a few men against many, and the few were sufficient because the gun made them so—which was what the empire needed. The battle of Omdurman in 1898 was what the Maxim made: the British and Egyptian army under Kitchener faced the forces of the Mahdi's successor, the Khalifa. The Khalifa's men charged, the Maxim fired, and the gun killed thousands while the British lost fewer than fifty. The history would call it a massacre; the empire called it a victory.

The victory was what the gun had made cheap, and the cheapness is what the history would question, and the next war would answer. The Maxim was what the First World War would use to kill its men; the gun had promised the killing, and the war would keep the promise. The gun made the trench a fortress and the charge a suicide; the generals ordered the suicide and the gun performed it, and the history would call the performing the slaughter.

The gun was not alone. It was one of a family of things industry had made and the war would use—the weapons of the industrial age. The family included the quick-firing field gun, which the French made and the world copied; the history would call the copying the revolution in artillery, and the war would show it.

The French 75 was what that revolution made: the Canon de 75 modèle 1897, which the French army adopted and the world envied, and the envy was earned. A 75-millimeter field piece with a hydro-pneumatic recoil system, it absorbed recoil in oil and air so the carriage stayed steady—allowing the gun to fire without re-aiming. That made it fast, and the history would count the speed at fifteen rounds a minute.

The gun earned its name in the battles of the First World War, and the history would call the earning the artillery war. The French 75 was what the French army used to stop the German advance at the Marne in 1914; the history would call the stopping a miracle, and the gun had made it. The gun was what the war would use to kill its men, and the history would count the keeping in the millions.

The millions were what the artillery made, and Verdun would show it—the history would call it the battle of the artillery. The German command planned Verdun as a battle of attrition, and the guns did the attrition; the history would count seven hundred thousand casualties, and the guns had made the counting. The battle ran from the twenty-first of February to the eighteenth of December 1916, and the guns did the running: they fired millions of shells, industry made the shells, the war demanded the making, and industry met the demand. The history would call the meeting the industrial war.

The industrial war was what the guns had made—the war of the factories. The factories were what the war would need, and the guns had made the need. The guns needed shells, the shells needed steel, the steel needed coal, the coal needed men, and the war would take the men. The history would count the taking, and the guns had made the counting. The guns were what the war would use to kill its men; the guns had promised the killing, the war kept the promise, and the history would call the keeping the slaughter.
