paragraphs: The trench was a machine for making the artillery necessary, and the artillery was a machine for making the trench necessary, and the loop between them was the loop the war could not break because the war was the loop. By the winter of 1915 the Western Front had become a continuous industrial work, three hundred miles of it, and the work was the work of digging and the digging was the work of the guns, for every shell that fell required a trench to hide from it, and every trench that was dug required a shell to reach it, and the two grew together in a terrible arithmetic that neither side could solve by adding more of either. The generals asked for more guns, and the factories gave them more guns, and the guns demanded more shells, and the factories gave them more shells, and the shells demanded more trenches, and the trenches demanded more shells, and the whole apparatus turned on itself like a wheel geared to its own axle. The wheel was the war, and the war was the wheel, and the history of the weapons in the middle years of the First World War is the history of a machine that had learned to feed on itself.

The numbers were the first thing the war taught the accountants to count, and the accountants counted them because the generals could not fight without them. In the first months of the war the British Expeditionary Force had gone to France with a few hundred field guns and a ration of shells the staff had calculated on the experience of the Boer War, and the calculation had been wrong by an order of magnitude, and the wrongness was discovered at the Battle of Neuve Chapelle in March 1915, when the gunners fired more ammunition in three days than the staff had allotted for a month, and the ammunition ran out, and the attack stalled, and the stall was blamed on the gunners, and the gunners on the staff, and the staff on the politicians, and the politicians on the factories, and the factories on the workers, and the workers on the war. The war was the thing that could not be blamed because the war was the thing that did the blaming, and so the blame moved down the chain until it reached the shell, and the shell was the thing that was missing, and the missing shell became the scandal the newspapers called the shell shortage, and the shortage became the thing the government had to answer for, and the answer was more factories and more workers and more shells, and the more was the thing the war would demand for the next three years.

The shell crisis of 1915 was not a crisis of production in the way the newspapers imagined it; it was a crisis of expectation, and the expectation was the thing the prewar staffs had gotten wrong. The prewar staffs had calculated that a battle would last a few days and that a few hundred rounds per gun would be enough, and the calculation was based on the wars of the nineteenth century, when the infantry had done the killing and the artillery had done the softening, and the softening had been a prelude and not a performance. In the trenches the artillery became the performance, and the infantry became the audience, and the audience was expected to walk out onto the stage when the performance was over and occupy the ground the performance had cleared, and the performance had to be long enough and loud enough and thorough enough to clear the ground, and the clearing was the thing the shells did, and the shells were the thing the factories had to make. The factories made them, and the making was the thing the war had taught the factories to do, and the teaching is the thing the history records as the mobilization of industry, and the mobilization was the thing that turned the war from a war of armies into a war of economies, and the economies were the thing the war would consume.

The French had learned the lesson earlier and harder, because the French had been fighting on their own soil and had lost the industrial north in the first weeks of the war, and the loss had taken the coal and the iron and the factories the French army needed, and the French army had been forced to buy its shells from Britain and America and to build new factories in the south, and the building was the thing the French did with a ferocity the history has never quite forgiven, because the ferocity was the thing the war demanded and the war was the thing the French could not lose. By 1916 the French were producing more shells than they had ever produced before the war, and the production was the thing that made Verdun possible, and Verdun was the thing the production had been built for, and the building is the thing the history calls the battle.

Verdun was the battle the German staff had designed to bleed the French army white, and the design was the design of a gunner, because the German chief of staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, had calculated that if he attacked a place the French could not abandon, the French would throw their army into the defense, and the German artillery would kill them, and the killing would be the victory, and the victory would be the thing the guns would do without the infantry having to take the ground. The place was Verdun, a fortress town on the Meuse the French had held since before the revolution, and the holding was the thing the French could not give up because the giving up would be the thing the French could not bear, and the bearing was the thing the German staff had counted on. The German staff massed more than a thousand guns on a front of eight miles, and the guns were the thing the battle would be, and the battle began on the twenty-first of February 1916 with a bombardment the French survivors described as a storm that did not end, and the storm did not end for ten months, and the ten months are the thing the history calls the Battle of Verdun, and the battle produced roughly seven hundred thousand casualties, and the casualties were the thing the guns had made.

The guns at Verdun were the guns the factories had made, and the factories had made them because the factories had been told to make them, and the telling was the thing the war had taught the states to do, and the states had learned the lesson because the states had been forced to learn it. The French had a gun the history remembers as the seventy-five, and the seventy-five was the thing the French had built before the war, and the building was the thing the French had done with a mechanical genius the history has never quite explained, because the genius was the thing the French had and the French had it because the French had been thinking about the next war since the last one. The Canon de 75 modèle 1897 was the first field gun with a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady, and the steadiness was the thing that allowed the gun to fire without being re-aimed after every shot, and the firing was the thing the gun could do at a rate the history often cites as roughly fifteen rounds per minute, and the fifteen was the thing the gun could do if the crew was good and the ammunition was there, and the ammunition was the thing the factories had to make, and the making was the thing the war had made necessary. The seventy-five was the icon of the French army, and the icon was the thing the French believed in, and the belief was the thing the French took to Verdun, and Verdun was the thing the belief could not survive, because the seventy-five was a field gun and the field gun was the thing the war had outgrown, and the war had outgrown it because the war had dug in, and the digging in was the thing that required the heavy howitzer, and the heavy howitzer was the thing the French had not built enough of, and the not building was the thing the French would pay for at Verdun.

The German guns at Verdun were the heavy howitzers the German factories had built, and the building was the thing the German staff had ordered before the war, and the ordering was the thing the German staff had done because the German staff had read the lessons of the siege of Port Arthur, where the Japanese had used heavy howitzers to break the Russian forts, and the breaking was the thing the German staff had wanted to do to the French forts, and the French forts were the thing the German staff had aimed at, and the aiming was the thing the German staff had done with a precision the history records as the thing that made Verdun a siege rather than a battle. The German guns fired more than twenty million shells at Verdun, and the firing was the thing the German factories had to supply, and the supplying was the thing the German railways had to carry, and the carrying was the thing the German army had to protect, and the protecting was the thing the German infantry had to do, and the doing was the thing the German infantry could not do forever, because the infantry was the thing the guns were supposed to spare, and the sparing was the thing the guns could not do, because the guns could not take the ground, and the ground was the thing the infantry had to take, and the taking was the thing the infantry died doing, and the dying was the thing the battle was, and the battle was the thing the guns had made.

The battle of the Somme was the British answer to Verdun, and the answer was the thing the British had been preparing since the shell crisis, and the preparing was the thing the British had done with a thoroughness the history records as the thing that made the first day of the Somme the worst day in the history of the British army. The British had massed more than fourteen hundred guns on a front of eighteen miles, and the guns had fired a preliminary bombardment that lasted a week, and the week was the thing the British staff had calculated would destroy the German defenses, and the calculation was the thing the British staff had gotten wrong, because the German defenses were deep and the German trenches were dug into the chalk and the chalk was the thing the shells could not break, and the breaking was the thing the British staff had counted on, and the counting was the thing the British infantry had to pay for. The British infantry went over the top on the first of July 1916, and the going was the thing the British infantry did with a courage the history has never been able to describe without the word slaughter, and the slaughter was the thing the German machine guns did, and the machine guns were the thing the British staff had underestimated, and the underestimating was the thing the British staff had done because the British staff had believed the bombardment would have killed the German gunners, and the killing was the thing the bombardment had not done, because the German gunners had sheltered in deep dugouts and had come up when the bombardment lifted, and the coming up was the thing the British infantry saw when they were halfway across no man's land, and the seeing was the thing the British infantry could not survive.

The first day of the Somme cost the British army more than fifty-seven thousand casualties, of whom nearly twenty thousand were killed, and the killing was the thing the machine gun did, and the machine gun was the thing the history had been building toward since the Maxim had demonstrated its recoil-operated mechanism in 1884. The Maxim gun had been the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun, and the self-powering was the thing the gun did with the recoil of its own firing, and the firing was the thing the gun could do at a rate the history often cites as six hundred rounds per minute, and the six hundred was the thing the gun could do if the ammunition was fed and the barrel was cooled and the crew was trained, and the training was the thing the armies had done before the war, and the doing was the thing the armies had done because the armies had believed the machine gun was a defensive weapon, and the defensive was the thing the machine gun was, and the defensive was the thing the infantry attacked into, and the attacking was the thing the infantry did because the infantry had been ordered to attack, and the ordering was the thing the staffs did because the staffs believed the attack was the thing that would win the war, and the winning was the thing the attack could not do, because the attack was the thing the machine gun was built to stop, and the stopping was the thing the machine gun did with a thoroughness the history records as the thing that made the trench deadlock.

The machine gun was not a new weapon in 1914, but the trench was a new thing, and the trench was the thing that made the machine gun decisive, because the trench was the thing that forced the infantry to attack across open ground, and the open ground was the thing the machine gun could sweep, and the sweeping was the thing the machine gun did with a precision the infantry could not match, and the matching was the thing the infantry tried to do with more men and more courage and more artillery, and the more was the thing the machine gun killed, and the killing was the thing the war became. The machine gun was the thing the armies had to answer, and the answer was the thing the armies developed in the middle years of the war, and the developing is the thing the history records as the invention of the tactics the war would need, and the tactics were the thing the weapons had made necessary.

The first answer to the machine gun was the trench raid, and the raid was the thing the infantry did at night, and the night was the thing the machine gun could not sweep, and the sweeping was the thing the machine gun did in daylight, and the daylight was the thing the infantry could not survive, and the surviving was the thing the infantry did in the dark. The raid was a small thing, a few men with grenades and wire cutters and a knife, and the knife was the thing the raid used when the grenades were gone, and the grenades were the thing the raid used when the knife was not enough, and the enough was the thing the raid could not be, because the raid was a raid and the raid did not take ground, and the ground was the thing the war required, and the requiring was the thing the raid could not satisfy. The raid was the thing the infantry did to keep the infantry alive, and the alive was the thing the raid could not guarantee, because the raid was the thing the machine gun could kill if the machine gun was awake, and the awake was the thing the raid tried to prevent, and the preventing was the thing the raid did with the knife, and the knife is the thing the history records as the weapon of the trench raid, and the trench raid was the thing the war made necessary, and the necessary was the thing the war always was.

The second answer to the machine gun was the tank, and the tank was the thing the British developed in secret under the cover name of the water carrier, and the water carrier was the thing the workers called the tank because the tank was a tank and the name stuck, and the sticking is the thing the history records as the birth of the armored vehicle, and the birth was the thing the war had made necessary, and the necessary was the thing the tank answered. The tank was a box of steel on tracks, and the tracks were the thing the tank used to cross the trench, and the crossing was the thing the tank did because the tank could, and the could was the thing the tank had because the tank was tracked and the tracks were the thing the tank had borrowed from the agricultural tractor, and the borrowing is the thing the history records as the thing that made the tank possible, and the possible was the thing the tank became at the Battle of Flers-Courcelette in September 1916, when the British sent forty-nine tanks into action, and the action was the thing the tanks did with a mechanical unreliability the history records as the thing that kept the tanks from being decisive, and the decisive was the thing the tanks would become, and the becoming was the thing the war would not live to see.

The tank was the thing the war had been building toward since the first armored train, and the armored train was the thing the nineteenth century had built, and the building was the thing the railway had made possible, and the possible was the thing the tank inherited, and the inheriting was the thing the tank did with the engine and the armor and the gun, and the gun was the thing the tank carried, and the carrying was the thing the tank did because the tank was a moving fortress, and the fortress was the thing the tank had been designed to be, and the designing was the thing the British navy had done, because the British navy had been given the job of breaking the trench deadlock, and the deadlock was the thing the navy could not break with ships, and the ships were the thing the navy had, and the having was the thing the navy used to build the tank, and the building was the thing the navy did with the armor plate and the naval gun and the naval engine, and the engine was the thing the tank needed, and the needing was the thing the navy understood, and the understanding was the thing that made the tank a naval weapon in its bones, and the bones were the thing the tank would keep, and the keeping is the thing the history records as the thing that made the tank a ship on land.

The third answer to the machine gun was the storm trooper, and the storm trooper was the thing the German army invented, and the inventing was the thing the German army did because the German army had learned the lesson of the trench, and the lesson was the thing the German army had learned from the French, and the French had learned it from the Russians, and the Russians had learned it from the Japanese, and the Japanese had learned it from the Germans, and the learning was the thing the war had made a circle, and the circle is the thing the history records as the thing that made the tactics of the trench. The storm trooper was a small group of men with light machine guns and grenades and flamethrowers, and the flamethrower was the thing the storm trooper used to clear the trench, and the clearing was the thing the storm trooper did by infiltration, and the infiltration was the thing the storm trooper did by finding the weak point in the line and passing through it and attacking the strong point from behind, and the behind was the thing the storm trooper could reach because the storm trooper did not attack the strong point from the front, and the front was the thing the machine gun swept, and the sweeping was the thing the storm trooper avoided, and the avoiding was the thing that made the storm trooper a new kind of soldier, and the soldier was the thing the war had made, and the making is the thing the history records as the thing the war did to the infantry.

The storm trooper was the thing the German army used at Riga in September 1917, and the using was the thing that broke the Russian line, and the breaking was the thing the German army had been trying to do for three years, and the three years were the thing the storm trooper had been developed in, and the developing was the thing the German army had done in secret, and the secret was the thing the German army had kept because the German army had learned that the trench was a problem of tactics and not a problem of weapons, and the weapons were the thing the storm trooper carried, and the carrying was the thing the storm trooper did with a lightness the ordinary infantryman could not match, and the matching was the thing the storm trooper did not try to do, because the storm trooper was not trying to hold ground, and the holding was the thing the ordinary infantryman did, and the doing was the thing the ordinary infantryman died doing, and the dying was the thing the storm trooper was designed to avoid, and the avoiding was the thing that made the storm trooper a weapon, and the weapon was the thing the war had made, and the making is the thing the history records as the thing the war did to the infantry.

The fourth answer to the machine gun was the gas, and the gas was the thing the war had not asked for, and the asking was the thing the war had done without, and the without was the thing the gas filled, and the filling was the thing the gas did to the trench, and the trench was the thing the gas could reach because the gas was heavier than air, and the air was the thing the gas displaced, and the displacing was the thing the gas did when it rolled down into the dugouts, and the dugouts were the thing the gas filled, and the filling was the thing the gas did with a thoroughness the history records as the thing that made gas the most feared weapon of the war. The gas was first used by the Germans at the Second Battle of Ypres in April 1915, and the using was the thing the Germans did with chlorine, and the chlorine was the thing the Germans released from cylinders, and the releasing was the thing the wind carried, and the wind was the thing the gas could not control, and the controlling was the thing the gas required, and the requiring was the thing that made the gas a weapon of opportunity and not a weapon of decision, and the decision was the thing the gas could not force, because the gas was a cloud and the cloud was a thing the wind could take away, and the taking away was the thing the gas did at the wrong moment, and the wrong moment was the thing the gas did not forgive.

The gas was the thing the war had made a crime, and the crime was the thing the war had not been able to prevent, because the war was the thing that made the crime possible, and the possible was the thing the gas was, and the gas is the thing the history records as the first weapon of mass destruction, and the destruction was the thing the gas did to the men who breathed it, and the breathing was the thing the gas made impossible, and the impossible was the thing the gas masks were built to prevent, and the preventing was the thing the gas masks did with a filter and a seal and a drill, and the drill was the thing the infantry had to learn, and the learning was the thing the gas made necessary, and the necessary was the thing the war always was.

The gas was the thing the war had made a treaty about, and the treaty was the Hague Convention of 1899, and the convention was the thing the war had signed and the war had broken, and the breaking was the thing the gas did, and the gas was the thing the war had promised not to use, and the using was the thing the war did anyway, and the anyway is the thing the history records as the thing that made the gas a weapon of the twentieth century, because the twentieth century was the thing the war had made, and the making was the thing the war did with the treaty and the gas and the machine gun, and the machine gun was the thing the treaty had not forbidden, and the forbidding was the thing the treaty had done for the dumdum bullet and the balloon and the gas, and the gas was the thing the treaty had forbidden and the war had used, and the using was the thing the war did because the war was the thing the treaty could not stop, and the stopping was the thing the treaty was supposed to do, and the doing was the thing the treaty could not do, and the not doing is the thing the history records as the thing that made the war a war of weapons without limits.

The gas was the thing the war had made a science, and the science was the thing the chemists did, and the chemists were the thing the war had gathered, and the gathering was the thing the war did with the universities and the laboratories and the industries, and the industries were the thing the war had mobilized, and the mobilizing was the thing the war did to the chemists, and the chemists did the science, and the science made the gas, and the gas was the thing the war used, and the using was the thing the war did with the science, and the science was the thing the war had made a weapon, and the weapon is the thing the history records as the thing that made the war a war of scientists, and the scientists were the thing the war would need, and the needing was the thing the war would not stop, and the stopping was the thing the war would not do, because the war was the thing the science served, and the serving was the thing the science did, and the doing is the thing the history records as the thing that made the twentieth century a century of science at war.

The gas was the thing the war had made a mask, and the mask was the thing the war had made necessary, and the necessary was the thing the mask answered, and the answering was the thing the mask did with a canister and a tube and a rubber face, and the rubber face was the thing the mask was, and the mask was the thing the infantry wore, and the wearing was the thing the infantry did when the gas came, and the coming was the thing the infantry could not see, and the seeing was the thing the mask prevented, and the preventing was the thing the mask did with the rubber and the glass, and the glass was the thing the mask used to see, and the seeing was the thing the infantry needed, and the needing was the thing the mask could not satisfy, because the mask fogged and the mask leaked and the mask was hot and the mask was heavy and the mask was the thing the infantry hated, and the hating was the thing the mask made the infantry feel, and the feeling was the thing the gas had made, and the making was the thing the war did to the infantry, and the infantry was the thing the war was, and the war was the thing the gas had made a war of masks.

The gas was the thing the war had made a deterrent, and the deterrent was the thing the gas became when both sides had it, and the having was the thing the gas did to the war, and the war was the thing the gas made a war of restraint, because the gas was the thing neither side could use without the other side using it, and the using was the thing the gas did not do in the last year of the war, and the not doing was the thing the gas did because the gas was the thing the war had made a weapon of the second use, and the second use was the thing the gas could not be, because the gas was the thing the wind could take away, and the taking away was the thing the gas did to the gas, and the gas was the thing the war had made a weapon that could not be aimed, and the aiming was the thing the gas could not do, and the not doing was the thing the gas did to itself, and the self was the thing the gas could not control, and the controlling was the thing the gas required, and the requiring was the thing the gas could not satisfy, and the satisfying was the thing the gas could not do, and the doing was the thing the gas did to the war, and the war was the thing the gas had made a war of fear.

The war had made a weapon of the air, and the air was the thing the war had not expected, and the expecting was the thing the war had done with the balloon and the airship and the airplane, and the airplane was the thing the war had made a weapon, and the making was the thing the war did with the Wright brothers and the Blériot and the Farman and the Voisin, and the Voisin was the thing the French had built, and the building was the thing the French had done before the war, and the war was the thing the French had not expected, and the expecting was the thing the French had done with the airplane, and the airplane was the thing the war had made a scout, and the scout was the thing the airplane became in the first months of the war, and the becoming was the thing the airplane did because the airplane could see, and the seeing was the thing the airplane did over the trench, and the trench was the thing the airplane saw, and the seeing was the thing the airplane did with a camera and an observer and a pilot, and the pilot was the thing the airplane needed, and the needing was the thing the airplane did with the young men who flew, and the flying was the thing the young men did with a courage the history records as the thing that made the airplane a weapon, and the weapon was the thing the airplane became when the pilot carried a gun, and the gun was the thing the pilot used to shoot the other pilot, and the other pilot was the thing the pilot was trying to kill, and the killing was the thing the airplane did in the air, and the air was the thing the war had made a new battlefield, and the battlefield was the thing the war had made in the sky.

The airplane was the thing the war had made a fighter, and the fighter was the thing the airplane became when the gun was fixed to fire through the propeller, and the propeller was the thing the gun had to fire through, and the firing was the thing the gun did with an interrupter gear, and the gear was the thing the gun used to stop firing when the propeller was in the way, and the way was the thing the gear could not see, and the seeing was the thing the gear did with a cam and a rod, and the rod was the thing the gear used to time the gun, and the timing was the thing the gear did with a precision the history records as the thing that made the fighter possible, and the possible was the thing the fighter became at the hands of the German ace Oswald Boelcke, who wrote the rules of air combat, and the rules were the thing the fighter pilots learned, and the learning was the thing the fighter pilots did because the fighter pilots had to, and the having to was the thing the war made, and the making was the thing the war did to the air.

The airplane was the thing the war had made a bomber, and the bomber was the thing the airplane became when the airplane carried a bomb, and the bomb was the thing the airplane dropped on the trench, and the trench was the thing the bomb could not hit, and the hitting was the thing the bomb could not do because the bomb was dropped by hand and the hand was not accurate, and the accurate was the thing the bomb would become, and the becoming was the thing the war would not live to see, but the war would see the beginning, and the beginning was the thing the German zeppelins did to London in 1915, and the doing was the thing the zeppelins did with a bomb load the history records as the thing that made the air raid a weapon, and the weapon was the thing the war had made a terror, and the terror was the thing the air raid did to the city, and the city was the thing the war had made a target, and the target was the thing the air raid would become, and the becoming was the thing the war would not live to see, but the war would see the beginning, and the beginning is the thing the history records as the thing that made the twentieth century a century of air war.

The airplane was the thing the war had made a reconnaissance, and the reconnaissance was the thing the airplane did with a camera, and the camera was the thing the airplane used to photograph the trench, and the trench was the thing the photograph showed, and the showing was the thing the photograph did with a clarity the history records as the thing that made the airplane indispensable, and the indispensable was the thing the airplane became because the airplane could see what the general could not, and the general was the thing the airplane served, and the serving was the thing the airplane did with a photograph and a report and a map, and the map was the thing the airplane made, and the making was the thing the airplane did with a pencil and a camera and a pilot, and the pilot was the thing the airplane needed, and the needing was the thing the war made, and the making was the thing the war did to the air.

The airplane was the thing the war had made a weapon of the ground attack, and the ground attack was the thing the airplane did with a machine gun and a bomb and a rocket, and the rocket was the thing the airplane did not have, and the having was the thing the war would not give, and the giving was the thing the war would do in the next war, and the next war was the thing the airplane would make, and the making is the thing the history records as the thing that made the airplane the weapon of the twentieth century, and the century was the thing the airplane would define, and the defining was the thing the airplane did with a speed and a height and a bomb load the history records as the thing that made the airplane a weapon of terror, and the terror was the thing the airplane did to the city, and the city was the thing the airplane would make a target, and the target was the thing the airplane would bomb, and the bombing was the thing the airplane would do, and the doing is the thing the history records as the thing that made the twentieth century a century of air war.

The war had made a weapon of the submarine, and the submarine was the thing the war had not expected, and the expecting was the thing the war had done with the Holland and the Lake and the Germaniawerft, and the Germaniawerft was the thing the German navy had built, and the building was the thing the German navy had done before the war, and the war was the thing the German navy had not expected, and the expecting was the thing the German navy had done with the U-boat, and the U-boat was the thing the war had made a commerce raider, and the raider was the thing the U-boat became when the U-boat was used against the merchant ship, and the merchant ship was the thing the U-boat could not sink without warning, and the warning was the thing the U-boat could not give because the U-boat was a submarine and the submarine was a thing that could not surface without being sunk, and the sinking was the thing the U-boat did to the merchant ship, and the merchant ship was the thing the U-boat made a target, and the target was the thing the U-boat could not distinguish from a warship, and the distinguishing was the thing the U-boat could not do, and the doing was the thing the U-boat did to the war, and the war was the thing the U-boat made a war of starvation.

The U-boat was the thing the war had made a crisis, and the crisis was the thing the Lusitania made, and the Lusitania was the thing the German U-boat sank on the seventh of May 1915, and the sinking was the thing that killed more than a thousand people, and the people are the thing the history records as the thing that made the U-boat a weapon of terror, and the terror was the thing the U-boat did to the neutral, and the neutral was the thing the U-boat could not distinguish from the enemy, and the distinguishing was the thing the U-boat could not do, and the doing was the thing the U-boat did to the war, and the war was the thing the U-boat made a war of the world, because the world was the thing the U-boat brought into the war, and the bringing was the thing the U-boat did with the sinking of the Lusitania, and the sinking is the thing the history records as the thing that made the United States a belligerent, and the belligerent was the thing the United States became in 1917, and the becoming was the thing the U-boat made, and the making was the thing the U-boat did to the war, and the war was the thing the U-boat ended, and the ending was the thing the U-boat did not intend, and the intending was the thing the U-boat did not have, because the U-boat was a weapon and the weapon was the thing the war used, and the using was the thing the war did to the weapon, and the weapon was the thing the war had made, and the making is the thing the history records as the thing that made the submarine a weapon of the twentieth century.

The war had made a weapon of the convoy, and the convoy was the thing the war had not expected, and the expecting was the thing the war had done with the cruiser and the destroyer and the dreadnought, and the dreadnought was the thing the war had built, and the building was the thing the war had done before the war, and the war was the thing the dreadnought had not expected, and the expecting was the thing the dreadnought had done with the battle fleet, and the battle fleet was the thing the war had not used, and the using was the thing the war did not do because the war was afraid of the mine and the torpedo and the submarine, and the submarine was the thing the war had made a threat, and the threat was the thing the convoy answered, and the answering was the thing the convoy did with a screen of destroyers and a zigzag and a depth charge, and the depth charge was the thing the convoy used to kill the submarine, and the killing was the thing the depth charge did with a can of

chapters.preview: Part 19
paragraphs: Part 19

The convoy was not a weapon. It was a schedule. And yet the schedule, in the spring of 1917, proved more decisive than any gun the Admiralty had built, because it solved a problem no gun could solve: how to move a hundred thousand tons of coal and grain and shell across four thousand miles of water while a hundred and twenty German submarines hunted them. The submarine was one of the earliest great weapons of the twentieth century that could not be answered by a counter-weapon. No anti-submarine gun could out-range a torpedo, no armor could stop a detonation beneath the waterline, no formation could prevent a U-boat from choosing its moment. The answer was not a weapon at all. It was a system: a schedule that concentrated the targets, a screen that detected the threat, and a doctrine that made the attack unprofitable. The convoy was an early weapon of the information age, and it was built out of nothing but coordination.

The arithmetic that made the convoy necessary was brutal and simple. In February 1917, Germany declared unrestricted submarine warfare. That month, U-boats sank 464,000 tons of British shipping. In March, 507,000 tons. In April, 860,000 tons. The Admiralty's own figures showed that if losses continued at the April rate, Britain would have fewer than six weeks of grain in reserve by the end of the summer. The First Sea Lord, Admiral John Jellicoe—who had commanded the Grand Fleet at Jutland and warned that the submarine was the weapon that could lose the war—told the War Cabinet in June 1917 that he could not guarantee the food supply. The War Cabinet told him the war would end in starvation if the losses were not cut. The tonnage was not a statistic. It was the measure of a nation's ability to keep fighting, and it was falling faster than any replacement program could build.

The Admiralty had resisted the convoy for three years. The reasons were not stupid. A convoy concentrated ships in one place, making a single submarine's attack more productive if it found the convoy; it required merchant captains to sail in formation, which many had never done; it required escorts, which were scarce; and it slowed the fast ships to the speed of the slow ones, reducing the number of voyages a ship could make in a year. The Admiralty calculated that the losses from concentration would exceed the losses from dispersion. The calculation was wrong, and it was wrong because it treated the submarine's attack as a matter of probability rather than detection. A submarine on the surface, running at ten knots, could see a single ship's smoke from fifteen miles away and close on it. A submarine could not see a convoy's smoke without also being seen by the convoy's escorts, and the escorts could force it to dive, and a dived submarine could not keep up with a convoy making nine knots. The convoy did not reduce the number of targets. It reduced the number of attacks, because an attack required the submarine to be in the right place at the right time, and the convoy made the right place a place where the submarine was hunted.

The first convoy sailed from Gibraltar on 10 May 1917 and arrived without loss. The second sailed on 20 May and also arrived without loss. By the end of June, the Admiralty had extended the system to the North Atlantic, and the losses began to fall. In July, 557,000 tons; in August, 511,000 tons; in September, 351,000 tons; in October, 458,000 tons; in November, 289,000 tons. By the end of 1917, the monthly loss had fallen to a third of the April figure, and the grain reserves had begun to recover. The convoy had not sunk a single U-boat. It had made the U-boat's attack unprofitable, and that was enough. What defeated the submarine in 1917 was not a depth charge or a hydrophone or a destroyer but a schedule, a formation, and a doctrine—and the proof lay less in any single engagement than in the shape of the loss curve, which bent downward the moment the system was adopted.

The depth charge was the second half of the answer, and it was a weapon that could only work within a system. The depth charge was a canister of high explosive fitted with a hydrostatic fuse, designed to detonate at a set depth. It was invented in 1916 and carried by destroyers and sloops and, later, by converted trawlers and motor launches. The depth charge was not accurate. Its lethal radius was perhaps twenty feet, and a submarine more than twenty feet from the detonation would survive. It was not a precision weapon. It was a weapon of probability, and its probability depended on the escort knowing where the submarine was. The hydrophone, which could detect a submarine's propellers at a range of a few miles, was the sensor. The depth charge was the effector. The escort was the platform that carried both, and the convoy was the system that brought the submarine into range. The depth charge killed perhaps thirty U-boats in the whole of the war. The convoy saved perhaps a million tons of shipping. The weapon was the least important part of the system—and the record of the U-boat commanders bears this out. Otto Steinbrinck, one of the most successful of them, complained in his war diary that the convoys had turned the Atlantic into "a hunt in which we are the hunted," and that the approach he had perfected against independent sailings—surface shadowing, night surface attack, escape on the surface—collapsed once the escorts forced him under. The weapon had not changed. The conditions of its use had.

The same pattern repeated in the Second World War, and with greater force because the technology had improved. The convoy system was reinstated on the first day of the war and extended to the whole of the Atlantic by 1940. The escorts were fitted with radar, which could detect a submarine on the surface at a range of several miles, and with high-frequency direction-finding, which could fix a U-boat's radio transmission to within a few miles. The depth charge was supplemented by the Hedgehog, a forward-firing mortar that threw a pattern of bombs ahead of the attacking ship, and by the Leigh Light, an airborne searchlight that illuminated a submarine on the surface at night. The escort carrier, a small aircraft carrier built on a merchant hull, closed the mid-Atlantic gap, the stretch of ocean beyond the range of land-based aircraft where the U-boats had done their worst. The system grew more complex, and the complexity was the point. The U-boat was defeated not by a single weapon but by a network of sensors, effectors, and platforms—and the network, not any one node, was what the Allies actually built.

The Battle of the Atlantic was the longest campaign of the Second World War, and it was the campaign in which the relationship between weapon and system was most clearly visible. The U-boat was a weapon of ambush, and it depended on finding a target and attacking it without being detected. The convoy system denied the U-boat the easy target. The radar and the direction-finding denied it the undetected approach. The escort carrier and the Leigh Light denied it the safe surface transit. The Hedgehog and the depth charge denied it the safe dive. Each was a weapon or a sensor, and each was useless without the others. But the system had limits, and the limits are instructive. In March 1943, at the height of the crisis, the system nearly broke: the U-boats penetrated the mid-Atlantic gap in wolf-pack strength, sank ninety-five ships in twenty days, and came close to severing the lifeline. What saved the convoys in that month was not the system as designed but the system as reinforced—escort groups rushed from other theaters, very-long-range aircraft borrowed from Bomber Command, and the decision to fight the U-boats at sea rather than merely avoid them. The system worked because it was revised under pressure; it did not work because it was complete.

The development of the convoy system was not a matter of invention. It was a matter of organization, and the organization was the hardest part. The Admiralty had to allocate escorts to convoys, balancing the need to protect merchant ships against the need to hunt submarines. It had to route the convoys around known U-boat concentrations, and the routing had to change as the concentrations moved. It had to coordinate the convoys with aircraft and escort groups, and the coordination had to be done in real time, which meant radio, which meant signals intelligence, which meant codebreaking. The routing orders themselves are the evidence. A Western Approaches convoy instruction from 1943 reads, in the flat language of the staff, that a given convoy was to be diverted south of a reported patrol line, that escorts were to be reinforced at a stated meridian, and that aircraft were to be provided from a named squadron for the final approach—three separate organizations coordinated on a single sheet of paper. The system was not a metaphor. It was a document, and the document was what a convoy routing officer actually worked from.

The codebreaking was the most secret part of the system, and it showed how far the system had come. The British had broken the German naval codes in the First World War, and they broke them again in the Second, and the breaking told the Admiralty where the U-boats were. The intelligence was called Ultra, and it was distributed to the convoy routing officers, who used it to steer the convoys away from the U-boat patrol lines. Ultra did not sink a single U-boat. It saved hundreds of ships, because it allowed the convoys to avoid the ambush—and here too the case has limits, because for much of 1942 the German naval Enigma was unreadable after the introduction of the fourth rotor, and the convoys sailed blind through the worst months of the American coastal slaughter. The intelligence was decisive when it was available and absent when it was most needed, which is the ordinary condition of information in war.

The pattern was not confined to the sea, but the sea is where it can be demonstrated most cleanly, and the land and air cases belong to their own parts. It is enough here to note that the same shift from weapon to system appeared on land, where the tank of 1916 achieved little at Flers-Courcelette because it was used without doctrine, infantry support, or numbers, and that it appeared in the air, where the unescorted bomber of 1943 was shot down at an unsustainable rate until the fighter escort made the campaign survivable. In both cases the weapon existed before the system that made it effective, and in both cases the weapon alone was not enough.

The system principle was not a new idea in the Second World War. It was as old as war itself. The phalanx was a system. The Roman legion was a system. The Mongol tumen was a system. The English longbow was a weapon, and it was effective because it was part of a system that included the archer's training, the arrow's manufacture, and the tactical doctrine that concentrated the fire. The Mary Rose longbows, recovered from the wreck of 1545, had draw weights of 100 to 185 pounds, and those draw weights are the physical evidence of a training system that began in childhood and continued for a lifetime. The longbow could not be improvised. It required a system, and the system was the thing that made the weapon.

The development of the firearm was the development of a weapon simpler to use than the longbow, and the simplicity made the firearm a weapon of the masses. But the ease of learning is only part of the explanation, and the tidy version—that the musket replaced the longbow because it took weeks rather than a lifetime to master—flatters the case. The musket was adopted because it was cheaper to equip, because it could be supplied from state arsenals rather than from the archer's own household, because it could be mass-produced to a standard, and because the state that could field mass armies could also pay for them. Ease of learning mattered; it was not sufficient on its own. The musket needed powder and ball manufactured to a standard, a flint replaced every twenty or thirty shots, and a bayonet that made it a weapon that could hold a line. The musket was a system, and the system was the thing that made the weapon work.

The Minié ball was a development that showed how a small change in a weapon could change the system. The Minié ball was a hollow-base bullet that expanded into the rifling when the musket was fired, and the expansion made the rifled musket as fast to load as the smoothbore. The rifled musket had been a specialist weapon before the Minié ball, because the rifling made the ball hard to ram down the barrel, and the ramming slowed the loading. The Minié ball solved the problem, and the solution made the rifled musket a general-issue weapon, and the general issue changed the tactics. The rifled musket had an effective range of several hundred yards, and the smoothbore musket had an effective range of less than a hundred, and the difference made the frontal assault suicidal. The Minié ball was a small invention, and it made the American Civil War the first modern war, because the modern war was the war in which the defender's firepower made the attacker's mass formation obsolete.

The Minié ball was adopted by the British army in the Pattern 1853 Enfield and by the American army in the Springfield Model 1861, and the adoption made the rifled musket the standard weapon of the infantry. The Enfield was a .577-caliber weapon, and the Springfield was a .58-caliber weapon, and the difference in caliber was a difference of standardization, and the standardization made the supply of ammunition possible. The Minié ball depended on a system of manufacture, because the hollow base had to be formed precisely, and the precision made the expansion reliable. The Minié ball was not a simple weapon. It required a factory, and the factory made it possible to arm a mass army, and the mass army made the Civil War the first industrial war.

The Civil War was the first war in which the railroad and the telegraph were integral to the conduct of operations, and the integration made the war a system war. The railroad moved the armies and the supplies, and the telegraph moved the orders and the intelligence, and the movement made the war possible at the scale it was fought. The Battle of First Bull Run was fought within a day's march of Washington, and the Battle of Gettysburg was fought three years later at a distance that would have been impossible without the railroad. The railroad was a system, and the system made the war a war of masses, and the masses made the war a war of attrition.

The telegraph was the system that made the command possible, and the command made the masses effective. The telegraph allowed the president to communicate with the generals in the field, and the communication made the strategy, and the strategy made the war. The telegraph was not a weapon, and it was more important than any weapon, because it made the weapons coordinated, and the coordination made the weapons effective. The telegraph was one of the earliest great military systems of the industrial age, and it made the railroad and the rifled musket and the mass army into a single system, and the system was the thing that won the war.

The system principle was visible in the development of the machine gun, and the machine gun was a weapon that was itself a system. The Maxim gun, demonstrated in 1884, was the first self-powered machine gun, and the self-power made it a system. The Maxim used the recoil of the cartridge to operate the mechanism, and the operation made the gun automatic, and the automatic fire made the gun a weapon of mass destruction. The Maxim was adopted by the British army in 1891, and the adoption made the machine gun a standard weapon, and the standard made the machine gun a weapon of the colonial wars, and the colonial wars showed the machine gun's power.

The Maxim gun depended on a system of supply, because automatic fire consumed ammunition at a rate no previous weapon had consumed it, and the supply made the gun effective. The Maxim needed a water jacket to cool the barrel, and the water jacket needed water, and the water made the gun a weapon that could fire for minutes rather than seconds. The Maxim needed a belt of cartridges, and the belt had to be manufactured, and the manufacture made the gun a weapon that could be sustained. The Maxim was a system, and the system was the thing that made the weapon work.

The machine gun changed the tactics of the infantry, and the change made the First World War a war of trenches. The machine gun made the frontal assault suicidal, and the suicidal assault made the armies dig in, and the digging in made the war a war of position. The machine gun was not the only weapon that made the war a war of position. The quick-firing artillery was the other, and the quick-firing artillery made the artillery the dominant arm of the war. The French 75mm field gun, adopted in 1897, was the first artillery piece with a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady, and the steadiness made the rapid fire possible, and the rapid fire made the artillery devastating. The 75 could fire fifteen rounds a minute, and the rate made it a weapon of suppression, and the suppression made the infantry's attack possible, and the attack made the war a war of attrition.

The French 75 depended on a system of supply, because the rapid fire consumed shells at a rate no previous artillery had consumed them, and the supply made the gun effective. The 75 needed shells, and the shells had to be manufactured, and the manufacture made the gun a weapon that could be sustained, and the sustainment made the war a war of industry. The 75 was a system, and the system was the thing that made the weapon work.

The Battle of Verdun showed the artillery's dominance, and the dominance made the battle a battle of attrition. Verdun ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916 and produced roughly 700,000 casualties, and the casualties made the battle a symbol of the war's futility. The artillery was the dominant weapon of the battle, and the dominance made the battle a battle of shell production, and the shell production made the battle a battle of industry. The German army fired two million shells in the first eight hours of the battle, and the firing made the battle a battle of logistics, and the logistics made the battle a battle of railroads and factories. The artillery was the weapon, and the system was the thing that made the weapon work.

Verdun was also the battle that showed the importance of the truck, and the truck was a system that made the logistics possible. The French army supplied Verdun over the Bar-le-Duc road, and the road made the defense possible, and the defense made the battle a French victory. The road was called the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way, and the name made the road a symbol of the war's endurance. The road carried 6,000 trucks a day at the height of the battle, and the trucks made the supply possible, and the supply made the defense possible. The truck was not a weapon, and it was more important than any weapon, because it made the weapons effective, and the effectiveness made the battle a French victory.

The truck was a system, and the system made the First World War a war of mobility as well as a war of position. The war was a war of position on the Western Front and a war of mobility on the Eastern Front, and the mobility made the Eastern Front a war of movement, and the movement made the Eastern Front a war of German victory. The German army used the railroad to concentrate its forces, and the concentration made the victory at Tannenberg possible, and the victory made the Eastern Front a German victory. The railroad was the system, and the system made the mobility possible, and the mobility made the victory possible.

The First World War was the first war in which the system principle was visible in every arm, and the visibility made the war a war of systems. The infantry was a system of rifle, machine gun, and artillery; the artillery was a system of gun, shell, and supply; the supply was a system of railroad, truck, and factory; and the factory was a system of machine, labor, and raw material. The war was a war of systems, and the systems made the war a war of attrition, and the attrition made the war a war of exhaustion. The war ended when the systems of the Central Powers exhausted their raw materials, their labor, and their will, and the exhaustion made the armistice possible, and the armistice made the peace, and the peace made the next war.

The Second World War was the war in which the system principle became the organizing principle of military development, and the organizing principle made the war a war of production as well as a war of tactics. The German army's blitzkrieg was a system, and the system made the German army effective in the first years of the war, and the effectiveness made the German army the master of Europe. The British and American armies were systems, and the systems made them effective in the last years of the war, and the effectiveness made the Allies the masters of the world. The Soviet army was a system, and the system made the Soviet army effective in the last years of the war, and the effectiveness made the Soviet Union a superpower.

The system principle was visible in the development of the tank, and the tank was a weapon that was itself a system. The tank was a system of armor, engine, gun, and radio, and the balance of the system determined its effectiveness. The German tank was a system of armor, engine, gun, and radio, and the balance made the German tank effective in the early years of the war, and the effectiveness made the blitzkrieg possible. The Soviet T-34 was a system of armor, engine, gun, and radio, and the balance made the T-34 the best tank of the war, and the best made the Soviet army effective, and the effectiveness made the Soviet victory possible.

The T-34 was optimized for production, and the optimization made it a weapon of mass production, and the mass production made it possible to build fifty thousand of them, and the fifty thousand made the Soviet army a weapon of mass. The T-34 had sloped armor, and the sloped armor made it survivable, and the survivability made it effective. It had a diesel engine, and the diesel made it reliable, and the reliability made it sustainable. It had a wide track, and the wide track made it mobile in mud and snow, and the mobility made it effective in the Russian winter. The T-34 was a system, and the system was the thing that made the weapon work.

The American tank was optimized for reliability and transportability, and the optimization made it a weapon of mass production, and the mass production made it possible to build fifty thousand Shermans, and the fifty thousand made the American army a weapon of mass. The Sherman was not the best tank of the war in armor or gun; it was the best in reliability and transportability, and the reliability and transportability made it effective, because the American army fought a war of movement, and the movement required reliability, and the reliability made the movement possible. The Sherman was a system, and the system was the thing that made the weapon work.

The system principle was visible in the development of the aircraft, and the aircraft was a weapon that was itself a system. The fighter was a system of engine, airframe, and armament, and the balance determined its effectiveness. The bomber was a system of engine, airframe, bomb load, and defensive armament, and the balance determined its effectiveness. The aircraft depended on a system of production, because it was the most complex weapon of the war, and the complexity made it a weapon of mass production, and the mass production made it possible to build a hundred thousand aircraft, and the hundred thousand made the Allies masters of the air.

The aircraft depended on a system of training, because the pilot was the most important part of the aircraft, and the pilot was the product of a system of training, and the training made the aircraft effective. The German air force was optimized for quality, and the quality made it effective in the early years of the war, and the effectiveness made the blitzkrieg possible. The American air force was optimized for quantity, and the quantity made it effective in the last years of the war, and the effectiveness made the strategic bombing possible. The British air force was optimized for night bombing, and the night bombing made it effective, and the effectiveness made the bombing of Germany possible.

The system principle was visible in the development of the atomic bomb, the most complex weapon ever built, and the complexity made it a weapon of systems. The Manhattan Project was a system of science, engineering, industry, and security, and the system made the bomb possible, and the possible made the bomb a weapon, and the weapon ended the war. The bomb could not be built by a single laboratory or a single factory. It required a system of laboratories and factories and mines and railroads, and the system made it possible, and the possible made it a weapon.

The Manhattan Project employed 130,000 people at its peak, and the employment made it a system, and the system made the bomb possible. The project cost two billion dollars, and the cost made it a weapon of state, and the state made it possible, and the possible made it a weapon. The project was a system of systems, and the systems made the bomb, and the bomb made the project a weapon, and the weapon made the project a turning point in the history of war.

The Trinity test on 16 July 1945 was the moment when the system principle became the atomic principle, and the atomic principle made the bomb a weapon of deterrence, and the deterrence made the bomb a weapon of peace, and the peace made the bomb a weapon of the Cold War. The Trinity device was a plutonium implosion bomb, and the implosion made it possible to use plutonium, and the plutonium made the bomb a weapon of mass production, and the mass production made it possible to build more bombs. The Trinity yield was about 21 kilotons, and the yield made the bomb a weapon of mass destruction, and the destruction made the bomb a weapon of terror, and the terror made the bomb a weapon of deterrence.

The atomic bomb made the system principle visible to everyone, and the visibility made the bomb a political weapon, and the political made the bomb a weapon of state, and the state made the bomb a weapon of the Cold War. The bomb was not a weapon that could be used in a battle. It was a weapon that could destroy a city, and the destruction made it a weapon of terror, and the terror made it a weapon of deterrence, and the deterrence made it a weapon of peace. The bomb was a system, and the system was the thing that made the weapon work, and the work made the bomb a turning point in the history of war.

The Cold War was the war in which the system principle became the organizing principle of the entire military establishment, and the organizing principle made the Cold War a war of systems, and the systems made the Cold War a war of deterrence, and the deterrence made the Cold War a war without fighting. The Cold War was a war of nuclear weapons, and the nuclear weapons made the war a war of deterrence, and the deterrence made the war a war of stability, and the stability made the war a war of peace. The Cold War was a war of systems, and the systems made the war a war of technology, and the technology made the war a war of innovation, and the innovation made the war a war of the future.

The nuclear weapons were the center of the Cold War system, and the center made the system stable, and the stability made the war a war of deterrence. The nuclear weapons were organized into a triad, and the triad made the deterrence survivable, and the survivability made the deterrence credible, and the credibility made the deterrence effective. The triad was a system of bombers, missiles, and submarines, and the system made the deterrence work, and the work made the Cold War a war without fighting.

The nuclear triad was a system of systems, and the systems made the triad survivable, and the survivability made the triad credible, and the credibility made the triad effective. The bomber was the first leg of the triad, and the bomber made the deterrence possible in the early years of the Cold War, and the possible made the deterrence credible. The missile was the second leg, and the missile made the deterrence fast, and the fast made the deterrence credible. The submarine was the third leg, and the submarine made the deterrence survivable, and the survivable made the deterrence credible.

The submarine-launched ballistic missile was the most important leg of the triad, and the importance made it the center of the deterrence, and the center made the deterrence stable, and the stable made the Cold War a war without fighting. The submarine made the deterrence survivable, because it could hide in the ocean, and the hiding made it survivable, and the survivable made it credible. The submarine was a system of submarine, missile, and navigation, and the system made the deterrence work, and the work made the Cold War a war without fighting.
The nuclear deterrence was a system that depended on information as much as
