paragraphs: The radio-direction-finding set—*Huff-Duff*—was the other half of the same revolution, and it is worth pausing on what these two devices together did, because they mark the moment when the electromagnetic spectrum became a battlefield in its own right rather than a convenience for communicating across it. *ASDIC*—the Allied name for sonar, chosen partly to disguise the fact that it was an echo-ranging technique the Germans also possessed—sent a pulse of sound into the water and listened for its return, giving a destroyer or corvette a bearing and range to a submerged U-boat at a few thousand yards. It was imperfect: a submarine that went deep, or lay silent in a layer of water of different temperature, could hide from it, and the early sets were clumsy and their operators inexperienced. But it converted the escort from a blind shepherd into a hunter, and it made the convoy system—which had nearly collapsed in 1917 for want of exactly this capability—viable from the first weeks of the war. *Huff-Duff* did a different thing. A U-boat coordinating its attack had to talk to its headquarters and to the other boats of its pack by high-frequency radio, and a radio transmission, however brief, can be intercepted and its bearing taken by two or more receivers and plotted as a fix. The British built a chain of shore stations and fitted sets aboard escorts, and by 1943 a convoy escort that caught a U-boat's transmission could turn toward it and run it down. Neither device was decisive alone. Together, with the codebreakers at Bletchley Park reading the German naval Enigma traffic, they constituted a system, and the Battle of the Atlantic was won by a system rather than by a weapon.

This is the central lesson of the Second World War, and the lesson this book has been building toward across every preceding chapter. The great industrial war of 1939 to 1945 was not won by the side with the best single weapon. It was won by the side that could assemble weapons, sensors, communications, logistics, and intelligence into a functioning whole, and adapt that whole faster than the enemy could adapt his. The German tanks of 1940 were not, tank for tank, markedly superior to the French; the German victory in the west was won by radio, by doctrine, by the integration of armor with close air support, and by the fact that a German tank commander could talk to his headquarters and his neighbors while a French one could not. The British fighter of 1940 was not markedly superior to the German; the Battle of Britain was won by a command-and-control system that *Chain Home* radar made possible. The American war economy did not merely outproduce the Axis; it outproduced it in the specific sense that mattered—the ability to deliver the right thing to the right place at the right time in quantities that made attrition arithmetic decisive. And the atomic bomb, which ended the war, was the most system-dependent weapon ever built: it required the industrial capacity of a continental power, the intellectual capital of the world's best physics, and a security apparatus capable of keeping a secret from an enemy who was also building it.

Consider the tank, that most emblematic of the war's weapons, and trace how it developed not as a machine but as a component of a system. The tank of 1939 was a descendant of the rhomboids of the Somme, and the interwar years had done to it what they did to everything: some armies thought hard about it and some did not. The British, who had invented it, divided their armor into "infantry tanks" and "cruiser tanks," a doctrinal split that produced machines like the Matilda—heavily armored, slow, armed with a two-pounder gun that could fire only solid shot—and the Crusader, fast, lightly armored, and mechanically unreliable. The French dispersed their tanks among infantry formations in support, a reasonable reading of 1918 and a fatal one for 1940. The Germans, forbidden by the Treaty of Versailles from having tanks at all, had built a doctrine in secret around the training of officers, and when they came to build machines they built them to fit the doctrine: the Panzer III and IV were not wonder weapons, but they were designed to be commanded by a man with a radio, to be refueled and repaired in the field, and to be concentrated at a point of decision rather than spread along a line. The German victory in France was not a triumph of the tank. It was a triumph of the tank *formation*—the panzer division, with its integrated infantry, artillery, engineers, and anti-aircraft—over the tank *battalion*, which was what the French and British had.

Then the war taught its brutal lessons. The Soviet T-34, which appeared in 1941, was in several respects the best-designed tank of the war: sloped armor that deflected shot, a diesel engine less flammable than gasoline, wide tracks for mud and snow, and a 76mm gun in a turret that could be traversed by hand or power. It was crude—the transmission was poor, the crew commander doubled as gunner, and the interior was a hell of noise and heat—but it was built to be produced in enormous numbers by a nation that had moved its factories east of the Urals and was prepared to spend lives to buy time. The German response was the Panther and the Tiger, better tanks and worse weapons: overengineered, expensive, mechanically fragile, and produced in quantities that could never match Soviet output. The Tiger could kill any Allied tank at ranges at which the Allied tank could not reply, and there were never enough of them to matter. The Panther was a superb machine that broke its final drive after a few hundred kilometers and could not be recovered from the mud because it was too heavy for the recovery vehicles. By 1944 the Western Allies were landing Shermans by the thousand, and the Sherman was in every respect an inferior tank to the Panther except in the respects that won the war: it was reliable, easy to repair, built to a standard that allowed a crew to survive a hit and bail out, and it could be shipped across an ocean and landed on a beach. The Sherman's worst features—thin armor and a tendency to burn—were addressed by the crews themselves, who welded sandbags and spare track links to the hull, and by the Ordnance Department, which up-gunned it with a British 17-pounder in the Firefly variant. The lesson was not that the Sherman was a good tank. The lesson was that a good-enough tank produced in overwhelming numbers and sustained by a logistics system that could deliver fuel, ammunition, and spare parts to the front is a better weapon than a superb tank produced in handfuls and abandoned when it breaks.

The same arithmetic governed the air war, and here the system character of the weapon was even more explicit. The strategic bombing campaign against Germany, which the British and Americans conducted from 1940 to 1945, was the most expensive single undertaking of the war in lives and treasure, and its results were fiercely debated then and remain debated now. What is not debated is what it did to the *development* of weapons. The British bombed at night, which required navigational aids—the *Gee* and *Oboe* radio-navigation systems, the *H2S* ground-scanning radar—pathfinder forces to mark the target, electronic countermeasures to blind the German night fighters, and a German night-fighter force directed by a ground-controlled interception system that the British learned to jam. The Americans bombed by day, which required long-range escort fighters, and the P-51 Mustang, fitted with the British Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, gave the Americans a fighter that could escort the bombers all the way to Berlin and back. The German response was the jet fighter—the Me 262, the first operational jet aircraft, faster than anything the Allies had and capable of sweeping the bombers from the sky if produced in numbers and used as a fighter rather than, at Hitler's insistence, as a bomber. It was not, and the reason was not technical. It was that the German industrial system was being bombed into ruins while the Allied system was producing aircraft at a rate the Germans could not match. The jet was a weapon of the future that arrived too late, in too few numbers, in a system already collapsing.

The bombing campaign's most important product, in the long run, was not the destruction it caused but the *instruments* it forced into existence: radar, radio navigation, electronic countermeasures, the proximity fuze, and the whole apparatus of signals intelligence. The proximity fuze—a small radar set inside an artillery shell that detonated it when it came near its target—was one of the war's most closely guarded secrets, and it multiplied the lethality of anti-aircraft fire and, later, of artillery against ground troops, because a shell that bursts in the air above a trench kills far more than one that buries itself in the earth before exploding. The fuze required a miniature ruggedized radio transmitter-receiver that could survive the acceleration of being fired from a gun, and it was produced in millions by American industry and used to devastating effect in the Pacific and at the Battle of the Bulge. It was a weapon that existed only because a system of laboratories, factories, and military users had been built to convert scientific insight into fielded hardware in months rather than decades.

That system had several names. In the United States it was the National Defense Research Committee and its successor, the Office of Scientific Research and Development, led by Vannevar Bush, which contracted with universities and industry to develop radar, proximity fuzes, rockets, and the components of the atomic bomb. In Britain it was the Directorate of Scientific Research and the establishments at Malvern and Fort Halstead and the Telecommunications Research Establishment, which moved from Swanage to Malvern to escape the bombing and there developed much of the radar that won the Battle of Britain and the night bombing campaign. In Germany it was the Reich Research Council and the various service laboratories, well funded until they were not, and hampered by the Nazi regime's preference for weapons that could be fielded quickly over research that might bear fruit in years. The difference was not scientific talent; German physics was the best in the world, and German engineers built the first operational jet, the first ballistic missile, and the first guided air-to-surface weapon. The difference was the *organization* of science for war—the willingness to fund long-shot research, to share results across services and across the Atlantic, and to accept that the most important weapons of the war would be the ones that did not exist when the war began.

The V-2 proves the point. The German *Aggregat 4*—the A4, which propaganda renamed *Vergeltungswaffe 2*, "vengeance weapon 2"—was a ballistic missile fourteen meters tall, weighing twelve and a half tons at launch, burning alcohol and liquid oxygen, and able to throw a one-ton warhead two hundred miles. It was a genuine engineering triumph, the first object to reach the edge of space, developed by a team under Wernher von Braun at Peenemünde on the Baltic coast. It was also, as a weapon, a failure. It could not be aimed accurately enough to hit a target smaller than a city; it killed an estimated nine thousand people in Britain and the Low Countries, most of them civilians, and the Germans fired some three thousand of them. The resources that went into it—the equivalent of a bomber fleet, according to Albert Speer, who as Reich Minister of Armaments knew—were resources not spent on fighters that could have defended German cities against the bombing that was destroying them. The V-2 was a weapon of the future used in the present to no strategic purpose, and its most important legacy was not the damage it did but the fact that the engineers who built it—von Braun and many of his team—were brought to the United States after the war and became the core of the American rocket program. The weapon that could not win a war became the foundation of the technology that would define the next half-century.

The V-1 was the other vengeance weapon, and in some ways the more interesting because it was cheaper and more effective. The *Fieseler Fi 103* was a pulse-jet-powered flying bomb, a small aircraft with a warhead, launched from a ramp and guided by a simple autopilot that counted the revolutions of a propeller and cut the fuel when the count reached a set number. It flew at about four hundred miles an hour at two to three thousand feet, within reach of anti-aircraft guns and fighters, and the British developed a layered defense—barrage balloons, guns, and fighters—that shot down most of those launched. But some got through, killing some six thousand people and injuring many more, and forcing the diversion of enormous resources to the defense of London. The V-1 was a weapon of terror, and it failed as a weapon of war, but it was the ancestor of the cruise missile, and the fact that it was cheap and could be produced in numbers made it a more rational weapon than the V-2, which was a magnificent dead end.

The Pacific war developed its own systems, naval and amphibious to a degree the European war was not. The aircraft carrier displaced the battleship as the capital ship of the fleet in a few months of 1942, and the reason was not that the carrier was a better ship but that the aircraft was a better weapon. At Pearl Harbor the Japanese demonstrated that a carrier strike could cripple a battle fleet at anchor; at Midway the Americans demonstrated that a carrier could sink another carrier at a range of a hundred miles, which meant the two fleets never saw each other. The battleship, for all its armor and sixteen-inch guns, could only engage what it could see, and the carrier's aircraft could see far beyond the horizon. The American response to the carrier's vulnerability—it was, as the war would show, a ship that could be sunk by a single well-placed bomb or torpedo—was to build the *Essex*-class carriers in numbers, develop damage-control procedures that could keep a burning carrier afloat and fighting, and build a fleet train of oilers, ammunition ships, and supply vessels that could keep the fleet at sea for months. The *Essex* class was the most successful capital ship design of the war by any measure that matters: twenty-four were built, none were sunk, and they carried the war to Japan's doorstep.

The amphibious assault was the other great Pacific system, developed by the U.S. Marine Corps and the Navy in the interwar years and perfected under fire from Guadalcanal to Okinawa. The problem was to land a division of troops with their equipment on a defended beach, and the solution was a whole family of specialized vehicles and ships: the Landing Ship, Tank, which could beach itself and disgorge tanks through bow doors; the Landing Craft, Vehicle, Personnel—the Higgins boat, designed by a Louisiana boatbuilder named Andrew Higgins, who had built shallow-draft boats for the swamps of the bayou and whose design was adopted over the objections of the Navy's bureau chiefs; the amphibious tractor, the *Amtrac*, which could swim from ship to shore and then crawl up the beach; and the whole apparatus of naval gunfire support, air support, and beach logistics that made the assault possible. None of these was a weapon in the narrow sense. Each was a component of a system, and the system was what won the war in the Pacific—the ability to project power across an ocean, land it on a defended shore, and sustain it there.

The Japanese, by contrast, developed weapons of a different character: the *kamikaze*, the suicide aircraft, and the *kaiten*, the human torpedo, and the *Ohka*, the rocket-powered suicide bomb. These were weapons of a system that had lost the ability to compete in a war of production, an attempt to substitute will and sacrifice for industrial capacity. They were terrifying and caused real losses—the *kamikaze* sank or damaged hundreds of American ships and killed thousands of sailors—but they could not change the outcome, because the American system could replace ships faster than the Japanese could sink them. The *kamikaze* was the last resort of a system that had run out of options, and a preview of a kind of warfare that would reappear in the decades to come, when weaker powers would seek asymmetric means to counter the overwhelming conventional superiority of stronger ones.

The war at sea also produced the weapon that would define the next half-century: the submarine. The German U-boat campaign, which nearly starved Britain in 1917 and came close again in 1940 and 1942, was the most effective strategic weapon the Germans deployed, and it was defeated not by a single counter-weapon but by a system of systems: convoys, escorts, *ASDIC*, *Huff-Duff*, radar, Leigh lights, escort carriers, long-range aircraft, and the codebreakers who read the U-boat's Enigma traffic. The American submarine campaign against Japan was equally decisive and less celebrated: the U.S. Navy's submarines, operating from Pearl Harbor and Australia, sank some five million tons of Japanese shipping, and by 1944 had effectively destroyed the Japanese merchant marine. The American submarines were armed with the Mark 14 torpedo, which was a scandal—it ran too deep, failed to explode when it hit, and its magnetic exploder detonated prematurely—and it took two years and the efforts of a determined officer named Charles Lockwood to fix the problems. The lesson was that a weapon is only as good as its components, and a torpedo that does not explode is worse than no torpedo at all, because it costs a submarine a firing opportunity that may not come again.

The submarine itself changed in the war. The German Type XXI, which appeared too late to affect the outcome, was the first true submarine rather than a submersible: it could run submerged on batteries for most of its voyage, it was faster underwater than on the surface, and it had a streamlined hull and a snorkel that allowed it to charge its batteries while submerged. It pointed directly at the future, and after the war both the Americans and the Soviets built submarines on its principles, then added the nuclear reactor that would allow a submarine to stay submerged for months and the ballistic missile that would make it the most survivable leg of the nuclear triad. The submarine most completely realized the ideal of stealth, and in the nuclear age it became the weapon that made deterrence stable, because a missile submarine at sea could not be found and destroyed, and therefore could not be disarmed by a first strike.

The war also produced the weapon that would make the submarine's nuclear role possible: the atomic bomb. The Manhattan Project was the largest single scientific and engineering undertaking in history up to that time, employing some 130,000 people and costing about two billion dollars—some thirty billion in today's money. It produced the two bombs that destroyed Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and it produced the Trinity test of 16 July 1945, the first nuclear detonation, with a yield of about twenty-one kilotons. The bomb was the ultimate system weapon: it required the industrial capacity to produce fissile material—the enormous plants at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and Hanford, Washington, which between them consumed a significant fraction of the entire American electrical generating capacity—the intellectual capacity to solve the problems of implosion and neutron initiation, and a security apparatus capable of keeping the secret from the Germans, who were also working on it. The German atomic program was never close to a bomb, but the fear that it might be was one of the reasons the Americans built one, and the fear was real enough that the Allies bombed the Norwegian heavy-water plant at Vemork and assassinated its German overseers.

The bomb changed the calculus of war in a way no weapon had since the introduction of gunpowder. The strategists of the prewar years had calculated that a future war would be won by the nation that could mobilize its industry fastest and endure the most casualties, and the bomb made both calculations obsolete, because a single weapon could destroy a city and a single nation could destroy the world. The doctrine that emerged, after a period of confusion in which the Americans believed they had a monopoly and the Soviets raced to break it, was deterrence: the idea that the best use of a nuclear weapon was never to use it, and that the way to prevent a nuclear war was to make the consequences of starting one unacceptable to any rational adversary. Deterrence depended on the weapon's existence rather than its employment, and it required a whole system of systems to make it credible: bombers, missiles, submarines, early-warning radars, command-and-control networks, and the political institutions that would manage the whole apparatus. The bomb was the weapon that made the system the point.

The Second World War was the first war in which the laboratory was a battlefield. It was the first war in which a nation's scientific capacity was a decisive military asset, and the first in which the government, the university, and the corporation were welded into a single apparatus for the production of new weapons. It was the first war in which the outcome was determined as much by the ability to invent as by the ability to produce, and the first in which the weapons invented during the war—radar, the proximity fuze, the jet engine, the ballistic missile, the atomic bomb—defined the wars of the next half-century. The weapons that ended the war were not the weapons that began it, and the difference was made by the system built to invent them.

This is the argument the rest of this book will develop, and it is worth stating plainly here, at the hinge of the narrative. The history of weapons is not a history of clever devices. It is a history of systems—of the ways in which societies organize themselves to produce, deploy, and sustain the means of violence—and the decisive changes in that history have come not when a new weapon was invented but when a new system for producing and using weapons was invented. The bronze sword was a system: it required the mining of copper and tin, the trade routes that brought them together, the foundries that cast them, the smiths who finished them, and the social arrangements that put them in the hands of a warrior class and kept them out of the hands of everyone else. The longbow was a system: it required the yew trees of Spain and Italy, the bowyers who shaped them over years, the arrow-makers who produced the millions of shafts and heads, and the social arrangements that required every Englishman to practice archery on Sunday and forbade him to play football. The gun was a system: it required the saltpeter of the Indies, the sulfur of Sicily, the charcoal of the forests, the foundries that cast the bronze and iron, the powder mills that ground the meal, and the financial institutions that could pay for it all. The machine gun was a system: it required the precision manufacturing that could make interchangeable parts, the ammunition factories that could produce millions of cartridges, and the logistics that could carry them to the front. And the atomic bomb was the system of systems, the one that required everything else and added to it the organized intellect of the modern world.

The Second World War was the moment when the system character of weapons became explicit, when the nations that fought it came to understand that they were fighting not a war of weapons but a war of systems, and when the weapons developed during the war were designed, for the first time, as components of systems rather than as individual instruments of combat. Radar was not a better telescope; it was a component of an air-defense system. The proximity fuze was not a better shell; it was a component of an anti-aircraft system. The atomic bomb was not a bigger bomb; it was a component of a strategic system that would dominate the next half-century. And the nations that won the war were the nations that built the systems, and the nations that lost were the nations that built, in the end, only weapons.

Consider, as a final case, the German V-weapons and the American atomic bomb side by side, because they are the two great technological projects of the war and they illustrate the difference between a weapon and a system. The V-2 was a weapon: a single, magnificent, expensive device that could be fired at a city and would kill some people and destroy some buildings. It was produced by a system, but not one designed to produce it; it was a system built for other purposes and turned, late and desperately, to the production of a wonder weapon. The atomic bomb was a system: it was produced by a system built specifically to produce it, and that system—the laboratories, the factories, the security apparatus, the command structure—was as much a part of the weapon as the plutonium core. The V-2 could be captured, and was; the atomic system could not be captured, because it was distributed across a continent and embedded in the industrial and intellectual life of a nation. The V-2 was a weapon a nation could build; the atomic bomb was a weapon only a system could build, and the nation that built the system won the war and dominated the peace.

The years after 1945 would test this proposition to destruction. The Cold War was a war of systems, fought with weapons that were never fired, and the systems built to fight it—the nuclear triad, the early-warning networks, the command-and-control apparatus, the alliance structures, the arms-control regimes—were the most elaborate and expensive systems ever constructed by human beings. The wars that were fought—in Korea, in Vietnam, in Afghanistan, in Iraq—were fought by nations that had the systems against nations or movements that did not, and the results were not always what the systems predicted. The systems that won the Second World War were designed to fight a war of mass and firepower against an enemy who fought the same way, and they were not always suited to a war against an enemy who did not. The history of weapons after 1945 is the history of the attempt to adapt the systems of industrial war to the wars that actually occurred, and it is a history of partial success and repeated failure.

But that is the subject of the chapters that follow. Here, at the end of the Second World War, the argument can be stated in its simplest form. The weapons of the industrial age were not merely tools; they were the visible tips of vast systems of production, organization, and knowledge, and the history of their development is the history of those systems. The nations that built the systems won the wars, and the nations that built only weapons lost them. The atomic bomb was the most dramatic proof of this proposition, but not the only one: the radar that won the Battle of Britain, the convoy system that won the Battle of the Atlantic, the amphibious system that won the Pacific, and the logistics system that put a million men on the beaches of Normandy were all proofs of the same proposition, and all were developed, in the space of a few years, by nations that had learned to organize themselves for the production of new means of war.

The war ended with two cities in ruins and a weapon that could destroy the world, and the nations that had built the weapon began, almost immediately, to build the systems that would keep it from being used. The paradox of the postwar world was that the most destructive weapon ever built was the weapon that prevented the great-power war the strategists had feared for a century. The systems built to fight the Cold War were, in the end, systems for preventing war, and they were successful to a degree no one had predicted. The history of weapons after 1945 would be a history of the attempt to make the systems of deterrence stable and the systems of conventional war usable, and of the ways in which the weapons themselves—the bombers, the missiles, the submarines, the precision-guided munitions, the drones—shaped the systems that used them.

The Second World War was the last war in which the outcome was determined by the production of weapons in the traditional sense. The wars that followed would be determined by the production of systems, and the weapons would be components of the systems rather than the systems themselves. The nations that understood this—the United States, the Soviet Union, and, in time, China—would build systems that could project power across the world, and the nations that did not would find themselves unable to compete. The history of war after 1945 is the history of the systems, and the weapons are the visible signs of their existence. The bomb was the first weapon that was also a system, and the systems that followed it—the missile, the satellite, the computer, the drone—were all, in their different ways, descendants of the great wartime systems built to win the war and, in winning it, changed the nature of war itself.

The atomic bomb was the product of a system, and it created a system. The system it created was the nuclear weapons complex: the laboratories at Los Alamos and Livermore, the production plants at Oak Ridge and Hanford and Savannah River, the testing grounds at Bikini and Eniwetok and the Nevada desert, the delivery systems—the bombers and missiles and submarines—and the command-and-control apparatus that would manage them. This complex was, and remains, one of the largest and most expensive enterprises in human history, and it was built in the decades after the war by the nations that had built the bomb and by the nations that raced to catch up. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949, four years after Hiroshima, and its first hydrogen bomb in 1953, less than a year after the American test. The British tested in 1952, the French in 1960, the Chinese in 1964. Each of these programs was a system, and each was built by a nation that had decided the system was necessary for its security.

The proliferation of nuclear weapons was the first great test of the system-of-systems argument in the postwar world, and it produced the first great arms-control regime, the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. The treaty was an attempt to manage the system by limiting the number of nations that could build it, and it was remarkably successful: 191 states are party to it, and only a handful—India, Israel, and Pakistan, which never joined, and North Korea, which announced its withdrawal in 2003—have acquired nuclear weapons outside its framework. The treaty was not a weapon and not a system in the military sense; it was a political system, built on the recognition that the spread of the weapon would make the world more dangerous for everyone, including the nations that already had it. It was the first acknowledgment by the great powers that the systems they had built to win the war had created a world in which the unrestricted spread of those systems would be a threat to all of them.

The postwar systems were not only nuclear. The conventional systems built after 1945—the tank formations of the Cold War, the fighter aircraft, the aircraft carriers, the logistics networks—were descendants of the wartime systems, and they were built to fight a war that never came. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, founded in 1949, was a system for the collective defense of Western Europe, and it integrated the forces of its member states into a command structure that could, in theory, fight a war against the Soviet Union. The Warsaw Pact, founded in 1955, was the Soviet answer, and the two alliances faced each other across the plains of Germany for four decades. The weapons built for that confrontation—the tanks, the artillery, the aircraft, the missiles—were the most advanced and expensive in history, and they were never used in the war for which they were designed. The systems built to fight the Third World War were, in the end, systems for preventing it, and they were successful because the consequences of failure were understood by both sides to be unacceptable.

The wars that were fought after 1945 were fought at the edges of the systems, in Korea and Vietnam and Afghanistan and Iraq, by nations that had the systems against nations or movements that did not. The results were not always what the systems predicted. The Korean War, which began in 1950, was fought to a stalemate by a Chinese army that had no air force and no navy and fought with small arms and mortars and the willingness to absorb casualties that the industrial systems could not match. The Vietnam War was lost by the most technologically advanced nation in the world to a peasant army that used the jungle and the night and the political will of its own people as weapons. The lesson of these wars was not that the systems were useless but that they were designed for a kind of war that did not always occur, and that the nations that built them had to learn to adapt them to wars they had not anticipated.

The adaptation was the work of the decades after 1945, and it produced the weapons that would define the wars of the twenty-first century: the precision-guided munition, the drone, the satellite, the computer network, and the whole apparatus of what would come to be called the revolution in military affairs. The precision-guided munition was the descendant of the proximity fuze and the guided missile, and it promised to make the systems of industrial war obsolete by allowing a single aircraft to destroy a target that had previously required a formation of bombers. The drone was the descendant of the radio-controlled aircraft of the Second World War, and it promised to remove the pilot from the cockpit and allow a nation to strike at its enemies without risking its own soldiers. The satellite was the descendant of the V-2, and it promised to make the whole world transparent to the nation that controlled the sky. And the computer network was the descendant of the radar and the codebreaking machines of the war, and it promised to make the systems of command and control vulnerable to attack in a way no previous weapon had been.

These weapons were developed over decades, and their development was shaped by the same logic that had shaped the weapons of the Second World War: the logic of the system. The precision-guided munition was not a better bomb; it was a component of a system that included the satellite that guided it, the aircraft that carried it, the computer that programmed it, and the intelligence that identified the target. The drone was not a better aircraft; it was a component of a system that included the satellite link that controlled it, the ground station that flew it, and the intelligence apparatus that told it what to look for. The satellite was not a better telescope; it was a component of a system that included the launch vehicle, the ground station, and the network of computers that processed its data. And the computer network was not a better radio; it was a component of a system that included the whole apparatus of modern communications and the whole apparatus of modern surveillance.

The wars of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries would test these systems as the wars of the mid-twentieth century had tested the systems of industrial war, and the results would be equally instructive. The Gulf War of 1991 was the first war in which precision-guided munitions were used on a large scale, and it convinced the world that the revolution in military affairs was real. The coalition dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs in Desert Storm, and about 6,520 tons of them were precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent of the total. The percentage was small, but the effect was disproportionate: the precision-guided munitions struck the command bunkers, the bridges, the power plants, and the air-defense sites that the coalition had identified as its most important targets, and they did so with an accuracy the unguided bombs of previous wars could not match. The images of laser-guided bombs falling down the ventilation shafts of Iraqi bunkers were broadcast around the world, and they created an expectation that air power could now do what it had always promised: destroy the enemy's ability to fight without destroying the enemy's society.

The expectation was premature. The Gulf War was fought against an enemy who had no air force worth the name, no navy, and no ability to interfere with the coalition's control of the air and space. The precision-guided munitions worked because the coalition had absolute command of the air, of space, and of the electromagnetic spectrum, and because the Iraqi army was a conscript force equipped with Soviet weapons designed for a war against NATO and never used against a technologically superior enemy. The war was a demonstration of what a system could do against an enemy who had no system, and not a demonstration of what a system could do against an enemy who had one.

The wars that followed—in Kosovo, in Afghanistan, in Iraq—tested the systems against enemies who had even less of a system than Iraq, and the results were mixed. The precision-guided munitions continued to work, and the drones became the weapon of choice for a nation that wanted to strike at its enemies without risking its own soldiers. But the wars were not won. The systems designed to destroy the enemy's ability to fight were not designed to build a new society in the enemy's country, and the nations that had built the systems discovered that the weapons that could destroy a state could not create one. The lesson of the post-1945 wars was the lesson the Second World War had already taught: the weapon is a component of a system, and the system is only as good as the purpose it is designed to serve. The systems of industrial war were designed to win a war of mass and firepower, and they were very good at it. They were not designed to win a war of counterinsurgency, and they were not very good at it.

The wars of the twenty-first century would test the systems in a new way, against enemies who had learned to use the systems' own weaknesses against them. The drone was the weapon that made this possible: a nation could use a drone to strike at an enemy without risking its own soldiers, but the enemy could use the drone's own communications links to find the ground station that controlled it and

chapters.title: Part 24
chapters.preview: The Predator’s pilot sat in a containerized ground-control station at Creech Air Force Base in Nevada, seven time zones and roughly seven thousand miles from the Afghan valley on his screen. He flew the aircraf
paragraphs: The Predator’s pilot sat in a containerized ground-control station at Creech Air Force Base in Nevada, seven time zones and roughly seven thousand miles from the Afghan valley on his screen. He flew the aircraft to the target, held the crosshairs on a compound, and pressed the button. The missile came off the rail. The video feed showed a bloom of dust and debris. Then, in the same shift, he drove home to his family for dinner. The weapon had separated the act of killing from the physical presence of the killer more completely than any weapon in the history of war, and the separation was not incidental to its design. It was the design. The drone made it possible for a nation to strike an enemy without risking its own soldiers—and made it possible for the enemy, using the drone’s own communications links, to find the ground station that controlled it and, in principle, attack the people who were not there. That paradox—the operator made both invulnerable and, through the satellite link, newly findable—was the signature of the twenty-first-century battlefield. The previous section ended on the drone as the hinge. This part follows that hinge through the wars, technologies, and doctrines that turned the weapon from a tool of industrial mass into a tool of persistent, networked, and increasingly automated violence, and it follows the countermeasures that grew up around it. The story runs from the first armed Predator sorties over Afghanistan in 2001 through the drone war over Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 and the contested claims of autonomous strike in Libya in 2021, and it keeps asking the question the whole book has asked: what does a weapon do to the political and moral order that builds it?

The armed drone did not arrive out of nowhere. It was the convergence of three long-running strands: the remotely piloted vehicle, the precision-guided munition, and the persistent surveillance platform. The remotely piloted vehicle stretched back to the First World War, when Britain and the United States experimented with small radio-controlled aircraft intended as flying bombs. The Radioplane company, founded in 1934, built target drones for anti-aircraft gunnery practice; a young photographer named David Conover, sent by the U.S. Army to photograph workers at the Radioplane plant in 1944, discovered a model named Norma Jeane Dougherty, who later became Marilyn Monroe. The drone was already a mass-produced industrial object before it was a weapon. The Ryan Firebee, developed in the 1950s, was a jet-powered target drone adapted for reconnaissance over North Vietnam and China; the Model 147 Lightning Bug flew hundreds of missions over North Vietnam, Laos, and China in the 1960s and 1970s, demonstrating that an unmanned aircraft could survive in defended airspace and return imagery. Israeli experience in the 1973 Yom Kippur War and the 1982 Lebanon War pushed the technology further: Israel Aircraft Industries developed the Scout and the Mastiff, small drones that could loiter over the battlefield and send back video in real time. In the 1982 Bekaa Valley, Israeli drones baited Syrian air-defense radars into turning on, exposing their emissions for anti-radiation missiles, and provided real-time reconnaissance for strike aircraft. The drone was already a system weapon—sensor, communications link, and shooter bound together—before the United States armed it.

The precision-guided munition was the second strand. The laser-guided bomb, developed in the 1960s and used with devastating effect in the 1972 Linebacker II campaign and again in the 1991 Gulf War, had already shown that a bomb could be steered to a point target rather than dropped in a pattern around it. The Gulf War’s precision weapons—about 7.4 percent of the roughly 88,500 tons of bombs dropped in Desert Storm, or about 6,520 tons—struck bridges, command bunkers, and aircraft shelters with a reliability unguided bombs could not match. Television images of a laser-guided bomb going down a ventilation shaft became the emblem of a new kind of air power: precise, surgical, and politically presentable. The third strand was persistence. The Predator, originally designated the RQ-1 (the “R” for reconnaissance), was developed in the 1990s from a design by Abraham Karem, an Israeli-American engineer who had built drones for the Israeli Air Force. It was a slow, propeller-driven aircraft with a wingspan of about forty-eight feet, a ceiling of around 25,000 feet, and an endurance of more than twenty hours. It carried a sensor ball—electro-optical and infrared cameras and a laser designator—and could loiter over a target for a full day, watching. The RQ-1 was a surveillance platform. The MQ-1, the “M” for multi-role, carried two Hellfire missiles.

The Hellfire was itself a product of the Cold War. It had been developed in the 1970s as an anti-tank missile, a precision weapon designed to be fired from helicopters against massed Soviet armor. It was small—about five feet long and a hundred pounds—with a shaped-charge warhead and a laser seeker. Mounted on a Predator, it became something new: a weapon that could be fired from a platform that had been watching a target for hours, by an operator who had been watching the target for hours, at a moment of choosing. The first armed Predator strike was flown in Afghanistan in October 2001, against Taliban leader Mullah Omar’s compound in Kandahar. The missile missed—Omar was not there, and the strike killed a small number of people, including, reportedly, a family—but the precedent was set. By 2002 the armed Predator was a regular part of the American air campaign in Afghanistan, and by the middle of the decade it was the centerpiece of a new kind of war.

The drone war that followed was not a single campaign but a set of campaigns, conducted in Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, Somalia, Pakistan, Libya, and Syria by the United States and, increasingly, by other states. The numbers are contested and incomplete, because the programs were largely classified and the strikes were often conducted by the Central Intelligence Agency rather than the Department of Defense, but the broad outlines are clear. In Pakistan’s Federally Administered Tribal Areas, the United States conducted hundreds of drone strikes between 2004 and 2018, targeting al-Qaeda and Taliban leaders and, according to critics, killing large numbers of civilians. The Bureau of Investigative Journalism, a London-based nonprofit, compiled a database of the strikes and estimated that between 2004 and 2018 there were between 430 and 450 strikes in Pakistan, killing between 2,500 and 4,000 people, of whom between 400 and 1,000 were civilians. The New America Foundation estimated lower civilian casualties. The dispute over the numbers was itself part of the politics of the drone: the United States claimed extraordinary precision and minimal civilian harm; critics claimed the strikes were a form of extrajudicial killing that created more enemies than it killed. Both claims had evidence behind them, and the evidence was hard to adjudicate because the programs were secret.

The drone’s military logic was straightforward. It offered persistence—a Predator could watch a target for twenty hours, far longer than a manned aircraft could loiter—and a low risk of friendly casualties, because the crew was on the ground, often in the United States. It offered precision, because the Hellfire was a guided weapon and the sensor could identify a target before the shot. And it offered a low political cost, because a drone strike did not put American pilots at risk of being shot down and captured, and could be conducted without a large ground presence. The drone was, in the language of the time, a “light footprint” weapon. It was the ideal instrument for a war the American public was willing to continue at a low level of visible commitment but not willing to fight with large ground forces. The drone was the weapon of the forever war.

But the drone’s logic cut both ways. The persistence that made it a good surveillance platform also made it a good target for the enemy’s intelligence. The drone’s video feed and control signals traveled over satellite links, and those links could be intercepted, jammed, or exploited. In 2009, Iraqi insurgents were reported to have used off-the-shelf software, reportedly a program called SkyGrabber, to intercept the unencrypted video feeds from American Predators. The feeds were not encrypted because the bandwidth cost of encryption was high and because the military had assumed the enemy could not exploit the signal. The assumption was wrong. The insurgents could watch what the drone was watching and use that knowledge to hide, to ambush, or to bait the drone into striking a decoy. The military encrypted the feeds after the breach was reported, but the episode revealed a structural vulnerability: the drone was a networked weapon, and a networked weapon could be hacked.

The vulnerability was not only technical. The drone’s ground-control station was a physical facility, and it was a target. In 2011, Iranian forces claimed to have brought down an American RQ-170 Sentinel, a stealthy reconnaissance drone, by spoofing its GPS signal and tricking it into landing in Iran. The claim was disputed—the United States said the drone had malfunctioned—but the episode showed that the drone’s dependence on navigation and communications links was a point of attack. In 2019, Iran shot down an American RQ-4 Global Hawk, a large, high-altitude surveillance drone, with a surface-to-air missile, nearly triggering a military response. The drone was a weapon that could be used against its owner. The enemy could use the drone’s own communications links to find the ground station that controlled it, and it could attack the people who were not there—the operators, the analysts, the contractors—through cyber operations, through targeting their bases, or through the political costs of a strike gone wrong. The drone had separated the killer from the killing, but not the killer from the consequences.

The drone also changed the moral economy of war. The pilot in the ground-control station was not in physical danger, but he was in psychological danger. Studies of drone operators found high rates of stress, fatigue, and post-traumatic stress disorder, in part because the operators watched their targets for hours, saw the aftermath of their strikes in high-resolution video, and then went home to their families. The distance that made the drone politically attractive made it morally complicated. The operator could see the target’s face, watch him play with his children, follow him for days, and then kill him. The intimacy of the surveillance was unprecedented. A bomber pilot in the Second World War saw a city from five miles up; a drone operator saw a man’s face from five miles away and could see the blood afterward. The drone did not remove the moral weight of killing; it relocated it.

The legal questions were equally complicated. The drone strikes were conducted under the Authorization for Use of Military Force, passed by Congress on 14 September 2001, which authorized the president to use “all necessary and appropriate force” against the nations, organizations, or persons who planned, authorized, committed, or aided the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001. The authorization was broad, and the executive branch interpreted it to permit lethal strikes against suspected terrorists and their associates far from any conventional battlefield, in countries with which the United States was not at war. The strikes raised questions under international humanitarian law: who was a lawful target, what constituted a “direct participation in hostilities,” and whether the strikes met the requirements of distinction and proportionality. The legal debate was conducted in law reviews, in congressional hearings, and in the court of public opinion, and it was never fully resolved. The drone had created a new category of warfare—the targeted killing of individuals by remote-controlled aircraft—and the law had not caught up with it.

The drone’s proliferation was the next chapter. The United States was the first state to arm drones on a large scale, but not the last. Israel had armed drones—the Hermes 450 and the Heron—and used them in Lebanon, Gaza, and elsewhere. Britain, France, Italy, and other NATO countries acquired armed drones, often American-built Reapers. Turkey developed its own armed drone, the Bayraktar TB2, a relatively cheap, propeller-driven aircraft built by a company founded by Selçuk Bayraktar, an MIT-trained engineer who was also President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s son-in-law. The TB2 was a different kind of weapon from the Predator: smaller, cheaper, easier to operate, and designed for export. It carried a maximum payload of about 150 kilograms, could stay aloft for more than twenty hours, and could be operated by a crew with limited training. It was the drone as a commodity, and it would change the balance of power in several regional conflicts.

The first place the TB2 made a decisive difference was Libya, where the Turkish-backed Government of National Accord used it against the forces of Khalifa Haftar, who was backed by the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, and Russia. The TB2 struck Haftar’s supply lines, his artillery, and his air defenses, and helped turn the tide of the war. The second place was Nagorno-Karabakh, a mountainous enclave that had been the subject of a frozen conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan since the collapse of the Soviet Union. The conflict had erupted into war in the early 1990s, and a ceasefire in 1994 had left Armenia in control of Nagorno-Karabakh and several surrounding districts of Azerbaijan. The ceasefire held, more or less, for twenty-six years. Then, on 27 September 2020, Azerbaijan launched an offensive to retake the territory.

The war that followed lasted forty-four days. It was fought with a mix of old and new weapons: tanks, artillery, and infantry, but also drones, loitering munitions, and electronic warfare. Azerbaijan had invested heavily in Turkish and Israeli drones, including the Bayraktar TB2 and the Israeli Harop and SkyStriker loitering munitions. Armenia had invested in Russian air-defense systems, including the S-300 and the Tor-M2, and in older Soviet-era equipment. The Azerbaijani drones hunted the Armenian air defenses, and the Armenian air defenses could not shoot them down. The TB2s flew at medium altitude, above the effective range of some of the Armenian short-range systems, and used their sensors to find and destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, and supply trucks. The videos Azerbaijan released—grainy, green-tinted footage of tanks exploding, of soldiers running, of air-defense systems being destroyed—were a new kind of propaganda. They showed the drone’s-eye view of war, and they showed that a relatively small, relatively cheap drone could destroy a tank that cost millions of dollars and carried a crew of three.

The RUSI study of the conflict, published in 2021, described it as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and suppression of air defense. The study’s authors, Justin Bronk and colleagues, argued that the conflict demonstrated the vulnerability of traditional, short-range air defenses to medium-altitude drones and loitering munitions, and that it showed the importance of electronic warfare, dispersion, and camouflage. The study also noted that Azerbaijani success was not simply a matter of technology; it depended on the integration of drones with artillery, electronic warfare, and a coherent operational plan. The drone was a system weapon, and the system mattered as much as the weapon. The war ended with a Russian-brokered ceasefire on 9 November 2020, and Azerbaijan regained control of much of Nagorno-Karabakh and the surrounding districts. The drone had changed the outcome of the war, and it had changed the way militaries around the world thought about air power.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was not the first time drones had been used in a conventional conflict—Israel had used them in Lebanon in 2006, and the United States had used them in Iraq and Afghanistan—but it was the first time they had been the decisive weapon in a war between two states with modern, if uneven, air defenses. The war was a demonstration, and militaries studied it. The lesson many drew was that the era of the manned aircraft and the heavy tank might be ending, that cheap drones could overwhelm expensive platforms, and that air defenses needed to be rethought. The lesson was overstated—tanks and manned aircraft would continue to matter, and the Armenian air defenses were poorly handled as well as outmatched—but it was not wrong. The drone had become a weapon of first resort, and the counter-drone industry was born.

The counter-drone problem was hard. A small drone was a difficult target: slow, small, and flying low, and it could be made of plastic and powered by an electric motor, which made it hard to detect by radar and hard to shoot down with missiles. The solutions that emerged were a mix of old and new: guns, nets, jammers, lasers, and cyber. The gun was the simplest: a radar or an acoustic sensor detected the drone, and a gunner shot at it. The net was a variation: a projectile that deployed a net to entangle the drone’s rotors. The jammer was electronic: it disrupted the drone’s control signal or its GPS, causing it to hover, return home, or crash. The laser was directed energy: it burned a hole in the drone’s airframe or its sensor. The cyber was the most exotic: it hacked the drone’s control system and took it over. Each solution had limitations. Guns were cheap but inaccurate. Jammers were effective but could disrupt friendly communications. Lasers were expensive and power-hungry. Cyber was fragile and required intelligence. The counter-drone problem was a microcosm of the larger problem of twenty-first-century warfare: the offense was cheap, the defense was expensive, and the advantage lay with the attacker.

The drone also changed the relationship between the state and the individual. A state could now kill a single person, in a country far away, without putting a soldier at risk, and it could do so on the basis of intelligence that might be wrong. The strikes were conducted by the CIA and by the military, and the decision to strike was made by officials who were not on the battlefield and who often relied on pattern-of-life analysis—the observation of a person’s movements over time—to identify targets. The strikes killed people who were not the intended targets, including, in some cases, people attending funerals or weddings, and the United States sometimes characterized the dead as militants on the basis of their presence at the scene. The drone strike became a symbol of a new kind of war, a war that was permanent, invisible to most Americans, and conducted by remote control.

The political scientist Grégoire Chamayou, in his book *A Theory of the Drone* (2013), argued that the drone created a new kind of sovereignty, a “cybernetic” sovereignty in which the state exercised power through the control of information and the capacity for violence at a distance. The drone, he wrote, was a weapon of “hunter” warfare, in which the state tracked and killed individuals rather than fighting armies. The philosopher Peter Singer, in *Wired for War* (2009), had earlier described the rise of robotics in warfare and the ethical questions it raised. The debate was not merely academic. The drone strikes were the subject of litigation in the United States and in Europe, and of investigations by the United Nations and by human-rights organizations. The UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary, or arbitrary executions, Philip Alston, reported in 2010 that the United States was conducting targeted killings in a way that raised serious questions under international law, and he called for greater transparency. The United States did not provide it.

The drone’s proliferation was not limited to states. Non-state actors could buy or build drones, and they did. The Islamic State used commercial quadcopters to drop small bombs in Iraq and Syria, and used them for reconnaissance. Hezbollah used drones to surveil Israel. Houthi forces in Yemen used drones to attack Saudi Arabia, including a 2019 attack on the Abqaiq oil processing facility that knocked out about half of Saudi Arabia’s oil production for a time. The attack was conducted with a mix of drones and cruise missiles, and it demonstrated that a non-state actor could use relatively cheap technology to strike a strategic target. The drone had become a weapon of the weak as well as the strong.

The drone’s development was also shaped by the commercial sector. The same technology that made a Predator possible—miniaturized sensors, GPS, satellite communications, lightweight materials—was being developed for consumer and commercial uses, and the consumer drone market exploded in the 2010s. Companies like DJI, a Chinese firm founded in 2006, sold millions of small quadcopters for photography, agriculture, and recreation. The military adapted: soldiers bought commercial drones and used them for reconnaissance, and militaries developed small, cheap drones for infantry units. The line between the military and civilian drone blurred, and the regulation of drones became a problem for governments around the world. The drone was a dual-use technology, and its spread was driven by markets as much as by states.

The next step in the drone’s evolution was autonomy. A drone remotely piloted by a human was one thing; a drone that could fly, navigate, and select targets on its own was another. The technology for autonomy was developing rapidly: computer vision, machine learning, and cheap sensors made it possible for a machine to identify a person or a vehicle and track it. The military applications were obvious: a loitering munition that could find its own target, an autonomous drone that could swarm with others, a robot that could navigate a building and clear it. The ethical and legal questions were profound: if a machine killed a person, who was responsible? Could a machine distinguish between a combatant and a civilian? Could it comply with the laws of war? The debate over lethal autonomous weapons systems began in earnest in the 2010s, at the United Nations, in the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, and in civil society. The Campaign to Stop Killer Robots, founded in 2012, called for a preemptive ban on fully autonomous weapons. The states parties to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons established a Group of Governmental Experts to discuss the issue, and the discussions continued for years without a binding agreement.

The contested case of the Kargu-2 loitering munition in Libya was a preview of the debate. In March 2021, a UN Panel of Experts report on Libya stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition “may have been” used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The Kargu-2 was a Turkish-built quadcopter that could be operated in a “fire and forget” mode, in which it would autonomously find and attack a target. The report’s language was careful—“may have been”—and the claim was not independently confirmed. The Panel of Experts was reporting on the basis of information it had received, and the information was not conclusive. But the report was widely reported as the first confirmed case of an autonomous drone killing a human being, and it became a landmark in the debate. The claim remains contested and should be treated with caution. It is not a confirmed autonomous strike. But it is a sign of what was coming: the technology for autonomous targeting existed, it was being deployed, and the legal and ethical frameworks for controlling it were not in place.

The Kargu-2 was a loitering munition, a weapon that combined the drone and the missile. A loitering munition was a small, inexpensive aircraft that could fly to a target area, loiter overhead, and then dive onto a target when commanded—or, in some modes, on its own. The Israeli Harop, developed in the 2000s, was one of the first; it was a “fire and forget” weapon that could loiter for hours and then attack a radar emitter. The loitering munition was a weapon of the “sensor-to-shooter” era: a sensor and a shooter in one package, usable against targets that appeared suddenly, such as a mobile air-defense system or a tank. It was also a weapon of the “fog of war” era: it could be launched into an area and left to find a target, which meant that the decision to kill was delegated to a machine, or to a human who was not present.

The loitering munition was used extensively in Nagorno-Karabakh, and in the war in Ukraine that began in 2022. The Ukrainian military used Turkish TB2 drones and American loitering munitions, including the Switchblade, against Russian forces, and the Russian military used Iranian-made Shahed-136 drones to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The Shahed was a cheap, propeller-driven drone that carried a warhead and was designed to fly to a target and explode. It was not a precision weapon in the sense that a Hellfire was; it was a terror weapon, designed to overwhelm air defenses and strike civilian infrastructure. The war in Ukraine became a laboratory for drone warfare, and it demonstrated that drones were not a panacea: they could be shot down, jammed, and countered, and their effectiveness depended on the integration of the drone with other systems.

The drone was also changing the way wars were fought on the ground. The small quadcopter, equipped with a camera and a grenade, became a standard infantry weapon in Ukraine and elsewhere. A squad could send up a drone to see over a hill, spot an enemy position, and drop a grenade into a trench. The drone was cheap, expendable, and easy to use, and it gave small units a capability once reserved for aircraft. It was also a weapon of the “transparent battlefield”: both sides could see each other, and concealment became harder. The drone was a surveillance device as much as a weapon, and its effect on the conduct of war was as much about information as about firepower.

The drone’s rise was part of a larger shift in the character of war. The industrial-age battlefield, with its massed armies, its trenches, and its artillery barrages, had been replaced by a battlefield that was dispersed, networked, and persistent. The weapons that mattered were not the biggest guns but the most precise and the most connected. The drone was a symbol of this shift, but not the only weapon. Precision-guided munitions, cyber weapons, space-based sensors, and autonomous systems were all part of the same transformation, driven by the same forces that had driven the industrial revolution in warfare: technology, economics, and politics. But the direction was different. The industrial revolution in warfare had been about mass production and mass destruction; the information revolution in warfare was about precision, speed, and control.

The history of the drone was also a history of the state’s changing relationship to violence. The drone allowed a state to kill individuals without a battlefield, without a declaration of war, and without the consent of the country in which the killing took place. It allowed a state to conduct a war that was invisible to most of its citizens, and to continue a war indefinitely. The drone was a weapon of the “forever war,” and a weapon of the “surveillance state.” The same technology that allowed a state to watch a suspected terrorist also allowed it to watch its own citizens, and the boundary between foreign intelligence and domestic surveillance was blurred. The drone was a technology of control as well as a technology of destruction.

The drone’s history also intersected with the history of arms control. The nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, had 191 states parties; India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The NPT was a landmark of the Cold War arms-control regime, but it did not address drones, cyber weapons, or autonomous systems. The new technologies of the twenty-first century were not covered by the old arms-control treaties, and efforts to create new regimes were slow and contested. The drone was a weapon that could be used by any state with the money to buy one, and the export of drones was regulated by the Missile Technology Control Regime, a voluntary arrangement among thirty-five countries, but the regime was not universal and did not cover small drones. The proliferation of drones was a proliferation of precision strike, and it was changing the balance of power in regional conflicts.

The drone was also changing the way wars were represented. The video feed from a drone was a new kind of war imagery: intimate, detailed, real-time, and often released by militaries as propaganda. The Azerbaijani videos of tanks exploding were watched millions of times and shaped public perceptions of the war. The drone’s-eye view was a view from above, a view of targets as objects, and it made war look like a video game. The comparison was made often, and it was not entirely wrong: the drone operator used a joystick, watched a screen, and killed people who were represented as pixels. But the comparison was also misleading: the drone operator knew that the pixels were people, and the psychological burden of that knowledge was part of the story. The drone did not make war into a game; it made war into a different kind of reality, one in which the killer was close enough to see and far enough to be safe.

The drone’s history was also a history of the people who built and operated it. The engineers who designed the Predator, the Hellfire, and the ground-control station were part of a military-industrial complex transformed by the information revolution. The companies that built drones—General Atomics, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, and others—were part of a defense industry that was consolidating and globalizing. The operators who flew the drones belonged to a new kind of military profession, one that required technical skill, emotional resilience, and a capacity for detachment. The analysts who watched the video feeds were part of a new kind of intelligence apparatus, one that processed vast amounts of data and turned it into targets. The drone was a system, and the system was made of people as well as machines.

The drone’s history was also a history of resistance. The drone strikes were protested in Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia, and the protests were sometimes violent. The Pakistani politician Imran Khan, who later became prime minister, was a vocal critic of the strikes and called them a violation of Pakistani sovereignty. The Yemeni journalist and activist Nasser Arrabyee documented the strikes and their aftermath, and described the anger and fear they produced. The drone was a weapon that created enemies as well as killed them, and the political consequences were part of its history. The strikes were also challenged in court: in 2010, the American Civil Liberties Union and the Center for Constitutional Rights filed a lawsuit on behalf of Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen who had been placed on a kill list, seeking to prevent the government from killing him without due process. The lawsuit was dismissed on the grounds that the courts could not review military decisions. Al-Awlaki was killed by a drone strike in Yemen in 2011, and his sixteen-year-old son, Abdulrahman, was killed by a separate strike two weeks later. The killings raised questions about citizenship, due process, and the limits of executive power, and they were part of the drone’s moral ledger.

The drone’s history was also a history of the future. The technologies that made the drone possible—artificial intelligence, robotics, miniaturization, and connectivity—were advancing rapidly, and the drone was a preview of the weapons that were coming. The autonomous drone, the drone swarm, the drone that could operate in a city, the drone that could be built by a non-state actor from commercial parts—these were not science fiction. They were engineering problems, and they were being solved. The question was not whether the drone would become more autonomous and more ubiquitous, but how the world would manage the consequences. The drone was a weapon that had already changed the history of war, and it would change it further.

The history of the drone was, in the end, a history of a paradox. The drone was a weapon that promised to make war more precise, more humane, and more controllable. It promised to reduce civilian casualties, protect soldiers, and allow states to act with discrimination. It delivered some of these promises: the Hellfire was more precise than a bomb, and the drone operator could see the target before firing. But the drone also made war more permanent, more secret, and more remote. It made it easier for states to kill without consequence, and harder for the public to know what was being done in its name. The drone was a weapon of the twenty-first century, and it carried the contradictions of the twenty-first century: the promise of precision and the reality of proliferation, the promise of control and the reality of blowback, the promise of humanity and the reality of distance.

The drone’s story was not over. The wars in Ukraine and Gaza, the proliferation of drones to non-state actors, the development of autonomous systems, and the debate over killer robots were all part of the same story. The drone was a weapon that had changed the history of war, and it would continue to change it. The question that the history of the drone posed was the question that the history of weapons had always posed: what kind of world do we build when we build a weapon? The drone had given a new answer, and the answer was still being written.
