chapters.preview: The drone’s story was not over. The wars in Ukraine and Gaza, the spread of drones to non-state actors, the development of autonomous systems, and the debate over killer robots were all part of the same story.
paragraphs: The drone’s story was not over. The wars in Ukraine and Gaza, the spread of drones to non-state actors, the development of autonomous systems, and the debate over killer robots were all part of the same story. The drone was a weapon that had changed the history of war, and it would continue to change it. The question the drone posed was the question the history of weapons had always posed: what kind of world do we build when we build a weapon? The drone had given a new answer, and that answer was still being written.

To understand what came next, it is necessary to go back to a small town in the Donbas in the spring of 2014, when a ragtag volunteer battalion of Ukrainian soldiers, many of them amateurs, discovered that a cheap quadcopter bought off the shelf could do something a platoon of scouts could not. The war in eastern Ukraine began that April, after Russia’s annexation of Crimea and the outbreak of fighting between Ukrainian forces and Russian-backed separatists. The Ukrainian army was then a shadow of what it would become: underfunded, poorly equipped, and short of almost everything, including reconnaissance aircraft. Into that gap flew the consumer drone. Volunteers bought Chinese-made quadcopters—DJI Phantoms, mostly—and sent them to the front. Soldiers taped cameras to them, or used the cameras they came with, and flew them over separatist positions to see what was there. The images were grainy, the range was short, the batteries lasted twenty minutes, and a determined rifleman could jam or shoot down the whole thing. But it worked. For the first time, a squad of infantry could see over the next hill without sending a man to die looking.

The innovation spread the way innovations spread in war: by imitation and necessity. By 2015, both sides were using drones, and the Ukrainians had begun to weaponize them, dropping small grenades and improvised explosives from commercially available machines. The Russian-backed forces did the same. The drones were not elegant weapons. They were the kind of thing a clever sergeant improvises when the supply chain has failed and the enemy is close. But they changed the texture of the war. A drone overhead meant that movement was observed, that artillery could be corrected in real time, that a trench could be mapped before an assault. The drone did not replace the artillery; it made the artillery smarter. It did not replace the infantry; it made the infantry more exposed.

What happened in Ukraine between 2014 and 2022 was a preview, and the full-scale invasion of February 2022 turned the preview into a transformation. When Russian forces crossed the border, they expected a short war. They did not expect the skies over their columns to fill with small, cheap, buzzing machines. The Ukrainian military, having spent eight years learning to fight with drones, deployed them at scale. The results were visible to the world: videos of Russian tanks struck by munitions dropped from quadcopters, of artillery batteries corrected by drone observers, of infantry positions identified and destroyed within minutes. The images were often shaky, often taken from a camera looking straight down, and they had a quality new to war footage: they were intimate, close, and strangely quiet. The drone hovered, the target moved, the munition fell, and the screen went white or black. The war was being watched from above, and the watching was the fighting.

The drone war in Ukraine was not a war of large, expensive, high-altitude machines. It was a war of small, cheap, low-altitude machines, and that was the point. A quadcopter costing a few hundred dollars could destroy a tank costing several million. A loitering munition—a drone designed to crash into its target and explode—could be manufactured in a workshop and used to strike a command post. The economics of the battlefield had been inverted. The side with the cheaper weapon could impose costs on the side with the more expensive one. This was not entirely new; the improvised explosive device had done something similar in Iraq and Afghanistan. But the drone made it systematic, made it visible, and made it a matter of everyday tactics rather than occasional atrocity.

The Russian military adapted, as militaries do. It developed electronic warfare systems to jam drone signals and fielded its own drones, including the Iranian-designed Shahed loitering munitions it used to strike Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The Shahed was a different kind of weapon: a one-way attack drone, cheap and crude, powered by a small engine and guided by satellite, designed to fly hundreds of kilometers and explode. It was a poor man’s cruise missile, used the way cruise missiles are used: to strike power stations, terrorize cities, exhaust air defenses. Ukrainian air defenses, meanwhile, had to learn to shoot down small, slow, low-flying targets that were hard to detect and cheap to replace. A missile costing hundreds of thousands of dollars was being used to intercept a drone costing tens of thousands. The exchange was unfavorable, and everyone knew it.

The war in Ukraine also demonstrated something the history of weapons had shown repeatedly: that the adoption of a new weapon is never just a matter of technology. It is a matter of organization, doctrine, training, supply, and politics. The Ukrainian military could use drones effectively because it had spent years building the institutions to do so—units dedicated to drone operations, training programs for operators, a culture that encouraged improvisation. The Russian military, with its more centralized and hierarchical structure, was slower to adapt, though it eventually did. The lesson was not that drones were decisive; it was that drones were a tool, and the tool was only as good as the hand that held it.

The war in Gaza, which escalated dramatically after the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, added another chapter. Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups used drones in ways both tactical and symbolic: to drop munitions on Israeli positions, conduct reconnaissance, and attack vehicles. The Israeli military, one of the most technologically advanced in the world, used drones extensively for surveillance and strike, and also faced the problem of drones used against it. The conflict was fought in a dense urban environment, where the drone’s ability to see over walls and into streets was both an advantage and a liability. The drone made the battlefield more transparent, and transparency in war is not always a good thing; it can mean that civilians are more exposed, that combatants are more easily targeted, that the distinction between the two is harder to maintain.

The proliferation of drones to non-state actors was one of the most significant developments of the early twenty-first century. Hezbollah used drones against Israel. The Houthis in Yemen used drones to attack Saudi Arabia and, later, shipping in the Red Sea. ISIS used drones in Iraq and Syria. The Taliban used drones in Afghanistan. Mexican drug cartels used drones to drop explosives and conduct surveillance. The technology was cheap, widely available, and easy to use, and the barriers to entry were low. A group that could not afford a fighter jet could afford a drone. A group that could not build a missile could buy a drone and strap a bomb to it. The monopoly on air power that had belonged to states since the invention of the airplane was eroding.

This erosion had consequences beyond the battlefield. It changed the way states thought about security. It changed the way borders were defended. It changed the way wars were fought and the way they were imagined. The drone was a weapon that could be used by anyone, against anyone, and that fact meant the old distinctions between combatant and non-combatant, between the front line and the rear, between war and peace, were becoming harder to sustain. The drone was not the cause of this blurring, but it was an accelerant. It made the world more dangerous in a way that was diffuse and hard to address.

The development of autonomous systems was the next step, and it raised questions the history of weapons had been building toward for centuries. The drone was a weapon controlled by a human, even if that human was thousands of miles away. The autonomous weapon was a weapon that made its own decisions. The distinction was not always clear—a loitering munition that selects its target based on a pre-programmed set of criteria is partly autonomous—but the direction of travel was clear. The technology was moving toward machines that could find, identify, and kill targets without human intervention. The debate over whether this was acceptable was one of the most important debates of the era, and it was a debate the history of weapons had been preparing for.

The UN Panel of Experts report on Libya in 2021 offered a glimpse of what was coming. The report stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition, a Turkish-made weapon, “may have been” used in autonomous mode against retreating forces in Libya in 2020. The claim was contested and not independently confirmed. The wording was careful, hedged, and uncertain. But the fact that the claim was made at all was significant. It suggested that the technology was not just theoretical, that it was being used in real conflicts, and that the international community was not sure how to respond. The report was a warning: the line between human-controlled and autonomous weapons was being crossed, and the crossing was happening without a clear legal or ethical framework to govern it.

The debate over killer robots, as autonomous weapons were sometimes called, was a debate about accountability. If a machine kills a person, who is responsible? The operator? The programmer? The commander who deployed the machine? The manufacturer? The state that built it? The law of armed conflict required that someone be accountable for every death, and the autonomous weapon made accountability difficult. It also made the distinction between combatant and civilian harder to maintain, because a machine that could not distinguish between the two was a machine that could kill indiscriminately. The technology was not there yet, but the trajectory was clear, and the international community was struggling to keep up.

The campaign to ban autonomous weapons was led by a coalition of non-governmental organizations, including Human Rights Watch and the International Committee for Robot Arms Control, and supported by a number of states, including Austria, Brazil, and the Vatican. The campaign argued that autonomous weapons crossed a moral line, that they were inherently indiscriminate, and that they should be prohibited by international law. It was opposed by states developing the technology, including the United States, Russia, China, and Israel, which argued that autonomous weapons could be more precise and more humane than human soldiers, and that a ban would be unenforceable. The debate was ongoing, and it was a debate the history of weapons had seen before: over the crossbow, the machine gun, the bomber, the nuclear bomb. Each time, the argument was made that the new weapon was uniquely terrible, and each time, the weapon was adopted anyway.

The history of weapons was not a history of progress in the sense of moral improvement. It was a history of escalation, of adaptation, of the constant search for advantage. The drone was the latest chapter, and the autonomous weapon was the chapter being written. The question was not whether the technology would be developed—it would—but how it would be used, and by whom, and under what constraints. The history of weapons suggested that the answer would be determined not by ethics alone but by politics, by power, and by the interests of the states and groups that wielded the weapons. It also suggested that the answer would be contested, that the debate would continue, and that the outcome would be shaped by the same forces that had shaped every previous chapter: the desire for security, the fear of the enemy, and the belief that the next weapon would be the one that finally made war safe, or at least survivable.

The drone had changed the history of war, and it would continue to change it. But the drone was not the end of the story. It was a step in a longer story, a story that had begun with a sharpened stone and would continue with whatever came next. The history of weapons was a history of human ingenuity applied to the problem of killing, and the problem was not going away. The question was what kind of world we would build with the weapons we built, and the answer was still being written.

The drone’s rise was inseparable from a broader transformation in the way wars were fought and understood. To see the drone clearly, it is necessary to place it in the context of the longer history of air power, of precision, and of the relationship between technology and strategy. The drone was not the first weapon to promise precision; it was the latest in a long line. The history of precision was a history of promises made and broken, of technologies that were supposed to make war clean and instead made it more complicated. The drone was the heir to that history, and it carried its contradictions.

The dream of precision was old. The archer who could hit a target at a hundred paces was a precise weapon. The rifleman who could hit a target at three hundred paces was a precise weapon. The bomber that could hit a factory instead of a city was a precise weapon. The dream was always the same: to hit the thing you aimed at, and only the thing you aimed at. It was a dream of control, of limiting the violence of war to the people and things that deserved it. It was also a dream of efficiency, of using force in a way that achieved the political objective without the waste and horror of indiscriminate destruction. The dream was noble, and it was also dangerous, because it made war seem more acceptable than it was.

The history of precision in the twentieth century was a history of technological ambition and strategic disappointment. The bomber was supposed to be a precision weapon; the bombardiers of the 1930s trained with bombsights that were marvels of mechanical engineering, and they believed they could hit a target from twenty thousand feet. The war proved them wrong. The bombs fell where they fell, and the cities burned. The lesson was not that precision was impossible; it was that precision was hard, and the technology of the time was not up to the task. The lesson was learned, forgotten, and learned again.

The laser-guided bomb, developed in the 1960s and used in Vietnam and later in the Gulf War, was the first weapon to make precision a practical reality. The bomb was guided by a laser pointed at the target, and it could hit with a degree of accuracy that had been impossible before. The Gulf War of 1991 was the coming-out party for precision-guided munitions. Images of laser-guided bombs falling down the ventilation shafts of buildings, of cruise missiles turning corners, of targets destroyed with a single bomb, were broadcast around the world. The war was presented as a new kind of war, a war of precision and cleanliness, a war in which the violence was surgical and the collateral damage minimal.

The reality was more complicated. The Gulf War was not a clean war. The bombing of the Amiriyah shelter in Baghdad, which killed hundreds of civilians, was a reminder that precision was not the same as infallibility. The use of precision weapons was also uneven; only a small fraction of the bombs dropped in the Gulf War were precision-guided. The rest were dumb bombs, and they killed indiscriminately. The war was not a revolution in the nature of war; it was a revolution in the image of war. The image was of precision, and the image was powerful, and it shaped the way the public understood the war and the way the military understood itself.

The drone was the next step in the history of precision. It was a weapon that could loiter over a target for hours, be controlled by a human who could see the target in real time, and strike with unprecedented precision. The drone was the ultimate expression of the precision dream: a weapon that could kill one person and leave the rest of the world untouched. It was also the ultimate expression of the precision nightmare: a weapon that made killing easy, that made it remote, that made it a matter of pushing a button and watching a screen.

The drone was used extensively in the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and in the broader campaign against terrorism that followed the attacks of September 11, 2001. It was used to kill leaders of al-Qaeda and the Taliban, to conduct surveillance, to support troops in contact. It was also used in countries that were not at war with the United States, including Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia. The drone was a weapon that could be used anywhere, at any time, and that fact meant the war on terror was a war without a battlefield. The war was everywhere, and the drone was the weapon that made it so.

The drone strikes in Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia were controversial. They killed people who were described as militants, and they also killed people who were not. The exact number of civilians killed was disputed, and the dispute was part of the problem. The United States claimed the strikes were precise and that civilian casualties were rare; critics claimed they were indiscriminate and that civilian casualties were significant. The truth was hard to establish, because the strikes were conducted in secret and the evidence was classified. The drone was a weapon that operated in the shadows, and the shadows made accountability difficult.

The drone was also a weapon that created new kinds of trauma. The people who lived under the drones—in the tribal areas of Pakistan, in the villages of Yemen, in the towns of Somalia—lived in constant fear. The drone was always overhead, or it might be overhead, and the sound of the drone was the sound of death. The people who lived under the drones described a condition sometimes called “living under drones”: anxiety, sleeplessness, the sense that the sky itself was hostile. The drone was a weapon that did not just kill; it terrorized. It made the everyday life of a community a kind of war.

The drone was also a weapon that changed the way the United States thought about itself. It was a weapon used by a democracy, in secret, in countries that were not at war with it, to kill people who had not been tried or convicted of any crime. It raised questions about the rule of law, about sovereignty, about the morality of assassination. The United States had built the drone, and it had to decide what it meant to use it. The decision was not easy, and the debate was not resolved. The United States used the drone because it was effective, and it was effective because it was precise, and it was precise because it was a machine. The machine was the problem and the machine was the solution.

The drone was not just a weapon; it was a system. It was a combination of technologies—the aircraft, the sensors, the communications links, the command and control, the munitions—and the system was what made it powerful. It was also a combination of institutions—the military, the intelligence agencies, the contractors, the lawyers—and the institutions were what made it possible. The drone required a vast infrastructure to operate, and the infrastructure was part of the weapon. The drone was not a single thing; it was a network, and the network was the weapon.

The network was also a vulnerability. The drone depended on communications links, and those links could be jammed or hacked. It depended on GPS, and GPS could be spoofed. It depended on intelligence, and intelligence could be wrong. The drone was only as good as the information it was given, and the information was often imperfect. The drone promised precision, and the promise was only as good as the data. The data was often wrong, and the wrong data meant that the wrong people died.

The drone was also changing the way the military thought about air power. It was cheaper than a fighter jet, could stay in the air longer, and did not risk a pilot’s life. It could be used in situations where a manned aircraft could not, and the military was beginning to see the drone as a complement to, and eventually a replacement for, the manned aircraft. The drone was the future of air power, and the future was already here.

The future of air power was also the future of the pilot. The drone was flown by a pilot, but the pilot was on the ground, and the pilot was not in danger. The pilot was a technician, sitting in a trailer in Nevada, flying a mission in Afghanistan, and then going home to dinner. The pilot was a new kind of warrior, and the warrior was a new kind of person. The drone pilot killed by remote control, and the remote control was a new kind of distance—physical, psychological, and moral. The pilot was close enough to see the target and far enough away to be safe, and the combination was a new kind of experience. The drone pilot could see the face of the person they were about to kill, and the seeing was a kind of intimacy, and the intimacy was a kind of horror.

The drone pilot was also subject to a new kind of stress. Pilots worked long shifts, watching a screen, waiting for something to happen. They were exposed to the violence of war without the camaraderie of the battlefield, without the adrenaline of combat, without the physical exertion that made the violence bearable. The drone pilot killed from a chair, and the killing was a kind of work, and the work was a kind of trauma. The drone pilot was a new kind of veteran, and the veteran was a new kind of casualty—a person who had been to war without going to war, and the war had followed them home.

The drone was changing the way the public thought about war. It was used in secret, and the secrecy was a kind of protection, and the protection was a kind of lie. The public was not asked to sacrifice, not asked to pay, not asked to notice. The drone made war easy for the public, and the ease was a kind of danger. It allowed a country to fight a war without the consent of its people, and consent was the foundation of democracy. The drone was undermining the relationship between the government and the governed, and the undermining was quiet, and the quiet was the problem.

The drone was also changing the way the world thought about the United States. It was used by the United States more than by any other country, and its use was a projection of power. The drone could reach anywhere, and the reach was a kind of empire. It was resented, and the resentment was a kind of blowback. The drone created enemies, and the enemies were the reason the drone was used. The drone was caught in a cycle, and the cycle was hard to break.

The drone was not the first weapon to create blowback. The history of weapons was full of examples of weapons that solved a problem and created a new one. The machine gun solved the problem of massed infantry attacks and created the problem of trench warfare. The bomber solved the problem of the stalemate and created the problem of civilian bombing. The nuclear bomb solved the problem of the invasion of Japan and created the problem of nuclear proliferation. The drone solved the problem of terrorism and created the problem of anti-Americanism. The pattern was old, and it was likely to continue.

The drone was also changing the way wars were fought by non-state actors. It was cheap, easy to use, and available to anyone who wanted one. It leveled the playing field, or at least tilted it, and the tilting was a kind of democratization of violence. It allowed a small group to attack a large state, and the attack was a kind of asymmetry. It was used by Hezbollah, by Hamas, by the Houthis, by ISIS, and the use was a kind of proliferation. The drone was spreading, and the spread was a kind of inevitability.

The spread of the drone was also the spread of a new kind of war. The drone was used in the gray zone, the space between war and peace, and the gray zone was a kind of permanent conflict. It was used in countries that were not at war, and the use was a kind of intervention. It was used to kill people who were not soldiers, and the killing was a kind of assassination. It was used to send a message, and the message was a kind of diplomacy. It was used in ways the old rules did not cover, and the old rules were not adequate to the new weapon.

The old rules were the laws of war, the Geneva Conventions, the customs of armed conflict. They were built around the distinction between combatants and civilians, between the battlefield and the home front, between war and peace. The drone blurred those distinctions. It could kill a combatant in a country that was not at war, and the killing was not covered by the laws of war. It could kill a civilian by mistake, and the mistake was hard to investigate. It could be used by a non-state actor, and the non-state actor was not bound by the laws of war. The drone was challenging a legal framework built over centuries, and the challenge was not being met.

The legal challenge was also a moral challenge. The drone made killing easy, and the ease was a kind of temptation. It allowed a person to kill without seeing the consequences, and the not seeing was a kind of moral blindness. It allowed a person to kill without risk, and the lack of risk was a kind of asymmetry. It allowed a person to kill without the possibility of being killed, and the asymmetry was a kind of injustice. The drone was changing the moral calculus of war, and the change was not being acknowledged.

The moral challenge was also a psychological challenge. The drone was changing the way people thought about killing. It made killing a matter of pressing a button, and the button was a kind of abstraction. It made killing a matter of watching a screen, and the screen was a kind of distance. It made killing a matter of following a procedure, and the procedure was a kind of routine. It made killing a matter of work, and the work was a kind of normalization. The drone was making killing ordinary, and the ordinariness was the danger.

The ordinariness of killing was not new. The history of weapons was a history of making killing easier, and the ease was the point. The spear made killing easier than the rock. The bow made killing easier than the spear. The gun made killing easier than the bow. The machine gun made killing easier than the gun. The bomb made killing easier than the machine gun. The drone made killing easier than the bomb. Each step made killing more efficient, more distant, more mechanical. Each step made killing more ordinary. The drone was the latest step, and it was a big one, and the bigness was the problem.

The problem was not that the drone was a weapon. The problem was that it was changing the relationship between the killer and the killed. It allowed the killer to be far away, and the distance was a kind of protection. It allowed the killer to be safe, and the safety was a kind of privilege. It allowed the killer to be anonymous, and the anonymity was a kind of impunity. It allowed the killer to be a machine, and the machine was a kind of excuse. The drone was changing the meaning of responsibility, and the change was not being discussed.

The discussion was happening, but on the margins—in academic journals, in human rights reports, in the corridors of the United Nations. It was not happening in the mainstream, and the mainstream was where the decisions were made. It was not happening because the drone was used by the powerful, and the powerful did not want to discuss it. It was not happening because the drone was effective, and the effective was the enemy of the good. It was not happening because the drone was popular, and the popular was the enemy of the critical. The discussion was not happening, and the not happening was a kind of failure.

The failure was not just a failure of discussion. It was a failure of imagination. The drone was changing the world, and the world was not imagining the change. It was creating a new kind of war, and the new kind of war was not being understood. It was creating a new kind of peace, and the new kind of peace was not being imagined. It was creating a new kind of world, and the new kind of world was not being seen. The failure of imagination was a kind of blindness, and the blindness was a kind of danger.

The danger was not just the danger of the drone. It was the danger of all weapons. The history of weapons was a history of danger, and the danger was the point. It was the reason weapons were built, and the reason they were feared. It was the reason they were controlled, and the reason they were not. It was the reason they were used, and the reason they were not. It was the reason they were studied, and the reason they were not. It was the reason weapons were the subject of this book, and the reason the book was necessary.

The book was necessary because the history of weapons was not just a history of technology. It was a history of politics, economics, culture, and psychology. It was a history of the human condition, and the human condition was a condition of conflict. It was a history of the ways humans had tried to solve the problem of conflict, and those ways had often made the problem worse. It was a history of the ways humans had tried to protect themselves, and the protection had often been a kind of trap. It was a history of the ways humans had tried to build a better world, and the building had often been a kind of destruction.

Destruction was the theme of the history of weapons, and it was not a happy one. It was a history of violence, and the violence was the point. It was the reason weapons were built, and the reason they were feared. It was the reason they were controlled, and the reason they were not. It was the reason they were used, and the reason they were not. It was the reason they were studied, and the reason they were not. It was the reason weapons were the subject of this book, and the reason the book was necessary.

The book was necessary because the history of weapons was a history of the ways humans had tried to control violence, and the control had often failed. It was a history of the ways humans had tried to limit violence, and the limits had often been exceeded. It was a history of the ways humans had tried to end violence, and the ends had often been violent. It was a history of the ways humans had tried to make violence acceptable, and the acceptability had often been a kind of horror. It was a history of the ways humans had tried to make violence meaningful, and the meaning had often been a kind of lie.

The lie was the lie of the just war, the clean war, the necessary war. The lie was that violence could be controlled, limited, ended. The lie was that weapons could solve the problem of conflict, and the problem was not the kind of problem weapons could solve. The problem was human nature, and human nature was not a problem that could be solved by a weapon. The problem was politics, and politics was not a problem that could be solved by a weapon. The problem was power, and power was not a problem that could be solved by a weapon. The problem was fear, and fear was not a problem that could be solved by a weapon. The problem was the human condition, and the human condition was not a problem that could be solved by a weapon.

The history of weapons was a history of the failure to solve the problem, and the failure was the lesson. The lesson was that weapons were not the answer, and the answer was something else. The answer was politics, the art of the possible. The answer was diplomacy, the art of the deal. The answer was law, the art of the rule. The answer was culture, the art of the shared. The answer was education, the art of the learned. The answer was empathy, the art of the understood. The answer was not a weapon, not a technology, not a machine. The answer was human, and the human was the problem and the solution.

The solution was not easy, not quick, not certain. It was a process, and the process was slow and painful. It was the process of building a world in which weapons were not necessary, and the building was the work of generations. It was the process of building a world in which conflicts were resolved without violence, and the building was the work of institutions. It was the process of building a world in which the strong did not prey on the weak, and the building was the work of justice. It was the process of building a world in which the fear of the other was replaced by trust, and the building was the work of the human heart. It was the process of building a world in which the history of weapons was a history of the past, and the building was the work of the future.

The future was uncertain, and the uncertainty was the condition. It was uncertain because weapons were changing, and the change was fast. It was uncertain because politics were changing, and the change was unpredictable. It was uncertain because the world was changing, and the change was global. It was uncertain because humans were changing, and the change was slow. It was uncertain because uncertainty was the nature of the future, and the nature was the condition. The future was uncertain, and the uncertainty was the reason for hope, the reason for fear, and the reason for the book.

The book was a history, and the history was a story. It was the story of the ways humans had tried to kill each other, and the ways had been ingenious and terrible. It was the story of the ways humans had tried to protect themselves, and the ways had been clever and futile. It was the story of the ways humans had tried to build a better world, and the ways had been ambitious and tragic. It was the story of the ways humans had tried to understand themselves, and the ways had been profound and incomplete. It was the story of the human condition, and the condition was a condition of conflict, and the conflict was the reason for the weapons, and the weapons were the reason for the story.

The story was not over. It was continuing, and the continuing was the point. It was continuing in Ukraine, in Gaza, in the Red Sea, in the mountains of the Hindu Kush, in the deserts of the Sahel, in the jungles of the Amazon, in the cities of the world. It was continuing in the laboratories, in the factories, in the war rooms, in the parliaments, in the streets. It was continuing in the minds of the people who built the weapons, the people who used them, the people who feared them, and the people who studied them. The story was continuing, and the continuing was the reason for the book, and the book was a way of understanding the continuing, and the understanding was a way of shaping it, and the shaping was a way of hoping.

The hope was not a naive hope. It was tempered by history, and history was a history of failure, and the failure was the reason for the temper. It was informed by knowledge, and knowledge was a knowledge of the worst, and the worst was the reason for the information. It was grounded in reality, and reality was a reality of conflict, and the conflict was the reason for the grounding. It was not a certainty, and the uncertainty was the reason for the hope. It was a choice, and the choice was the reason for the hope. It was a risk, and the risk was the reason for the hope. It was a gamble, and the gamble was the reason for the hope. It was a bet, and the bet was the reason for the hope. It was a wager, and the wager was the reason for the hope. The

paragraphs: The wager was not abstract. It was made, again and again, by people who had seen the worst and chose to act anyway, and the record of their wagers is the record of the arms race itself. Part 26 takes up the moment when the nuclear competition between the United States and the Soviet Union became a competition not only in warheads but in the machines that would carry them, and it argues that the delivery system, not the explosive, became the true currency of strategy. A bomb that cannot reach its target is a laboratory curiosity; a bomb that can arrive in thirty minutes from the other side of the planet reorganizes world politics. The shift from bomber to missile was therefore no technical footnote to the nuclear age. It was the event that made the nuclear age permanent, because it removed the human decision time that the bomber had, however briefly, preserved.

To understand why, begin with the aircraft. The Boeing B-29 Superfortress, which entered combat in 1944, was the most advanced heavy bomber of the Second World War: pressurized, with remote-controlled gun turrets, capable of carrying a substantial payload above twenty thousand feet over ranges exceeding three thousand miles. It carried the atomic bombs to Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, and in the years immediately after the war it carried the entire American nuclear deterrent. The logic of the early Cold War was the logic of the bomber: the United States held a monopoly on atomic weapons until 1949, and it possessed the only fleet capable of delivering them against the Soviet Union from bases in Europe, the Middle East, and the Pacific. The Strategic Air Command, under General Curtis LeMay from 1948, built its identity around the manned bomber, and that identity persisted long after the technology that justified it had been superseded. The bomber was a weapon, but it was also an institution, and institutions resist replacement.

The Soviet Union, which tested its first atomic device in August 1949, faced a delivery problem of a different kind. It had no fleet of intercontinental bombers comparable to the B-29, and its attempts to produce one—the Tupolev Tu-4, reverse-engineered from three B-29s that had made emergency landings in Soviet territory during the war—were a stopgap rather than a solution. The Tu-4 could reach targets in Western Europe, but it could not reach the United States and return. The Soviet answer, developed under Sergei Korolev and a team of German and Soviet engineers, was the ballistic missile, and the R-1, a copy of the German V-2, was the first step. The V-2 itself, fired against London and Antwerp in 1944 and 1945, was a weapon of terror rather than strategy: it carried a one-ton warhead about two hundred miles with an accuracy measured in miles, and it killed more people in production than in use. But it established the principle that a rocket could carry a payload over the horizon and beyond the reach of any defense, and that principle, once established, could be scaled.

The scaling was rapid. The Soviet R-5, deployed in the mid-1950s, had a range of about twelve hundred kilometers. The R-7 Semyorka, the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile, was tested in August 1957 and flew more than six thousand kilometers. It was cumbersome, requiring a massive launch complex and a fueling process measured in hours, and it was never deployed in large numbers. But it carried Sputnik into orbit in October 1957, and the political shock of that launch—the realization that the same rocket that placed a satellite in orbit could place a warhead on Washington—transformed the American strategic debate. The "missile gap," a central issue in the 1960 presidential election, was in fact a myth: the United States possessed a substantial advantage in bombers and was rapidly closing the missile gap that briefly existed. But the myth had consequences: a massive expansion of the American missile program—Minuteman, Atlas, Titan—and the doctrine of mutual assured destruction that came to define the strategic relationship between the superpowers.

The Minuteman I, deployed in 1962, was a solid-fueled missile that could be launched from a hardened silo in about a minute, a dramatic improvement over the liquid-fueled Atlas and Titan, which required lengthy fueling and could not be kept at readiness. Solid fuel was a genuine revolution in strategic affairs, because it made the missile a weapon that could be launched on warning rather than after prolonged preparation. The silo, hardened against blast and buried in the wheat fields of the American Midwest, made the missile survivable against all but a direct hit, and the dispersal of silos across thousands of miles made a disarming first strike against the entire force essentially impossible. The Soviet Union, which deployed its own silo-based missiles in the 1960s, followed the same logic. By the end of the decade, both sides possessed forces that could survive a first strike and retaliate, and the doctrine of mutual assured destruction—MAD, in the grim acronym that entered the language—became the de facto strategic policy of both superpowers, whether or not their leaders were willing to say so in public.

The submarine-launched ballistic missile added a third leg to the triad and a dimension the silo could not provide. The USS George Washington, commissioned in 1959, was the first ballistic missile submarine, carrying sixteen Polaris missiles with a range of about twelve hundred nautical miles. The Polaris A-3, deployed in 1964, extended the range to twenty-five hundred nautical miles, which meant a submarine could remain submerged in the Atlantic or Pacific and still strike targets deep inside the Soviet Union. The submarine was the most survivable leg of the triad, because a submerged submarine is extraordinarily difficult to detect and track, and the deterrent value of even a single submarine on patrol was enormous. The Soviet Union developed its own ballistic missile submarines—the Hotel, Yankee, and Delta classes—and the competition in submarine quieting, the technology that determines how easily a submarine can be detected, became one of the Cold War's most closely guarded secrets. The American advantage in quieting, which persisted through the 1970s and 1980s, was one of the most significant and least visible factors in the strategic balance.

The bomber, the silo, and the submarine together constituted the triad, designed to ensure that no single attack could disarm the United States or the Soviet Union. The logic was redundancy: if the bombers were destroyed on the ground, the silos would survive; if the silos were targeted, the submarines would survive; if the submarines were tracked, the bombers would survive. The triad was expensive, redundant, and, by the standards of any rational cost-benefit analysis, absurd. But the absurdity was the point. Its purpose was not to win a war but to make the prospect of war so terrible that no rational leader would initiate one, and the redundancy was the mechanism by which the terror was made credible.

The credibility problem was the central problem of nuclear strategy, and the theorists of the 1950s and 1960s struggled with it in ways that reveal the limits of rational analysis when applied to the unthinkable. Bernard Brodie, in The Absolute Weapon (1946), argued that the atomic bomb made the prevention of war, rather than the winning of it, the central task of military strategy. But prevention required credibility, and credibility required the willingness to carry out a threat that would destroy one's own society. The French strategist General Pierre Gallois argued that the deterrent value of nuclear weapons was independent of the number of warheads, because the destruction of a few cities was sufficient to deter any rational adversary. The American strategist Herman Kahn, in On Thermonuclear War (1960), argued that the United States should be prepared to fight and win a nuclear war, and his willingness to think the unthinkable made him a figure of controversy and a central influence on the strategic debate. Robert McNamara, Secretary of Defense under Kennedy and Johnson, brought a systems-analysis approach to the Pentagon and attempted to impose rational criteria on the nuclear force, with the doctrine of "mutual assured destruction" and the "counterforce" targeting of military rather than civilian targets. Counterforce was intended to make the deterrent more credible by limiting damage to civilian populations, but it had the paradoxical effect of making nuclear war seem more thinkable, and therefore more likely, and it was criticized by strategists who argued that any attempt to limit nuclear war was an illusion.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was the moment when theory met reality, and the reality was more frightening than the theory. The Soviet Union, under Nikita Khrushchev, had placed medium-range ballistic missiles in Cuba, and the United States, under John F. Kennedy, imposed a naval quarantine and demanded their removal. The crisis was resolved after thirteen days when Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove American Jupiter missiles from Turkey. It was a victory for Kennedy and a humiliation for Khrushchev, but it was also a lesson in the fragility of the strategic balance. The two leaders had come close to war, and the closeness was a function of misperception and miscommunication as much as of the objective balance of forces. The crisis led directly to the Moscow-Washington hotline of 1963, a teletype link designed to prevent the kind of miscommunication that had nearly led to catastrophe, and to the Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space, and underwater.

The test ban treaty was the first significant arms control agreement of the nuclear age, significant not because it reduced the number of weapons but because it established the principle that the two superpowers could negotiate limits on their competition. That principle was extended in the 1960s and 1970s through the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks, SALT I and SALT II, which produced the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty of 1972 and the Interim Agreement on offensive arms. The ABM Treaty was a landmark: it limited each side to two ABM sites—later reduced to one—and thereby preserved the principle of mutual vulnerability that was the foundation of deterrence. The logic was counterintuitive: by limiting defenses, the treaty made offense more stable, because neither side could hope to shield itself from retaliation. It was a recognition that the offense-defense relationship was a zero-sum game, and that the pursuit of defense would only provoke a more intense offense.

The SALT process continued through the 1970s, and SALT II, signed in 1979, placed limits on the number of strategic nuclear delivery vehicles and on the warheads each missile could carry. The treaty was never ratified by the Senate—withdrawn by President Carter after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan—but both sides observed its limits until the mid-1980s. The SALT process was accompanied by the ABM Treaty and by the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987, which eliminated an entire class of weapons—ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges between five hundred and fifty-five hundred kilometers—and was the first treaty to actually reduce the number of nuclear weapons rather than merely limit their growth. The INF Treaty was a product of the Reykjavik summit of 1986, where Reagan and Gorbachev came close to agreeing on the abolition of all nuclear weapons, and it was a sign that the arms race was not an inexorable force but a human institution that could be changed by human decisions.

The strategic competition was not confined to the two superpowers. Britain, France, and China developed their own nuclear forces, each with a doctrine reflecting its particular strategic circumstances. The British deterrent, based on Polaris and later Trident submarines, was assigned to NATO and justified by the argument that it provided a second center of decision that complicated Soviet planning. The French force de frappe, developed under de Gaulle, was explicitly independent of NATO and justified by the doctrine of "dissuasion du faible au fort," the deterrence of the strong by the weak, which held that a French nuclear strike against Soviet cities would suffice to deter an attack on France. The Chinese program, which tested its first device in 1964, was justified by the doctrine of no first use and by the argument that a minimal deterrent was sufficient to deter a nuclear attack. Each of these forces was small by superpower standards, but each was significant because it added a new center of decision and a new set of risks to the strategic equation.

The proliferation of nuclear weapons was a central concern of the post-war order, and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, was its principal instrument. The treaty recognized five nuclear-weapon states—the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France, and China—and committed the other signatories to refrain from acquiring nuclear weapons. It also committed the nuclear-weapon states to pursue negotiations on disarmament, a commitment honored more in rhetoric than in practice. The treaty has 191 states parties, but India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. It was a landmark of international law, but it was also a recognition that the nuclear club was a closed shop, and the tension between its non-proliferation and disarmament provisions was a source of persistent controversy.

The arms race was not only a competition in numbers but a competition in technology, and the technology of the 1970s and 1980s transformed the strategic balance in ways the theorists of the 1950s had not anticipated. The multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle, MIRV, allowed a single missile to carry several warheads, each aimed at a different target. It was first deployed by the United States on the Minuteman III in 1970 and by the Soviet Union on the SS-9 and SS-18 in the 1970s. MIRV multiplied the number of warheads without multiplying the number of missiles, and it made the arithmetic of the strategic balance enormously more complicated. Missile accuracy also improved, from a circular error probable of a mile or more in the 1950s to a few hundred feet by the 1980s, making it possible to target hardened silos with a reasonable prospect of destruction. The combination of MIRV and accuracy created a "window of vulnerability" in the American silo-based force, a source of intense political controversy in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

The response to the window of vulnerability was the MX missile, later named the Peacekeeper, a large MIRVed missile originally intended to be deployed in a mobile mode, shuttling between silos in a "shell game" that would make it impossible for the Soviets to target. The shell game was abandoned as impractical, and the Peacekeeper was eventually deployed in existing Minuteman silos, where it was as vulnerable as the missiles it replaced. The strategic competition of the 1980s was therefore one in which the offense was dominant and the defense was, at best, a marginal factor. The Strategic Defense Initiative, announced by President Reagan in March 1983, was an attempt to change that equation by developing a defense against ballistic missiles, and it was a source of intense controversy. The "Star Wars" program, as it was known, was criticized by scientists who argued that a leak-proof defense was technically impossible and by strategists who argued that even a partial defense would undermine deterrence by making a first strike seem more feasible. It was never deployed as envisioned, but it was a significant factor in the strategic debate, and it contributed to the Soviet Union's sense that it could not compete in the high-technology competition that the American economy could sustain.

The Soviet response to the American buildup was a massive expansion of its own forces, and by the early 1980s the Soviet Union had deployed more warheads and more missiles than the United States. The SS-18, a heavy MIRVed missile with ten warheads, was the most powerful weapon in the Soviet arsenal, and the Soviet Union deployed more than three hundred of them. The Soviet Union also deployed a mobile missile, the SS-20, in Europe, a deployment that created tension with NATO, which responded with the deployment of Pershing II and ground-launched cruise missiles in 1983. The Euromissile crisis was one of the most dangerous moments of the Cold War, resolved only by the INF Treaty of 1987, which eliminated the entire class of intermediate-range missiles.

The end of the Cold War was not the end of the arms race, but it was a transformation. The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 left the United States as the sole superpower, and the strategic competition of the Cold War was replaced by a different set of challenges: the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction to regional powers, the threat of nuclear terrorism, and the management of the vast nuclear arsenals that remained. The START treaties, signed in 1991 and 1993, reduced the number of strategic warheads, and the Moscow Treaty of 2002 and New START of 2010 continued the process. The number of nuclear warheads in the world, which peaked at more than seventy thousand in the mid-1980s, declined to fewer than fifteen thousand by the 2010s. The decline was a genuine achievement, but it was also a reminder that the weapons themselves remained, and that the knowledge of how to make them could not be unlearned.

The strategic competition of the Cold War was the context in which the modern technology of precision and autonomy was developed, and the connection between the nuclear competition and the conventional revolution is often overlooked. The Global Positioning System, which made precision navigation possible, was developed by the United States Department of Defense for military purposes, with the first satellites launched in 1978. The system was fully operational in 1995, and it was the foundation of the precision-guided munitions that transformed air warfare in the 1990s. Stealth technology, which made aircraft less visible to radar, was developed in the 1970s and 1980s as a response to the Soviet air defense system, and it was first deployed in the F-117 Nighthawk in 1983. The cruise missile, which combined precision guidance with long range and low observability, was developed in the 1970s and 1980s and first used in combat in the 1991 Gulf War.

The Gulf War of 1991 was the first war in which precision-guided munitions played a significant role, and the statistics are instructive. Coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs in Desert Storm, of which about 6,520 tons were precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent of the total. The percentage was small, but the effect was disproportionate, because the precision weapons were used against the most important targets: command bunkers, bridges, power plants, and air defense sites. Images of laser-guided bombs falling down the ventilation shafts of the Iraqi Ministry of Defense were broadcast around the world, creating an expectation that air power could achieve strategic effects with minimal collateral damage. The expectation was not entirely justified—the bombing of the Amiriyah shelter in Baghdad in February 1991 killed more than four hundred civilians, and the "highway of death" in the retreat from Kuwait was a scene of enormous destruction—but it was a political fact, and it shaped the way air power was used in the decades that followed.

The precision revolution was not only a matter of accuracy but of information. The weapons of the 1991 war were guided by laser designators and television cameras, and they required a human operator to designate the target or confirm the image. The weapons of the 1999 Kosovo war were guided by the Global Positioning System, and they could be launched from aircraft at high altitude and in bad weather, which reduced the risk to the attacking aircraft but also reduced the operator's ability to confirm the target. The bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade in May 1999, which killed three Chinese journalists, resulted from a targeting error that the GPS-guided weapons could not correct. The error was a reminder that precision is not the same as accuracy, and that the information on which the weapons depend is only as good as the intelligence that produces it.

The development of the unmanned aerial vehicle, the drone, was a further step in the same direction. The Predator drone, developed in the 1990s and armed with Hellfire missiles in 2001, allowed the United States to strike targets in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia without risking the lives of American pilots. The drone was a weapon of precision and persistence, and also of surveillance, because the same aircraft that carried the missile carried the cameras that identified the target. It was a significant technological achievement, but also a source of legal and ethical controversy, because the strikes were conducted in countries with which the United States was not at war, and because the intelligence on which the strikes depended was often unreliable. The drone was a weapon of the strong against the weak, and one difficult to counter with conventional means of air defense.

The drone became a weapon of the many as well as the few, and the diffusion of the technology was one of the most significant developments of the early twenty-first century. The Turkish Bayraktar TB2, a medium-altitude drone developed in the 2010s, was sold to more than a dozen countries and used to decisive effect in the Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020. That war, which lasted forty-four days, was a landmark in the history of drone warfare, because Azerbaijan used the TB2 and loitering munitions to destroy Armenian armor, artillery, and air defense systems. The Armenian air defense system, based on the Soviet-era Buk and Tor systems, was unable to detect and engage the small, slow, low-flying drones, and the destruction of the air defenses opened the way for the drones to attack ground forces with impunity. The RUSI study of the conflict, published in 2021, described it as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and suppression of air defense, and argued that it demonstrated the vulnerability of conventional forces to unmanned systems.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was a small conflict in a small region, but it was a preview of a larger transformation. The drone combined precision, persistence, and low cost, and it could be produced by countries that could not produce a modern fighter aircraft. The diffusion of the drone was a diffusion of air power, and the diffusion of air power was a diffusion of the ability to strike at a distance. The implications were profound: a country with a few dozen drones could threaten the armor and artillery of a country with a much larger and more expensive conventional military, and the threat was difficult to counter without a comprehensive air defense system that was itself expensive and vulnerable.

The loitering munition, which combined the drone with the missile, was a further development in the same direction. A loitering munition can cruise over a battlefield for an extended period, identify a target, and then attack it with a warhead. The Israeli Harop, developed in the 2000s, was one of the first, and it was followed by a range of systems from Turkey, Russia, and the United States. The loitering munition was a weapon of the small and the many, and it blurred the line between the drone and the missile, between surveillance and strike.

The question of autonomy was the most controversial aspect of the new weapons, and the war in Libya brought it into sharp relief. A United Nations Panel of Experts report, published in March 2021, stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces in Libya, and the report was widely cited as evidence that the era of autonomous warfare had begun. The claim was contested and not independently confirmed, and it should be treated with caution. The Kargu-2, a Turkish-built quadcopter loitering munition, is capable of autonomous operation in the sense that it can navigate to a target area and identify a target without human intervention, but the extent to which it was used in a fully autonomous mode in Libya is unclear. The report was a warning rather than a confirmation, and the warning was that the technology of autonomy was advancing more rapidly than the law and ethics supposed to govern it.

The ethical question was not new. The crossbow, the longbow, the musket, and the machine gun had all been criticized as inhuman or as undermining the warrior ethic, and each had been adopted anyway. But the autonomous weapon was different in kind, because it could select and attack a target without a human decision. The distinction between a weapon that is aimed by a human and a weapon that aims itself goes to the heart of the laws of war, which require that a combatant distinguish between combatants and civilians and that the use of force be proportionate. A human can make that distinction, however imperfectly; a machine can make it only if it has been programmed to do so, and the programming is only as good as the information and values built into it.

The debate over autonomous weapons was conducted in the United Nations Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, and it produced a group of governmental experts that met regularly from 2014 onward. The debate was inconclusive, because the major military powers were reluctant to accept a binding prohibition, and because the definition of autonomy was itself contested. It was a reminder that the law of war has always lagged behind the technology of war, and that the lag is not a bug but a feature: the law is made by states, and states are reluctant to limit their own military options.

The cyber domain was the other great new arena of the twenty-first century, and an arena in which the relationship between offense and defense was even more uncertain than in the nuclear domain. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, was a cyber weapon designed to sabotage the Iranian nuclear program by causing the centrifuges at the Natanz enrichment facility to spin out of control. It was a precision weapon in the sense that it targeted a specific industrial control system, and it was attributed to the United States and Israel, though neither government confirmed its role. Stuxnet was a landmark because it demonstrated that a cyber weapon could produce physical effects on an air-gapped target—one isolated from the internet—and because it demonstrated that the offense in cyberspace had a significant advantage over the defense. That advantage was a function of the complexity of modern computer systems, riddled with vulnerabilities that cannot all be patched, and of the difficulty of attributing an attack to its source, which makes deterrence difficult.

The cyber domain blurred the traditional distinctions between war and peace and between combatant and civilian. A cyber attack on a power grid could kill civilians, but it might be conducted by a non-state actor, or by a state actor operating through proxies, and the response might be a cyber attack, a diplomatic protest, or a military strike. The uncertainty was itself a source of instability, because the lack of clear rules of the road increased the risk of escalation. The Tallinn Manual, published in 2013 and updated in 2017, was an attempt by a group of international lawyers to apply the existing law of armed conflict to cyberspace, but it was a scholarly exercise rather than a binding legal instrument, and its influence on state behavior was limited.

The return of great-power competition in the 2010s and 2020s was the context in which these new technologies were deployed, and in which the nuclear balance remained the foundation of strategic stability. The United States, Russia, and China all modernized their nuclear forces, and New START, signed in 2010, was the last remaining arms control agreement between the United States and Russia. The treaty limited each side to 1,550 deployed strategic warheads and 700 deployed delivery vehicles, and it was extended in 2021 for a further five years. The extension was a modest achievement, but an achievement nonetheless, because it preserved a channel of communication and a framework of verification built over decades.

The hypersonic missile was the most prominent new development in the strategic competition, and one that threatened to undermine the stability the arms control agreements had preserved. A hypersonic missile travels at more than five times the speed of sound and can maneuver in flight, which makes it difficult to intercept and difficult to predict. The Russian Avangard, a hypersonic glide vehicle, was deployed in 2019, and the Chinese DF-17, a hypersonic glide vehicle mounted on a ballistic missile, was displayed in 2019. The United States was developing its own hypersonic weapons, and the competition was a source of concern because the flight time of a hypersonic missile is so short that the decision time for a response is measured in minutes. The concern was that the compression of decision time would increase the risk of accidental escalation, and that uncertainty about the capabilities of the new weapons would increase the risk of miscalculation.

The history of the nuclear age is therefore a history of a competition that was never fought, and the paradox of the competition is that its success was measured by the absence of war. The weapons built to be used were never used, and the strategy designed to deter was never tested. The absence of a third world war was a remarkable achievement, purchased at enormous cost, both in money and in the moral burden of maintaining weapons designed to kill millions. The cost was borne by the societies that built the weapons, and the burden by the leaders who held the power to use them.

The question the nuclear age posed, and continues to pose, is whether the deterrence that prevented war can be sustained indefinitely, and whether the technology that made deterrence possible can be managed without catastrophe. History cannot answer it, because the future is not determined by the past. But the history of the nuclear age offers lessons relevant to the present, and the most important is that the technology of war is not autonomous. It is made by people, used by people, and can be controlled by people. The control is never perfect, and the risk is never zero, but control is possible, and the history of the arms control agreements is the history of attempts to exercise it.

The second lesson is that the offense-defense balance is not a fixed law of nature but a product of technology and politics, and that it can be changed by human decisions. The ABM Treaty was an attempt to preserve the dominance of the offense, and the Strategic Defense Initiative an attempt to change it. The debate between the two was a debate about whether defense was possible and whether it was desirable, and it was never fully resolved. The lesson is that the balance is a choice, and that the choice has consequences.

The third lesson is that the proliferation of weapons is a diffusion of power, and that the diffusion of power is a source of both stability and instability. The proliferation of nuclear weapons to Britain, France, and China added new centers of decision and new risks, but it also added new constraints on the behavior of the superpowers. The proliferation of drones and precision weapons to smaller states and non-state actors has added new capabilities to the weak, but it has also added new threats to the strong. The lesson is that the diffusion of weapons is neither a simple good nor a simple evil, but a complex process that must be managed with care.

The fourth lesson is that the law and ethics of war lag behind the technology, and that the lag is a source of danger. The laws of war were developed in an era of conventional weapons and have been adapted, with difficulty, to the era of nuclear weapons, precision weapons, and drones. The adaptation is never complete, and the gap between technology and law is a gap in which atrocities can occur. The lesson is that the law must be updated, and that the updating requires the attention of lawyers, ethicists, and soldiers, as well as politicians.

The fifth lesson is that the history of war is a history of unintended consequences, and that weapons built for one purpose were often used for another. The V-2 was built to terrorize London and became the foundation of the space program. The atomic bomb was built to end the Second World War and became the foundation of the Cold War. The drone was built for surveillance and became a weapon of assassination. The lesson is that the future is not predictable, and that the weapons of the future will be used in ways their designers did not intend.

The history of the nuclear age is therefore a history of a gamble, and the gamble was the bet that the weapons would never be used. The bet was made by the leaders who built the weapons, and by the societies that accepted them. It was a rational bet, in the sense that the alternative—a world without nuclear weapons—seemed impossible, and a moral bet, in the sense that it accepted the risk of catastrophe in exchange for the avoidance of a different catastrophe. The bet was never resolved, because the weapons remain, and the risk remains, and the gamble continues.

The gamble was made in the context of a competition that was also a cooperation, and the cooperation was the cooperation of the arms control agreements. The agreements were a recognition that the competition was too dangerous to be left unregulated, and that the adversaries had a common interest in survival. That common interest was the foundation of the agreements, and the agreements were the foundation of the stability the world enjoyed in the second half of the twentieth century. The stability was not perfect, and it was not permanent, but it was real, and it was the product of human decisions.

The history of the development of weapons is therefore not a history of inevitable progress but a history of choices, made by people who were often frightened and often uncertain. The choices were not always wise, and the consequences were not always foreseen, but the choices were made, and the world that resulted is the world we inhabit—one in which the weapons of the past remain, the weapons of the future are being developed, and the choices that will determine the future are being made now.

The gamble was a gamble on the future, and the future is not a place that can be visited. It is a place that is made, by the decisions of the present, and the decisions of the present are informed by the history of the past. The history of the nuclear age is a history of decisions made in the shadow of catastrophe, and the shadow has not lifted. The shadow is the reason for the caution, and the caution is the reason for the hope. The hope is not a certainty, and the uncertainty is the reason for the hope. The hope is a choice, and the choice is the reason for the hope. The hope is a risk, and the risk is the reason for the hope. The hope is a gamble, and the gamble is the reason for the hope. The hope is a bet, and the bet is the reason for the hope. The hope is a wager, and the wager was the bet that the weapons would never be used.

The wager was not a single bet but a series of bets, made in the laboratories and the war rooms and the negotiating halls. The bets were made by the scientists who designed the weapons, the soldiers who deployed them, and the diplomats who tried to limit them. They were made by the societies that paid for the weapons and by the leaders who threatened to use them. They were made in the hope that the weapons would deter, and the hope was informed by the knowledge of the worst.

The knowledge of the worst was the knowledge of what the weapons could do, and that knowledge was the product of the tests and the calculations and the photographs of the aftermath. It was the knowledge of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and of the tests in the Pacific and in the atmosphere and underground. It was the knowledge of the casualties and the radiation and the firestorms, and it was the reason for the caution. The caution was the reason for the arms control, and the arms control was the reason for the stability, and the stability was the reason for the hope.

The hope was grounded in reality, and the reality was a reality of conflict, and the conflict was the reason for the grounding. The hope was not a certainty, and the uncertainty was the reason for the hope. The hope was a choice, and the choice was the reason for the hope. The hope was a risk, and the risk was the reason for the hope. The hope was a gamble, and the gamble was the reason for the hope. The hope was a bet, and the bet was the reason for the hope. The hope was a wager, and the wager was the reason for the hope. The wager was the wager that the weapons would never be used, and the wager was the foundation of the strategy that kept the peace. It was a wager made by the generation that built the bomb, and inherited by the generations that followed. It was a wager that was never won, and never lost, and never resolved. The wager was the condition of the world, and the condition of the world was the reason for the history, and the history was the reason for the book.

chapters.title: Part 27
chapters.preview: The wager had a geography, and the geography had a name. The name was the Fulda Gap: a corridor of low ground between the mountains of the Rhön and the forests of the Knüll, running northwest from the Czechoslo
paragraphs: The wager had a geography, and the geography had a name. The name was the Fulda Gap: a corridor of low ground between the mountains of the Rhön and the forests of the Knüll, running northwest from the Czechoslovak border toward the West German plain. Thirty to forty kilometers wide in places, it was the most heavily defended piece of ground on the planet. The reason was simple arithmetic. East of the gap lay the Group of Soviet Forces in Germany—half a million men and thousands of tanks, organized into armies that could reach the Rhine in a week if the ground permitted. West lay the American V Corps; behind V Corps lay the Rhine crossings; behind the crossings lay the ports; behind the ports lay the Atlantic; and behind the Atlantic lay the United States. The gap was where the arithmetic of the Cold War became a terrain problem, the terrain problem became a weapons problem, and the weapons problem became the thing soldiers on both sides trained to solve for forty years.

The weapons problem had a shape. The shape was the tank, and the tank had a number: the ratio of armored vehicles to kilometers of front. The ratio favored the attacker, and the attacker was the one who chose the time and place. NATO's answer was not to match the ratio tank for tank but to make it irrelevant—to make the attacker's tanks die faster than they could be replaced. The instrument was the antitank guided missile, a child of the same years that produced the recoilless rifle and the shaped charge, its family tree running back to the bazooka, the Panzerfaust, and the crumpled cones of copper that turned armor into a problem of chemistry rather than thickness.

The first generation of antitank missiles were manual. The gunner tracked the target through a telescopic sight and steered the missile with a joystick along a wire that unspooled behind it; the steering was an art. The French SS.10 and SS.11, the British Vigilant, the American SSM-A-23 Dart and its successor the MGM-32 Entac, the Soviet 3M6 Shmel—these required the gunner to keep his thumb on a stick and his eye on a flare at the missile's tail while it flew toward a tank that was shooting back. The wire was the guidance link and also the vulnerability: it could be cut by terrain or by the blast of the missile's own warhead, and the gunner was exposed for the entire flight—ten to twenty seconds, an eternity under fire. The second generation solved the exposure problem with semiautomatic command to line of sight. The gunner put his crosshairs on the target and kept them there; an infrared sensor at the launcher tracked a flare on the missile's tail; a computer computed the deviation between the line of sight and the missile's flight path and sent corrections down the wire. The gunner's job became pointing rather than steering, and pointing was something a conscript could learn in a week. The American BGM-71 TOW, the European MILAN and HOT, the Soviet 9M113 Konkurs and 9M114 Shturm—these armed the infantry of the 1970s and 1980s. Their shaped-charge warheads could penetrate the frontal armor of any tank then in service, and their ranges of three to four kilometers exceeded the effective range of the tank's own main gun in the hands of a moving gunner. The third generation removed the wire. The gunner put his crosshairs on the target and fired, and the missile guided itself—by imaging infrared, millimeter-wave radar, or laser designation from the launcher or a forward observer. The American FGM-148 Javelin, fielded in 1996, was the archetype: fire-and-forget, climbing above the battlefield, locking its seeker on the tank's thermal signature, and diving onto the thin armor of the turret roof, where no frontal glacis could save the crew. Its warhead was a tandem shaped charge—two cones in line, the first to detonate the explosive reactive armor the Soviets had developed to defeat single charges, the second to penetrate the armor beneath. The missile cost about eighty thousand dollars in its early production lots; the tank it killed cost four to five million. That exchange was the arithmetic that made the infantryman dangerous again.

The infantryman's danger was not only the missile. It was the rocket-propelled grenade, the bazooka's descendant and the most widely distributed antitank weapon in history. The Soviet RPG-7, introduced in 1961, was a recoilless launcher firing a fin-stabilized rocket with a shaped-charge warhead. It weighed seven kilograms loaded, cost a few hundred dollars, could be carried by a single soldier, could penetrate three hundred millimeters of armor, and was produced in the millions, copied in dozens of countries, and used in every war from Vietnam to Ukraine. The RPG-7 made the tank cautious in cities—the terrain where the tank's advantages of speed and standoff range disappeared. That disappearance drove armies to develop specialized urban warfare tactics and specialized armored vehicles with short-barreled guns, remote weapon stations, and slat armor to detonate the RPG's warhead before it reached the hull. The RPG also made the helicopter cautious, and the helicopter's caution made the Soviet experience in Afghanistan a case study in the vulnerability of rotary-wing aviation to ground fire. The case study drove the American response in the 1980s: the AH-64 Apache, with its mast-mounted sight that let the helicopter hide behind terrain and expose only the sensor, and its Hellfire missile, fired from behind cover and guided to the target by a laser pointed by the crew or a ground observer.

The helicopter was the other half of the antitank equation.
