The mitrailleuse was a weapon that required a doctrine, and the French did not have one. The lesson was that a new weapon without a doctrine is a weapon that will be misused, and the misuse will be blamed on the weapon rather than on the doctrine. The machine gun would have to wait for Hiram Maxim and for the colonial wars of the 1880s and 1890s to find its doctrine, and the doctrine would be found in the slaughter of colonial campaigns.

The colonial wars of the late nineteenth century were the wars in which the industrial powers tested their new weapons against enemies who did not have them, and the tests were not merely military. They were political and moral and psychological, and they shaped the way the industrial powers thought about war. The Battle of Omdurman in 1898 was the most famous of these tests. A British-Egyptian army under Kitchener, armed with Lee-Metford rifles and Maxim guns and supported by gunboats on the Nile, destroyed a Mahdist army of perhaps fifty thousand men in a few hours. The British lost fewer than fifty men killed. The disparity was not a matter of courage; the Mahdists were brave and charged with determination. The disparity was a matter of firepower, and the firepower was the product of the industrial revolution. The Maxim gun, which could fire six hundred rounds a minute, was the decisive weapon, and the men who saw it work understood that the age of the massed charge was over. The lesson was learned in the Sudan and in the other colonial wars, and it was learned by the wrong people. The British and French and Germans learned that their weapons could defeat any enemy who did not have them, and they concluded that their weapons would defeat any enemy. The conclusion was wrong, because the enemies they would face in 1914 would have the same weapons.

The Maxim gun was the weapon that made the colonial wars possible, and it was also the weapon that made the First World War inevitable in its shape. Hiram Maxim demonstrated his recoil-operated automatic machine gun in 1884, and the British Army adopted a .303-caliber version in 1891. The Maxim was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun, and it was a template for automatic warfare. It used the recoil of the cartridge to operate the mechanism, which meant it could fire continuously as long as the ammunition held out and the barrel did not overheat. The water-cooled barrel allowed it to fire for long periods, and the result was a weapon that could produce a volume of fire no infantry formation could survive. The Maxim was not a subtle weapon. It was a machine for killing, and it killed with an efficiency that had no precedent. The men who used it in colonial wars were impressed by its power, and the men who faced it in 1914 were destroyed by it.

The Maxim was not the only automatic weapon of the period. The Gatling gun, invented in 1861, was a hand-cranked multi-barrel weapon that could fire hundreds of rounds a minute, and it was used in the Civil War and the colonial wars. The Gatling was reliable and effective, but it required a man to turn the crank, and the crank was a point of failure. The Maxim was self-powered, and the self-powering was the innovation. The Maxim could be operated by a single man, and a single man with a Maxim could hold a position against a battalion. The doctrine of the machine gun was developed in the colonial wars, and the doctrine was simple: put the gun where the enemy must come, and let it fire. The doctrine would be applied on the Western Front, and it would produce the trenches.

The magazine rifle was the companion weapon of the machine gun, and it changed the infantryman's relationship to firepower. The bolt-action magazine rifle, adopted by every major army in the 1880s and 1890s, could fire five or more rounds without reloading and could be reloaded quickly with a clip. The German Mauser, the British Lee-Enfield, the French Lebel, and the Russian Mosin-Nagant were all products of this period, and all were effective weapons. The Lee-Enfield, with its ten-round magazine and fast bolt, was the best of them, and the British infantryman could produce a rate of fire that amazed the Germans in 1914. The magazine rifle was not revolutionary in the way the machine gun was, but it multiplied the firepower of the infantryman, and the multiplication was decisive. A battalion armed with magazine rifles could produce a volume of fire no battalion armed with single-shot rifles could match, and the result was that the infantry fight became a contest of firepower rather than a contest of maneuver.

Smokeless powder was the third element of the triad, and it made the other two possible. Black powder produced a cloud of smoke that obscured the battlefield and revealed the position of the shooter, and it limited the rate of fire because the smoke would choke the gunner and blind the aim. Smokeless powder, developed in France in the 1880s, burned cleanly and produced almost no smoke, and it allowed the machine gun and the magazine rifle to be used effectively. It also increased the range and velocity of the bullet, and it made the battlefield a place where the enemy could kill you from a distance you could not see. The combination of smokeless powder, magazine rifles, and machine guns made the open battlefield a killing ground, and the men who commanded armies in 1914 did not understand what had happened.

The artillery was the fourth element, and it dominated the First World War. The French 75mm field gun, adopted in 1897, was the most advanced artillery piece in the world. It used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady, which meant the gun did not have to be re-aimed after each shot. The result was a rate of fire of roughly fifteen rounds per minute, and the shells could be fused to burst in the air and shower the ground with shrapnel. The French 75 was a superb weapon, and it was the reason the French army believed that the offensive spirit could overcome any defense. The French doctrine of 1914, Plan XVII, was based on the assumption that the 75 would support a rapid advance, and the assumption was wrong. The 75 was a superb weapon, but it was a light field gun, and it could not destroy entrenched positions. The heavy artillery that could destroy trenches was in short supply, and the shortage would cost the French dearly.

The German artillery was heavier and more numerous, and the Germans had learned the lessons of the Russo-Japanese War and the Balkan Wars. The German army had a preponderance of heavy howitzers, and the howitzers could fire shells at a high angle and drop them into trenches. The German artillery was the decisive weapon of 1914, and it was the reason the German army advanced so far so fast. The German guns could smash the Belgian and French forts, and the forts were supposed to be impregnable. The fall of Liège and Namur in August 1914 demonstrated that modern artillery could reduce fortifications designed to withstand it, and the demonstration changed the calculus of defense. The fort was no longer a refuge; it was a target. The trench would replace the fort, and the trench would be the dominant form of fortification for the next four years.

The First World War was the war in which the industrial revolution caught up with the battlefield, and the catching up was catastrophic. The war began with the assumption that it would be short, an assumption based on the experience of the Franco-Prussian War and the belief that the offensive could win. The assumption was wrong, and the wrongness was revealed in the first months. The Battle of the Marne in September 1914 stopped the German advance, and the race to the sea that followed produced a line of trenches stretching from the Swiss border to the North Sea. The trenches were the product of the firepower the industrial revolution had produced, and the firepower made the trenches necessary. An army that tried to advance across open ground against machine guns and magazine rifles and rapid-fire artillery would be destroyed, and the armies learned this lesson in the first weeks. The trenches were not a choice; they were a necessity, and the necessity was produced by the weapons.

The trench was a weapon in itself, or at least a system that made weapons effective. A trench was a ditch in the ground, and a ditch in the ground was a shelter from artillery and small-arms fire. The trench was not a new invention; it had been used in sieges for centuries. But the trench as a continuous line of fortification, stretching for hundreds of miles and defended by machine guns and artillery, was new. The trench system was a machine for holding ground, and the machine was effective. An attacker who tried to cross no man's land would be exposed to machine gun fire and artillery, and the exposure would be fatal. The trench system made the defense dominant, and the dominance would last until the tank, stormtrooper tactics, and the creeping barrage broke it.

The machine gun was the weapon that made the trench system work. A single Maxim gun, well emplaced, could cover a hundred yards of front, and a few guns could cover a mile. The guns were placed to create interlocking fields of fire, and the fields of fire made no man's land a killing zone. The attacker who tried to cross the zone would be cut down before he reached the enemy trench, and the cutting down was mechanical and impersonal. The machine gun made the First World War a war of attrition, and the attrition was measured in hundreds of thousands of casualties. The Battle of the Somme, which began on 1 July 1916, cost the British army nearly sixty thousand casualties on the first day, and most were caused by machine guns and artillery. The first day of the Somme was the worst day in the history of the British army, and it was the product of a doctrine that had not caught up with the weapons.

The artillery was the weapon that made the trenches a hell. The shelling of the trenches was continuous, and the shelling killed men who were not in battle and destroyed the trenches they were living in. The artillery was the principal cause of casualties in the First World War, and it was the weapon the generals used to try to break the deadlock. The preliminary bombardment before an attack was supposed to destroy the enemy's defenses, and the bombardment was measured in days and in millions of shells. The bombardment at the Somme lasted a week and fired more than a million and a half shells. It did not destroy the German defenses, because the German defenses were deep and the shells were not heavy enough. The lesson was that the artillery had to be heavier and the bombardment more accurate, and the lesson was learned slowly and at great cost.

The Battle of Verdun was the purest expression of the artillery war. The battle ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916 and produced roughly seven hundred thousand casualties. The German plan was to bleed the French army white by attacking a position the French would have to defend, and the position was Verdun. The German artillery fired more than twenty million shells during the battle, and the French artillery fired a comparable number. The battlefield was a moonscape of craters and shattered trees, and the men who fought there lived in holes in the ground. The battle was not a contest of maneuver; it was a contest of logistics and production. The side that could produce more shells and move them to the front could keep firing, and the side that could not would be destroyed. The French army was supplied by a single road, the Voie Sacrée, and the road was kept open by a continuous stream of trucks. The trucks moved ammunition and food and men, and the movement was the difference between victory and defeat. Verdun was a battle of the industrial age, and the industrial age was the age of the factory and the railway and the truck.

The tank was the weapon that broke the deadlock, and it was invented by the British and the French in response to the trench. The tank was an armored vehicle that could cross no man's land and crush barbed wire and machine gun nests, and the first tanks were used at the Battle of Flers-Courcelette in September 1916. The tanks were slow and unreliable and broke down frequently, but they demonstrated that a vehicle could cross the killing zone and survive. The tank was the answer to the machine gun, and the answer was armor. The tank would be developed throughout the war, and by 1918 the British and French were using tanks in mass, and the German army was forced to develop anti-tank weapons. The tank was the first weapon that combined mobility and protection and firepower, and the combination would define the armored warfare of the twentieth century.

Stormtrooper tactics were the German answer to the deadlock, and they were a revolution in infantry doctrine. The German army developed a system of infiltration tactics in which small groups of specially trained soldiers would advance under cover of a short bombardment, bypass strong points, and penetrate deep into the enemy's defenses. The tactics were used at Riga in September 1917, at Caporetto in October 1917, and in the spring offensives of 1918, and they were effective. The stormtroopers were armed with light machine guns, flamethrowers, and hand grenades, and they were trained to act independently. The tactics required a high level of training and initiative, and the German army had both. The stormtrooper tactics were the precursor of the modern infantry squad, and they demonstrated that a small unit with the right weapons and the right training could break a defensive line.

The creeping barrage was the artillery answer to the deadlock, and it was a technique rather than a weapon. The creeping barrage was a wall of artillery fire that moved forward ahead of the attacking infantry, and the infantry followed close behind it. The barrage was designed to keep the enemy's head down and prevent him from manning his machine guns, and it required a high level of coordination between the artillery and the infantry. The creeping barrage was used at the Somme, at Arras, and at Passchendaele, and it was effective when properly executed. The technique was a product of the industrial age, because it required a huge number of shells and a sophisticated system of communication. The creeping barrage was the first time artillery and infantry were integrated into a single system, and the integration would become the basis of modern combined arms.

The First World War was also the war in which the aircraft became a weapon. The airplane was invented in 1903, and it was used in the First World War for reconnaissance and for artillery spotting. The reconnaissance aircraft was a weapon of information, and the information it provided was decisive. The side that could see the enemy's movements could plan its own, and the side that could not was blind. The airplane also became a weapon of attack, and the first aerial combat took place in 1914. The fighter aircraft was developed to shoot down reconnaissance aircraft, and the fighter became an icon of the war. The bomber was developed to attack ground targets, and the German Zeppelin raids on London and the Gotha raids of 1917 demonstrated that aircraft could attack cities. The aircraft was the weapon that would dominate the next war, and the First World War was its infancy.

The submarine was the weapon that changed the relationship between war and the civilian, and it did so in a way that was morally and politically explosive. The German U-boat campaign against merchant shipping was an attempt to starve Britain into submission, and it was effective. The U-boats sank millions of tons of shipping, and the sinking of the *Lusitania* in May 1915 killed more than a thousand people, including 128 Americans. The *Lusitania* sinking turned American public opinion against Germany and contributed to the American entry into the war in 1917. Unrestricted submarine warfare was a weapon that attacked civilians, and the attack on civilians was a moral threshold. The First World War was the first war in which civilians were deliberately targeted on a large scale, and the targeting was a product of the weapons. The submarine could not distinguish between a warship and a merchant ship, and the bomber could not distinguish between a factory and a house. The weapons made the distinction impossible, and the impossibility changed the ethics of war.

The First World War ended on 11 November 1918, and the peace that followed tried to prevent another war. The Treaty of Versailles imposed heavy reparations on Germany and limited its armed forces, and the limits were designed to prevent Germany from rearming. The treaty also created the League of Nations, which was supposed to provide a forum for the peaceful resolution of disputes. The treaty failed, and the failure was due in part to the weapons the war had produced. The weapons had made war so terrible that the victors wanted to prevent it, but the weapons had also made the victors afraid of each other, and the fear made cooperation difficult. The interwar period was a period of arms races and alliances and crises, and the crises led to the Second World War.

The Second World War was the war in which the weapons of the industrial age reached their culmination, and the culmination was the atomic bomb. The war began in 1939 with the German invasion of Poland, and it was fought with weapons developed in the interwar period. The tank, the aircraft, the submarine, and the aircraft carrier were all products of the interwar period, and all were used in the war. The German blitzkrieg was a combination of tanks, aircraft, and infantry, and it was a doctrine that integrated the weapons into a single system. The blitzkrieg was effective in Poland, France, and the Soviet Union, and it demonstrated that the tank and the aircraft could break a defensive line if used together.

The Battle of Britain was the first battle fought entirely in the air, and it was a battle of radar and fighters and bombers. The British developed a system of radar stations and fighter control that allowed them to intercept German bombers, and the system was a weapon of information. The radar could detect incoming aircraft, and the fighter control could direct the fighters to intercept them. The system was a product of the industrial age, and it was decisive. The German air force could not destroy the British air force, and the failure of the air offensive forced Hitler to postpone the invasion of Britain. The Battle of Britain was a battle of systems, and the better-integrated system won.

The aircraft carrier was the weapon that changed naval warfare, and the change was demonstrated at Pearl Harbor and at Midway. The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 was carried out by aircraft launched from carriers, and the attack destroyed the American battleship fleet. The battleship was the symbol of naval power, and the attack demonstrated that it was vulnerable to aircraft. The Battle of Midway in June 1942 was fought between carrier fleets, and the American carriers sank four Japanese carriers and changed the balance of power in the Pacific. The carrier made the battleship obsolete, and the obsolescence was a product of the aircraft. The aircraft could strike from beyond the range of the battleship's guns, and the strike was decisive.

The strategic bombing campaign was the weapon that attacked the enemy's industrial base, and it was a weapon that killed civilians. The British and American air forces bombed German and Japanese cities, and the bombing killed hundreds of thousands of civilians. The bombing was designed to destroy the enemy's capacity to produce weapons and to break the enemy's will to fight, and it was effective in destroying the capacity but not in breaking the will. The bombing of Dresden in February 1945 killed perhaps twenty-five thousand people, and the bombing of Tokyo in March 1945 killed perhaps a hundred thousand. The bombing was a weapon that attacked the civilian population, and the attack was a moral threshold. The bombing was justified by the argument that it would shorten the war and save lives, and the argument was contested then and is contested now. The bombing was a product of the weapons, and the weapons made the argument possible.

paragraphs: opened the argument that would define the next half century. When the B-29 *Enola Gay* released "Little Boy" over Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, the uranium gun-type device exploded with a force of roughly fifteen kilotons; three days later, "Fat Man," a plutonium implosion bomb, detonated over Nagasaki at an estimated twenty-one kilotons. Between them, the two attacks killed on the order of a hundred thousand people by the end of 1945 and many more in the years that followed from burns, radiation sickness, and cancers. The weapons were the culmination of a program—the Manhattan Engineer District—that had employed more than a hundred and twenty thousand people at its peak, cost roughly two billion contemporary dollars, and compressed into three years a body of physics, metallurgy, chemistry, and engineering that might otherwise have taken a generation. The bomb was not simply a bigger explosive. It changed the relationship between war and politics, because it made the destruction of an entire city achievable by a single aircraft on a single mission, and because it made the prospect of mutual destruction the organizing fact of international life.

The scientific foundations had been laid in the preceding decades. The discovery of nuclear fission by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann in 1938, and its interpretation by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, established that a heavy nucleus could split and release energy on the order of two hundred million electron volts per event—millions of times the energy released in a chemical reaction of the same mass. The realization that a chain reaction might be sustained in a suitable assembly of fissile material followed quickly. Enrico Fermi's team achieved the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in a squash court beneath the west stands of Stagg Field at the University of Chicago on 2 December 1942, using a lattice of graphite and uranium. The pile was crude and its power output trivial, but the achievement was the hinge on which the entire enterprise turned: it demonstrated that the release of nuclear energy could be controlled, and therefore that it could be weaponized.

The institutional history matters as much as the physics, because the bomb was the first great weapon produced by a state through the deliberate mobilization of science and industry rather than through the incremental improvisation of arsenals and inventors. The British, alarmed by the possibility of a German bomb, had commissioned the MAUD Committee, whose 1941 report concluded that a weapon was feasible. The report reached the United States, where Vannevar Bush's National Defense Research Committee and then the Office of Scientific Research and Development had already begun to organize American science for war. The Manhattan Project, formally established in August 1942 under the Army Corps of Engineers and directed from September 1942 by Brigadier General Leslie Groves, with J. Robert Oppenheimer as scientific director of the weapons laboratory at Los Alamos, was an unprecedented fusion of academic physicists, industrial contractors, and military administration. Its scale was reflected in its geography: the Clinton Engineer Works at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, where uranium was enriched by electromagnetic separation, gaseous diffusion, and liquid thermal diffusion in parallel because no one was certain which method would work; the Hanford Engineer Works in Washington, where plutonium was produced in the first large reactors; and Los Alamos, where the physics of the weapon itself was worked out.

The two bomb designs reflected two approaches to the central problem of assembling a supercritical mass quickly enough to prevent the assembly from blowing itself apart before the chain reaction could consume a significant fraction of the material. The gun-type design, used in Little Boy, fired a subcritical uranium projectile into a subcritical uranium target, combining them into a supercritical mass; it was conceptually simple and was never tested before use. The implosion design, used in Fat Man and tested at Trinity, surrounded a subcritical plutonium core with conventional explosives arranged to compress it symmetrically into a supercritical density; it was far more difficult to engineer and far more efficient. The Trinity test, conducted at Alamogordo, New Mexico, on 16 July 1945, detonated a plutonium implosion device nicknamed "Gadget" with a yield of about twenty-one kilotons. The test validated the implosion design and, in the words of the test director, Kenneth Bainbridge, turned the desert sand into a green glassy substance later called trinitite. Oppenheimer later recalled that a line from the Bhagavad Gita came to mind: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." The quotation has been repeated so often that it has become a cliché, but the sentiment it records was genuine and was shared by many of the scientists who watched the test.

The decision to use the bomb against Japan was made in a context that is often flattened in retrospect. The war in the Pacific had been fought with a ferocity that had already made civilian casualties routine: the firebombing of Tokyo in March 1945 had killed perhaps a hundred thousand people, and the bombing of other Japanese cities had killed many more. The invasion of Japan, planned for November 1945 and codenamed Olympic, with a follow-on operation called Coronet, was expected to produce casualties that planners estimated in the hundreds of thousands. The Japanese government had not surrendered, and its military leadership was prepared to fight a war of national annihilation. The bomb offered a way to end the war without an invasion, and President Truman made the decision to use it after consulting his advisers. The moral argument has never been settled, and the historical record does not support a simple verdict in either direction. What the record does show is that those who made the weapon understood it as one that would change the terms of war itself, and that the understanding was correct.

The immediate effect was the Japanese surrender, announced on 15 August 1945 and formalized on 2 September aboard the battleship *Missouri* in Tokyo Bay. The longer effect was the transformation of international politics. The Soviet Union, informed of the bomb's existence at the Potsdam Conference but not of its details, accelerated its own program; the first Soviet test, "First Lightning," detonated at Semipalatinsk on 29 August 1949, ended the American monopoly four years earlier than many Western estimates had predicted. The British tested their first device in 1952, the French in 1960, and the Chinese in 1964. The proliferation that followed was slower and more constrained than many had feared, but it was real, and it produced a world in which the possession of nuclear weapons became the defining marker of great-power status.

The strategic logic that emerged from the bomb was deterrence, and deterrence was a theory before it was a policy. Early American planners assumed that nuclear weapons would be used in a future war much as conventional bombs had been used in the last one—as a means of destroying the enemy's industrial capacity and will to fight. The doctrine of massive retaliation, articulated by Secretary of State John Foster Dulles in 1954, promised that the United States would respond to aggression with nuclear weapons "at places and with means of our own choosing." The doctrine was a product of the Eisenhower administration's determination to contain the costs of conventional defense, and it was credible only so long as the United States possessed a decisive advantage in nuclear forces. That advantage eroded as the Soviet Union built its own arsenal, and by the early 1960s the two superpowers had arrived at a condition that came to be called mutually assured destruction—MAD, an acronym whose grim aptness was not lost on the people who used it.

The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was the moment at which the logic of deterrence was tested most directly. The Soviet Union, under Nikita Khrushchev, had begun to deploy medium-range ballistic missiles in Cuba in response to the American deployment of Jupiter missiles in Turkey and to the failure of the Bay of Pigs invasion. President Kennedy imposed a naval "quarantine" on Cuba and demanded the removal of the missiles; the world waited for thirteen days while the two governments negotiated. The crisis ended when Khrushchev agreed to withdraw the missiles in exchange for an American pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey. The crisis was resolved, but it demonstrated that the deterrent relationship between the superpowers was unstable in ways that no theory had anticipated. It also produced a direct communications link between Washington and Moscow—the "hotline"—and a series of arms-control agreements that began with the Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space, and underwater.

The arms race that followed was quantitative and qualitative at once. The United States and the Soviet Union built arsenals that peaked at more than thirty thousand warheads each, deployed on bombers, land-based intercontinental ballistic missiles, and submarine-launched ballistic missiles—the "triad" designed to ensure that a first strike could not disarm the victim. Warhead technology improved dramatically: the fission weapons of the 1940s gave way to thermonuclear weapons, which used a fission explosion to ignite a fusion reaction in deuterium and tritium and could produce yields in the megaton range. The first American thermonuclear test, "Ivy Mike," detonated at Enewetak Atoll on 1 November 1952, produced a yield of about ten megatons. The Soviet Union tested its own thermonuclear device in 1953, and the British, French, and Chinese followed. Delivery systems improved as well: the bombers of the 1940s gave way to jet-powered bombers, and the bombers gave way, in part, to missiles that could reach their targets in thirty minutes rather than ten hours.

The missile age transformed the geography of deterrence. The first American ICBM, the Atlas, became operational in 1959; the Soviet R-7 had been tested in 1957 and was used to launch Sputnik. The submarine-launched ballistic missile, first deployed by the United States in 1960 aboard the *George Washington*, made the deterrent force survivable in a way that land-based missiles and bombers were not, because a submarine at sea could not be located and destroyed with confidence. The result was a strategic condition in which each side could destroy the other even after absorbing a first strike—the condition that made deterrence stable in theory and terrifying in practice.

The Cuban crisis also accelerated the development of command-and-control systems and of procedures designed to prevent accidental war. The hotline was the first of these; later agreements included the 1971 Agreement on Measures to Reduce the Risk of Outbreak of Nuclear War, the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, and the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks, which produced the SALT I interim agreement and the ABM Treaty in 1972. The ABM Treaty was particularly significant because it codified the logic of mutual vulnerability: by restricting defenses against ballistic missiles, it ensured that each side remained vulnerable to the other's arsenal, and it thereby made the deterrent relationship more stable. The treaty was a recognition that defense and deterrence were in tension, and that the pursuit of defense could undermine the stability that deterrence provided.

The proliferation of nuclear weapons beyond the original five powers was slower than many had predicted but more consequential than the optimists had hoped. India tested a "peaceful nuclear explosive" in 1974 and conducted a series of weapon tests in 1998; Pakistan followed with its own tests in 1998. Israel is widely believed to have possessed nuclear weapons since the late 1960s, though it has never acknowledged doing so. South Africa built a small arsenal in the 1970s and 1980s and dismantled it in the early 1990s, the only state to have done so. North Korea announced its withdrawal from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 2003 and conducted its first nuclear test in 2006. The NPT, which opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, became the most widely adhered-to arms-control agreement in history, with 191 states parties; India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The treaty's bargain was that the nuclear powers would pursue disarmament while the non-nuclear states would forgo the acquisition of weapons; the bargain has been imperfectly kept on both sides, and the result is a world with nine nuclear-armed states and a persistent anxiety about the tenth.

The nuclear revolution also transformed the relationship between war and the state in ways that went beyond the battlefield. The cost of nuclear weapons programs concentrated power in the executive branches of the states that pursued them, because the secrecy and speed the programs required were incompatible with legislative oversight. The weapons themselves became the ultimate expression of the industrial state's capacity for organized violence, and the states that possessed them acquired a status unavailable to states that did not. The bomb was, in this sense, the culmination of a long trend in the history of weapons: the trend toward weapons that were produced by states, controlled by states, and that defined the states that possessed them.

The nuclear age also produced a new kind of war: the proxy war, fought by client states and movements while the patrons stood back from direct confrontation. The logic was simple: because direct war between the nuclear powers risked escalation to annihilation, the powers competed through proxies in the spaces that the nuclear balance left open. Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola, and a dozen other conflicts were shaped by this logic. The proxy wars were not less destructive than the direct wars they replaced; they were often more destructive, because the patrons supplied their clients with the most advanced conventional weapons available and because the conflicts were fought without the restraints that the fear of escalation imposed on the patrons themselves. The Korean War, which began in June 1950 when North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel, was fought to a stalemate that ended with an armistice in July 1953; the American commander, General Douglas MacArthur, was relieved of his command in April 1951 after publicly advocating the bombing of Chinese territory and the use of Nationalist Chinese forces, a proposal that President Truman rejected because it risked a wider war. The Vietnam War, which lasted from the 1950s to 1975, was fought with a vast American arsenal of helicopters, bombers, and chemical defoliants, and it ended with the unification of Vietnam under a communist government. The Afghan War, which began with the Soviet invasion in December 1979, was fought by the mujahideen with American-supplied Stinger missiles, and it contributed to the collapse of the Soviet Union.

The conventional weapons of the Cold War were transformed as well, driven by the same industrial and scientific capacities that produced the bomb. The jet engine, developed independently by Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany in the 1930s, made possible aircraft that could fly faster than sound and carry heavier bomb loads. The German Me 262, the first operational jet fighter, entered combat in 1944; the American F-86 Sabre and the Soviet MiG-15 fought each other over Korea in the first jet-versus-jet air battles. The helicopter, developed in the 1930s and 1940s, became a weapon of war in Korea and Vietnam, where it gave commanders an unprecedented ability to move troops and firepower across difficult terrain. The tank, developed in the First World War, became the centerpiece of land warfare in the Second World War and the Cold War, and its design was shaped by the same competition between armor, gun, and mobility that had driven the naval arms races of the preceding century.

The infantry weapon was transformed as well, driven by the same logic of industrial production that had produced the rifled musket and the machine gun. The German StG 44, introduced in 1944, was the first mass-produced assault rifle, a weapon that fired an intermediate cartridge and could be used in both semi-automatic and fully automatic modes. The Soviet AK-47, designed by Mikhail Kalashnikov and adopted in 1949, became the most widely produced firearm in history, with estimates of total production ranging from seventy-five million to a hundred million. The American M16, adopted in the 1960s, was the product of a different design philosophy—lighter, faster-firing, and more accurate at range—and it became the standard infantry weapon of the American military for half a century. The assault rifle reflected the industrialization of war in its materials and its methods of manufacture, and it reflected the politics of the Cold War in its distribution: the AK-47 became the weapon of the Soviet bloc and of the insurgencies that the Soviet Union supported, and the M16 became the weapon of the American alliance.

The artillery of the Cold War was transformed by the same developments that had transformed the artillery of the First World War, driven by the same competition between firepower and mobility. The self-propelled howitzer, which mounted a gun on a tracked or wheeled chassis, became the standard field artillery of the major armies; the American M109 Paladin, introduced in the 1960s, and the Soviet 2S1 Gvozdika and 2S3 Akatsiya, introduced in the 1970s, were typical of the type. The rocket artillery of the Second World War was developed into the multiple rocket launcher, which could deliver a large volume of fire on a target in a short time; the Soviet BM-21 Grad, introduced in 1963, became one of the most widely used artillery weapons in the world. The development of radar and of electronic computers made it possible to compute firing solutions with a speed and accuracy unimaginable in the First World War, and the development of the proximity fuse, which detonated a shell when it came near its target, made anti-aircraft artillery far more effective than it had been.

The naval weapons of the Cold War were dominated by the aircraft carrier and the submarine, and both were transformed by the technology of the nuclear age. The carrier, which had replaced the battleship as the capital ship of the fleet in the Second World War, became the centerpiece of American power projection; the nuclear-powered carrier, first commissioned in 1961 as the *Enterprise*, could operate for years without refueling. The submarine, which had been a commerce raider in the two world wars, became a strategic weapon platform with the development of the ballistic missile submarine, and it became a hunter of other submarines with the development of the nuclear-powered attack submarine. The Soviet Union invested heavily in submarines, and the competition between American and Soviet submarine forces became one of the most intense and least visible arenas of the Cold War arms race.

The electronics revolution transformed weapons in ways as profound as the nuclear revolution, though less visible. The vacuum tube, developed in the early twentieth century, made possible radio communications, radar, and the first electronic computers; the transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, made possible the miniaturization of electronic systems; the integrated circuit, developed in the late 1950s, made possible the guidance systems of modern missiles. The result was a generation of weapons that could find their targets without a human operator aiming them: the air-to-air missile, the surface-to-air missile, the anti-ship missile, and the precision-guided bomb. The guided missile changed the relationship between the platform and the target, because it made the platform less important than the missile it carried, and it changed the relationship between the soldier and the weapon, because it made the soldier a supervisor of a machine rather than an aimer of a gun.

The Vietnam War was the first war in which precision-guided munitions were used on a significant scale, and the results were mixed. The American "smart bombs" of the late 1960s and early 1970s—the laser-guided bombs developed under the Paveway program—were used with considerable effect against bridges and other point targets, but they were expensive, dependent on favorable weather, and available only in small numbers. The war also demonstrated the limits of air power against a determined guerrilla enemy, and it produced a generation of American officers determined to use technology to overcome the disadvantages the war had exposed. The result was the "military-technical revolution" of the 1970s and 1980s, which sought to use information technology to make weapons more precise, communications more rapid, and command more centralized.

The 1973 Yom Kippur War was a turning point in the development of conventional weapons, because it demonstrated the lethality of the new guided weapons in a way that no exercise had. The Egyptian and Syrian forces, equipped with Soviet-supplied anti-tank guided missiles and surface-to-air missiles, inflicted heavy losses on the Israeli armored forces and air force in the first days of the war. The Israeli counterattacks, which had been expected to be rapid and decisive, were slowed by the density of the new weapons on the battlefield. The war was a shock to the military establishments of both superpowers, and it accelerated the development of the weapons that would dominate the battlefields of the 1980s and 1990s: the main battle tank with composite armor, the attack helicopter, the precision-guided munition, and the unmanned aerial vehicle.

The 1982 Falklands War was a smaller conflict with a disproportionate influence on naval thinking, because it demonstrated the vulnerability of surface ships to anti-ship missiles. The Argentine Air Force, equipped with French-made Exocet missiles, sank the British destroyer *Sheffield* and the container ship *Atlantic Conveyor*, and the British task force was forced to adapt its tactics to the threat. The war also demonstrated the importance of air-to-air refueling, satellite communications, and vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, and it was watched closely by navies around the world as a preview of the kind of conflict that might be fought in the missile age.

The 1980s saw the development of a generation of weapons designed to fight a war in Europe that never came. The American M1 Abrams tank, introduced in 1980, was equipped with composite armor, a turbine engine, and a sophisticated fire-control system; the Soviet T-80 and T-72 tanks were upgraded with reactive armor and improved guns. The American AH-64 Apache attack helicopter, introduced in 1986, was designed to destroy tanks with Hellfire missiles; the Soviet Mi-24 Hind was designed to carry troops and to provide fire support. The multiple launch rocket system, the tactical missile system, and the precision-guided artillery projectile were all developed in this period, and all were designed to deliver accurate fire on a battlefield expected to be dense with targets.

The end of the Cold War did not end the development of weapons; it changed the context in which weapons were developed. The Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 left the United States as the world's dominant military power, and the American military used the decade that followed to demonstrate the capabilities that the Cold War had produced. The Gulf War of 1991 was the first war in which precision-guided munitions were used on a large scale, and the results were dramatic. Coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs in Desert Storm; about 6,520 tons were precision-guided, roughly 7.4 percent of the total. The percentage was small, but the weapons struck high-value targets—command bunkers, bridges, air-defense sites, and armored vehicles—with an effectiveness that changed the expectations of air power. The images of laser-guided bombs falling down ventilation shafts and of cruise missiles turning corners in Baghdad were broadcast around the world, and they created a public impression of precision more complete than the reality. The war demonstrated what the new weapons could do, and also what they could not do: the Iraqi army was defeated in the field, but the Iraqi government survived, and the sanctions and no-fly zones that followed the war became a permanent feature of the region's politics.

The revolution in military affairs that the Gulf War seemed to announce was more gradual than the public impression suggested. The precision-guided munitions of 1991 were dependent on favorable weather, on laser designators that had to be aimed at the target, and on a communications and command system still largely based on voice radio. The improvements of the following decade—the global positioning system, satellite communications, digital data links, unmanned aerial vehicles—made the precision revolution more complete, and they made it possible to plan and execute a campaign with a speed and coordination that had not been possible before. The Kosovo War of 1999 was fought entirely from the air, with precision-guided munitions and cruise missiles, and it demonstrated that a campaign could be conducted without ground troops, though it also demonstrated the limits of air power against a dispersed and concealed enemy.

The wars that followed the attacks of 11 September 2001 were fought in a different context, and they shaped the development of weapons in ways that the planners of the 1990s had not anticipated. The invasion of Afghanistan in October 2001 and the invasion of Iraq in March 2003 were rapid and successful in their initial phases, and they were followed by insurgencies that lasted for years and that were fought with a different kind of weapon: the improvised explosive device, the rocket-propelled grenade, the sniper rifle, and the unmanned aerial vehicle. The American military responded with a new generation of armored vehicles designed to resist mines and ambushes—the Mine-Resistant Ambush-Protected vehicle, or MRAP—and with a new generation of surveillance and strike systems designed to find and kill individual insurgents. The armed drone, developed in the 1990s as a reconnaissance platform, became a strike weapon in the 2000s, and its use raised legal and ethical questions that are still being debated.

The drone was not a new idea in the 2000s; it was the culmination of a long line of development that went back to the First World War, when both the British and the Americans experimented with unmanned aircraft. The German V-1 flying bomb of 1944 was a cruise missile in all but name, and the American Firebee drones of the Vietnam War were used for reconnaissance. The Predator drone, developed by General Atomics and first flown in 1994, was a reconnaissance platform that could loiter over a target for hours and transmit video to operators on the ground. The addition of Hellfire missiles in 2001 turned the Predator into a strike weapon, and the combination of persistent surveillance and precision strike became the defining capability of the American way of war in the 2000s. The drone changed the relationship between the operator and the target, because the operator could be thousands of miles away and could watch the target for hours before deciding to strike, and it changed the relationship between the state and the battlefield, because the state could conduct hostilities in countries with which it was not formally at war.

The drone also changed the economics of air power. A Predator cost a fraction of the price of a manned fighter, and it could be flown for a fraction of the cost per hour. The result was that air power became available to states and to non-state actors that could never have afforded a manned air force. The Turkish Bayraktar TB2, a drone developed in the 2010s, was sold to more than a dozen countries and was used with devastating effect in Libya, in Nagorno-Karabakh, and in Ukraine. The drone democratized air power in the way that the assault rifle had democratized firepower, and the consequences of that democratization are still unfolding.

The 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war was the conflict in which the drone's potential was most clearly demonstrated. The war lasted forty-four days, from 27 September to 10 November 2020, and it was fought between Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed region of Nagorno-Karabakh. Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and Israeli-made loitering munitions—the Harop and the SkyStriker—against Armenian armor, artillery, and air-defense systems. The drones located and destroyed Armenian tanks and air-defense systems with a precision that the Armenian forces could not counter, and the video of the strikes was broadcast around the world. The Royal United Services Institute's 2021 study of the conflict treated it as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense, and it noted that the drones had been effective because the Armenian air defenses were not designed to detect and engage small, slow, low-flying targets. The war ended with a Russian-brokered ceasefire that ceded significant territory to Azerbaijan, and it demonstrated that a middle power with a modest budget could use drones to defeat a conventional opponent.

The use of drones in Nagorno-Karabakh also demonstrated the limits of the drone. The drones were effective against an opponent that lacked the means to detect and engage them, and in a conflict fought in open terrain with clear weather. They were less effective against an opponent with sophisticated air defenses, as the war in Ukraine would later demonstrate. The drone was not a wonder weapon that made all other weapons obsolete; it was a weapon that changed the terms of the competition, and the competition continued.

The war in Ukraine, which began with the Russian invasion of February 2022, became the largest land war in Europe since the Second World War, and it became a laboratory for the weapons of the twenty-first century. The war demonstrated the continued importance of artillery, which inflicted the majority of casualties on both sides, and the importance of precision-guided artillery—the American HIMARS rocket system, the French Caesar self-propelled howitzer, and the German PzH 2000—which allowed the Ukrainian forces to strike Russian command posts and ammunition depots with a precision the Russians could not match. The war also demonstrated the importance of drones, used by both sides for reconnaissance and for strike, and the importance of electronic warfare, used to jam the drones and the communications systems on which they depended. The war was a reminder that the weapons of the twenty-first century are not a single technology but a system of technologies, and that the side that integrates them most effectively has an advantage not reducible to any single weapon.

The war in Ukraine also demonstrated the continued importance of the tank, which some analysts had declared obsolete after the Gulf War and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. The tank was vulnerable to drones, to anti-tank guided missiles, and to artillery, and the Russians lost hundreds of tanks in the first months of the war. But the tank was also indispensable for the combined-arms operations the Ukrainians used to retake territory, and the Ukrainians and the Russians both continued to use tanks throughout the war. The tank was not obsolete; it was one weapon among many, and its effectiveness depended on how it was used and on what it was used with.

The war in Ukraine was also a demonstration of the importance of air defense, which many Western militaries had neglected after the end of the Cold War. The Russians used cruise missiles and ballistic missiles to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, and the Ukrainians used a combination of Soviet-era air-defense systems and Western-supplied systems—the American Patriot, the German IRIS-T, the Norwegian NASAMS—to defend against them. The air-defense systems were effective, but they were expensive, and the Ukrainians were forced to choose which targets to defend and which to leave exposed. The war was a reminder that air defense is a weapon in its own right, and that the competition between offense and defense is as old as war itself.

The war in Ukraine also accelerated the development of autonomous weapons, which had been a subject of debate for decades. The Ukrainian forces used drones that could be programmed to fly to a target and detonate, and drones that could be operated by a single soldier with a tablet. The Russian forces used the Lancet loitering munition, which could loiter over a battlefield and strike a target when it was found. The autonomous weapon was not a science-fiction fantasy; it was a weapon being used in a war, and the debate about its legality and its ethics was no longer academic.

The question of autonomous weapons had been raised by a 2021 report from the United Nations Panel of Experts on Libya, which stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The claim was contested and was not independently confirmed, and it should be treated with caution. The report was significant not because it proved that autonomous weapons had been used, but because it showed that the technology was available and that the legal and ethical frameworks for its use had not been developed. The debate about autonomous weapons is a debate about the relationship between the soldier and the weapon, and it is a debate that the history of weapons has prepared us for: every generation of weapons has raised the question of whether the new weapon is compatible with the moral restraints that the previous generation had developed, and every generation has answered the question in its own way.

The nuclear weapons that ended the Second World War did not end the development of conventional weapons; they changed the context in which conventional weapons were developed. The nuclear balance made direct war between the great powers too dangerous to contemplate, and it pushed the competition into proxy wars, into the development of conventional weapons that could be used in those wars, and into the development of the command-and-control systems designed to prevent the nuclear balance from breaking down. The result was a world in which the most powerful weapons were never used, and in which the weapons that were used were developed with an intensity that the nuclear balance did not diminish. The history of weapons in the nuclear age is the history of a competition conducted in the shadow of the bomb, and the shadow shaped the competition in ways that are still being worked out.

The nuclear age also produced a new kind of arms control, designed to manage the competition rather than to end it. The Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963 was followed by the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968, the Seabed Treaty of 1971, the Biological Weapons Convention of 1972, the ABM Treaty of 1972, the SALT agreements of 1972 and 1979, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987, and the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaties of 1991 and 1993. The treaties were imperfect, and some were abandoned—the United States withdrew from the ABM Treaty in 2002 and from the INF Treaty in 2019—but they were a recognition that the weapons of the nuclear age required a new kind of politics, and they were a partial answer to the question that the bomb had raised.

The history of weapons is not a history of progress in the sense of improvement in the human condition; it is a history of the accumulation of capabilities, and the accumulation has been driven by the same forces that have driven the history of war. The weapons of the twenty-first century are the product of a long development shaped by the interaction of technology, politics, and culture. The bomb was the weapon that made the interaction most visible, because it changed the relationship between war and politics in a way that no previous weapon had. The drone and the precision-guided munition are the weapons that have made the interaction most recent, because they have changed the relationship between the soldier and the battlefield in a way that the bomb did not.

The history of the bomb is also a history of the scientists who made it and of the moral questions they raised. The Franck Report, written in June 1945 by a committee of scientists at the University of Chicago and signed by James Franck, Donald Hughes, J. J. Nickson, Eugene Rabinowitch, Glenn Seaborg, J. C. Stearns, and Leo Szilard, argued that the bomb should be demonstrated before it was used against a populated city, and that the demonstration should be conducted in a way that would persuade the Japanese government to surrender. The report was not accepted, and the bomb was used without a demonstration. The scientists who made the bomb were not unanimous in their views, and the debate among them was a preview of the debate that would follow. Oppenheimer, who had directed the laboratory at Los Alamos, later opposed the development of the hydrogen bomb, and his opposition cost him his security clearance in 1954. The scientists who made the bomb were the first of a new kind of weapon maker: the scientist who works for the state and who is asked to accept the state's judgment about how the weapon will be used. The history of weapons in the nuclear age is in part the history of that new kind of weapon maker, and the history is not yet complete.

The bomb also changed the relationship between the state and the citizen, because it made the citizen a potential target in a way that no previous weapon had. The bombing of cities in the Second World War had already made civilians the targets of war, but the bomb made the destruction of a city a single event, and it made the destruction of a society a possibility. The civil-defense programs of the 1950s—the fallout shelters, the air-raid drills, the "duck and cover" films—were an attempt to prepare the citizen for a war that could not be survived, and they were a recognition that the bomb had changed the meaning of defense. The bomb was a weapon that could not be defended against, and the recognition of that fact was the beginning of the strategic thought that produced deterrence.

The history of weapons in the nuclear age is also a history of the proliferation of weapons to states that were not party to the original competition. The Soviet Union's acquisition of the bomb in 1949 was followed by the British in 1952, the French in 1960, and the Chinese in 1964. The Indian test of 1974 was followed by the Pakistani test of 1998, and the North Korean test of 2006 was followed by a series of tests that continued into the 2010s. The proliferation was slower than many had feared, and more constrained than the pessimists had predicted, but it was real, and it produced a world in which the possession of nuclear weapons was the defining marker of great-power status. The NPT was the attempt to manage the proliferation, and it succeeded in slowing it, but not in stopping it.

The history of weapons is also a history of the attempts to control them. The laws of war, developed in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, were extended in the twentieth century to cover the new weapons. The Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols of 1977 established the principle that the right of the parties to a conflict to choose methods and means of warfare is not unlimited, and that the weapons used must be discriminate and proportionate. The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 prohibited the development, production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons, and it established a verification regime that was unprecedented
