paragraphs: The Chemical Weapons Convention entered into force on 29 April 1997, and its verification machinery—the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, based at The Hague—became the most intrusive international inspection regime ever built for a class of weapons. Its inspectors could arrive at declared facilities on short notice, sample and analyze materials, seal equipment, and monitor destruction. By the early 2020s the OPCW had verified the destruction of more than 70,000 metric tons of declared chemical warfare agents—roughly 98 percent of the world's declared stockpile—across dozens of states parties. The convention rested on a bargain: states that gave up their chemical weapons would receive assurance that their rivals were doing the same, and that assurance would be produced by inspectors rather than by promises.

That bargain held better than most arms-control arrangements of the twentieth century, but it held unevenly. The convention banned the weapons; it did not eliminate the underlying chemistry, the industrial infrastructure that could produce precursor chemicals, or the knowledge of how to weaponize them. The gap between "no stockpiles" and "no capability" is the central problem of all modern arms control, and the chemical case illustrates it with unusual clarity. When the OPCW reported in the 2010s that it had verified the destruction of the last declared Syrian chemical weapons precursor facilities, it simultaneously documented that chemical attacks were still occurring inside Syria—chlorine-filled barrel bombs dropped from helicopters, sarin released in the towns of the Damascus suburbs in August 2013. The weapons had been declared destroyed, but the war continued to produce new ones from industrial chemicals that were never on any weapons list. Chlorine is a common industrial disinfectant; the convention's schedules were designed to capture chemicals whose only plausible large-scale use was warfare, and chlorine fell through the gaps until its use in war forced the OPCW's member states to amend the schedules in 2019, adding certain dual-use chemicals and expanding the organization's mandate to attribute attacks.

The pattern recurs across the history of arms control: the instrument is written to control the weapons of the war that prompted it, and the next war finds the seams. The Geneva Protocol of 1925, which prohibited the use in war of asphyxiating and poisonous gases, was drafted after the gas warfare of the Western Front, and it said nothing about the herbicides and riot-control agents the United States would use in Vietnam in the 1960s, and nothing about the nerve agents discovered in the 1930s. The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 banned an entire class of weapons before any state had used them in war on a large scale, but it was built without a verification regime, because the Soviet Union refused to accept the inspections the chemical convention would later make routine. The result was a treaty with no inspectors, no sampling rights, and no formal mechanism for establishing whether a state party was cheating—a gap that became acute during the 1990s, when the defection of Soviet biological-weapons scientists and the testimony of defectors from the former Soviet program revealed a massive covert enterprise the convention had never been designed to detect.

The modern history of weapons is therefore not a story of technology advancing while law trails behind. It is a story of technology and law advancing together, each shaping the other, each sometimes outrunning the other, with the outcome depending on the willingness of states to build institutions with real authority. The Chemical Weapons Convention worked as well as it did because the great powers of the 1990s—the United States and Russia in particular, which held the overwhelming majority of the world's declared stockpile—decided that a verified regime was in their interest, because they feared the proliferation of chemical weapons to Iraq, Iran, Libya, and other states more than they feared the inspections themselves. The convention's authority was borrowed from the interests of the strong, and it is worth remembering that the same interests had, only a decade earlier, been perfectly willing to tolerate chemical weapons when they were held by allies or by states that were not yet a problem.

The history of arms control is inseparable from the history of the weapons themselves, because every treaty is written against the background of what the weapons can do and what the states that hold them can be persuaded to give up. The nuclear case is the most consequential, and it most clearly shows the pattern: a technology that appeared to make war unwinnable, followed by an attempt to manage it, followed by partial success, followed by proliferation, followed by a second attempt. The Manhattan Project produced the first nuclear weapons in 1945, and within four years the Soviet Union had tested its own. The United States had entered the nuclear age with a monopoly and a set of ideas—international control of atomic energy, a United Nations commission, a plan proposed by Bernard Baruch in 1946—that presumed the monopoly would last long enough to be converted into a system of control. The Soviet Union's first test in August 1949 ended that presumption. The Baruch Plan, which had called for the international ownership and management of all atomic energy activities, was never ratified; the Soviet Union proposed instead that the United States destroy its stockpile first, and neither side was willing to move first.

The result was the arms race, and the arms race produced the weapons that shaped the second half of the twentieth century. The United States tested the first hydrogen device in 1952; the Soviet Union followed in 1953. Yields climbed from the twenty-one kilotons of the Trinity device to the megaton range, and by the early 1960s both sides were deploying intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles, and bombers in numbers that made the phrase "overkill" a commonplace. The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was the moment when the logic of the arms race became visible to everyone: the two superpowers had come within a decision of a general war that would have killed tens of millions, and the crisis ended not with a treaty but with a withdrawal and a secret understanding. The following year, the Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space, and underwater, and it was signed by the United States, the Soviet Union, and the United Kingdom—the first of the great nuclear arms-control agreements, and one driven as much by public health concern over radioactive fallout as by strategic calculation.

The history of the nuclear age is usually told through its treaties—the Partial Test Ban, the Non-Proliferation Treaty, SALT I and II, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, START—and through its crises. But the treaties are the visible surface of a deeper change in the relationship between war and the state. The nuclear weapon did what no previous weapon had done: it made the total war that had been the organizing principle of military planning since Napoleon into a project that could not be carried out without destroying the state that carried it out. The strategists of the 1950s and 1960s built a vocabulary for this—deterrence, assured destruction, counterforce and countervalue, escalation ladders—and the vocabulary was an attempt to think about war in conditions where the traditional measures of victory and defeat had lost their meaning. Bernard Brodie wrote in 1946 that "thus far the chief purpose of our military establishment has been to win wars. From now on its chief purpose must be to avert them." The sentence became the founding statement of nuclear strategy, and it was true in a way that went beyond the nuclear weapon: the industrialization of war had been making the same point since 1914, and the nuclear weapon made it unavoidable.

The Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970, was the attempt to prevent the spread of the weapon that had produced this change. It rests on three pillars: non-proliferation, disarmament, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy. The nuclear-weapon states—the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, France, and China—undertook to pursue negotiations on disarmament; the non-nuclear states undertook not to acquire nuclear weapons and to accept safeguards administered by the International Atomic Energy Agency; and all states parties were guaranteed access to nuclear technology for peaceful purposes. The treaty has 191 states parties, making it the most widely adhered-to arms-control agreement in history. India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined; North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003 and subsequently tested nuclear devices. The treaty's success is real but partial: it slowed proliferation and created a norm against acquisition that has made going nuclear costly, but it did not stop the five recognized nuclear-weapon states from maintaining and modernizing their arsenals, and it did not prevent the emergence of de facto nuclear states.

The NPT's weakness was built into its structure. The treaty drew a distinction between the states that had tested a nuclear device before 1 January 1967 and those that had not, and it froze that distinction in place. The nuclear-weapon states were permitted to keep their arsenals; the others were forbidden to acquire them. From the perspective of the non-nuclear states, this looked less like a bargain than a hierarchy, and the review conferences of the 1990s and 2000s became forums in which the non-nuclear states pressed for concrete progress on disarmament—the "13 steps" agreed at the 2000 review conference, the action plan of 2010—while the nuclear-weapon states responded with commitments that were real but limited. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, adopted in 2017 and entering into force in 2021, was the response of the non-nuclear states to the perceived failure of the NPT's disarmament pillar: a ban treaty negotiated without the participation of the nuclear-weapon states, which have argued that it is unrealistic and counterproductive. The ban treaty has the moral clarity of the chemical and biological conventions, and the same weakness—it binds only those who join, and the states that hold the weapons have not joined.

The history of the nuclear age is also a history of near-misses, and the near-misses are the best evidence of how the institutions of control actually function. The Cuban Missile Crisis was the first and most famous. The 1973 Yom Kippur War produced a nuclear alert in the United States and, according to some accounts, a Soviet threat that was read in Washington as a possible prelude to nuclear use. The 1983 NATO exercise Able Archer, combined with the Soviet Union's genuine fear of a first strike and its flawed early-warning system, brought the world closer to nuclear war than the public understood at the time; the Soviet officer Stanislav Petrov's decision on 26 September 1983 not to report a satellite warning of incoming missiles, on the grounds that the warning was probably a malfunction, is often cited as the moment when a single individual's judgment prevented a catastrophe. The 1995 Norwegian rocket launch, a scientific sounding rocket briefly mistaken by Russian radar operators for a submarine-launched missile, produced an alert that reached the Russian president's nuclear briefcase before it was stood down. Each of these episodes is a story about technology and institutions: the technology of warning and command, the institutions of decision-making, and the human beings who stand between them.

The end of the Cold War produced the largest reductions in nuclear arsenals in history, and it also produced the most serious proliferation crises. The United States and Russia signed START I in 1991 and START II in 1993; the Lisbon Protocol brought Belarus, Kazakhstan, and Ukraine into the NPT as non-nuclear states, and the three countries transferred the Soviet weapons on their territory to Russia in exchange for security assurances—the Budapest Memorandum of 1994, in which Russia, the United States, and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to Ukraine's territorial integrity and independence. The Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction program, initiated in 1991, funded the dismantlement of Soviet weapons and the securing of nuclear materials across the former Soviet Union. The reductions were real: by the early 2000s the United States and Russia each held roughly a quarter of the warheads they had held at the height of the Cold War, and the New START treaty of 2010 capped deployed strategic warheads at 1,550 for each side.

But the post-Cold War period also produced the proliferation the NPT had been designed to prevent. Iraq's nuclear program was discovered after the 1991 Gulf War to have been far more advanced than the IAEA had known; the inspections that followed, and the cat-and-mouse game between the UN Special Commission and the Iraqi government, became the template for a decade of confrontation that ended in the 2003 invasion. Libya gave up its weapons of mass destruction program in 2003, in a negotiation held up as a model until the 2011 intervention that overthrew Muammar Gaddafi convinced other proliferators that giving up weapons was a way to invite attack. North Korea withdrew from the NPT in 2003 and tested its first nuclear device in 2006, and the six-party talks that were supposed to prevent it collapsed. Iran's nuclear program produced a decade of negotiations, sanctions, and the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action of 2015, which restricted Iran's enrichment program in exchange for relief from sanctions—an agreement the United States withdrew from in 2018, and which Iran subsequently began to violate. India and Pakistan tested nuclear devices in 1998 and have fought a conventional war since; their rivalry is the most dangerous unresolved nuclear confrontation in the world, and the 2019 clash over Kashmir, in which Indian and Pakistani aircraft engaged in the first aerial combat between nuclear-armed states, was a reminder that the nuclear taboo does not prevent conventional war between nuclear powers.

The nuclear weapon is the clearest case of a technology that changed the relationship between war and politics, but it is not the only one. The revolution in precision-guided munitions, which began in the 1960s and matured in the 1990s, changed the relationship between air power and ground war in a different way. The laser-guided bombs used in Vietnam in the late 1960s and early 1970s—the "smart bombs" that destroyed the Thanh Hoa Bridge in 1972 after years of unsuccessful conventional attacks—were the first indication that a bomb could be aimed at a target rather than at an area. The technology developed slowly through the 1970s and 1980s and reached maturity in the 1991 Gulf War, when coalition aircraft dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, of which about 6,520 tons were precision-guided. The precision-guided munitions were roughly 7.4 percent of the total tonnage, but they were used against the targets that mattered: command bunkers, bridges, air-defense sites, and the infrastructure of the Iraqi state. The images of laser-guided bombs falling into the ventilation shafts of the Ministry of Defense building in Baghdad became the defining images of the war, and they created an expectation—among the public, among politicians, and among the military itself—that air power could now achieve with a few aircraft what had previously required a fleet.

The expectation was not entirely wrong, but it was premature. The 1999 Kosovo campaign, in which NATO aircraft flew more than 38,000 sorties without a single combat loss, demonstrated the potential of precision air power against a state with a modern air-defense system; it also demonstrated its limits, because the campaign did not stop the Serbian forces in Kosovo from carrying out the ethnic cleansing the war was supposed to prevent, and the targets NATO eventually struck—bridges, power stations, television transmitters—were chosen as much for their political effect as for their military value. The 2003 invasion of Iraq was the apotheosis of precision air power in the service of a ground campaign: the "shock and awe" bombing of Baghdad was designed to decapitate the Iraqi regime and paralyze its command, and the ground forces that followed advanced to Baghdad in three weeks with fewer casualties than the planners had feared. But the same campaign produced the insurgency that would consume the next decade, and the precision weapons that had destroyed the Iraqi state proved far less useful against an enemy that fought from among the population.

The precision revolution was, in its own way, as profound as the nuclear revolution, because it changed the political calculus of using force. When a bomb can be aimed at a building, the state that drops it can claim to be attacking a military target and not a city; when the bomb misses, the claim becomes harder to sustain, and the political cost of civilian casualties rises. The result was a shift in the way wars were fought and justified: the "precision" label became a form of legitimacy, and states possessing precision weapons used them to conduct campaigns designed to be politically sustainable at home, which often meant campaigns limited in their aims and careful in their targeting. The 2011 NATO campaign in Libya, which relied heavily on precision air strikes and was conducted under a UN mandate to protect civilians, was the clearest example of this logic, and it also demonstrated its limits: the campaign achieved its immediate objective of preventing a massacre in Benghazi, but it produced a protracted civil war and a failed state.

The drone was the extension of the precision revolution into persistent surveillance and targeted killing. The Predator drone, developed in the 1990s from a surveillance platform, was armed with Hellfire missiles in 2001 and used in Afghanistan and Yemen in the years that followed. The Reaper, a larger and more capable platform, entered service in 2007. By the 2010s the United States was conducting drone strikes in Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, and Libya, and the legal and ethical debates that surrounded them—about sovereignty, civilian casualties, the definition of a battlefield, the psychology of remote warfare—became a permanent feature of public discussion. The drone changed the relationship between the state and the use of force in a way the precision bomb had not: it made it possible to kill a specific individual in a specific place, on a timetable chosen by the state, without putting a pilot at risk, and it therefore lowered the political cost of using force to a level that had not existed since the pre-industrial era.

The drone's military significance was demonstrated most dramatically in the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war, when Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air-defense systems. The war lasted forty-four days. The drones—cheap, slow, and vulnerable to a competent air-defense system—were devastating against an opponent whose air defenses were obsolete and whose forces were exposed. The images of Armenian tanks and artillery pieces destroyed by precision munitions from the air became the defining images of the conflict, and the Royal United Services Institute's 2021 study of the war treated it as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense. The lesson military establishments around the world drew was not that drones had made tanks obsolete—the war also showed that ground forces still mattered, and that the side with better tactics and better integration of reconnaissance and strike could prevail—but that the combination of persistent surveillance, precision munitions, and cheap unmanned platforms had changed the balance between offense and defense in ways no army could ignore.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was also a demonstration of how quickly a new military technology can spread. The Bayraktar TB2 was a Turkish design, sold to Azerbaijan and later to Ukraine, Poland, and other states. The loitering munitions used in the war—the Israeli-made Harop and the Turkish-made Kargu—were commercially available. The technology of precision strike, which had been the monopoly of the great powers in 1991, had by 2020 become accessible to middle-income states and even to non-state actors. The proliferation of drones was the proliferation of air power, and it raised the same questions the proliferation of nuclear weapons had raised: what happens when a technology once the preserve of a few states becomes available to many, and what institutions can manage the consequences?

The answer, in the case of drones, was that the institutions were much weaker than the nuclear ones. There is no drone non-proliferation treaty, no inspection regime, no international agency with the authority to verify the numbers and capabilities of armed drones. The export of armed drones is governed by national export-control laws and by the Missile Technology Control Regime, a voluntary arrangement among supplier states that has been only partially effective. The result is a world in which armed drones are spreading rapidly, the rules for their use are contested, and the states that pioneered them are now competing with states that have learned from their example.

The history of weapons is, at every stage, a history of this kind of asymmetry: a technology appears, it confers an advantage on the state that develops it, the advantage is temporary, and the technology spreads. The states that are ahead try to preserve their advantage through secrecy, export controls, and arms-control agreements; the states that are behind try to acquire the technology, sometimes by purchase, sometimes by espionage, sometimes by indigenous development. The process is as old as metallurgy—the spread of bronze-working, of iron-working, of gunpowder, of the rifled musket, of the machine gun, of the nuclear weapon, of the drone—and it has never been stopped, only slowed.

The First World War is the great case study of what happens when the spread of a technology outruns the institutions supposed to manage it. The war began in August 1914 with armies equipped with weapons whose implications their commanders only partly understood. The magazine rifle, the machine gun, the quick-firing field gun, and the railway had all been developed in the preceding decades, and each had been used in colonial wars or in the smaller European wars of the nineteenth century, but none had been used together, by mass armies, on a continental scale. The result was a war in which the offensive tactics the armies had inherited from the nineteenth century—the bayonet charge, the cavalry pursuit, the frontal assault on a fortified position—were repeatedly and catastrophically defeated by the defensive firepower of the new weapons.

The numbers are the most concise way to describe what happened. The French army, which began the war with a doctrine of the offensive à outrance, lost about 27,000 men killed on 22 August 1914 alone, in the first day of the Battle of the Frontiers; total French casualties in August and September 1914 exceeded 300,000. The British Expeditionary Force, small but professional, was nearly destroyed at Mons and Le Cateau in the last week of August. The German army, with the best artillery and the best-trained staff in Europe, was stopped at the Marne in September by a combination of French resilience, British intervention, and the exhaustion of its own logistics. By the end of 1914 the Western Front had stabilized into a line of trenches running from the North Sea to the Swiss border, and the war had become a siege on a continental scale.

The trench stalemate was not the result of stupidity or a failure of imagination, although both were present. It was the result of a technological balance in which the defensive had a decisive advantage. The magazine rifle, firing a high-velocity bullet, could kill at ranges of up to a kilometer; the machine gun, firing 400 to 600 rounds per minute, could stop an infantry assault at a few hundred meters; the quick-firing field gun, with a recoil system that allowed it to fire without re-aiming, could deliver shrapnel and high-explosive shells at a rate that made open ground lethal. The attackers had no weapon that could suppress these defenses long enough for an assault to reach the enemy line. Every attack was therefore a calculation of how many men would be killed before the survivors reached the enemy trench, and the calculation was usually unfavorable.

The war produced a series of attempts to break the balance. The first was artillery on an unprecedented scale: the preliminary bombardment at the Somme in June 1916 lasted a week and fired more than 1.7 million shells, and the bombardment at Verdun, which began in February 1916, was even more intense. The theory was that a sufficiently heavy bombardment would destroy the enemy's defenses and allow the infantry to walk across no man's land. It failed because the artillery could not destroy everything, because the defenders could shelter in deep dugouts, and because the bombardment announced the attack and allowed the defenders to bring up reserves. The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916, produced roughly 700,000 casualties on both sides and became the symbol of a war in which artillery was the dominant weapon and the infantry its victim. The German commander, Erich von Falkenhayn, had intended to "bleed the French army white" by attacking a position the French would defend to the last man; the French commander, Philippe Pétain, had intended to hold the position and rotate his divisions through it so the army would not be destroyed. Both succeeded, in a sense, and the result was a battle that consumed the resources of both armies without producing a decision.

The second attempt was chemical weapons. The German army released chlorine gas from cylinders at Ypres on 22 April 1915, and the gas cloud drifted into the French and Algerian trenches, killing and disabling thousands of soldiers and opening a gap in the Allied line that the Germans, who had not expected the attack to be so effective, were unable to exploit. The Allies responded with their own gas attacks, and by 1917 both sides were using phosgene and mustard gas, delivered by artillery shells. The chemical weapons of the First World War killed and injured hundreds of thousands of soldiers, but they did not break the stalemate, because the gas depended on the wind, because gas masks reduced its effectiveness, and because gas was as dangerous to the attacker as to the defender. The chemical weapon was a weapon of terror and attrition, not of decision.

The third attempt was the tank. The British developed the tank in secret in 1915 and 1916, and the first tanks went into action at the Somme on 15 September 1916. They were slow, unreliable, and mechanically fragile, and they were used in small numbers, but they demonstrated that a vehicle protected by armor could cross no man's land and attack the enemy's trenches. The tank was the first weapon to combine mobility, protection, and firepower in a way that could break the defensive balance, and the British and French armies developed it through 1917 and 1918. The Battle of Cambrai in November 1917, in which 476 British tanks attacked without a preliminary bombardment, was the first demonstration of the tank's potential; the German offensives of 1918 and the Allied counteroffensives that followed showed how the tank, combined with improved artillery tactics and infantry infiltration, could restore mobility to the battlefield.

The fourth attempt was new infantry tactics. The German army, after the failures of 1916, developed the "stormtrooper" tactics used in the spring offensives of 1918: small groups of specially trained infantry, armed with light machine guns, grenades, and flamethrowers, would infiltrate through the enemy's defenses, bypass strong points, and attack the command and supply nodes in the rear. The tactics were effective and produced the deepest advances of the war on the Western Front, but they were not enough to win the war, because the German army lacked the mobility and logistics to exploit its breakthroughs.

The combination of these innovations—the tank, the stormtrooper tactics, the improved artillery, the aircraft—produced the "combined arms" warfare that would define the twentieth century. The German army's 1918 offensives were the first large-scale demonstration of combined arms, and the Allied counteroffensives that followed, culminating in the Hundred Days that ended the war, were the first campaigns in which tanks, aircraft, artillery, and infantry were integrated into a single operational system. The war that had begun as a clash of mass armies with nineteenth-century tactics ended as a laboratory for the weapons and tactics of the next war.

The First World War also produced the first systematic attempt to control a weapon while the war was still being fought. The use of chemical weapons provoked an outcry that led, in 1925, to the Geneva Protocol, which prohibited the use in war of asphyxiating and poisonous gases. The protocol was signed by most of the major powers and was respected in the Second World War by all the major belligerents except Japan, which used chemical and biological weapons in China. Its success was partly a matter of deterrence—the fear of retaliation in kind—and partly a matter of the weapon's limited military utility. The chemical weapon had been shown to be a weapon of attrition rather than decision, and the states that possessed it had reasons of their own to avoid its use.

The Second World War was the war in which the industrialization of weapons reached its logical conclusion. It was fought by states that mobilized their entire economies, and the weapons they produced were the products of industrial systems designed for mass production. The numbers are almost impossible to comprehend: the United States produced about 300,000 aircraft during the war, the Soviet Union about 150,000, Germany about 120,000, and the United Kingdom about 130,000. The Soviet Union produced about 100,000 tanks and self-propelled guns, the United States about 90,000, Germany about 46,000, and the United Kingdom about 27,000. The United States alone produced about 40 billion rounds of small-arms ammunition. The war was a contest of production as much as of tactics, and the outcome was determined in large part by the ability of the Allied economies to outproduce the Axis.

The weapons that defined the war were the products of this industrial system. The tank, a fragile experiment in 1916, became the core of the armored divisions that fought the great battles of 1940–45. The German Panzer divisions, which combined tanks with motorized infantry, artillery, and close air support, were the instrument of the blitzkrieg that defeated France in six weeks in 1940; the Soviet T-34, which combined sloped armor, a powerful gun, and wide tracks, was the weapon that made the Soviet counteroffensives of 1943–45 possible; the American Sherman, produced in enormous numbers and shipped around the world, equipped the Allied armies in the West. The tank was not a single weapon but a system, and the armies that integrated it best—with radio communications, mobile artillery, and tactical air power—were the armies that won.

The aircraft was the other defining weapon. The strategic bombing campaigns against Germany and Japan were the largest and most sustained attempts in history to win a war by air power alone. The British Bomber Command and the American Eighth Air Force dropped about 1.4 million tons of bombs on Germany, and the Twentieth Air Force dropped about 160,000 tons on Japan. The campaigns killed hundreds of thousands of civilians—the bombing of Dresden in February 1945 killed an estimated 25,000 people, the firebombing of Tokyo in March 1945 an estimated 100,000—and destroyed the industrial and urban infrastructure of both countries. The strategic bombing campaign was justified by the theory that destroying the enemy's industrial capacity would collapse its ability to wage war; the theory was partly correct, in that the bombing did reduce German and Japanese production, but partly wrong, in that it did not break the enemy's will to fight and in that the resources devoted to it might have been used more effectively elsewhere.

The strategic bombing campaign also produced the weapon that ended the war. The Manhattan Project, which began in 1942 as a program to develop an atomic weapon before the Germans did, produced the first nuclear devices in July 1945. The Trinity test on 16 July 1945, in the New Mexico desert, detonated a plutonium implosion device with a yield of about 21 kilotons. The bomb dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, a uranium gun-type device, had a yield of about 15 kilotons; the bomb dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, a plutonium implosion device, had a yield of about 21 kilotons. The two bombs killed an estimated 100,000 to 200,000 people, most of them civilians, and they ended the war.

The decision to use the bomb has been debated for as long as the bomb has existed. The arguments for its use were that an invasion of Japan would have cost hundreds of thousands of American and Japanese lives, that the bomb would shock Japan into surrender, and that its use would demonstrate to the Soviet Union the power of the United States at the beginning of the postwar competition. The arguments against were that Japan was already defeated and that the bomb was used to intimidate the Soviet Union as much as to defeat Japan, that the bombing of cities violated the laws of war, and that the weapon was so terrible that its use set a precedent that could not be contained. The debate is unresolved, and it is likely to remain so, because the evidence is ambiguous and the stakes are so high.

What is not ambiguous is the effect of the bomb on the history of war. The nuclear weapon ended the era of total war between the great powers, because a total war between nuclear-armed states would be a war of mutual destruction. It did not end war; it changed its character. The wars of the postwar period were fought by proxy, or by states that did not have nuclear weapons, or by non-state actors. The great powers fought each other through clients and allies, and they competed through technology, espionage, and economic pressure rather than direct military confrontation. The result was a period of great-power peace unprecedented in the history of the modern state system, accompanied by a series of brutal wars on the periphery.

The Cold War was also the period in which the institutions of arms control were built. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963, the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968, the Biological Weapons Convention of 1972, the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty of 1972, the SALT I and II agreements, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987, and the Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 were all products of the Cold War, and all were attempts to manage the weapons the Cold War had produced. The institutions they created—the IAEA, the OPCW, the various bilateral commissions—were the first international bodies with the authority to inspect, verify, and enforce. They were imperfect and unevenly applied, but they represented a genuine change in the way states related to weapons: the recognition that some weapons were too dangerous to be left to the unilateral judgment of the states that held them.

The end of the Cold War raised the hope that the institutions might be extended and strengthened. The 1990s produced the Chemical Weapons Convention, the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty of 1996 (signed but never entered into force, because the United States and other states did not ratify it), the Ottawa Treaty banning anti-personnel landmines in 1997, and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court in 1998. The 1990s also produced the first serious attempts to control the proliferation of small arms and light weapons, which kill more people than any other class of weapon but have never been subject to a comprehensive international regime.

The small arms problem is the mirror image of the nuclear problem. Nuclear weapons are held by a handful of states, have been used twice in war, and are subject to the most extensive arms-control regime in history. Small arms are held by hundreds of millions of people, are used in every war, and are subject to almost no international control. The United Nations Programme of Action on Small Arms and Light Weapons, adopted in 2001, is a political commitment rather than a treaty; it has no verification mechanism and no enforcement provisions. The Arms Trade Treaty, adopted in 2013 and in force since 2014, regulates the international transfer of conventional weapons, but it has been signed by only about 110 states, and the largest exporters—the United States, Russia, and China—have not joined. The result is that the weapons that kill the most people are the least controlled, and the weapons that kill the fewest are the most controlled.

The disparity is not an accident. It reflects the interests of the states that dominate the international system. The great powers have been willing to accept restrictions on the weapons that threaten them—nuclear, chemical, biological—because those weapons could be used against them. They have been unwilling to accept restrictions on the weapons they use to project power and supply their allies, because those weapons are the instruments of their influence. The result is a hierarchy of arms control that mirrors the hierarchy of international power.

The post-Cold War period also produced a new kind of war, and the new kind of war produced a new kind of weapon. The wars of the 1990s and 2000s—in the Balkans, Somalia, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Iraq—were fought by states against non-state actors, by non-state actors against civilians, or by coalitions of states against failed states. The enemies were not armies but insurgencies, militias, and terrorist networks, and the weapons useful against them were not tanks and bombers but precision munitions, drones, special forces, and surveillance systems. The revolution in military affairs that the United States began to develop in the 1990s was a revolution in information technology: the integration of sensors, communications, and precision weapons into a system that could find, track, and destroy a target in minutes rather than hours.

The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq were the testing ground for this system, and they demonstrated both its power and its limits. The power was evident in the speed with which the Taliban and the Iraqi army were defeated in 2001 and 2003. The limits were evident in the years that followed, when the same precision weapons that had destroyed the enemy's conventional forces proved unable to defeat an insurgency that fought from among the population. The insurgents adapted: they used improvised explosive devices, which were cheap and effective; suicide attacks, which were difficult to prevent; the internet and social media, which allowed them to recruit and propagandize; and the political systems of the states they fought against, which allowed them to wait out the coalitions that opposed
