paragraphs: The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq did not end the era of precision warfare; they complicated it. The same technologies that had destroyed the Taliban’s and Saddam Hussein’s conventional forces in weeks proved unable to deliver decisive political outcomes against irregular adversaries who dispersed into cities, villages, and mountains and learned to fight the precision arsenal asymmetrically. The result was a period—roughly 2003 to the present—in which the world’s most advanced militaries invested enormous resources in weapons and systems designed not to win battles against comparable armies but to find, fix, and finish individual fighters, protect their own forces from cheap and ubiquitous threats, and operate where the enemy deliberately blurred the line between combatant and civilian. This period is the hinge between the industrial-mass warfare of the twentieth century and the distributed, algorithmic, and increasingly autonomous warfare of the twenty-first. It is defined by a paradox: the more precise and powerful the weapon, the less decisive it often proved, because precision addressed the wrong problem. The problem was not the destruction of targets but their identification, the protection of forces, and the political sustainability of long wars fought among populations whose allegiance could not be bombed into submission.

To understand this paradox, one must begin with the improvised explosive device, the weapon that more than any other defined the counterinsurgency era. An IED is not a single weapon but a category: a bomb assembled from commercial or military explosives, often augmented with metal fragments, triggered by a command wire, radio signal, pressure plate, or victim-operated switch, and emplaced along a road, in a culvert, under a pile of rubbish, or inside a vehicle. Its components are cheap—a few hundred dollars for a basic device, a few thousand for a sophisticated one—and its materials ubiquitous. Fertilizer, diesel fuel, and a detonator can be purchased in any agricultural market; artillery shells and mortar rounds can be scavenged from old battlefields or stolen from poorly secured depots; cell phones and garage-door openers can serve as triggers. The IED is the archetypal weapon of the weak against the strong: it requires no industrial base, no trained crew, and no exposure of the attacker to the defender’s fire. It exploits the defender’s dependence on roads, convoys, and predictable movement patterns, turning the defender’s own mobility into a liability.

The numbers tell the story of the IED’s centrality in Iraq and Afghanistan. By the time the United States withdrew from Iraq in 2011, IEDs had accounted for roughly half of all American combat deaths there, and a similar or higher proportion of wounded. In Afghanistan, the proportion was even higher in the later years, as the Taliban shifted from direct-fire engagements to roadside bombs. The devices were not merely lethal; they were psychologically corrosive. A convoy moving at walking pace through a village, every culvert and trash pile a potential bomb, was a convoy whose crew was exhausted, hypervigilant, and prone to mistakes—mistakes that alienated the population the convoy was supposed to protect. The IED was therefore not only a tactical weapon but a strategic one: it imposed costs, slowed operations, diverted resources, and eroded the political will of the intervening powers.

The response to the IED was a case study in the co-evolution of offense and defense, illustrating how weapon development in this period was driven less by greater lethality than by greater survivability and situational awareness. The first response was armor. Vehicles designed for mobility and payload—Humvees, trucks, even armored personnel carriers—were up-armored with bolt-on steel plates, then replaced by purpose-built mine-resistant ambush-protected vehicles, the MRAPs, whose V-shaped hulls deflected blast energy away from the crew compartment and whose raised suspensions kept occupants above the point of detonation. The MRAP program was one of the fastest major procurement efforts in American military history: from a few dozen vehicles in 2006 to more than twenty thousand by 2010, at a cost of tens of billions of dollars. The vehicles saved lives—units equipped with MRAPs saw casualty rates from underbody blasts fall dramatically—but they were heavy, expensive, and logistically demanding, and poorly suited to the narrow streets and soft ground of many Afghan and Iraqi environments. The MRAP was a technological fix to a tactical problem with strategic roots: the defender’s need to move along predictable routes among a population the enemy could mine at will.

The second response was electronic warfare. Because many IEDs were triggered by radio signals—cell phones, cordless phones, remote controls—the coalition deployed jammers that broadcast noise across the relevant frequency bands, preventing the trigger signal from reaching the device. Mounted on vehicles and carried by dismounted patrols, these jammers evolved rapidly as insurgents shifted frequencies and adopted new triggering methods. The result was an electronic arms race in the electromagnetic spectrum, each side seeking to exploit the other’s vulnerabilities. The insurgents moved from simple radio triggers to command wires, which could not be jammed, and to pressure plates, which required no signal at all. The coalition responded with route-clearance teams, ground-penetrating radar, and remotely operated robots that inspected suspicious objects. Each measure was countered, and each counter countered in turn. The IED war was a microcosm of the broader dynamic of the period: a continuous, iterative contest between cheap, adaptive, low-technology weapons and expensive, sophisticated, high-technology defenses, in which the advantage shifted constantly and neither side achieved a permanent edge.

The third response was intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. If the IED could not be defeated by armor and jamming alone, it had to be defeated before it was emplaced—by finding the bomb-makers, the bomb factories, and the networks that financed and supplied them. This required a vast expansion of surveillance: unmanned aerial vehicles, or drones, that loitered over roads and villages for hours, streaming full-motion video to analysts and commanders; signals-intelligence systems that intercepted insurgent communications; biometric systems that catalogued fingerprints and iris scans; and data-mining tools that sought patterns in the flood of information. The growth of this apparatus was one of the defining features of the period. The United States went from a handful of military drones in 2001 to thousands by the 2010s, and the number of analysts required to process the imagery grew accordingly. The drone became the emblem of the era, not because it was a new kind of weapon—armed drones had been developed in the early 2000s—but because it embodied the fusion of surveillance and strike that precision warfare promised: the ability to watch a target for hours, strike with a missile once the target was positively identified, and do so without risking a pilot.

The armed drone deserves close attention, because it most clearly connects the precision revolution of the 1990s to the autonomous warfare of the present. The Predator, a turboprop-powered unmanned aircraft developed in the 1990s for reconnaissance, was armed with Hellfire missiles in 2001 and used in Afghanistan and Yemen. The Reaper, a larger and more capable successor, entered service in 2007 and could carry a heavier payload, including laser-guided bombs and, later, small precision munitions. These aircraft were not fast or stealthy; they were slow, vulnerable to air defenses, and useful only in permissive airspace. But in the conflicts of the 2000s, the airspace over Afghanistan, Pakistan’s tribal areas, Yemen, Somalia, and later Libya and Syria was permissive, because the insurgents had no air force and only rudimentary anti-aircraft weapons. The drone therefore allowed the United States and its allies to conduct a persistent campaign of surveillance and strike against suspected militants in countries where they had no ground forces and where the local government either consented or could not object.

The drone campaign was controversial, and the controversy concerned not only legality and sovereignty but the nature of the weapon itself. A drone strike is a precision weapon in the sense that it can be aimed at a specific individual or vehicle, but not in the sense that it can reliably distinguish a combatant from a civilian in a crowded market or a wedding procession. The intelligence that identifies a target is often fragmentary, based on patterns of behavior, signals intercepts, and human sources of variable reliability. The decision to strike is made by operators thousands of miles away, watching a video feed, and the consequences of a mistake are visited on the people below. The drone thus intensified the moral and legal dilemmas of precision warfare: it made killing easier for the killer, because it removed the killer from the scene, and it made the consequences harder to see, because the evidence of civilian casualties was often disputed and difficult to verify.

The drone also changed the politics of war. Because it required no ground troops, it allowed the United States to conduct hostilities in countries with which it was not formally at war, and to do so with minimal congressional or public scrutiny. The campaign in Pakistan’s tribal areas, which peaked between 2008 and 2012, was conducted by the CIA and the military with the tacit consent of the Pakistani government, which publicly condemned the strikes while privately cooperating with them. The campaigns in Yemen, Somalia, and Libya followed a similar pattern. The drone thus became a tool of what some scholars called “remote warfare” or “light-footprint” operations: the use of air power, special forces, and intelligence to pursue limited objectives without committing large ground formations. This approach had real advantages—it was cheap, politically sustainable, and avoided the casualties that had eroded support for the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan—but also real limits. It could kill individual militants, but it could not hold territory, build institutions, or address the grievances that produced the militants in the first place. The drone was a weapon of attrition, not of pacification.

The broader trajectory of the period can be understood as a series of adaptations to the failure of precision warfare to deliver decisive political results. The first adaptation was counterinsurgency itself—the doctrine, codified in the U.S. Army and Marine Corps field manual of 2006, that emphasized protecting the population, building local institutions, and using force with restraint. Counterinsurgency was not a weapons program, but it had profound implications for weapons development. It demanded weapons that could be used with discrimination in populated areas: precision-guided munitions with small warheads, sniper rifles, non-lethal weapons, and surveillance systems that could distinguish insurgents from civilians. It demanded vehicles that could move among the population without destroying infrastructure, and air power that could support ground troops without causing the collateral damage that would drive the population into the arms of the insurgents. The result was a shift in the character of air power: from the destruction of fixed targets to the support of troops in contact, from the heavy bomb to the small, precise munition, and from the fast jet to the slow, persistent drone.

The second adaptation was a new generation of precision munitions designed for the counterinsurgency environment. The most important were the guided rocket and the small-diameter bomb. The 70mm rocket, a cheap and ubiquitous munition used since the 1940s, was fitted with a laser seeker and a precision guidance kit, turning it into a low-cost, low-collateral weapon that could be fired from helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft. The small-diameter bomb, a 250-pound weapon with a sophisticated guidance package, allowed aircraft to carry more munitions and strike targets with less blast effect. These weapons were not designed to destroy tanks or bunkers; they were designed to kill a handful of insurgents in a compound without destroying the surrounding houses. They reflected a new understanding of precision: not merely the ability to hit a target, but the ability to hit it with the minimum force necessary to achieve the desired effect.

The third adaptation was the expansion of special operations forces and the integration of precision strike into their operations. Special forces had always relied on stealth and surprise, but in the 2000s they acquired an unprecedented ability to call down precision fire from aircraft, drones, and naval platforms. A small team of operators could now direct a strike on a target that would previously have required a battalion. This fusion of special operations and precision air power was the model for the raid that killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad in May 2011, in which a team of Navy SEALs, supported by intelligence and surveillance, assaulted a compound in a Pakistani city and extracted without a firefight with Pakistani forces. The raid was a tactical success and a political triumph, but it also demonstrated the limits of the model: it required years of intelligence work, a permissive environment, and a target that was isolated and identifiable. It could not be replicated at scale.

The fourth adaptation was the development of counter-rocket, artillery, and mortar systems, known as C-RAM, and the broader effort to defend bases and forces against the cheap, unguided weapons insurgents used to attack them. The threat was simple: a few dozen rockets or mortar rounds fired at a base from a nearby village, causing casualties and disruption. The defense was complex: radar systems that detected the incoming projectiles, computers that calculated their trajectories, and rapid-fire guns or lasers that intercepted them. The Phalanx Close-In Weapon System, originally designed for ships, was adapted for land use and deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan, where it engaged incoming rockets with a stream of 20mm rounds. The system worked, but it was expensive—each intercept cost thousands of dollars—and vulnerable to saturation attacks. The C-RAM mission illustrated a broader problem of the period: the defender’s need to protect against cheap, plentiful threats with expensive, scarce interceptors.

This problem became acute with the rise of another cheap and ubiquitous weapon: the rocket-propelled grenade, or RPG, and its more sophisticated cousins, the anti-tank guided missile and the man-portable air-defense system. These weapons were not new, but their proliferation and their use against helicopters, aircraft, and armored vehicles forced the development of new defenses. Helicopters, the backbone of the American way of war since Vietnam, became increasingly vulnerable to ambushes by fighters armed with RPGs and machine guns. The response was to fly higher, to fly at night, and to use the aircraft’s sensors and weapons to find and kill attackers before they could fire. The result was a shift in helicopter operations: from low-level, high-speed runs to high-altitude, stand-off engagements, and from the transport helicopter as a battlefield taxi to the armed helicopter as a precision-strike platform.

The fifth adaptation was a new generation of armored vehicles designed specifically for the counterinsurgency environment. The MRAP was the most visible example, but it was part of a broader family that included the Stryker, a wheeled armored personnel carrier that could be fitted with remote-controlled weapons and sensors, and the Mine-Resistant Ambush-Protected All-Terrain Vehicle, a smaller, more mobile vehicle for Afghanistan’s rugged terrain. These vehicles were not designed to fight other armored vehicles; they were designed to survive ambushes, move among the population, and give the crew the situational awareness needed to detect and avoid threats. They reflected a new understanding of armored warfare: not the clash of tanks on the open plain, but the protection of forces in a complex environment where the enemy was everywhere and nowhere.

The sixth adaptation was a new generation of sensors and communication systems that allowed forces to share information in real time. The most important was the Blue Force Tracker, a GPS-based system that displayed the location of friendly forces on a digital map, along with the various systems that allowed dismounted soldiers to see the same picture as their commanders. These systems were not weapons in the traditional sense, but they were force multipliers: they allowed small units to coordinate their actions, avoid friendly fire, and call down precision strikes with unprecedented speed and accuracy. They also created new vulnerabilities: they depended on satellites, radio links, and electrical power, and could be jammed, hacked, or destroyed. Dependence on information systems became a defining feature of the period, and protecting those systems a central concern of military planners.

The seventh adaptation was a new generation of medical care that dramatically improved survival rates for wounded soldiers. The combination of forward surgical teams, rapid evacuation by helicopter, and new treatments for trauma—tourniquets, blood products, and damage-control surgery—meant that soldiers who would have died in previous wars now survived. This was a genuine humanitarian achievement, but it also had strategic implications: the number of wounded soldiers, many with severe and lasting injuries, grew, and the cost of caring for them over decades became a significant burden on the states that fought. The improvement in medical care also changed the calculus of risk: if a soldier was more likely to survive a wound, the political cost of a wound was lower, and the willingness to accept risk higher. The relationship between medicine and strategy was not often acknowledged, but it was real.

The cumulative effect of these adaptations was a transformation in the character of the armed forces of the advanced states. They became smaller, more professional, more dependent on technology, and more expensive per soldier. They became expert at finding and killing individual fighters, protecting their own forces from improvised threats, and operating in complex environments among populations. But they also became less capable of the kind of mass, industrial warfare that had defined the twentieth century. The stockpiles of artillery shells, tanks, and combat aircraft built up during the Cold War were allowed to shrink, and the industrial base that produced them was allowed to atrophy. The assumption was that future wars would resemble those of the 2000s: limited, irregular, and fought against technologically inferior adversaries. That assumption would be tested, and found wanting, in the second decade of the twenty-first century.

The wars of the 2000s also accelerated a development that would prove decisive in the following decade: the spread of precision weapons and drones beyond the advanced militaries that had pioneered them. Drone technology was not inherently difficult to acquire. The airframe could be built from commercial components; the sensors purchased off the shelf; the communications links adapted from civilian technology; and the munitions could be small, cheap, and widely available. The result was a proliferation of drones to states and non-state actors that had never before possessed an air force. Hezbollah flew Iranian-supplied drones over Israel in the 2000s. Hamas and other Palestinian groups developed crude rockets and, later, drones. The Islamic State used commercial quadcopters to drop small bombs and to film propaganda. The Houthis in Yemen, with Iranian assistance, developed a family of drones and cruise missiles that could strike targets deep inside Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The monopoly on precision air power that the United States had enjoyed in the 1990s was eroding, and the erosion would have profound consequences.

The proliferation of drones was part of a broader diffusion of military technology that characterized the period. The components of precision warfare—GPS receivers, laser designators, inertial navigation systems, digital communications, and imaging sensors—became cheaper and more widely available. States with modest industrial bases could now build or buy weapons that would have been beyond their reach a generation earlier. Iran, in particular, developed a sophisticated program of ballistic and cruise missiles, drones, and precision-guided munitions, and exported these weapons to its allies and proxies across the Middle East. The Houthi missile and drone campaign against Saudi Arabia, which began in 2015 and continued for years, demonstrated what a non-state actor with state sponsorship could do: it struck oil facilities, airports, and cities, disrupted global energy markets, and imposed costs on a wealthy and technologically advanced state. The campaign was not decisive, but it showed that precision strike was no longer the exclusive preserve of the world’s most powerful militaries.

The diffusion of precision weapons also changed the character of the arms trade. The United States, which had dominated the market for advanced weapons since the end of the Cold War, found itself competing with new suppliers: China, which offered drones and missiles at lower prices and with fewer political conditions; Turkey, which developed a family of armed drones that proved effective and affordable; Israel, long a leader in drone technology; and Iran, which supplied cheap and crude but effective weapons to its allies. The result was a more fragmented and competitive market, in which states could shop around for the capabilities they wanted and the leverage of any single supplier was reduced. The proliferation of precision weapons was thus both a cause and a consequence of the diffusion of power in the international system.

The second decade of the twenty-first century also saw the return of a kind of warfare the advanced militaries had assumed obsolete: the interstate conventional war. The Russian annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the war in eastern Ukraine that followed were the first signs. The Russian intervention in Syria in 2015, which combined air power, precision strike, and proxy forces, was another. But the full implications became clear only with the large-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the largest conventional war in Europe since 1945, which exposed the limits of the post-Cold War military model. The war in Ukraine was not a war of precision weapons against insurgents; it was a war of artillery, armor, and mass, in which both sides fired tens of thousands of shells a day, tanks and armored vehicles were destroyed in large numbers, and the industrial base that produced munitions and weapons proved decisive.

The war in Ukraine was a shock to the advanced militaries, and it is worth examining in some detail because it illustrates the central argument of this book: that the development of weapons is not a linear progression toward greater precision and smaller forces, but a dialectical process in which each new capability generates a counter-capability, and in which the character of war is shaped by the interaction of technology, tactics, and the industrial and political context. The war began with a Russian attempt at a rapid, precision-guided decapitation strike: missile attacks on airfields, command centers, and air defenses, followed by airborne and special forces operations aimed at seizing Kyiv and decapitating the government. The attempt failed. The missiles were not accurate enough or numerous enough to destroy the Ukrainian air defenses and command structure; the airborne assault on Hostomel airfield was repulsed; and the Russian ground forces, advancing along multiple axes, were ambushed and slowed by Ukrainian forces armed with anti-tank guided missiles, including the American Javelin and the British NLAW, and with drones that directed artillery fire.

The failure of the Russian precision blitzkrieg was a lesson in the limits of precision. The Russian military had invested heavily in precision weapons—the Iskander ballistic missile, the Kalibr cruise missile, the Kh-101 air-launched cruise missile—but not enough in the intelligence, surveillance, and command systems needed to find and fix targets in real time, nor in the munitions needed to sustain a long war. The result was that precision weapons were used against fixed targets—airfields, barracks, power stations—rather than against the mobile forces that mattered, and the Russian army found itself fighting a war of attrition for which it was poorly prepared.

The Ukrainian response was a case study in the creative use of limited resources. The Ukrainians had a small air force and no navy, but a large army, a motivated population, and access to Western weapons and intelligence. They used drones—both military models like the Turkish Bayraktar TB2 and commercial quadcopters—to find and target Russian columns. They used anti-tank guided missiles to ambush Russian armor. They used artillery, guided by drones, to strike Russian command posts and supply depots. They used the Starlink satellite internet system to maintain communications and coordinate their operations. And they used social media to shape the narrative of the war and mobilize international support. The result was a war both old and new: old in its dependence on artillery and attrition, new in its use of drones, precision weapons, and information technology.

The war in Ukraine accelerated the development of several categories of weapons. The first was the armed drone. The Turkish Bayraktar TB2, which had been used to devastating effect in Libya and Nagorno-Karabakh, became a symbol of Ukrainian resistance in the early months of the war. It was a medium-altitude, long-endurance drone, capable of carrying precision-guided munitions and loitering over the battlefield for hours. It was not stealthy or fast, and it was vulnerable to air defenses, but in the early months of the war, when the Russian air defense system was disorganized, it was effective. As the war continued, the TB2 became less useful, because the Russians improved their air defenses and the Ukrainians shifted to smaller, cheaper drones that could be used in large numbers.

The second category was the loitering munition, also known as the kamikaze drone. These are small, inexpensive drones that carry an explosive warhead and can loiter over a target area until a target is identified, then dive into it. The American Switchblade, the Russian Lancet, and the Iranian Shahed-136 were all used in the war, and they proved effective against armor, artillery, and air defenses. The loitering munition is a hybrid weapon: it combines the surveillance capability of a drone with the lethal effect of a missile, and it can be produced cheaply and in large numbers. It also raises difficult questions about autonomy, because the decision to strike can be made by the operator or, in some modes, by the weapon itself.

The third category was the anti-drone system. The proliferation of drones on the battlefield created an urgent need for defenses against them, and the war in Ukraine became a laboratory for anti-drone technology. The defenses ranged from electronic jammers that disrupted the drone’s control link, to guns and missiles that shot the drone down, to nets and cages that protected vehicles and positions, to acoustic sensors that detected the drone’s approach. The contest between drones and anti-drones became a defining feature of the war, and it illustrated the broader dynamic of the period: the rapid, iterative co-evolution of offense and defense, in which each new capability was met by a counter-capability, and in which the advantage shifted constantly.

The fourth category was the precision-guided artillery round. The Ukrainian military, armed with Western artillery systems like the American HIMARS and the French Caesar, used precision-guided rockets and shells to strike Russian command posts, ammunition depots, and bridges. The HIMARS, a truck-mounted rocket launcher that fires GPS-guided rockets with a range of about 80 kilometers, was particularly effective, because it could fire and move before the Russians could respond. The precision artillery round combined the accuracy of a guided missile with the low cost and high volume of artillery, demonstrating that precision was not only a matter of air power but of ground-based fire as well.

The fifth category was the unmanned surface vessel. The Ukrainians, who had no navy, developed small, explosive-laden boats that could be steered remotely or autonomously into Russian ships. These drones attacked the Russian Black Sea Fleet, sinking or damaging several vessels and forcing the fleet to withdraw from the western Black Sea. The success of the unmanned surface vessel demonstrated how cheap, autonomous technology could challenge a traditional naval power, and it foreshadowed a future in which the seas would be contested by swarms of small, unmanned craft.

The war in Ukraine also demonstrated the importance of the industrial base. Both sides fired enormous quantities of artillery ammunition—by some estimates, the Russians fired tens of thousands of shells a day at the height of the war, and the Ukrainians thousands—and both found their stockpiles inadequate. The Western countries supplying Ukraine discovered that their own production capacity was insufficient to meet demand, and they began to invest in expanding their ammunition factories. The war was a reminder that precision weapons do not replace mass; they complement it, and a military that lacks the industrial capacity to sustain a long war will find its precision weapons insufficient.

The war in Ukraine also illustrated the continuing importance of armored vehicles, despite predictions of their obsolescence. Tanks and armored personnel carriers were used extensively by both sides and proved vulnerable to anti-tank guided missiles, drones, and artillery. But they also proved essential for breakthrough operations, for protecting infantry, and for holding ground. The lesson was not that tanks were obsolete, but that they needed to be integrated with other systems—drones, electronic warfare, air defense—to survive on the modern battlefield. The tank, like the infantryman, had to adapt to an environment in which it was constantly observed and constantly targeted.

The war in Ukraine was the largest and most consequential conflict of the period, but not the only one. The Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020, between Azerbaijan and Armenia, was a landmark in the development of drone warfare. Azerbaijan, armed with Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and Israeli loitering munitions, used them to destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, and air defenses. The drones operated with impunity because Armenia’s air defenses were inadequate and because the terrain—mountainous, with narrow valleys—favored the attacker who could see and strike from above. The war lasted 44 days and ended with a decisive Azerbaijani victory, and it was widely interpreted as a demonstration of the power of drones against conventional forces. The RUSI study of the conflict, published in 2021, concluded that it was a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense, and that it offered lessons for future conflicts.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war also illustrated the vulnerability of traditional air defenses to drones. The Armenian air defense system, based on Soviet-era systems like the S-300 and the Tor, was designed to defend against aircraft and missiles, not against small, slow, low-flying drones. The drones exploited gaps in coverage, used terrain to mask their approach, and attacked the air defenses themselves, destroying radars and launchers. The result was that the Armenian air defense system collapsed, and the Azerbaijani drones operated freely. The lesson was that air defenses needed to be redesigned to counter drones, and that the integration of sensors, shooters, and command systems was essential.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war also raised the question of autonomy. The Azerbaijani drones were, for the most part, remotely piloted, but the loitering munitions had some autonomous capabilities—they could loiter over a target area and attack a target that matched a pre-programmed signature. The war was thus a step toward the autonomous battlefield, and it prompted a debate about the ethics and legality of autonomous weapons. The debate was intensified by a contested allegation from the Libyan civil war: a 2021 UN Panel of Experts report stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition “may have been” used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The claim was not independently confirmed and should be treated with caution, but it illustrated the direction of travel: the technology of autonomous targeting was advancing, and the legal and ethical frameworks for controlling it were lagging behind.

The Libyan civil war, which began in 2011 and continued intermittently for a decade, was another laboratory for the new weapons. The United Arab Emirates, supporting one side, deployed Chinese-made Wing Loong drones and other precision weapons. Turkey, supporting the other side, deployed Bayraktar TB2 drones and, later, armed drones and loitering munitions. The war became a proxy conflict in which regional powers tested their weapons and tactics, and it demonstrated how quickly drone technology could spread and how effective it could be against poorly defended forces. The war also demonstrated the vulnerability of drones to air defenses when the defender had modern systems: the Emirati drones were vulnerable to Turkish-made air defenses, and the Turkish drones to Emirati air defenses, and the contest between them shaped the course of the war.

The Syrian civil war, which began in 2011 and continued for more than a decade, was another conflict that shaped the development of weapons. The war began with peaceful protests against the regime of Bashar al-Assad, and it escalated into a multi-sided conflict involving the regime, its Russian and Iranian allies, a fragmented opposition, Kurdish forces, the Islamic State, and a coalition led by the United States. The war was a laboratory for drones, precision weapons, and cyber operations. The Russians used precision missiles and air power to support the regime; the Americans used drones and special forces to fight the Islamic State; the Turks used drones to support their proxies; and the Islamic State used commercial drones to drop small bombs and film propaganda. The war also demonstrated the importance of air defense: the Russian deployment of the S-400 air defense system to Syria deterred the United States and its allies from enforcing a no-fly zone, and it demonstrated how a sophisticated air defense system could shape the behavior of an adversary.

The Syrian war also illustrated the relationship between precision weapons and civilian casualties. The regime and its Russian allies used precision weapons, but they also used unguided bombs and barrel bombs, which caused enormous civilian casualties. The United States and its allies used precision weapons, but they also caused civilian casualties, particularly in the campaign against the Islamic State in Mosul and Raqqa, where the urban environment made it difficult to distinguish combatants from civilians. The war was a reminder that precision weapons do not eliminate civilian casualties; they can reduce them, but they cannot eliminate them, and the political and moral consequences of civilian casualties remain.

The conflicts of the 2010s and 2020s thus present a complex picture. On the one hand, precision weapons continued to improve: they became more accurate, more affordable, and more widely available. Drones became smaller, cheaper, and more capable. The integration of sensors, communications, and strike systems became tighter, and the speed of the kill chain—the time between the identification of a target and the delivery of a weapon—shrank from hours to minutes to seconds. On the other hand, the proliferation of these technologies to a wider range of actors meant that the advantage they conferred was temporary and contested. The United States and its allies might have pioneered precision warfare, but they no longer monopolized it, and the adversaries they faced—whether insurgents in Iraq and Afghanistan or state actors like Russia and Iran—learned to adapt.

The adaptation took several forms. The first was dispersal. Adversaries learned to disperse their forces, avoid concentrations that could be detected and destroyed, and operate in small, mobile units. The Islamic State, for example, operated from trucks and cars, moving constantly, and used tunnels and urban areas to hide from surveillance. The Taliban operated from villages and mountains, blending with the population and avoiding fixed positions. The Russians in Ukraine dispersed their ammunition depots and command posts, and used decoys and electronic warfare to confuse Ukrainian drones.

The second form of adaptation was concealment. Adversaries learned to hide from surveillance: to use camouflage, operate at night, avoid electronic emissions, and use tunnels and underground facilities. The North Korean nuclear program, dispersed and concealed in mountains, was an extreme example, but the principle applied to conventional forces as well. The Russians in Ukraine used camouflage and decoys to protect their vehicles, and electronic warfare to jam Ukrainian drones and communications.

The third form of adaptation was the use of cheap, numerous weapons to overwhelm defenses. The Houthis in Yemen used swarms of drones and missiles to attack Saudi Arabia, and the Saudis found that their expensive air defense systems—Patriot missiles costing millions of dollars each—were poorly suited to intercepting cheap drones costing thousands. The same problem confronted the Israelis, who faced rocket and drone attacks from Hamas and Hezbollah and developed the Iron Dome system to intercept rockets, but found that the system could be saturated by large numbers of cheap projectiles. The economics of defense against cheap drones became a central problem of the period: the defender’s interceptor often cost more than the attacker’s weapon, and the attacker could produce weapons faster than the defender could produce interceptors.

The fourth form of adaptation was the use of the electromagnetic spectrum. Adversaries learned to jam GPS signals, spoof navigation systems, disrupt communications, and hack into computer networks. The Russians, in particular, developed sophisticated electronic warfare capabilities and used them to disrupt Ukrainian drones, communications, and precision weapons. The Ukrainians responded by using alternative navigation systems, developing anti-jam techniques, and using fiber-optic cables to control their drones. The contest in the electromagnetic spectrum became as important as the contest in the physical domain, illustrating the extent to which modern weapons depend on information systems that can be disrupted.

The fifth form of adaptation was the use of the law and the media as weapons. Adversaries learned to exploit the legal and ethical constraints on the advanced militaries: to operate from civilian areas, use human shields, stage attacks from hospitals and schools, and publicize civilian casualties. The result was that the advanced militaries found themselves constrained by their own values and by the scrutiny of the international media, while their adversaries were not. This asymmetry was a central feature of the counterinsurgency era and continued into the era of great-power competition. The law of armed conflict, developed to limit the suffering of war, became a battleground in itself.

The cumulative effect of these adaptations was to complicate the promise of precision warfare. The promise was that precision weapons would allow the advanced militaries to achieve their objectives with fewer casualties, less collateral damage, and greater political sustainability. The reality was more complex. Precision weapons did reduce casualties and collateral damage in many cases, but they also created new vulnerabilities, new dependencies, and new dilemmas. The advanced militaries became dependent on satellites, communications networks, and complex supply chains, and these dependencies could be exploited by adversaries. The precision weapons themselves became more expensive and more complex, and the industrial base that produced them became more concentrated and more fragile.

The period also saw the emergence of a new domain of warfare: cyberspace. Cyber operations were not new—they had been conducted since the 1980s—but they became an integral part of military operations in the 2000s and 2010s. The United States established Cyber Command in 2009, and other states followed. Cyber operations were used for espionage, disruption, and attack. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, was a landmark: a cyber weapon designed to sabotage Iran’s nuclear enrichment program, it demonstrated that cyber operations could cause physical damage to industrial facilities.
