The static front demanded a different kind of gun, and the belligerents built one. The howitzer, firing its shell in a high arc, could drop projectiles into trenches and onto the reverse slopes of hills where flat-trajectory field guns could not reach. The Germans entered the war with a heavy siege train, including 420mm “Big Bertha” mortars and 305mm Skoda guns borrowed from Austria-Hungary, and used them to smash the Belgian forts at Liège and Namur in August 1914. The British and French, who had gone to war with far fewer heavy guns, spent the next four years catching up. By 1916 the British had the 60-pounder gun and the 6-inch and 8-inch howitzers; by 1918 they had the 9.2-inch howitzer in numbers, a weapon that could throw a 290-pound shell nearly ten miles. The artillery park of a single British corps grew from a few dozen guns in 1914 to several hundred by 1917, and ammunition expenditure grew with it. The British fired about 1.5 million shells in the preliminary bombardment at the Somme in June 1916, which lasted a week. It did not destroy the German defenses, because the Germans had dug deep dugouts thirty feet below the surface and because a large share of the British shells were shrapnel, designed to kill men in the open and nearly useless against earthworks. The lesson, learned at enormous cost, was that the shell had to match the target: high-explosive for earthworks, shrapnel for open ground, gas for the flanks, and smoke to blind the defenders.

The Battle of Verdun, from 21 February to 18 December 1916, was the purest expression of the artillery war. The German plan, devised by chief of the general staff Erich von Falkenhayn, was not to capture the fortress town but to bleed the French army white by forcing it to defend a position it could not abandon. The Germans massed more than 1,200 guns along a front of about eight miles and fired about two million shells in the first four days. The French, under General Philippe Pétain, answered with the famous phrase “On ne passe pas”—they shall not pass—and fed divisions into the meat grinder along the one road that remained open, the Voie Sacrée, which carried about 90,000 men and 50,000 tons of supplies a week at the battle’s height. The battle produced roughly 700,000 casualties, French and German combined, on a battlefield that never moved more than a few miles in either direction. Verdun was not a battle of maneuver but of logistics, in which the side that could keep its guns fed and its men supplied held on. Artillery had become the arm that decided battles, and infantry the arm that occupied ground the artillery had already destroyed.

The shell shortage of 1915 was the first great industrial crisis of the war. The British Expeditionary Force had gone to France with a ration of shells per gun that assumed a short war, and by the spring of 1915 the guns were firing faster than the factories could supply them. The Battle of Neuve Chapelle in March 1915, the first British offensive of the war, was fought with a bombardment that lasted only thirty-five minutes because there were not enough shells for a longer one. The political fallout was severe: the Asquith government fell in May 1915 and was replaced by a coalition, and a new Ministry of Munitions under David Lloyd George took control of production. The ministry built new factories, conscripted skilled labor, and by 1916 the British were producing shells on a scale that would have seemed impossible two years earlier. The lesson was not lost on the other belligerents. The war had become a contest of industrial capacity, and the nation that could mobilize its factories as thoroughly as its armies would win.

The machine gun completed the transformation of the battlefield that the magazine rifle had begun. The Maxim gun, demonstrated by Hiram Maxim in 1884 and adopted by the British Army in .303 caliber in 1891, was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun. It used the recoil of the fired cartridge to cycle the action, so that a single gunner could fire 450 to 600 rounds per minute without any external power source. The Germans adopted a version of the Maxim as the Maschinengewehr 08, and by 1914 each German infantry regiment had a machine-gun company of six guns. The British, slow to adopt the weapon, went to war with two guns per battalion. The disparity mattered. A single well-sited machine gun, firing from a concrete pillbox or a trench parapet, could stop a battalion attack in the open, and the Germans built their defensive doctrine around the weapon. The British learned the lesson at the cost of tens of thousands of casualties on the first day of the Somme, 1 July 1916, when about 57,000 men were killed or wounded, most of them in the first hour, most by machine-gun and rifle fire from German positions that the week-long bombardment had failed to destroy.

The machine gun also changed the economics of killing. A trained infantryman with a bolt-action rifle could fire perhaps fifteen aimed rounds a minute. A machine-gun crew could fire several hundred, and the gun could be kept in action as long as the ammunition held out. The weapon did not require a large crew—two men could serve it—and it could be mounted on a tripod or a sledge and moved from position to position. The result was that a defensive line held by a few hundred men with machine guns could not be carried by an attack of several thousand infantry unless the attackers first suppressed the guns with artillery. The whole tactical problem of the war reduced to this: how to cross the open ground between the trenches before the machine guns cut the attackers down. The answer, when it came, was not a better infantry weapon but a combination of artillery, gas, tanks, and aircraft, coordinated into a single plan.

The tank was the most ambitious attempt to solve the problem. The idea of an armored vehicle that could cross trenches and crush wire had been proposed before the war, but the technical obstacles—a sufficiently powerful engine, a track that could grip soft ground, and armor heavy enough to stop machine-gun bullets—had not been overcome. The British Admiralty, under Winston Churchill, funded the development of a vehicle called a “land ship” and, for secrecy, a “tank.” The first prototype, “Little Willie,” ran in September 1915, and the first production model, the Mark I, went into action at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916. The Mark I was a rhomboid vehicle weighing about 28 tons, powered by a 105-horsepower Daimler engine, armed with either two 6-pounder guns or four machine guns, and crewed by eight men. It could cross a trench up to about nine feet wide and moved at about four miles an hour on good ground. Of the forty-nine tanks committed at Flers, only about a third reached the German lines, and their effect was more psychological than decisive. But the tank had shown that a vehicle could survive machine-gun fire and cross the wire, and the armies spent the rest of the war developing the weapon. The French built the Renault FT, a light tank with a rotating turret carrying a single gun, which became the template for almost every tank that followed. The Germans, slow to develop their own tanks, captured Allied machines and used them, and built only about twenty of their own A7V tanks. By 1918 the British and French had thousands of tanks, and they used them in mass at Amiens on 8 August 1918, when more than 400 British tanks broke through the German lines and the German commander Erich Ludendorff called it “the black day of the German Army.”

The tank was not a wonder weapon, and its early record was mixed. The machines broke down constantly, the crews suffered from heat, fumes, and noise, and the armor could be penetrated by field guns and the new anti-tank rifles. But the tank was the first weapon that could carry protected firepower across the killing zone, and it pointed toward the combined-arms tactics that would define the next war. The tank was also a weapon that required an industrial base: the British and French could build thousands because they had the factories, the steel, and the engineering capacity. The Germans, cut off from raw materials by the Allied blockade, could not match them. The blockade itself was a weapon, perhaps the most important of the war. The British Royal Navy’s distant blockade of the German coast, maintained from 1914 onward, cut Germany off from imported food, fertilizer, and industrial raw materials. By the winter of 1916–17 the German civilian population was living on turnips and ersatz bread, and the “turnip winter” killed hundreds of thousands of civilians. The blockade was a slow strangulation, and it contributed as much to the German collapse of 1918 as any battle.

The submarine was the German answer to the blockade, and it nearly brought Britain to its knees. The U-boat was a fragile weapon—early boats could dive only to about 150 feet and were slow underwater—but it was nearly invisible when submerged, and a single torpedo could sink a merchant ship. The Germans declared unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1917, and by April they were sinking about 880,000 tons of Allied and neutral shipping a month. The British Admiralty calculated that if the losses continued, Britain would run out of food and munitions within six months. The crisis was met by the convoy system, in which merchant ships sailed in groups escorted by warships, and by the entry of the United States into the war in April 1917. The convoy reduced losses dramatically, and the U-boat campaign failed. But the submarine had shown that a relatively cheap weapon, operated by a small crew, could threaten the survival of a great power. It was the first weapon of mass interdiction, and it changed the strategic calculus of naval warfare.

The aircraft was the newest weapon of the war, and its development was the fastest. The Wright brothers had flown in 1903, and by 1914 the airplane was a fragile machine of wood, wire, and fabric, capable of perhaps seventy miles an hour and carrying no armament. Its military uses were reconnaissance and artillery spotting, and the first months of the war were fought with aircraft that carried observers with binoculars and, later, cameras. The need to prevent enemy reconnaissance led to the arming of aircraft, first with pistols and rifles, then with machine guns mounted on the fuselage. The Germans developed a synchronizing gear that allowed a machine gun to fire through the propeller arc, and the Fokker Eindecker of 1915 gave the Germans a period of air superiority that the British called the “Fokker scourge.” The fighter aircraft was born, and the war produced increasingly capable machines: the Sopwith Camel, the SE5a, the Fokker D.VII, the SPAD XIII. By 1918 aircraft could fly at 130 miles an hour, climb to 20,000 feet, and carry two machine guns and a bomb load. The bomber had also appeared, and the Germans used Zeppelins and Gotha bombers to raid London, killing about 1,400 people and injuring about 3,400. The raids did little military damage, but they showed that the airplane could carry the war to the enemy’s homeland, and they prompted the creation of the world’s first independent air force, the British Royal Air Force, in April 1918.

The air war was a war of production and training as much as of tactics. The British and French built about 150,000 aircraft during the war, and the Germans about 48,000. The life expectancy of a fighter pilot on the Western Front was measured in weeks, and the aces—men who shot down five or more enemy aircraft—became the public face of the war in the air. The most famous, the German Manfred von Richthofen, the “Red Baron,” was credited with eighty victories before he was killed in April 1918. But the air war was also a war of attrition, in which the side that could replace its pilots and aircraft faster would prevail, and the Allies, with their larger industrial base, won that war.

The war on the Eastern Front was different, and it showed how much geography and technology shape the character of a war. The front was longer, the forces more dispersed, and the fighting more mobile than in the west. The Russians had enormous manpower but inadequate industry, and their armies were chronically short of rifles, shells, and even boots. The German and Austro-Hungarian armies, better equipped and better led, won a series of spectacular victories: the Battle of Tannenberg in August 1914, in which the Germans encircled and destroyed the Russian Second Army; the Gorlice-Tarnów offensive of 1915, which drove the Russians out of Poland; and the Brusilov offensive of 1916, the Russians’ greatest success but also the beginning of the collapse of the Russian army. The Eastern Front also saw the first large-scale use of poison gas, at Bolimów in January 1915, and the development of the trench mortar and hand grenade into essential infantry weapons. The Russians, short of artillery, relied on the bayonet and the shovel, and their soldiers dug in with the same desperate ingenuity as the soldiers in the west.

The Ottoman Empire entered the war on the side of the Central Powers in November 1914, and the fighting in the Middle East and the Caucasus opened new fronts. The Gallipoli campaign of 1915, in which British, French, Australian, New Zealand, and Indian troops attempted to force the Dardanelles and knock the Ottomans out of the war, was a failure that cost about 250,000 casualties on each side. The campaign was a lesson in the difficulty of amphibious operations against a defended shore, and in the limits of naval power: the British and French battleships that bombarded the Ottoman forts could not force the straits without minesweepers, and the minesweepers could not operate under the Ottoman guns. The campaign was also the first in which aircraft played a significant role in spotting for naval gunfire, and the first in which a submarine—the British E11—sank an Ottoman battleship in the Sea of Marmara.

The war in the Middle East was a war of cavalry and railways, of camels and armored cars. The British and their Arab allies, encouraged by T. E. Lawrence, waged a guerrilla campaign against the Ottoman railway that supplied Medina, showing how a small force with modern weapons—rifles, machine guns, explosives—could tie down a much larger force. The Battle of Megiddo in September 1918, in which British and Indian troops broke the Ottoman army in Palestine, was a model of combined-arms warfare: cavalry, infantry, artillery, and aircraft working together to destroy an enemy in a single battle. The war in the desert also saw the first use of aircraft for strategic bombing against Ottoman supply lines, and the first use of motorized transport to move troops across long distances.

The war at sea was dominated by the dreadnought battleship, the most expensive weapon system of its day. The British Royal Navy had launched HMS Dreadnought in 1906, a battleship armed with ten 12-inch guns and powered by steam turbines, and the ship had made every previous battleship obsolete overnight. The naval arms race between Britain and Germany that followed was one of the causes of the war, and the Battle of Jutland on 31 May 1916 was the only major fleet engagement of the war. The British Grand Fleet, under Admiral John Jellicoe, and the German High Seas Fleet, under Admiral Reinhard Scheer, fought for about twelve hours in the North Sea. The British lost fourteen ships and about 6,000 men; the Germans lost eleven ships and about 2,500 men. The battle was a tactical draw and a strategic British victory, because the German fleet retreated to port and never again challenged the British blockade. Jutland showed that the battleship was vulnerable to mines, torpedoes, and plunging fire, and that the decisive weapon at sea might be the submarine and the mine rather than the big gun.

The war ended on 11 November 1918, and the weapons developed during it did not disappear. The tank, the airplane, the submarine, the machine gun, and poison gas all remained in the arsenals of the victorious powers, and the lessons of the war were studied by a generation of officers who would command the armies of the next war. The most important lesson, at least for the Germans, was that the trench deadlock could be broken by a combination of speed, surprise, and concentrated firepower. The German stormtrooper tactics of 1918, in which small groups of heavily armed infantry infiltrated the enemy lines and bypassed strong points, were the prototype of the modern infantry squad. The British and French, by contrast, drew the lesson that the war had been won by firepower and attrition, and they built their postwar armies around the defensive power of the machine gun and the artillery. The difference in doctrine would matter in 1940.

The interwar years were a period of intense experimentation and, in some countries, of deliberate neglect. The tank developed rapidly in Britain and France, where the technical problems of armor, suspension, and engine power were gradually solved. The British built the Vickers Medium tank and the experimental “Mother” tank, and the theorists J. F. C. Fuller and Basil Liddell Hart argued that tanks, supported by aircraft and motorized infantry, could break through an enemy front and exploit the breakthrough to a depth of hundreds of miles. The French built the Char B1, a heavy tank with a powerful gun and thick armor, and the SOMUA S35, a cavalry tank with good speed and armor. But the French army, which had borne the brunt of the war, was committed to the doctrine of the continuous front and the methodical battle, and it distributed its tanks among the infantry divisions rather than concentrating them in armored divisions. The Germans, forbidden by the Treaty of Versailles from having tanks, studied the British theorists and built a doctrine of armored warfare around the panzer division, a combined-arms formation of tanks, motorized infantry, artillery, and engineers. The German tank, the Panzerkampfwagen I, was a light training vehicle, but the doctrine was sound, and the Germans tested it in the Spanish Civil War and in the invasion of Poland.

The airplane developed even faster. The monoplane replaced the biplane, the radial engine replaced the inline engine, and the all-metal stressed-skin fuselage replaced the fabric-covered frame. By the mid-1930s the bomber could carry a ton of bombs at 200 miles an hour over a range of a thousand miles, and the fighter could fly at 350 miles an hour. The theorists of air power, most notably the Italian Giulio Douhet and the American Billy Mitchell, argued that the bomber would be the decisive weapon of the next war, that a fleet of bombers could destroy an enemy’s cities and industry and break its will to fight without the need for a land battle. The theory was influential and shaped the rearmament programs of the 1930s, but it was also wrong in important respects. The bomber of the 1930s could not carry enough bombs to destroy a modern city, and the fighter could intercept it. The air war of 1939–45 would be a war of attrition between bombers and fighters, and the bomber would not break civilian morale.

The naval powers developed the aircraft carrier, the weapon that would replace the battleship as the capital ship of the next war. The British had converted the battlecruiser Furious and the battleship Eagle to carriers during the First World War, and the Americans and Japanese built purpose-built carriers in the 1920s and 1930s. The Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 limited the size of battleships and carriers, and it encouraged the development of the carrier as a way of preserving naval power within the treaty limits. The Japanese built the Akagi and Kaga, the Americans the Lexington and Saratoga, and the British the Courageous and Glorious. The carrier was a floating airfield, and its striking power was its aircraft, which could attack ships at a range of hundreds of miles, beyond the range of any battleship gun. The theory of carrier warfare was developed by the Japanese and American navies in the 1920s and 1930s, and it would be tested at Pearl Harbor and Midway.

The Second World War was the most destructive war in human history, and it was also the war in which weapons development reached a new level of intensity. The war began on 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, and it ended on 2 September 1945, when Japan surrendered on the deck of the USS Missouri. In between, about seventy million people died, and the weapons that killed them were the products of the most intensive scientific and industrial effort ever mounted. The war was fought on land, at sea, and in the air, and with weapons that ranged from the rifle to the atomic bomb.

The German invasion of Poland in 1939 was a demonstration of the new combined-arms warfare. The German army attacked with sixty divisions, including six panzer divisions and four motorized divisions, supported by about 2,000 aircraft. The Polish army, smaller and less well equipped, was overwhelmed in about five weeks. The German tactics—the concentrated use of tanks and aircraft to break through a weak point in the enemy line and then exploit the breakthrough with motorized infantry—were called Blitzkrieg, “lightning war,” and they were the most important tactical innovation of the war. The Blitzkrieg was not a new weapon but a new way of using existing ones. The tank, the dive bomber, the motorized infantry, and the radio were all available before the war, but the Germans were the first to combine them into a single doctrine and to organize their army around it.

The French campaign of May 1940 was the decisive test of the Blitzkrieg. The French army was larger than the German army and had more and better tanks. The French Char B1 bis was a heavy tank with a 47mm gun and 60mm of armor, and the SOMUA S35 was a well-armored cavalry tank. But the French army was organized for a methodical battle, and it had distributed its tanks among its infantry divisions. The German army attacked through the Ardennes, a region the French had considered impassable for tanks, and broke through the French line at Sedan on 13 May 1940. The German panzer divisions then drove to the English Channel, cutting the Allied armies in two. The British Expeditionary Force was evacuated from Dunkirk in late May and early June, and France surrendered on 22 June 1940. The campaign had lasted six weeks and had destroyed the French army, which had been considered the best in Europe. The lesson was that doctrine and organization mattered as much as the weapons themselves.

The Battle of Britain, from July to October 1940, was the first major battle fought entirely in the air. The German Luftwaffe, under Hermann Göring, attempted to destroy the Royal Air Force and gain air superiority over southern England as a prelude to invasion. The RAF, under Hugh Dowding, had the advantage of an integrated air defense system that included radar, ground observers, and a centralized command and control network. The British radar stations, the Chain Home network, could detect incoming German aircraft at a range of about 100 miles, and the RAF could concentrate its fighters against the bombers. The German fighters, the Messerschmitt Bf 109, were superior to the British Hawker Hurricane and Supermarine Spitfire in some respects, but the British had the advantage of fighting over their own territory, where shot-down pilots could be recovered. The battle was a German defeat and the first major setback for the German war machine. The RAF lost about 1,000 aircraft and the Luftwaffe about 1,900, and the German bombing campaign against British cities, the Blitz, killed about 40,000 civilians but did not break British morale.

The war at sea was a war of convoys and submarines, of carriers and battleships. The German U-boat campaign against Allied shipping in the Atlantic was the most dangerous threat to Britain’s survival. The Germans built about 1,100 U-boats during the war, and they sank about 2,600 Allied and neutral merchant ships, totaling about 14 million tons. The British and their allies developed the convoy system, the escort carrier, the long-range patrol aircraft, and the radar and sonar that could detect a submerged submarine. The codebreakers at Bletchley Park, who broke the German Enigma cipher, gave the Allies advance warning of U-boat movements, and the combination of these measures defeated the U-boat campaign by 1943. The Battle of the Atlantic was a war of technology and intelligence as much as of ships and guns, and it was won by the side that could innovate faster.

The aircraft carrier replaced the battleship as the decisive naval weapon in the Pacific. The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 was carried out by six Japanese carriers and about 350 aircraft, and it sank or damaged eight American battleships and destroyed about 180 American aircraft. The attack was a tactical success and a strategic failure, because it did not destroy the American carriers, which were at sea, and it brought the United States into the war. The Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942 was the first naval battle in which the opposing ships never saw each other, and the Battle of Midway in June 1942 was the decisive carrier battle of the war. The Americans, under Chester Nimitz, had broken the Japanese naval code and knew that the Japanese planned to attack Midway. The American carriers Yorktown, Enterprise, and Hornet ambushed the Japanese fleet and sank four Japanese carriers—Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, and Hiryu—in a single day. The Japanese lost about 3,000 men, including many of their best pilots, and the balance of naval power in the Pacific shifted to the Americans. Midway was the most important naval battle of the war, and it was fought entirely by aircraft.

The war on the Eastern Front was the largest land war in history. The German invasion of the Soviet Union, Operation Barbarossa, began on 22 June 1941, and it involved about 3.8 million Axis troops, 3,600 tanks, and 2,700 aircraft. The Germans advanced to the outskirts of Moscow by December 1941, but they were stopped by the Soviet counteroffensive and the Russian winter. The Battle of Stalingrad, from August 1942 to February 1943, was the turning point of the war in the east. The German Sixth Army, under Friedrich Paulus, attempted to capture the city of Stalingrad on the Volga River, and the Soviets, under Georgy Zhukov, defended it street by street. The Soviets then launched a counteroffensive, Operation Uranus, which encircled the German Sixth Army and cut it off from its supplies. Paulus surrendered on 2 February 1943, and about 91,000 German soldiers were taken prisoner. The battle cost the Germans about 800,000 casualties and the Soviets about 1.1 million, and it destroyed the German Sixth Army. The Battle of Kursk in July 1943 was the largest tank battle in history and the last German offensive in the east. The Soviets had about 3,600 tanks and the Germans about 2,700, and the battle ended in a Soviet victory that gave the Red Army the initiative for the rest of the war.

The Soviet T-34 tank was the best tank design of the war. It had a 76mm gun, 45mm of sloped armor, and a 500-horsepower diesel engine, and it was simple, rugged, and easy to mass-produce. The German tanks of 1941, the Panzer III and Panzer IV, were outgunned and outarmored by the T-34, and the Germans were shocked by the quality of the Soviet tank. The Germans responded with the Tiger tank, which had an 88mm gun and 100mm of armor, and the Panther, which had a 75mm gun and 80mm of sloped armor. The Tiger and Panther were superior to the T-34 in firepower and armor, but they were complex, expensive, and unreliable, and the Germans could not build enough of them. The Soviet Union built about 57,000 T-34s during the war, and the United States built about 49,000 Sherman tanks. German tank production was about 20,000 tanks of all types. The lesson was that the best tank is not the one with the best specifications but the one that can be built in the largest numbers and kept in action.

The strategic bombing campaign against Germany was the most ambitious attempt to use air power to win a war. The British Bomber Command, under Arthur Harris, and the American Eighth Air Force, under Carl Spaatz, bombed German cities and industry from 1942 to 1945. The British bombed at night and the Americans by day, and the combined campaign dropped about 1.5 million tons of bombs on Germany. The campaign killed about 400,000 German civilians and destroyed or damaged about 3.6 million homes. It did not break German morale, and it did not stop German war production, which actually increased until 1944. The bombing campaign did divert German resources—about a million men and a large share of German fighter production—to the defense of the Reich, and it did destroy the German oil industry by 1945. But the campaign was enormously costly: the British lost about 55,000 aircrew and the Americans about 26,000, and the German defenses shot down about 40,000 Allied aircraft. The strategic bombing campaign was a war of attrition in the air, won by the side with the larger industrial base.

The bombing of Japan was even more destructive. The American B-29 Superfortress, which entered service in 1944, could carry a bomb load of about 20,000 pounds at a range of 1,500 miles and an altitude of 30,000 feet. The B-29 was the most advanced bomber of the war, and it was used to firebomb Japanese cities. The raid on Tokyo on 9–10 March 1945 killed about 100,000 people and destroyed about 16 square miles of the city, and it was the deadliest air raid of the war. The firebombing campaign destroyed about 60 percent of the built-up area of Japan’s major cities and killed about 300,000 people. The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 were the culmination of the bombing campaign, and they killed about 200,000 people. The atomic bomb was a new kind of weapon, and it changed the nature of war.

The Manhattan Project was the largest scientific and industrial effort of the war. It began in 1942, under the direction of Leslie Groves and Robert Oppenheimer, and it employed about 130,000 people and cost about $2 billion. The project produced two types of atomic bomb: a uranium gun-type device, code-named “Little Boy,” and a plutonium implosion device, code-named “Fat Man.” The first nuclear detonation, the Trinity test, took place on 16 July 1945 at Alamogordo, New Mexico. The device, a plutonium implosion bomb code-named “Gadget,” was detonated on a steel tower and produced a yield of about 21 kilotons, roughly equivalent to 21,000 tons of TNT. The Trinity test was the first detonation of a nuclear weapon, and it opened the nuclear age. The bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, and Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945. The atomic bomb ended the war and began a new era in which the survival of humanity depended on the restraint of the nations that possessed the weapon.

The Second World War was a war of production as much as of tactics. The United States, which entered the war in December 1941, produced about 300,000 aircraft, 100,000 tanks, and 6,000 ships during the war, and it supplied its allies with weapons and equipment on a scale that no other nation could match. The Soviet Union produced about 150,000 aircraft and 100,000 tanks, and it bore the brunt of the land war in Europe. The British produced about 130,000 aircraft and 30,000 tanks. Germany produced about 120,000 aircraft and 60,000 tanks, and Japan about 75,000 aircraft and 5,000 tanks. Allied production was about three times that of the Axis, and the disparity was decisive. The war was won by the side that could build the most weapons and get them to the front.

The lessons of the Second World War shaped the weapons and doctrines of the Cold War. The atomic bomb made a direct war between the great powers unthinkable, and the two superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union, competed through proxy wars, arms races, and technological competition. The nuclear arms race produced weapons of enormous destructive power: the hydrogen bomb, first tested by the United States in 1952 and by the Soviet Union in 1953, had a yield of megatons, hundreds of times more powerful than the atomic bombs of 1945. The intercontinental ballistic missile, developed in the 1950s, could deliver a nuclear warhead to a target on the other side of the world in about thirty minutes. The submarine-launched ballistic missile, developed in the 1960s, gave the nuclear powers a second-strike capability that made a first strike futile. The result was the doctrine of mutually assured destruction, which held that a nuclear war would destroy both sides and that the only rational policy was deterrence.

The Cold War was also a period of intense conventional weapons development. The jet engine, developed independently by British and German engineers in the 1930s, replaced the piston engine in the fighters of the 1950s. The swept wing, developed by the Germans during the war, allowed aircraft to fly near the speed of sound, and the afterburner allowed them to exceed it. The air-to-air missile, developed in the 1950s, replaced the gun as the primary weapon of the fighter, and the radar-guided missile allowed a fighter to attack a target beyond visual range. The helicopter, developed during the war, became a weapon of mobile warfare in the 1960s, and the armed helicopter, the gunship, was used extensively in the Vietnam War. The assault rifle, developed by the Germans during the war as the StG 44, became the standard infantry weapon of the postwar armies. The StG 44 fired an intermediate cartridge, the 7.92mm Kurz, less powerful than a full-power rifle cartridge but more powerful than a pistol cartridge, and it allowed a soldier to fire on full automatic with some control. The Soviet AK-47, designed by Mikhail Kalashnikov in 1947, was the most widely produced assault rifle in history, and it became the symbol of the guerrilla fighter and the insurgent.

The Vietnam War was the first war in which the helicopter and the precision-guided weapon played a significant role. The American strategy was to use air mobility—the helicopter—to move troops quickly to the point of contact, and to use air power to destroy the enemy’s supply lines. The helicopter gunship, the Bell AH-1 Cobra, was used to escort the transport helicopters and attack enemy positions, and the Boeing B-52 bomber was used to drop massive loads of bombs on suspected enemy base areas. The laser-guided bomb, developed in the 1960s, was used to destroy bridges and other point targets with a single bomb, and it was the first precision-guided munition used in combat. The Vietnamese communists, who lacked air power and heavy weapons, used guerrilla tactics, tunnels, and the Ho Chi Minh Trail to sustain their forces, and they won the war by wearing down American public support. The Vietnam War was a lesson in the limits of technology: the most advanced weapons in the world could not defeat a determined enemy who was willing to accept heavy casualties and who had the support of the local population.

The 1973 Yom Kippur War was a demonstration of the new precision-guided weapons. The Egyptian and Syrian armies attacked Israel on 6 October 1973, and they used Soviet-supplied anti-tank guided missiles and shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles to inflict heavy losses on the Israeli armored and air forces. The Egyptian infantry, equipped with the AT-3 Sagger missile, destroyed about 250 Israeli tanks in the first days of the war, and the Syrian and Egyptian air defenses, equipped with the SA-6 missile, shot down about 100 Israeli aircraft. The Israeli air force, which had dominated the skies in 1967, was forced to change its tactics, and the Israeli army, which had relied on the tank, was forced to develop combined-arms tactics to defeat the missile. The war was a warning that the precision-guided weapon would change the nature of conventional warfare, and the armies of the world studied it closely.

The 1982 Lebanon War was the first war in which a modern air force destroyed an integrated air defense system. The Israeli air force, using drones to locate the Syrian SA-6 and SA-8 missile batteries in the Bekaa Valley, destroyed the Syrian air defense system in a single day, then shot down about 80 Syrian aircraft without losing a single plane. The Israeli success was the result of a combination of technology—the drone, the precision-guided weapon, the airborne warning and control aircraft—and tactics—

chapters.title: Part 37
chapters.preview: The Bekaa Valley campaign of June 1982 became the template for air power over the next four decades. The Israelis did not simply buy better missiles; they built a system in which every element fed every other.
paragraphs: The Bekaa Valley campaign of June 1982 became the template for air power over the next four decades. The Israelis did not simply buy better missiles; they built a system in which every element fed every other. Days before the main strike, small remotely piloted vehicles—the Scout and the Mastiff—loitered over the valley and, in deliberate provocation, flew low enough to be engaged. The Syrians, relying on doctrine absorbed from their Soviet advisers, switched on their radars and launched missiles. The missiles missed the small, slow, hard-to-see drones, but the launch signatures were recorded. The Israelis now knew where the batteries were, what frequencies they radiated on, and how long they took to go from cold to firing. When the main attack came on 9 June, the air force used a coordinated package: drones to draw fire and locate, electronic warfare to jam and blind the command links, precision-guided bombs to kill the launchers, and fighter-bombers with anti-radiation missiles to hunt the radars. The Syrians lost the equivalent of a full air-defense division in hours, and the Israeli air force, shielded by the collapse of the Syrian umbrella, was free to operate over the battlefield. The lesson the world drew was not that one weapon had triumphed but that the integration of sensors, communications, and precision munitions had produced a new kind of military system—one in which the speed of information transfer mattered more than the mass of firepower.

That lesson matured unevenly. The United States, which had watched the Bekaa Valley with professional interest, spent the rest of the 1980s building the architecture to do the same thing on a much larger scale: the Joint Surveillance Target Attack Radar System, the airborne warning and control aircraft, the global positioning system, and the communications links that would eventually be called the "military-technical revolution" and then, more grandly, the "revolution in military affairs." The Soviet Union drew a different and ultimately fatal conclusion. Soviet theorists understood the implications of precision-guided weapons and reconnaissance-strike complexes, and they wrote about them with real sophistication; but the Soviet economy could not produce the electronics, and the Soviet system could not reform fast enough to field them. The gap that opened in the 1980s between what the Americans could see and do and what the Soviets could see and do was one of the deep causes of the Soviet collapse. Weapons development, in other words, is never only about weapons. It is a test of industrial capacity, of organizational flexibility, and of a society's willingness to pay for capabilities whose payoff may not arrive for a generation.

The 1991 Gulf War was the first large-scale demonstration of what the new system could do. The coalition air campaign, which ran for thirty-eight days before the ground offensive, was built around a target list of unprecedented specificity: command bunkers, air-defense nodes, bridges, power stations, and Iraqi nuclear, chemical, and biological facilities. The weapons that struck these targets were, for the most part, precision-guided. The numbers are worth setting down carefully, because they are often misremembered. Coalition aircraft dropped roughly 88,500 tons of bombs during Desert Storm. Of that total, about 6,520 tons—roughly 7.4 percent—were precision-guided. The overwhelming majority of the tonnage was still unguided, "dumb" bombs dropped by aircraft that had to fly into the teeth of Iraqi air defenses. Yet the precision fraction, small as it was, did most of the visible damage to the things that mattered. Laser-guided bombs dropped down ventilation shafts, destroyed bridges with single hits, and severed the Iraqi command network. The television images of a bomb falling through a building's roof and exploding inside became the defining visual of the war, and they shaped public expectations of air power for a generation.

The gap between the 7.4 percent and the public perception was itself a strategic fact. The coalition had achieved something new: it had made war look clean, at least on television. The precision weapon promised that war could be surgical, that the right targets could be struck and the wrong ones spared, that the awful arithmetic of area bombing could be replaced by the careful arithmetic of the single bomb. That promise was partly true and partly a story told by the people who benefited from it. The same war saw the bombing of the Amiriyah shelter in Baghdad, where hundreds of civilians were killed by two precision-guided bombs aimed at what was believed to be a military command bunker; the guidance was precise, but the intelligence was wrong. Precision did not eliminate error; it changed the relationship between the weapon and the error. A dumb bomb that missed by a hundred meters was a tragedy of imprecision. A precision bomb that hit exactly the wrong target was a tragedy of knowledge. The distinction would matter more and more as the decades passed.

The ground war, when it came, lasted a hundred hours. The Iraqi army in Kuwait was destroyed from the air before it could maneuver, and the coalition's tanks and infantry advanced against an enemy that had been blinded and paralyzed. The American M1 Abrams tank, the Bradley fighting vehicle, and the multiple-launch rocket system performed as designed, but the decisive advantage was not in any single platform. It was in the coalition's ability to see the battlefield in real time, to pass information from sensor to shooter faster than the Iraqis could react, and to concentrate firepower with a precision impossible a generation earlier. The "left hook" that swept around the Iraqi defenses was a maneuver out of the textbook, but it was executed with a situational awareness the textbook had never imagined. The Iraqis, who had fought a long and bloody war against Iran in the 1980s, were not incompetent; they were operating in a different information age.

The Gulf War also revealed the limits of the new system. The Iraqi Scud launches against Israel and Saudi Arabia were a political problem the coalition's air power could not solve. The coalition flew thousands of sorties hunting mobile Scud launchers and destroyed very few; the launchers moved at night, hid in culverts and under bridges, and were replaced faster than they could be killed. The Patriot missile, rushed into service to defend against the Scuds, was later shown to have had a poor record of actually intercepting them, though the political effect of the deployment was real. The lesson was that precision and information dominance did not automatically translate into the ability to find and kill a small, mobile, dispersed target—a lesson that would be relearned, painfully, in Afghanistan and Iraq.

The 1990s were the decade in which the precision revolution became the organizing principle of Western military procurement. The budget battles of the post-Cold War period were fought over what kind of military the United States and its allies should have. Advocates of the "revolution in military affairs" argued that information technology had changed the nature of war, that the age of mass armies and heavy armored formations was over, and that the future belonged to small, networked, precision-strike forces. Advocates of the older model argued that the world was still dangerous, that the peace dividend was a fantasy, and that the ability to fight a conventional war against a peer competitor should not be traded away for a technological vision. The outcome was a compromise that satisfied no one: the Americans kept their heavy formations but lavished money on precision munitions and the networks to guide them, while the Europeans, with smaller budgets and different strategic cultures, struggled to keep up.

The wars of the 1990s were the testing ground. The 1999 Kosovo campaign was fought entirely from the air, at high altitude, by aircraft that rarely saw their targets. The precision weapons did enormous damage to the Serbian military and infrastructure, but they also killed civilians—in a refugee convoy, in a television station, in the Chinese embassy, where a misidentified building was struck by precision-guided bombs. The Chinese embassy bombing was a particularly instructive case. The intelligence was wrong, the targeting was precise, and the political consequences were enormous. The Chinese government, which had been watching the American way of war with growing alarm, concluded that precision weapons were a strategic threat and that China needed the means to counter them. The Chinese anti-access/area-denial strategy, which would dominate military thinking in the 2010s and 2020s, had one of its origins in a bomb that hit the wrong building in Belgrade.

Kosovo also exposed a structural problem that would only grow worse. The Europeans, who flew a significant share of the sorties, discovered that their aircraft could not communicate with American aircraft, that their munitions were not precision-guided, and that their intelligence was not integrated into the American system. The capability gap, widening since the 1980s, became a political embarrassment. The European Union launched a series of initiatives to close it, with limited success. The lesson was that the precision revolution was not a set of gadgets that could be bought off the shelf; it was a system, and a system required a level of investment and integration only the United States could afford.

The wars after 2001 changed the terms of the debate again. The invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq were conventional campaigns against conventional armies, won quickly and with remarkably few American casualties. The precision weapons did their job. But the occupations that followed were a different kind of war, and the weapons that had won the conventional phase were often irrelevant to the guerrilla phase. The insurgents in Iraq and Afghanistan had no air defenses, command bunkers, or armored divisions. They had improvised explosive devices, small arms, and the ability to blend into the population. The American military, which had spent two decades preparing to fight a precision war against a peer competitor, found itself fighting a counterinsurgency with equipment designed for a different conflict.

The response was a new wave of weapons development, driven by the immediate needs of the battlefield rather than long-range planning. The most important was the Mine-Resistant Ambush-Protected vehicle, or MRAP, rushed into production to protect soldiers from IEDs. The MRAP was not a precision weapon; it was a heavy, ungainly truck with a V-shaped hull that deflected blast energy away from the occupants. It saved thousands of lives, and it was a reminder that the history of weapons is not a simple story of ever-greater precision and sophistication. Sometimes the most important development is a humble piece of engineering that solves a specific, dirty problem. The MRAP also illustrated how fast a modern industrial system could respond to a battlefield requirement: within a few years, the United States had produced tens of thousands of vehicles and shipped them to the war zone, a mobilization that would have impressed the planners of the Second World War.

The other great development of the counterinsurgency era was the armed drone. The Predator, originally a reconnaissance platform, was fitted with Hellfire missiles and used to kill individual insurgent leaders in Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, and Afghanistan. The drone was a precision weapon in the most literal sense: it allowed a remote pilot, sitting in a trailer in Nevada, to watch a target for hours and then fire a missile with a very small margin of error. The drone also changed the politics of war. It allowed the United States to kill people in countries with which it was not at war, without risking American lives, and without the visible military presence that would have provoked a political crisis. The drone was, in that sense, the perfect weapon for the post-9/11 era: precise, deniable, and cheap.

But the drone also raised questions the precision revolution had been dodging since 1991. If a weapon can kill a specific person, who decides which person to kill? What evidence is required? What happens when the intelligence is wrong and a wedding party is struck instead of a militant convoy? The drone strikes in Pakistan and Yemen killed many militants, but they also killed civilians, and the political cost of those deaths was high. The debate over drone warfare was, at bottom, a debate about the ethics of precision: whether the ability to strike a target with minimal collateral damage made it easier to go to war, and whether the people who operated the drones were morally responsible for the deaths they caused. The answers were not obvious, and they were not settled.

The technological trajectory of the drone pointed toward something even more consequential. If a drone could be flown remotely, why not autonomously? The military had been developing autonomous systems for decades—cruise missiles that navigated by terrain matching, missiles that homed on radar emissions, mines that waited for a target to pass. But the combination of cheap computing, satellite navigation, and advanced sensors made it possible to imagine weapons that could find and engage targets without a human in the loop. The ethical and legal questions raised by autonomous weapons were profound, and the international community began to debate them in earnest in the 2010s. The debate was complicated by the fact that the technology was dual-use, that the line between a "semi-autonomous" weapon and a "fully autonomous" one was blurry, and that the major military powers had no interest in a treaty that would constrain their development.

The 2006 Lebanon War was a preview of how precision weapons would reshape the battlefield in the hands of a non-state actor. Hezbollah, the Lebanese militia, had spent years building an arsenal of rockets and missiles, and it had learned from the Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in 2000 how to fight a modern army. During the thirty-four-day war, Hezbollah fired thousands of rockets into Israel, using mobile launchers that could be set up, fired, and hidden in minutes. The Israeli air force, which had dominated the skies in 1982 and 1991, found it difficult to suppress the rocket fire. The rockets were small, dispersed, and often fired from civilian areas. The Israelis responded with precision strikes against launchers and infrastructure, but the strikes did not stop the rocket fire, and the ground war that followed was bloody and inconclusive. The lesson was that precision weapons were not a magic solution to asymmetric warfare; a determined, well-organized non-state actor could use simple, cheap weapons to impose costs on a technologically superior opponent.

The 2006 war also demonstrated the growing importance of air-defense systems in the hands of non-state actors. Hezbollah used man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS, to threaten Israeli helicopters and low-flying aircraft, and it used anti-ship missiles to strike an Israeli corvette off the coast. The corvette strike was a shock: a small, cheap missile, fired by a militia, had damaged a modern warship. The lesson was that the proliferation of precision-guided weapons was not confined to the great powers. The same technologies that had given the Americans and the Israelis their edge were now available, in degraded but still lethal forms, to anyone with the money and the connections to buy them.

The proliferation problem was the dark side of the precision revolution. The technologies that made precision weapons possible—satellite navigation, cheap microprocessors, miniaturized sensors, and secure communications—were commercial technologies, available to anyone who could buy them. The genie could not be put back in the bottle. The result was a gradual leveling of the battlefield, in which the gap between the most advanced military and its opponents narrowed, not because the opponents became as capable as the advanced military, but because the advanced military's advantages became less decisive. A precision-guided artillery shell, fired by a poorly trained crew with a cheap drone spotting for it, could destroy a tank that cost a hundred times as much. The economics of warfare were shifting in ways that favored the defense.

The wars in Iraq and Syria against the Islamic State, from 2014 to 2019, were fought with a combination of precision air power and local ground forces. The coalition air campaign was one of the most precise in history, with thousands of strikes against ISIS targets, and it was supported by a vast intelligence and surveillance apparatus. The results were impressive: the caliphate was destroyed, and the territorial defeat of ISIS was achieved with a relatively small number of Western ground troops. But the campaign also showed the limits of precision. The city of Mosul was reduced to rubble in the fighting, and thousands of civilians were killed. The precision weapons could destroy a building with a single bomb, but they could not rebuild it, and they could not prevent the political chaos that followed the military victory.

The Syrian civil war, which began in 2011, was a laboratory for a different kind of weapons development. The Syrian government, backed by Russia and Iran, used barrel bombs, chemical weapons, and indiscriminate artillery fire against rebel-held areas. The rebels, backed by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and the United States, used anti-tank guided missiles, improvised explosive devices, and, eventually, armed drones. The war was a showcase for the proliferation of precision-guided munitions to non-state actors: the TOW missile, supplied by the United States, became a symbol of the rebels' ability to destroy government tanks, and the footage of TOW strikes, uploaded to YouTube, became a form of propaganda. The war also demonstrated the growing role of Russia in the global arms market, as Moscow used the conflict to test new weapons and to advertise them to foreign buyers.

The Russian intervention in Syria, which began in 2015, was a turning point in the history of precision warfare. The Russians, who had watched the American precision campaigns of the 1990s and 2000s with a mixture of envy and alarm, had spent a decade rebuilding their military. They had developed new precision weapons, new drones, and new command-and-control systems, and they used Syria as a proving ground. The Russian air campaign was less precise than the American one—the Russians used unguided bombs and cluster munitions, and they killed many civilians—but it was effective. The Russians demonstrated that a modern military could achieve its objectives with a combination of precision and mass, and that the American way of war was not the only way.

The Russian experience in Syria fed into a new generation of Russian weapons, unveiled in 2018 in a carefully staged presentation by President Vladimir Putin. The weapons included the Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missile, the Avangard hypersonic glide vehicle, the Poseidon nuclear torpedo, and the Burevestnik nuclear-powered cruise missile. The presentation was a political statement as much as a military one: a declaration that Russia would not accept permanent technological inferiority to the United States, and that it was willing to invest in exotic weapons to offset American advantages. Some of these weapons were real, some were aspirational, and some were probably propaganda, but the message was clear. The precision revolution had not ended; it had entered a new phase, in which the great powers competed to develop weapons that could defeat the defenses the others had built.

The most important of these new weapons was the hypersonic missile. A hypersonic missile flies at more than five times the speed of sound, and it can maneuver in flight, which makes it difficult to intercept. The American, Russian, and Chinese militaries all invested heavily in hypersonic technology in the 2010s and 2020s, and the result was a new arms race that resembled, in some ways, the nuclear arms race of the Cold War. The hypersonic missile was a precision weapon, but it was also a strategic weapon, because it could carry a nuclear warhead and because its speed and maneuverability made it a first-strike weapon. The development of hypersonic missiles raised the same questions the atomic bomb had raised in 1945: how do you defend against a weapon that can reach its target before you can react?

The answer, at least in the early 2020s, was that you could not defend against it with any confidence. American missile-defense systems, built to intercept ballistic missiles on predictable trajectories, were not designed to intercept maneuvering hypersonic vehicles. The Russians and the Chinese, who had invested in hypersonic technology earlier and more aggressively than the Americans, had a temporary advantage. The Americans responded with a crash program to develop their own hypersonic weapons and to build new sensors and interceptors to defend against them. The program was expensive and technically difficult, and it was not clear, even to its advocates, that it would work. The hypersonic race was a reminder that the history of weapons is a history of action and reaction, of measures and countermeasures, and that every new weapon provokes a response that may be more dangerous than the weapon itself.

The 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war was a landmark in the history of precision warfare, and it deserves to be examined in detail. The war, which lasted forty-four days, was fought between Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed territory of Nagorno-Karabakh. Azerbaijan, which had spent years building up its military with Turkish and Israeli help, used armed drones—particularly the Turkish Bayraktar TB2—and loitering munitions to devastating effect against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses. The Bayraktar TB2 was a medium-altitude, long-endurance drone that could carry laser-guided bombs and anti-tank missiles. It was not a particularly advanced drone by American standards, but it was cheap, reliable, and available in quantity, and it was integrated into a Turkish command-and-control system that gave the Azerbaijanis a real-time picture of the battlefield.

The results were dramatic. The Armenian army, which had relied on Soviet-era tanks, artillery, and air-defense systems, was unable to cope with the drone threat. The Armenian air defenses, designed to shoot down aircraft, could not reliably detect and engage the small, slow-flying drones. The Armenian tanks, dug in along the front lines, were picked off one by one by the drones' precision munitions. The footage of these strikes, filmed by the drones themselves and posted to social media, became a defining image of the war. The Azerbaijani advance was slow and costly, but it was successful, and it ended with a ceasefire that gave Azerbaijan control of much of the disputed territory.

The lessons of the Nagorno-Karabakh war were studied closely by militaries around the world. The first was that drones had become a decisive weapon in conventional warfare, not just in counterinsurgency. The second was that air defense had to be redesigned to deal with small, slow, low-flying targets. The third was that the integration of sensors and shooters—the same integration the Israelis had pioneered in 1982—was now available to middle-income countries, not just to the great powers. The fourth was that the cost-exchange ratio favored the offense: a cheap drone could destroy an expensive tank, and the defender had to spend far more to shoot down the drone than the attacker had spent to build it. The war was a warning that the precision revolution had democratized, and that the era in which a technologically superior army could dominate a battlefield with impunity was coming to an end.

The war also raised the question of autonomy. The loitering munitions used in the war—the Israeli Harop and the Turkish Kargu-2, among others—were capable of operating in a semi-autonomous mode, in which they could search for a target and attack it without a human operator. The Kargu-2 became the subject of a contested allegation in a United Nations report on Libya, which stated that the weapon "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces in 2021. The report was carefully hedged, and the claim was never independently confirmed. But the mere fact that it was made—and that it was plausible—was significant. It suggested that the line between semi-autonomous and fully autonomous weapons was being crossed, not by deliberate decision, but by the incremental development of technology that made autonomy easier and more attractive.

The debate over autonomous weapons was, in some ways, a replay of the debate over precision weapons in the 1990s. Advocates argued that autonomy would make weapons more precise, more reliable, and more humane, because a machine would not panic or make mistakes under stress. Critics argued that autonomy would make war easier to start, because it would remove the human cost of killing, and that it would create a moral and legal vacuum in which no one could be held responsible for the deaths of civilians. The debate was complicated by the fact that the technology was advancing faster than the law, and that the major military powers had no interest in a treaty that would constrain their development. The result was a stalemate: the United Nations convened a series of meetings on lethal autonomous weapons systems, but no binding agreement was reached, and the development of the technology continued.

The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine was the largest conventional war in Europe since 1945, and it became a laboratory for the weapons of the twenty-first century. The war was fought with a combination of old and new weapons: tanks, artillery, and infantry, as in the wars of the twentieth century, but also drones, precision-guided missiles, satellite communications, and cyberattacks. The Russians, who had invested heavily in precision weapons and electronic warfare, expected a quick victory. They did not get one. The Ukrainians, with Western help, mounted a stubborn defense, and the war settled into a grinding attritional conflict that resembled the First World War more than the precision wars of the 1990s.

The war in Ukraine revealed the strengths and weaknesses of the precision revolution. The strengths were obvious: Ukrainian drones, guided by satellite communications and operated by soldiers with laptops, destroyed Russian tanks and artillery with remarkable efficiency. The Turkish Bayraktar TB2, the star of Nagorno-Karabakh, was used to devastating effect in the early weeks of the war, and the footage of its strikes became a symbol of Ukrainian resistance. The Javelin anti-tank missile, supplied by the United States, proved highly effective against Russian armor, and the Stinger anti-aircraft missile, supplied by the Europeans, proved effective against Russian helicopters and low-flying aircraft.

The weaknesses were equally obvious. The Russians, who had invested heavily in electronic warfare, were able to jam Ukrainian drones and communications, and the Ukrainians had to adapt by using different frequencies and different tactics. The precision weapons were expensive and scarce, and the Ukrainians ran through their stocks of Javelins and Stingers faster than the West could replace them. The war became a contest of industrial production as much as of technology: the side that could produce more shells, more drones, and more missiles would win, and the West, which had spent decades shrinking its defense industrial base, found that it could not produce munitions fast enough to keep up with the demands of the war.

The war also demonstrated the growing importance of cheap, expendable drones. The Ukrainians used commercial quadcopters, modified to carry small bombs, to attack Russian positions, and they used first-person-view drones, piloted by soldiers wearing video goggles, to fly into Russian tanks and bunkers. These drones were cheap—a few hundred dollars each—and they were produced in enormous quantities by volunteers and small workshops. The Russians responded with their own drones, and the skies over the front lines became a dense, contested environment in which small, cheap machines fought for dominance. The era of the precision weapon as an expensive, scarce, high-technology artifact was giving way to an era in which precision was cheap, ubiquitous, and disposable.

The war also revealed the vulnerability of the modern battlefield to surveillance. The Ukrainians, using commercial satellite imagery and signals intelligence, were able to track Russian movements in near real time, and they used that information to target artillery and drones. The Russians, who had invested heavily in electronic warfare, were able to disrupt some of this surveillance, but not all of it. The result was a battlefield that was, in some ways, more transparent than any in history, and a war in which the ability to hide was as important as the ability to shoot. The lessons of the war were being absorbed by militaries around the world, and the next generation of weapons would be designed to fight in a world in which everything could be seen.

The history of precision weapons, from the first laser-guided bombs in Vietnam to the drone swarms of the twenty-first century, is a history of a single idea: that the ability to see and to strike with accuracy is more important than the ability to strike with mass. That idea has transformed warfare, but it has not eliminated the fundamental truths that have governed war since the beginning. Precision weapons are still weapons; they still kill people, and they still destroy things. They have made war more efficient, but they have not made it less terrible. They have given the strong new advantages, but they have also given the weak new tools. They have changed the way wars are fought, but they have not changed the reasons wars are fought. The precision revolution is a chapter in the history of war, not the end of it.

The story of precision weapons is also a story about the relationship between technology and strategy. The technology of precision guidance did not emerge in a vacuum; it was developed by people who had a theory of how war should be fought, and it was used by militaries that had a doctrine for how to use it. The Americans, who pioneered precision weapons, had a doctrine of air power that emphasized the destruction of specific targets—command centers, bridges, factories—rather than the destruction of cities. The precision weapon was the perfect tool for that doctrine, and the doctrine shaped the weapon as much as the weapon shaped the doctrine. The Israelis, who faced a different strategic problem, developed precision weapons for a different purpose: to strike at the enemies of a small state without provoking a wider war. The Russians, who faced a different problem again, developed precision weapons to compensate for their numerical inferiority in other areas. The technology was the same, but the strategy was different, and the results were different.

The precision revolution also changed the relationship between war and politics. In the era of mass warfare, the destruction of cities was a political act: it was intended to break the will of the enemy population. In the era of precision warfare, the destruction of specific targets is a political act of a different kind: it is intended to signal resolve, to punish a regime, or to shape the behavior of an adversary without causing the kind of mass casualties that would provoke international outrage. The precision weapon has made it possible to fight a war with a smaller political footprint, but it has also made it easier to fight a war without a clear political goal. The wars of the post-Cold War era—Kosovo, Iraq, Libya, Syria—were fought with precision weapons, and they were fought without the kind of mass mobilization that had characterized the wars of the twentieth century. The result was a series of wars that were relatively cheap in blood and treasure, at least for the intervening powers, but that were also inconclusive and, in some cases, counterproductive.

The precision revolution has also changed the relationship between the soldier and the battlefield. In the era of mass warfare, the soldier was a small part of a vast machine, and his individual actions were rarely decisive. In the era of precision warfare, the soldier is a node in a network, and his individual actions—calling in a precision strike, operating a drone, designating a target—can be decisive. The infantryman with a laser designator can destroy a tank with a single shot, and the drone operator in a trailer in Nevada can kill a man on the other side of the world. The precision weapon has empowered the individual soldier, but it has also isolated him, because the act of killing has become more remote, more mediated by technology, and more distant from the physical reality of the battlefield.

The history of weapons is, in the end, a history of human ingenuity applied to the problem of killing. The precision weapon is one of the most ingenious of these applications, and it has changed the world in ways its inventors could not have imagined. But it has not solved the problem of war, and it has not made war obsolete. The precision weapon is a tool, and like all tools, it can be used for good or for ill. The question that faces the world in the twenty-first century is not whether precision weapons will be used—they will be—but whether the people who use them will be wise enough to use them well. The history of the twentieth century suggests that the answer is not obvious, and that the consequences of getting it wrong are terrible.

The development of precision weapons was not a single event but a long, uneven process, shaped by the same forces that have shaped every other aspect of weapons development: the competition between states, the pressure of war, the availability of technology, and the choices of individuals. The story of the precision revolution is a story about the interaction of these forces, and it is a story that is still being written. The wars of the twenty-first century—in Ukraine, in Nagorno-Karabakh, in Gaza—are the latest chapters, and they are being written in real time, with consequences that are not yet clear. What is clear is that the precision weapon has become the defining weapon of our age, and that the age of precision is not over. It is just beginning.

The precision revolution was, in a sense, the culmination of a process that had begun with the first firearms. The gunpowder weapon had always promised to make war more controllable, more predictable, more rational. The cannonball that flew in a predictable arc, the musket ball that hit what it was aimed at, the rifled bullet that extended the range of the individual soldier—each of these was a step toward the precision weapon. The precision weapon was the fulfillment of that promise, but it was also a reminder that the promise was always partly illusory. War is never fully controllable, never fully predictable, never fully rational. The precision weapon has made war more precise, but it has not made it less chaotic, and it has not made it less human. The history of war is a history of human beings trying to impose order on chaos, and the precision weapon is the latest tool in that effort. It is a powerful tool, but it is not a magic wand, and the people who use it would do well to remember that.

The precision weapon has also changed the way we think about the laws of war. The laws of war, which were codified in the Geneva Conventions and their protocols, are based on the principle of distinction: combatants must be distinguished from civilians, and civilians must not be targeted. The precision weapon makes it possible to strike a military target with a high degree of confidence that civilians will not be harmed, and it therefore makes it possible to comply with the laws of war more fully than was possible in the era of area bombing. But the precision weapon also creates new legal problems. If a weapon can strike a target with precision, does that mean that the user has an obligation to use it? If a commander has a choice between a precise weapon that will kill the target and a few civilians and a less precise weapon that will kill the target and many civilians, is he obligated to use the precise weapon? The law has not fully answered these questions, and the answers will depend on the development of new legal doctrines and new ethical frameworks.

The precision weapon has also changed the way we think about responsibility. In the era of mass bombing, the responsibility for civilian deaths was diffuse: the crews who dropped the bombs, the commanders who ordered the raids, the politicians who set the policy, the scientists who designed the weapons. In the era of precision warfare, the responsibility is more concentrated: the person who designates the target, the person who pulls the trigger, the person who approves the strike. The precision weapon has made it possible to assign responsibility more precisely, but it has also made it possible to evade responsibility more easily. The drone operator who kills a man in a distant country can say that he was following orders, that the intelligence was good, that the target was a legitimate military objective. The precision weapon has not resolved the ancient problem of moral responsibility in war; it has merely given it a new form.

The history of precision weapons is, in the end, a history of the human desire to control the uncontrollable. War is the most uncontrollable of human activities, and the precision weapon is the most ambitious attempt to control it. The attempt has succeeded in part, and it has failed in part. It has succeeded in making it possible to destroy specific targets with a high degree of accuracy, and it has failed in making it possible to win wars without the messy, bloody, unpredictable business of ground combat. The precision weapon is a tool, and like all tools, it is only as good as the people who use it. The history of the twenty-first century will be, in part, the history of how well or how badly the world's militaries use the precision weapons they have built. The stakes are high, and the outcome is not certain.

The precision revolution has also had a profound effect on the relationship between the military and the society it serves. In the era of mass warfare, the military was a mirror of society: it drew its soldiers from the general population, and it fought wars that affected the entire population. In the era of precision warfare, the military is increasingly a specialized, professional force that fights wars with a small number of highly trained personnel and a large number of highly sophisticated machines. The result is a growing gap between the military and the society it serves, a gap that is reflected in the way wars are fought, the way they are reported, and the way they are remembered. The precision weapon has made it possible to fight a war with a small number of casualties, at least on one side, and it has made it possible for the public to ignore the war, or to support it without understanding it. The precision weapon has not made war less political; it has made it more political, because it has made it possible to fight a war without the kind of public mobilization that would have been necessary in the past.

The precision revolution has also changed the way wars are remembered. The wars of the twentieth century were remembered through the experiences of the soldiers who fought them, and through the images of the battlefields they left behind. The wars of the twenty-first century are remembered through the images captured by drones and satellites, and through the data collected by sensors and computers. The precision weapon has made it possible to record a war in unprecedented detail, but it has also made it possible to forget a war more easily, because the images are abstract, the data is overwhelming, and the experience of the people on the ground is often invisible. The precision weapon has not made war more humane; it has made it more remote, and remoteness is not the same as humanity.

The history of weapons is a history of the human capacity for both creation and destruction. The precision weapon is a creation of the human mind, and it is a tool of destruction. It has been used to kill people, to destroy cities, and to change the course of history. It has also been used to protect people, to deter aggression, and to bring wars to a faster end.
