paragraphs: The moral character of a tool is never settled in the abstract. It is settled in the moment of use, by the hands that hold it and the institutions that direct those hands—and settled again and again, because the tool does not stay still. Every weapon ever built was built to a purpose, and every purpose has been revised the moment the weapon reached the field. This is the rhythm that has governed the long history of war and weapons development, and it is the rhythm Part 38 must examine in its most recent and consequential phase: the age in which the weapon itself began to think, or to appear to think, and in which the distance between the person who decides and the person who dies grew from the length of a bowshot to the circumference of the earth.

To understand how that distance was closed and then reopened in new forms, we must return once more to the beginning—not to repeat covered ground but to see it whole. The first weapons were extensions of the arm: the club, the stone, the spear. Their range was the range of the human body, and their moral character was inseparable from the body that wielded them. A man who killed with a spear looked into the face of the man he killed, or at least into the space where that face had been. The act was intimate, and because it was intimate it was bounded by the limits of intimacy: fatigue, fear, the reluctance to kill one's own kind that soldiers have reported across many centuries and cultures. The spear did not permit the killer to forget the killed. Weapon and wound occupied the same place at the same time.

The bow changed this, but only slightly. A longbowman at Agincourt, drawing a bow of perhaps 150 pounds—as the surviving bows recovered from the *Mary Rose* suggest—could kill at two hundred yards, and the killing remained visible, personal, bounded by the archer's own strength and skill. The *Mary Rose* bows, raised from the Solent in 1982 along with 137 longbows, are a physical record of what that intimacy cost: draw weights estimated at 100 to 185 pounds imply bodies deformed by years of training, shoulder blades thickened and spines curved, the skeleton itself reshaped by the weapon it served. The archer paid for his range with his body. The weapon was an extension of him, and the moral cost was an extension of him too.

Gunpowder broke the connection. The first recipes in the *Wujing Zongyao* of 1044 were incendiaries and smoke-makers, not true explosives, and the earliest metal-barreled firearms—like the Heilongjiang hand cannon dated by inscription to 1288—were crude tubes that threw a ball a short distance with uncertain effect. But the principle was already revolutionary: the energy came from chemistry, not muscle, and the person who pulled the trigger did not need to be strong, trained from childhood, or able to see the face of the man he killed. A peasant could kill a knight. A boy could kill a master. The gunpowder weapon democratized killing and, in doing so, began the long separation of killer from killed.

That separation accelerated with every technological step. The rifled musket and the Minié ball, developed by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, extended the infantryman's effective range to several hundred yards and made Civil War volley fire murderous in a way smoothbore warfare had not been. The soldier who fired a Springfield Model 1861 at a line of men he could barely see was already several steps removed from the spearman. The Maxim gun, demonstrated in 1884 and adopted by the British Army in .303 caliber in 1891, removed him further still: self-powered and recoil-operated, it could fire hundreds of rounds a minute without human intervention beyond a trigger pull and the feeding of a belt. The gunner did not aim at a man; he aimed at a sector, and the sector was filled with men.

The French 75, the Canon de 75 modèle 1897, with its hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady and allowed roughly fifteen rounds a minute without re-aiming, completed the transformation of the individual weapon into an industrial process. By Verdun in 1916, the battlefield was dominated not by men with weapons but by weapons with men as their servants. The battle ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916 and produced roughly 700,000 casualties, the great majority caused by artillery. The shell was the true infantryman of the First World War. The men in the trenches were targets, and the men who fired the guns were, in a sense, already operators of a system rather than warriors in any recognizable older sense.

The Second World War extended the system to the scale of continents. Strategic bombing, the firebombing of cities, the V-2 rocket, and finally the atomic bomb at Trinity on 16 July 1945, with a yield of about 21 kilotons, completed the arc that had begun with the hand cannon. The weapon could now destroy a city without its operator ever seeing the city, and the decision to use it could be made by a committee in a room thousands of miles away. The nuclear age added a new dimension: the weapon that could not be used without destroying the user, and therefore the weapon whose primary function became deterrence rather than employment. The NPT, opened for signature in 1968 and in force since 1970, with 191 states parties and notable non-signatories in India, Israel, and Pakistan, and North Korea's announced withdrawal in 2003, is the institutional expression of that paradox: the most powerful weapons ever built are the ones that must never be used, and the entire architecture of arms control exists to keep them unused.

But the nuclear weapon, for all its enormity, did not end conventional weapons development. It accelerated it, because the nuclear threshold made conventional war the only war that could actually be fought—and the conventional weapons that could be fought with became more precise, more lethal, and more autonomous. The precision-guided munition was the answer to the problem of the nuclear age: how to achieve military effect without escalation, destroy a target without destroying a city, make war usable again. In Desert Storm in 1991, coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, of which about 6,520 tons—roughly 7.4 percent—were precision-guided. The percentage was small, but the effect was disproportionate. The PGM struck high-value targets—command bunkers, bridges, radar sites—with an accuracy that changed the expectations of air power forever. The public saw grainy footage of a bomb entering a ventilation shaft and believed, for a time, that war had become surgical.

It had not. The other 92.6 percent of the bombs were unguided, and they killed indiscriminately, as unguided bombs always have. The precision weapon did not eliminate collateral damage; it concentrated it, made it visible, and made it a political problem in a way that the area bombing of the Second World War had not been. It also created a new kind of distance: the operator in a ground station in Nevada, watching a screen, pressing a button, killing a man in Kandahar or Fallujah. The moral character of that act is not settled by the accuracy of the weapon. It is settled by whether the operator knows who he is killing, whether he can see the consequences, and whether the institution that employs him holds him accountable.

The drone wars of the twenty-first century made that question urgent. The Bayraktar TB2, the Turkish drone that became famous in the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war, is a relatively simple machine, but its effect was revolutionary. In the 44-day war, Azerbaijan used TB2s and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses, and the RUSI study of 2021 treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and suppression of air defense. The drone did not merely kill; it changed the calculus of the battlefield. A tank that could be destroyed from the air by a machine costing a fraction of its price was no longer a decisive weapon. The loitering munition, which circles above a target area and then dives, collapsed the distinction between reconnaissance and strike, between observer and killer.

And then there is the contested claim of autonomy. The UN Panel of Experts report on Libya in 2021 stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The claim remains contested and not independently confirmed, and it must be treated with explicit caveat: this is a contested allegation, not a confirmed autonomous strike. But that the allegation could be made at all is the significant thing. The technology exists to allow a machine to select and attack a target without a human in the loop, and whether it has been used that way is a question of fact, not of possibility. The possibility is already here. The moral character of the autonomous weapon is not a future problem; it is a present one, and it is the problem Part 38 must confront directly.

The central argument of this book has been that weapons and wars develop together, each shaping the other, and that weapons development is never merely technical. It is a social, economic, political, and moral process. The weapon is never just a tool; it expresses the society that builds it, and it in turn reshapes that society. The longbow required a society that could afford to train archers for a lifetime, and it produced a society in which the archer was a valued and feared member. The Maxim gun required an industrial economy that could produce ammunition in the millions of rounds, and it produced a society in which the machine gun became the symbol of colonial domination. The atomic bomb required a scientific establishment of unprecedented scale, and it produced a society in which the scientist became a political actor and the physicist a strategist.

The autonomous weapon requires something new: a society willing to delegate the decision to kill to a machine. That is not a technical question, and it cannot be answered by engineers. It is a question about the kind of society we want to be, and it is being answered now—not in the future—by the choices governments, militaries, and corporations are making about what to build and what to deploy. The history of weapons is a history of choices, and the choices are always made by people, even when the weapon itself is a machine.

To see how those choices have been made in the past, and to understand what is at stake in the present, we must examine the long relationship between the warrior and the weapon, and between the weapon and the society that produces it. That relationship has passed through several distinct phases, each identifiable by how it answered a single question: who decides who dies? In the age of the spear, the answer was the man with the spear. In the age of the longbow, the answer was the archer, but the archer was constrained by his own body and by the training that had shaped it. In the age of the firearm, the answer was the man with the gun, but the gun was increasingly produced by an industrial system that determined its characteristics and its supply. In the age of the artillery, the answer was the gunner, but the gunner was part of a system that told him where to fire. In the age of the bomber, the answer was the bombardier, but the bombardier was part of a system that told him what to bomb. In the age of the precision weapon, the answer is the operator, but the operator is part of a system that tells him what to target—and the system is increasingly capable of making the decision itself.

The trajectory is clear: the decision to kill has been progressively removed from the person who actually does the killing and transferred to systems that are larger, more abstract, and more remote. The spear did not require a system. The drone requires a system that includes satellites, data links, intelligence analysts, commanders, lawyers, and politicians. The autonomous weapon requires all of those and also the algorithm that makes the final decision. The question is whether that final transfer is acceptable, and the answer depends on what we believe about the moral status of machines and the moral responsibility of the people who build and deploy them.

The history of weapons suggests that the transfer will happen, because it always has. Every generation has resisted the new weapon on moral grounds, and every generation has been overruled by the exigencies of war. The crossbow was condemned by the Church, and then it was used. The longbow was seen as unchivalrous, and then it was used. The machine gun was seen as inhuman, and then it was used. The bomber was seen as a weapon of terror, and then it was used. The atomic bomb was seen as the end of civilization, and then it was built and used and built again. The pattern is not a law of nature, but it is a strong tendency, driven by the fact that war is a competition in which the side that adopts the new weapon first gains an advantage the other side cannot afford to ignore.

But the autonomous weapon is different in one crucial respect: it is the first weapon that can make the decision to kill without a human being present in the decision. The other weapons required a human hand at the moment of use, even if the hand was far from the target. The autonomous weapon removes the hand. And the removal of the hand is not a technical detail; it is a moral threshold. It is the threshold at which responsibility for killing becomes diffuse, and diffuse responsibility is no responsibility at all. The history of war has been, in part, a history of the struggle to hold someone responsible for the deaths that war causes. The autonomous weapon threatens to end that struggle by making responsibility impossible to locate.

This is not a hypothetical concern. The Kargu-2 allegation, contested as it is, points to a real possibility already realized in some form. The technology for autonomous target selection exists, and it is being deployed in loitering munitions and in defensive systems that must react faster than a human can. The question is not whether the technology will be used, but under what constraints and with what accountability. The answer is being written now, in the procurement decisions of governments and the design choices of engineers, and it will determine the moral character of war for the next century.

To understand the stakes, we must look more closely at how the precision weapon and the autonomous weapon have changed the relationship between the military and the society it serves. The precision weapon was sold to the public as a way to make war more humane, and in some respects it did. It reduced the number of civilians killed in some campaigns, and it allowed militaries to strike targets that would have been impossible to strike without unacceptable collateral damage. But it also made war more remote, and remoteness has its own costs. The public that watches a war on a screen, seeing only the precision strikes and not the rubble they leave behind, is insulated from the reality of war. The precision weapon did not make war more humane; it made it more remote, and remoteness is not the same as humanity.

The autonomous weapon will make war more remote still. The operator who presses a button is at least present in the act, even if he is thousands of miles away. The machine that selects and kills without an operator is not present at all, and the people who built it and deployed it are even further removed. The chain of responsibility stretches from the engineer who wrote the code to the general who authorized the deployment to the politician who approved the budget, and at each link the responsibility becomes thinner. The result is a kind of moral evaporation, in which the act of killing becomes something that happens, like a natural event, rather than something someone does.

The history of weapons is full of attempts to solve this problem, and most have failed. The laws of war, from the Geneva Conventions to the Rome Statute, are attempts to hold individuals responsible for the acts of war, and they have had some success. But they were designed for a world in which the killer was a person, and they have struggled to adapt to a world in which the killer is a system. The autonomous weapon is the ultimate test of the laws of war, because it is the weapon that cannot be held accountable in the way the law requires. A machine cannot be tried, and the people who built it can always claim that they did not intend the specific act the machine carried out.

This is why the debate over autonomous weapons is not a technical debate. It is a debate about the nature of moral responsibility, and it is a debate the history of weapons has been building toward for centuries. The spear required the spearman to be responsible. The machine gun required the gunner to be responsible, but the gunner was part of a system. The bomber required the bombardier to be responsible, but the bombardier was part of a system. The drone requires the operator to be responsible, but the operator is part of a system. The autonomous weapon requires no one to be responsible, and that is the difference that matters.

The history of war and weapons development is, in the end, a history of human choices about how to kill and who to hold responsible for the killing. The choices have always been constrained by technology, but they have never been determined by it. The crossbow did not have to be used, the machine gun did not have to be used, the atomic bomb did not have to be used. They were used because people chose to use them, and the choices were made in specific historical circumstances by specific people who could have chosen otherwise. The autonomous weapon is the same. It does not have to be used, and the choice to use it is being made now, by people who can choose otherwise.

The rest of this book will examine those choices in detail. It will look at how the precision weapon changed the relationship between the military and the public, how the drone changed the relationship between the operator and the target, and how the autonomous weapon is changing the relationship between the machine and the moral law. It will argue that the history of weapons is not a story of inevitable progress but a story of contingent choices, and that the choices made in the present will determine the character of war for generations to come.

The precision weapon, as we have seen, was born out of the desire to make war usable in the nuclear age. The atomic bomb had made total war unthinkable, and the precision weapon was an attempt to make limited war thinkable again. The result was a weapon that could destroy a target without destroying a city, and that could be used in conflicts below the nuclear threshold. The precision weapon was used in Vietnam, the Gulf War, Kosovo, Afghanistan, and Iraq, and in each it demonstrated its ability to achieve military effects with relatively few civilian casualties, at least by the standards of earlier wars. But it also demonstrated its limits. The precision weapon could not win a war by itself, and it could not prevent the atrocities soldiers commit when they are on the ground. The precision weapon was a tool, and like all tools it was only as good as the people who used it.

The drone was a further development of the precision weapon, and it added a new dimension: persistence. A drone could loiter over a target for hours, watching and waiting, and strike when the moment was right. The drone was a surveillance platform and a weapon in one, and it collapsed the distinction between intelligence and action. It also removed the operator from the battlefield, and that removal had consequences that were not always foreseen. The operator could go home to his family after a shift, and the psychological distance between him and his targets was greater than that of any previous warrior. Drone operators who have spoken publicly describe a strange kind of war, fought in a trailer in the Nevada desert, in which the enemy is a pixel on a screen and the killing is done with a joystick. The intimacy of the spear is gone, and the distance of the drone is not the same as the distance of the bomber. The bomber pilot flew over the target and saw the city below; the drone operator sees only what the camera shows, and the camera shows only what the operator is looking for.

The autonomous weapon takes the final step. It removes the operator entirely and delegates the decision to kill to an algorithm. The algorithm is not a person, and it cannot be held responsible in the way a person can. The people who wrote the algorithm can be held responsible for its design, but not for the specific act it carries out in a specific situation. The result is a gap in the chain of responsibility, and that gap is the central problem of the autonomous weapon.

The history of weapons suggests that the gap will be filled by something, because societies cannot tolerate unaccountable killing for long. It may be filled by law, by regulation, by international agreement, or by the simple refusal of soldiers to use weapons they cannot control. But it will be filled, and how it is filled will determine the character of war in the twenty-first century. The history of weapons is a history of human choices, and the choice about autonomous weapons is the most important choice of our time.

The longbowmen of the *Mary Rose* paid for their range with their bodies, and the archers of Agincourt paid for their skill with their lives. The soldiers of the First World War paid for the artillery with their blood, and the civilians of the Second World War paid for the bomber with their cities. The people who will pay for the autonomous weapon are not yet known, but they will be the people killed by machines that no one is responsible for. The history of war and weapons development is a history of the human capacity for both creation and destruction, and the autonomous weapon is the latest expression of that capacity. The question is whether it will be the last.

The answer is not determined by technology. It is determined by the choices people make, and the choices are being made now. The history of weapons is a history of choices, and the choices are always made by people, even when the weapon itself is a machine. The autonomous weapon is a machine that makes choices, but the choice to build it and deploy it is a human choice, and it can be unmade by human choice. Whether it will be the last expression of that capacity is a question the future will answer, but the answer will be determined by the choices made in the present.

The precision weapon, the drone, and the autonomous weapon are not separate developments. They are stages in a single process: the process by which the decision to kill has been removed from the person who does the killing and transferred to systems that are larger, more abstract, and more remote. The process began with the crossbow and the longbow, continued with the firearm and the artillery, accelerated with the bomber and the missile, and has now reached the point at which the system can make the decision itself. The process is not inevitable, but it is powerful, driven by the logic of war as a competition in which the side that adopts the new weapon first gains an advantage. That logic is real, but it is not the only logic. The history of weapons also shows that societies can and do impose limits on the weapons they use, and that those limits are often the result of moral and political pressure rather than military necessity. The bans on chemical weapons, blinding lasers, anti-personnel mines, and cluster munitions are all examples of limits imposed despite military objections. The autonomous weapon is a candidate for the same kind of limit, and the debate over whether to impose it is the most important debate in the history of weapons since the debate over the atomic bomb.

That earlier debate was resolved, in part, by the NPT, which opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, and which now has 191 states parties. The NPT did not eliminate nuclear weapons, but it created a framework in which their spread was slowed and their use made less likely. The debate over the autonomous weapon has no equivalent framework, and the absence of a framework is itself a choice. The choice is being made by default, through the development and deployment of autonomous weapons without any international agreement to govern them. The default is not neutral; it favors the states and corporations developing the weapons, and it disadvantages the people who will be killed by them.

The history of weapons is a history of the human capacity for both creation and destruction, and the autonomous weapon is the latest expression of that capacity. The question is whether it will be the last. The answer is not determined by technology. It is determined by the choices people make, and the choices are being made now.

paragraphs: states parties. The NPT did not abolish the bomb, but it created a framework in which the bomb’s spread could be slowed, monitored, and in some cases reversed. The treaty rested on a bargain: states without nuclear weapons would forswear them, states with them would eventually disarm, and all would have access to peaceful nuclear technology under safeguards. The bargain was unequal and imperfect, and the nuclear powers never fully honored it. But it established a principle that had not existed before—that possession of a weapon could be made a matter of international law rather than raw capability alone. The NPT is the clearest example in the history of weapons of a technology constrained not by its own limits but by a political decision to constrain it. The question the autonomous weapon debate raises is whether the same decision can be made again, for a technology far more diffuse, far more commercially driven, and far less concentrated in the hands of a few states than the atomic bomb ever was.

The answer is not obvious, and the history of arms control suggests reasons for both optimism and pessimism. The optimistic case rests on the record of the last century, which shows that states have repeatedly agreed to limit or abolish categories of weapons when political pressure was strong enough. The pessimistic case rests on the fact that almost every successful arms control agreement has been built on concentrated, observable, and expensive technology—the kind only a handful of states could build, and that could be counted, inspected, and verified. The autonomous weapon does not fit that model. It is built from commercially available components, it is software rather than hardware, and it is being developed by corporations as well as states. The NPT worked, in part, because the bomb was hard to make and easy to count. The autonomous weapon is neither.

To understand why the NPT succeeded where other arms control efforts failed, it is necessary to look at the conditions that made it possible. The first was the sheer destructive power of the weapon. The atomic bomb was not simply a more efficient way of killing; it threatened the existence of the state that used it, the state that was targeted, and eventually the entire planet. The scale of the threat created a political constituency for control that crossed national boundaries. The second condition was the concentration of the technology. In 1945 only one state possessed the bomb, and by 1970 only five had tested one. The technology was expensive, it required industrial infrastructure that could be detected, and it produced unmistakable signatures—a nuclear test cannot be hidden. The third condition was the existence of a forum in which the bargain could be struck. The United Nations provided the stage, and the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union provided the incentive, because both superpowers eventually concluded that the spread of the bomb to other states was more dangerous than the continued possession of the bomb by each other.

The NPT was the product of all three conditions, and it is worth remembering how close it came to failing. The treaty was opened for signature in 1968, at a moment when the United States was mired in Vietnam and the Soviet Union was still recovering from the Cuban Missile Crisis. The negotiations were difficult, and the treaty that emerged was full of compromises. The nuclear weapons states—the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France, and China—were not required to disarm on any timetable. The treaty simply committed them to “pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament.” That language was vague enough to be ignored, and it was ignored for decades. The non-nuclear states, meanwhile, were required to accept safeguards on their peaceful nuclear programs, which many regarded as an infringement on their sovereignty. The treaty was extended indefinitely in 1995, but only after the nuclear powers agreed to a set of principles and objectives that included the elimination of nuclear weapons—a commitment that has never been fulfilled.

The NPT’s record is therefore mixed. It did not prevent India, Israel, and Pakistan from acquiring nuclear weapons, and it did not prevent North Korea from announcing its withdrawal in 2003 and subsequently testing a device. But it did slow the spread of the bomb, and it created a norm that made acquisition costly. States that pursued nuclear weapons after 1970 did so in the face of international sanctions, export controls, and diplomatic isolation. South Africa built a small arsenal and then dismantled it in the early 1990s, the only state to have done so. Brazil and Argentina abandoned their nuclear programs in the 1980s and 1990s. Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Belarus gave up the Soviet weapons that remained on their territory after the collapse of the USSR. These outcomes were not the result of the treaty alone, but the treaty provided the framework within which they became possible.

The lesson for the autonomous weapon debate is that arms control works best when the weapon in question is concentrated, observable, and catastrophic. The autonomous weapon is catastrophic in the sense that it could kill without human intervention, but it is not concentrated and it is not observable. It is a software capability that can be embedded in existing platforms, and it can be developed by any state or non-state actor with access to the relevant technology. The campaign to ban fully autonomous weapons—weapons that can select and engage targets without human control—has therefore focused on a different strategy. Rather than trying to eliminate the technology, it has tried to establish a norm that human control over the use of force is a moral and legal requirement. The norm is not a treaty, and it may never become one, but it has already begun to shape the behavior of states and the development of weapons.

The campaign has been led by a coalition of non-governmental organizations, including Human Rights Watch and the International Committee for Robot Arms Control, which formed the Campaign to Stop Killer Robots in 2012. The campaign has argued that fully autonomous weapons would cross a moral threshold, because they would delegate the decision to kill to a machine. It has also argued that such weapons would be inconsistent with international humanitarian law, which requires that attacks distinguish between combatants and civilians, that they be proportionate, and that they be necessary. A machine, the campaign argues, cannot make those judgments in the way the law requires, and the result would be a lowering of the legal and moral barriers to the use of force. The campaign has had some success. The United Nations has held discussions on the issue since 2014, first under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons and then in the General Assembly. In 2023 the UN Secretary-General called for a legally binding instrument to prohibit fully autonomous weapons, and a growing number of states have endorsed the idea of a treaty.

But the campaign has also run into the same obstacles that have frustrated other arms control efforts. The major military powers—the United States, Russia, China, and India—have resisted a binding ban. They have argued that existing international humanitarian law is sufficient to regulate autonomous weapons, and that a ban would be premature because the technology is still developing. They have also argued that autonomy in weapons is a spectrum, and that a ban on fully autonomous weapons would be difficult to define and enforce. The United States has issued a policy that requires human control over the use of force, but it has not agreed to a treaty. Russia has been openly hostile to the campaign, and China has taken a more nuanced position, supporting a ban on the use of fully autonomous weapons but opposing a ban on their development. The result is a stalemate that resembles the stalemate in other areas of arms control, and it is likely to persist for as long as the major powers believe that the military advantages of autonomy outweigh the political costs of a ban.

The stalemate is not the end of the story, however. The history of arms control shows that norms can change even when treaties do not. The ban on blinding lasers, for example, was adopted in 1995 as Protocol IV to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, but it was preceded by a decade of lobbying by the International Committee of the Red Cross and by a growing consensus among states that the weapon was unnecessarily cruel. The ban on anti-personnel mines was adopted in 1997 as the Ottawa Treaty, outside the UN framework, after a coalition of NGOs and middle powers decided that the major powers would never agree to a ban within the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. The Ottawa Treaty has been signed by 164 states, but not by the United States, Russia, China, or India. The ban on cluster munitions, adopted in 2008, followed a similar pattern. These treaties did not eliminate the weapons, but they stigmatized them, and the stigma has changed the behavior of states that have not signed. The United States has not used anti-personnel mines since 1991, and it has not used cluster munitions in populated areas since 2003, even though it has not joined the treaties that ban them.

The autonomous weapon campaign hopes to achieve a similar stigma. The goal is not necessarily a treaty that binds the major powers, but a norm that makes the use of fully autonomous weapons politically costly. The campaign has already had some effect. The UN Secretary-General’s call for a ban, the growing number of states that support a treaty, and the attention the issue has received in the media have all raised the political cost of developing fully autonomous weapons. The question is whether the cost will be high enough to deter the major powers from deploying them. The history of the NPT suggests that it might be, but the history of the anti-personnel mine ban suggests that it might not. The difference is that the bomb was a weapon that could destroy the world, and the mine was a weapon that maimed civilians long after the war was over. The autonomous weapon is somewhere in between. It could make war more humane, by reducing the risk to soldiers, or it could make war more brutal, by lowering the threshold for the use of force. The outcome depends on the choices that states make, and those choices are not determined by the technology alone.

The debate over autonomous weapons is the most recent chapter in a longer history of the relationship between technology and restraint. That history has a pattern, and the pattern is not one of steady progress toward either more destructive weapons or more effective controls. It is a pattern of oscillation, in which periods of rapid technological change are followed by periods of consolidation and restraint. The invention of gunpowder was followed by centuries in which the technology spread slowly and was adapted to existing social and military structures. The invention of the machine gun was followed by a period of colonial warfare in which the weapon was used against opponents who did not have it, and then by the First World War, in which it was used against opponents who did. The invention of the atomic bomb was followed by a period of nuclear proliferation and then by the NPT. The invention of precision-guided munitions was followed by a period of optimism about surgical air power and then by the realization that precision does not solve the political problems that cause war. The invention of the drone was followed by a period of remote warfare and then by the proliferation of the technology to non-state actors and middle powers.

Each of these periods has been shaped by the interaction of three factors: the technology itself, the political and social context in which it is developed, and the moral and legal norms that govern its use. The technology sets the outer limits of what is possible. The political context determines who has access to the technology and how it is used. The norms determine what is acceptable and what is not. The interaction is complex, and it is not always predictable. The machine gun was invented in the 1880s, but it did not transform warfare until the First World War, because the military establishments of the great powers were slow to recognize its potential and because the social and political context of the late nineteenth century did not create the conditions for its use. The atomic bomb was invented in the 1940s, and it transformed warfare immediately, because the political context of the Second World War created the conditions for its use and because the norms that might have restrained it did not yet exist.

The history of the last century suggests that the norms are the most important of the three factors, because they are the only one that can be changed by human agency. The technology is what it is. The political context is the product of history. But the norms are the product of choice, and they can be changed by persuasion, by protest, and by political action. The ban on chemical weapons is the clearest example. Chemical weapons were used on a large scale in the First World War, and they were used again in the 1980s by Iraq and Iran. But the norm against their use was strong enough to prevent their use in the Second World War, and it was strong enough to produce the Chemical Weapons Convention in 1993, which has been signed by 193 states. The convention did not eliminate chemical weapons, and it did not prevent the Syrian government from using them in the 2010s. But it created a norm that made their use a crime, and it created a mechanism for holding states accountable. The norm did not stop the use of chemical weapons, but it changed the consequences of using them.

The autonomous weapon debate is an attempt to create a similar norm before the technology is widely deployed. The campaign’s strategy is to establish the principle that human control over the use of force is a moral and legal requirement, and to make the development and use of fully autonomous weapons politically costly. The strategy has had some success, but it faces a fundamental obstacle: the technology is being developed by states and corporations that have a strong interest in deploying it, and the states that are most likely to use it are the states that are least likely to accept a ban. The United States, Russia, China, and India have all invested heavily in autonomous systems, and they have all resisted a binding treaty. The result is a stalemate that is likely to persist until the technology is actually used in a way that shocks the conscience of the world, or until a major power decides that the political cost of deploying it is too high.

The stalemate is not unique to autonomous weapons. It is the same stalemate that has frustrated arms control efforts in other areas, from nuclear testing to space weapons. The history of arms control suggests that progress is possible, but it also suggests that progress is usually the result of a crisis. The NPT was preceded by the Cuban Missile Crisis, which brought the world to the brink of nuclear war. The Chemical Weapons Convention was preceded by the use of chemical weapons in the Iran-Iraq War, which shocked the international community. The ban on anti-personnel mines was preceded by a campaign that highlighted the suffering of civilians in Cambodia, Angola, and Afghanistan. The ban on cluster munitions was preceded by the use of the weapons in Kosovo and Lebanon, which produced widespread civilian casualties. In each case, the crisis created a political opening that allowed the campaign to succeed. The autonomous weapon campaign has not yet had its crisis, and it may not have one until the weapons are used in a way that produces a public outcry.

The question that the history of weapons raises is whether the world can create a norm before the crisis occurs. The answer is not clear. The history of the last century suggests that prevention is possible, but it also suggests that prevention is rare. The NPT was a preventive measure, but it was adopted after the bomb had already been used. The Chemical Weapons Convention was a preventive measure, but it was adopted after chemical weapons had been used on a large scale. The bans on anti-personnel mines and cluster munitions were preventive measures, but they were adopted after the weapons had caused widespread civilian suffering. The pattern is consistent: the world tends to act after the damage has been done, not before. The autonomous weapon campaign is an attempt to break the pattern, and its success or failure will be a test of whether the world has learned anything from the history of the last century.

The history of weapons is not a story of inevitable progress. It is a story of choices, made by people shaped by the institutions and cultures in which they live. The institutions that develop weapons are not designed to restrain themselves. They are designed to produce the most effective weapons possible, and they are rewarded for doing so. The cultures that surround them are often shaped by the assumption that technological superiority is the key to security. The result is a system that produces weapons faster than it produces the norms to govern them. The gap between the technology and the norms is the central problem of the history of weapons, and it is the problem that the autonomous weapon debate is trying to solve.

The gap is not new. It has existed since the first stone axe was used to kill another human being. The difference is that the gap is now wider and more dangerous than ever before, because the technology is more powerful and more diffuse. The stone axe could only kill one person at a time, and it could only be used by someone close enough to swing it. The autonomous weapon can kill many people at once, and it can be used by someone thousands of miles away. The gap between the technology and the norms is the space in which the history of weapons unfolds, and the history of the last century suggests that the gap is not closing. It is widening.

The widening of the gap is not inevitable. It is the result of choices made by governments, by corporations, and by individuals. The choices are not always conscious, and they are not always made in the name of security. They are often made in the name of profit, or prestige, or bureaucratic inertia. But they are choices, and they can be made differently. The history of weapons shows that the gap can be narrowed, but it also shows that narrowing the gap requires political will, and political will is not always available. The autonomous weapon debate is an attempt to generate that will, and its outcome will depend on whether the world can muster the political will to impose limits on a technology that is still in its infancy.

The history of the last century provides some grounds for hope. The NPT, the Chemical Weapons Convention, the Ottawa Treaty, and the Convention on Cluster Munitions are all examples of the world imposing limits on weapons that were once considered essential. They are imperfect, and they have not eliminated the weapons they were designed to control. But they have changed the political and moral landscape in which those weapons are used. They have made it harder to use the weapons, and they have made it easier to hold states accountable when they do. The autonomous weapon campaign is trying to do the same thing, and it has already had some success. The question is whether it can build on that success, or whether it will be overwhelmed by the same forces that have frustrated other arms control efforts.

The answer will depend on the choices that are made in the next decade. The technology is developing rapidly, and the window for action is closing. The campaign to ban fully autonomous weapons has argued that the window is already closing, and that the world must act now or never. The major powers have argued that the technology is not yet mature enough to regulate, and that a ban would be premature. The debate is a familiar one, and it is likely to continue for as long as the technology continues to develop. The history of weapons suggests that the debate will be resolved not by argument alone, but by events. The events that will resolve it are likely to be a use of autonomous weapons that produces a public outcry, or a decision by a major power that the political cost of deploying the weapons is too high. Until then, the debate will continue, and the gap between the technology and the norms will continue to widen.

The history of weapons is a history of the gap between what is possible and what is acceptable. The gap is not fixed. It moves as the technology changes and as the norms change. The history of the last century shows that the gap can be narrowed, but it also shows that narrowing the gap is difficult and that it often requires a crisis. The autonomous weapon debate is an attempt to narrow the gap before the crisis occurs. Whether it succeeds will depend on the same factors that have determined the outcome of every previous arms control effort: the nature of the technology, the political context in which it is developed, and the norms that govern its use. The technology is new, but the factors are old, and the history of the last century provides a guide to what is likely to happen. The guide is not a prediction, but it is a warning. The warning is that the gap between the technology and the norms is not self-correcting. It must be closed by human action, and human action is not guaranteed. The history of weapons is a history of choices, and the choices that are made in the next decade will determine whether the autonomous weapon becomes a tool of restraint or a tool of escalation. The outcome is not predetermined. It is up to us.

The history of choices is also a history of unintended consequences. The weapons that were designed to make war more humane have often made it more brutal. The machine gun was designed to replace the volley fire of massed infantry, which was inaccurate and wasteful, with a weapon that could deliver sustained and accurate fire. The result was the trenches of the First World War, in which millions of soldiers died in a war of attrition that the machine gun made possible. The atomic bomb was designed to end the Second World War and to prevent a third, and it did both, but it also created a world in which the survival of humanity depends on the restraint of a handful of leaders. The precision-guided munition was designed to reduce civilian casualties by allowing bombs to be aimed at specific targets, and it did reduce civilian casualties in some conflicts, but it also made air power more attractive as an instrument of policy, and it lowered the political cost of using force. The drone was designed to allow surveillance and strike without putting pilots at risk, and it did, but it also made it easier for states to kill people in countries with which they were not at war, and it created a new kind of psychological warfare in which the sound of a drone overhead became a source of terror.

The pattern is consistent: every weapon that is designed to solve a problem creates a new problem. The new problem is usually not the one that the designers anticipated. The machine gun was not designed to create trench warfare. The atomic bomb was not designed to create a world of mutually assured destruction. The precision-guided munition was not designed to make war more palatable. The drone was not designed to create a permanent state of undeclared war. The unintended consequences are the product of the interaction between the technology and the social and political context in which it is used. The technology sets the possibilities, but the context determines which possibilities are realized. The history of weapons is therefore not a history of technology alone. It is a history of the interaction between technology and society, and the interaction is complex and unpredictable.

The complexity and unpredictability of the interaction is the reason why arms control is so difficult. The designers of weapons cannot anticipate how their weapons will be used, and the regulators cannot anticipate what weapons will be designed. The result is a constant game of catch-up, in which the norms are always one step behind the technology. The NPT was adopted after the bomb had been used. The Chemical Weapons Convention was adopted after chemical weapons had been used on a large scale. The bans on anti-personnel mines and cluster munitions were adopted after the weapons had caused widespread civilian suffering. The pattern is consistent, and it suggests that the world will not regulate autonomous weapons until they have been used in a way that produces a public outcry. The question is whether the outcry will come before or after the weapons have become so widespread that regulation is impossible.

The history of the last century suggests that the outcry usually comes after the damage has been done. The use of chemical weapons in the First World War produced an outcry that led to the Geneva Protocol of 1925, which banned the use of chemical and biological weapons in war. But the protocol did not prevent the use of chemical weapons in the 1980s, and it did not prevent the development of new chemical weapons. The use of nuclear weapons in 1945 produced an outcry that led to the NPT, but the NPT did not prevent the spread of nuclear weapons to India, Pakistan, Israel, and North Korea. The use of anti-personnel mines in the 1980s and 1990s produced an outcry that led to the Ottawa Treaty, but the treaty did not prevent the use of mines by states that did not sign it. The pattern is consistent: the outcry produces a treaty, but the treaty does not solve the problem. It creates a norm, and the norm changes behavior, but the change is slow and incomplete.

The autonomous weapon campaign hopes to break the pattern by creating a norm before the weapons are widely used. The campaign’s strategy is to establish the principle that human control over the use of force is a moral and legal requirement, and to make the development and use of fully autonomous weapons politically costly. The strategy has had some success, but it faces the same obstacle that has frustrated every previous arms control effort: the states that are most likely to use the weapons are the states that are least likely to accept a ban. The result is a stalemate, and the stalemate is likely to persist until the technology is used in a way that produces a public outcry, or until a major power decides that the political cost of deploying the weapons is too high.

The stalemate is not a reason for despair. The history of arms control shows that stalemates can be broken, but they are usually broken by events rather than by argument. The events that break stalemates are usually crises, and crises are usually the result of the use of the weapons that the stalemate was supposed to control. The logic is circular, and it is the logic that has governed the history of weapons for as long as weapons have existed. The world develops a weapon, the weapon is used, the use produces a crisis, the crisis produces a norm, and the norm changes behavior. The cycle is not inevitable, but it is the most common pattern, and there is no reason to believe that autonomous weapons will be exempt from it.

The cycle is not the only pattern, however. There are cases in which the world has acted before the crisis. The ban on blinding lasers is one example. The weapon was developed in the 1980s, and it was banned in 1995, before it had been widely used. The ban was the result of a campaign by the International Committee of the Red Cross, which argued that the weapon was unnecessarily cruel, and by a group of states that were willing to accept the ban. The campaign succeeded because the weapon was not essential to any state’s military strategy, and because the ban did not impose a significant cost on the states that accepted it. The lesson is that prevention is possible when the weapon is marginal and the cost of banning it is low. The autonomous weapon is not marginal, and the cost of banning it is high, which is why the campaign has had less success.

The lesson is not encouraging, but it is not the whole story. The history of weapons also shows that norms can change even when the technology is not marginal. The ban on chemical weapons was adopted even though chemical weapons were considered essential by many states. The ban on anti-personnel mines was adopted even though mines were considered essential by many military establishments. The bans succeeded because the campaigns that promoted them were able to mobilize public opinion and to persuade states that the weapons were not worth the political cost. The autonomous weapon campaign is trying to do the same thing, and it has had some success. The question is whether it can build on that success, or whether it will be overwhelmed by the same forces that have frustrated other arms control efforts.

The answer will depend on the choices that are made in the next decade. The technology is developing rapidly, and the window for action is closing. The campaign to ban fully autonomous weapons has argued that the window is already closing, and that the world must act now or never. The major powers have argued that the technology is not yet mature enough to regulate, and that a ban would be premature. The debate is a familiar one, and it is likely to continue for as long as the technology continues to develop. The history of weapons suggests that the debate will be resolved not by argument alone, but by events. The events that will resolve it are likely to be a use of autonomous weapons that produces a public outcry, or a decision by a major power that the political cost of deploying the weapons is too high. Until then, the debate will continue, and the gap between the technology and the norms will continue to widen.

The gap is not the only problem. The history of weapons also shows that the development of weapons is shaped by the political and economic systems in which it takes place. The weapons that are developed are not always the weapons that are needed. They are the weapons that the institutions that develop them are capable of producing, and the institutions are shaped by the interests of the states and corporations that fund them. The result is a system that produces weapons for reasons that have little to do with the security of the states that use them. The system produces weapons because the institutions that develop them are rewarded for producing them, and because the states that buy them are rewarded for buying them. The rewards are not always financial. They are often political, and they are often the result of the desire for prestige, or the fear of being left behind, or the bureaucratic inertia of institutions that have been developing weapons for decades.

The history of the last century is full of examples of weapons that were developed for reasons that had little to do with military necessity. The battleship was developed because states wanted to project power and prestige, and because naval institutions were dominated by officers who believed that the battleship was the measure of a navy’s strength. The result was a naval arms race that culminated in the First World War, and a generation of battleships that were obsolete almost as soon as they were built. The bomber was developed because air power theorists believed that bombing would win wars by destroying the enemy’s will to fight, and because air forces wanted to justify their existence as independent services. The result was a strategy that killed hundreds of thousands of civilians and did not achieve its objectives. The missile was developed because states wanted to deliver nuclear weapons quickly and reliably, and because the technology was available. The result was a world in which the survival of humanity depends on the restraint of a handful of leaders.

The pattern is consistent: the development of weapons is driven by institutional interests as much as by military necessity. The institutions that develop weapons are not neutral. They have their own interests, their own cultures, and their own ways of seeing the world. The result is a system that produces weapons that are often more expensive, more complex, and more destructive than they need to be. The autonomous weapon is likely to follow the same pattern. It is being developed because the institutions that develop it believe that it will give them an advantage, and because the states that fund it believe that it will enhance their prestige. The development is not driven by a careful assessment of the costs and benefits, and it is not driven by a democratic debate about the kind of world that the weapons will create.

The absence of a democratic debate is one of the most important features of the history of weapons. The decisions that shape the development of weapons are usually made by a small group of officials, scientists, and military officers, and they are usually made in secret. The public is informed after the decisions have been made, and the information that is provided is often incomplete or misleading. The result is a system in which the most important decisions about the future of humanity are made without the knowledge or consent of the people who will be affected by them. The atomic bomb is the clearest example. The decision to develop the bomb was made by a small group of officials and scientists, and it was kept secret from the public until the bomb was used. The decision to use the bomb was made by a handful of people, and it was not subject to a democratic debate. The result was a weapon that changed the world, and the change was not the result of a democratic choice.

The autonomous weapon is following the same pattern. The decisions that shape its development are being made by a small group of officials, scientists, and military officers, and they are being made in secret. The public is informed after the decisions have been made, and the information that is provided is often incomplete or misleading. The result is a system in which the most important decisions about the future of warfare are being made without the knowledge or consent of the people who will be affected by them. The campaign to ban fully autonomous weapons is an attempt to change the pattern, and it has had some success in raising public awareness. But the campaign is fighting against a system that is designed to keep the decisions secret, and the system has a long history of resisting attempts to open it up.

The history of weapons is therefore not only a history of technology. It is a history of power, and of the ways in which power is exercised. The states and corporations that develop weapons have a vested interest in keeping the decisions secret, because secrecy gives them an advantage over their competitors and over the public. The result is a system in which the most important decisions are made by the people who have the most to gain from them, and in which the people who have the most to lose are excluded from the process. The autonomous weapon is the latest example of this pattern, and the campaign to ban it is the latest attempt to change it. The outcome will depend on whether the campaign can mobilize enough public pressure to overcome the resistance of the institutions that develop the weapons. The history of the last century suggests that the campaign can succeed, but it also suggests that success is not guaranteed.

The history of the last century also suggests that the development of weapons is shaped by the international system. The system is anarchic, in the sense that there is no world government to enforce the rules, and the states that make up the system are sovereign. The result is a security dilemma: each state’s efforts to increase its security decrease the security of other states, and the result is an arms race. The security dilemma is the driving force behind the development of weapons, and it is the reason why arms control is so difficult. The states that are caught in the dilemma cannot afford to be left behind, and the result is a system that produces weapons faster than it produces the norms to govern them. The autonomous weapon is the latest example of the dilemma, and the campaign to ban it is the latest attempt to escape it. The outcome will depend on whether the states that are caught in the dilemma can find a way to cooperate, and the history of the last century suggests that cooperation is possible but difficult.

The difficulty of cooperation is the reason why the history of weapons is a history of cycles. The cycles are driven by the interaction between the technology, the institutions that develop it, and the international system in which it is used. The technology sets the possibilities, the institutions determine which possibilities are realized, and the international system determines the context in which the institutions operate. The interaction is complex, and it is not always predictable. The result is a history that does not follow a straight line, but that oscillates between periods of rapid development and periods of consolidation and restraint. The autonomous weapon is the latest example of the oscillation, and the campaign to ban it is the latest attempt to push the world toward restraint. The outcome will depend on the choices that are made in the next decade, and the choices will be shaped by the same factors that have shaped every previous period of the history of weapons.

The history of weapons is therefore a history of the human condition. It is a history of the desire for security, the fear of the other, the pursuit of power, and the search for meaning. It is a history of the ways in which human beings have tried to solve the problem of violence, and of the ways in which their solutions have created new problems. The autonomous weapon is the latest solution, and it is likely to create new problems. The problems will not be solved by the technology alone, and they will not be solved by the norms alone. They will be solved by the interaction between the technology, the norms, and the political context in which they are developed. The interaction is complex, and it is not always predictable. But it is the only way forward, and the history of the last century provides a guide to what is likely to happen. The guide is not a prediction, but it is a warning. The warning is that the gap between the technology and the norms is not self-correcting. It must be closed by human action, and human action is not guaranteed. The history of weapons is a history of choices, and the choices that are made in the next decade will determine whether the autonomous weapon becomes a tool of restraint or a tool of escalation. The outcome is not predetermined. It is up to us.

The history of choices is also a history of the ways in which the choices are constrained by the past. The past is not a dead weight, but it is a weight, and it shapes the range of options that are available in the present. The states that develop weapons are shaped by the wars that they have fought, by the institutions that they have built, and by the cultures that they have inherited. The result is a system that is resistant to change, and that tends to reproduce the patterns of the past. The autonomous weapon is being developed in a world that is shaped by the history of the last century, and the history of the last century is a history of the failure of arms control. The failure is not total, but it is significant, and it has created a world in which the development of weapons is driven by the fear of being left behind. The result is a system that is likely to produce autonomous weapons, and the question is whether the system can also produce the norms to govern them.

The answer will depend on the choices that are made in the next decade. The choices will be shaped by the same factors that have shaped every previous period of the history of weapons: the technology, the institutions, the international system, and the norms. The technology is new, but the factors are old, and the history of the last century provides a guide to what is likely to happen. The guide is not a prediction, but it is a warning. The warning is that the gap between the technology and the norms is not self-correcting. It must be closed by human action, and human action is not guaranteed. The history of weapons is a history of choices, and the choices that are made in the next decade will determine whether the autonomous weapon becomes a tool of restraint or a tool of escalation. The outcome is not predetermined. It is up to us.

The history of the last century is also a history of the ways in which the development of weapons has been shaped by the experience of war. The experience of war is not a single thing. It is different for the soldiers who fight, for the civilians who are caught in the middle, and for the societies that send them. The experience of the First World War shaped the development of weapons in the interwar period, and the experience of the Second World War shaped the development of weapons in the Cold War. The experience of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan shaped the development of drones and precision-guided munitions, and the experience of the war in Ukraine is shaping the development of autonomous weapons. The experience of war is therefore a feedback loop: the weapons shape the war, and the war shapes the weapons.
