paragraphs: The feedback loop between war and weapons has never run in only one direction, and the twentieth century offers the clearest evidence of how a single battlefield experience can redirect the trajectory of military technology for decades. The trench stalemate of the First World War did not merely produce new machines; it produced a new way of thinking about what a weapon was for. Before 1914, European general staffs assumed that firepower served maneuver—that artillery and rifles existed to enable infantry to close with and break the enemy line. By the winter of 1916, that assumption had been inverted. Firepower had become the purpose of battle rather than its servant, and the armies of the Western Front were organized around the production and delivery of shells to an extent no previous conflict had demanded. The consequence was a set of design priorities that shaped weapons for the next thirty years: mobility to escape the trench, armor to survive the machine gun, and indirect fire to reach unseen targets. Every major weapons system of the Second World War can be traced, in part, to a lesson learned in the mud of Flanders and the chalk of the Somme.

The scale of that redirection is difficult to overstate. Between 1914 and 1918, the combatants fired an estimated one billion artillery shells. The French alone produced more than 300 million rounds of 75mm ammunition, a figure that required expanding the Schneider and Renault works into industrial complexes employing hundreds of thousands of workers. The British shell crisis of 1915, which toppled the government of H.H. Asquith and brought David Lloyd George to the Ministry of Munitions, was not a failure of generalship but of industrial forecasting. The War Office had calculated prewar ammunition requirements on the assumption that battles would be short and decisive; when they proved neither, the entire economy had to be reorganized around the production of high-explosive filler. By 1917, the British were manufacturing more than 50 million shells a year, and the Ministry of Munitions controlled more than 20,000 factories and workshops. This was a transformation not just of weapons but of the relationship between the state and industry—one that would prove permanent.

The artillery experience of the First World War produced a specific set of technical innovations whose influence extended far beyond the armistice. The first was predicted fire. Before the war, artillery relied on observed fire: a forward observer watched where a shell landed and corrected the gun's aim. This was slow, vulnerable to counter-battery fire, and useless against targets that could not be seen. By 1917, the British and French had developed techniques for predicting where a shell would land based on meteorological data, barrel wear, and precise survey of gun positions, allowing accurate concentrations without prior registration. The Canadian Corps under Sir Arthur Currie used predicted fire to devastating effect at Vimy Ridge in April 1917, and the technique became standard for the remainder of the war. Predicted fire required not just better mathematics but better instruments: theodolites, sound-ranging equipment, and calibration devices that could measure barrel wear to a fraction of a millimeter. These instruments were the ancestors of the fire-control systems that would later guide naval guns, anti-aircraft batteries, and eventually ballistic missiles.

The second innovation was the creeping barrage, in which artillery fire advanced in a timed sequence ahead of the infantry, forcing defenders to remain in their dugouts until the attackers were almost upon them. First used in a limited way at the Somme in 1916, it was refined at Arras and Vimy in 1917. It required extraordinary coordination between artillery and infantry and depended on the reliable supply of shells and the accurate prediction of where each would fall. The creeping barrage was not a weapon in itself but a system—a way of combining existing weapons into a new form of tactical organization. The same logic of system integration would later produce the combined-arms teams of the Second World War, the armored spearheads of the Blitzkrieg, and the networked strike packages of the twenty-first century.

The third innovation was counter-battery fire as a distinct artillery mission. Before the war, counter-battery work was an afterthought; by 1916, it had become a specialized science. The British developed sound-ranging, locating enemy guns by triangulating the sound of their fire from a network of microphones, and flash-spotting, which used a gun's flash at night to determine its position. These techniques required dedicated survey sections, specialized equipment, and a centralized intelligence apparatus to process the data. The counter-battery organization of the British Expeditionary Force grew from a handful of officers in 1914 to a corps-level directorate by 1918. The lesson was clear: in a war of massed artillery, the side that could locate and destroy the enemy's guns would win the firefight, and the side that won the firefight would win the battle.

The First World War also demonstrated, with brutal clarity, the limitations of the weapons developed in the decades before 1914. The magazine rifle, the machine gun, and the quick-firing field gun had all been designed for open warfare, against targets that were visible and moving. In the trench environment, these weapons were often ineffective. The rifle could not be aimed accurately over the parapet without exposing the shooter; the machine gun was too heavy to move easily and too conspicuous to fire from a fixed position without attracting counter-battery fire; the field gun's flat trajectory could not hit targets in deep dugouts. The response was a wave of new weapons designed specifically for trench warfare: the trench mortar, the hand grenade, the flamethrower, and the submachine gun. Each was a direct response to a specific tactical problem, and each would have a long afterlife in the conflicts of the twentieth century.

The trench mortar was perhaps the most important. The British Stokes mortar, introduced in 1915, was a simple tube that fired a bomb from a fixed firing pin at the base. It was light enough for two men to carry, could be fired from a trench without exposing the crew, and could drop a bomb into an enemy trench with reasonable accuracy. It was the invention of Sir Wilfred Stokes, an engineer asked by Lloyd George to design a weapon that could break the deadlock of the trenches. By the end of the war, the British had produced more than 11,000 Stokes mortars and millions of bombs. The mortar became a standard infantry support weapon in every army in the world, and its descendants—the 60mm, 81mm, and 120mm mortars of the modern battlefield—remain in service today.

The hand grenade was another weapon reinvented for trench warfare. Before 1914, grenades were a curiosity, used mainly in sieges and by specialist troops. The trench environment made them essential: a grenade could be thrown around a corner, into a dugout, or over a parapet, and it could be carried by any infantryman. The British Mills bomb, introduced in 1915, was a segmented cast-iron sphere with a time fuse that could be thrown accurately and produced lethal fragmentation. More than 75 million Mills bombs were produced during the war. The grenade became a standard item of infantry equipment, and its design would evolve through the fragmentation grenades of the Second World War, the rifle grenades of the Cold War, and the 40mm grenade launchers of the modern era.

The flamethrower was a German invention, first used at Hooge in July 1915. It consisted of a portable tank of pressurized fuel and a nozzle that ignited the fuel as it was sprayed. It was a terrifying weapon but also a limited one: it had a range of only a few dozen yards, was dangerous to the operator, and was most effective against fixed positions. The Germans used flamethrowers in specialized assault units, the Sturmtruppen, trained to infiltrate enemy lines and attack strongpoints from the flanks. The flamethrower would be used again in the Second World War, most notably by the Americans against Japanese bunkers in the Pacific and by the Germans against Soviet fortifications on the Eastern Front. Its legacy is visible in the thermobaric weapons of the modern era, which use fuel-air explosives to achieve a similar effect over a larger area.

The submachine gun was the fourth major innovation of trench warfare. The first true submachine gun, the German MP18, was introduced in 1918. A shoulder-fired weapon that fired pistol ammunition at a high rate, it was ideal for the close-quarters combat of trench raids and urban fighting. The MP18 was used by the Sturmtruppen in the spring offensives of 1918 and was so effective that the Treaty of Versailles specifically prohibited Germany from producing submachine guns. The weapon was copied and improved by every major power in the interwar period: the Thompson in the United States, the Sten in Britain, the PPSh-41 in the Soviet Union, and the MP40 in Germany. The submachine gun became the signature weapon of the infantryman in the Second World War, and its descendants—the assault rifles and personal defense weapons of the modern era—remain the standard infantry weapon today.

The development of these weapons was not a matter of pure technological innovation. It was driven by the experience of combat, by the reports of officers who had been in the trenches, and by the demands of soldiers who needed weapons that would work in the conditions they faced. The British army, for example, had gone to war in 1914 with a doctrine that emphasized the rifle as the primary infantry weapon. By 1916, that doctrine had been revised to emphasize the grenade, the mortar, and the machine gun as the weapons that actually decided trench fights. The revision was not the work of a single theorist or committee; it was the product of a thousand after-action reports, a hundred training manuals, and the accumulated experience of millions of soldiers. The same process would repeat itself in every major conflict of the twentieth century.

The First World War also shaped weapons development more indirectly: it created a generation of military leaders determined never to fight another war of attrition. The French doctrine of the interwar period, embodied in the Maginot Line and the fortifications of the Metz region, was a direct response to the memory of Verdun. The French high command calculated that a fortified line could hold an attacker at bay long enough for the nation to mobilize, and that the cost of building the line was far less than the cost of another war of attrition. The Maginot Line was a technological solution to a tactical problem, but it was also a psychological one: it was designed to reassure a nation that had lost 1.4 million men that it would never again have to fight the kind of war that had killed them.

The German response was different. The Treaty of Versailles limited the German army to 100,000 men and prohibited the production of tanks, aircraft, and submarines. The German general staff, under Hans von Seeckt, responded by developing a doctrine that emphasized mobility, speed, and the concentration of force at a decisive point. This doctrine, later called Blitzkrieg, was designed to avoid the trench stalemate by using tanks and aircraft to break through the enemy line and exploit the breakthrough before the defender could react. It was not a weapon in itself, but it drove the development of specific weapons: fast tanks, dive bombers, and motorized infantry. The German army of 1939 was the product of a twenty-year effort to learn the lessons of 1914-1918 and build a force that could win the next war without repeating the mistakes of the last.

The British response was different again. The British army of the interwar period was small and poorly funded, but it produced a remarkable series of experimental mechanized formations. The Experimental Mechanized Force of 1927, under Colonel J.F.C. Fuller, demonstrated that a force of tanks, motorized infantry, and self-propelled artillery could move faster and strike harder than a traditional infantry division. Fuller's ideas, which emphasized the concentration of armored force at a decisive point and the exploitation of breakthrough, were influential in the development of British armored doctrine. But the British army was never able to fully implement them: the financial constraints of the 1930s and the priority given to imperial defense meant that the British army of 1939 was only partially mechanized. The British would spend the first years of the Second World War learning the lessons Fuller had taught in 1927.

The American response was shaped by a different set of experiences. The United States had entered the First World War late, and its army had seen only limited combat. But the American army of the interwar period was influenced by the writings of Fuller, Basil Liddell Hart, and other theorists of mechanized warfare. It developed a doctrine of armored warfare that emphasized the concentration of tanks in armored divisions, and it produced a series of tanks—the M2, the M3, and eventually the M4 Sherman—that would become the backbone of the Allied armored forces in the Second World War. The American experience of the First World War was less traumatic than the French or German experience, and the American response was correspondingly less radical. But the American army was still shaped by the lessons of 1914-1918, and the weapons it developed in the interwar period reflected those lessons.

The Second World War was, in many ways, the culmination of the trends that had begun in 1914. It was fought with weapons designed in response to the experience of the First World War, and its own experience would in turn shape the weapons of the Cold War. The tank, the aircraft, and the submarine—all developed in the First World War or in the years immediately before it—became the decisive weapons of the Second World War. The tank, in particular, was transformed from a slow, unreliable infantry support weapon into a fast, heavily armed vehicle that could break through enemy lines and exploit the breakthrough. The German Panzer divisions of 1939-1941 were the most effective armored force in the world, and their success was due as much to doctrine and organization as to the quality of their tanks. The Soviet T-34, introduced in 1940, was arguably the best tank of the war: it combined thick sloped armor, a powerful 76mm gun, and a reliable diesel engine in a package that was simple to produce and easy to maintain. The T-34 was a direct response to the experience of the First World War: it was designed to survive artillery fire, to cross trenches, and to break through enemy lines.

The aircraft was the other decisive weapon of the Second World War. The First World War had demonstrated the potential of aircraft for reconnaissance and ground attack, but it was the Second World War that made air power a decisive factor in land warfare. The German Ju-87 Stuka dive bomber, used in close coordination with armored columns, was a key element of the Blitzkrieg. The British and American strategic bombing campaigns against Germany and Japan demonstrated the destructive potential of air power, but they also revealed its limitations: strategic bombing did not break the will of the German or Japanese people, and it did not shorten the war as much as its advocates had predicted. The experience of the Second World War would shape the development of air power in the Cold War, when the bomber and the ballistic missile became the primary means of delivering nuclear weapons.

The submarine was the third decisive weapon of the Second World War. The German U-boat campaign against Allied shipping in the Atlantic was one of the most important campaigns of the war: it threatened to cut Britain off from its supplies and starve the British people into submission. The Allied response—the convoy system, the escort carrier, and the development of radar and sonar—was a case study in the feedback loop between weapons and tactics. The Germans developed new submarine designs, such as the Type XXI, which could stay submerged longer and travel faster underwater; the Allies developed new anti-submarine weapons, such as the Hedgehog and the Leigh Light, which could detect and destroy submarines more effectively. The Battle of the Atlantic was a technological arms race, and its outcome depended on the ability of each side to develop and deploy new weapons faster than the other.

The Second World War also saw the development of entirely new categories of weapons. The most important was the ballistic missile. The German V-2, first launched in September 1944, was the world's first operational ballistic missile. It was a terrifying weapon: it traveled at supersonic speed, could not be intercepted by the air defenses of the time, and carried a one-ton warhead that could destroy an entire city block. The V-2 killed an estimated 9,000 people in Britain and Belgium, but its strategic impact was limited: it was too inaccurate to be used against specific targets and too expensive to be produced in large numbers. But it was a technological breakthrough that would shape weapons development for the next fifty years. The ballistic missile would become the primary means of delivering nuclear weapons, and the technology developed for the V-2 would be used by both the United States and the Soviet Union in their space programs.

The other new category was the jet aircraft. The German Me-262, first flown in 1942, was the world's first operational jet fighter. It was faster than any Allied fighter and could have been a decisive weapon if produced in large numbers and used effectively. But it was hampered by engine problems, by the interference of Hitler, who wanted it used as a bomber, and by the shortage of skilled pilots and fuel. The British Gloster Meteor, first flown in 1943, was the first jet fighter to enter service with an Allied air force. The jet engine would transform air warfare in the postwar period, and the development of jet fighters and bombers would become a central element of the Cold War arms race.

The most important weapon of the Second World War, however, was not a tank or an aircraft or a missile. It was the atomic bomb. The Manhattan Project, which began in 1942 and culminated in the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, was the largest scientific and industrial undertaking in history. It employed more than 130,000 people and cost more than $2 billion—the equivalent of about $30 billion today. The project produced two types of bomb: a uranium gun-type device, code-named Little Boy, dropped on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, and a plutonium implosion device, code-named Fat Man, dropped on Nagasaki on August 9, 1945. The bombs killed an estimated 200,000 people, most of them civilians, and ended the war in the Pacific.

The atomic bomb was a weapon of a different kind. It was not an incremental improvement on existing weapons; it was a qualitative leap that changed the nature of warfare. The bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki demonstrated that a single weapon could destroy an entire city, and that a war fought with such weapons could destroy civilization. The international community responded by attempting to control the spread of nuclear weapons and prevent their use. The United Nations, founded in 1945, made nuclear disarmament one of its central goals. The Baruch Plan of 1946 proposed to place all nuclear weapons under international control, but it was rejected by the Soviet Union. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, established a framework for the control of nuclear weapons. The treaty has 191 states parties, but India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The NPT has been partially successful: it has slowed the spread of nuclear weapons but has not prevented it. The number of nuclear-armed states has grown from one in 1945 to nine today.

The development of nuclear weapons also shaped the development of conventional weapons. The Cold War, which lasted from 1947 to 1991, was a period of intense competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. The two superpowers competed in every category of weapon: tanks, aircraft, submarines, missiles, and nuclear warheads. The arms race was driven by a combination of technological competition, ideological rivalry, and bureaucratic inertia. Each side sought to maintain a qualitative advantage over the other and feared that the other would achieve a breakthrough that would give it a decisive advantage. The result was a period of unprecedented technological innovation, in which the weapons of the Second World War were replaced by entirely new systems: jet fighters, guided missiles, nuclear submarines, and precision-guided munitions.

The Cold War also saw the development of new categories of weapons designed to fight a nuclear war. The most important was the intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM). The Soviet R-7, first tested in 1957, was the world's first ICBM. It was a two-stage rocket that could deliver a nuclear warhead to a target more than 5,000 miles away. The American Atlas, first tested in 1958, was the first American ICBM. The development of ICBMs was accompanied by the development of submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs), which could be fired from submarines hidden beneath the ocean. The combination of ICBMs and SLBMs created the condition known as mutually assured destruction (MAD): each side had the ability to destroy the other, even after absorbing a first strike. MAD was a paradoxical strategy: it was designed to prevent war by making war unthinkable, and it succeeded in preventing a direct conflict between the United States and the Soviet Union for more than forty years.

The Cold War also saw the development of precision-guided munitions (PGMs). The first PGMs were developed during the Second World War: the German Fritz X and Henschel Hs 293 were radio-guided bombs used against Allied ships in the Mediterranean. But it was not until the 1960s and 1970s that PGMs became a significant part of the military arsenal. The American laser-guided bomb, first used in Vietnam in 1972, was a revolutionary weapon: it could be guided to a target by a laser designator and hit with an accuracy of a few meters. It was used to destroy bridges, bunkers, and other high-value targets that had previously required dozens or hundreds of unguided bombs to hit. The development of PGMs was driven by the experience of the Vietnam War, in which the American air campaign against North Vietnam had been frustrated by the inability of unguided bombs to hit precision targets.

The experience of the Vietnam War shaped weapons development in other ways as well. The war was fought in a jungle environment against an elusive enemy who used guerrilla tactics. The American response was to develop new weapons and tactics designed for counterinsurgency warfare: helicopter gunships, defoliants, and precision-guided munitions. The helicopter, in particular, became a signature weapon of the Vietnam War. The Bell UH-1 Iroquois, known as the Huey, was used to transport troops, provide fire support, and evacuate casualties. It was a versatile aircraft that could operate in conditions that would have been impossible for a fixed-wing aircraft. The experience of Vietnam demonstrated the importance of air mobility in counterinsurgency warfare and shaped the development of helicopter doctrine in the decades that followed.

The Vietnam War also demonstrated the limitations of air power in a counterinsurgency campaign. The American bombing campaign against North Vietnam, Operation Rolling Thunder, lasted from 1965 to 1968 and dropped more than 600,000 tons of bombs. It did not break the will of the North Vietnamese government, and it did not stop the flow of supplies to the Viet Cong in South Vietnam. The experience of Vietnam led to a reconsideration of the role of air power in warfare. The American air force of the 1970s and 1980s focused on developing weapons that could strike specific targets with precision, rather than weapons that could destroy large areas. The result was the precision-guided munitions that would be used to such devastating effect in the Gulf War of 1991.

The Gulf War was a turning point in the history of weapons. It was the first war in which precision-guided munitions played a significant role, and it demonstrated the potential of air power to achieve strategic effects with minimal casualties. The coalition air campaign, which began on January 17, 1991, was designed to destroy Iraq's command and control, its air defenses, and its weapons of mass destruction. The campaign used a combination of stealth aircraft, cruise missiles, and precision-guided bombs to strike targets with unprecedented accuracy. The F-117 Nighthawk, a stealth fighter invisible to radar, was used to strike high-value targets in Baghdad. The Tomahawk cruise missile, launched from ships and submarines in the Persian Gulf, was used to strike targets deep inside Iraq. The precision-guided bombs, guided by laser or television, were used to destroy bridges, bunkers, and command centers.

The statistics of the Gulf War air campaign are instructive. Coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs during Desert Storm. Of that total, about 6,520 tons were precision-guided, roughly 7.4 percent; the remaining 92.6 percent were unguided. Yet the precision-guided munitions struck high-value targets with an effectiveness that far exceeded their share of the tonnage. The images of laser-guided bombs destroying bridges and bunkers with a single hit were broadcast around the world, and they reshaped public and military expectations of air power. The Gulf War created the impression that precision-guided munitions had revolutionized warfare and that future wars would be fought with surgical precision and minimal collateral damage. That impression was not entirely accurate—the vast majority of the bombs dropped in the Gulf War were unguided, and they caused significant civilian casualties—but it shaped weapons development for the next two decades.

The Gulf War also demonstrated the importance of space-based systems in modern warfare. Coalition forces relied on GPS satellites for navigation, communications satellites for command and control, and reconnaissance satellites for intelligence. The GPS system, developed by the United States Department of Defense in the 1970s and 1980s, was used to guide aircraft and ground vehicles across the featureless desert of Iraq and Kuwait. GPS would become an essential element of precision-guided munitions, allowing bombs and missiles to navigate to their targets without a laser designator or a human operator. The development of GPS-guided weapons in the 1990s and 2000s would make precision-guided munitions cheaper, more reliable, and more widely available.

The experience of the Gulf War shaped weapons development in the post-Cold War period. The United States, which had emerged from the Cold War as the world's sole superpower, invested heavily in precision-guided munitions, stealth aircraft, and space-based systems. The goal was to create a military that could strike any target in the world with precision and minimal risk to American forces. The development of the Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM), a GPS-guided bomb that could be attached to any unguided bomb, was a key element of this strategy. The JDAM was first used in the Kosovo War of 1999 and used extensively in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. It was cheap, accurate, and easy to use, and it transformed the way air power was employed. By the 2000s, the majority of bombs dropped by American aircraft were precision-guided.

The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which began in 2001 and 2003 respectively, shaped weapons development in a different way. These wars were fought against insurgent forces dispersed among the civilian population, and they required a different kind of weapon from those developed for the Gulf War. The American military needed weapons that could strike specific targets with minimal collateral damage, and it needed weapons that could be used in urban environments where the distinction between combatants and civilians was blurred. The response was the development of smaller precision-guided munitions, such as the 250-pound Small Diameter Bomb, and new sensors and surveillance systems that could identify and track individual insurgents. These wars also saw the widespread use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), or drones, which could loiter over a target for hours and strike with precision when the opportunity arose.

The development of drones was one of the most significant weapons innovations of the post-9/11 period. The Predator drone, developed in the 1990s for reconnaissance, was armed with Hellfire missiles in 2001 and used to strike Taliban and al-Qaeda targets in Afghanistan. The Reaper drone, introduced in 2007, was larger and more capable, and it could carry a heavier payload of weapons. The drones were controlled by operators sitting in air-conditioned trailers in Nevada, thousands of miles from the battlefield. They could loiter over a target for hours, waiting for the right moment to strike, and transmit live video to commanders anywhere in the world. The drones transformed the way the United States fought its wars: they allowed the military to strike targets in countries where it had no ground forces and reduced the risk to American pilots. But they also raised new questions about the ethics and legality of remote warfare and provoked resentment among the populations that were targeted.

The experience of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan shaped weapons development more indirectly as well. The American military found that its conventional weapons—tanks, artillery, and fighter aircraft—were often ineffective against insurgents who used improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and guerrilla tactics. The response was a shift in investment toward intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) systems, toward special operations forces, and toward weapons that could be used in close-quarters combat. The development of the Mine Resistant Ambush Protected (MRAP) vehicle, designed to protect soldiers from IEDs, was a direct response to the experience of the Iraq War. The MRAP was a heavy, V-hulled vehicle that could withstand a blast from a roadside bomb, and it saved thousands of American lives. Its development was a case study in the feedback loop between war and weapons: the experience of the Iraq War created a demand for a new kind of vehicle, and the military and industry responded by developing one.

The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan also demonstrated the limitations of precision-guided munitions in counterinsurgency warfare. Precision-guided munitions were designed to destroy fixed targets, such as bridges and bunkers, but they were less effective against insurgents who moved frequently and hid among the civilian population. The American military found that it needed weapons that could strike with even greater precision, and sensors that could distinguish between combatants and civilians. The response was the development of new technologies, such as the Gorgon Stare, a wide-area surveillance system that could track multiple targets across a city, and smaller, more precise munitions. But these technologies were not a solution to the fundamental problem of counterinsurgency: the difficulty of distinguishing between insurgents and civilians in a crowded urban environment.

The experience of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan shaped weapons development in the twenty-first century, but it was not the only experience that did so. Wars between states—the conflicts in Georgia in 2008, in Ukraine in 2014, and in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020—also shaped weapons development. These conflicts demonstrated that the weapons and tactics developed for counterinsurgency warfare were not necessarily effective against a conventional opponent. The Russian army, which had learned from its experience in Chechnya and Georgia, developed a doctrine that emphasized electronic warfare, artillery, and drones. The Ukrainian army, which had learned from its experience in the Donbas, developed a doctrine that emphasized small-unit tactics, anti-tank missiles, and drones. The conflict in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 was a particularly important case: Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions to devastating effect against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses. The RUSI study of the conflict, published in 2021, treated it as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and the suppression of air defense. The conflict demonstrated that drones could be used not just for reconnaissance and precision strikes against individual targets but as a central element of a combined-arms campaign against a conventional opponent.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was a 44-day conflict that began on September 27, 2020, and ended with a ceasefire on November 10, 2020. Azerbaijan, supported by Turkey, launched an offensive to recapture territories occupied by Armenia since the early 1990s. The Azerbaijani forces used a combination of drones, loitering munitions, and long-range artillery to destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, and air defense systems. The Bayraktar TB2, a Turkish-made drone that could carry laser-guided missiles, was particularly effective. It could loiter over the battlefield for hours, identify targets, and strike them with precision. The Armenian air defenses, designed to counter traditional aircraft, were unable to detect or engage the drones. The result was a one-sided conflict in which Azerbaijan was able to destroy Armenian forces with impunity.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was a landmark in the history of weapons because it demonstrated the potential of drones to change the balance of power in a conventional conflict. It also demonstrated the vulnerability of traditional air defenses to drones and loitering munitions. The lessons of the conflict were studied by military forces around the world and shaped the development of new weapons and tactics. The United States, which had been developing drones for decades, accelerated its efforts to develop counter-drone systems. The Russians, who had sold air defense systems to Armenia, were forced to reconsider their assumptions about the effectiveness of those systems. The Chinese, who were developing their own drones and counter-drone systems, studied the conflict closely. The Nagorno-Karabakh war was a case study in the feedback loop between war and weapons: the experience of the conflict shaped the development of new weapons, which would in turn shape the experience of future conflicts.

The development of autonomous weapons is the most recent chapter in the history of the feedback loop between war and weapons. Autonomous weapons can select and engage targets without human intervention. They range from loitering munitions that can autonomously identify and strike targets to robotic sentries that can guard a perimeter without human supervision. Their development has been driven by advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and robotics, and it has been shaped by the experience of recent conflicts. The war in Ukraine, in particular, has accelerated the development of autonomous weapons: both Russia and Ukraine have used drones and loitering munitions extensively, and both sides have experimented with autonomous systems that can operate without human control.

The most controversial claim about autonomous weapons concerns an incident in Libya in 2021. A United Nations Panel of Experts report on Libya stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The Kargu-2 is a Turkish-made loitering munition that can be programmed to autonomously identify and strike targets. The UN report suggested that the weapon had been used in autonomous mode, without a human operator, to attack soldiers retreating from a battlefield. The claim was contested and has not been independently confirmed. It is important to treat it with caution: it is a contested allegation, not a confirmed autonomous strike. But the fact that the claim was made at all is significant. It suggests that autonomous weapons are no longer a theoretical possibility; they are a reality that the international community must confront.

The development of autonomous weapons raises profound ethical and legal questions. The laws of armed conflict require that combatants distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects and take precautions to minimize civilian casualties. Can an autonomous weapon make these distinctions reliably? Can it be held accountable for its actions? Who is responsible if an autonomous weapon kills civilians—the programmer, the commander, or the machine itself? These questions have been debated in the United Nations, in academic institutions, and in the militaries of the world. The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which meets in Geneva, has established a Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems to study the issue. But progress has been slow, and there is no international treaty that specifically regulates autonomous weapons.

The history of the feedback loop between war and weapons suggests that autonomous weapons will follow a familiar pattern. The experience of war will create a demand for weapons that can operate faster and more precisely than humans, and the development of those weapons will in turn shape the experience of future wars. The pattern is not deterministic: human choices, political decisions, and ethical considerations can shape the direction of weapons development. But the pattern is powerful, and it has been repeated in every major conflict of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. The development of autonomous weapons is the latest iteration of a process that began with the first stone axe and the first spear.

The feedback loop between war and weapons is not a simple cycle. It is a complex system in which many factors interact: technological innovation, industrial capacity, military doctrine, political leadership, and the experience of combat. The development of a new weapon is not simply a response to a battlefield problem; it is also a product of the institutions that develop it, the budgets that fund it, and the politics that shape it. The history of weapons is therefore a history of institutions as much as a history of technology. The Manhattan Project, for example, was not just a scientific undertaking; it was an industrial and bureaucratic one, involving the coordination of thousands of scientists, engineers, and workers across the United States. The development of the atomic bomb was shaped by the institutions that built it, and those institutions in turn shaped the weapons that were produced.

The history of weapons is also a history of unintended consequences. The tank, developed to break the trench stalemate of the First World War, became the decisive weapon of the Second World War. The atomic bomb, developed to end the Second World War, became the central weapon of the Cold War. The drone, developed for reconnaissance, became a precision-strike weapon. The internet, developed for military communications, became a tool of global commerce and social media. The history of weapons is full of examples of technologies developed for one purpose and used for another, and of weapons that had effects their designers never anticipated.

paragraphs: The feedback loop between war and technology is not a simple cycle in which conflict produces inventions and inventions produce new conflicts. It is a ratchet. Each turn adds capability that cannot be subtracted, and each addition raises the stakes of the next. A weapon, once demonstrated, cannot be undiscovered. A fortress, once breached, must be rebuilt on a new principle or abandoned. The ratchet does not turn at a constant speed. It lurches—during the industrial wars of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the naval arms race before 1914, the nuclear decades after 1945—and sometimes seems to stall, as in the long centuries when sword and bow coexisted without either displacing the other. But it does not run backward. This chapter examines the ratchet in detail, through the institutions and industries that turned ideas into arsenals, and through the moments when a new capability forced every rival to respond or perish.

Begin with an institution easy to overlook because it is so familiar: the arsenal. The word comes from the Arabic *dār al-ṣināʿa*, a house of manufacture, and entered European languages through Venetian and Genoese trade with the Islamic Mediterranean. By the fourteenth century the Venetian Arsenal, the *Arsenale di Venezia*, was a state enterprise of extraordinary scale—a walled complex of shipyards, ropewalks, foundries, and armories that could, according to the often-repeated but probably exaggerated chronicle, launch a fully equipped galley a day at its height. Whether or not the daily galley was literally achieved, the principle was real: the concentration of specialized labor, standardized components, and stored reserves under public control. Venice kept a reserve of seasoned timber and pre-fitted hulls, so a fleet could be assembled from parts rather than built from scratch. This was the first great lesson of military-industrial organization—that the decisive advantage often lies not in the weapon but in the capacity to replace it.

The lesson recurred wherever states built arsenals. The Ottoman Tophane-i Amire, the imperial cannon foundry at Constantinople, cast the great bombards that battered the walls of Constantinople in 1453, including colossal pieces the Venetian and Genoese defenders could not match. The Ottoman state maintained foundries, gunpowder mills, and saltpeter works across its territories, and its ability to sustain siege artillery was a principal reason for its expansion through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. In Muscovy, the Cannon Yard (*Pushkarsky Dvor*) in Moscow, established in the late fifteenth century, became a center of bronze casting; by the sixteenth century Russian foundries were producing guns of every caliber, and the great Tsar Cannon, cast in 1586, remains a monument to the ambition if not the utility of the enterprise. In Sweden, the crown under Gustavus Adolphus organized copper mining, cannon founding, and gunpowder production into a coordinated system that made the small kingdom a major exporter of artillery to the rest of Europe. The pattern was consistent: the state that could organize production on a large scale could field and, crucially, re-field its forces after losses.

The shift from artisan production to something recognizably industrial occurred first in small arms, through the division of labor. The traditional gunsmith made a gun entire, fitting lock, stock, and barrel by hand so that no two weapons were interchangeable. In the eighteenth century, the French, then the British and Americans, began to break the process into steps. The crucial figure in the American story is often said to be Eli Whitney, who in 1798 contracted with the United States government to produce ten thousand muskets with interchangeable parts. Historians have long since established that Whitney did not fully achieve interchangeability—his demonstration of swapping parts before officials was carefully staged with preselected components—but the idea had been planted, and the goal was pursued with increasing success by the federal armories at Springfield and Harpers Ferry and by private contractors such as Simeon North and John Hall. Hall's rifles, produced at Harpers Ferry from 1819, were built on the principle of interchangeable parts and were among the first firearms in the world to be so manufactured in quantity.

The significance of interchangeability was not merely logistical, though it was enormously that. A weapon whose parts could be swapped in the field could be repaired by a soldier rather than a specialist. An armory that could produce standardized parts could subcontract and could scale. But the deeper significance was conceptual: the weapon became a manufactured commodity rather than a crafted object, and the state that mastered its manufacture could equip armies on a scale artisanal production could never approach. The British, watching the American experiments with interest, established their own armory production at Enfield and elsewhere, and the "American system of manufactures," as they called it, became a template for industrial production far beyond weapons. The sewing machine, the bicycle, and eventually the automobile all drew on techniques refined in the making of guns.

The industrialization of firearms reached a threshold with the percussion cap and the rifled musket. The flintlock, dominant for two centuries, was vulnerable to weather and misfires; the percussion lock, using a small fulminate cap struck by a hammer, was more reliable and could be made in quantity. The next step was the Minié ball, developed by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849. The problem it solved was ancient: a spherical ball dropped down a smoothbore barrel was quick to load but inaccurate, while a ball fitting tightly into rifling was accurate but slow to ram home. Minié's bullet was a hollow-based lead projectile that expanded when the powder charge drove it forward, engaging the rifling even though it had been dropped loosely down the barrel. The result was a weapon that loaded as quickly as a smoothbore but fired with the accuracy of a rifle.

The consequences were immediate and terrible. The British Pattern 1853 Enfield and the American Springfield Model 1861, both firing Minié-type bullets, extended the infantryman's effective range from perhaps a hundred yards to several hundred. In the American Civil War, the rifled musket transformed the battlefield. Defenders behind earthworks could sweep open ground at ranges attackers could not cross without ruinous loss. The war's casualty figures—roughly 620,000 dead from a population of about thirty-one million—reflected not only the scale of the armies but the lethality of their weapons. Generals on both sides had learned their trade in the age of the smoothbore, and they repeatedly ordered frontal assaults against positions the new rifles made impregnable. The lesson, relearned at enormous cost in 1914, was that a change in the range and accuracy of the individual weapon could invalidate the tactical doctrine of an entire generation of officers.

The same decades saw the industrialization of artillery. Casting cannon in iron and bronze gave way to boring solid castings and then to rifling gun barrels. The French, under the artillery officer and later emperor Napoleon III, developed rifled field guns that could throw a conical shell accurately at ranges far beyond the smoothbore. The British responded with the Armstrong and Whitworth rifled guns, which used breech-loading mechanisms and, in Whitworth's case, a hexagonal bore that imparted a rapid spin. The race between armor and projectile, which would become a defining contest of the industrial age, had begun in earnest.

Then came the machine gun. Hiram Maxim, an American inventor working in London, demonstrated in 1884 a gun that used the recoil of the previous shot to load and fire the next. The Maxim gun was the first widely adopted self-powered automatic weapon; it could fire hundreds of rounds per minute, sustained by a water-cooled barrel and a belt of cartridges. The British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891, and the weapon and its descendants—the Vickers, the German Maschinengewehr 08, the Russian Maxim—became the backbone of defensive firepower in the First World War. The Maxim was not merely a faster rifle; it was a different category of weapon. A single gun crew could deliver the fire of a company, and the gun could be kept in action as long as ammunition and water lasted. The tactical implications were grasped slowly. In the colonial wars of the 1890s, the Maxim was used to devastating effect against opponents armed with spears and older firearms, as at Omdurman in 1898, where a British-Egyptian force under Kitchener destroyed a much larger Mahdist army with massed machine-gun and rifle fire. In the Boer War and the Russo-Japanese War, the machine gun began to show what it could do against European-style armies, but the full lesson was not absorbed until the trenches of the Western Front.

The industrialization of war required not only factories but systems of supply. An army in the field consumes ammunition, food, fuel, and replacement parts at rates preindustrial economies could not sustain. The railway was the first technology that made it possible to move and supply mass armies. The Prussian General Staff, under Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, built its plans around the railway timetable; the mobilization of 1870 was a triumph of logistics as much as of tactics, and the Prussian victory over France in the Franco-Prussian War demonstrated that the state that could move its armies fastest and supply them longest would win. The railway also reshaped strategy in a deeper sense: it made possible the concentration of forces at a chosen point, and it made the destruction of an enemy's rail network a strategic objective in its own right. The American Civil War had already shown this, with Sherman's March to the Sea and the raids on Confederate railroads; the wars of the twentieth century would make the railway, the road, and eventually the pipeline and the airfield the central objects of strategic attack.

The telegraph was the companion technology. For the first time, a commander could receive intelligence and issue orders in something close to real time, and a government could direct its generals from a capital hundreds of miles away. The Crimean War saw the first use of the electric telegraph to connect a field army with its capital, and the American Civil War saw the telegraph integrated into the operations of both armies. The effect was to centralize command and increase the tempo of decision. It also created a new vulnerability: the telegraph line, the cable, and the signal station became targets, and the interception of messages became a branch of military art. The telegraph and its successors—the telephone, the radio, the encrypted network—would become as important to the conduct of war as the weapons themselves, and the contest over communications would become one of the defining struggles of the twentieth century.

The naval dimension of the industrial ratchet turned on the same principles. The wooden sailing ship of the line, which had dominated naval warfare since the seventeenth century, was displaced within a few decades by the ironclad, the steam engine, and the rifled naval gun. The Crimean War demonstrated the vulnerability of wooden ships to explosive shells, and the American Civil War produced the first duel between ironclads, the *Monitor* and the *Merrimack* (rebuilt as the *Virginia*) at Hampton Roads in 1862. The lesson was unmistakable: armor had to be thick enough to resist the new guns, and the guns had to be powerful enough to penetrate the new armor. The result was a spiral in which each new class of battleship was rendered obsolete by the next class of gun, and the cost of naval competition rose to levels that strained the finances of every great power. The British *Dreadnought*, launched in 1906, was a deliberate break with the past: an all-big-gun ship, turbine-powered, heavily armored, that made every existing battleship obsolete overnight. The *Dreadnought* triggered a naval arms race with Germany that poisoned Anglo-German relations and contributed to the outbreak of the First World War.

The First World War was the ratchet's most terrible demonstration. The war began with the weapons and doctrines of the nineteenth century and ended with weapons that would define the twentieth. The opening campaigns were fought with rifles, machine guns, and field artillery, and the result was a stalemate on the Western Front that neither side could break. The response was a series of innovations, each intended to restore movement and each deepening the war's lethality. Poison gas, first used on a large scale by the Germans at Ypres in 1915, was a chemical weapon both sides soon adopted; it killed and maimed hundreds of thousands and left a legacy of fear and revulsion that shaped the chemical-weapons treaties of the later century. The tank, developed by the British and first used at Flers-Courcelette in September 1916, was an attempt to combine armor, firepower, and mobility in a single vehicle; its early performance was unreliable, but its potential was clear, and the tank would become the decisive weapon of the next war. The airplane, first used for reconnaissance, was armed for combat and then for ground attack; the strategic bomber, which would become a defining weapon of the Second World War, was conceived during the First.

Artillery was the war's dominant weapon, and its development illustrates the ratchet at its most relentless. The French 75mm field gun, the *Canon de 75 modèle 1897*, was a revolutionary design. Its hydro-pneumatic recoil system absorbed the force of the recoil and returned the barrel to its firing position, so the gun did not have to be re-laid after each shot. The result was a rate of fire—often cited at roughly fifteen rounds per minute—far beyond anything a smoothbore or a conventionally mounted rifled gun could achieve. The 75 became an icon of French artillery and a symbol of the offensive spirit of the prewar French army. But the war that came was not a war of rapid maneuver; it was a war of entrenched positions, and the 75's flat trajectory was less useful than the heavy howitzers that could drop shells into trenches. The great artillery battles of the war—Verdun, the Somme, Passchendaele—consumed shells at rates no prewar planning had anticipated. The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916, produced roughly 700,000 casualties and was dominated from beginning to end by artillery. The German bombardment that opened the battle fired more than a million shells in the first hours, and the French response, the *Voie Sacrée*, the "Sacred Way" supply route that kept the fortress supplied, became a legend of logistics. The war taught that industrial shell production was as decisive as tactical skill, and the belligerents built vast new capacities to manufacture explosives, propellants, and fuses. The lesson was not lost on the planners of the next war.

The Second World War was the ratchet at full speed. The tank, the airplane, the aircraft carrier, the submarine, the radar, the proximity fuse, the rocket, and the atomic bomb all reached maturity within six years. The war was fought by industrial economies mobilized entirely for production, and the outcome was determined as much by factory output as by battlefield courage. The German *Blitzkrieg* of 1939–1941 was a doctrine built around the tank and the dive bomber, and it demonstrated that a combined-arms force could break through a defensive line and exploit the breakthrough at a speed the defenders could not match. The Soviet response, the deep battle doctrine and the massive production of the T-34 tank, showed that the ratchet could be turned by a state that organized its industry for war on an unprecedented scale. The American "arsenal of democracy"—the Liberty ships, the B-24 bombers, the Sherman tanks, the escort carriers—demonstrated that production capacity could be a strategic weapon in its own right.

The air war illustrated the ratchet's moral as well as its material dimension. The doctrine of strategic bombing, developed between the wars by theorists such as Giulio Douhet and Hugh Trenchard, held that bombing an enemy's cities and industry could break its will to fight. The British and American bombing campaigns against Germany and Japan put the doctrine to the test. The results were ambiguous at best. The bombing of Hamburg in 1943 and Dresden in 1945, the firebombing of Tokyo in March 1945, and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki killed hundreds of thousands of civilians, but the extent to which they shortened the war remains debated. What is not debated is that the bombing campaigns diverted enormous resources from other uses, forced the defenders to build vast networks of fighters and anti-aircraft guns, and demonstrated the vulnerability of industrial societies to attack from the air. The bomber, in other words, was a weapon whose effects were as much psychological and political as physical, and the moral questions it raised—about the targeting of civilians, about the proportionality of means to ends—became central to the ethics of war in the nuclear age.

The atomic bomb was the ratchet's most dramatic turn. The Manhattan Project, which produced the first nuclear weapons, was a mobilization of scientific and industrial resources without precedent. The Trinity test of 16 July 1945, in the New Mexico desert, detonated a plutonium implosion device with a yield of about twenty-one kilotons—roughly equivalent to twenty-one thousand tons of TNT. The bomb dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 was a uranium gun-type device with a yield of about fifteen kilotons; the bomb dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August was a plutonium implosion device with a yield of about twenty-one kilotons. The two bombs killed an estimated 110,000 to 210,000 people by the end of 1945, and the survivors—the *hibakusha*—carried the physical and psychological scars for the rest of their lives. The strategic effect was immediate: Japan surrendered, and the world entered the nuclear age.

The nuclear age transformed the ratchet's logic. Before 1945, the competition between offense and defense was a contest in which each side could hope to gain an advantage by superior technology, numbers, or tactics. After 1945, the destructive power of a single weapon was so great that the traditional calculus broke down. The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949, and the United States responded by developing the hydrogen bomb, tested in 1952 with a yield of about ten megatons—roughly a thousand times the yield of the Hiroshima bomb. The Soviet Union tested its own hydrogen bomb in 1953. The result was a condition strategists called mutual assured destruction: each side had enough nuclear weapons to destroy the other many times over, and any use of nuclear weapons would be suicidal. The ratchet had reached a point where further turning could not produce a usable military advantage; it could only produce more destruction.

The response to this condition was arms control. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, was an attempt to stop the spread of nuclear weapons to additional states while committing the existing nuclear powers to eventual disarmament. It has 191 states parties. India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined; North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003 and subsequently tested nuclear devices. The treaty has been only partially successful: it has slowed but not stopped proliferation, and the commitment to disarmament has not been fulfilled. The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks of the 1970s and the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaties of the 1980s and 1990s reduced the arsenals of the United States and Russia from their Cold War peaks, but thousands of warheads remain deployed, and new delivery systems—hypersonic glide vehicles, maneuverable reentry vehicles, and autonomous systems—have raised new questions about the stability of deterrence.

The nuclear ratchet also produced a counter-ratchet in conventional weapons. Because nuclear weapons could not be used without risking annihilation, the great powers fought their wars through proxies and with conventional forces, and they invested heavily in the precision and lethality of those forces. The development of precision-guided munitions was the most important conventional innovation of the late twentieth century. In the Vietnam War, the United States used laser-guided bombs to destroy bridges and other point targets that had resisted repeated conventional bombing. The technology matured through the 1970s and 1980s and was demonstrated on a large scale in the Gulf War of 1991. Coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs in Desert Storm; about 6,520 tons were precision-guided, roughly 7.4 percent of the total. The percentage was small, but the effect was disproportionate. Precision-guided munitions struck command bunkers, bridges, power plants, and air-defense sites with an accuracy unguided bombs could not match, while reducing collateral damage. The images of laser-guided bombs falling precisely onto targets, broadcast around the world, reshaped public and military expectations of air power. The promise of "precision" became a central justification for the use of force, and the development of GPS-guided munitions in the 1990s made precision available in all weather and at longer ranges.

The revolution in precision was accompanied by a revolution in surveillance and communications. The satellite, the drone, the encrypted radio, and the networked computer made it possible for a commander to see the battlefield in something close to real time and to direct fires with unprecedented accuracy. The "revolution in military affairs" that theorists proclaimed in the 1990s was, in essence, the application of information technology to the age-old problem of finding and hitting the enemy. The result was a military that could, in the favorable conditions of the 1991 and 2003 Iraq wars, destroy an opponent's command and control and paralyze its defenses within days. But the revolution also revealed its limits. Precision weapons are expensive, and they depend on intelligence, communications, and air superiority. Against an opponent who can deny those conditions—by dispersing, by hiding among civilians, by using unjammable communications, or by fielding sophisticated air defenses—the advantage of precision is reduced.

The drone was the emblem of the new warfare. Unmanned aerial vehicles, developed for reconnaissance in the Vietnam War and refined through the 1980s and 1990s, became armed strike platforms in the first decade of the twenty-first century. The American Predator and Reaper drones, armed with Hellfire missiles, allowed the United States to strike targets in Pakistan, Afghanistan, Yemen, Somalia, and elsewhere without risking pilots. The drone was a weapon of persistence—it could loiter over a target for hours—and of precision, and it became a central tool of counterterrorism. But the drone also raised profound legal and ethical questions. Who is a combatant in a war against a nonstate actor? What is the legal basis for killing a suspected militant in a country with which the United States is not at war? What is the effect on civilians who live under the constant threat of drone strike? The debate over drones was, in miniature, the debate over all precision weapons: the ability to strike a specific target with minimal collateral damage is a genuine moral advance over area bombing, but it also makes the decision to use force easier, and it places the power to kill in the hands of officials who may be far from the consequences.

The drone war reached a new stage in the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh conflict. In the forty-four-day war between Azerbaijan and Armenia, Azerbaijani forces used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions—"kamikaze" drones that circle a target and then dive into it—to destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, and air-defense systems. The Royal United Services Institute, in a 2021 study, treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense. The lesson military analysts drew was that cheap, widely available drones could defeat expensive, traditional systems, and that air defense, designed to counter manned aircraft and missiles, was vulnerable to small, slow, low-flying drones. The conflict also demonstrated the power of imagery: drone footage of destroyed tanks, broadcast on social media, became a weapon of information warfare as well as a record of physical destruction.

The next step in the ratchet is autonomy. The loitering munitions used in Nagorno-Karabakh were, for the most part, remotely controlled or preprogrammed, but the technology for autonomous targeting exists and is being developed. A United Nations Panel of Experts report on Libya, issued in 2021, stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The claim is contested and has not been independently confirmed, and it should be treated with caution. But the possibility it raises is real: a weapon that selects and attacks its own targets, without a human in the loop, would be a genuine revolution in the ethics and law of war. The debate over autonomous weapons is now one of the most active in international humanitarian law, and the outcome will shape the ratchet's next turn.

The ratchet does not turn only through new weapons. It also turns through new defenses, and the contest between the two is the oldest pattern in the history of war. The castle wall was answered by the siege tower and the battering ram; the siege tower by the moat and the sloping wall; the sloping wall by the cannon; the cannon by the bastion; the bastion by the mortar and the mine. The First World War's trenches were answered by the tank, and the tank by the anti-tank gun and the shaped-charge warhead. The airplane was answered by the fighter and the anti-aircraft gun, and the bomber by the radar-directed interceptor and the surface-to-air missile. The missile was answered by the anti-missile, and the anti-missile by the maneuverable warhead and the decoy. This is the "offense-defense balance," the central variable in the history of weapons. When offense has the advantage, wars tend to be short and decisive; when defense has the advantage, wars tend to be long and bloody. The First World War was long and bloody because the defense—the trench, the machine gun, the rapid-firing artillery—had the advantage. The Second World War was more mobile because the tank and the airplane restored the advantage to the offense. The nuclear age reversed the balance again, because the offense—the missile—could not be reliably stopped, and the result was a stalemate of terror.

The offense-defense balance is not a purely technical matter. It depends on doctrine, training, geography, and the willingness of societies to bear costs. A weapon decisive in one context may be useless in another. The machine gun was decisive in the defensive conditions of the Western Front but less useful in the mobile conditions of the Eastern Front, where vast distances and poor roads favored cavalry and armored cars. The tank was decisive in the open plains of Poland and Ukraine but less useful in the mountains of Italy and the jungles of the Pacific. The history of weapons is full of technologies developed for one environment that proved inadequate in another, and of armies that failed because they assumed the conditions of the last war would be those of the next.

The ratchet is also driven by competition between states. The security dilemma—the condition in which one state's defensive measures appear threatening to its neighbors, who respond with measures of their own—is the engine of arms races. The naval race between Britain and Germany before 1914 was a classic example: each new British battleship was seen in Berlin as a threat, each new German battleship was seen in London as a challenge, and the result was a spiral of construction that consumed vast resources and poisoned relations. The nuclear arms race of the Cold War was another: each new American missile was answered by a new Soviet missile, and each new Soviet missile by a new American one, and the result was an arsenal of tens of thousands of warheads that could never be used. The security dilemma is not irrational; it is a structural feature of a system of sovereign states without a common authority. But it can be mitigated by arms control, by transparency, and by institutions that allow states to reassure one another. The history of the twentieth century is, in part, the history of attempts to mitigate the security dilemma—the League of Nations, the United Nations, the nuclear nonproliferation regime, the conventional arms control treaties of the Cold War's end—and of the limits of those attempts.

The institutions that shape weapons development are not only international. They are also domestic: the bureaucracies, industries, and political coalitions that surround the production of arms. The "military-industrial complex," a phrase made famous by President Dwight Eisenhower in his farewell address of 1961, describes the network of relationships among the armed forces, the defense industry, and the political establishment that sustains and expands military production. Eisenhower, who had commanded the Allied armies in Europe, warned that the "conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry" was new in the American experience and that its "total influence—economic, political, even spiritual—is felt in every city, every statehouse, every office of the federal government." The warning was prescient. The defense industry became a major employer and a major source of political contributions, and the services became a major consumer of advanced technology. The result was a system in which the development of new weapons was driven as much by bureaucratic and industrial interests as by strategic need.

The same dynamic operated in the Soviet Union, where the military-industrial complex was even more deeply embedded in the state. The Soviet defense industry employed millions of workers and consumed a vast share of the national product. The design bureaus—Tupolev, Mikoyan, Sukhoi, Korolev—were centers of technological innovation, and competition among them produced some of the most advanced weapons of the Cold War. But the system also produced waste, duplication, and a chronic inability to convert military technology to civilian use. The Soviet economy was, in a sense, a war economy that never demobilized, and its collapse in 1991 was in part the collapse of a system organized around the production of weapons.

The ratchet has a cultural dimension as well. Weapons are not only tools; they are symbols, and the symbolism shapes the way societies think about war. The sword was the symbol of the knightly class, and the rifle the symbol of the citizen-soldier. The battleship was the symbol of national power, and the aircraft carrier is the symbol of power projection. The nuclear bomb is the ultimate symbol of annihilation, and the drone is the symbol of a new kind of war in which the warrior is distant and unseen. The symbolism matters because it shapes the decisions societies make about which weapons to build and which to forswear. The campaign against chemical weapons, which began in the nineteenth century and culminated in the Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993, was driven in part by a moral revulsion expressed in cultural terms: the gas attack was seen as a violation of the laws of war and of the dignity of the soldier. The campaign against land mines, which produced the Ottawa Treaty of 1997, was driven by images of maimed civilians and the testimony of deminers. The campaign against autonomous weapons is being driven by a similar moral concern: the fear that machines will be allowed to make life-and-death decisions that should be reserved for human beings.

The ratchet is also shaped by the law. The laws of war—the Geneva Conventions, the Hague Conventions, the customary rules that govern the conduct of hostilities—are not merely constraints on the use of weapons; they also shape the development of weapons. A state that wants to use a weapon must consider whether its use will be legal, and that consideration can influence the weapon's design. The development of precision-guided munitions was driven in part by the desire to comply with the principle of distinction—the rule that combatants must distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects. The development of nonlethal weapons was driven in part by the desire to use force in situations where lethal force would be legally or politically unacceptable. The law is not always effective; states sometimes violate it, and the enforcement mechanisms are weak. But the law sets a standard against which the use of weapons is judged, and that standard shapes the political and moral environment in which weapons are developed.

The ratchet's future is uncertain. The technologies now emerging—artificial intelligence, hypersonic weapons, directed-energy weapons, quantum computing, biotechnology—have the potential to transform warfare as profoundly as gunpowder, the steam engine, and the atomic bomb. Hypersonic weapons, which travel at more than five times the speed of sound and can maneuver in flight, threaten to defeat existing missile defenses and to compress the time available for decision-making. Directed-energy weapons—lasers and high-power microwaves—offer the possibility of defeating drones and missiles at the speed of light. Artificial intelligence offers the possibility of autonomous systems that can process information and make decisions faster than human beings. Each raises profound questions about stability, about the ethics of autonomous killing, and about the control of escalation. The ratchet will continue to turn, and the task of statesmen and citizens will be to manage its turning in a way that preserves the possibility of peace.

The history of the ratchet is, in the end, a history of choices. Technologies do not develop on their own; they are developed by people, in institutions, under political and economic conditions that can be changed. The decision to build a weapon is a decision that can be made differently. The decision to use a weapon is a decision that can be refused. The history of the twentieth century is full of examples of weapons developed but never used, of arms races halted by negotiation, of wars prevented by deterrence. The ratchet is not a natural force; it is a human construction, and it can be managed by human action. The question facing the twenty-first century is whether the institutions built to manage the ratchet—the treaties, the alliances, the international organizations, the norms—are strong enough to bear the strain of the new technologies. The answer is not yet known, but the history of the ratchet suggests it will depend on the wisdom and the will of the people who make the decisions.

The ratchet's turning is visible most clearly in the great wars, but it is also visible in the small wars, the colonial wars, the insurgencies, and the police actions that have filled the spaces between the great conflicts. The colonial wars of the nineteenth century were laboratories for new weapons: the Maxim gun, the repeating rifle, the steel-hulled gunboat, and the telegraph were all tested in Africa and Asia before they were used in Europe. The small wars of the twentieth century—the Boer War, the Spanish Civil War, the Vietnam War, the Soviet war in Afghanistan—were also laboratories, and the lessons learned in them shaped the weapons and doctrines of the great powers. The Spanish Civil War, in particular, was a proving ground for the tank, the dive bomber, and the strategic bombing of cities, and the lessons were absorbed by the Germans, the Soviets, and the Western allies in the years before 1939. The Vietnam War was a proving ground for the helicopter, the precision-guided bomb, and the electronic sensor, and the lessons shaped the American military's "revolution in military affairs" in the 1990s. The Soviet war in Afghanistan was a proving ground for the shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missile and for the guerrilla tactics that would be used against the Americans in Afghanistan and Iraq.

The small wars also reveal the limits of the ratchet. A technologically superior force can win every battle and still lose the war, because the ratchet's logic applies to the means of destruction but not to the ends of politics. The United States in Vietnam, the Soviet Union in Afghanistan, and the United States in Iraq and Afghanistan all discovered that the most advanced weapons in the world could not build a legitimate government, could not win the loyalty of a population, and could not defeat an insurgency willing to absorb punishment and wait. The lesson is not that technology is irrelevant; it is that technology is a means, not an end, and that the political and social dimensions of war are as important as the technical. The ratchet turns, but it does not turn the whole of war. The human element—the courage, the fear, the loyalty, the betrayal, the hope—remains at the center, and no weapon has yet been invented that can replace it.

The history of the ratchet is also a history of the state. The state that could organize production, mobilize manpower, and finance the costs of war could compete; the state that could not was conquered or absorbed. The rise of the modern state in early modern Europe was driven in large part by the demands of war: the need for revenue to pay for artillery, fortifications, and standing armies led to the development of taxation, bureaucracy, and public credit. The military revolution of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—the "gunpowder revolution" that transformed European warfare—was also a fiscal revolution, and the states that mastered it became the great powers of the modern world. The relationship between war and the state is reciprocal: war made the state, and the state made war. The ratchet turned, and the state grew, and the growth of the state made the ratchet turn faster.

The twentieth century pushed this relationship to its limit. The two world wars mobilized entire societies, and the state that could organize the whole of its economy for war—the "total war" state—was the state that could win. The Soviet Union, the United States, and the United Kingdom all demonstrated that a modern industrial society could produce weapons on a scale unimaginable in the nineteenth century. The cost was enormous: the Second World War killed an estimated seventy to eighty-five million people, and the destruction of cities, industries, and infrastructure took decades to repair. The nuclear age then made total war suicidal, and the state's relationship to war changed again. The great powers could no longer fight each other directly without risking annihilation, so they fought through proxies, through economic pressure, through information operations, and through the development of ever more sophisticated conventional weapons. The state's military institutions became professionalized, technologized, and expensive, and the gap between the military and the society it defended widened.
