paragraphs: The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan also produced new ways of understanding the relationship between war and the grotesque. Those wars were fought in the name of the grotesque and against it. They were a reminder that war is a grotesque act, and that how wars are fought and understood is shaped by the grotesque.

The same wars produced new ways of understanding the relationship between war and the beautiful. They were fought in the name of the beautiful and against it. They were a reminder that war is a beautiful act

—and that the two categories cannot be held apart. The weapon that kills a man at a thousand meters is a beautiful object; the wound it makes is grotesque. The aircraft that levels a city block is a triumph of engineering; the city block is a ruin. This doubleness is not a paradox to be resolved but a condition to be described, and it is the condition under which every weapon since the first sharpened stone has been made, admired, used, and mourned.

By the second decade of the twenty-first century, the tools of war had entered a phase in which the old categories of weapon and platform, soldier and machine, front line and rear area, had begun to dissolve. The dissolution was not sudden. It had been underway since at least the mid-twentieth century, when the guided missile first promised to make the bomber obsolete and the computer first promised to make the gunner obsolete. But the wars of the 2000s and 2010s accelerated it, and the conflicts of the 2020s—in Nagorno-Karabakh, Ukraine, Gaza, the Red Sea—made it visible to anyone who cared to look. The history of weapons had reached a point where the most consequential developments lay no longer in the explosive power of the warhead or the range of the gun, but in the software that guided the warhead, the sensor that found the target, and the network that connected the two.

This shift had a date, or a cluster of dates, and the most instructive is 1991. In the air campaign of Operation Desert Storm, coalition forces dropped approximately 88,500 tons of bombs. About 6,520 tons were precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent. The number is small: the kind a skeptic could use to argue that the "revolution in military affairs" was hype, that the Gulf War was won by the same mass and firepower that had won the Second World War, and that precision weapons were a footnote. But the footnote did the work. The 7.4 percent was aimed at the targets that mattered: command bunkers, bridges, power stations, air-defense nodes, the infrastructure of the Iraqi state. The other 92.6 percent was aimed at area targets—troop concentrations, supply dumps, the things mass bombing had always been aimed at. Precision weapons did not replace mass; they complemented it, and in complementing it they changed what air power could promise. Before 1991, the promise was attrition: we will destroy so much of your army that you cannot fight. After 1991, it was decapitation: we will destroy the things that make your army an army, and we will do it on the first night.

The public understood this before the military did, or at least before the military's doctrine caught up. The images from Baghdad in January 1991—green tracers arcing into the night, the flash of a bomb hitting its target with the camera rolling, the neat crosshairs of the cockpit video—became the visual vocabulary of a new kind of war. The crosshairs were the key image. They showed the viewer what the weapon saw, and what the weapon saw was a target: a building, a bridge, a tank, a truck. They made the war legible as a series of precise, discrete acts of destruction, each justified by the thing in the center of the frame. What they did not show was everything outside it: the people in the building, the traffic on the bridge, the family in the truck. The precision weapon did not eliminate collateral damage; it reorganized the viewer's relationship to it. The bomb that missed by ten meters was no longer a bomb that missed; it was a bomb that hit the wrong thing, and the wrong thing could be shown or not shown depending on the edit.

The military learned the lesson slowly and unevenly. The 1999 air campaign over Kosovo—Operation Allied Force—was fought entirely from the air, at altitudes above 15,000 feet, to protect the crews. The result was a campaign that destroyed a great deal of Serbian military equipment and infrastructure but did not stop the expulsion of Kosovo Albanians until ground threat and diplomacy converged. The precision weapons worked; the strategy did not. The Pentagon drew the lesson that precision was necessary but not sufficient, that the network of sensors and shooters had to be integrated, and that the targeting cycle—the time between finding a target and destroying it—had to be compressed. This was the origin of the "kill chain" as a doctrinal concept: find, fix, track, target, engage, assess. The kill chain described a process, but it also described a weapon. The weapon was no longer the bomb; the weapon was the chain.

By the 2000s, the chain had become the organizing principle of American military power. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq were fought by small units connected to vast networks of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. A Special Forces team on a mountainside in Afghanistan could call in an airstrike from a bomber circling at 30,000 feet, guided by a Predator drone's camera feed, coordinated by a command center in Qatar, and authorized by a commander in Florida. The team was the point of the spear; the network was the shaft. The Taliban and later the Iraqi insurgency learned to fight the network by disappearing into the population, using civilians as cover, communicating through couriers and disposable phones, and accepting that any concentration of force would be destroyed from the air. The result was a war of small actions—ambushes and IEDs, night raids and drone strikes—in which the most important weapon was often the one not fired: the camera, the radio, the biometric scanner, the database.

The drone was the emblem of this phase. The MQ-1 Predator, first flown as a reconnaissance platform in the 1990s and armed with Hellfire missiles after 2001, was a slow, unglamorous aircraft with a propeller and a bulging sensor turret. It was not fast or stealthy or particularly survivable in contested airspace. What it was, was persistent. It could loiter over a target for twenty hours, watching, waiting, then strike. The persistence changed the temporal structure of war. A commander with a Predator overhead did not have to decide whether to strike now or wait for a better opportunity; he could wait, and the waiting was itself a form of pressure. The people below knew they were being watched, or suspected it, and the suspicion shaped their behavior. The drone was a weapon that worked by being present.

The drone also changed the politics of war. A Predator strike in a country with which the United States was not at war—Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, Libya—was not an act of war in the constitutional sense, because it committed no ground troops and risked no American lives. It was a "targeted killing," a "kinetic strike," a "disposition matrix" entry. The euphemisms were not incidental. They were the linguistic technology that made a new kind of violence possible. The drone strike required a new vocabulary because it fit none of the old categories: it was not a battle, not a bombing campaign, not an assassination in the classic sense, though it had elements of all three. It was a continuous, low-level, globally distributed use of force, authorized by secret legal opinions and conducted by the CIA and the military's Joint Special Operations Command. The weapon and the law evolved together, each shaping the other.

The drone's critics called it a coward's weapon, a weapon that killed by remote control, that turned war into a video game. The criticism had force, but it misdescribed the experience of the people who flew the drones. The pilots sat in air-conditioned trailers in Nevada, watching a screen, then went home to their families at the end of the shift. They were not in physical danger, but they were in a psychological danger of a kind the military had not anticipated. The surveillance was intimate. The drone's camera could see a man's face, follow him for days, watch him play with his children, see him say goodbye to his wife, and then kill him. The pilots reported symptoms of trauma resembling those of combat veterans, and the military struggled to understand why. The answer, perhaps, was that the drone had collapsed the distance that had always separated the killer from the killed—not by bringing them closer in space but by bringing them closer in time and attention. The pilot knew his target as a person before he killed him, and that knowledge was a kind of wound.

The drone was also the first widely used weapon that was partly autonomous. The Predator was flown by a human pilot, but it relied on autopilot, GPS, and software to stay aloft and find its way. The Hellfire missile was guided by a laser or a radar seeker. The sensor turret was stabilized by gyroscopes and controlled by software. The human was in the loop, but the loop was made of code. As the 2000s gave way to the 2010s, the code grew more capable. The Reaper replaced the Predator, carrying more weapons and better sensors. The Gorgon Stare pod gave a single drone the ability to watch a whole city at once. The Army's Gray Eagle and the Navy's Fire Scout added new platforms. And the software that processed the video, flagged moving objects, and suggested targets became more sophisticated. The human's role shifted from operator to supervisor, from the person who flew the aircraft to the person who approved what the aircraft's software had found.

This shift was the subject of intense debate within the military and among scholars of war. The debate was about autonomy: how much decision-making could be delegated to a machine, and under what conditions. It was about accountability: if a machine killed the wrong person, who was responsible—the pilot, the programmer, the commander who authorized the strike? It was about ethics: was it permissible to kill by algorithm, and if so, what did that say about the value of human life? And it was about strategy: would autonomous weapons make war more likely, because they lowered the cost of using force, or less likely, because they made its use more precise and therefore more proportionate?

The debate was not resolved, but it was given a concrete test in the 2020s. The 44-day war between Armenia and Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, fought from 27 September to 10 November 2020, was the first conflict in which drones and loitering munitions played a decisive role. Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones, armed with precision-guided munitions, and Israeli-made loitering munitions—the Harop and the SkyStriker—to destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, air-defense systems, and supply columns. The Armenian air defenses, designed to counter manned aircraft, could not reliably detect or engage the small, slow, low-flying drones. The TB2s flew at altitudes and speeds that exploited gaps in Armenian radar coverage, and the loitering munitions loitered—circling over the battlefield, waiting for a target to appear, then diving onto it. The videos of the strikes, filmed by the drones' own cameras and posted to social media by the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense, showed tanks exploding, artillery pieces flipping into the air, soldiers running from vehicles that had been hit. The videos were propaganda, but they were also evidence: a relatively small, relatively cheap force of drones could defeat a larger, more traditional force.

The RUSI study of the conflict, published in 2021, described it as a landmark. The authors, led by Justin Bronk, argued that the war demonstrated the vulnerability of traditional ground forces to drone-enabled strike and suppression of air defense. They noted that the TB2 was not a wonder weapon—it was slow, vulnerable to fighters and sophisticated surface-to-air missiles, and dependent on a data link that could be jammed. But in a conflict where the defender lacked modern fighters and modern air defenses, the TB2 was decisive. The drone had not made tanks obsolete, the study concluded, but it had made the tank's survival dependent on a layered defense of electronic warfare, short-range air defense, and camouflage and concealment. It had raised the cost of operating armor in the open, at a fraction of the cost of a manned aircraft.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was followed, sixteen months later, by the Russian invasion of Ukraine, which became the largest land war in Europe since 1945 and the most intensive test of drones and precision weapons in a high-intensity conflict. The war began on 24 February 2022 with a Russian attempt to decapitate the Ukrainian government by seizing Kyiv. The attempt failed, and the war settled into a grinding attritional struggle along a front stretching from the Black Sea to the Russian border. The drones were everywhere. Ukrainian forces used Turkish TB2s in the early weeks to strike Russian supply columns, then, as Russian air defenses adapted, shifted to smaller, cheaper drones: the American Switchblade loitering munition, the Polish Warmate, and a vast array of commercial quadcopters adapted to carry grenades and mortar shells. Russian forces used their own drones—the Orlan-10 for reconnaissance, the Lancet loitering munition for strike, and Iranian-made Shahed-136 one-way attack drones for deep strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The Shahed was a simple, cheap, propeller-driven aircraft with a warhead and a GPS guidance system; slow and noisy and easy to shoot down, but cheap enough to be launched in swarms, and the swarms overwhelmed Ukrainian air defenses and forced the expenditure of expensive interceptors on cheap targets.

The drone war in Ukraine was a war of adaptation. The Russians learned to jam the GPS signals that guided Ukrainian drones, and the Ukrainians learned to fly without GPS, using inertial navigation and visual piloting. The Russians learned to hide their tanks under camouflage nets and move them only at night, and the Ukrainians learned to use thermal cameras to find them anyway. The Ukrainians learned to use Starlink satellite internet to control their drones and coordinate their artillery, and the Russians learned to target the Starlink terminals. Each adaptation was a small chapter in the history of weapons, and each was made in weeks or months rather than the years or decades that had characterized weapons development in the industrial age. The drone war was a war of software updates.

The artillery war in Ukraine was equally instructive. By most measures it was an artillery war: the majority of casualties on both sides were caused by artillery, and the rate of shell consumption was enormous. The Ukrainians fired thousands of shells a day, and the Russians fired more. The supply of shells became a strategic problem. The United States and its allies scoured the world for 155mm shells, and the production capacity of the Western defense industry—shrunk after the Cold War—proved inadequate to the demand. The war revealed that the precision revolution had not eliminated the need for mass. Precision weapons were used extensively—the American HIMARS rocket launcher, with its GPS-guided rockets, destroyed Russian ammunition depots and command posts far behind the front—but they were used alongside the old unguided artillery, and the old unguided artillery was still the backbone of the war.

The HIMARS was a case study in the value of precision. The M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System was a truck-mounted launcher that fired GPS-guided rockets with a range of about 80 kilometers. The Ukrainians used it to strike Russian ammunition depots, forcing the Russians to move their depots farther from the front, which lengthened their supply lines, which made their logistics more vulnerable. The HIMARS did not win the war, but it changed the geometry of the war. It was a weapon that worked by changing the enemy's behavior rather than by destroying his forces directly. The Russians dispersed their depots, moved their command posts, stopped using fixed headquarters. The HIMARS was a weapon that made the enemy hide.

The war in Ukraine also saw the first large-scale use of hypersonic missiles in combat. The Russian Kinzhal, an air-launched ballistic missile with a claimed hypersonic speed, was used against Ukrainian targets, including, in March 2022, a large underground ammunition depot in western Ukraine. The Kinzhal was not a true hypersonic glide vehicle—it was an air-launched ballistic missile with a maneuvering warhead—but it was fast and difficult to intercept. The Ukrainians claimed to have shot down Kinzhals with American Patriot air-defense systems, and the claims were disputed. The significance of the hypersonic missile was not that it was unstoppable—it was not—but that it compressed the reaction time of the defender. A hypersonic missile launched from a few hundred kilometers away could reach its target in minutes, leaving the defender almost no time to detect, decide, and intercept. The hypersonic missile was a weapon that worked by shrinking time.

The war in Gaza, which began on 7 October 2023 with the Hamas attack on Israel and continued into 2024 and beyond, was another test of the new weapons in a different environment. The Hamas attack was a low-tech assault—paragliders, motorcycles, pickup trucks, rifles—that overwhelmed a high-tech defense. The Israeli response was a high-tech campaign that used precision-guided munitions, drones, and artificial intelligence to identify and strike targets in a dense urban environment. The Israeli military used an AI system called Lavender to generate targets, and another called the Gospel to identify buildings and structures associated with Hamas. The systems were reported to have generated thousands of targets at a speed human analysts could not match, and the strikes that followed killed thousands of civilians. The war in Gaza raised the question the drone debate had been circling for two decades: what happens when the kill chain is automated, when the machine finds the target and the human merely approves? The answer, in Gaza, was that the human approved more targets than he could meaningfully evaluate, and the result was a scale of destruction that the precision weapons had promised to prevent.

The war in the Red Sea, which began in late 2023 when Houthi forces in Yemen began attacking commercial shipping, was a test of a different kind. The Houthis used anti-ship ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones to attack ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Gulf of Aden. The attacks were cheap—a drone cost a few thousand dollars—and the defenses were expensive: a Standard Missile-2 interceptor cost millions. The United States and its allies shot down dozens of drones and missiles, and the cost exchange ratio was deeply unfavorable. The Houthi campaign demonstrated the asymmetric logic of the new weapons: a poor, non-state actor could impose costs on a rich, technologically advanced adversary using cheap, commercially available technology. The drone had democratized precision strike, and the democratization had consequences the inventors of the Predator had not foreseen.

The thread running through all these conflicts is the convergence of the sensor, the network, and the weapon. In the industrial age, the weapon was a discrete object—a gun, a tank, a bomb—and the history of weapons was the history of improvements to that object. In the information age, the weapon is a system, and the history of weapons is the history of the integration of the system. The system includes the sensor that finds the target, the network that transmits its location, the computer that calculates the firing solution, the guidance system that steers the weapon, and the warhead that destroys the target. It also includes the human who decides whether to fire, and the legal and political framework that authorizes the decision. The system is the weapon, and the system is distributed across space and time in ways that make it difficult to say where the weapon begins and ends.

This convergence has a history, and it is longer than the drone. It begins with radar in the 1930s, which made it possible to detect aircraft beyond visual range. It continues with the proximity fuze in the 1940s, which made anti-aircraft fire far more lethal; the guided missile in the 1950s; the laser-guided bomb in the 1960s; the cruise missile in the 1970s; GPS in the 1980s; and the drone in the 1990s. Each was a step toward the integration of the system and away from the discrete weapon. The history of weapons in the twentieth century is the history of the weapon becoming a system, and the history of the twenty-first century is the history of the system becoming autonomous.

The autonomy question is the question the history of weapons has been building toward since the first time a human being used a tool to kill another human being. The tool was an extension of the human's will, and the human was responsible for what the tool did. The bow and arrow extended the human's reach, but the human aimed and released. The firearm extended it further, but the human still aimed and pulled the trigger. The artillery piece extended the reach to miles, but the human still calculated the trajectory and gave the order to fire. The guided missile extended it to hundreds of miles; the human programmed the target, but the missile did the flying and the finding. The drone extended it to thousands of miles; the human watched the screen and pressed the button. The autonomous weapon extends the reach to the point where the human is no longer in the loop at all, and the machine decides whom to kill.

The debate over autonomous weapons has been conducted largely in the language of ethics and law, and that is appropriate, because the stakes are ethical and legal. But it has also been conducted in the language of speculation, because the autonomous weapon has not yet been widely used in combat. The UN Panel of Experts report on Libya, published in March 2021, stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces in Libya in 2020. The report was carefully hedged, and the claim was not independently confirmed. The Kargu-2, manufactured by the Turkish company STM, was a quadcopter loitering munition that could be operated in autonomous mode, using onboard cameras and machine-learning algorithms to identify and attack targets. The report's authors were cautious, but the report was a milestone: the first official document to suggest that a machine might have killed a human being without a human being deciding to kill that human being. The suggestion was contested, and it remains contested. But the fact that it could be made at all was a sign that the history of weapons had reached a threshold.

The threshold is not a cliff. The autonomous weapon is not a single thing that either exists or does not exist. Autonomy is a spectrum, and most weapons called autonomous are partly autonomous. The Patriot air-defense system has an automatic mode in which it engages targets without human intervention, but the mode is used under human supervision and can be overridden. The Aegis combat system on Navy ships has a similar mode. The Israeli Iron Dome system decides which incoming rockets to intercept and which to ignore, faster than a human could. The loitering munitions used in Nagorno-Karabakh and Ukraine have autonomous modes that let them track a target after it has been designated, but a human designates the target. The question is not whether autonomy exists but where the human is in the loop, and how much time and information the human has to exercise judgment.

The history of weapons suggests that the answer will be determined not by ethics but by tactics. The side that can compress the kill chain will win the engagement, and compression requires the removal of the human from the loop, because the human is slow. A human takes a second or more to decide whether to fire; a machine takes a millisecond. In a fight between a machine that decides in a millisecond and a human who decides in a second, the machine will win. This is the logic that drives autonomy, and no ethical objection has yet been able to defeat it. Ethical objection can slow the development of autonomous weapons, and it can shape the rules under which they are used, but it cannot stop the development, because the tactical advantage is too great. The history of weapons is a history of tactical advantages pursued regardless of ethical cost, and there is no reason to think the autonomous weapon will be an exception.

The history of weapons is also a history of the unintended consequences of tactical advantages. The machine gun was developed to give a small number of soldiers the firepower of a large number, and it did, but it also made the frontal assault suicidal and produced the trench stalemate of the First World War. The bomber was developed to strike behind the lines, and it did, but it also made civilians the target and produced the doctrine of strategic bombing that killed hundreds of thousands. The nuclear weapon was developed to end the Second World War, and it did, but it also produced a decades-long arms race and the possibility of human extinction. The autonomous weapon will have unintended consequences, and the most likely is that it will make war faster and more frequent, because it will lower the cost of using force and remove the human hesitation that has sometimes prevented war. The autonomous weapon will be a weapon that works by removing the human from the decision, and the removal of the human from the decision is the removal of the last check on the use of force.

The check was never reliable. Humans have always been willing to kill, and the history of war is a history of humans killing other humans in large numbers. But the check was a check, and its removal is a change in kind, not just in degree. The human in the loop is the person who can say no. The machine in the loop is the person who has delegated the decision to a machine that cannot say no. The delegation is the essence of the autonomous weapon, and the delegation is the thing the history of weapons has been building toward.

The history of weapons has also been building toward the integration of the human and the machine. The soldier of the twenty-first century is not a man with a rifle; he is a node in a network, carrying a radio, a GPS receiver, a night-vision device, a thermal sight, a laser rangefinder, and a computer. The rifle is the least important thing he carries. The network is the weapon, and the soldier is the sensor. His eyes and ears are the network's eyes and ears, and his rifle is the network's smallest and most intimate effector. The integration of the soldier into the network is the integration of the human into the system, and it mirrors the integration of the system into the weapon. The soldier and the weapon are becoming the same thing, and the thing they are becoming is a distributed, networked, intelligent system that finds and kills.

The integration has a history, and it is the history of the infantryman's load. In the eighteenth century, a soldier carried a musket, a bayonet, a cartridge box, a canteen, and a knapsack—about thirty pounds. In the nineteenth century, the rifle replaced the musket, and the load grew. In the twentieth century, the machine gun, the radio, the helmet, the gas mask, and the entrenching tool were added, and the load grew to sixty or eighty pounds. In the twenty-first century, the night-vision device, the body armor, the GPS, the radio, the computer, and the batteries were added, and the load grew to a hundred pounds or more. The soldier was carrying more and more equipment to connect him to the network, and the equipment was making him slower and more exhausted. The integration of the soldier into the network was making the soldier less able to fight as a soldier. The solution, in the 2020s, was the exoskeleton, the powered suit that would carry the load for the soldier, and also the robot, the machine that would carry the load instead of the soldier. The robot was the next step in the integration, and the integration was the next step in the history of weapons.

The robot was not a new idea. The Germans used the Goliath tracked mine in the Second World War, a small, remote-controlled vehicle that carried a bomb. The Soviets used teletanks, remote-controlled tanks, in the Winter War. The Americans used the MQ-1 Predator, a remote-controlled aircraft, in the 1990s. But the robots of the twenty-first century were different, because they were autonomous or semi-autonomous, and because they were cheap. The commercial drone, the quadcopter with a camera and a GPS, cost a few hundred dollars, and it could be adapted to carry a grenade or a mortar shell. The adaptation was made by soldiers in the field, not by engineers in a laboratory, and it spread through the ranks in weeks. The drone was a weapon invented by its users, and the users were not the people who had designed it. The history of weapons had become a history of improvisation.

The improvisation was visible in Ukraine, where soldiers on both sides modified commercial drones to carry munitions, drop grenades, relay communications, and conduct reconnaissance. The modifications were posted to social media, the posts were studied by soldiers on the other side, and the other side made its own modifications. The cycle of innovation was measured in days. A new drone tactic would appear on the front, and within a week the other side would have a counter, and within another week the first side would have a counter to the counter. The drone war was a war of rapid iteration, and the iteration was driven by the soldiers, not the generals. The generals were trying to catch up with their own troops.

The generals were also trying to catch up with the technology. The procurement systems of the world's militaries were designed for the industrial age, when a weapon took a decade to develop and a generation to field. The drone took a month to develop and a week to field. The procurement systems could not keep up, and the soldiers bypassed them. Soldiers bought commercial drones with their own money or with crowdfunded donations and used them in ways the procurement systems had not anticipated. The result was a gap between what the military had and what the military needed, and the gap was filled by improvisation. The history of weapons had become a history of the gap between the institution and the technology, and the gap was widening.

The gap was not new. The history of weapons is full of institutions failing to adapt to new technology. The French army in 1940 had more and better tanks than the German army, but it used them as infantry support, while the Germans used them as a concentrated striking force. The British army in 1914 had the best rifle in the world, the Lee-Enfield, but not the doctrine to use it in the way the war required. The Roman legions in the fourth century had the best infantry in the world, but they could not adapt to the cavalry armies of the barbarians. The gap between institution and technology is a constant in the history of weapons, and the constant is the source of the surprises that decide wars. The side that closes the gap first wins, and the side that closes it second loses.

Closing the gap is a matter of culture as much as technology. The military that can learn faster wins, and the military that can learn faster tolerates dissent, encourages initiative, and rewards improvisation. The Ukrainian military in 2022 was such a military, at least at the small-unit level. The Russian military was not. The Ukrainians decentralized decision-making, allowing junior officers and non-commissioned officers to adapt their tactics to the situation; the Russians centralized it, requiring junior officers to seek approval from higher headquarters. The result was that the Ukrainians could exploit the new technology faster than the Russians, and the exploitation of the new technology was a decisive advantage in the early months of the war. The history of weapons is not just the history of the weapons; it is the history of the institutions that use them, and the institutions that learn faster are the institutions that win.

The learning was visible in the artillery war. The Ukrainians used a commercial software system, GIS Arta, to coordinate their artillery fire. The system allowed a drone operator to send a target's coordinates to a gun crew in seconds, and the gun crew to fire and adjust in minutes. It was a force multiplier, because it compressed the kill chain from the minutes or hours of a traditional artillery unit to the seconds of a networked one. The Russians had a similar system, but it was less flexible and less widely used. The result was that the Ukrainians could hit Russian targets faster than the Russians could hit Ukrainian targets, and the speed was a form of precision. The artillery war was a war of software, and the software was the weapon.

The software was also the vulnerability. The Ukrainians relied on Starlink, the satellite internet system built by SpaceX, to connect their drones and their artillery. The Starlink terminals were small, portable, and hard to jam, and they gave the Ukrainians a communications advantage the Russians could not match. But the terminals were also a single point of failure. If SpaceX had decided to turn them off, or if the Russians had found a way to jam them, the Ukrainian advantage would have disappeared. Dependence on a commercial system was a new kind of vulnerability, one the history of weapons had not seen before. The weapon was not just the system; the weapon was the company that owned the system, and the company was not a state.

The privatization of the kill chain was a development the history of weapons had been building toward since the first time a state hired a mercenary. The mercenary was a soldier who fought for pay, and the state that hired him did not control him as it controlled its own soldiers. The private military company was a mercenary in corporate form, and the private technology company was a mercenary in the form of a software vendor. The state that relied on a private company for its communications, its drones, its satellites, and its software was a state that had outsourced part of its sovereignty. The history of weapons had become a history of the state's dependence on the private sector, and the dependence was a vulnerability its enemies could exploit.

The exploitation was visible in the cyber domain. The cyber weapon was the weapon that did not kill, or did not kill directly, but could disable the systems the other weapons depended on. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, attacked the industrial control systems of Iran's nuclear enrichment program, causing centrifuges to spin out of control and destroy themselves. It was a precision weapon, in the sense that it targeted a specific facility and a specific process, and it worked by exploiting the software that controlled the machinery. The cyber weapon was the logical extension of the precision revolution: if the weapon is a system, then the way to defeat the system is to attack its software. The cyber weapon was a weapon that worked by making the enemy's weapons stop working.

The cyber weapon also had the advantage of deniability. The Stuxnet attack was attributed to the United States and Israel, but the attribution rested on journalistic investigation and circumstantial evidence, not a formal declaration. The cyber weapon allowed a state to attack another state without admitting that it was attacking, and the deniability made it a tool of covert action rather than open war. The cyber weapon was a weapon that worked by blurring the line between war and peace, and the blurring was the point. The history of weapons had reached a point where the most consequential attacks were the ones not acknowledged, and the ones not acknowledged were the hardest to deter.

The deterrence problem was the central problem of the new weapons. The nuclear weapon was deterrable because it was visible, expensive, controlled by a state, and because the state could be threatened with retaliation. The cyber weapon was hard to deter because it was invisible, cheap, usable by non-state actors, and because the state that used it could deny that it had. The drone was hard to deter because it was cheap, usable by non-state actors, and because the state that used it could claim self-defense. The autonomous weapon was hard to deter because it removed the human decision that could be threatened with retaliation. The new weapons were eroding the foundations of deterrence, and the erosion was a strategic problem the history of weapons had not prepared the world to solve.

The history of deterrence was the history of the nuclear age. The nuclear weapon was the first weapon too powerful to use, and the strategy of deterrence was the strategy of not using it. The strategy rested on the threat of retaliation, and the threat was credible because the retaliation would be devastating. It worked, in the sense that no nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945, but it worked at a cost. The cost was the maintenance of arsenals large enough to survive a first strike and still retaliate, and the arsenals were expensive and dangerous. The cost was also the proliferation of nuclear weapons to more states, and the proliferation was a constant worry. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, was an attempt to limit the proliferation, and it had 191 states parties. India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 200
