paragraphs: The treaty’s arithmetic told only part of the story. Of the roughly two hundred states in the international system, 191 had signed on to forswear the bomb, but the states that mattered most for the treaty’s survival were the ones that had not. India tested a “peaceful nuclear explosive” at Pokhran in 1974—a device the world politely declined to call a weapon and which everyone understood to be one. Pakistan, watching its rival cross the threshold, began a covert enrichment program under the cover of a civilian nuclear-energy effort, a program that would not detonate a device until 1998 but that shaped South Asian strategy for a quarter century before that. Israel maintained a policy of deliberate ambiguity, neither confirming nor denying a stockpile that outside analysts had estimated since the 1970s. The treaty had created a world divided into nuclear haves and have-nots and then discovered that the have-nots with the most reason to want the bomb were precisely those the treaty could not reach. The NPT was a landmark of arms control, and it was also a lesson in the limits of any agreement that depends on the cooperation of the states it most needs to constrain.

That lesson had been learned before, in other domains, and it is the thread that runs through the last half-century of weapon development. The history of weapons is not a history of technology alone. It is a history of the interaction between technology and the institutions that try to control it—treaties, alliances, procurement bureaucracies, defense industries, and the shifting coalitions of domestic politics that fund and constrain them. The NPT was one such institution, and its mixed record set the pattern for everything that followed: the partial test-ban treaty of 1963, the SALT and START agreements, the Chemical Weapons Convention, the Ottawa Convention on landmines, the cluster-munitions convention, the various export-control regimes that tried to keep sensitive technologies from spreading. Each of these agreements did something real. Each also left gaps, and the gaps were where the weapons went.

Consider the test ban. The Limited Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space, and underwater, but not underground. The United States and the Soviet Union signed it in the aftermath of the Cuban Missile Crisis, when both governments had been frightened by how close they had come to catastrophe, and the treaty’s immediate purpose was to reduce the radioactive fallout that atmospheric testing had spread across the globe. It succeeded at that. Fallout levels dropped sharply after 1963, and the public-health rationale was genuine. But the treaty also had a strategic logic that its framers understood perfectly well. By banning atmospheric tests, it froze the advantages the established nuclear powers already held. The United States and the Soviet Union had conducted hundreds of atmospheric tests between 1945 and 1963, gathering the data they needed to design reliable weapons. A new entrant to the nuclear club could not do the same without violating the treaty and inviting sanctions. The test ban was arms control and it was also a cartel.

The cartel did not hold. France and China, neither of which had signed, continued atmospheric testing into the 1970s and 1980s. France tested in the Algerian Sahara and then at Mururoa in the Pacific; China tested at Lop Nur in Xinjiang. The tests were a demonstration of independence, a refusal to accept a regime the two states had not helped to build, and they were also a necessity: without testing, neither country could be confident in its weapons designs. France conducted its last atmospheric test in 1974 and moved underground; China continued atmospheric testing until 1980. The underground tests continued much longer. The Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which would have banned all nuclear explosions, was opened for signature in 1996 and has never entered into force because a handful of states—including the United States, China, India, Pakistan, Israel, Iran, and North Korea—have not ratified it. The treaty’s verification regime, a global network of seismic, hydroacoustic, infrasound, and radionuclide monitoring stations, is a genuine technical achievement, and it has detected every nuclear test conducted since the network became operational. But detection is not prohibition. North Korea tested six nuclear devices between 2006 and 2017, and each test was detected, condemned, and sanctioned, and each test moved the program forward.

The pattern repeated across the other domains. The Chemical Weapons Convention, which entered into force in 1997, banned the development, production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons and established the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons to verify compliance. By the 2010s the OPCW had supervised the destruction of the great majority of declared stockpiles, a logistical achievement of the first order. The United States and Russia, which had built the largest arsenals, spent decades and billions of dollars dismantling them, and the destruction was verified, inspected, and documented. Yet the convention did not prevent the use of chemical weapons in Syria, where the Assad government employed sarin and chlorine against civilians in 2013 and again in 2017, or in Iraq, where Saddam Hussein had used them in the 1980s with the knowledge of the great powers, or in Malaysia, where a nerve agent was used in a political assassination at an airport in 2017. The convention changed the norm, and the norm mattered, but it did not stop determined states and non-state actors from using the weapons when they judged the benefits to outweigh the costs.

The landmine convention told a similar story. The Ottawa Convention, signed in 1997 and in force since 1999, banned antipersonnel landmines and required states parties to destroy their stockpiles and clear their minefields. It was the product of an unusual coalition of middle powers, nongovernmental organizations, and survivors, and it accomplished something the traditional arms-control process had not: it put a class of weapons beyond the pale and stigmatized their use so thoroughly that even states that had not signed—the United States, Russia, China, India, Pakistan—found themselves constrained by the norm. The number of new mine casualties fell, and the number of states producing mines shrank. But the convention did not eliminate mines. The United States continued to use them in limited circumstances, and the major producers continued to stockpile them. The cluster-munitions convention, adopted in 2008, followed the same arc: a ban that most states joined, a few important states that did not, and a norm that changed behavior without eliminating the weapon. The pattern was consistent enough to be a rule: international law could stigmatize a weapon and could constrain its use by states that cared about their reputations, but it could not disarm the states that judged the weapon essential to their security.

The reason was structural. A weapon is developed because someone believes it confers an advantage, and a state will give up the advantage only if it receives something it values more. The NPT was a bargain of this kind: the non-nuclear states agreed not to acquire weapons in exchange for access to civilian nuclear technology and a commitment by the nuclear powers to pursue disarmament in good faith. The bargain was asymmetric, and the asymmetry was the treaty’s weakness. The nuclear powers promised to disarm but set no timetable, and the non-nuclear states watched the arsenals remain in place decade after decade. The treaty’s review conferences became recurring exercises in managed disappointment, with the non-nuclear states pressing for concrete commitments and the nuclear powers offering language that committed them to very little. The 1995 review conference extended the treaty indefinitely, which the nuclear powers wanted, in exchange for a set of principles and objectives that the nuclear powers largely ignored. The 2000 review conference produced an “unequivocal undertaking” by the nuclear powers to accomplish the total elimination of their arsenals, a phrase negotiated with great care and implemented with none.

The asymmetry had consequences beyond the review conferences. It gave the non-nuclear states a grievance they could use to justify their own programs, and it gave the nuclear states a credibility problem that undermined their non-proliferation efforts. When the United States invaded Iraq in 2003 on the premise that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction—a premise that proved false—the invasion did lasting damage to the non-proliferation regime, because it demonstrated that a state that gave up its weapons program could still be attacked while a state that kept one, like North Korea, was treated with caution. The lesson was not lost on the governments that were watching. Muammar Gaddafi’s decision to abandon Libya’s weapons program in 2003, celebrated at the time as a triumph of non-proliferation, looked very different after 2011, when a NATO intervention helped topple his regime and he was killed by rebels. The leaders who had watched the sequence drew the obvious conclusion: disarmament was safe only if the great powers could be relied upon to protect you, and the great powers could not always be relied upon.

The NPT’s deeper problem was that it had been designed for a world of a handful of nuclear powers and had to operate in a world where the technology of enrichment and reprocessing was spreading. The treaty’s safeguards, administered by the International Atomic Energy Agency, were built around the assumption that a state’s nuclear program could be inspected and declared. The IAEA’s authority was limited: it could verify that declared materials were not diverted, but it could not search for undeclared facilities without additional protocols, and the additional protocols were voluntary. Iraq had a covert program that the IAEA did not detect until after the 1991 Gulf War, when the inspectors went in under the terms of the ceasefire and found a program far larger than anyone had suspected. North Korea kicked the inspectors out, withdrew from the treaty, and built a bomb. Iran built a vast enrichment infrastructure under the cover of a civilian program and was caught by a combination of intelligence, inspections, and the discovery of undeclared facilities at Natanz and Fordow. The safeguards were a speed bump, not a wall.

The Iran case was instructive because it showed how the non-proliferation regime actually worked in practice. It worked through a combination of intelligence, sanctions, diplomacy, and covert action. The Stuxnet computer worm, reportedly developed by the United States and Israel and which damaged centrifuges at Natanz around 2010, was a weapon of a new kind: malicious software designed to destroy physical equipment, delivered through the internet, and attributed only years later. Stuxnet was the first widely recognized cyber weapon, and it opened a domain of warfare that would grow rapidly over the following decade. It was also a demonstration that the non-proliferation regime had developed a covert arm, and that the covert arm could be used to slow a program without the risks of a military strike. The 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, which Iran signed with the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Russia, and China, was a diplomatic settlement that traded sanctions relief for limits on Iran’s enrichment program and enhanced inspections. It was, by the standards of arms control, a substantial achievement. It was also fragile: the United States withdrew from it in 2018, and Iran began to exceed its limits, and the agreement’s collapse showed how much of the non-proliferation regime depended on the domestic politics of a single country.

That dependence was the regime’s central vulnerability, and it grew as the weapons themselves changed. The NPT and the arms-control treaties of the Cold War had been built around a particular kind of weapon: a fission or fusion device, large, expensive, and difficult to build, whose development left detectable traces and whose use would be unmistakable. The treaties assumed that a state’s nuclear program could be monitored because it required large facilities—reactors, enrichment plants, reprocessing facilities—that were hard to hide. The assumption held for the first generation of nuclear powers. It held less well for the second generation, which learned to build smaller and more dispersed facilities, and it held even less well for the technologies that emerged at the end of the twentieth century and the beginning of the twenty-first. The revolution in computing, communications, and precision manufacturing that transformed the civilian economy also transformed the weapons, and it did so in ways the arms-control architecture was not designed to address.

The most important of these changes was the precision revolution in munitions. The idea of a guided weapon was old—the torpedo had been guided since the nineteenth century, and the German V-1 and V-2 had been guided in a crude sense—but the technologies that made precision practical at scale emerged in the 1970s and matured in the 1980s and 1990s. Laser guidance, which used a spot of laser light on a target to steer a bomb or missile toward it, was developed in the 1960s and used in Vietnam, where the Paveway series of laser-guided bombs was employed against bridges and other point targets. The results were dramatic: a bridge that had required dozens of unguided bombs to destroy could be dropped with a handful of guided ones, and the aircraft could attack from outside the range of the defenses. Television guidance, which used a camera in the nose of the weapon to let the operator steer it, was used in the same period. The technologies were expensive and the weapons were few, but the trend was clear.

The trend accelerated in the 1970s with the development of the cruise missile. The modern cruise missile was a small, pilotless aircraft that carried a warhead, flew at low altitude to evade radar, and navigated by matching the terrain beneath it to a stored map. The United States began developing the Tomahawk in the 1970s, and the missile entered service in the 1980s. The Soviet Union developed its own equivalents. The cruise missile was significant because it combined precision with range: it could be launched from a ship or a submarine hundreds of miles from the target and could strike a specific building. It was also significant because it was cheap enough to be built in large numbers, unlike the ballistic missile, which was expensive and whose accuracy was limited by the physics of reentry. The cruise missile made precision a mass commodity.

The other half of the precision revolution was the satellite navigation system. The United States began developing the Global Positioning System in the 1970s, launched the first satellites in 1978, and declared the system fully operational in 1995. The Soviet Union developed its own system, GLONASS, and Europe, China, and others followed with their own systems in the decades that followed. GPS was a civilian system with military applications, and its military applications were transformative. A weapon that could determine its own position to within a few meters could be guided to a target with an accuracy that had previously required a human operator or a laser designator. The combination of GPS and inertial navigation made possible the family of weapons that came to be known as joint direct attack munitions—unguided bombs fitted with a guidance kit that turned them into precision weapons at a fraction of the cost of a purpose-built guided missile. The JDAM, which entered service in the late 1990s, cost tens of thousands of dollars rather than hundreds of thousands, and it could be dropped from any aircraft that could carry a bomb.

The effect on air power was profound. In the Second World War, the bombing campaign against Germany had required thousands of aircraft dropping tens of thousands of tons of bombs to destroy targets that could have been destroyed by a handful of precision weapons, and the accuracy of the bombing had been so poor that many bombs fell miles from their targets. The postwar surveys of strategic bombing had documented the inaccuracy, and the militaries had spent decades trying to improve it. The precision revolution did not merely improve accuracy; it changed the logic of air power. A single aircraft carrying a few precision weapons could now accomplish a mission that had previously required a formation of bombers, and it could do it at night and in bad weather, without exposing the aircrew to the defenses. The number of aircraft required for a given mission fell, and the value of each aircraft rose, and the calculus of attrition changed.

The first large-scale demonstration of the new air power came in the Gulf War of 1991. The coalition that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait began its air campaign on 17 January 1991 with a barrage of cruise missiles and stealth aircraft strikes against command-and-control facilities, air defenses, and communications. The F-117 stealth fighter, which had been developed in secret and which was designed to be nearly invisible to radar, attacked targets in Baghdad that had been considered impenetrable. The cruise missiles, launched from ships and submarines in the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, flew through the city’s defenses and struck their targets. The air campaign was not perfect—the coalition dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs in Desert Storm, and only about 6,520 tons, roughly 7.4 percent, were precision-guided—but the precision weapons struck the high-value targets that mattered, and the images of the strikes, broadcast around the world, reshaped public and military expectations of what air power could do. The war was a demonstration that a military could be paralyzed by the destruction of a relatively small number of targets, and the demonstration was widely studied.

The Gulf War was also a demonstration of the limits of precision. The coalition’s air campaign did not destroy Iraq’s nuclear program, which was larger than the intelligence had estimated, and it did not kill Saddam Hussein, and it did not prevent Iraq from launching Scud missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia. The Scud hunt became a symbol of the gap between the promise and the reality: the coalition devoted enormous resources to finding and destroying mobile missile launchers, and it destroyed far fewer than it claimed. The precision weapons were precise, but the intelligence that told them where to go was not, and the combination of imprecise intelligence and precise weapons produced a great deal of destruction with a limited strategic effect. The lesson was that precision was a multiplier, not a substitute, for intelligence and judgment.

The 1999 Kosovo war tested the new air power again. NATO conducted a 78-day bombing campaign against Yugoslavia to stop the ethnic cleansing in Kosovo, and the campaign was fought from high altitude to minimize allied casualties. The high-altitude restriction meant that the aircraft were largely immune to Yugoslav air defenses, but it also meant that the crews could not visually identify their targets, and the result was a series of mistakes: a refugee convoy was struck, a passenger train was hit, and the Chinese embassy in Belgrade was bombed. The embassy bombing was a particularly instructive error. The intended target was a Yugoslav military procurement facility, and the coordinates that were used were wrong, and the result was a diplomatic crisis between the United States and China. The precision weapons had hit exactly the wrong building. The campaign achieved its objective—Yugoslavia withdrew from Kosovo—but the mistakes demonstrated that precision did not eliminate the fog of war; it only changed its character.

The Kosovo campaign also marked the first sustained use of the unmanned aerial vehicle as a weapons platform. The Predator drone, which had been developed as a reconnaissance platform in the 1990s, was fitted with Hellfire missiles and used to attack targets in Afghanistan and later in Yemen, Somalia, and Pakistan. The armed drone was a new kind of weapon: it could loiter over a target for hours, it could be flown by a crew thousands of miles away, and it could strike with precision when the target appeared. The first armed Predator strike was conducted in Afghanistan in October 2001, and the use of armed drones expanded rapidly over the following two decades. The drone was a weapon of counterinsurgency and counterterrorism, and it was controversial for reasons that went beyond its military effectiveness: it made killing easy for the state that operated it, and it raised questions about sovereignty, civilian casualties, and the legal framework for targeted killing that the international system had not resolved.

The drone was also a preview of a larger shift. The technology that made the Predator possible—satellite communications, precision navigation, miniature sensors, and lightweight materials—was the same technology that would make possible the small, cheap drones that would transform the battlefield in the 2010s and 2020s. The military drone of the early 2000s was expensive and complex, and only a few states could build and operate it. The commercial drone of the 2010s was cheap and simple, and anyone could buy one. The spread of the technology followed the pattern of the spread of every previous military technology: the great powers developed it first, and then it diffused to smaller states and non-state actors, and the diffusion changed the balance of power in ways the developers had not anticipated.

The precision revolution was one of two technological shifts that reshaped warfare in the decades after the Cold War. The other was the information revolution, and the two were intertwined. The same computing and communications technologies that made precision guidance possible also made possible the collection, transmission, and processing of enormous quantities of information about the battlefield. The result was what came to be called the “military-technical revolution” and later the “revolution in military affairs”: the idea that the combination of precision weapons, advanced sensors, and networked communications would transform warfare as profoundly as the combination of the tank, the aircraft, and the radio had transformed it in the Second World War. The idea was promoted by a group of American military thinkers in the 1990s, and it shaped the way the United States built its forces for the next two decades.

The revolution in military affairs had a specific strategic context. The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 left the United States as the world’s only superpower, with a defense budget larger than the next several powers combined and with a technological lead that no rival could match in the near term. The Gulf War had demonstrated what American air power could do against a Soviet-equipped army, and the demonstration was read in capitals around the world as a sign that the American way of war was the way of the future. The Chinese military studied the Gulf War closely and concluded that it needed to transform its own forces, and the transformation it undertook over the following decades—the development of precision weapons, the modernization of its air force and navy, the creation of a networked command-and-control system—was a direct response to what it had seen. The Russians drew similar conclusions, and the reforms they undertook after the Cold War were shaped by the same lessons.

The American way of war that emerged from the 1990s was built around a set of assumptions. The first was that precision weapons and advanced sensors would allow the United States to see the battlefield and to strike any target on it, and that the combination would produce a decisive advantage. The second was that the American military would fight as part of a coalition, and that the coalition would provide legitimacy and basing and additional forces. The third was that the American public would not tolerate casualties, and that the military therefore had to fight in a way that minimized them, which meant relying on air power and precision weapons and avoiding ground combat where possible. The fourth was that the conflicts of the future would be short and decisive, and that the military did not need to be sized for long occupations or protracted counterinsurgencies.

The wars of the 2000s tested every one of those assumptions, and most of them failed. The invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 and the invasion of Iraq in 2003 were rapid and decisive in the conventional sense: the Taliban government fell within weeks, and the Iraqi army was defeated in three weeks. The precision weapons worked as advertised, and the casualty toll on the American side was low. But the wars did not end. The conventional victories were followed by insurgencies that lasted for years, and the insurgencies were fought with improvised explosive devices, small arms, and suicide attacks, not with the tanks and aircraft that the precision revolution had been designed to defeat. The American military found itself fighting a kind of war for which its precision weapons were of limited use, and it spent the next decade and a half trying to adapt.

The adaptation took several forms. The first was the development of mine-resistant ambush-protected vehicles, designed to survive the blast of an IED and rushed into production in large numbers. The MRAP was a case study in rapid procurement: the military identified the need, the industry responded, and thousands of vehicles were built and fielded within a few years. The vehicle was heavy and expensive and not suited to all terrain, but it saved lives, and its development showed that the procurement system could move quickly when the political pressure was sufficient. The second was the expansion of the drone program, which allowed the military to surveil and strike targets without exposing ground forces. The third was the development of biometric and signals-intelligence systems that could identify and track insurgents, and the fourth was the expansion of special-operations forces, which conducted raids and trained local forces.

The counterinsurgency era also produced a body of doctrine. The American military published a counterinsurgency field manual in 2006 that emphasized protecting the population, building local institutions, and using force with restraint. The manual was a significant intellectual achievement, and it reflected a genuine effort to learn from the failures of the early occupation of Iraq. But the doctrine was difficult to implement, and the results were mixed. The “surge” of additional troops into Iraq in 2007 reduced the violence, but the reduction was produced by a combination of factors—the surge, the alliance with Sunni tribal leaders known as the Anbar Awakening, the exhaustion of the insurgents, and the ethnic cleansing that had already separated the communities—and it was not clear how much of the credit belonged to the doctrine. The Afghan surge of 2009–2012 produced similar ambiguity. The violence fell in some areas and rose in others, and the Afghan government remained weak and corrupt, and the Taliban remained resilient.

The counterinsurgency era was expensive. The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan cost trillions of dollars, and the cost was borne not only in money but in lives: thousands of American service members were killed and tens of thousands were wounded, and the Iraqi and Afghan casualties were far higher. The wars also strained the military, which found itself deploying units repeatedly and struggling to recruit and retain enough soldiers. The strain was a reminder that the precision revolution had not eliminated the need for ground forces, and that the ground forces were the ones who bore the burden of the long wars. The American public’s tolerance for casualties, which the revolution in military affairs had assumed to be low, proved more complicated than the assumption suggested: the public tolerated the casualties of the long wars, but it also grew weary of the wars, and the weariness shaped the politics of the later withdrawals.

The wars of the 2000s also changed the character of the weapons themselves. The insurgencies were fought at close range, in cities and villages, and the weapons that mattered were not the precision-guided munitions but the rifles, machine guns, grenades, and rockets that the infantry carried. The American military had spent the Cold War preparing for a conventional war in Europe, and its small arms and infantry equipment had been designed for that war. The experience of the insurgencies exposed the gaps: the body armor was inadequate at first, the vehicles were not armored, and the radios and communications equipment were not suited to the dispersed operations of counterinsurgency. The military responded with a wave of procurement: new body armor, new vehicles, new radios, new rifles, and new sensors. The procurement was rapid and expensive, and it demonstrated that the weapons of a counterinsurgency are different from the weapons of a conventional war.

The most important of these procurement efforts was the program to develop a new infantry rifle. The American military had used the M16 and its variants since the 1960s, and the rifle had been improved over the decades, but the experience of the insurgencies suggested that a new rifle with better range and lethality was needed. The Army launched the Individual Carbine competition in 2011 and then cancelled it, and the Marine Corps adopted a new rifle, the M27, in 2011. The larger effort, the Next Generation Squad Weapon program, was launched in 2017 and selected a new rifle and a new light machine gun in 2022. The new weapons fired a 6.8mm cartridge, designed to penetrate modern body armor at longer range than the 5.56mm cartridge the M16 had used. The program was a reminder that the infantry rifle, the oldest and most basic of weapons, was still being redesigned, and that the redesign was driven by the same logic that had driven the development of every previous weapon: the interaction between the threat and the countermeasure.

The counterinsurgency era ended, in the American experience, with the withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021. The withdrawal was chaotic, and it was followed by the collapse of the Afghan government and the return of the Taliban to power. The collapse was a strategic defeat for the United States and its allies, and it demonstrated that two decades of investment in precision weapons and counterinsurgency doctrine had not produced a durable political outcome. The Taliban had not been defeated by precision weapons; they had waited out the coalition, and they had won by not losing. The lesson was one the history of irregular warfare had taught many times before: a technologically superior force can win every battle and still lose the war, because the war is not decided on the battlefield but in the political and social terrain that the weapons cannot reach.

The withdrawal from Afghanistan coincided with a shift in the great-power competition that had been building for a decade. The United States had been focused on counterinsurgency, and while it was focused there, China and Russia had been modernizing their militaries and developing weapons designed to counter the American advantages. The Chinese military had built a large inventory of precision missiles, including the DF-21D and DF-26 ballistic missiles designed to strike aircraft carriers from long range, and it had developed a dense integrated air-defense system and a large fleet of modern warships. The Russian military had developed hypersonic missiles, electronic-warfare systems, and a range of precision weapons, and it had demonstrated them in Syria and Ukraine. The American advantage in precision weapons, which had seemed decisive in 1991, had narrowed, and the narrowing changed the strategic calculus.

The Chinese anti-access/area-denial strategy was the most significant development. The strategy was designed to keep American forces out of the western Pacific in the event of a conflict, and it relied on a combination of long-range missiles, submarines, mines, and air defenses. The DF-21D, which entered service around 2010, was the first ballistic missile designed to strike a moving ship at sea, and it was widely described as a “carrier killer.” The missile was a response to the American strategy of using aircraft carriers to project power, and it demonstrated that the precision revolution had diffused: the technology that had given the United States a decisive advantage in 1991 was now available to its rivals, and the rivals were using it to threaten the platforms on which American power depended.

The diffusion of precision technology was not limited to states. The wars of the 2000s and 2010s demonstrated that non-state actors could acquire and use precision weapons. Hezbollah used anti-ship missiles against an Israeli warship in 2006, and it used guided rockets and drones in subsequent conflicts. Hamas and other Palestinian groups developed rockets and, later, drones. The Houthis in Yemen used anti-ship ballistic missiles and drones to attack shipping in the Red Sea in 2023 and 2024, demonstrating that a non-state actor with access to relatively cheap precision weapons could disrupt a global trade route. The diffusion was a consequence of the same forces that had diffused every previous military technology: the spread of manufacturing, the availability of commercial components, and the willingness of states to export weapons to proxies.

The diffusion of drones was the most dramatic example. The armed drone had been an American monopoly in the early 2000s, but by the 2010s Turkey, China, Iran, Israel, and others were producing drones, and the drones were being sold to a wide range of states. The Turkish Bayraktar TB2, a relatively cheap and effective drone, was sold to Azerbaijan, Ukraine, Libya, and Ethiopia, and it was used with devastating effect in each conflict. The drone was a weapon of the middle powers: cheap enough for a state with a modest defense budget to afford, and effective enough to change the outcome of a conflict. The drone also lowered the political cost of using force, because a drone strike did not put a pilot at risk, and the lowered cost made the drone attractive to governments that wanted to act without paying the political price of casualties.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020 was the landmark. The war was fought between Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed territory of Nagorno-Karabakh, and it lasted 44 days. Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and Israeli loitering munitions to destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, air defenses, and supply lines, and the drones were decisive. The Armenian air defenses, designed to counter aircraft, were not effective against small, slow, low-flying drones, and the Armenian armor, exposed and poorly concealed, was destroyed in large numbers. The war ended with a ceasefire favorable to Azerbaijan, and the outcome was widely interpreted as a demonstration of the power of drones against conventional forces. The Royal United Services Institute, a British defense think tank, published a study in 2021 that treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense, and the study was read widely in military establishments around the world.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was also a demonstration of the vulnerability of conventional forces to precision weapons in the hands of a determined opponent. The Armenian army had been equipped with Soviet-era tanks and air defenses, and it had been considered a capable force, but it was defeated by a smaller and less well-equipped opponent that had invested in drones and precision munitions. The lesson was that the traditional measures of military power—the number of tanks, the size of the army, the sophistication of the air force—were not reliable indicators of combat effectiveness in the new environment. The lesson was reinforced by the war in Ukraine, which began with the Russian invasion in February 2022 and which became the largest land war in Europe since the Second World War.

The Ukraine war was a test of nearly every assumption that had shaped weapon development since the end of the Cold War. The Russian military invaded with a force designed for a short, decisive campaign, equipped with modern tanks, aircraft, and precision missiles. The invasion failed to achieve its objectives in the first weeks, and the war settled into a protracted conflict fought with artillery, drones, and infantry. The precision weapons that Russia used—the Kalibr cruise missiles, the Iskander ballistic missiles, the Kinzhal hypersonic missiles—were used against Ukrainian infrastructure and military targets, and they caused significant damage, but they did not produce a decisive effect. The Ukrainian military, equipped with Western anti-tank missiles and air-defense systems, and later with precision artillery and drones, fought the Russians to a standstill in many areas, and the war became a war of attrition.

The Ukraine war demonstrated the continuing importance of mass. The precision weapons were effective, but they were expensive, and the war consumed them at a rate the producing states had not anticipated. The United States and its allies found that their production of artillery shells and precision munitions was inadequate for a war of this scale, and they scrambled to increase production. The war also demonstrated the importance of drones: both sides used small, cheap drones for reconnaissance and for attack, and the drones were integrated into the artillery fire-control system in a way that made the artillery far more lethal. The war also demonstrated the vulnerability of tanks and armored vehicles to precision anti-tank weapons and drones, and it produced a debate about whether the tank was obsolete. The debate was premature—tanks were still used, and they were still effective when employed with infantry and air support—but it reflected a real change in the character of ground warfare.

The Ukraine war also demonstrated the importance of electronic warfare. Both sides jammed the other’s drones and communications, and the jamming was effective enough that the drones had to be designed to operate in a contested electromagnetic environment. The war became a contest of adaptation: a new drone or a new jamming technique would be introduced, and the other side would develop a countermeasure, and the cycle would repeat. The cycle was fast—weeks rather than years—and it demonstrated that the development of weapons had become a continuous process rather than a series of discrete innovations. The lesson was that the advantage in a modern war belongs to the side that can adapt faster, and the adaptation depends on the industrial base, the technical skills of the engineers and operators, and the willingness of the political system to support the effort.

The Ukraine war also brought the nuclear question back to the center of strategic thinking. Russia possessed the world’s largest nuclear arsenal, and its leadership made repeated references to the possibility of using nuclear weapons, and the references were widely interpreted as an attempt to deter Western intervention. The deterrence worked, in the sense that the West did not intervene directly, but it also demonstrated the continuing importance of nuclear weapons in the strategic calculus. The war was a reminder that the nuclear revolution of 1945 had not been superseded by the precision revolution of the 1990s: the threat of nuclear escalation still set the limits within which conventional wars were fought, and the limits were real.

The nuclear arsenals themselves had been transformed since the Cold War. The United States and Russia had reduced their stockpiles dramatically under the START treaties, from a peak of more than 60,000 warheads each in the 1980s to a few thousand each by the 2010s. But the reductions had been accompanied by modernization: both countries replaced their older missiles and bombers with new ones, and both developed new delivery systems, including hypersonic glide vehicles and nuclear-armed cruise missiles. The modernization was expensive, and it was controversial, and it demonstrated that the nuclear arms race had not ended; it had changed its character. The arsenals were smaller, but they were more capable, and the capabilities were more diverse.

The other nuclear powers had also modernized. China expanded its arsenal and built new silos, and it developed a submarine-launched ballistic missile that gave it a secure second-strike capability. India and Pakistan expanded their arsenals and developed new delivery systems, including submarine-launched missiles. North Korea built a small but growing arsenal and tested missiles that could reach the United States. Israel maintained its undeclared arsenal. The NPT had not prevented proliferation; it had slowed it and shaped it, and the shape was a world with nine nuclear-armed states and a handful of others that could build a bomb within a few years if they chose.

The arms-control architecture that had been built during the Cold War had eroded. The United States withdrew from the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty in 2002, and the treaty’s restrictions on missile defenses lapsed. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear
