paragraphs: The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty collapsed in 2019, when the United States withdrew, citing Russian violations, and Russia suspended its participation. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, the last major bilateral cap on American and Russian strategic warheads, was extended in 2021 but faced an uncertain future. The architecture had not vanished, but it had thinned, and the thinning mattered. Arms control had never been a substitute for strategy; it was a tool that made strategy legible—a set of agreed numbers and inspection regimes that told each side what the other had and what it could do. When the numbers became uncertain, the strategies built on them became uncertain too.

By the early twenty-first century, the nuclear age had settled into a strange equilibrium. The weapons were terrible enough that their use was almost unthinkable, and the unthinkability had become a kind of stability. But that stability rested on assumptions rarely examined: that command-and-control systems would work, that decision-makers would be rational, that warning systems would not produce false alarms indistinguishable from real attacks. Each assumption had been tested and had held—but sometimes barely. In 1983, a Soviet early-warning system reported the launch of American missiles; the officer on duty, Stanislav Petrov, judged the report a malfunction and did not pass it up the chain. The report was indeed a malfunction, a rare alignment of sunlight on high-altitude clouds and the satellite's orbit. The system had worked because a human being refused to believe it.

The problem of false alarm did not disappear with the end of the Cold War. It grew more complicated as nuclear-armed states multiplied and as the sensors feeding the warning systems became more numerous and varied. A launch detected by satellite, radar, seismic sensor, or radiation monitor—each sensor had its own failure modes, and integrating them into a single picture created new ones. The picture could be wrong in ways no single sensor would have been. Integration was necessary, because warning time was short and the decision window narrow, but it also created a system that could fail in ways hard to predict and hard to diagnose.

The history of weapons development is, in large part, a history of integration. A weapon is rarely a single device; it is a system of devices, and the system is often more fragile than its components. The longbow was a system: the bow, the arrow, the archer, the supply of bowstaves, the training that produced the archer, the tactical doctrine that placed him in the line. The system could fail at any point. The Mary Rose carried 137 longbows when it sank in 1545, and the surviving bows have estimated draw weights of 100 to 185 pounds—meaning the archers who drew them had trained for years and had bodies shaped by the training. A longbowman was not a soldier who happened to carry a bow; he was a specialist whose skill could not be quickly replaced. The system that produced him was expensive and slow, and when it broke, it could not easily be repaired.

The same logic applied to the rifled musket. The Minié ball, developed by Claude-Étienne Minié in 1849, was a hollow-base bullet that expanded into the rifling when the powder charge fired, allowing a soldier to load a rifled musket as quickly as a smoothbore. The British Pattern 1853 Enfield and the American Springfield Model 1861 used the Minié ball, producing a weapon that could hit a man at several hundred yards—far beyond the effective range of the smoothbore muskets that had dominated the battlefield for two centuries. The Minié ball was a small technological change with large tactical consequences. It extended the range at which infantry could engage, which made frontal assaults more costly, which contributed to the casualty lists of the American Civil War. Weapon and tactics were coupled; a change in one forced a change in the other.

The Maxim gun, demonstrated by Hiram Maxim in 1884, was another integration. The gun used the recoil of the fired cartridge to operate its mechanism, so it could fire continuously as long as ammunition was fed to it. The British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891, and the weapon became the template for automatic warfare. But the Maxim was not just a gun; it was a gun, a mount, an ammunition supply, a cooling system, and a crew. It could fire hundreds of rounds per minute, consuming ammunition faster than any previous weapon, so the supply system had to be redesigned to keep it fed. The water jacket had to be maintained. The crew had to be trained to keep the gun from overheating and to clear jams. The Maxim was a system, and the system was what mattered.

The French 75mm field gun, adopted in 1897, was a system in the same sense. Its hydro-pneumatic recoil system kept the carriage steady when the gun fired, so the gun did not have to be re-aimed after each shot. The result was a rate of fire of roughly fifteen rounds per minute, far faster than any previous field gun. But that rate depended on a supply of shells, a supply of propellant, a crew trained to load and fire quickly, and a fire-control system that could direct the fire. The gun was a machine, and the machine was part of a larger machine. When the larger machine worked, the gun was devastating; when it did not, the gun was a heavy piece of metal that could not easily be moved and could not be fed.

The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916 and produced roughly 700,000 casualties, was the clearest demonstration of what the integrated system could do. The battle was fought with artillery, and the artillery was fought with shells. The German army fired millions of shells in the opening bombardment, and the French army fired millions more in response. The guns were not the bottleneck; the shells were. The factories that produced the shells, the railways that carried them to the front, the depots that stored them, the crews that loaded them into the guns—these were the components of the system, and the system determined the outcome. The infantry, once the decisive arm, became the force that occupied the ground after the artillery had done its work. The weapons had changed the tactics, and the tactics had changed the war.

The pattern repeated in the Second World War, at a larger scale and with more terrible weapons. The strategic bombing campaigns against Germany and Japan were systems: the bombers, the bombs, the crews, the bases, the fuel, the navigation aids, the fighter escorts, the intelligence that identified the targets. The campaigns did not achieve the decisive results their advocates had promised, but they forced the defenders to divert resources to air defense, weakening them elsewhere. The bombing worked indirectly, by imposing costs rather than by destroying targets. The atomic bomb was a different kind of weapon, one that worked directly, destroying a city with a single aircraft. The Trinity test on 16 July 1945 produced a yield of about 21 kilotons, and the bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki were of similar yield. These were not just more powerful versions of earlier bombs; they were qualitatively different, because they could destroy a city with a single delivery—and because the delivery could not be stopped.

The nuclear age changed the logic of weapons development in ways still being worked out. Before 1945, weapons development was driven by the search for advantage: a better bow, a faster-firing gun, a more accurate rifle, a more powerful explosive. After 1945, it was driven by the search for stability: a survivable second-strike force, a reliable command-and-control system, a warning system that could not be fooled. Weapons were still developed for advantage, but advantage was measured in terms of deterrence rather than victory. A weapon that could not be used was not useless; it was useful precisely because it could not be used. The logic was counterintuitive, and it took decades to work out.

The counterintuitive logic produced strange artifacts. The intercontinental ballistic missile, which could deliver a warhead to the other side of the world in half an hour, was a weapon of enormous power and enormous vulnerability. The missile silos were fixed and their locations known, so they could be targeted. The submarines that carried ballistic missiles were survivable, because their locations were not known, but they were expensive and their communications were difficult. The bombers were flexible, but they could be shot down. Each leg of the triad had its own strengths and weaknesses, and the triad as a whole was more survivable than any single leg. The triad was a system, and the system was designed to survive the loss of any of its parts.

The command-and-control system was the most fragile part of the system, and the part that received the least attention. It had to detect an attack, assess it, decide whether to respond, and transmit the response to the forces. Each step could fail. Detection could produce a false alarm. Assessment could be wrong. The decision could be delayed or confused. Transmission could be interrupted. The system had been designed to work under the worst conditions, but the worst conditions were hard to simulate and harder to test. It was tested in exercises, and the exercises revealed problems, and the problems were fixed, but the fixing was never complete.

The problem of command and control was not new. It had been present in every war, in every army, in every era. The difference was that the consequences of failure had grown. A failure of command and control in the Napoleonic era could lose a battle; a failure in the nuclear era could end a civilization. The growth of consequences had not been matched by a growth in the reliability of the systems. The systems had improved, but not enough to make the consequences acceptable. The gap between consequences and reliability was the central problem of the nuclear age, and it had not been solved.

The problem was managed, not solved. The management took the form of doctrine, procedures, safeguards, redundancies. The doctrine specified when the weapons could be used and who could authorize their use. The procedures specified how the authorization would be transmitted and verified. The safeguards prevented unauthorized use. The redundancies ensured that a single failure would not be decisive. The management was elaborate, expensive, and never complete. It was a system, and the system had its own failure modes, which were the subject of constant study and constant worry.

The worry was justified, but it was also a distraction. Nuclear weapons were the most dramatic weapons ever built, and they absorbed the attention of strategists and policymakers for decades. But the history of weapons development did not stop with them. Conventional weapons continued to develop, driven by the same logic that had driven them before 1945: the search for advantage, the integration of systems, the coupling of weapons and tactics. Conventional weapons were less dramatic than nuclear ones, but they were used more often, and their development shaped the wars that were actually fought.

The precision-guided munition was the most important conventional development of the late twentieth century. The PGM was a bomb or missile that could be steered to its target, usually by a laser designator or a satellite navigation system. The steering made the weapon accurate, and the accuracy made it possible to destroy a target with a single weapon rather than a salvo. The first widespread use of PGMs was in the Persian Gulf War of 1991, when coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, of which about 6,520 tons—roughly 7.4 percent—were precision-guided. The percentage was small, but the PGMs struck high-value targets—bridges, command bunkers, air-defense sites—and the strikes were shown on television, and the images reshaped public and military expectations of air power. The war was not won by the PGMs alone, but the PGMs made the war look different from the wars that had come before.

The difference was partly a matter of accuracy and partly a matter of information. The PGM was not just a bomb; it was a bomb that was part of a system that included the sensors that found the target, the communications that passed the target coordinates to the aircraft, the aircraft that carried the bomb, the designator that illuminated the target, and the bomb itself. The system made the accuracy possible, and the system made the accuracy useful. A bomb that could hit a target was not useful unless the target was known and the bomb could be delivered. The system provided the knowledge and the delivery.

The system was expensive, and the expense limited its use. PGMs were a small fraction of the bombs dropped in 1991, and they remained a small fraction for years afterward. The expense was a barrier to widespread adoption, and the barrier was lowered only gradually, as the cost of guidance kits fell and the number of weapons equipped with them rose. The lowering of the barrier changed the character of air warfare. By the early twenty-first century, PGMs were the default weapon for many missions, and the unguided bomb was reserved for targets that did not require precision. The change was gradual but profound. The air campaign that had once meant dropping many bombs on a general area became a matter of dropping a few bombs on specific targets.

The change was not limited to air warfare. Precision guidance was applied to artillery, naval gunfire, mortars, rockets. The guided artillery shell could hit a target at a range of tens of kilometers with an accuracy of a few meters. The guided rocket could be fired from a truck and hit a target designated by a drone. The guidance made the weapons more effective, the effectiveness made them more attractive, and the attractiveness drove the development of more guidance and more precision. The cycle was self-reinforcing, and it produced a steady improvement in accuracy.

The improvement in accuracy was accompanied by an improvement in sensors. The sensors were the eyes of the system, and the eyes were getting better. Drones were the most visible example. A drone was an aircraft without a pilot, controlled from the ground or programmed to fly a predetermined route. It could carry cameras, radar, signals-intelligence equipment, and weapons. It could loiter over a target for hours, watching and waiting, and strike when the target appeared. The drone was a system, and the system was cheap enough to be used where a manned aircraft would have been too expensive or too risky.

The drone was not a new idea. The United States had used drones for reconnaissance since the Vietnam War, and Israel had used them extensively in the 1982 Lebanon War. But the drones of the early twenty-first century were different. They were armed, networked, and integrated into the command-and-control system. The armed drone could find a target, identify it, and destroy it within a single chain of command. The chain was short, and the shortness made the drone a responsive weapon. Responsiveness was the drone's advantage, and the advantage was demonstrated in the wars of the early twenty-first century.

The demonstration was clearest in the Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020. The war lasted forty-four days and was fought between Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed territory of Nagorno-Karabakh. Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses. The drones were not advanced by major-power standards, but they were effective against an opponent that lacked adequate air defense. They destroyed tanks, artillery pieces, and air-defense systems, and the destruction was recorded on video and posted to the internet. The videos showed the drones circling above the targets and then striking, and the strikes were precise and devastating. The war was a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense, and it was studied by militaries around the world.

The study produced a debate. One side argued that the drone had changed the character of war, that the combination of persistent surveillance and precision strike had made the traditional armored formation obsolete. The other argued that the drone was effective only against an opponent that lacked air defense, that a competent air defense would have shot down the drones, and that the war had demonstrated the importance of air defense rather than the obsolescence of armor. The debate was not resolved, because the evidence was ambiguous and the conditions of the Nagorno-Karabakh war were not general. The war was fought between two small states with limited resources, and the lessons were not necessarily transferable to a war between major powers.

The debate was a reminder that the history of weapons development is not a history of progress toward a single endpoint. Weapons develop in response to threats, and threats develop in response to weapons. The cycle is a competition, and the competition has no final winner. The drone was a response to the threat of air defense, and air defense was a response to the threat of aircraft, and aircraft was a response to the threat of air defense. The cycle had been running since the first aircraft flew over a battlefield, and it showed no sign of stopping.

The cycle was visible in the development of the loitering munition. A loitering munition could fly to a target area, loiter over it, search for a target, and strike when the target was found. It was a cross between a drone and a missile, combining the drone's persistence with the missile's lethality. It was used in Nagorno-Karabakh and in other conflicts, and it was adopted by militaries around the world. The weapon was controversial, because it could be used in autonomous mode, with the weapon itself deciding when to strike. The autonomy raised legal and ethical questions, and the questions were not resolved.

The questions were raised most sharply by an incident in Libya in 2021. A United Nations Panel of Experts report stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The claim was contested and was not independently confirmed, and it should be treated with caution. The report did not establish that an autonomous strike had occurred; it stated that the munition may have been used in autonomous mode, which is a weaker claim. The distinction matters, because the difference between a weapon capable of autonomous operation and a weapon that has actually operated autonomously is the difference between a potential and an event. The potential is real and is being developed, but the event has not been confirmed. Caution is necessary, because the claim has been repeated and amplified in ways the evidence does not support.

The caution does not diminish the significance of the development. The autonomous weapon is a real technology, and it is being developed by several states. It raises questions that existing legal frameworks do not answer. The laws of war require that a weapon distinguish between combatants and civilians, avoid disproportionate harm, and be used in a way that is accountable. An autonomous weapon that makes its own targeting decisions cannot be held accountable the way a human being can, and the accountability gap is the core of the legal and ethical problem. The problem has been studied by international organizations, militaries, and scholars, and the studies have produced proposals for regulation, but the proposals have not been adopted.

The proposals have not been adopted because the states developing the technology do not want to be constrained, and the states that are not developing it lack the leverage to constrain them. The dynamic is familiar from the history of arms control. States that have a weapon want to keep it, and states that do not have it want to acquire it or prevent others from acquiring it. The dynamic has produced treaties, the treaties have produced limits, and the limits have been imperfect. The history of arms control is a history of imperfect limits, and the imperfection is not a failure; it is the nature of the enterprise.

The enterprise was most successful in the nuclear realm, where the limits were embodied in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The treaty opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, and it has 191 states parties. India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The treaty did not prevent proliferation, but it slowed and shaped it. The slowing was the result of the treaty's inspection regime, which made it harder for a state to develop a nuclear weapon in secret, and the shaping was the result of the treaty's norms, which made it costly for a state to withdraw. The treaty was a system, and the system worked imperfectly, and the imperfection was the price of the system's existence.

The system was under strain in the early twenty-first century. The strain came from several directions. The nuclear-armed states were modernizing their arsenals, undermining the commitment to disarmament that the treaty's non-nuclear signatories had accepted. The non-nuclear states were growing impatient with the slow pace of disarmament, and some pursued the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which entered into force in 2021. The prohibition treaty was supported by the non-nuclear states and opposed by the nuclear-armed states, and the opposition meant that the treaty did not have the support of the states that possessed the weapons it prohibited. The treaty was a statement of intent, not a mechanism of control, and the gap between intent and control was the gap the arms-control system had always struggled to close.

The struggle was not new. It had been present since the first attempts to limit weapons, which were as old as war itself. The ancient world had rules about the conduct of war, and the rules sometimes limited the weapons that could be used. The medieval church tried to limit the use of the crossbow, which was considered too deadly to be used against Christians. The attempt failed, because the crossbow was too useful to be abandoned. The failure was a pattern, and the pattern repeated with the longbow, the musket, the machine gun, the bomber, the nuclear weapon. The weapons were too useful to be abandoned, and the attempts to limit them were too weak to succeed. The limits that did succeed were the limits that were in the interest of the powerful states, and the interests of the powerful states changed over time.

The change was visible in the history of the laws of war. The laws of war were codified in the nineteenth century, in the Geneva Conventions and the Hague Conventions, and the codification was driven by the experience of war. The Crimean War and the American Civil War had shown the cost of the new weapons, and the cost prompted the codification. The codification was a response to the weapons, and the weapons were a response to the codification. The cycle was the same cycle that drove the development of the weapons themselves, and it produced a body of law that was always slightly behind the technology.

The lag was a problem, because the law was supposed to constrain the technology, and the constraint was supposed to prevent the worst outcomes. The lag meant that the constraint was always applied to the technology of the previous war, and the technology of the next war was always unconstrained. The pattern was visible in the history of aerial bombing. The Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 prohibited the bombardment of undefended towns, but the prohibition did not anticipate the strategic bombing campaigns of the Second World War, which targeted cities that were defended but whose populations were not. The law had not anticipated the technology, and the technology had not been constrained by the law.

The pattern was visible again in the history of the drone. The drone was a new technology, and the law had not anticipated it. The law of armed conflict applied to the drone, because the drone was a weapon and the law applied to weapons, but the application was contested. The contested questions included the definition of a battlefield, the status of the drone operator, the legality of targeted killing, and the accountability for civilian casualties. The questions were debated, the debates produced arguments, and the arguments did not produce answers. The law was applied, but the application was uncertain, and the uncertainty was a feature of the system rather than a bug.

The uncertainty was also a feature of strategy. The strategists who planned the wars of the early twenty-first century had to plan for a world in which weapons were precise, sensors were ubiquitous, and information was abundant. The abundance of information was supposed to make planning easier, because commanders would know more about the battlefield than their predecessors had. But the abundance also made planning harder, because the information was noisy and the noise could overwhelm the signal. Commanders had more data than they could process, and the processing required tools that were themselves complex and fallible. The tools were computers, software, networks, and algorithms, and they were the newest and least understood part of the system.

The tools were the subject of the newest debate in the history of weapons development. The debate was about artificial intelligence, and whether machines could be trusted to make decisions previously made by human beings. The debate was not new; it had been present since the first automated systems were introduced, and in the debate about the autonomous weapon. But it was sharpened by the rapid improvement in the machines. The machines could now recognize images, translate languages, play games, and drive cars. They could also target weapons, and the targeting was the part of the debate that mattered most.

The targeting mattered because targeting was the moment when the weapon became lethal. A weapon that could find its own target was a weapon that could kill without a human being in the loop, and the absence of the human being was the source of the concern. The concern was not that machines would become conscious and decide to kill; it was that machines would make mistakes, and the mistakes would be attributed to no one. The accountability gap was the core of the concern, and the gap was the reason the debate had not been resolved.

The debate had produced a range of positions. At one end were the states and organizations that wanted a binding treaty prohibiting autonomous weapons. At the other were the states that wanted no treaty at all, arguing that existing law was sufficient and that a treaty would stifle innovation. In the middle were the states that wanted a non-binding code of conduct, or a treaty that regulated some autonomous weapons but not others. The positions were staked out, the negotiations were slow, and the slowness was the pattern of arms control. The negotiations took longer than the technology, and the technology advanced while the negotiations stalled.

The advance was visible in the wars of the early twenty-first century. The wars in Ukraine, Syria, Libya, Nagorno-Karabakh, and the disputed waters of the South China Sea all showed the increasing use of drones, precision weapons, electronic warfare, and cyber operations. These wars were not fought with the weapons of the future; they were fought with the weapons of the present, and the present was a mixture of the old and the new. The old weapons—artillery, tanks, infantry—were still present, and still decisive in many situations. The new weapons—drones, precision munitions, cyber tools—were present too, and they were changing the way the old weapons were used.

The change was most visible in the war in Ukraine, which began in 2014 and escalated in 2022. The war was fought with artillery, as the wars of the twentieth century had been, but the artillery was guided by drones and targeted with precision. Drones were used for reconnaissance, artillery spotting, strike, and electronic warfare. The war showed that the drone was not a substitute for artillery; it was a complement. The drone found the target, and the artillery destroyed it. The combination was more effective than either alone, and the combination was the system.

The system was what the history of weapons development had always been about. The weapons were the components, and the system was the whole. The whole was greater than the sum of its parts, and the whole was also more fragile than the parts. The fragility was the price of integration, and the price was paid in the wars that were fought. The wars showed the system working, and the wars showed the system failing, and the failures were as instructive as the successes.

The failures were instructive because they revealed the assumptions on which the system rested. The assumptions were rarely stated and rarely examined, and they were the source of the surprises the wars produced. The assumption that drones would be effective was tested in Nagorno-Karabakh and confirmed, but the assumption that drones would be effective against a competent air defense was tested in Ukraine and not confirmed. The assumption that precision weapons would reduce civilian casualties was tested in the wars of the early twenty-first century and not confirmed, because the precision weapons were accurate but the intelligence that guided them was not always accurate, and the errors were sometimes catastrophic.

The errors were the subject of the newest scholarship on the history of weapons. The scholarship had moved beyond the study of the weapons themselves to the study of the systems the weapons were part of. It had shown that weapons were never just tools; they were social artifacts, shaped by the societies that produced them and shaping those societies in turn. The longbow was a social artifact, because it required a society that could produce and sustain the archers. The Maxim gun was a social artifact, because it required a society that could produce the ammunition and the factories and the railways that fed it. The nuclear weapon was a social artifact, because it required a society that could produce the fissile material and the delivery systems and the command-and-control apparatus.

The social dimension of weapons was the dimension traditional histories had neglected. Traditional histories focused on inventors and inventions, dates and specifications, battles and campaigns. New histories focused on systems and societies, networks and institutions, the people who built and used and suffered from the weapons. The new histories were richer than the old, and also more complicated, because systems were more complicated than weapons. The complication was the point. Weapons were simple compared to systems, and systems determined the outcomes.

The outcomes were determined by the interaction of weapons and societies. A society that could produce a weapon could use it, and a society that could not produce it could not use it, or could use it only in limited ways. The asymmetry was the source of advantage, and advantage was the source of conquest. The history of war was a history of asymmetries, and the asymmetries were produced by differences among societies. The differences were not just technological; they were economic, political, and cultural. The society that could mobilize its resources for war had an advantage over the society that could not, and the advantage was often decisive.

The advantage was not permanent. Conquered societies learned from their conquerors, and the learning was the source of the next asymmetry. The pattern was visible in the history of gunpowder. The Chinese developed gunpowder, and the knowledge spread to the Islamic world and to Europe, and the Europeans developed gunpowder weapons to a degree the Chinese had not. The Europeans used the weapons to conquer the world, and the world learned from the Europeans, and the learning produced new asymmetries. The pattern was a cycle, and the cycle was the engine of the history.

The engine was still running in the early twenty-first century. The states that had developed precision weapons, drones, and cyber tools had an advantage over the states that had not, and the advantage was demonstrated in the wars. The advantage was not absolute, because states that lacked the advanced weapons could use older weapons effectively, and because advanced weapons could be countered by tactics that exploited their weaknesses. Drones could be shot down by air defenses, precision weapons could be jammed, cyber tools could be defended against. The advantage was a matter of degree, and the degree was contested.

The contest was the subject of the newest chapter in the history of weapons development. The chapter was being written in real time, and the writing was difficult because the events were recent and the evidence incomplete. Historians who would write the chapter in the future would have the advantage of hindsight, and hindsight would reveal patterns invisible to the participants. The patterns would be the patterns of the past, because the history of weapons development was a history of continuity as well as change. Weapons changed, but the logic of weapons did not. The logic was the logic of advantage, of integration, of asymmetry, of contest. The logic was the logic of war, and war was the constant.

The constant was the reason the history of weapons development was worth studying. The study revealed the logic, and the logic was the key to understanding the present and anticipating the future. The future was not determined, but it was shaped by the past, and the shape was visible in the weapons being developed. The weapons of the future would be more precise, more autonomous, more networked, more integrated. They would be part of systems more complex than the systems of the past, and the complexity would produce new vulnerabilities and new opportunities. The vulnerabilities would be exploited, the opportunities seized, and the cycle would continue.

The cycle was the theme of the history, and the theme was the answer to the question the history posed. The question was whether weapons determined wars or wars determined weapons. The answer was that neither determined the other; they determined each other. Weapons and wars were a single system, and the system was the subject of the history. It was not a history of weapons alone, nor of wars alone. It was a history of the system, and the system was the whole.

The whole was greater than the sum of its parts, and the whole was also more fragile than the parts. The fragility was the lesson of the history, and the lesson was the warning. The warning was that the systems the weapons were part of could fail, and the failures could be catastrophic. The failures could be prevented, but prevention required understanding, and understanding required study. The study was the purpose of the history, and the history was the record of the study. The record was long, detailed, and incomplete. The incompleteness was the nature of the record, because the record was written by human beings who could not know everything. The human beings did their best, and their best was the history.

The history was the story of weapons and wars and the societies that produced them. The story was told in the chapters that followed, organized around the themes the history had revealed. The themes were advantage and integration and asymmetry and contest. They were the threads that ran through the story, and the threads were the key to understanding it. The story was long, complicated, and worth telling. The telling was the task, and the task was the book.

The book was a history of war and the development of weapons, and the history was a history of the systems the weapons were part of. The systems were the subject, and the weapons were the evidence. The evidence was abundant, and the abundance was the challenge. The challenge was to select the evidence that revealed the systems and to ignore the evidence that obscured them. The selection was the historian's task, and the task was never complete. The historian selected, the selection was judged by readers, and the judgment was the historian's reward and punishment.

The punishment was the criticism that the selection was wrong, and the criticism was often justified. A historian who selected only the evidence that supported the thesis was a propagandist; one who selected the evidence that challenged it was a scholar. The distinction was the distinction between history written to prove a point and history written to understand. Understanding was the goal, and the goal was never fully achieved. The historian approached the goal, and the approach was the history.

The approach was the method, and the method was the comparative study of systems. The comparative study revealed patterns that the single case could not. The pattern was the repetition of the logic across cases, and the repetition was the evidence of the logic's power. The logic was the logic of the system, and the system was the unit of analysis. The unit was not the weapon, nor the war, nor the society. The unit was the system that included all three, and the system was the subject of the history.

The subject was large, the history was long, and the book was the record. The record was the contribution to understanding, and understanding was the contribution to peace. Peace was the goal, and the goal was never fully achieved, but the approach was the history, and the history was the record of the approach. The record was the book, and the book was the history, and the history was the story of the systems the weapons were part of. The story was the story of the human beings who built and used and suffered from the systems, and the story was the story of the human condition. The condition was the condition of a species that had learned to make weapons and had not learned to stop making them. The learning was the task, and the task was the history, and the history was the book.

The book was a history of war and the development of weapons, and the history was a history of the systems the weapons were part of. The systems were the subject, the weapons were the evidence, and the evidence was the story. The story was told in the chapters that followed, organized around the themes the history had revealed. The themes were advantage and integration and asymmetry and contest, and they were the threads that ran through the story. The threads were the key to understanding the story, and the story was the history, and the history was the book. The book was the record of the study, the study was the purpose, and the purpose was understanding. Understanding was the goal, the goal was peace, and peace was the hope. The hope was the hope of a species that had learned to make weapons and had not learned to stop making them. The learning was the task,

paragraphs: The learning was the task, and the task was unfinished. In the century after the first industrial war, weapons makers confronted a paradox no earlier generation had faced: their instruments had become so destructive that their use threatened to abolish the purposes for which wars were fought. The history of the following decades would be, in large measure, the history of how states tried to live inside that paradox—how they built arsenals they could never fully use, planned for wars they could not afford to win, and kept advancing the technology of killing even as the doctrine of killing grew more cautious.

Consider the machine gun, which had reached maturity by the opening of the twentieth century and would be refined into a family of weapons so varied that the term itself became imprecise. The Maxim gun of 1884 had been a single answer to a single problem: how to convert the energy of a fired cartridge into the work of loading and firing the next. Its descendants multiplied along axes of weight, caliber, and role. The heavy machine gun, water- or air-cooled, mounted on a tripod or vehicle, could sustain fire for minutes at a time and was expected to hold a line. The light machine gun, fed from a magazine or belt, was carried by one soldier and served as the automatic spine of the infantry squad. The submachine gun, firing pistol ammunition, was a close-quarters tool for trench raiders and, later, urban combat. Each was a different answer to a different question, and the questions were dictated by the conditions of battle.

The First World War had taught that the machine gun, properly sited and supplied, could stop an assault cold. It had also taught that the gun was voracious. A single water-cooled gun could consume thousands of rounds in an hour, and feeding it—ammunition, water, spare barrels, replacement parts—became a problem in itself. The armies of the Great War learned to organize machine-gun companies as specialized units with their own transport, supply trains, and doctrine. The gun was no longer a curiosity attached to a regiment; it was a system, and the system had to be managed.

Between the wars, refinement continued. The German MG 34, introduced in 1934, was among the first general-purpose machine guns—light enough for one man to carry, heavy enough to mount on a tripod for sustained fire. It fired from a belt, could be switched from light to heavy configuration in the field, and was built to tolerances that made it expensive but precise. Its successor, the MG 42, was cheaper, faster to build, and fired at so high a rate—some 1,200 rounds per minute—that its sound was described as a ripping canvas. The MG 42 was not subtle. It was designed to suppress, pin, and kill, and it did so with an economy of material that made mass production possible. The American Browning M2, chambered for the .50-caliber cartridge, was a different kind of answer: a heavy gun mountable on vehicles, aircraft, and ships that would remain in service for nearly a century because no one could improve on its combination of power and reliability.

The machine gun's development illustrated a principle that would recur throughout the century: weapon and doctrine evolved together, each shaping the other. The gun made the squad a unit of firepower rather than maneuver. The squad's tactics changed to exploit the gun's suppressive effect. The gun's weight and ammunition consumption dictated the squad's transport, which dictated its mobility, which dictated its role. And so on, in a loop that never quite closed.

Artillery followed a similar path on a larger scale. The French 75 of 1897 was a revolution because its hydro-pneumatic recoil system kept the carriage steady, letting the gun fire without re-aiming after each shot. The principle was simple: if the gun does not move, the crew does not have to reset it, and the rate of fire increases. The 75 could fire roughly fifteen rounds per minute, a rate unimaginable to Napoleonic-era gunners. But the 75 was also a light field gun, and the war that began in 1914 demanded heavier weapons. The howitzers and siege guns that followed were designed to throw larger shells over longer distances, and their recoil systems grew more elaborate to handle the greater forces.

By the Second World War, artillery had become the dominant arm of land warfare by weight of fire. A single field army might dispose of hundreds of guns, and a major offensive might be preceded by a bombardment lasting days and consuming millions of shells. Artillery logistics—producing, transporting, storing, and delivering shells to the guns—became a branch of industrial management as much as a military art. The German army, which had pioneered railway guns and heavy siege artillery, found itself outproduced by the Soviet Union, whose factories turned out tens of thousands of guns and millions of shells after 1941. The Soviet preference for massed artillery, concentrated on narrow sectors and fired in preparation for infantry and armor attacks, became a signature of Soviet doctrine and persisted into the Cold War.

Artillery's development also drove counter-battery fire—locating the enemy's guns and destroying them. In the First World War, counter-battery work relied on aerial observation, sound ranging, and flash spotting. In the Second, it relied increasingly on radar, which could track a shell's trajectory and calculate the position of the gun that fired it. The radar sets of the 1940s were crude by later standards, but they worked, making the artillery duel a matter of electronics as well as explosives.

The tank, born in the trenches of the First World War as a solution to the machine gun, matured in the Second into the principal weapon of maneuver. Early tanks were slow, unreliable, and thinly armored; they had been designed to crush wire and cross trenches, not to fight other tanks. The war that began in 1939 was different. German Panzer divisions, built around fast, radio-equipped tanks, demonstrated that armor could be a concentrated striking force, punching through a defended line and exploiting the breakthrough before the defender could react. The French and British, who had more tanks, dispersed them in support of infantry and were defeated in detail.

The lesson was learned, and tanks of the later war years grew heavier, better armed, and better protected. The Soviet T-34, with its sloped armor, wide tracks, and reliable diesel engine, was a design of genius that could be produced in enormous numbers. The German response—the Panther and the Tiger—was technically superior in armor and armament but produced in smaller numbers and plagued by mechanical complexity. The American Sherman was not the best tank by any single measure, but it was reliable, easy to produce and repair, and available in quantities that made it decisive. Its story illustrated a truth the history of weapons had demonstrated repeatedly: the best weapon is not always the one with the best specifications, but the one that can be produced, maintained, and supplied under the conditions of actual war.

The tank's development also drove anti-tank weapons. Early anti-tank rifles, firing heavy bullets from long barrels, were effective against thin-skinned vehicles but useless against the thicker armor of later tanks. The answer was the shaped-charge warhead, which used the explosive force of a hollow cone to project a jet of molten metal through armor. The principle had been discovered in the nineteenth century, but only in the Second World War was it exploited in practical weapons. The German Panzerfaust, a disposable recoilless launcher firing a shaped-charge grenade, was cheap, simple, and deadly at short range. It was copied and improved by the Soviet Union, whose RPG-7 would become one of the most widely distributed weapons in history. The shaped charge made armor vulnerable in a new way: it depended not on velocity or mass but on the chemistry of the warhead and the geometry of the cone. A single infantryman with a rocket launcher could destroy a tank that had cost a hundred times as much to build.

The aircraft, a fragile observation platform in 1914, became a weapon of strategic significance in the Second World War. The bomber, in particular, was seen by its advocates as a means of bypassing the trench stalemate and striking directly at the enemy's industrial heartland. The theory of strategic bombing, developed between the wars by theorists such as Giulio Douhet and Hugh Trenchard, held that a sustained campaign against an enemy's cities and factories would break its will to fight. The theory was tested in the war and found wanting in its original form. The bombing of Germany and Japan caused enormous damage and killed hundreds of thousands of civilians, but it broke the will of neither nation. The German war economy continued to expand until late in the war, and the Japanese government did not surrender until the atomic bombings and the Soviet declaration of war made its position untenable.

The bomber's failure to achieve decisive results did not end strategic air power; it shifted the emphasis from mass to precision, from area bombing to the destruction of specific targets. Radar, radio navigation aids, and better bombsights made it possible to attack a factory or a bridge with some hope of hitting it. The fighter-bomber, carrying a modest bomb load and delivering it accurately, gave ground forces a new kind of close support. And the jet engine, pioneered in Germany and Britain during the war, promised speeds and altitudes that would transform the bomber into a weapon that could strike before the defender could react.

The atomic bomb, which ended the war in the Pacific, culminated a development program that had drawn on the best scientific minds of the Allied nations and cost more than the Manhattan Project's managers cared to calculate. The bomb was not a weapon in the traditional sense. It released energy on a scale without precedent, and its effects—blast, heat, radiation—were so extensive that they could not be confined to a battlefield. The bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki killed more than a hundred thousand people, most of them civilians, and survivors suffered radiation sickness and cancers that would claim more lives in the years that followed. The bomb was a weapon that could destroy a city, and the city was a unit of human organization thousands of years old. The bomb made the city a target in a way no earlier weapon had.

The hydrogen bomb, which followed the Soviet Union's first atomic test in 1949, multiplied destructive power by a factor of a thousand. The first hydrogen device, tested by the United States in 1952, produced a yield of more than ten megatons—roughly a thousand times that of the Hiroshima bomb. The Soviet Union tested its own hydrogen device in 1953, and the arms race that followed produced warheads of twenty megatons and more. Delivery systems—bombers, then intercontinental ballistic missiles, then submarine-launched missiles—grew more numerous and more capable. By the 1960s, the United States and the Soviet Union each possessed thousands of warheads, enough to destroy the other's society many times over.

The doctrine that emerged was deterrence, and its logic was simple: if both sides can destroy the other, neither will attack. The logic was simple; the implementation was not. The doctrine required that weapons be survivable—that they could not be destroyed in a first strike—and survivability drove the development of hardened silos, mobile launchers, and submarines that could hide in the ocean. It required that weapons be reliable—that they would work if ordered—and reliability drove redundant systems, failsafe mechanisms, and elaborate command-and-control networks. It required that weapons be credible—that the enemy would believe they would be used—and credibility drove war plans that contemplated the unthinkable.

The nuclear arms race was not a race in the ordinary sense. It was a competition in which each side sought not to win but to avoid losing, and success was measured not in territory or resources but in warheads, missile accuracy, and speed of response. The competition was expensive and dangerous, and it produced a series of crises—Berlin, Cuba, the Middle East—in which the world came close to the war the weapons were supposed to prevent. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962, when the United States and the Soviet Union confronted each other over the placement of Soviet missiles in Cuba, was the closest the world came to nuclear war. The crisis was resolved through negotiation, but the lesson was clear: the weapons had created a situation in which a single miscalculation could lead to catastrophe.

The response was arms control. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space, and underwater, and it was followed by agreements limiting the growth of arsenals and the deployment of defensive systems. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970, sought to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons to additional states. It was signed by 191 states parties, but India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The treaty was not a solution to the problem of nuclear weapons, but a framework within which the problem could be managed.

The nuclear age also transformed the relationship between war and politics. In Carl von Clausewitz's classical formulation, war was the continuation of politics by other means. In the nuclear age, total war between the major powers ceased to be a rational instrument of policy, because its costs would exceed any conceivable political gain. The result was a shift in the character of war: the major powers fought through proxies, through limited wars on the periphery, and through the competition of intelligence and technology that came to be called the Cold War. The wars that were fought—Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan—were fought with conventional weapons, and the nuclear arsenals remained in the background as a guarantee that the conflicts would not escalate into a general war.

The Korean War, which began in 1950 when North Korean forces invaded the South, was the first test of the post-war order. The United States, acting under the auspices of the United Nations, intervened to defend South Korea, and the war that followed was a seesaw conflict that ended in a stalemate near the 38th parallel. It was fought with the weapons of the Second World War—rifles, machine guns, artillery, tanks, aircraft—but it also saw the introduction of the jet fighter and the helicopter as a medical evacuation and transport vehicle. The war ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty, and the Korean peninsula remained divided, a reminder that the conflicts of the nuclear age could be frozen rather than resolved.

The Vietnam War, which lasted from the mid-1950s to 1975, was a different kind of conflict: a guerrilla war fought in jungles and rice paddies, against American forces equipped with the technology of a conventional army. The helicopters that carried troops into battle, the bombers that struck targets in the North, the defoliants that stripped the jungle of cover—all were attempts to use technology to overcome the advantages of the guerrilla. The attempts failed. The guerrillas, willing to accept casualties the Americans were not and fighting on their own terrain, sustained the war until the Americans withdrew. Vietnam demonstrated that technology could not compensate for a failure of strategy, and that the most sophisticated weapons were useless in a war the public did not support.

Vietnam also drove the development of precision-guided munitions. The first laser-guided bombs, developed by the United States in the late 1960s, were used to destroy bridges and other point targets that had resisted conventional bombing. They were expensive and required a laser designator to illuminate the target, but they were accurate—a single bomb could destroy a target that would have required dozens of unguided ones. The success of the laser-guided bomb in Vietnam previewed the revolution in precision that would transform air power in the decades that followed.

The precision revolution was made possible by electronics—miniaturized computers, sensors, and guidance systems that could be packed into a bomb or missile. The first generation of precision munitions relied on laser guidance, which required a clear line of sight to the target and a designator operated by a ground team or an aircraft. The second relied on the Global Positioning System, a satellite-based signal that could guide a weapon to a set of coordinates with accuracy measured in meters. The third combined both and added the ability to track a moving target or loiter over a battlefield until a target appeared.

The effect on air power was profound. In the Second World War, bombing a target required hundreds of aircraft and thousands of bombs, and the damage was often scattered over a wide area. In the Gulf War of 1991, a single aircraft could destroy a target with a single bomb. The statistics told the story: coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, of which about 6,520 tons were precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent. The precision-guided munitions were a small share of the total tonnage, but they struck high-value targets—bridges, command bunkers, power plants, air-defense sites—with a precision that had not been possible before. Images of bombs falling down ventilation shafts and through the doors of bunkers became the defining images of the war and reshaped public and military expectations of what air power could do.

The Gulf War was also a demonstration of the revolution in military affairs predicted by theorists in the 1980s. The theory held that precision weapons, advanced sensors, and information networks would let a smaller, more agile force defeat a larger, less sophisticated opponent. It was tested in the deserts of Kuwait and Iraq and found to work—at least in a conventional war against a technologically inferior opponent. The Iraqi army, one of the largest in the world, was defeated in a hundred hours of ground combat, and coalition casualties were remarkably low.

The revolution did not end with the Gulf War. It continued through the 1990s as the United States and its allies invested in the technologies that had made the Gulf War possible—satellite navigation, stealth aircraft, precision munitions, and the information networks that connected them. The wars in Kosovo and Iraq in the 1990s and 2000s were fought with these technologies and demonstrated both their power and their limits. The bombing of Kosovo in 1999, conducted without ground troops, forced the Serbian government to withdraw from the province, but only after seventy-eight days of bombing that caused widespread damage to civilian infrastructure and killed hundreds of civilians. The invasion of Iraq in 2003 was a rapid conventional victory followed by an insurgency that lasted for years, and the precision weapons so effective in the conventional phase were less useful against an enemy that fought from among the population.

The Iraq War also saw the development of a new kind of weapon: the improvised explosive device. The IED was not a product of a defense industry; it was a weapon of the weak, made from artillery shells, fertilizer, and cell phones, and used to attack the armored vehicles coalition forces relied on. The response was a competition between attackers and defenders that drove the development of armored vehicles, electronic jammers, and robots that could disable or destroy the devices. The competition was a reminder that the history of weapons was not a story of progress in one direction but of adaptation and counter-adaptation, in which each new weapon provoked a new defense and each new defense a new weapon.

The drone, or unmanned aerial vehicle, was another chapter. The first drones were developed during the Cold War as target drones and reconnaissance platforms, and they were used in Vietnam for reconnaissance and in the Balkans for surveillance. The armed drone, which could carry a missile and strike a target, was developed in the early 2000s and used extensively in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia. It had advantages no manned aircraft could match: it could loiter over a target for hours, be operated from a base thousands of miles away, and strike with precision without putting a pilot at risk. It also had disadvantages: it was vulnerable to air defenses, required a communications link that could be jammed, and raised legal and ethical questions about targeted killing and civilian casualties.

The drone war in the tribal areas of Pakistan, conducted by the CIA and the U.S. military from 2004 to 2018, was the most intensive use of armed drones in history. The strikes killed thousands of militants, but also civilians, and the program became a source of tension between the United States and Pakistan. Supporters defended it as a precise and effective tool against terrorism; opponents criticized it as extrajudicial killing that violated international law. The debate previewed those that would follow as autonomous weapons became more capable.

Autonomous weapons—weapons that can select and engage targets without human intervention—were the next step. The technology had been developed in the laboratory for decades, and it was deployed in limited form in the loitering munitions used in the Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020. In that forty-four-day war, Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses. The drones were effective because they were cheap, could loiter over the battlefield, and could strike with precision. Armenian air defenses, designed to counter manned aircraft, were not effective against the small, slow drones. The war was a landmark in drone warfare and was studied by militaries around the world as a preview of the future.

Nagorno-Karabakh also raised the question of autonomy. The loitering munitions used in the war were capable of autonomous operation—they could be programmed to search for a target and attack it without further human input. Whether they were actually used in autonomous mode was contested. A United Nations Panel of Experts report on Libya in 2021 stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces, but the claim was not independently confirmed. The hedge was appropriate, because the evidence was not conclusive. The question of autonomous weapons remained open, and the debate over their use was one of the most important in the history of weapons.

That debate was not only technical. It was moral and legal, about the nature of killing and the responsibility for it. The laws of war, developed over centuries, rested on the principle that combatants must distinguish between combatants and civilians and take precautions to avoid civilian casualties. The principle required judgment, and judgment required a human being. A machine could be programmed to recognize a tank, but could it recognize a child? Could it distinguish a soldier who was surrendering from one preparing to fire? Could it make the kind of judgment the laws of war required? The answers were not obvious, and the debate over them was likely to continue for years.

Cyber weapons were another chapter in the history of weapons that did not fit traditional categories. A cyber weapon was software or a set of techniques used to attack an adversary's computer systems, with effects ranging from the disruption of a website to the destruction of a centrifuge. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, had been designed to attack the centrifuges at Iran's Natanz enrichment facility. It caused the centrifuges to spin at the wrong speed and destroyed about a thousand of them. The attack was a milestone because it demonstrated that a piece of code could cause physical damage to a facility thousands of miles away.

Stuxnet also demonstrated the difficulty of attributing a cyber weapon to its author. The worm was designed to cover its tracks, and it was not immediately clear who had built it. The evidence eventually pointed to the United States and Israel, but attribution took years and was never officially confirmed. The difficulty was a problem for deterrence, because deterrence required that an adversary be identified and held responsible. If a cyber attack could not be attributed, it could not be deterred.

Cyber weapons also raised the question of what counted as an act of war. A cyber attack that destroyed a power grid or a financial system could cause more damage than a conventional military strike, but it did not involve the use of force in the traditional sense. The laws of war had been written for a world of physical violence and did not easily accommodate a weapon that could cause physical violence without a physical presence. The debate over the rules that should govern cyber warfare was one of the most active areas of international law in the twenty-first century.

The history of weapons in the twentieth century was also a history of the industrialization of war. The two world wars had demonstrated that the outcome of a conflict depended as much on the capacity to produce weapons as on the skill of the soldiers who used them. The United States, a minor military power in 1914, became the arsenal of democracy in 1941 because its factories could produce tanks, aircraft, and ships in quantities no other nation could match. The Soviet Union, which had lost much of its industrial base in the German invasion, rebuilt it east of the Urals and produced more tanks than Germany in every year of the war. The lesson was not lost on the nations that emerged from the war: the capacity to produce weapons was a component of national power, and the nations that could produce the most weapons could win the wars.

The industrialization of war also changed the relationship between soldier and weapon. In the age of the musket, a soldier was a craftsman who understood his weapon and could repair it. In the age of the machine gun and the tank, a soldier was a technician operating a weapon designed and built by others. The soldier's skill was still important—a good tank crew could outperform a poor one—but the weapon's quality was determined by the factory, not the workshop. Training shifted from the care of the weapon to its use, and the weapon's complexity grew to the point where specialized technicians were required to maintain it.

Industrialization also changed the relationship between soldier and state. In the age of the citizen army, the soldier was a citizen called to serve. In the age of the industrial army, the soldier was a specialist trained to operate a particular system. The soldier's loyalty was to the unit and the state, but the soldier's identity was increasingly defined by the weapon. The infantryman was a rifleman, the tanker a tank crewman, the pilot a pilot. The weapon was not just a tool; it was part of the soldier's identity.

The assault rifle showed how weapon and identity were intertwined. The assault rifle could fire in automatic or semi-automatic mode and was designed to be carried by a single soldier. The German StG 44, introduced in 1944, was the first mass-produced assault rifle, and it was followed by the Soviet AK-47, designed in 1947, which became the most widely distributed firearm in history. The AK-47 was simple, reliable, and cheap to produce, and it was adopted by armies and insurgent groups around the world. Its design was a compromise between the power of a full-size cartridge and the controllability of a smaller one, and the compromise was so successful that it became the standard for infantry weapons in the second half of the twentieth century.

The AK-47 was also a symbol. It appeared on the flag of Mozambique, on the currency of several nations, and in the iconography of revolutionary movements. It was a tool of liberation for some and of oppression for others, and its meaning depended on who was holding it. Its ubiquity was a measure of its success as a weapon, but also of the proliferation of weapons in the post-war world. Produced in millions of copies and sold or given to governments and insurgents on every continent, it made it possible for small groups to challenge states and contributed to the proliferation of conflicts that characterized the post-war era.

The proliferation of small arms was a problem the international community tried to address through treaties and conventions. The United Nations Programme of Action on Small Arms and Light Weapons, adopted in 2001, was an attempt to control the trade and reduce the number of weapons in circulation. It was not binding, and its effect was limited. The trade continued, and the weapons continued to kill. The problem was not the weapon itself but the demand for it, and the demand was driven by conflict, crime, and insecurity. The history of weapons had shown that a weapon, once invented, could not be uninvented, and the AK-47 was a case in point.

The rifle's development was also a story of accuracy. The musket of the eighteenth century was accurate to perhaps fifty yards; the rifle of the nineteenth to several hundred; the rifle of the twentieth to a thousand yards and more; the sniper's rifle to a mile. The increase was driven by improvements in manufacturing, optics, and ammunition, and it changed the nature of infantry combat. A single sniper could hold a position against a company, and the threat of a sniper could slow an advance to a crawl.

The sniper's rifle was a weapon of precision, and its development paralleled precision in artillery and air power. It was also a weapon of psychology: the knowledge that a sniper was watching could demoralize a unit, and the fear of the sniper could be as effective as the sniper's bullet. The sniper was a specialist whose training was long and demanding, and the sniper's craft was one of the oldest in the history of weapons.

Body armor developed in response to the rifle and the machine gun. The steel helmet of the First World War was designed to protect the soldier's head from shrapnel, and it was effective. The body armor of the Second World War, designed to protect the torso from fragments, was less so. The body armor of the late twentieth century, designed to stop bullets, was made possible by new materials—ceramics, aramid fibers, and polyethylene—that could stop a bullet without weighing the soldier down. By the twenty-first century, body armor was a system of helmet, vest, and plates that could stop a rifle bullet, issued to soldiers in combat zones around the world. The armor saved lives, but it added weight, and the weight was a burden the soldier had to carry.

Body armor exemplified the competition between offense and defense that had characterized the history of weapons. The rifle made the soldier vulnerable; the armor made him less so. The armor made him heavier, and the weight made him slower. The slower soldier was more vulnerable to artillery and the machine gun. The competition continued, and the soldier was caught in the middle.

The history of weapons in the twentieth century was also a history of the soldier's experience. The soldier of the First World War lived in trenches, exposed to artillery, machine-gun fire, and gas. The soldier of the Second fought in cities, deserts, and jungles, and his experience was shaped by the weapon he carried. The soldier of Vietnam fought a guerrilla war, and his experience was shaped by the helicopter, the radio, and the rifle. The soldier of the twenty-first century fought a war of drones and IEDs, and his experience was shaped by armor, radio, and robot.

The soldier's experience was also shaped by the weapon's failure. The history of weapons was not a history of perfect machines but of machines that jammed, misfired, broke down, and killed the soldiers who used them. Early machine guns jammed frequently, and gunners had to clear jams under fire. Early tanks broke down, and crews had to abandon them. Early aircraft crashed, and pilots died. The history of weapons was a history of trial and error, and the errors were often fatal.

The development of weapons was also a story of the people who made them. It was not an anonymous history but one of inventors, engineers, and industrialists. Hiram Maxim, who invented the machine gun that bore his name, was a prolific inventor who had also designed a mousetrap and a curling iron. Claude-Étienne Minié, who invented the bullet that bore his name, was a French army officer frustrated by the slow reloading of the rifle. Mikhail Kalashnikov, who designed the AK-47, was a Soviet tank commander wounded in the war who turned to designing weapons while he recovered. The inventors were not always soldiers, but they were always shaped by the wars of their time.

The history of weapons was also a history of the organizations that produced them. The arsenals of the early modern state—the Venice Arsenal, the Woolwich Arsenal, the Springfield Armory—were among the first industrial organizations, pioneering mass-production techniques later applied to consumer goods. The private contractors of the nineteenth century—Krupp, Vickers, Schneider—were among the first multinational corporations, selling weapons to governments around the world. The defense industry of the twentieth century was a hybrid of public and private enterprise and one of the largest industries in the world. Its products shaped the history of war, and its interests shaped the history of peace.

The history of weapons was also a history of the treaties that tried to limit them. The Geneva Conventions, first adopted in 1864 and revised in 1949, established rules for the treatment of wounded soldiers, prisoners of war, and civilians. The Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 established rules for the conduct of war, including the prohibition of certain weapons. The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 prohibited the production and use of chemical weapons, and the Ottawa Treaty of 1997 prohibited the use of anti-personnel landmines. The treaties were not always effective, but they established norms that shaped the behavior of states.

They were also a history of the treaties' failures. The Chemical Weapons Convention was signed by most of the world's nations, but chemical weapons were used in Iraq in the 1980s and in Syria in the 2010s. The Ottawa Treaty was signed by most nations, but the United States, Russia, and China did not join, and landmines continued to kill civilians in dozens of countries. The treaties measured the international community's desire to limit the horrors of war, but also the difficulty of doing so.

The history of weapons in the twentieth century was a history of the transformation of war. The war of the eighteenth century was a war of maneuver, fought by professional armies on open fields. The war of the twentieth was a war of mass, fought by conscript armies in trenches and cities. The war of the twenty-first was a war of precision, fought by professional armies with drones and precision weapons. The transformation was driven by technology, but also by politics, economics, and the changing nature of the state.

The transformation of war was also a transformation of the soldier's experience. The soldier of the eighteenth century fought in a line, shoulder to shoulder with his comrades, and his experience was shaped by the discipline of the line. The soldier of the twentieth fought in a trench, alone or in a small group, and his experience was shaped by the isolation of the trench. The soldier of the twenty-first fought in a network, connected to comrades and commanders by radio and satellite, and his experience was shaped by the network. The soldier was never alone, but he was also never free.

The transformation of war was also a transformation of the enemy. The enemy of the eighteenth century was a professional soldier who fought for a king. The enemy of the twentieth was a conscript who fought for a nation. The enemy of the twenty-first was a guerrilla who fought for a cause, a terrorist who fought for a god, or a hacker who fought for a state. The enemy was never the same, the weapon was never the same, and the history of weapons was the history of the changing enemy.

The history of weapons in the twentieth century was also a history of the changing relationship between war and society. The war of the eighteenth century was a war of kings, fought by armies separate from the society that supported them. The war of the twentieth was a war of nations, fought by armies drawn from society and mobilizing its resources. The war of the twenty-first was a war of states and non-states, fought by armies smaller and more specialized, and by networks dispersed and invisible. The
