paragraphs: The armies that fought the First World War were the first in history organized around the factory rather than the harvest. When the German General Staff drafted its plan for the invasion of France in 1905, it did not begin with maps of the frontier or estimates of enemy divisions. It began with the railway timetable. The Schlieffen Plan was, at bottom, a logistics document—a calculation of how many trains could pass through the rail junctions at Herbesthal and Malmedy in a given hour, how many days it would take to concentrate seventy divisions on the Belgian border, and how many weeks would remain before Russian mobilization forced a redeployment eastward. The plan was a bet that the industrial state could move men faster than the agrarian one, and that speed of concentration would decide the war before the slower belligerent could bring its weight to bear. It was a bet on the factory, and the factory won it in the first weeks and then lost it in the next four years, because the same industrial capacity that could move an army in August could also produce shells in October—shells needed in quantities no planner had imagined.

The transformation had been underway for half a century. The railway, the telegraph, the steamship, and the rifled musket had already remade the American Civil War into something the European observers who flocked to the battlefields of Virginia did not fully recognize. The Prussian observers at Gettysburg and in the Crimea took notes; the notes were folded into the staff work of the 1860s and 1870s, and the staff work became the doctrine that the conscript armies of the continent carried into 1914. Prussia's victories over Austria in 1866 and over France in 1870 were read across Europe as proof that mobilization speed, railway concentration, and breech-loading rifles were the decisive variables. What the observers missed was that the American war had also demonstrated what happened when those variables met entrenched infantry armed with rifled muskets and supported by railroads that could feed an army in the field for four years. The Europeans took the lesson of concentration and ignored the lesson of attrition. The first four months of the First World War taught them the lesson they had skipped.

The numbers tell the story of the shift more clearly than any single battle. In the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71, the Prussian army fired roughly 200,000 rounds of artillery ammunition in the entire campaign. In the first months of the First World War, the French and German armies each fired more shells in a single engagement than the entire Prussian army had fired in the war that made Germany. By 1916, the French army was consuming shells at a rate that exceeded the entire pre-war production of the French munitions industry within a matter of weeks. The statistic British artillery officers cited most bitterly in the winter of 1914–15 was that the army had enough shells for a single day of the bombardment the Western Front demanded. The "shell shortage" that dominated British politics in 1915 was not a shortage of courage or of guns but of the industrial capacity to feed the guns at the rate the front consumed them.

The shell crisis of 1915 is one of the clearest cases in the history of weapons where a weapon's tactical promise outran the state's ability to supply it. The British Expeditionary Force went to France in August 1914 with about 1,200 field guns and a doctrine that assumed a short war of movement. The doctrine collapsed at Mons, Le Cateau, and the Marne; the army dug in, and the guns settled into the routine of the trench line. That routine was a daily exchange of fire in which each side sought to suppress the other's batteries and cut the wire in front of the opposing trenches, and it consumed shells at a rate the War Office had never modeled. The British government responded by creating the Ministry of Munitions under David Lloyd George in May 1915, and the Ministry did what no British government had done before: it took direct control of private industry, built national factories, and conscripted labor into the munitions trades. By 1917 the Ministry was producing shells in quantities that would have seemed absurd in 1914, and the British army was firing them at a rate that would have seemed equally absurd. The war had become a contest between two industrial systems rather than two armies.

The French response to the same crisis was to make the artillery the center of the army. The Canon de 75 modèle 1897, the famous "French 75," had entered service with a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady when the gun fired, so the gun did not have to be re-laid after every shot. The result was a rate of fire contemporary observers put at roughly fifteen rounds per minute, and in the hands of a well-drilled crew it could be higher for short bursts. The 75 was a superb field gun, and it was the wrong weapon for the war that arrived. Its flat trajectory made it excellent for shrapnel against troops in the open and useless against troops in trenches and dugouts. The French army discovered in 1915 that it needed howitzers and heavy guns, and it had spent the pre-war years building the finest light field gun in the world and almost nothing else. The lesson was not that the 75 was a bad weapon. The lesson was that a weapon optimized for one kind of war can become a liability when the war changes, and the industrial system that produced it could not be re-tooled overnight.

The German army made the same discovery from the other direction. Its pre-war artillery was organized around the 77mm field gun and the light field howitzer, with heavy artillery a secondary arm, and by 1916 the German army had learned at Verdun and the Somme that the heavy gun was the decisive instrument. The German response was to build the heaviest concentration of artillery on the Western Front. German artillery at Verdun fired more than twenty million shells in the course of the battle, and the German army still lost the battle. The lesson of Verdun was not that artillery was decisive. The lesson was that artillery was necessary and not sufficient, and that a defender who could feed his guns and rotate his divisions could absorb a bombardment that would have annihilated an army of the previous century.

The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916, is the canonical example of the artillery war. The German plan, drafted by Chief of the German General Staff Erich von Falkenhayn, was not to break the French line in a single stroke but to attack a position the French would feel compelled to defend to the last man, and to bleed the French army white in the defense. The position was the fortress complex around Verdun, a salient the French had held since 1914 and that had become a symbol of national resolve. The German attack opened with a bombardment of unprecedented weight, followed by infantry assaults that gained ground slowly and at enormous cost. The French held, and the battle became a grinding exchange that consumed roughly 700,000 casualties on both sides before it ended in December. Artillery dominated every phase. The German guns fired more than twenty million shells, the French guns fired a comparable number, and the infantry on both sides spent most of the battle in dugouts and trenches waiting for the bombardment to lift or shift. The battle was decided not by a single tactical innovation but by the ability of each side to keep its guns supplied, replace its losses, and rotate its divisions through the meat grinder. The side that could not do those things lost ground; the side that could held.

The logistics of Verdun were as important as the guns. The French army supplied the salient over a single road, the Voie Sacrée, which became the most famous supply route of the war. The road was a two-lane highway built for peacetime traffic, pressed into service as the lifeline of an army; the French organized a truck convoy system that kept a continuous stream of vehicles moving day and night, carrying ammunition, food, and reinforcements to the front and casualties back. The road was the reason the French could hold. The German army, by contrast, supplied its guns over a rail network built for the pre-war economy that could not be expanded fast enough to meet demand, and German artillery at Verdun was constrained by the tonnage that could be moved forward—a constraint that shaped the battle. The lesson was that the weapon was only as good as the supply chain behind it, the supply chain only as good as the transport network that supported it, and the transport network a product of the industrial state.

The railway had already remade war in the nineteenth century, and the First World War was the first war in which the railway was the primary instrument of strategic movement. The German concentration in August 1914 moved more than three million men to the frontiers in a matter of days, and the French concentration moved a comparable number, and the Russian mobilization moved an army across the width of an empire on a rail network thinner than the German one—the subject of a famous German intelligence estimate. The estimate was wrong, the Russian army mobilized faster than the Germans expected, the German plan had to be adjusted, and the adjustment contributed to the failure of the Schlieffen Plan at the Marne. The railway was a weapon, and the side that understood its timetable better won the opening campaign.

The railway also shaped the trench line. The Western Front stabilized where it did because the opposing armies ran out of the ability to move supplies forward faster than the other side could dig in, and the line that formed in the autumn of 1914 ran from the North Sea to the Swiss border and stayed within a few miles of that position for four years. The trench line was a supply line, the supply line was a rail line, and the rail line was a product of the industrial geography of northern France and Belgium. The armies fought over the rail junctions, and the battles of 1915 and 1916 were fought to break the rail-based stalemate, and the stalemate held because neither side could break the other's rail network without breaking its own.

The trench itself was a weapon, and its development was one of the quiet innovations of the war. The trench was not a new idea—siege warfare had used approach trenches for centuries—but the trench system of the Western Front was a new kind of fortification: a continuous line of earthworks stretching for hundreds of miles, designed to absorb artillery fire and shelter infantry from machine-gun fire. It was dug in a zigzag so that a shell landing in one traverse could not kill the men in the next, revetted with timber and sandbags, provided with dugouts deep enough to shelter from heavy shells, and wired with barbed wire in belts that could be dozens of yards deep. The trench system was a machine for surviving artillery, built by the labor of millions of soldiers who spent more time digging than fighting, and the digging was as important to the war as the shooting.

The barbed wire fronting the trenches was itself a weapon of considerable importance. Invented in the 1870s for the American cattle industry, it had been adapted for military use in the Boer War and the Russo-Japanese War, and by 1914 it was a standard article of military equipment. The wire was cheap, easy to deploy, and extraordinarily effective at slowing an infantry assault. A belt twenty yards deep could stop a battalion for minutes, and minutes were enough for the machine guns to find their range. The wire was cut by artillery fire, and the cutting of the wire became one of the central problems of the offensive; the failure to cut it was one of the reasons the first day of the Somme was a catastrophe. The wire was a weapon that cost pennies and defeated attacks that cost thousands of lives.

The machine gun was the other great defensive weapon of the trench war, and its development had been underway since Hiram Maxim demonstrated his recoil-operated automatic gun in 1884. The Maxim gun was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun, the British Army adopted a .303-caliber version in 1891, and by 1914 the major armies had machine guns in their inventories and had not yet worked out how to use them. Pre-war doctrine treated the machine gun as a support weapon, a way to add firepower to an infantry battalion, and it underestimated the weapon's defensive potential. In the trench war the machine gun was not a support weapon. It was the anchor of the defense, and a single well-sited gun could stop an attack across open ground, and the attackers learned to fear it more than any other weapon on the battlefield. The German army, which had fewer machine guns than the British and French at the start of the war, built up its machine-gun establishment faster and used it more effectively, and the German defensive doctrine of 1916 and 1917 was built around the machine gun and the deep trench system.

The machine gun was also a weapon of the offensive, and the development of the light machine gun and the submachine gun in the later years of the war was an attempt to give the attacking infantry the firepower the defensive machine gun had given the defender. The Lewis gun, the Chauchat, the Bergmann MP18—these were weapons designed to be carried forward in an assault, to provide the volume of fire a rifle could not, and to allow a small group of men to suppress a trench position while the rest of the assault closed. The submachine gun was a particularly revealing innovation. It fired pistol ammunition, was short and light, and was designed for the close-quarters fighting of trench raids and urban combat. The MP18, introduced by the German army in 1918, was the first submachine gun to see widespread service, and it was a weapon of the stormtrooper tactics the German army developed in the last year of the war. The stormtrooper was an infantryman trained to infiltrate the enemy line, bypass strong points, and attack the enemy's command and supply nodes, and the submachine gun was his tool. The tactics and the weapon were developed together, and the combination was one of the most important infantry innovations of the war.

The stormtrooper tactics were a response to the failure of massed assault. The trench war had demonstrated that a linear attack across open ground against a wired and entrenched defense was a slaughter, and the German army responded by developing a technique of infiltration that concentrated force at weak points and avoided the strong ones. The stormtroopers were organized into small units, armed with light machine guns, flamethrowers, and grenades, and trained to move fast and keep moving. The tactics worked: the German offensive of March 1918 broke the British line and advanced further than any offensive since 1914, and the offensive still failed because the German army could not supply the advance and could not replace the losses. The stormtrooper was a weapon of the offensive, the offensive was a weapon of the industrial state, and the industrial state could not sustain the offensive beyond the reach of its railheads.

The flamethrower was another weapon of the trench war, and its development illustrates the way the war forced innovation in directions pre-war planners had not anticipated. The flamethrower projected burning liquid into a trench or dugout; it was first used by the German army in 1915, and it was terrifying, effective, and limited. The weapon had a short range, was dangerous to its operator, and required a crew of two or three men to carry the fuel and the propellant. It was not a war-winning weapon, but it was a weapon the trench war demanded, because the trench war was a war of close-quarters fighting in confined spaces, and the flamethrower was a way to clear a dugout without sending men into it.

The grenade was the most widely used weapon of the trench war, and its development was a return to an older tradition. The hand grenade had been a standard infantry weapon in the eighteenth century and had fallen out of use in the nineteenth as armies moved to linear tactics and long-range fire, and the trench war brought it back. The grenade was ideal for trench fighting because it could be thrown around a corner, into a dugout, or over a parapet, and the armies of 1914 improvised grenades from jam tins and empty shell cases before developing purpose-built models. The Mills bomb, introduced by the British army in 1915, was a segmented cast-iron grenade that became the standard British grenade of the war, and the German army developed the "potato masher" stick grenade, which had a longer throwing range and a wooden handle that made it easier to throw. The grenade was cheap, could be produced in enormous quantities, and was the weapon the infantryman carried into the trench raid and the assault. The trench war made the grenade a central infantry weapon again, and it has remained one ever since.

The trench mortar was another weapon the trench war brought back into service. The mortar had been a standard siege weapon since the fifteenth century and had been superseded by the howitzer in the nineteenth, and the trench war revived it because it needed a weapon that could drop a bomb into an enemy trench from short range. The British army developed the Stokes mortar, a simple tube with a base plate that fired a bomb from a fixed firing pin, and the Stokes became the standard British mortar of the war and the ancestor of the modern infantry mortar. The mortar was cheap, portable, and could be operated by a small crew; it was the infantryman's artillery. The trench war made the mortar a central infantry weapon, and it has remained one ever since.

The tank was the most famous innovation of the trench war, and its development was a direct response to the stalemate. The tank was a vehicle that could cross a trench, crush barbed wire, and carry a gun and armor, and it was conceived by the British as a way to break the trench line. The first tanks went into action at the Battle of Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916; they were slow, unreliable, and mechanically fragile, and they still had an effect on the battle out of proportion to their numbers. The tank was a weapon the industrial state could build and improve, and by 1918 the British and French armies were fielding tanks in numbers that could make a difference. The Battle of Cambrai in November 1917 was the first battle in which tanks were used in mass; the German army was shocked by the breakthrough, and the shock was a preview of the mobile warfare that would dominate the next war.

The tank was not a decisive weapon in the First World War, but it was a decisive innovation, because it demonstrated that the trench line could be broken and that the machine gun and the wire were not invincible. The tank combined the firepower of the artillery, the mobility of the cavalry, and the protection of the fortification—the first weapon in history to combine those three properties in a single machine. It was a product of the internal combustion engine, and the internal combustion engine was the technology that would transform warfare in the twentieth century as thoroughly as the railway had transformed it in the nineteenth.

The internal combustion engine also transformed the air. The First World War was the first war in which aircraft played a significant role, and the development of military aviation during the war was one of the most rapid technological transformations in the history of weapons. The aircraft of 1914 were fragile machines of wood and fabric, powered by engines of less than a hundred horsepower and capable of speeds of less than a hundred miles per hour. The aircraft of 1918 were robust machines of metal and plywood, powered by engines of several hundred horsepower, capable of speeds of more than a hundred and fifty miles per hour, armed with machine guns and capable of carrying bombs. The transformation was driven by the war, the war was driven by the industrial state, and the industrial state could produce aircraft in quantities that would have seemed impossible in 1914.

The aircraft's first military role was reconnaissance. The airplane could see over the trench line and report on the enemy's dispositions, and the reconnaissance aircraft became the most valuable aircraft of the early war. The airplane was the answer to the trench stalemate's central problem—that neither side could see what the other was doing behind the line—and it gave commanders the eyes they had lost when the front stabilized. The reconnaissance aircraft was soon joined by the fighter, designed to shoot down reconnaissance aircraft, and the fighter was joined by the bomber, designed to attack the enemy's supply lines and cities, and by 1918 the air war had become a separate theater with its own tactics, its own aces, and its own industrial base.

The air war was a war of technology, and the technology changed so fast that a fighter superior in January could be obsolete by June. The German air force, the Luftstreitkräfte, dominated the air over the Western Front in 1915 and 1916 with the Fokker Eindecker and the Albatros series; the British and French responded with new aircraft and new tactics, and the pendulum swung back and forth. The air war was a war of attrition in the air as well as on the ground, the losses were heavy, and the pilots who survived became the celebrities of the war. It was also a war of production: the side that could build more aircraft and train more pilots won, and the Allies won the air war by 1918 because they had more industrial capacity than the Central Powers.

The air war also produced the first strategic bombing campaign in history. The German army used Zeppelin airships to bomb London in 1915 and 1916, and the German air force used Gotha bombers to bomb London in 1917; the British responded by forming the Royal Air Force in 1918 and by planning a strategic bombing campaign against Germany. The strategic bombing campaign of the First World War was small in scale compared to those of the Second World War, but it established the principle that a nation's cities and industries were legitimate targets in total war—a principle developed to its logical conclusion in the next war.

The naval war was transformed as thoroughly as the land war. The First World War was the first war in which the dreadnought battleship was the capital ship, and the dreadnought was a product of the naval arms race between Britain and Germany that had dominated the pre-war decade. The dreadnought was a battleship armed with a uniform battery of large-caliber guns and powered by steam turbines, designed to fight a decisive battle at long range, and the decisive battle never came. The Battle of Jutland, fought on 31 May and 1 June 1916, was the only major fleet action of the war, and it was indecisive; the German fleet retreated to port and never came out again in force. The dreadnought was a weapon too expensive to risk, and the navies that built it discovered that the risk of losing it was greater than the value of using it, and the naval war was fought by cruisers, destroyers, and submarines instead.

The submarine was the naval weapon that mattered most in the First World War. The German U-boat campaign against British commerce was an attempt to starve Britain into submission; it came close to succeeding in 1917 and was defeated by the convoy system and by the entry of the United States into the war. The submarine attacked the enemy's supply chain rather than his battle fleet; it was a weapon the industrial state could build in quantity, and a weapon the international law of the sea had not anticipated. The German submarine campaign was a war on commerce, the war on commerce was a war on civilians, and the war on civilians was one of the defining features of the twentieth century's total war.

The First World War was the first war in which the distinction between combatant and civilian began to erode. The submarine attacked merchant ships, the airplane bombed cities, the blockade starved populations, and the propaganda demonized the enemy. The war was fought by nations, not by armies; the nations mobilized their entire populations for the war effort, and the mobilization of the population made the population a target. The First World War taught the twentieth century that total war was possible, and the lesson was learned and applied in the Second World War.

The casualties of the First World War were the price of the lesson. The war killed roughly nine million soldiers and perhaps ten million civilians, wounded more than twenty million, and left a generation of survivors changed by the experience. It was fought by conscript armies drawn from every class and every region, and it touched every family in Europe. The war was a catastrophe that the industrial state had made possible, and the states that fought it were never the same afterward.

The peace that ended the war tried to prevent the next war by disarming the defeated. The Treaty of Versailles, signed in 1919, limited the German army to 100,000 men, forbade Germany an air force, submarines, and tanks, and imposed reparations designed to cripple the German economy. The treaty failed, its failure was one of the causes of the Second World War, and the failure was a lesson in the limits of arms control. The treaty tried to control weapons by controlling the state that possessed them; the state found ways around the controls, and the controls became a grievance that fueled the next war.

The interwar years were a period of intense technological development in weapons, much of it driven by the memory of the First World War. The armies of the 1920s and 1930s tried to solve the problems the trench war had exposed, developing new doctrines and new weapons to solve them. The German army developed the doctrine of blitzkrieg, which combined tanks, aircraft, and infantry into a coordinated offensive, as a response to the failure of the trench war's massed assault. The British army developed the doctrine of mechanized warfare, the American army the doctrine of amphibious warfare, and the Soviet army the doctrine of deep battle. The doctrines were different, but they shared a common assumption: that the next war would be a war of movement, and that the weapons that would win it would be the tank, the aircraft, and the radio.

The tank was the central weapon of interwar development. The tanks of 1918 were slow, unreliable, and mechanically fragile, and interwar designers set out to build tanks that were fast, reliable, and mechanically robust. The result was a generation of tanks faster and more reliable than their predecessors; the tanks of the 1930s were capable of speeds of twenty or thirty miles per hour and ranges of a hundred miles or more. Tanks were also armed with better guns and protected by better armor, and the tank became the primary offensive weapon of the mechanized army.

The development of the tank was accompanied by the development of the doctrine that would use it. The German doctrine of blitzkrieg was developed by officers such as Heinz Guderian, who argued that the tank should be concentrated in armored divisions and used to break through the enemy line and exploit the breakthrough. The doctrine was tested in the Spanish Civil War and the Polish campaign of 1939, and validated in the French campaign of 1940, when German armored divisions broke through the Ardennes and drove to the English Channel in ten days. Blitzkrieg was a weapon system as much as a doctrine, combining the tank, the dive bomber, the radio, and motorized infantry into a single instrument of offensive warfare.

The aircraft was the other central weapon of interwar development. The aircraft of the 1930s were metal monoplanes powered by engines of a thousand horsepower or more and capable of speeds of three hundred miles per hour or more. Armed with cannon and machine guns and able to carry bombs, the aircraft was the most versatile weapon of the interwar period. It was also the weapon that made strategic bombing possible, and interwar theorists of strategic bombing such as Giulio Douhet and Billy Mitchell argued that the next war would be won by bombing the enemy's cities and industries into submission. The theory was tested in the Second World War, the results were ambiguous, and the ambiguity would shape the nuclear age.

The Second World War was the war in which the industrial state reached its full potential as a war-making machine. It was fought by the major industrial powers of the world, on a scale that dwarfed the First World War, with weapons the First World War had only begun to develop. It killed an estimated seventy to eighty-five million people, making it the deadliest war in human history, and it introduced the nuclear weapon.

The tank was the central weapon of the land war in the Second World War, and the tanks of the war were the most advanced armored vehicles ever built. The German Panzer III and Panzer IV, Tiger and Panther were the most famous tanks of the war, the Soviet T-34 the most influential, and the American Sherman the most numerous. The T-34 was a revelation to the German army when it appeared in 1941, because it combined sloped armor, a powerful gun, and a reliable diesel engine in a package cheaper and easier to build than the German tanks, and it was produced in quantities German industry could not match. The T-34 was a weapon of the industrial state, and the Soviet Union was an industrial state built for the purpose of fighting a war, and the T-34 was the expression of that purpose.

The tank was also a weapon the infantry needed to fear, and the development of the anti-tank weapon was one of the central stories of the war. The anti-tank rifle, the anti-tank gun, the bazooka, the Panzerfaust, and the shaped-charge warhead were all developed during the war to give the infantryman a way to kill a tank. The shaped-charge warhead was the most important of these innovations, because it used an explosive charge to create a jet of molten metal that could penetrate armor, and the shaped charge was the basis of the bazooka, the Panzerfaust, and the modern anti-tank missile. It allowed a single infantryman to destroy a tank, and it changed the balance between the tank and the infantry.

The aircraft was the other central weapon of the Second World War, and the air war of the Second World War was the largest and most destructive air war in history. The strategic bombing campaign against Germany and Japan was an attempt to destroy the enemy's industrial capacity and break his will to fight; it killed hundreds of thousands of civilians and destroyed large parts of the enemy's cities, and it did not break the enemy's will. The bombing of Hamburg in 1943, the bombing of Dresden in 1945, and the firebombing of Tokyo in 1945 were the most destructive air raids in history—the product of a doctrine developed in the interwar years, tested in the war, and found less effective than its proponents had claimed.

The strategic bombing campaign was also a campaign of technological innovation. The four-engine heavy bomber, the Norden bombsight, radar, the jet engine, and the ballistic missile were all driven by the air war, and all shaped the postwar world. The jet engine was the most important, because it made possible the jet fighter, the jet bomber, and the jet airliner, and it transformed the world's transportation system as thoroughly as it transformed its air forces.

The naval war of the Second World War was a war of aircraft carriers and submarines. The aircraft carrier replaced the battleship as the capital ship of the world's navies; it projected air power across the ocean, and it was the weapon that won the war in the Pacific. The Battle of Midway, fought in June 1942, was the decisive carrier battle of the war; it was fought entirely by aircraft, the Japanese lost four carriers and the Americans one, and the battle changed the balance of power in the Pacific. The carrier was a weapon of the industrial state: the United States built more than a hundred carriers during the war, the Japanese fewer than twenty, and the difference in production was the difference in the war.

The submarine was the other decisive naval weapon of the war. The German U-boat campaign against the Atlantic convoys was an attempt to cut the supply line between the United States and Britain; it came close to succeeding in 1942 and was defeated by the convoy system, by radar, and by the code-breaking at Bletchley Park. The American submarine campaign against Japanese shipping was one of the most effective campaigns of the war, destroying the Japanese merchant marine and starving the Japanese economy—a campaign the Japanese had not anticipated and could not counter. The submarine attacked the enemy's supply chain, the supply chain was the enemy's weakness, and the submarine was the weapon that exploited it.

The code-breaking at Bletchley Park was one of the most important weapons of the war, and it was not a weapon in the conventional sense. The British code-breakers, working with the Polish intelligence service, broke the German Enigma and Lorenz ciphers, and the intelligence they produced was used to defeat the U-boat campaign, win the Battle of the Atlantic, and support the Normandy invasion. Code-breaking was a weapon of the information age and a preview of the role information would play in the wars of the twenty-first century. It was also a weapon that depended on the industrial state, because it required electromechanical computers and a large organization of mathematicians, linguists, and technicians—an organization as important as the technology.

The atomic bomb was the weapon that ended the Second World War and defined the postwar world. It was the product of the Manhattan Project, a research and development program that employed more than a hundred thousand people and cost more than two billion dollars, the largest scientific and engineering project in history up to that time. The project produced the first nuclear weapon, tested at Trinity, New Mexico, on 16 July 1945; the test was a success, the bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August and on Nagasaki on 9 August, and Japan surrendered on 15 August. The bomb killed more than a hundred thousand people in the two cities, was the most destructive weapon ever used in war, and changed the nature of war.

The Trinity test was the moment the nuclear age began. The device, code-named "Gadget," was a plutonium implosion bomb, detonated on a tower in the New Mexico desert with a yield of about twenty-one kilotons, roughly equivalent to twenty-one thousand tons of TNT. The explosion was brighter than the sun, created a mushroom cloud that rose to a height of more than seven miles, and shattered windows in towns more than a hundred miles away. The scientists who watched the test understood that they had made a weapon that could destroy a city, that the weapon would change the world, and some understood that it would change the world in ways they could not control.

The bomb was the ultimate weapon of the industrial state, and it made the industrial state's total war obsolete. It was so destructive that it could not be used without destroying the civilization that used it, and the states that possessed it understood that it was a weapon of deterrence rather than a weapon of war. The logic of deterrence was simple: if both sides have the bomb, neither side can use it without being destroyed, and the balance of terror that resulted was the basis of the postwar peace. That peace was maintained by the threat of annihilation for more than forty years, at the cost of living under the constant threat of nuclear war.

The nuclear age transformed the relationship between war and society as thoroughly as the industrial revolution had transformed it. The nuclear weapon could destroy a society in a single day, and the societies that possessed it organized themselves around the threat of its use. The civil defense programs of the 1950s, the fallout shelters, the "duck and cover" drills, and the emergency broadcasting system were all attempts to prepare the population for a nuclear war, and all were doomed to fail, because no civil defense program could protect a population from a full-scale nuclear attack. The nuclear age was an age of anxiety, the anxiety was a product of the weapon, and the weapon was a product of the industrial state.

The nuclear weapon also transformed the relationship between the state and the military. It could be used only by the highest authority, and the authority to use it was concentrated in the hands of a few people—a departure from the tradition of military command. The nuclear weapon required a command and control system that was centralized and secure, a product of the Cold War designed to ensure that the weapon could be used if necessary and could not be used by accident. The command and control system was a weapon in itself, and it was as important as the bomb.

The Cold War was a war fought without direct combat between the major powers, with weapons developed during the Second World War and with weapons developed after it. It was a war of nuclear deterrence, and it was also a war of proxy

paragraphs: wars, and it was a war of technology, and the three were inseparable. The command and control system that grew up around the bomb was the first weapon system in history whose most important components were not steel and high explosive but procedures, communications links, and human reliability. It was also the first whose designers had to assume the enemy might one day capture it whole, so it was built with locks inside locks. The permissive action link, the two-man rule, the sealed authenticator system, the fail-safe and fail-deadly arrangements of bombers and missiles on alert: each was a small invention in the technology of obedience. None fired a shot. All shaped the war that was never fought.

The proxy wars were fought with the surplus of the last war and the prototypes of the next. In Korea, the United States discovered that its wartime arsenal had been allowed to decay and that its new jet fighters, the F-80 and F-86, had to be rushed into combat against Soviet-built MiG-15s over the Yalu. The air war over MiG Alley became a laboratory for swept wings, afterburners, and air-to-air radar ranging, and the lessons were written directly into the next generation of aircraft. On the ground, the war settled into trench lines a soldier of 1916 would have recognized, supported by the same 105mm and 155mm howitzer families that would serve for the next half century. The war ended where it began, near the thirty-eighth parallel, and the weapons tested there did not decide it. What decided it was the threat of escalation—the nuclear arsenal held in reserve—and the willingness of the belligerents to accept a stalemate rather than risk weapons that would have made the stalemate irrelevant.

Vietnam was different in kind. It was a war in which the most advanced industrial power in the world deployed helicopters, guided bombs, chemical defoliants, and electronic sensors against an enemy who moved on foot and by bicycle and chose the time and place of every engagement. The helicopter was the emblem of the war, a weapon system in the fullest sense: the UH-1 Huey was a transport, a gunship, a medevac platform, and a command post, and the tactics of air mobility were invented around it in the field. The AC-47 gunship, a transport fitted with side-firing miniguns, was improvised to circle a target and pour fire onto it, and it became the ancestor of a family of gunships that served into the twenty-first century. The laser-guided bomb, first used in quantity in 1972 against bridges north of the demilitarized zone, was the true revolution, though its significance was not widely understood at the time. A bomb guided to a point target by a spot of laser light changed the arithmetic of air power: a bridge that had once required dozens of sorties and hundreds of bombs could be dropped by a single aircraft with a handful of weapons. The technology was crude by later standards, and weather, smoke, and jungle canopy often defeated it, but the principle was established: precision was a weapon in its own right.

The Soviet Union drew different lessons. It had supplied the North Vietnamese with surface-to-air missiles, the SA-2, and with radar and fighters, and it had watched the Americans build a complex apparatus of electronic countermeasures to defeat them. The SA-2 forced American aircraft to fly low, where they were vulnerable to anti-aircraft artillery, and the cat-and-mouse game of radar, jammer, and anti-radiation missile became a permanent feature of air warfare. The Soviet answer was layered air defense and tanks in enormous numbers, reflecting a doctrine that assumed a war in Europe would be decided by mass and momentum. NATO answered with precision and the tank-killing guided missile, and the two doctrines met in the tank designs of the 1960s and 1970s: the Soviet T-64 and T-72 with their low silhouettes and autoloaders, the American M60 and the German Leopard with their rangefinders and stabilized guns. The main battle tank was the most heavily engineered vehicle in the world, its development driven by the arithmetic of armor penetration and slope and standoff distance—an arithmetic that had begun with the first iron plates bolted to the sides of a Holt tractor in 1916.

The Middle East became the proving ground for the weapons the superpowers sold to their clients. The 1967 war demonstrated the value of air power used preemptively and the vulnerability of aircraft on the ground. The 1973 war demonstrated the value of the anti-tank guided missile, when Egyptian infantry with the Soviet AT-3 Sagger and the RPG-7 inflicted heavy losses on Israeli armor in the first days of the Suez Canal crossing, and the value of the man-portable air-defense system, when SA-7 missiles fired by infantrymen threatened Israeli aircraft. The lessons were absorbed everywhere. Every army reexamined its tank tactics, every air force its low-level tactics, and the infantryman with a shoulder-fired missile became a more dangerous opponent than he had been since the rifled musket. The cost of a tank rose into the millions of dollars while the cost of the missile that could kill it remained in the tens of thousands, and the asymmetry was noted in every defense ministry on earth.

The 1973 war also demonstrated the value of the precision-guided weapon in a form that would become central. The Israeli Air Force, using early electro-optical and television-guided bombs supplied by the United States, attacked bridges and command posts with a success rate conventional bombs could not match. The weapons were scarce and the tactics improvised, but the direction of travel was clear. The guided bomb had been a curiosity in 1943, when the Germans sank the Italian battleship Roma with a radio-controlled glide bomb, and a specialist tool in Vietnam, and now it was becoming a category of ordnance. The engineers who built the guidance kits understood that the hard part was not the explosive or the airframe but the seeker and the control loop—products of the electronics revolution that was transforming everything else.

The electronics revolution was the deepest current running beneath the weapons of the late twentieth century. The vacuum tube had made radar and radio possible, the transistor made them small, and the integrated circuit made them cheap. A guided missile that had required a truckload of vacuum tubes and a crew of technicians in 1955 could be built around a single circuit board in 1975. Miniaturization changed the kinds of weapons that could be built and the kinds of wars that could be fought. A radio that had weighed fifty pounds and required a dedicated operator became a handheld set every squad could carry. A computer that had filled a room became a fire-control system that fit in the nose of a shell. The infantryman of 1980 carried more computing power in his radio than the entire German army had possessed in 1940, and that power was not a luxury; it was the difference between a unit that could call fire on a target in minutes and one that could not.

The precision revolution reached its first maturity in the 1991 Gulf War. The coalition that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait deployed weapons developed during the Cold War for a war in Europe, now used against a different kind of enemy. The F-117 stealth fighter, its faceted surfaces designed to scatter radar energy, attacked Baghdad on the first night and was not detected by the air defense system built with Soviet help. The Tomahawk cruise missile, a small jet-powered aircraft with terrain-following radar and a guidance system that compared the ground beneath it to a stored map, flew through the streets of the city and struck targets with a precision impossible a decade earlier. The M1 Abrams tank, with composite armor, thermal sight, and stabilized 120mm gun, destroyed Iraqi armor at ranges beyond which the Iraqi crews could see. The Apache helicopter, with its fire-control radar and Hellfire missiles, hunted tanks at night. The coalition dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, about 6,520 tons of them precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent of the total. The figure was small, and it was the figure that mattered. Precision weapons struck the command bunkers, bridges, and air defense nodes, and the effect was disproportionate to their weight; the public and the military alike drew the conclusion that precision was the future of air power.

The conclusion was not wrong, but it was incomplete. The precision weapons of 1991 were guided by laser, television, infrared, and terrain matching, and each method had limits. Laser guidance required a clear line of sight and a designator—often a soldier on the ground or an aircraft circling overhead, both vulnerable. Television guidance required contrast between target and background, and smoke, dust, and darkness defeated it. Infrared guidance required a heat signature, which could be masked. Terrain matching required a detailed map, which could be wrong. The weapons worked when conditions were right, and conditions were often right in a desert war against an enemy who had not prepared for them—and would not always be right. The engineers understood this, and they built the next generation around satellite navigation, immune to smoke and darkness and able to put a weapon within a few meters of a coordinate from any altitude in any weather.

The Global Positioning System was a military program before it was a civilian one. The constellation of satellites that provided the signal was launched by the United States Air Force beginning in 1978, and the system reached initial operational capability in 1993 and full operational capability in 1995. The signal was deliberately degraded for civilian users until 2000, when the degradation was turned off, and the effect on the world was enormous. For weapons, it made possible the joint direct attack munition, a tail kit and guidance unit bolted onto an ordinary gravity bomb to turn it into a precision weapon for a fraction of the cost of a purpose-built guided missile. The JDAM entered service in 1997 and changed the economics of precision. A weapon that had cost a hundred thousand dollars could now be built for twenty thousand, and the number of targets that could be struck with precision rose accordingly. The same logic applied to artillery: the Excalibur projectile, guided by GPS and inertial navigation, gave a 155mm howitzer a first-round hit probability at forty kilometers that had previously required dozens of rounds and a forward observer.

The satellite navigation revolution also changed the way armies moved and communicated. A unit that knew its own position to within a few meters could call fire on a target it could see and be confident the round would land where aimed. A convoy that knew its route could move at night without headlights. A commander who could see his units' positions on a screen could direct them in a way impossible when positions were reported by voice and plotted by hand. The digital battlefield was the logical extension of the command and control system that had grown up around the bomb, built on the same foundation of satellites, computers, and secure communications. The difference was that it was distributed rather than centralized, putting computing power in the hands of junior leaders rather than a few senior officers in a bunker.

The 1990s were the decade in which the precision weapon and the digital network came together, and the wars of the decade were the demonstrations. The Kosovo campaign of 1999 was fought entirely from the air, with precision weapons to a degree impossible in 1991. NATO aircraft flew at high altitude, above the reach of Serbian air defenses, and dropped guided bombs on bridges, factories, and television stations. The campaign was controversial—criticized for the targets it struck and the damage it did to civilian infrastructure, and also for the targets it failed to strike and the time it took to achieve its aims. But it demonstrated that a modern air force could conduct a sustained campaign against a determined opponent without suffering a single combat loss, and the demonstration was noted in every capital that might one day face such a campaign.

The revolution in precision was accompanied by a revolution in sensing. The sensors that guided the weapons were also the sensors that found the targets, and the two were increasingly the same. A Predator drone, first flown as a reconnaissance platform in the Balkans in the mid-1990s, carried a camera and a datalink that let an operator on the ground see what the drone saw in real time. The next step was to arm it, and the first armed Predator fired a Hellfire missile in Afghanistan in 2001. The combination of a persistent sensor and a precision weapon in a single unmanned aircraft was a new kind of weapon system—one that could loiter over a target for hours and strike with a precision impossible when sensor and shooter were separate. The armed drone was the direct descendant of the guided bomb, the cruise missile, and the reconnaissance satellite, and the ancestor of a family of systems that would dominate the wars of the next two decades.

The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq were fought with the weapons of the precision revolution against enemies who did not oblige by presenting the kind of targets those weapons were designed to destroy. The Taliban and Al Qaeda fought in small, dispersed groups, using civilian populations as cover and the terrain as concealment. The Iraqi insurgency used improvised explosive devices, cheap and effective, which killed more coalition soldiers than any other weapon. The response to the IED was a case study in adapting technology to a threat. The Americans armored their vehicles with add-on kits and then built the Mine-Resistant Ambush Protected vehicle, a truck with a V-shaped hull that deflected blast energy away from the crew compartment. They deployed jammers to defeat the bombs' radio triggers. They flew drones and tethered aerostats to watch the roads. They developed ground-penetrating radar to find buried bombs and robots to inspect them. The IED was a weapon of the weak, and it forced the strongest military in the world to spend billions on defenses that had not been foreseen—a reminder that the cost of a weapon is not the same as its price.

The wars also demonstrated the limits of precision. A precision weapon can destroy a target if the target can be found and identified, and in a counterinsurgency the target is often a person in a crowd or a house in a village, and the decision to strike carries legal and moral weight. The drone campaign in Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia became a subject of intense debate—about the accuracy of the intelligence that fed the targeting and the number of civilians killed alongside intended targets. The weapons themselves were accurate to within meters, and that accuracy did not resolve whether the target was the right one. The precision revolution had solved the problem of hitting what you aimed at; it had not solved the problem of knowing what to aim at, and the second problem was older than gunpowder.

The same lesson had been learned in the air campaigns of the Second World War, when the bombers of the Eighth Air Force attacked ball-bearing plants and oil refineries with courage beyond dispute and accuracy measured in hundreds of meters. The Norden bombsight, the most celebrated precision instrument of its day, was designed to put a bomb in a pickle barrel from twenty thousand feet; in practice the bombs fell across a city. The difference between then and now was that the modern weapon could hit the pickle barrel, and the modern intelligence system could sometimes tell which pickle barrel was the right one, and the combination was a genuine revolution. The revolution was not in the explosive or the airframe; it was in the information.

The information revolution was the theme of the wars of the early twenty-first century, and of the weapons developed for them. The military acronym was network-centric warfare: the idea that sensors, shooters, and commanders should be linked into a single network so that information gathered by one could be used by another in real time. The idea was attractive and oversold, and it had a vulnerability its proponents did not always acknowledge: a network is a target. An enemy who can disrupt the network can blind the sensors and silence the shooters—with electronic jamming, cyber attacks, or the destruction of the satellites on which the network depends. The precision revolution had made the military dependent on information, and the dependency was a new kind of weakness.

The vulnerability was demonstrated in the wars that followed. In 2008, in the opening hours of the Russo-Georgian War, Russian forces and their allies disrupted Georgian communications and attacked Georgian government websites, slowing the Georgian response and shaping the narrative of the war. In 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea, the operation was conducted by soldiers without insignia, supported by electronic warfare that jammed Ukrainian communications and cyber attacks that disabled Ukrainian government systems. The weapons of the information age were not all kinetic, and the non-kinetic ones were often the ones that mattered most in the first hours of a conflict.

The war in eastern Ukraine, which began in 2014 and escalated into the full-scale invasion of 2022, became the most important laboratory for the weapons of the twenty-first century. The conflict was a hybrid of old and new: a war of trenches and artillery, with both sides firing tens of thousands of shells a week, and a war of drones, electronic warfare, and precision missiles. The artillery was the same kind that had fought at Verdun, but the way it was used was transformed by the drone. A drone that could see a target and correct a battery's fire in real time made every gun more lethal, and the drone became the most important weapon on the battlefield not because it killed the most but because it made everything else more effective. The Ukrainians used commercial quadcopters, bought off the shelf and modified to carry grenades, and used them in swarms. The Russians used loitering munitions, electronic jamming, and their own drones, and the contest between drone and jammer became a running battle of adaptation fought in weeks rather than years.

The drone war in Ukraine demonstrated a principle visible in the Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020 and destined to become central to the thinking of every military in the world. In the forty-four-day war between Azerbaijan and Armenia, Azerbaijani forces used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions to destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, and air defense systems. The TB2 was a slow, propeller-driven aircraft with a modest payload, effective because Armenian air defenses were not designed to detect and engage it and because Azerbaijani forces used it in combination with other systems to suppress the air defenses first. The Royal United Services Institute studied the conflict and treated it as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and the suppression of air defense, noting that the drones were not invincible and that their success depended on the defender's failure to adapt. The lesson was not that drones had made tanks obsolete, as some commentators claimed, but that persistent surveillance combined with precision strike had made the battlefield transparent in a new way, and that any force that could not hide from the air would be destroyed from the air.

Nagorno-Karabakh also demonstrated the importance of the loitering munition, a weapon combining the drone and the guided missile. A loitering munition is a small aircraft that can circle over a target area for minutes or hours, searching for a target, then dive onto it and explode. Sometimes called a suicide drone, the name captures its essential feature: it is a guided missile that can wait. Developed in Israel in the 1980s and used in the 1990s and 2000s, it became a central weapon in the wars of the 2020s. The Russians used the Lancet and the KUB; the Ukrainians used the Switchblade, the Phoenix, and a range of improvised models. The weapons were cheap enough to be expended in large numbers and precise enough to destroy tanks, artillery, and command posts.

The question of autonomy was raised by the loitering munition, and the question was not resolved. A loitering munition that searches for a target and attacks it without a human in the loop is an autonomous weapon, and the ethics and law of autonomous weapons were the subject of intense debate in the 2010s and 2020s. The debate was given a concrete example by a 2021 report from the United Nations Panel of Experts on Libya, which stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition may have been used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The report was carefully hedged, and the claim was contested and not independently confirmed, but it was significant as the first official document to suggest an autonomous weapon might have been used in combat. The distinction between a weapon autonomous in its navigation and one autonomous in its decision to kill is the distinction that matters, and the Kargu-2, like most loitering munitions, was designed to be operated by a human who made the final decision. The report suggested that in at least one engagement the human may have been bypassed, and the suggestion was enough to fuel a debate that would shape the next generation of weapons.

The debate over autonomy was a debate about the relationship between human and machine, and that relationship had been changing since the first fire-control computer was installed on a warship. The computer took over the calculation of the firing solution; the human retained the decision to fire. The guided missile took over terminal guidance; the human retained the decision to launch. The loitering munition took over the search; the human retained the decision to attack, at least in principle. The next step—the one the Kargu-2 report hinted at—was the removal of the human from the decision, and that removal raised questions not only ethical but practical. A machine that decides to kill must be trusted to distinguish combatants from civilians, and that trust requires a confidence in the machine's perception and judgment that no machine had yet earned.

The wars of the 2020s were fought with weapons increasingly networked and increasingly autonomous, in domains added to the traditional battlefield. The cyber domain was the most important of the new domains, its weapons software and exploits and the skills of the people who wrote them. A cyber attack could disable a power grid, a pipeline, or a command and control system without a single shot being fired. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, was a case study: designed to damage the centrifuges of the Iranian nuclear program by manipulating the industrial control systems that ran them, it was the first known cyber weapon to cause physical damage to a target. It was a weapon of precision, designed to be used without being seen, and it opened a new chapter in the history of weapons that was still being written.

The space domain was the other new frontier. The satellites that made precision possible also made communication, navigation, and early warning possible, and the satellites were vulnerable. A missile that could reach low earth orbit could destroy a satellite, a laser could blind one, a cyber attack could disable the ground stations that controlled one. The anti-satellite weapon was tested by the United States in 1985, by China in 2007, by India in 2019, and by Russia repeatedly, and each test created a cloud of debris that threatened the satellites of every nation. The weaponization of space was a slow-motion crisis, made more urgent by the dependence of modern militaries on the systems space provided.

The hypersonic weapon was the most prominent new kinetic weapon of the 2020s, promising to defeat the defenses built to stop the ballistic missile. A hypersonic glide vehicle is launched by a rocket and then glides to its target at Mach 5 or more, maneuvering in flight, and the combination of speed and maneuverability makes it difficult to track and intercept. Developed by Russia, China, and the United States, it was deployed by Russia as the Kinzhal and the Avangard and by China as the DF-17. It was not a revolution in destructive power; its warhead was conventional or nuclear and its yield no greater than a ballistic missile's. It was a revolution in the arithmetic of warning time, and the arithmetic of warning time was the arithmetic on which deterrence depended.

The revolution in warning time was the theme connecting the weapons of the twenty-first century to those of the Cold War. The command and control system built around the bomb assumed that a missile attack would be detected by radar and that there would be minutes—perhaps half an hour—to decide how to respond. The hypersonic weapon compressed those minutes, and the compression made the decision harder. The autonomous system compressed them further, raising the question of whether a human could be in the loop at all. The answer the militaries of the world gave was that the human would be in the loop for the decision to use nuclear weapons, and might not be for the decision to use conventional weapons in a fast-moving engagement. The answer was a compromise, and the compromise was unstable.

The instability was visible in the way the weapons were marketed and sold. The arms trade was a business, and the business had shaped weapons development since the first bronze swords were traded across the Mediterranean. The twentieth century saw the rise of the arms exporter as a state instrument, with the United States and the Soviet Union arming clients and proxies to gain influence and subsidize their own defense industries. The twenty-first century saw new exporters, most importantly Turkey, whose Bayraktar drones were sold to Azerbaijan, Ukraine, Poland, and dozens of other countries. The drone was a weapon a middle-income country could buy and use to change the regional balance of power, and its sale was a foreign policy instrument as much as a commercial transaction. The proliferation of precision weapons was a proliferation of power, and that power was no longer confined to the great powers.

The proliferation of drones was accompanied by a proliferation of defenses against them. The counter-drone system became a category of weapon in its own right: jammers, guns, nets, lasers, and missiles. Gun-based systems like the German Gepard and the American C-RAM used radar-directed cannon to shoot down small aircraft; missile-based systems like the Israeli Iron Dome used interceptor missiles to destroy rockets and artillery shells; laser-based systems like the Israeli Iron Beam and the American HELIOS used a directed-energy beam to burn a hole in the target, with the advantage of an unlimited magazine and the disadvantage of dependence on clear weather and a steady power supply. The counter-drone system was designed to defeat a weapon that was cheap and plentiful, and the economics of the exchange favored the attacker: a drone costing a few thousand dollars could be defeated by a missile costing a hundred thousand, and a defender who fought a swarm with missiles would run out of missiles before the attacker ran out of drones.

The economics of the exchange was a theme running through the history of weapons. The longbow was cheap and the knight expensive, and the longbow won. The rifle was cheap and the ship of the line expensive, and the rifle changed the balance of power on land and at sea. The IED was cheap and the armored vehicle expensive, and the IED shaped the wars of the early twenty-first century. The drone was cheap and the air defense missile expensive, and the drone was reshaping the wars of the 2020s. The pattern was not a law and did not always hold, but it held often enough to be a guide to how weapons development worked. The weapon that was cheap, effective, and easy to use spread faster than the weapon that was expensive, effective, and hard to use, and the spread changed the character of war.

The character of war in the 2020s was shaped by the return of great-power conflict. The wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Nagorno-Karabakh were not the counterinsurgency wars the American and NATO militaries had prepared for in the 2000s and 2010s. They were wars between states with artillery, tanks, air defense, and drones, and wars in which the industrial base mattered. The Ukrainian army fired tens of thousands of artillery shells a week, and the supply of shells became a strategic problem for the entire Western alliance. Producing a 155mm shell required steel, explosives, fuzes, and the factory capacity to assemble them, and that capacity had been allowed to shrink during the decades of low-intensity war. The lesson was that the precision revolution had not abolished the need for mass, and that a war of attrition still consumed material at a rate a peacetime economy could not sustain.

The return of mass was accompanied by the return of the trench. The war in Ukraine settled into a line of fortifications stretching for hundreds of kilometers, dug with excavators, reinforced with concrete, and protected by mines and drones. The trench was a weapon in the sense that it shaped the battlefield and forced the attacker into a killing zone, and it was as old as the first siege. The difference was that the modern trench was watched by drones and targeted by precision artillery, and the soldier in the trench was more exposed than the soldier of 1916 had been, because the drone could see him and the artillery could reach him within minutes. The battlefield had become transparent, and transparency had made the trench a more dangerous place—and the trenches were still dug because there was no alternative.

The transparency of the battlefield was the product of the drone, the satellite, and the sensor, and of the network that connected them. The network was the central weapon system of the twenty-first century, built by the same companies that built the civilian internet. The military network was a version of the civilian network with encryption, redundancy, and security added; the addition was expensive and the security imperfect. A cyber attack on a military network could disable the sensors, the communications, and the command and control, launched from anywhere by anyone with the skill and resources. The network was a weapon that could be turned against its owner, and the vulnerability was a permanent feature of the information age.

The history of weapons had always been a history of vulnerabilities. The bronze sword was vulnerable to the iron sword, the iron sword to the crossbow, the crossbow to the firearm, the firearm to the rifled musket, the rifled musket to the machine gun, the machine gun to the tank, the tank to the guided missile, the guided missile to the electronic countermeasure, and the electronic countermeasure to the anti-radiation missile. The cycle of measure and countermeasure was the engine of weapons development, running since the first arms race between the tribes of the Stone Age. The cycle was faster in the twenty-first century because the information technology that drove it could be updated in months rather than decades, and the speed of the cycle was itself a weapon.

The speed of the cycle was visible in how the Ukrainians adapted to the Russian invasion. A commercial drone bought in a shop could be modified in a workshop and fielded in a week. A software update could change the behavior of a whole fleet of drones overnight. A new tactic could be shared on a messaging app and adopted by thousands of soldiers in a day. The speed of adaptation was a form of asymmetric advantage, one a small and agile force could hold over a large and bureaucratic one. The Russian military, which had invested in centralized command and heavy formations, was slow to adapt; the Ukrainians, who had invested in decentralized initiative and light formations, were fast. The contrast was not absolute—the Russians adapted too—and the war became a contest of learning as much as a contest of firepower.

The contest of learning was the theme theorists of the 2020s used to describe the wars of the future. The phrase was the learning battlefield: the side that could observe the effects of its weapons and adjust its tactics and technology faster would win. The idea was not new; the German army of 1917 had developed stormtroop tactics in response to the stalemate of the trenches, and the British army of 1918 had developed the combined-arms attack in response to the failure of the Somme. The difference was the speed and scale of the learning, and the technology that made it possible. Drone feeds, satellite images, and signals intercepts could be analyzed in real time and the analysis fed back to the unit in the field, closing the loop from observation to action in minutes rather than days.

The closed loop was the essence of the weapon system the militaries of the 2020s were trying to build. It was called by different names in different countries, and the names all meant the same thing: a network of sensors, shooters, and commanders that could find a target and destroy it faster than the enemy could find and destroy the network. It was a weapon in the sense that it was designed to kill, and in the sense that it was designed to protect, and it was made of software, radio links, and trained people. The history of weapons had begun with a stone that could be thrown and passed through bronze, iron, gunpowder, steel, high explosive, and nuclear fission, and it had arrived at a weapon made of information. Information was the latest material in the long history, and the next chapter would be written in it.

The nuclear weapon remained the exception to the rule that weapons were made of information. The bomb was a physical object requiring fissile material and a delivery system; the information that went into it was the information of physics and engineering, and the information that controlled it was the command and control system. The bomb had not been used in war since 1945, and the taboo against its use had grown stronger with each decade, and the taboo was a weapon in its own right. It was enforced by the fear of retaliation, the fear of the consequences, and the moral revulsion the images of Hiroshima and Nagasaki had produced. It was also enforced by the treaties built around it, most importantly the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. The treaty had 191 states parties; India, Israel, and Pakistan had never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. It was a bargain: the nuclear powers would work toward disarmament and share the benefits of nuclear technology, and the non-nuclear powers would forgo the bomb. The bargain had been only partly kept, and the treaty had not prevented the spread of the bomb to states that refused to join, nor produced the disarmament it promised. It had nevertheless created a norm that held for more than half a century, and the norm was a weapon that had prevented a war.

The arms control treaties were the diplomatic counterpart of the weapons they regulated. The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks of the 1970s and the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaties of the 1980s and 1990s capped and then reduced the number of warheads and delivery systems, and the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987 eliminated an entire class of weapons. The treaties were verified by inspections, satellites, and the exchange of data, and the verification was a technology in its own right. They were also a recognition that the weapons had become so powerful that their use would be self-defeating, and that recognition was the foundation of mutual assured destruction. The doctrine was grim and stable, its stability the product of the certainty that a first strike would be answered by a second—and that certainty the product of the command and control system built to ensure the second strike could be launched even if the first had destroyed the leadership and the cities.

The command and control system was the most important weapon that had never been used, and it was what the history of the Cold War had been about. The system was a network of radar, satellites, computers, communications links, and people, designed to detect an attack, decide whether to respond, and transmit the order to the forces. It had been tested by accident and false alarm, and it had nearly failed. In 1979, a training tape was loaded into the computer at NORAD and the computer reported a massive Soviet attack, and the officer on duty judged the report a false alarm and did not retaliate. In 1983, the Soviet satellite early-warning system reported the launch of five American missiles, and the officer on duty, Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov, judged the report a false alarm and did not retaliate. The judgment was correct, and it was made by a human being with the authority to override the machine—the most important safety feature of the system.
The lesson of the false alarms was that the human in the loop was not a formality but a necessity, and
