The necessity was not self-sustaining. It had to be built into the machine, and the building was never finished. The false alarms of the early 1980s taught a generation of officers and engineers that a human being with the authority to say no was the most important component in a nuclear command system, and the lesson was written into doctrine, into procedures, into the design of the consoles and the wording of the checklists. But the lesson was also a product of a particular moment in warning technology, and as the technology changed, the moment passed. The sensors multiplied. The computers grew faster. The time between detection and decision shrank. Each change was a technical improvement, and each eroded the margin in which a human being could exercise judgment, and the erosion was gradual enough that no single step seemed to require abandoning the principle. The principle survived in the language. In the machinery, it was quietly being hollowed out, and the hollowing was the central dynamic of the last decades of the twentieth century and the first decades of the twenty-first.

The pattern was not new. It had appeared before, in every period in which a weapon system became so fast or so complex that the human operator could no longer keep up, and the response had always been the same: the human was moved from the inside of the loop to the outside, from operator to supervisor, from the one who pulled the trigger to the one who authorized the pulling. The crossbowman of the twelfth century aimed and loosed his bolt with his own hands, and the decision and the act were the same motion. The gunner of the sixteenth century aimed and touched a match to a touchhole, and the decision and the act were separated by a second or two. The artilleryman of the nineteenth century laid his piece and pulled a lanyard, and the decision and the act were separated by the length of the lanyard and the time of the fuse. The machine gunner of 1916 held a trigger and swept a beaten zone, and the decision and the act were separated by the rate of fire and the supply of ammunition; the decision was made once and the act continued for as long as the belt held out. The bombardier of 1943 pressed a button and the bomb fell, and the decision and the act were separated by the time of fall and the drift of the wind, and the bombardier could not see what he had done. The missileer of 1962 turned a key and the missile rose, and the decision and the act were separated by thirty minutes and the curve of the earth, and the missileer would never see what he had done. At each step the human being was pushed further from the point of impact, and at each step the act became more abstract, and the abstraction was the price of range and power and speed.

The abstraction had a consequence that the designers of the systems did not always acknowledge. A human being who cannot see the consequences of his act must rely on the system's representations to know what he is doing, and the representations are made by the same machinery that carries out the act. The bombardier looked through a bombsight and saw a crosshair on a target, and the crosshair was a representation produced by a gyroscope and a telescope, and the bombardier trusted the representation because he had been trained to trust it and because the alternative was to refuse to bomb. The missileer looked at a console and saw a light, and the light was a representation produced by a computer and a communications link, and the missileer trusted the representation because the system had been designed to be trustworthy and because the alternative was to disobey a lawful order. The trust was necessary. Without it the system could not function. But the trust was also a vulnerability, because a representation can be wrong, and the human being who trusts it has no independent way to check it. The independence that the false-alarm officers of 1983 exercised was the independence of a man who had another source of information—the absurdity of the number, the implausibility of the pattern—and who was willing to act on it against the representation.

Stanislav Petrov had that independence because he had been trained in a system that still expected officers to think, because the number of missiles reported was small enough to be implausible, and because he had a suspicion, never proven, that the new satellite system was unreliable. The independence was a residue of an older culture of command, and it was not guaranteed by the design of the system. The system had been built to report, and the reporting was what it did, and the officer who overrode the report was overriding the system, not fulfilling it. The distinction mattered. A system that depends on the operator to override it is a system that has not solved the problem of the operator, and the solution, when it came, was to remove the operator from the position where overriding was possible.

The removal happened first in the air-defense systems, where the tempo of the threat was fastest. The Aegis combat system, deployed from the early 1980s, was designed to detect, track, and engage multiple targets simultaneously, and its engagement was governed by a computer that assigned weapons to threats according to a set of rules. The human operators monitored the display and could intervene, but the intervention was a break in the automatic sequence, and the sequence was designed to run without breaks. The Patriot system, deployed in the same years, had a similar architecture, and its performance in the Gulf War of 1991 became a case study in the gap between the representation and the reality. The Patriot was credited during the war with intercepting a large proportion of the Iraqi Scud missiles fired at Israel and Saudi Arabia, and the credit was reported in the press and repeated by officials, and the repetition made the system a symbol of the precision and effectiveness of American arms. The postwar analysis was less flattering. The intercepts had been fewer than claimed, the debris from the intercepts had caused casualties on the ground, and the system had failed to engage some of the missiles it was designed to stop. The failures were traced in part to the software, which had been designed to track aircraft and had difficulty with the different flight profile of a ballistic missile, and in part to the clock, which drifted by a fraction of a second and caused the system to look in the wrong place at the wrong time. The drift was a small thing, a rounding error in the timing of the radar, and it was the kind of thing that a human being with a stopwatch and a clear view might have noticed, and the system had no human being in that position. The representation said the missile was there, and the missile was not there, and the system acted on the representation.

The lesson of the Patriot was not that the system was bad. The lesson was that the system was a system, with its own internal logic and its own internal errors, and that the human beings who supervised it could not see the errors because the errors were inside the representation. The supervisors saw the display, and the display was consistent with itself, and the consistency was the problem. A human being who checks a machine against the world needs access to the world, and the access had been removed when the machine was built to be the only source of information. The removal was not a conspiracy. It was an engineering convenience. The machine could see farther and faster than the human, and the human's senses were redundant, and redundancy is expensive, and the expense was cut.

The cutting accelerated in the decades that followed, as the sensors proliferated and the networks that connected them grew. The Revolution in Military Affairs, as it was called in the 1990s, was a vision of a battlefield in which sensors, communications, and precision weapons were linked into a single system that could see everything and strike anything, and the human being was a component in the system, a decision node, not a sensor and not an effector. The vision was articulated in the Pentagon and in the defense journals, and it was tested in the Balkans and in Iraq, and it was found to work, in the narrow sense that the system could find targets and destroy them with a precision that earlier generations of airmen had only imagined. The narrow sense was the sense that mattered to the people who built the system, and the broader sense—the sense in which the system changed the relationship between the human being and the act of killing—was left to the philosophers and the ethicists, who wrote papers that the engineers did not read.

The change was visible in the cockpit. The pilot of a 1944 fighter aircraft flew by feel, by the seat of his pants, by the sound of the engine and the buffet of the air over the wings, and his senses were the primary instruments of the machine. The pilot of a 1991 fighter aircraft flew by display, by a head-up display that projected symbols onto the canopy and a set of multifunction screens that showed the radar picture and the status of the systems, and his senses were secondary to the representations. The pilot of a 2011 fighter aircraft flew by a helmet-mounted cueing system that tracked his eye movements and a set of displays that fused the data from the aircraft's own sensors and from other aircraft and from satellites and from ground stations, and the fusion was the picture, and the picture was the world. The pilot who flew the aircraft that bombed a target in Libya in 2011 saw the target on a screen, and the screen was fed by a pod on the wing, and the pod was a camera, and the camera was a sensor, and the pilot's eye was the last link in a chain that began with a photon and ended with a trigger, and the chain was long enough that the pilot could not have said, with confidence, what he was seeing. He saw a shape on a screen. The shape was a tank, or a truck, or a house, or a group of people, and the resolution was good enough to distinguish a tank from a truck and not good enough to distinguish a combatant from a farmer, and the distinction was the one that mattered.

The distinction had mattered in every war, and the technologies of the earlier eras had managed it in different ways. The musketeer of the eighteenth century stood in a line and fired into a line, and the distinction between combatant and noncombatant was made by the formation, which was visible and legible and had been agreed upon by the conventions of the age. The rifled-musket skirmisher of the 1860s fired at a target he could see, and the distinction was made by the uniform, which was visible at the range at which he fired. The machine gunner of 1916 fired at a beaten zone, and the distinction was made by the map, which showed the trench line and the ground beyond it, and the gunner who fired too far was firing into the enemy's rear, where the noncombatants were, and the conventions of the age did not much care. The bomber of 1943 dropped his bombs on a city, and the distinction was abandoned, and the abandonment was justified by the doctrine of strategic bombing, which held that the morale of the enemy population was a legitimate target and that the workers in the factories were as much a part of the war effort as the soldiers in the field. The drone pilot of 2011 fired a missile at a compound in a village, and the distinction was made by the intelligence that had identified the compound as a target, and the intelligence was a product of the same network that flew the drone, and the pilot who fired had never seen the village and would never see the village and could not have said whether the intelligence was right.

The drone was the purest expression of the trend, because the drone removed the pilot from the aircraft entirely and placed him in a container in Nevada, and the removal made the abstraction complete. The pilot sat in a chair and looked at a screen and moved a joystick, and the joystick moved a control surface on an aircraft on the other side of the world, and the aircraft was a machine that flew and watched and, when commanded, killed. The pilot could see the target for hours before he fired, and the seeing was a form of intimacy that earlier generations of airmen had never had, and the intimacy was also a form of distance, because the pilot was not in the sky and not in danger and not subject to the physical and psychological stresses that had always attended the act of killing from the air. The pilot went home at the end of his shift. He ate dinner with his family. He slept in his own bed. The war was a place he visited, and the visiting was mediated by a screen, and the mediation was the point.

The psychologists who studied the drone pilots found a pattern that the designers had not anticipated. The pilots reported high levels of stress, not because they were in danger but because they were not, and the stress came from the combination of intimacy and distance, from the hours of watching a target and the sudden act of destroying it, from the knowledge that the people on the screen were real and the inability to act on that knowledge in any way except by killing them. The stress was different from the stress of combat, and the difference was instructive. The combat pilot of 1944 had a clear and present danger that organized his fear and gave it a shape, and the fear was the fear of death, which is a fear that human beings have evolved to manage. The drone pilot of 2011 had no such danger, and his fear was the fear of himself, of what he was doing and what he had become, and the fear had no shape and no end. He was killing people from a chair in Nevada, and the killing was real, and the reality was the problem. The system had been designed to make the killing easier, and it had succeeded, and the success had produced a new kind of casualty, and the casualty was the operator.

The operator was not the only casualty. The people on the screen were casualties in the ordinary sense, and the ordinary sense was the one that the system was designed to produce, and the production was efficient. The drone was a weapon of precision, and precision meant that the weapon could be aimed at a particular person or a particular building, and the aiming was done by intelligence that was gathered by the same network that flew the drone, and the network was global and persistent and patient. The patience was the novelty. The drone could loiter over a target for twenty hours or more, and the loitering allowed the operators to wait for the right moment, and the right moment was the moment when the target was alone or in a vehicle or in a compound with no civilians nearby, and the waiting was a form of surveillance that had never been possible before. The surveillance was also a form of power, because the people on the ground could not see the drone and did not know they were being watched, and the asymmetry was total. The drone was a panopticon in the sky, and the panopticon was armed.

The arming of the panopticon was the achievement of the first decade of the twenty-first century, and the achievement was celebrated in the press and in the policy journals as a revolution in warfare, and the celebration was not wrong. The drone did change warfare. It changed the cost of a strike, which fell from the price of an aircraft and a pilot and a bomb to the price of a missile and a few hours of a contractor's time, and the fall in cost changed the calculus of when a strike was worth making. It changed the political risk of a strike, because a drone that was shot down did not produce a prisoner of war or a funeral with a flag-draped coffin, and the absence of risk changed the willingness of governments to use force. It changed the geography of war, because a drone could strike anywhere in the world from a base in Nevada or Djibouti or Sicily, and the change in geography changed the meaning of borders and sovereignty. And it changed the psychology of the people who ordered the strikes, because the strikes were easy and clean and remote, and the ease and the cleanliness were the qualities that the policymakers valued, and the valuing was human and understandable and corrosive.

The corrosion was visible in the count. The United States conducted hundreds of drone strikes in Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, and Libya in the years after 2001, and the strikes killed thousands of people, and the people included militants and bystanders and people whose status was disputed, and the disputes were never resolved because the intelligence that justified the strikes was classified and the classification was justified by the need to protect sources and methods. The protection was real. The sources and methods were the network, and the network was the weapon, and the weapon would have been compromised by disclosure. But the protection also meant that the strikes were beyond scrutiny, and the beyond-scrutiny was the condition in which errors could persist, and the errors did persist. The drone pilots and the analysts who supported them were human beings, and human beings make mistakes, and the mistakes were made in a system that had no mechanism for correcting them except the after-action review, and the after-action review was conducted by the same organization that had made the mistake.

The pattern was familiar from the history of every weapon that had promised precision. The rifled musket had promised accuracy and delivered it, and the accuracy had encouraged the infantryman to fire at individuals rather than formations, and the firing at individuals had required a new kind of discipline and a new kind of training, and the training had not kept pace with the weapon, and the result was a battlefield on which the soldiers fired high and the officers could not understand why. The machine gun had promised volume of fire and delivered it, and the volume had encouraged the tacticians to believe that the machine gun could replace the line, and the belief had produced the trench stalemate, in which the machine gun was so effective that neither side could advance. The bomber had promised the destruction of the enemy's will and delivered the destruction of the enemy's cities, and the destruction had not broken the will, and the failure had been explained by the doctrine's adherents as a matter of insufficient weight, and the insufficient weight had justified the firebombing of Hamburg and Tokyo and the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The drone promised precision and delivered it, and the precision encouraged the belief that the strikes were surgical and the surgery was clean, and the belief was a form of self-deception that the operators shared with the policymakers and the public, and the self-deception was the system's most important product.

The self-deception was not unique to the drone. It was the general condition of the precision age, and the precision age had begun, by most accounts, on a January night in 1991, when an F-117 stealth fighter dropped a laser-guided bomb on the Iraqi air-defense headquarters in Baghdad and the bomb went down the ventilation shaft and the building was destroyed and the television cameras in the hotel across the river recorded the explosion and the recording was broadcast around the world. The broadcast was the point. The bomb was a demonstration, and the demonstration was aimed at the American public and the Iraqi government and the world, and the message was that the United States could destroy any building in Baghdad without destroying the city around it, and the message was received. The war that followed was a war of precision, or at least a war in which precision was the advertised feature, and the advertisement was effective. The coalition dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs in Desert Storm, and about 6,520 tons were precision-guided, roughly 7.4 percent, and the small share was enough to create the impression that the age of the dumb bomb was over. The impression was not accurate. The vast majority of the tonnage was unguided, and the unguided bombs did what unguided bombs have always done, which is to fall where they are dropped and to kill whoever is there, and the killing was extensive. The Amiriya shelter in Baghdad was struck by two laser-guided bombs on 13 February 1991, and the bombs penetrated the reinforced concrete and exploded inside, and the people inside were families who had taken shelter from the bombing, and the number who died was in the hundreds, and the United States explained that the shelter had been on a target list as a military command-and-control facility and that the intelligence had been wrong. The intelligence was wrong. The precision was real. The two facts were compatible, and the compatibility was the lesson that the precision age had to learn and did not learn, which is that a precise weapon aimed at the wrong target is a precise weapon that kills the wrong people.

The lesson was learned again in the years that followed, in Serbia and Afghanistan and Iraq, and the learning was always local and always incomplete. The F-117 that was shot down over Serbia in 1999 was a reminder that stealth was not invisibility and that precision was not invulnerability, and the reminder was absorbed by the engineers who designed the next generation of aircraft. The bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade in 1999 was a reminder that the intelligence that guided the precision weapons was a human product and subject to human error, and the error was explained as a mistake in the targeting database, and the explanation was accepted by the Chinese government after a period of outrage and a payment of compensation, and the acceptance was a diplomatic settlement, not a technical one. The bombing of a wedding party in Afghanistan in 2002 was a reminder that the people on the ground could not distinguish a precision weapon from an unguided one, and the reminder was not absorbed by anyone in a position to change the system. The pattern repeated, and the repetition was the system working as designed, because the system was designed to deliver precision and not to deliver judgment, and the judgment was supposed to come from the human beings in the loop, and the human beings in the loop were the ones who made the errors.

The errors were not random. They clustered around the points where the representation diverged from the reality, and the divergence was greatest where the representation was most abstract. A pilot who saw a tank on a screen was seeing a representation of a tank, and the representation was produced by a sensor and processed by a computer and displayed on a screen, and each of those steps was a place where an error could enter. The sensor could be fooled by a decoy. The computer could misclassify a truck as a tank. The screen could be misread by a tired pilot. The errors compounded, and the compounding was invisible to the pilot, because the pilot saw only the final representation and had no way to audit the chain that produced it. The audit was possible in principle, because the data was recorded, and the recording was used in the after-action reviews, and the reviews found errors and the errors were corrected in the next version of the software. But the correction was always retrospective, and the next version of the software introduced new errors, and the cycle was the cycle of every complex system, which is a cycle of failure and patch and failure again.

The cycle was tolerable as long as the failures were small, and the failures were small as long as the weapons were aimed at things that could be distinguished from other things. A tank can be distinguished from a truck, and a truck from a car, and a car from a crowd, and the distinguishing was the work of the sensor and the analyst, and the work was good enough most of the time. But the work became harder as the targets became smaller and more dispersed and more intermingled with the things that were not targets, and the hardness increased as the wars of the twenty-first century became wars among populations rather than wars between armies. The insurgent who planted a roadside bomb was indistinguishable from the farmer who planted a field, and the distinction required intelligence that was human and local and slow, and the intelligence was not what the precision system was designed to provide. The system was designed to provide a picture, and the picture was a picture of things, and the things were not the same as the people, and the people were the targets.

The gap between the picture of things and the knowledge of people was the gap that the next generation of weapons was designed to close, and the closing was the work of the second decade of the twenty-first century. The weapons were the drones and the sensors and the networks, and the networks were the thing that made the weapons a system, and the system was called by many names and the names changed as the fashion changed. It was called network-centric warfare, and then it was called the revolution in military affairs, and then it was called multi-domain operations, and then it was called the kill chain, and the names were marketing as much as doctrine, and the marketing obscured a simple fact, which was that the system was a system for finding things and killing them, and the finding was becoming faster and the killing was becoming more automatic.

The automation was the trend that mattered, and the trend was visible in every domain. The air-defense system that had been designed to assist a human operator was redesigned to operate without one, and the redesign was justified by the speed of the threat, which was too fast for a human being to react to. The missile that had been designed to be guided by a human operator was redesigned to guide itself, and the self-guidance was justified by the accuracy it could achieve and the number of missiles that could be controlled at once. The drone that had been designed to be flown by a remote pilot was redesigned to fly itself, and the self-flying was justified by the endurance it could achieve and the bandwidth it could save. Each of the redesigns was a technical improvement, and each of them moved the human being further from the act, and the movement was cumulative, and the cumulative effect was a system in which the human being was a supervisor of a process that ran without him.

The process ran without him in the air-defense systems of the 2000s, and the running was tested in the wars of the 2010s, and the tests were not always successful. The Iron Dome system, deployed by Israel in 2011, was designed to intercept short-range rockets, and its interception was governed by a computer that calculated the trajectory of each rocket and decided whether it was a threat to a populated area, and the decision was made in seconds and the interceptor was launched automatically, and the human operators monitored the system and could override it, and the override was rarely used because the system was faster and more accurate than the operators. The system worked, in the sense that it intercepted a large proportion of the rockets that threatened populated areas, and the working was a triumph of automation, and the triumph was celebrated as a model for the defense of cities against missile attack. But the system also made a decision that the operators did not make, which was the decision of which rockets to intercept and which to let fall, and the decision was based on an algorithm that weighed the trajectory against a map of populated areas, and the map was a representation, and the representation was not the same as the reality. A rocket that fell in an open field was not intercepted, and the people in the field were not consulted, and the calculation was correct by the standards of the algorithm and not necessarily by the standards of the people on the ground.

The same logic governed the missile defenses that were deployed by the United States and its allies in Europe and Asia, and the logic was the logic of the machine, which is to say that it was a logic of probabilities and thresholds and rules, and the rules were written by engineers who had never been in a war. The engineers wrote the rules to be safe, and the safety was defined as the avoidance of false positives, because a false positive could start a war. But the avoidance of false positives meant the acceptance of false negatives, and a false negative meant a missile that got through, and the trade-off between the two was a trade-off that the engineers could not make on their own authority, and the authority was supposed to come from the political leadership, and the political leadership did not understand the trade-off and did not want to understand it, and so the trade-off was made by default, in the design of the system, by people who were not accountable for the consequences.

The default was the pattern. The most important decisions about the use of force in the twenty-first century were made by engineers, in the design of systems, and the decisions were made without public debate and without political oversight and often without the awareness of the engineers themselves, who thought they were solving technical problems. The engineer who designed the targeting software for a drone was solving a technical problem, which was how to identify a target from a video feed, and the solution was a set of rules, and the rules encoded a judgment about what a target looked like, and the judgment was a moral judgment disguised as a technical one. The engineer who designed the rules of engagement for an autonomous air-defense system was solving a technical problem, which was how to distinguish a hostile aircraft from a friendly one, and the solution was a set of criteria, and the criteria encoded a judgment about who was likely to be hostile, and the judgment was a political judgment disguised as a technical one. The disguises were necessary, because the engineers were not elected and not authorized to make moral or political judgments, and the disguises allowed them to make the judgments anyway, and the making was the way the system worked.

The system worked, and the working was the problem. The history of weapons is a history of the transfer of judgment from the person who acts to the system that enables the act, and the transfer has always been justified by the same argument, which is that the system is faster and more accurate and more reliable than the person, and the argument has always been true in the narrow sense and false in the broad sense. The system is faster and more accurate and more reliable at the tasks it was designed to perform, and the tasks it was designed to perform are the tasks that the designers understood, and the designers understood the physics of the weapon and not the politics of its use. The gap between the two was the space in which the great crimes of the twentieth century were committed, and the gap was not closed by the precision weapons of the twenty-first, and the precision weapons widened it, because they made the act of killing easier and the consequences of killing harder to see.

The widening was visible in the numbers, and the numbers were the numbers of the people who died. The twentieth century killed more people in war than any century before it, and the killing was done with weapons that were designed to be efficient, and the efficiency was measured in the number of people a weapon could kill per unit of effort, and the measurement was the measure of progress. The machine gun killed more people per unit of effort than the rifle, and the artillery killed more than the machine gun, and the bomber killed more than the artillery, and the atomic bomb killed more than the bomber, and the trend was clear and the trend was the trend of the whole history. The twenty-first century did not reverse the trend. The precision weapons killed fewer people per strike than the area weapons, and the strikes were more numerous, and the total was smaller than the total of the great wars of the twentieth century, and the smallness was a relief and not an achievement. The precision weapons made war more tolerable to the societies that waged it, and the tolerability was the danger, because a war that is tolerable is a war that can be continued, and the continuation was the point.

The point was made explicitly by the theorists of the precision age, who argued that the new weapons would make war more humane, because they would allow the destruction of the enemy's military capacity without the destruction of the enemy's society, and the argument was attractive and the argument was wrong. The argument was wrong because it assumed that the enemy's military capacity could be separated from the enemy's society, and the separation was possible in a war between states with professional armies and impossible in a war between a state and an insurgency, and the wars of the twenty-first century were mostly wars between a state and an insurgency. In those wars the enemy's military capacity was embedded in the enemy's society, and the precision weapons could not destroy the capacity without destroying the society, and the attempt to do so produced the destruction of the society and the strengthening of the insurgency, and the strengthening was the outcome that the theorists had not predicted.

The failure of prediction was not a failure of intelligence. It was a failure of imagination, and the imagination was the imagination of the engineers, who could imagine a weapon that hit exactly what it was aimed at and could not imagine a war in which the aiming was the problem. The aiming was the problem because the aim was a judgment, and the judgment was made by people who were not in the war and did not know the people in the war, and the judgment was made on the basis of representations that were produced by the same system that carried out the strike. The system was a closed loop, and the closure was the danger, and the danger was the danger of every closed loop, which is that it can be stable in its errors. The system could be wrong and not know it was wrong, and the not-knowing was the condition of the people inside it, and the people inside it were the pilots and the analysts and the commanders and the policymakers, and none of them could see the whole, and the whole was the thing that mattered.

The whole was visible to the people on the ground, and the people on the ground were the ones who were being killed. They saw the drones and they heard the drones and they knew the drones were there, and the knowing changed their lives in ways that the system did not measure. They changed the times they gathered and the places they slept and the routes they walked, and the changes were a form of control that the system exercised without intending to, and the control was the most important effect of the drone, and the effect was invisible to the people who operated the drone. The drone was a weapon that killed a few people and controlled many, and the control was the strategic effect, and the strategic effect was not measured because it could not be measured, and the unmeasured effect was the one that determined the outcome of the wars.

The outcome of the wars was not determined by the precision weapons, and the failure was visible in the long wars of the twenty-first century, which were fought with the most precise weapons ever built and were not won. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq were fought with precision weapons and drones and networks, and the networks were the most sophisticated in history, and the wars lasted for twenty years and ended in the return of the Taliban to power and the persistence of the insurgency in Iraq, and the persistence was the outcome that the precision age had not anticipated. The precision age had anticipated that the new weapons would make war quick and decisive, and the wars were slow and indecisive, and the slowness and the indecisiveness were the product of the same weapons, because the weapons made it possible to fight without committing, and the commitment was the thing that had won the wars of the earlier eras. The earlier eras had won their wars by mobilization, by the commitment of the whole society to the war, and the commitment had been terrible and effective, and the precision age had tried to win wars without the commitment, and the trying had failed.

The failure was the failure of the theory of the precision age, and the theory was the theory of the Revolution in Military Affairs, and the revolution had been proclaimed in the 1990s and had been tested in the 2000s and had been found wanting in the 2010s, and the finding was slow because the people who had proclaimed the revolution were the people who were evaluating it. The evaluation was conducted in the defense journals and the war colleges and the think tanks, and the evaluators were the same people who had built the systems, and the systems were their careers, and the careers were not served by the finding of failure. The finding was made anyway, by the soldiers who fought the wars and by the historians who studied them, and the finding was that the precision weapons had changed the tactics of war and not the strategy, and the strategy was still the strategy of politics and will and commitment, and the weapons were still the tools of the strategy and not its substitute.

The distinction between tactics and strategy was the distinction that the precision age had blurred, and the blurring was the source of its errors. The precision weapons were tactical tools, and they were excellent tactical tools, and the excellence was mistaken for strategic effect, and the mistake was made by people who should have known better. The mistake was made because the tactical effects were visible and the strategic effects were not, and the visibility was the bias of the age, which was an age of images and metrics and displays. The images showed the bombs hitting the targets, and the metrics showed the targets destroyed, and the displays showed the progress of the war, and the progress was a representation, and the representation was produced by the same system that was fighting the war. The system was measuring itself, and the measurement was favorable, and the favorability was the problem.

The problem was not new. It was the problem of every system of measurement that measures what it can measure and ignores what it cannot, and the history of war is full of such systems. The body counts of the Vietnam War were a system of measurement, and the counts were favorable and the war was lost, and the loss was not understood until the counts were abandoned and the war was seen as a whole. The bombing campaigns of the Second World War were a system of measurement, and the tonnage dropped was favorable and the effect on the enemy's will was not, and the effect was not understood until the war was over and the surveys were done. The precision weapons of the twenty-first century were a system of measurement, and the targets destroyed were favorable and the wars were not won, and the not-winning was the finding that the system could not produce.

The finding was produced by the people who were outside the system, and the outside was the place where the history of weapons was written. The historians who studied the precision age saw the pattern that the participants could not see, and the pattern was the pattern of every revolution in military affairs, which is that the revolution changes the means of war and not the ends, and the ends are political and the politics is human and the human is not changed by the means. The revolution in military affairs of the sixteenth century was the revolution of gunpowder and the trace italienne and the standing army, and it changed the means of war and not the ends, and the ends were still the ends of dynastic ambition and religious conflict, and the wars were still the wars of the earlier era, fought with new tools. The revolution in military affairs of the nineteenth century was the revolution of the railroad and the telegraph and the rifled musket, and it changed the means of war and not the ends, and the ends were still the ends of nationalism and empire, and the wars were larger and deadlier and not different in kind. The revolution in military affairs of the twentieth century was the revolution of the internal combustion engine and the aircraft and the radio, and it changed the means of war and not the ends, and the ends were still the ends of ideology and power, and the wars were total and the totality was the new thing and the totality was a means and not an end. The revolution in military affairs of the twenty-first century was the revolution of the computer and the network and the precision weapon, and it changed the means of war and not the ends, and the ends were still the ends of politics, and the politics was still the politics of the people who waged the wars.

paragraphs: The precision revolution did not arrive all at once, and it did not arrive where most people think. It arrived first in the laboratory and the budget line, then in the targeting pod and the cockpit, and only last in the newspaper and the evening news. By the time the public saw a bomb go down a chimney, the chimney had been measured by a laser, the coordinates passed through three layers of command, and the weapon designed, tested, and paid for over twenty years by people whose names nobody remembers. The history of weapons is always like this. The visible moment is the end of a long chain, and the chain is made of metallurgy and mathematics and procurement and the stubbornness of a few engineers who believed a bomb could be made to fall where it was aimed.

The idea of the guided weapon is older than the airplane. Naval torpedoes were steered by gyroscopes before the First World War, and the Whitehead torpedo, perfected in the 1860s and 1870s, was in its way the first practical self-propelled guided munition—a device that carried its own propulsion and its own sense of direction through the water. The torpedo was a weapon of the industrial age, and it changed naval tactics because it made the small boat dangerous to the battleship, which had to be defended with nets and torpedo boats and eventually destroyers. It was also a lesson in the economics of precision: a torpedo was expensive relative to a shell, and a navy that fired them recklessly would bankrupt itself, so the torpedo was reserved for the moment when it could be aimed with confidence. The same economics would govern the precision-guided bomb a century later, and the same tension between cost and accuracy would define the debate about air power in the 1990s.

The Second World War produced a burst of guided-weapon development remarkable for its ambition and disappointing for its results. The German Fritz X was a radio-controlled glide bomb, used with some success against Italian battleships after the Italian armistice in 1943, and the Hs 293 was an anti-ship missile that sank several Allied ships in the Mediterranean. The Japanese developed the Ohka, a rocket-powered suicide aircraft that was a guided weapon only in the sense that a pilot was the guidance system, and the Americans developed the Azon, a radio-controlled bomb used in Burma with mixed results. These weapons were the ancestors of the precision munition, and they shared the ancestor's defects: they were fragile, they required a skilled operator with a clear line of sight, and they were easily jammed or decoyed. The Germans in particular understood that a guided weapon multiplies the effectiveness of a small force—understood it because they were losing the war of mass production and needed a way to strike disproportionate blows. The lesson was not lost on the victors, and after 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union both invested in guided-weapon research, though the investment was modest and the results slow.

The real breakthrough came not from the bomb but from the computer. The development of the digital computer in the 1940s and 1950s made it possible to calculate a ballistic trajectory in real time, and the transistor and the integrated circuit in the 1950s and 1960s made it possible to put a computer inside a weapon. The first generation of practical precision weapons was built around these technologies: the laser-guided bomb, developed by the United States in the 1960s and used with dramatic effect in Vietnam, was a bomb with a seeker that homed on a laser spot designated by a forward air controller or a strike aircraft. The laser-guided bomb was not a new explosive and it was not a new aircraft; it was a new way of connecting the two, and it turned a dumb bomb into a weapon that could hit a bridge or a bunker with a single sortie. The Thanh Hoa Bridge in North Vietnam, which had resisted hundreds of unguided bombing runs, was finally dropped in 1972 by laser-guided bombs—a demonstration that precision was not a marginal improvement but a change in kind.

The precision revolution of the 1970s and 1980s was driven by the same logic that had driven the torpedo and the Fritz X: the desire to make a small force strike a large target, and the recognition that unguided weapons waste most of their energy on the ground. The United States invested heavily in precision guidance because it expected to fight outnumbered in Europe against the Warsaw Pact, and a weapon that could hit a tank with one shot was worth a great deal to an army that could not afford to fire ten. The Soviet Union invested too, though less successfully, and the difference would become visible in the 1990s. The precision weapon was also a weapon of the rich, because it required satellites and computers and skilled operators, and the countries that could afford it were the countries that already had the most powerful air forces. The precision revolution therefore reinforced the existing hierarchy of military power rather than overturning it—one of the reasons it was so attractive to the powers already at the top.

The Tomahawk cruise missile, first used in combat in 1991, was the emblem of the new era. It was a small, subsonic, winged missile that could be launched from a ship or a submarine and fly hundreds of miles to a target designated by coordinates, using terrain-following radar and an inertial navigation system to find its way. The Tomahawk was not a wonder weapon in the sense of being invulnerable; it was slow and could be shot down, and the Iraqis claimed to have shot down many of them. But it could be fired from the sea at a target deep inland without risking a pilot, and it could be fired in salvoes, and the salvo was the new unit of military action. The opening night of Desert Storm in January 1991 saw Tomahawks launched from ships in the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, and the missiles flew over the desert to strike command centers and air defenses in Baghdad, and the television cameras in Baghdad filmed the tracers and the explosions, and the world watched a war that seemed conducted by remote control.

The statistics of Desert Storm are worth setting down carefully, because they are often misquoted and because they carry the argument. Coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs during the war, and about 6,520 tons of those were precision-guided, roughly 7.4 percent of the total. The figure is often cited as evidence that precision was marginal, and in tonnage terms it was. But tonnage is the wrong measure, because a precision weapon is not designed to deliver tonnage; it is designed to destroy a target, and the targets it destroyed were the ones that mattered. The precision weapons in Desert Storm were used against bridges, command bunkers, air-defense sites, and leadership facilities, and post-war surveys found that they had achieved a much higher probability of destruction per weapon than unguided bombs. The Gulf War Air Power Survey, a massive official study, concluded that precision weapons had been decisive in the campaign against Iraq's command and control, and that the ability to strike a target with a single weapon had changed the calculus of air campaigning. The 7.4 percent was not a marginal share of the effort; it was the sharp end of the spear, and the rest of the tonnage was the shaft.

The precision revolution also changed the politics of war, perhaps its most important effect. A war fought with precision weapons can be presented as clean, or at least cleaner, because the images are of a single building destroyed and not of a city block flattened. The Pentagon learned in the 1990s to put a camera on the weapon and release the footage, and the footage of a bomb going through a window became the visual signature of American power. This was a form of propaganda, but it was also a form of accountability, because the footage could be checked and the claims tested, and the precision weapon made it possible to ask whether a particular target had been a military objective. The precision weapon did not eliminate civilian casualties, and the wars of the 1990s and 2000s produced plenty of them, but it changed the moral arithmetic of bombing, because a bomb that could hit a target could also be blamed for missing it. It made the bomber responsible in a way the area bomber had never been, and the responsibility was a new burden for air forces that had spent the twentieth century arguing that bombing was a blunt instrument and the bluntness unavoidable.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in intelligence, because a precision weapon is only as good as the coordinates it is given. The target must be found, identified, and located to within a few meters, and this requires satellites and drones and human sources and signals intercepts. The intelligence apparatus that grew up around precision weapons was vast and expensive, and it created a new kind of warfare in which the most important battle was the battle to know where the target was. The "targeted killing" campaigns of the 2000s and 2010s were the logical extension: a missile fired from a drone at a single person, guided by intelligence gathered over weeks or months. The drone was the precision weapon taken to its conclusion, a weapon that could loiter over a target for hours and then strike with a Hellfire missile weighing a hundred pounds and carrying a warhead of twenty. It was cheap relative to a fighter jet and could be flown by a pilot sitting in a trailer in Nevada, and it made the projection of force possible at a scale never before possible. It also raised profound questions about sovereignty and law and the ethics of killing at a distance, debated in the 2010s with a heat the weapons themselves did not seem to warrant, because the drone was not a new kind of explosive but a new kind of presence.

The drone was not a new idea in the 2000s. The United States had experimented with armed drones in the 1960s and 1970s, the Israelis had used drones for reconnaissance in the 1982 Lebanon War, and the Predator had been developed in the 1990s for reconnaissance and armed with Hellfire missiles only in 2001. The arming of the Predator was a decision made in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, because the United States wanted to strike at al-Qaeda leaders in Afghanistan and Pakistan without risking American lives. The first armed Predator strike was in October 2001, and the campaign that followed was a campaign of targeted killing that lasted two decades and killed thousands of people, some the intended targets and some not. The drone was a precision weapon, but precision is not the same as accuracy, and the intelligence that guided it was often wrong. The drone wars of the 2000s and 2010s were a laboratory for the precision weapon, and the laboratory produced both successes and failures, and the failures were often invisible because the footage was classified and the investigations internal.

The drone also changed the geography of war, because a drone can be flown from one continent and strike in another, and the pilot can go home to dinner after a shift. This was a new kind of soldiering, and it was controversial, and the controversy was about whether it was cowardly or humane. The drone pilot was not in danger, and this was either a moral advance or a moral degradation, depending on who was arguing. The drone made war easier to start, because it lowered the political cost of casualties, and the lowering of the cost was a change in the calculus of intervention. Countries with drones could intervene in places where they would not have intervened if the intervention required boots on the ground, and the interventions of the 2010s in Libya and Syria and Yemen were shaped by this new calculus. The drone changed the ends of war as well as the means, because it made it possible to wage a war that was not a war in the legal sense, and the legal sense was a thing governments could now avoid.

The precision revolution reached its first maturity in the air campaign of the 1999 Kosovo War, when NATO flew 38,000 sorties and dropped 23,000 munitions, and the precision share was much higher than in 1991. The Kosovo campaign was fought without a single NATO combat death, entirely from the air, and presented as a model of humanitarian war. It also demonstrated the limits of precision, because the targets were often decoys and the weather was bad and the intelligence imperfect, and the bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade was a catastrophe that exposed the fragility of the targeting chain. The embassy bombing was a case of a precision weapon hitting the wrong building because the coordinates were wrong, a reminder that a precision weapon is only as precise as the map it is given. The Kosovo campaign was also a demonstration that precision weapons could coerce a government without invading a country, and the coercion worked, and the model was copied in the 2000s and 2010s with less success.

The precision revolution was not confined to the air. The guided artillery shell and the guided rocket were developed in the 1980s and 1990s, and the Multiple Launch Rocket System was fitted with guided rockets that could hit a target at thirty or forty miles with an accuracy once the preserve of aircraft. The guided artillery shell, the Excalibur, was fielded in the 2000s and gave a howitzer the ability to hit a target with a single round at a range of twenty-five miles. The guided mortar round followed, and the guided bullet was developed for snipers, and the precision revolution spread downward through the hierarchy of weapons until even the infantryman had a guided weapon. The Javelin anti-tank missile, fielded in the 1990s, was a fire-and-forget weapon that could hit a tank at two miles, and a small infantry unit could use it to destroy a much more expensive armored vehicle. The Javelin democratized anti-tank warfare, and it would become famous in the 2022 Ukraine war, when it was used to destroy Russian armor on a scale no one had predicted.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in defense, because the same technologies that made a weapon precise made it possible to intercept a weapon that was precise. The Patriot missile, developed in the 1970s and 1980s, was an anti-aircraft missile that could be used against ballistic missiles, and it was used in 1991 with mixed results. The Aegis system, developed for the navy, was a radar and missile system that could track hundreds of targets and engage dozens simultaneously, and it became the basis of the missile-defense architecture of the 2000s. Missile defense was a precision weapon aimed at a precision weapon, and the race between offense and defense was a race that had been running since the first shield and the first spear. It was also a political weapon, because a country that could defend itself against missiles could act with more freedom than one that could not, and the deployment of missile defenses in Europe and Asia in the 2010s was a source of tension with Russia and China. The defense was not perfect, and interception rates were debated, but it changed the calculus of the offense, because a missile that might be intercepted had to be fired in greater numbers.

The next stage of the precision revolution was the integration of the weapon into a network, which the United States called the "military technical revolution," then the "revolution in military affairs," then "network-centric warfare." The idea was that sensors and shooters could be linked by a network so that a target detected by one platform could be engaged by another, and the network would make the whole force more effective than the sum of its parts. The idea was tested in Afghanistan and Iraq in the 2000s, and it worked well against an enemy with no air force and no electronic warfare, and less well against an enemy that could jam the network or hide from the sensors. The network was a fragile thing, and the fragility was exposed when the enemy learned to fight without radios and without vehicles and without the signatures the sensors were designed to detect. Network-centric warfare was a doctrine for a war against a peer competitor, and the wars of the 2000s were not against a peer competitor, and the doctrine was therefore never fully tested.

The precision revolution reached its second maturity in the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when the United States launched a "shock and awe" campaign designed to decapitate the Iraqi regime with precision strikes. The campaign was a demonstration of the new American way of war, and also of its limits, because the Iraqi regime did not collapse as quickly as the planners had hoped, and the war turned into an insurgency that precision weapons were not designed to fight. The insurgency was a war of improvised explosive devices and small arms and suicide bombers, and the precision weapon was irrelevant to it, because the enemy was not a target that could be found and fixed and finished. The American military spent the 2000s and 2010s trying to adapt its precision arsenal to a war among the people, and the adaptation was expensive and slow and only partly successful. The precision weapon was a weapon for a war of machines, and the war among the people was a war of humans, and the humans were harder to target.

The precision revolution was not an American monopoly, and the diffusion of precision technology was one of the great strategic stories of the early twenty-first century. China developed its own precision weapons, including the DF-21D anti-ship ballistic missile, designed to threaten American aircraft carriers at a range of a thousand miles—a response to the American precision revolution, because the carrier was the symbol of American power projection and the Chinese wanted a way to hold it at risk. Russia developed the Iskander missile and the Kalibr cruise missile, and the Kalibr was used in the Syrian war from ships in the Caspian Sea, a demonstration that precision was no longer a Western monopoly. Iran developed precision-guided munitions and supplied them to Hezbollah and the Houthis, and the Houthis used them against Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, and the precision weapon became a weapon of the weak as well as the strong. The diffusion of precision was a diffusion of power, and the diffusion of power was a change in the international system that the theorists of the 1990s had not predicted.

The precision revolution also changed the economics of war in a way not fully appreciated at the time. A precision weapon is expensive, and the expense constrains the number that can be fired. The Tomahawk cost about a million dollars in the 1990s, the laser-guided bomb about thirty thousand, the guided artillery shell about a hundred thousand. The expense meant a country could not fight a war of attrition with precision weapons, because the stockpiles would be exhausted in a few weeks. The wars of the 2000s and 2010s were fought against enemies who could not shoot back, and the stockpiles were adequate, but a war against a peer competitor would be a war of attrition, and the attrition would be measured in precision weapons. American stockpiles were large but not unlimited, and production capacity was limited by the number of factories and skilled workers, and the factories could not be expanded quickly. The precision weapon was a weapon of the first day of a war, and the war of the second day would be fought with whatever was left, and whatever was left might not be enough.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the cost of defense, because a precision weapon can be intercepted by a cheaper weapon, and the interceptor can cost less than the missile it intercepts. The Iron Dome system, developed by Israel and deployed in 2011, was a system of interceptor missiles that could shoot down rockets fired from Gaza, and the interceptor cost about fifty thousand dollars and the rocket about a thousand, and the economics were upside down. Iron Dome was a success in that it shot down most of the rockets it engaged, but a failure in that it cost more to defend than to attack, and the asymmetry was a problem the defenders of the twenty-first century would have to solve. The drone was the same problem in a different form, because a drone that costs a few thousand dollars can be shot down by a missile that costs a million, and the defender who fires the missile is losing the exchange. The cheap drone was the revenge of the poor against the precision weapon, and the revenge was a lesson the rich would have to learn.

The drone war in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 was the moment the lesson became impossible to ignore. The war lasted forty-four days, from September 27 to November 10, and was fought between Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed territory of Nagorno-Karabakh. Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and Israeli loitering munitions to find and destroy Armenian tanks, artillery, and air-defense systems. The Bayraktar TB2 was a relatively cheap drone, costing a few million dollars, carrying a few precision munitions, and slow and vulnerable to air defenses. But the Armenian air defenses were old and poorly maintained, and the drones operated with impunity, and the videos of Armenian tanks exploding under drone strikes were broadcast around the world. The war demonstrated that a middle-income country with a modest air force could use drones to defeat a larger and better-equipped army, and the demonstration was studied by every military in the world.

The Royal United Services Institute, a British think tank, published a study of the Nagorno-Karabakh war in 2021 concluding that the conflict was a landmark in the history of air power. The study found that the drones had suppressed the Armenian air defenses so effectively that the Azerbaijani air force could operate with impunity, and that drone strikes on Armenian armor and artillery had been so effective that the Armenian army was forced to abandon its positions. The study was careful to note that Azerbaijani success was due to a combination of factors, including the poor state of the Armenian air defenses and the skill of the Azerbaijani operators, and that the lessons of the war were not universal. But it was clear that the drone had changed the character of the battlefield, and that the change was not temporary.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was also a demonstration of the importance of the loitering munition, a weapon that flies to a target area, loiters over it, and strikes when a target is found. The loitering munition is a cross between a drone and a missile, designed to be cheap and expendable, and it can be used to attack targets not worth a missile. The Israeli Harop and the Turkish Kargu-2 were the loitering munitions used in Nagorno-Karabakh, and the Kargu-2 was later at the center of a controversy about autonomy. The Kargu-2 was a small quadcopter that carried an explosive charge and could be flown into a target, designed to be operated by a human but with an autonomous mode that could allow it to find and attack a target without human intervention. That mode was the subject of a United Nations report in 2021, which stated that a Kargu-2 "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces in Libya. The report was hedged and the claim contested, and no independent confirmation was ever produced, but it was a warning that the technology of autonomous weapons was advancing faster than the law and ethics supposed to govern it.

The autonomous weapon was the logical endpoint of the precision revolution, because a weapon that can find and identify and attack a target without a human in the loop can operate at a speed and scale a human cannot match. It also raised the deepest questions about the morality of war, because a machine that decides to kill is a machine given a moral authority no machine should have. The campaign to ban autonomous weapons, the "Campaign to Stop Killer Robots," was launched in 2012 and supported by a coalition of human-rights organizations and academics and a few governments. It was opposed by the major military powers, including the United States and Russia and China, on the argument that autonomous weapons could be more precise and more humane than human soldiers, because a machine does not panic and does not commit atrocities. The argument was not absurd, but the campaigners rejected it, and the debate was unresolved at the end of the 2010s and still unresolved in the 2020s.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the law of war, because the precision weapon made it possible to distinguish between combatants and civilians in a way the area bomber had not. The law of war, codified in the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols, requires that attacks be directed at military objectives and that civilians be spared, and the precision weapon made compliance possible in a way the area bomber had not. The precision weapon was therefore a weapon the lawyers could love, and they did, and military lawyers became an essential part of the targeting process. The targeting cell in a modern air campaign includes a lawyer who reviews the target list and advises on the legality of the strike, and the lawyer is there because the precision weapon has made the law relevant in a way it was not before. The lawyer is also there because the precision weapon has made the law enforceable, because a strike that kills civilians can be investigated and the investigators can find out what happened, and the finding can be embarrassing.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the image of war, because the precision weapon is a weapon that can be photographed. The footage of a precision strike is a small explosion and a puff of smoke, and it can be broadcast without offending the sensibilities of viewers. The footage of area bombing is a city on fire, and it offends. The precision weapon therefore made war more presentable, and presentability was a form of power, because a war that can be presented is a war that can be sustained. Presentability was also a form of deception, because the footage of a precision strike does not show the civilians killed by the strike, and civilians were often killed. The precision weapon did not eliminate the horror of war; it hid the horror behind a camera and a screen, and the hiding was a new kind of horror.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the relationship between the soldier and the enemy, because the soldier who fires a precision weapon may never see the enemy. The pilot who drops a laser-guided bomb from thirty thousand feet sees a target on a screen, and the target is a building or a vehicle or a person, and the person is a dot on a screen. The distance between soldier and enemy had been growing since the invention of the firearm, and the precision weapon was its culmination, because it allowed the soldier to kill without seeing and without being seen. The distance was a form of protection, and also a form of alienation, and the alienation was a theme of the literature and psychology of the wars of the twenty-first century. The drone pilot who kills a man in Yemen from a trailer in Nevada is a man who has killed and has not been to a funeral, and the psychology of that man was a subject of study and concern.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the weak, because the weak learned to use the precision weapon against the strong. The Hezbollah rocket attacks on Israel in 2006 demonstrated that a non-state actor could use rockets to disrupt the life of a modern state, and though the rockets were not precision weapons, they were a form of strategic precision because they were aimed where disruption would be greatest. The Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in the 2010s and 2020s demonstrated that a non-state actor could use precision weapons to strike at the heart of a wealthy state, and the attacks on the Saudi oil facilities at Abqaiq and Khurais in 2019 demonstrated that a precision strike could knock out half the oil production of a major exporter. The Abqaiq attack was carried out with cruise missiles and drones, and the missiles and drones were precision weapons, and the precision was the point, because the attackers wanted to hit the processing facilities and not the surrounding town. The attack was a strategic success, and a demonstration that the precision revolution had armed the weak as well as the strong.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the strong, because the strong learned that precision weapons could be used to coerce without invading. The air campaign against Serbia in 1999 was a coercion campaign, and it worked; the air campaign against Libya in 2011 was a coercion campaign, and it worked; the air campaign against the Islamic State in 2014–2019 was a coercion campaign, and it worked—but the coercion was always limited by the fact that the enemy could absorb punishment and continue to fight. The precision weapon was a weapon of punishment, and punishment works only if the enemy values what is being punished, and the enemies of the twenty-first century often did not. The Islamic State did not value its oil facilities, or its command centers, or its leaders, in the way a state values its infrastructure, and the precision weapon was therefore less effective against the Islamic State than against Serbia. The precision weapon was a weapon for a war of states, and the wars of the twenty-first century were wars of states against non-states, and the weapon was not always suited to the war.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the defense, because the defense learned to use precision weapons to intercept the offense. Missile defense was a precision weapon aimed at a precision weapon, and it could change the balance of power between offense and defense. The American missile defense system in Europe, the Aegis Ashore system in Romania and Poland, could intercept Iranian missiles aimed at Europe, and also Russian missiles aimed at Europe, and the Russians objected because they believed it was aimed at them. The objection was a source of tension, and the tension demonstrated that a defensive weapon can be as provocative as an offensive one. The precision revolution had made the defense as important as the offense, and the balance between the two was constantly shifting.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the offense, because the offense learned to use precision weapons to destroy the defense. The suppression of enemy air defenses, the SEAD campaign, used precision weapons to destroy radar and missile launchers, and had to be won before the air campaign could begin. The SEAD campaign was a campaign of the first day, and the first day was the day that decided the war, and the precision weapon was the weapon of the first day. It was also a campaign the defense could win, because the defense could use decoys and mobility and passive sensors to survive, and the survival of the defense could deny the offense the use of the air. The SEAD campaign was a duel between the precision weapon and the precision defense, fought in the electromagnetic spectrum as much as in the air.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the sea, because the precision weapon made the surface ship vulnerable in a way it had not been since the Second World War. The anti-ship missile could be fired from a small boat or a shore battery or an aircraft, could hit a ship at a range of hundreds of miles, and the ship could not defend itself against a missile faster than the ship and smarter than the ship. The sinking of the Israeli corvette Hanit by a Hezbollah anti-ship missile in 2006 demonstrated that a non-state actor could damage a modern warship, and the sinking was a shock to the navies of the world. The anti-ship missile made the sea a contested space, and the contest was one the navies of the world had to win if they were to project power. It also made the aircraft carrier vulnerable, and the vulnerability of the carrier was what the Chinese DF-21D was designed to exploit. The carrier was the symbol of American power, and the carrier was a target, and the target was one the precision weapon could hit.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the land, because the precision weapon made the tank vulnerable in a way it had not been since the Second World War. The anti-tank guided missile could be carried by a single soldier, could hit a tank at a range of two miles, and the tank could not defend itself against a missile faster than the tank and smarter than the tank. The Javelin missile was a fire-and-forget weapon that used an infrared seeker to home on the heat of a tank, and it was used in Iraq and Afghanistan and Syria, and it made the tank a liability as well as an asset. The tank was a weapon of the offensive, and the anti-tank missile was a weapon of the defensive, and the defensive could stop the offensive. The anti-tank missile changed the balance of power between offense and defense on land, and the change was one the armies of the world had to adapt to.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the air, because the precision weapon made the aircraft vulnerable in a way it had not been since the Second World War. The surface-to-air missile could hit an aircraft at a range of dozens of miles, guided by radar or infrared or a combination of both, and it made the air a contested space. The air-defense missile was a weapon the offense had to suppress, and the suppression required precision weapons, and the precision weapons were the weapons the air-defense missile was designed to shoot down. The air-defense missile made the air campaign expensive, and the expense was one the offense had to bear, and the bearing of the expense was one the offense could not always afford.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of space, because the precision weapon depended on satellites for navigation and communication and intelligence, and the satellites were vulnerable to attack. The anti-satellite weapon was a precision weapon aimed at a satellite, and it was tested by China in 2007 and by the United States in 2008, demonstrations that space was a contested domain. The contest in space was one the precision weapon had made necessary, because the precision weapon could not function without the satellite, and the satellite was a target. The precision revolution had made space a theater of war, and the theater was one the international community had tried to keep peaceful, and the trying had failed.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the electromagnetic spectrum, because the precision weapon depended on the spectrum for guidance and communication, and the spectrum was vulnerable to jamming and spoofing. Electronic warfare was a form of precision warfare, because the jammer could blind the precision weapon, and the blinding was a form of attack cheaper than the precision weapon. Russian electronic warfare in Ukraine in 2014 and 2022 demonstrated that a sophisticated electronic-warfare capability could degrade the precision weapon, and the degradation was one the offense had to overcome. The precision revolution had made the spectrum a battlefield, and the battlefield was one the offense and the defense both had to win.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the cyber domain, because the precision weapon depended on networks for command and control, and the networks were vulnerable to cyber attack. Cyber attack was a form of precision warfare, because it could disable a network without destroying it, and the disabling was a form of attack cheaper than the precision weapon. The cyber attacks on the Ukrainian power grid in 2015 and 2016 demonstrated that a cyber attack could disrupt a society, and the disruption was one the precision weapon could not achieve. The precision revolution had made the cyber domain a battlefield, and the battlefield was one the offense and the defense both had to win.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the information domain, because the precision weapon depended on information for targeting, and the information was vulnerable to manipulation. Information warfare was a form of precision warfare, because it could make the precision weapon hit the wrong target, and the wrong target was one the information warrior had chosen. Russian information warfare in Ukraine in 2014 and 2022 demonstrated that a sophisticated information-warfare capability could confuse the enemy, and the confusion was one the precision weapon could not overcome. The precision revolution had made the information domain a battlefield, and the battlefield was one the offense and the defense both had to win.

The precision revolution was also a revolution in the strategy of the economic domain, because the precision weapon depended on industry for production, and the industry was vulnerable to attack. Economic warfare was a form of precision warfare, because it could deny the enemy the means to produce precision weapons, and the denial was one the precision weapon could not achieve. The sanctions on Russia after 2014 and 2022 were a demonstration that economic warfare could degrade a military,
