The Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020 made the drone visible, and the visibility was the product of the drones themselves. The war lasted forty-four days; Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses, and the use was the use the Royal United Services Institute studied in 2021, treating the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense. The landmark was the landmark of the drone, and the drone was the weapon the study said would shape the future of strike and defense. The study was right, and the rightness was the rightness of the pattern, and the pattern was the pattern of the weapon shaping the war. The drone had shaped the war in Nagorno-Karabakh, the shaping was what the history had predicted, and the prediction was the prediction of increasing distance, increasing ease, and increasing spread.

The spread was the spread of the drone to the non-state actor and the small state, and the spread was the spread of the precision the strong had once monopolized. The strong had monopolized precision because precision was expensive, and expense was the barrier, and the barrier was what the cheap drone had removed. The cheap drone was the precision weapon of the poor, and the poor used it, and the use was what the strong had feared, and the fear was the fear of losing the advantage. The advantage had been the advantage of the strong, and the loss of the advantage was the loss of what had made the strong strong, and the loss was what the history had been building toward. The history had been the history of advantage, and advantage had been the advantage of the weapon, and the weapon had been the weapon of the strong, and the strong had been strong because of the weapon. The drone had broken the chain, and the breaking was the breaking of the history, and the breaking was the new thing.

The new thing was not the end of the history. It was the next phase—the phase in which the weapon was everywhere, the advantage was temporary, and the advantage was contested. The contest was the contest of the drone against the drone, of precision against precision, and it was a contest the strong would have to win without the monopoly that had made the strong strong. The strong would

chapters.title: Part 55
chapters.preview: The state’s monopoly on violence rests on controlling the technologies of force, and each major weapons revolution has redistributed that control. Bronze casting around 3000 BCE concentrated arms in palace work
paragraphs: The state’s monopoly on violence rests on controlling the technologies of force, and each major weapons revolution has redistributed that control. Bronze casting around 3000 BCE concentrated arms in palace workshops and made chariot-owning elites dominant; gunpowder, perfected in Song China by the eleventh century and fielded in European siege trains by the 1450s, let rulers level castles and fund standing armies; the rifled musket, mass-produced at the Enfield and Springfield armories by the 1850s, multiplied the killing power of ordinary infantry. Cheap commercial drones are the next rupture: a DJI Mavic 3, retailing near $2,000, gave Ukrainian platoon commanders in 2022–2023 precision observation and strike once reserved for states, and Houthi forces have used low-cost UAVs against Saudi and Emirati targets since 2019. When non-state actors can buy precision for the price of a used car, the strong must learn to fight without the monopoly—the hardest learning they have ever done, because the monopoly was their foundation.

chapters.title: Part 56
chapters.preview: The weakness of the many had a texture, and that texture was the texture of the weapon—the weapon the few had made, and the making of it was the making of the many into the weak.
paragraphs: The weakness of the many had a texture, and that texture was the texture of the weapon—the weapon the few had made, and the making of it was the making of the many into the weak.

Consider the pike. For more than two centuries it was queen of the battlefield: a length of ashwood eighteen feet long tipped with a steel head. It was cheap and simple. It required no training a village could not supply, no powder a treasury could not afford, no armorer a smith could not become. Yet the pike made the many into a formation, the formation made them into a weapon, and the weapon made them into a power the few had never faced.

The Swiss made the pike into an art. In the fourteenth century the cantons—poor, mountainous, pressed between Habsburgs, Burgundians, and French—discovered that men on foot with pikes could break the charge of knights. The discovery was not of the pike but of the discipline it demanded—a discipline of the many, and the many were the men of the cantons, who had no horses, no armor, no castles, and no lords to protect them. So they made themselves into a weapon, and the weapon was the pike, and the pike was the weapon of the many.

At Morgarten in 1315 the Swiss ambushed Duke Leopold of Austria's army in a mountain pass. The knights could not deploy their horses on the narrow ground; the Swiss rolled stones down the slopes and struck with halberds and pikes; the Austrian column was destroyed—the few destroyed by the many. At Sempach in 1386 the Swiss met the Austrian knights in the open field. The knights dismounted, since the soft ground would not let the horses charge; the Swiss pikes held the line; the Austrian duke was killed. It was a battle of the many against the few, and the many won. At Nancy in 1477 the Swiss pikes broke the army of Charles the Bold of Burgundy. Charles was killed, the Burgundian state collapsed, and a great power fell before the pikes of the many.

The pike was not a new weapon. It had been known since the Greek phalanx; the Macedonians had carried the sarissa, twenty-one feet long. The phalanx was a formation of the many and the weapon of the many, and the Roman legion defeated it—but the legion too was a formation of the many, and a weapon of the many.

Yet the Swiss pike was not the Greek phalanx. The Swiss formation could move. The many moved in step, and the step was the step of drum and fife—instruments of the many, and therefore instruments of the weapon.
The Swiss fought in squares three hundred men on a side, hollow, filled with halberdiers and crossbowmen. The crossbowmen trained at the butts on Sunday—the training of the many, men of the cantons.

The pike square was a machine for turning men into a wall of points eighteen feet long. The first five ranks leveled their pikes: the first rank's reached the ground, the second a horse's knees, the third a horse's chest, the fourth and fifth the rider. A horse will not charge a wall of points—not because it is a fool, but because it knows the points, and the points were the points of the many.

A pike cost perhaps a shilling, a halberd perhaps two; a knight's armor cost a village's income for a year, his horse two years'. The knight was the few, of horse and armor; the many were the many of pike and halberd. The many could buy a thousand pikes for the price of one knight, and the thousand pikes could kill the one knight—the killing of the few by the many.

The pike was a weapon of the commune—of burghers and peasants, free men of towns and valleys who had made themselves free by making themselves into a weapon. The pike was the weapon of the free, and the free were the many.

The few saw the pike and were afraid. Their fear was fear of the weapon, and fear of the weapon was fear of the many. So the few sought a weapon to answer the pike, and the weapon that answered it was the firearm—the weapon the few would make, and the making of it was the making of the many into the weak again.

The firearm was not new. The hand cannon had been known since the fourteenth century: a tube of iron or bronze on a wooden stock, fired by touching a hot wire to a touchhole. It was inaccurate, slow, and dangerous to the man who fired it—a curiosity and a terror, but no match for a pike square. The pike square was the weapon of the many; the hand cannon was the weapon of the few, and the few could not make it break the many.

The matchlock changed the hand cannon into a weapon, and the change was the change of the lock: a mechanism of springs, levers, and a burning cord—the match, a length of hemp soaked in saltpeter and dried, burning at a foot an hour. The match was the heart of the matchlock, and the matchlock was the weapon the few would use to break the many.

The matchlock was fired by pulling a trigger that lowered the burning match into a pan of priming powder. The priming flashed and ignited the main charge through the touchhole; the ball flew at a thousand feet a second and could kill a man at a hundred yards—the range of the matchlock, the range of the weapon, and the weapon was the weapon of the few.

But the matchlock was slow. A trained musketeer could fire perhaps once a minute, in a sequence of a dozen motions—the motions of the manual, and the manual was the manual of the few. The few had written the manual.

The musketeer carried a bandolier of a dozen wooden charges, each holding a measure of powder—the measure of the few, who had fixed it. He carried a flask of priming powder, a bag of bullets, a length of match, and a rest—a pole with a fork at the top to hold the heavy barrel.

The matchlock was a weapon of the state, and the state was the state of the few. It was expensive: powder, lead, armorer, drill—and the drill was the drill of the few, who drilled the many into a weapon.

The pike had been the weapon of the many because it was cheap and simple and required only courage and discipline—the discipline of the commune. The matchlock was the weapon of the few because it was expensive and complex and required powder, lead, a manufactory, a treasury, and a drill only a state could supply.

And so the pike square gave way to the tercio: a formation of pikes and muskets, the muskets the few and the pikes the many. The few stood at the corners of the square and the many in the middle; the few shot and the many held.
The tercio was the formation of the Spanish—the few of the empire. It was a square of three thousand men, of pikes with muskets at the corners.

The tercio fought at Cerignola in 1503, at Ravenna in 1512, at Bicocca in 1522, at Pavia in 1525—where it broke the French and captured the French king—at Mühlberg in 1547, at St. Quentin in 1557, and at Gravelines in 1558.
But the tercio was not the pike square. It was a formation of the few—the few of the state, the few of the musket—while the pike remained the weapon of the many.

The matchlock was the weapon of the state because the state could afford it, and the state that could afford it could tax the many. The matchlock made the state, and the state made the matchlock. It required a treasury, and the treasury a tax, and the tax a bureaucracy, and the bureaucracy a king. It required a manufactory, and the manufactory a guild, and the guild a charter, and the charter a king. It required a drill, and the drill a manual, and the manual a general, and the general a king. It required a powder mill, and the powder mill a water wheel, and the water wheel a stream, and the stream a valley, and the valley a king. It required a lead mine, and the lead mine a shaft, and the shaft a pump, and the pump an engine, and the engine a king. And the king was the few.

So the pike gave way to the musket—the many to the few—but slowly. The pike held the field for two hundred years after the matchlock was invented, because the musket was slow (the slowness of the match), inaccurate (the inaccuracy of the smoothbore), short-ranged (the short range of the ball), and vulnerable (the vulnerability of the reload).

And so pike and musket fought together—the many and the few—in the tercio, and in the Swedish brigade of Gustavus Adolphus, king of Sweden. Gustavus made the musket lighter, faster (through Swedish drill), cheaper, and standard—a weapon that could break the pike, the breaking of the many by the few.

The Swedish brigade was a formation of muskets and pikes, the muskets the few and the pikes the many, but it put the muskets in the front and the pikes in the rear. It was the brigade that broke the pike square.

And the pike square gave way to the line—the line of the musket, the weapon of the few, and the line of the many, and the line of the state, which was the state of the few. The line was both: the many and the few.

The flintlock made the line into a weapon. It struck a flint against a steel frizzen, replacing the slow match with a spark. It was faster, more reliable, and cheaper than the matchlock. It made the musket a weapon every man could carry, fire, and own—a weapon of the many, and of the few, and of the state.
The flintlock musket was the weapon of the line, and the line was the line of the few, and of the many, and of the state.
And the line was

chapters.title: Part 57
chapters.preview: The line broke at the Somme, and the breaking was not a metaphor. On 1 July 1916, along a front of some eighteen miles north of the river, the British Fourth Army sent its battalions forward in waves against Ge
paragraphs: The line broke at the Somme, and the breaking was not a metaphor. On 1 July 1916, along a front of some eighteen miles north of the river, the British Fourth Army sent its battalions forward in waves against German positions that had been bombarded for a week. The bombardment was meant to destroy the wire, the trenches, and the men who held them. It did not. The shells were numerous—more than a million and a half in the preparatory barrage—but a large proportion were shrapnel, which burst in the air and did little to cut the deep belts of barbed wire, and many were duds, and the German defenders had gone deep into dugouts cut thirty feet into the chalk, where they waited through the noise and came up when it stopped. When the whistles blew and the men climbed out, they walked into machine-gun fire sighted on the gaps in the wire. By the end of the day the British had suffered 57,470 casualties, of whom 19,240 were dead. It was the worst day in the history of the British Army, produced by the collision of two systems: a mass army trained to advance in extended lines, and a defensive apparatus built around the machine gun, the quick-firing field gun, and the trench.

The Somme is usually told as a story of futility, and there is truth in that telling, but the truth is more specific and more useful. The first day was not a failure of courage or of numbers. It was a failure of a particular theory of the offensive—that artillery could suppress a defense sufficiently to let infantry cross the open ground between the lines—against a particular theory of the defense developed precisely to defeat it. The weapons on both sides had changed, and the tactics had not changed with them. The machine gun was not new in 1916. Hiram Maxim had demonstrated his recoil-operated gun in 1884, and the British Army had adopted a .303-caliber version in 1891. What was new was the number of them, and the way they were used. A single Maxim could fire six hundred rounds a minute, and a well-sited pair could cover several hundred yards with interlocking fire. Against a line of men walking forward at a steady pace, the mathematics were not ambiguous. The men who designed the German defenses understood this. They sited their guns in depth, on reverse slopes, in concrete emplacements, so that the guns that survived the bombardment could cover the ground the bombardment had not.

The Somme was also a story about shells. The British artillery fired more shells in the week before 1 July than the British Army had fired in the entire first year of the war, and it was still not enough. The demand for shells had outrun the capacity to produce them, and the capacity to produce them had outrun the capacity to produce the machine tools, chemical plants, and skilled labor that made the shells. The result was a crisis—the Shell Crisis of 1915, which toppled the government of H. H. Asquith and brought David Lloyd George to the Ministry of Munitions—that revealed something the prewar planners had not fully grasped: that industrial war was a problem of production as much as of tactics. The weapon that mattered most in 1916 was not the rifle or the machine gun or the field gun. It was the factory. The nation that could produce the most shells, guns, explosives, steel, and men trained to use them would win the war of attrition, and the war of attrition was the war the Western Front had become.

The French 75 is the emblem of this transformation. The Canon de 75 modèle 1897 was not the first quick-firing field gun, but it was the first to solve the problem of recoil in a way that allowed the gun to stay on target between shots. Earlier field guns had to be re-laid after every round, because the recoil pushed the carriage back. The 75 used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system—a cylinder of oil and a cylinder of compressed air—that absorbed the recoil and returned the barrel to its firing position, so that the gun could fire as fast as the crew could load it. The rated rate of fire was fifteen rounds a minute, and in the hands of a well-drilled crew it could be higher. The 75 was light, mobile, and accurate, and it was the finest field gun in the world when the war began. It was also, by 1916, insufficient. The 75 was a flat-trajectory gun designed for direct fire against targets in the open, and trench war demanded high-angle fire against targets that were dug in. The French, the British, and the Germans all developed howitzers and mortars to fill the gap, and the artillery park of every army grew into a hierarchy of calibers, from the light field gun to the heavy howitzer to the railway-mounted siege gun that could throw a shell weighing a ton more than twenty miles.

The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916, was the purest expression of this logic. The German plan, devised by Erich von Falkenhayn, was not to take ground but to bleed the French army white. The Germans would attack a position the French could not afford to lose, and they would use their artillery to destroy the French reserves as they were fed into the battle. The French, under Philippe Pétain, adopted the slogan *On ne passe pas*—they shall not pass—and fed their army into the meat grinder because the alternative was to admit that the war could not be won. The battle produced roughly 700,000 casualties on both sides, and the ground that changed hands was measured in yards. The artillery fired more than twenty million shells. The battlefield was a moonscape of craters, shattered trees, and bodies that could not be buried because the ground was under fire. Verdun was not a battle in the old sense of a decisive engagement. It was a process, an industrial process for converting men and material into casualties, conducted with the same logic that governed a factory: inputs, throughput, output. The output was death.

The response to the machine gun and the trench was not a single weapon but a system of weapons, and the system took years to develop. The first response was the tank. The tank was conceived as a machine that could cross the wire and the trenches and survive machine-gun fire, and it was developed in Britain under the cover name "water carriers for Mesopotamia"—hence "tank." The first tanks went into action on 15 September 1916 at Flers-Courcelette, during the Somme offensive. There were forty-nine of them, and most broke down or got stuck, but the ones that worked did what they were designed to do: they crossed the wire, they crossed the trenches, and they frightened the German infantry. The tank was slow, unreliable, and mechanically fragile, and it would not become a decisive weapon until the 1930s, but it was the first machine designed to solve the specific tactical problem of the Western Front, and it pointed toward the future.

The second response was the infiltration tactic. The Germans developed it first, in the form of the *Stosstruppen*—storm troops—trained to bypass strong points and penetrate deep into the enemy's rear, leaving the strong points to be reduced by the following waves. The tactic was based on the recognition that the machine gun made frontal assault suicidal, and that the way to defeat a defense in depth was to find the gaps and exploit them. The storm troops were armed with light machine guns, flamethrowers, and hand grenades, and they were trained to move fast and to communicate by radio and by runner. The tactic worked, and it was used to devastating effect in the German offensive of March 1918, which broke the British Fifth Army and advanced forty miles in two weeks—the largest movement of the war on the Western Front since 1914. But the offensive outran its supply lines, the Allies counterattacked, and by the summer of 1918 the German army was exhausted. The war ended on 11 November 1918, and the weapons developed to fight it—the tank, the airplane, the submarine, the machine gun, the quick-firing artillery, the poison gas—would define the next war.

The airplane was the newest of these weapons, and its development during the First World War was astonishingly rapid. In 1914, the airplane was a fragile contrivance of wood and fabric that could carry a pilot, an observer, and a few bombs, and it was used mainly for reconnaissance. By 1918, it was a purpose-built fighting machine that could fly at 130 miles an hour, climb to 20,000 feet, and carry two machine guns and a bomb load. The key technical developments were the synchronization gear, which allowed a machine gun to fire through the propeller arc without shooting off the blades, and the aircraft engine, which went from 80 horsepower to 400 horsepower in four years. The tactical development was equally rapid: the fighter, the bomber, the ground-attack aircraft, and the strategic bombing campaign against cities and factories all emerged during the war. The airplane did not decide the war, but it established a principle that would govern the next century: that control of the air was a precondition for control of the ground.

The submarine was the other new weapon that changed the shape of the war. The German U-boat campaign against Allied shipping was an attempt to starve Britain into submission, and it came close to succeeding. In 1917, German submarines sank more than six million tons of Allied and neutral shipping, and the British Admiralty warned that Britain would run out of food by the end of the year. The response was the convoy system, which grouped merchant ships under the protection of warships, and it worked: the loss rate fell, and the U-boats were forced to attack the escorts, which were themselves armed. The submarine campaign was also the proximate cause of American entry into the war, because the German decision to resume unrestricted submarine warfare—sinking neutral ships without warning—outraged American opinion and led to the declaration of war in April 1917. The submarine had not been able to win the war for Germany, but it had brought the United States into the war against Germany, and that was decisive.

The First World War was the first war in which the weapons of the industrial revolution were deployed in their full maturity, and the result was a transformation in the relationship between the state and the battlefield. The armies of 1914 were mass armies, raised by conscription, equipped with mass-produced weapons, fed by mass-produced food, and moved by mass-produced railways and ships. The war was fought by societies, not by armies, and the distinction between the battlefield and the home front eroded. The bombing of cities, the blockade of ports, the rationing of food, the conscription of labor, the censorship of the press, and the mobilization of science and industry for war all became normal features of the belligerent states. The war also transformed the relationship between the state and the individual: the state demanded the lives of its citizens, and it developed the bureaucratic machinery to organize the demand. The passport, the identity card, the conscription register, the ration book, the propaganda ministry—all were either invented or perfected during the First World War.

The war ended with an armistice, not a surrender, and the peace that followed was unstable. The Treaty of Versailles imposed harsh terms on Germany—territorial losses, military limitations, and reparations—and the terms were resented by the German population and by the German army, which had not been defeated in the field. The treaty also created the League of Nations, intended to prevent future wars, but the League had no enforcement mechanism and the United States did not join. The interwar period was a period of rearmament and experimentation, and the weapons that would be used in the Second World War were developed during it. The tank became faster and more reliable, and the doctrine of armored warfare was developed by theorists such as J. F. C. Fuller and Basil Liddell Hart in Britain and Heinz Guderian in Germany. The airplane became faster and more powerful, and the doctrine of strategic bombing was developed by theorists such as Giulio Douhet in Italy and Hugh Trenchard in Britain. The aircraft carrier was developed by the United States and Japan, and the doctrine of carrier warfare was developed by the navies of both countries. The submarine became more capable, and the doctrine of unrestricted submarine warfare was refined.

The Second World War was the war in which these weapons were used in their full maturity, and the result was a transformation in the scale of destruction. The war began on 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, and it ended on 2 September 1945, when Japan surrendered on the deck of the USS *Missouri* in Tokyo Bay. It was fought on every continent and every ocean, and it involved every major power in the world. The death toll was between seventy and eighty-five million people, the majority of them civilians. The weapons that caused the most deaths were not the new weapons—the tank, the airplane, the submarine—but the old: the rifle, the machine gun, the artillery, and the bomb. The strategic bombing campaign against Germany and Japan killed hundreds of thousands of civilians, and the firebombing of Tokyo in March 1945 killed more people in a single night than the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima five months later. The war was a war of production as much as of tactics, and the Allies won because they out-produced the Axis. The United States produced more than 300,000 aircraft, more than 100,000 tanks, and more than 40 billion rounds of small-arms ammunition during the war. The Soviet Union produced more than 100,000 tanks and self-propelled guns. The German war economy was not fully mobilized until 1944, and by then it was too late.

The weapon that ended the war was the atomic bomb, and its development was the most significant scientific and industrial project of the war. The Manhattan Project employed more than 130,000 people and cost about two billion dollars, and it produced three bombs: a uranium gun-type device called "Little Boy," a plutonium implosion device called "Fat Man," and a plutonium implosion device called "Gadget" that was tested at Trinity, New Mexico, on 16 July 1945. The Trinity test produced a yield of about 21 kilotons, and it was the first nuclear detonation in history. The bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, and it killed between 100,000 and 200,000 people, most of them civilians. The bomb was the culmination of a process that had begun with the discovery of nuclear fission in 1938, and it opened a new era in the history of weapons. The atomic bomb was not a bigger bomb; it was a different kind of bomb. It derived its energy from the nucleus of the atom, and the energy released was millions of times greater than that of a chemical explosive. It was also a weapon that could not be used without threatening the existence of the state that used it, because the other side could build the same weapon and use it in return. The result was the doctrine of deterrence, which governed the strategic relationship between the United States and the Soviet Union for the next half century.

The atomic bomb was followed by the hydrogen bomb, tested by the United States in 1952 and by the Soviet Union in 1953. The hydrogen bomb used nuclear fusion rather than fission, and it was hundreds of times more powerful than the atomic bomb. Its development was followed by the intercontinental ballistic missile, which could deliver a nuclear warhead to the other side of the world in thirty minutes. The result was the doctrine of mutual assured destruction, which held that the only way to prevent a nuclear war was to make its consequences unacceptable to both sides. The doctrine was stable in that it prevented a nuclear war, but unstable in that it depended on the willingness of both sides to maintain a force that could survive a first strike and retaliate. The result was an arms race that consumed enormous resources and produced weapons that could destroy civilization many times over.

The nuclear arms race was accompanied by the development of conventional weapons that were increasingly precise and increasingly lethal. The precision-guided munition was developed during the Vietnam War, when the United States began using laser-guided bombs to attack bridges and other high-value targets that had resisted conventional bombing. The laser-guided bomb had a seeker that homed on a laser spot designated by a ground or air observer, and it could hit a target with a circular error probable of a few meters. The precision-guided munition was used in the Gulf War of 1991, when coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs, of which about 6,520 tons were precision-guided—roughly 7.4 percent. The percentage was small, but the effect was large: the precision-guided bombs struck high-value targets—command bunkers, bridges, power plants, air-defense sites—with an accuracy that had not been possible before, and they reshaped public and military expectations of air power. The Gulf War was also the first war in which stealth aircraft were used, and the first in which the global positioning system was used to navigate and to guide weapons.

The development of precision-guided munitions was part of a broader transformation in the nature of war that began in the 1970s and accelerated in the 1980s and 1990s. The transformation was driven by the microprocessor and the technologies that depended on it: the computer, the satellite, the data link, the sensor, and the guided weapon. The result was what military theorists called the "revolution in military affairs"—a transformation in the way wars were fought as profound as the one produced by the machine gun and the quick-firing field gun in the First World War. The revolution was based on the idea that information was the key to victory, and that the side that could collect, process, and act on information faster than the other side would win. The result was a new kind of warfare characterized by precision, by speed, and by the integration of sensors and shooters into a single network.

The revolution in military affairs was on display in the Gulf War of 1991, in the Kosovo War of 1999, and in the invasion of Iraq in 2003. In each, the United States and its allies used precision-guided munitions, stealth aircraft, and networked command and control to defeat an opponent that was numerically superior in some categories but technologically inferior. The result was a series of lopsided victories that seemed to confirm the theory that information technology had transformed the nature of war. But the theory was incomplete, because it did not account for the fact that the enemies of the United States and its allies were not trying to fight the same kind of war. They were fighting an asymmetric war, using improvised explosive devices, suicide bombers, and small arms to attack the forces that were trying to occupy their countries. The result was a series of long, inconclusive wars in Iraq and Afghanistan that cost the United States and its allies thousands of lives and trillions of dollars, and that ended without a clear victory.

The asymmetric war was a reminder that the history of weapons is not a history of progress in a simple sense. The most advanced weapons in the world were not able to defeat an enemy armed with rifles and bombs made from fertilizer and cell phones. The reason was that the advanced weapons were designed to fight a different kind of war—a war between states, fought by armies, with clear front lines and identifiable targets. The asymmetric war had no front lines and no identifiable targets, and the advanced weapons were often useless or counterproductive. The result was a rethinking of the relationship between weapons and strategy, and a recognition that the most important weapon in an asymmetric war was not a bomb or a missile but a soldier on the ground, working with local people, gathering intelligence, and building trust.

The rethinking was interrupted by the return of great-power competition, which began in the 2010s and accelerated in the 2020s. It was driven by the rise of China and the resurgence of Russia, and it was accompanied by the development of new weapons designed to fight a war between states. These included hypersonic missiles, which could fly at more than five times the speed of sound and maneuver in flight, making them difficult to intercept; directed-energy weapons, which used lasers and microwaves to destroy targets; and autonomous weapons, which could select and engage targets without human intervention. They also included cyber weapons, which could attack the computer systems that controlled the other side's weapons and infrastructure, and space weapons, which could attack the satellites the other side depended on for navigation and communication.

The most important of these new weapons, in terms of its effect on the battlefield, was the armed drone. The drone was not new in the 2020s—the United States had used armed drones to attack targets in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia since the early 2000s—but it became a weapon of mass effect in the 2020s, when it was used in large numbers by state and non-state actors in conflicts in Libya, Syria, Nagorno-Karabakh, and Ukraine. The drone was cheap, easy to operate, and hard to detect, and it could be used for reconnaissance, for strike, and for electronic warfare. It also changed the relationship between the operator and the battlefield, because the operator could be thousands of miles from the target, and the decision to kill could be made by someone who was not in danger of being killed.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020 was the landmark. The war was fought between Azerbaijan and Armenia over the disputed territory of Nagorno-Karabakh, and it lasted forty-four days. Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions—weapons that loiter over the battlefield and attack targets when they are found—against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses. The drones were effective: they destroyed hundreds of Armenian tanks and artillery pieces and suppressed the Armenian air-defense system, which was equipped with Soviet-era systems not designed to detect and track small, slow-flying drones. The result was a decisive Azerbaijani victory, and a demonstration that a relatively small, relatively cheap weapon could defeat a larger, more expensive force. The RUSI study of the conflict, published in 2021, treated it as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense, and argued that the conflict had lessons for the future of strike and defense.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war was followed by the war in Ukraine, which began with the Russian invasion of 24 February 2022 and became the largest war in Europe since the Second World War. The war in Ukraine was a war of drones, and also a war of artillery, tanks, infantry, and trenches. It combined the weapons of the twenty-first century with the tactics of the twentieth, and it demonstrated that the revolution in military affairs had not made the old weapons obsolete. The drones were used for reconnaissance and for strike, and they were used in large numbers—Ukraine and Russia both used thousands, many of them commercial quadcopters adapted for military use. They were also used for artillery spotting, which made the artillery more lethal, and for electronic warfare, which made the drones less effective. The result was a war characterized by a constant competition between the drone and the counter-drone, and by a constant adaptation of tactics and technology.

The war in Ukraine also demonstrated the importance of the industrial base. The war consumed enormous quantities of ammunition, and the Western countries that supported Ukraine found that their production capacity was insufficient to meet the demand. The result was a rethinking of the relationship between the military and the industrial base, and a recognition that the ability to produce weapons and ammunition in large quantities was as important as the ability to design them. The war was a reminder that the history of weapons is not only a history of technology but also a history of production, and that the side that can produce the most weapons and ammunition will often win, even if its weapons are not the most advanced.

The war in Ukraine was also a reminder that the history of weapons is a history of adaptation. The weapons used in the war were not the weapons designed for it. The drones were commercial quadcopters adapted for military use. The anti-tank missiles were designed to destroy tanks, but they were also used to destroy buildings and bunkers. The artillery was designed for a war of movement, but it was used in a war of position. The result was a war fought with a mixture of old and new weapons, and characterized by a constant process of improvisation and adaptation.

The history of weapons is also a history of arms control. The development of the atomic bomb was followed by the nuclear non-proliferation regime, intended to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons to other states. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty was opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, and it has 191 states parties. India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined the treaty, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The treaty was based on a bargain: the states that had nuclear weapons would agree to negotiate in good faith toward disarmament, and the states that did not would agree not to acquire them, in exchange for access to peaceful nuclear technology. The bargain was imperfect—the nuclear-weapon states did not disarm, and some non-nuclear-weapon states acquired nuclear weapons anyway—but the treaty slowed the spread of nuclear weapons and established a norm against nuclear proliferation that has held for more than half a century.

The arms-control regime was extended to other weapons. The Chemical Weapons Convention, which entered into force in 1997, banned the production, stockpiling, and use of chemical weapons, and it was ratified by 193 states. The Biological Weapons Convention, which entered into force in 1975, banned the development, production, and stockpiling of biological weapons, but it did not have a verification mechanism. The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which entered into force in 1983, regulated the use of weapons considered excessively injurious or indiscriminate, such as landmines, booby traps, and incendiary weapons. The Ottawa Treaty, which entered into force in 1999, banned anti-personnel landmines, and it was ratified by 164 states, but not by the United States, Russia, China, India, or Pakistan. The Cluster Munitions Convention, which entered into force in 2010, banned cluster munitions, and it was ratified by 123 states, but not by the United States, Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Israel, or Ukraine.

The arms-control regime was also extended to autonomous weapons. The debate over autonomous weapons began in the 2010s, when the development of drones and of artificial intelligence made it possible to imagine a weapon that could select and engage targets without human intervention. The debate was conducted in the United Nations Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which established a Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems in 2016. The group met regularly but did not reach a consensus on whether to ban autonomous weapons, and the debate continued into the 2020s. It was complicated by the fact that the definition of autonomy was contested, and by the fact that the technology was developing faster than the diplomacy. The result was a gap between the development of the technology and the development of the rules supposed to govern it.

The debate over autonomous weapons was also complicated by a contested allegation. In 2021, a UN Panel of Experts report on Libya stated that a Kargu-2 loitering munition "may have been" used in autonomous mode against retreating forces. The report was based on information that was not independently verified, and the claim was contested by the manufacturer and by other experts. The report did not claim that the weapon had definitely been used in autonomous mode; it said that it "may have been" used in that mode, and it called for further investigation. The claim was important because it was the first time a UN body had suggested that an autonomous weapon might have been used in combat, and it was used by both sides of the debate to support their positions. But the claim was not confirmed, and it should be treated with caution. The history of autonomous weapons is still being written, and the Kargu-2 allegation is a contested episode in that history, not a confirmed fact.

The history of weapons is also a history of the relationship between weapons and the state. The state has always been the most important producer and user of weapons, and the development of weapons has always been shaped by the state's need to defend itself and to project power. The state has also been the most important regulator of weapons, and the development of weapons has always been shaped by the state's need to control the means of violence. The result is a complex relationship in which the state is both the driver and the regulator of weapons development, and in which that development is shaped by the state's need to balance the demands of security against the demands of legitimacy.

The relationship between weapons and the state was transformed by the industrial revolution, which made it possible for the state to produce weapons in large quantities and to equip mass armies. The result was the mass army, the defining institution of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The mass army was based on conscription, which made every male citizen a potential soldier, and on mass production, which made it possible to equip the mass army with standardized weapons. The result was a transformation in the relationship between the state and the citizen: the citizen was no longer a subject who was protected by the state but a soldier who was called on to defend the state, and the state was no longer a distant authority but an institution that reached into every household to demand the lives of its sons.

The mass army was transformed by the development of nuclear weapons, which made it possible to destroy a state without defeating its army. The result was a shift in the basis of military power from the mass army to the nuclear arsenal, and a shift in the relationship between the state and the citizen from the citizen as soldier to the citizen as hostage. The nuclear weapon was a weapon that could not be used without destroying the state that used it, and the result was a strategic relationship based on the threat of mutual destruction rather than on the actual use of force. The result was a paradox: the most powerful weapons ever developed were weapons that could not be used, and the states that possessed them were forced to rely on the threat of use rather than on use itself.

The paradox was resolved, in part, by the development of conventional weapons precise and lethal enough to be used in limited wars. The precision-guided munition was a weapon that could be used without escalating to nuclear war, and it was used in the Gulf War, in Kosovo, in Afghanistan, and in Iraq. The result was a new kind of war characterized by precision and by discrimination, and by a new kind of relationship between the state and the citizen: the citizen was no longer a soldier or a hostage but a taxpayer who paid for the weapons and a spectator who watched the war on television. The result was a war fought by professionals and watched by civilians, and characterized by a gap between the experience of the soldiers and the experience of the citizens.

The gap was closed, in part, by the development of drones, which made it possible for the citizen to be both a soldier and a spectator. The drone operator was a soldier who was not in danger of being killed, and the citizen who watched the drone footage on television was a spectator who was not in danger of being killed either. The result was a war fought by remote control, and characterized by a new kind of relationship between the state and the citizen: the citizen was no longer a soldier or a hostage or a taxpayer or a spectator but a participant in a war fought on a screen. The result was a war characterized by a new kind of distance, a new kind of intimacy, and a new kind of moral ambiguity.

The moral ambiguity was the subject of the debate over autonomous weapons. The debate was based on the recognition that the development of weapons that could select and engage targets without human intervention raised fundamental questions about the relationship between humans and machines, and about the responsibility for the use of force. It was also based on the recognition that the development of autonomous weapons was inevitable, and that the question was not whether they would be developed but how they would be regulated. The result was a debate characterized by a tension between the desire to ban autonomous weapons and the desire to regulate them, and by a tension between the desire to preserve human control over the use of force and the desire to develop weapons faster and more precise than humans.

The tension was also present in the debate over the use of artificial intelligence in war. The development of artificial intelligence made it possible to process enormous quantities of data and to make decisions faster than humans, and the result was a new kind of warfare characterized by speed and by complexity. The result was also a new kind of risk: the risk that the machines would make mistakes that humans would not make, and the risk that they would be hacked or manipulated by the other side. The result was a debate over the role of humans in the decision to use force, and over the extent to which the machines should be allowed to make decisions on their own.

The debate over artificial intelligence was part of a broader transformation in the nature of war driven by the development of information technology. The transformation was characterized by the integration of sensors and shooters into a single network, by the use of data to make decisions, and by the use of algorithms to process the data. The result was a new kind of warfare that its proponents called "network-centric warfare," and that its opponents criticized as a form of warfare based on the illusion of control. The critics argued that the network was vulnerable to attack, that the data was often wrong, and that the algorithms were often biased. The result was a debate over the extent to which information technology had transformed the nature of war, and over the extent to which the old weapons and the old tactics still mattered.

The debate was resolved, in part, by the war in Ukraine, which demonstrated that the old weapons and the old tactics still mattered, and that the new weapons and the new tactics were not a substitute for them. The war was fought with artillery and tanks and trenches, and it was also fought with drones and precision-guided munitions and cyber weapons. The result was a war characterized by a mixture of old and new, and by a constant process of adaptation. The result was also a reminder that the history of weapons is not a history of progress in a simple sense, but a history of adaptation, in which the old and the new coexist, and in which the outcome of a war is determined by the ability of the combatants to adapt to the conditions of the battlefield.

The history of weapons is also a history of the relationship between weapons and society. The development of weapons has always been shaped by the society that produced them, and the development of weapons has always shaped the society that produced them. The result is a complex relationship in which weapons are both a product of society and a producer of society, and in which the development of weapons is shaped by the values of the society and the values of the society are shaped by the weapons. The result is a history that is not only a history of technology but also a history of culture, and a history of the ideas that people have about war and about the weapons used to fight it.

The relationship between weapons and society was transformed by the development of the mass army, which made every citizen a soldier and every soldier a citizen. The result was a transformation in the relationship between the individual and the state, and a transformation in the relationship between the individual and the community. The result was also a transformation in the relationship between the individual and death: the individual was no longer a person who died in his own time and in his own place but a person who died in the time and place of the state, and the result was a new kind of mortality that was organized and statistical and anonymous.

The relationship between weapons and society was transformed again by the development of nuclear weapons, which made it possible to destroy a society without defeating its army. The result was a transformation in the relationship between the individual and the state: the individual was no longer a soldier who was called on to defend the state but a hostage who was held by the state as a guarantee of its own survival. The result was also a transformation in the relationship between the individual and death: the individual was no longer a person who died in the time and place of the state but a person who could die at any time and in any place, and the result was a new kind of mortality that was universal and instantaneous and anonymous.

The relationship between weapons and society was transformed again by the development of precision-guided munitions, which made it possible to fight a war with fewer casualties and less destruction. The result was a transformation in the relationship between the individual and the state: the individual was no longer a soldier or a hostage but a taxpayer who paid for the weapons and a spectator who watched the war on television. The result was also a transformation in the relationship between the individual and death: the individual was no longer a person who could die at any time and in any place but a person who could watch other people die at any time and in any place, and the result was a new kind of mortality that was distant and mediated and spectacular.

The relationship between weapons and society was transformed again by the development of drones, which made it possible to fight a war without risking the lives of the soldiers who fought it. The result was a transformation in the relationship between the individual and the state: the individual was no longer a soldier or a hostage or a taxpayer or a spectator but a participant in a war fought on a screen. The result was also a transformation in the relationship between the individual and death: the individual was no longer a person who could watch other people die but a person who could cause other people to die without being in danger of dying himself, and the result was a new kind of mortality that was remote and surgical and asymmetrical.
