paragraphs: Ethical questions have changed as weapons have changed. A club raises the question of whether it is just to strike a man who cannot strike back. A crossbow raises the question of whether a peasant should be permitted to kill a knight. Gunpowder raises the question of whether it is honorable to kill at a distance. The machine gun raises the question of whether it is moral to kill so many so quickly. The bomber raises the question of whether it is permissible to kill civilians. The nuclear weapon raises the question of whether it is permissible to kill everyone. And the drone raises the question of whether it is permissible to kill without risk, and whether the absence of risk changes the moral calculus of killing itself. Each new weapon has met a version of the same objection—that it is unfair, dishonorable, disproportionate, inhuman—and each has, in time, been absorbed into the ordinary conduct of war, so that what once seemed monstrous comes to seem merely tactical. The history of weapons is therefore also a history of moral accommodation, of how societies learn to live with the means they have invented.

This is the argument that has run through the preceding fifty-seven parts, and it must now be brought to its conclusion. The central claim is not that weapons determine history—that would be a crude technological determinism the evidence does not support—but that weapons and the societies that make them are locked in a reciprocal relationship in which each shapes the other, and that the shape of that relationship has changed in a way that can be described and dated. For most of human history, the relationship was slow and local: a weapon was invented, it spread, it altered the balance of power between those who had it and those who did not, and then it stabilized, and the societies that used it adapted over generations. The pace was set by the limits of communication and production. A new way of making a spear point or a sword blade might take centuries to diffuse across a continent; a new way of casting a cannon might take decades. But the relationship was always the same in the long run: the weapon changed the war, the war changed the society, and the society changed the weapon.

What has changed in the modern period is the speed and scale of the loop. The industrial revolution compressed the cycle from centuries to decades, the twentieth century compressed it from decades to years, and the twenty-first century has compressed it from years to months. The Manhattan Project took three years to build a weapon that ended a world war and reordered international politics. Precision-guided munitions took roughly two decades to move from experimental prototypes to the dominant mode of American air power. The armed drone took roughly a decade to move from a curiosity to a central instrument of American counterterrorism, and another decade to become a commodity that non-state actors and middle powers could buy off the shelf. Autonomous systems, now under development, promise to compress the loop further still, because the weapon will no longer need a human being in the loop to decide when to fire, and the decision cycle will be measured in milliseconds rather than minutes.

The compression of the loop has a consequence that is easy to state and difficult to absorb: the moral accommodation that once took generations must now take place within a single career, sometimes within a single conflict. The soldiers who fought at Verdun in 1916 had grown up in a world where the machine gun was a novelty and the airplane a toy. By the time they were old men, the world had lived through the bombing of cities, the firebombing of Tokyo, the destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the standoff of mutual assured destruction. The moral framework they had inherited—one in which war was a contest between combatants and civilians were to be spared—had been stretched, broken, and remade, and they had watched it happen. The soldiers who fought in the Gulf War in 1991 had grown up in the shadow of nuclear weapons and trained to fight a war in which precision munitions would let them strike a target without destroying the city around it. By the time they were old, the same precision munitions had become cheap enough for a militia in Yemen to use, and the moral framework had been stretched again.

The point is not that the moral framework has collapsed. It is that the framework has been forced to do more work than any framework can bear, because weapons have changed faster than the language available to describe them. The vocabulary of just war—proportionality, discrimination, military necessity, the distinction between combatant and civilian—was developed for a world of bows and swords and siege engines, and it has been stretched to cover a world of stealth aircraft, cyber weapons, and autonomous drones. The vocabulary has proved remarkably elastic, but elasticity has a limit, and the limit is reached when the weapon makes the distinction between combatant and civilian meaningless, or makes the decision to kill so fast that no human being can deliberate about it, or makes the act of killing so remote that the killer no longer experiences the killing as an act at all.

At that limit, the history of weapons becomes something other than a history of technology. It becomes a history of the human relationship to violence, and of how that relationship has been transformed by the tools human beings have made. The transformation is not new—it has been underway since the first man picked up a stone—but it has reached a point at which it is visible in a single lifetime, and at which the question of what kind of creatures we are becoming is no longer a question for philosophers but for engineers and legislators and soldiers and citizens.

Consider the long arc of the transformation through a single thread: the distance between the killer and the killed. In the beginning, the distance was the length of an arm. A man killed another with a stone or a club or a fist, and the killing was intimate; the killer felt the resistance of the body and heard the breath leave it. The spear extended the distance to a few feet, the arrow to a few dozen yards, the sling further still, the crossbow and longbow to a few hundred yards, gunpowder to a few hundred more, the rifled musket to a thousand yards, the artillery piece to miles, the airplane to hundreds of miles, the intercontinental ballistic missile to thousands, and the drone to the other side of the world while keeping the killer in a chair in a room in Nevada.

At each step, the extension of distance changed the moral experience of killing. The man who killed with a club knew exactly what he had done. The man who killed with an arrow saw the man fall but did not feel the impact. The man who killed with a musket saw the smoke and heard the report and watched the enemy line waver, but did not know which of his shots had found a mark. The artilleryman who fired a shell at a grid coordinate did not see the explosion; the bombardier who dropped a bomb from twenty thousand feet saw only a flash; the drone operator who pressed a button in Nevada saw the explosion on a screen in real time, in high definition, with the sound delayed by the speed of light. The drone operator, in fact, sees more than any killer in history—the target's face, the target's family, the target's last moments—and yet he is thousands of miles away, and the killing is as remote as it has ever been. The drone has, in a sense, reversed the arrow: it has restored the intimacy of the club while preserving the distance of the missile.

This reversal is the source of the moral unease that surrounds the drone, and it is worth examining closely, because the unease is not, as it is sometimes said to be, a matter of squeamishness about new technology. The unease is a mismatch between what the drone operator sees and what the operator can do. The operator sees the target as a person, the way a man with a club sees his victim as a person, but the operator is not in danger the way a man with a club is, and is not subject to the constraints that proximity imposes. The man with a club cannot kill casually, because he is within reach of the man he is killing, and the man he is killing can fight back. The drone operator can kill casually, because he is not within reach, and the man he is killing cannot fight back. The drone has created a category of killing that is intimate and safe at the same time, and that combination is morally novel in a way the history of weapons has not prepared us for.

The military calls this asymmetry a virtue. The whole point of the drone, from the soldier's point of view, is that it allows him to kill the enemy without being killed, and the whole point of every weapon in history has been to allow the soldier to kill the enemy without being killed. The club was an improvement over the fist for the same reason. The spear was an improvement over the club. The bow was an improvement over the spear. The gun was an improvement over the bow. The drone is an improvement over the gun. From the soldier's point of view, the history of weapons is a history of increasing safety, and the drone is simply the latest step in a long progression.

But from the point of view of the society that sends the soldier, the drone is different, because it removes the soldier from the battlefield entirely, and in doing so removes the constraint that has, throughout history, limited the willingness of societies to go to war. That constraint is the risk of death. A society that sends its young men to fight will hesitate before sending them into a war that will kill many of them, and that hesitation is a check on the resort to war. A society that sends drones to fight does not pay that price, and the check is weakened. The drone has made it possible for a democracy to fight a war for twenty years without the war becoming a central issue in its politics, because the war has not cost the democracy very much—a few thousand lives, a few trillion dollars, but not the kind of mass casualty that would force a reckoning. The drone has, in this sense, made war easier, and the ease of war is a moral problem, because the whole thrust of the just war tradition has been to make war harder.

The same logic applies to the precision-guided munition, the subject of Part 57, which deserves to be revisited here, because the PGM and the drone are two expressions of the same underlying transformation. The PGM promised to make war more humane by making it more precise—by allowing the attacker to destroy the target without destroying the neighborhood around it. The promise was real, and it was kept, to a degree. The Gulf War of 1991 demonstrated that a coalition could destroy the command-and-control infrastructure of a modern state while leaving most of the civilian infrastructure intact, and the Kosovo campaign of 1999 demonstrated that a coalition could wage war for seventy-eight days without suffering a single combat death. But the promise had a hidden cost: the precision of the weapon made the resort to war more attractive, because the political cost of casualties—both one's own and the enemy's—was reduced. The PGM did not simply make war more humane; it made war more usable, and the usability of war is not the same thing as the humanity of war.

The history of weapons is full of this kind of trade-off, in which a weapon that is more humane in one respect is more inhumane in another. The machine gun was more humane than the bayonet in that it killed more quickly and with less suffering, but more inhumane in that it made mass slaughter routine. The bomber was more humane than the siege in that it could destroy a city without starving it, but more inhumane in that it killed civilians directly rather than as a by-product of starvation. The nuclear weapon was more humane than firebombing in that it killed instantly rather than over hours, but more inhumane in that it threatened to kill everyone. And the drone is more humane than the manned aircraft in that it does not put the pilot at risk, but more inhumane in that it removes the pilot from the moral experience of killing. The trade-off is not a sign that weapons are getting worse; it is a sign that the moral accounting of weapons is more complicated than the simple arithmetic of casualties.

The complication is compounded by the fact that the moral accounting is always done after the fact, by historians and lawyers and philosophers, while decisions about weapons are made before the fact, by engineers and generals and politicians operating under the pressure of immediate necessity. The decision to develop the atomic bomb was made in 1941, when the United States believed Nazi Germany might be developing one, and it was made on the basis of a calculation of national survival that left little room for moral deliberation. The decision to develop the drone was made in the aftermath of September 11, 2001, when the United States faced a non-state enemy that operated in failed states and could not be defeated by conventional means, and it was made on the basis of a calculation of military effectiveness that left little room for moral deliberation. The moral accounting came later, from outside the institutions that made the decisions, and too late to change them. This is the normal pattern in the history of weapons, and it should make us modest about our ability to control the weapons we make.

But modesty is not fatalism, and the history of weapons also contains examples of successful restraint. The most important is the nuclear non-proliferation regime, which has, since the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970, prevented the spread of nuclear weapons from the five original nuclear powers to the more than one hundred and eighty states that have renounced them. The regime has not been perfect—India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined, and North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003—but it has been remarkably successful by the standards of any previous attempt to control a weapon of mass destruction. It has worked because it combined a moral norm (that nuclear weapons are uniquely dangerous and should not spread) with a system of incentives and disincentives (the benefits of civilian nuclear cooperation and the costs of sanctions and isolation) and a system of verification (the inspections of the International Atomic Energy Agency). The regime is the closest thing the world has to a successful example of arms control, and it is worth studying as a model for the control of other weapons.

The model has been applied, with less success, to other categories of weapons. The Chemical Weapons Convention, in force since 1997, has largely succeeded in eliminating declared stockpiles of chemical weapons, but it has been unable to prevent their use in Syria and elsewhere. The Biological Weapons Convention, in force since 1975, has no verification mechanism and has been largely ineffective. The Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, in force since 1983, has been extended to cover blinding lasers and incendiary weapons, but not autonomous weapons, because the states developing them have blocked the extension. The pattern is clear: arms control works when the major powers have an interest in controlling the weapon, and fails when they do not. The nuclear regime worked because the nuclear powers had an interest in preventing the spread of nuclear weapons to their rivals. An autonomous weapons regime has not worked because the major powers believe autonomous weapons will give them an advantage, and they are not willing to give it up.

The question of autonomous weapons now confronts the history of weapons, and it will define the next century in the same way that the question of nuclear weapons defined the last. The autonomous weapon can select and engage targets without human intervention. It is not a remotely piloted drone, controlled by a human being; it is a weapon that makes the decision to kill on its own. The technology is not speculative. Loitering munitions, which can cruise over a battlefield and attack a target when they find it, are already in service. Air-defense systems that can detect and engage incoming missiles without human intervention have been in service for decades. The question is not whether the technology will exist; it is whether it will be used to kill human beings without a human being deciding to kill them.

The case for autonomous weapons is about speed and scale. A human being cannot react fast enough to counter a swarm of drones or a hypersonic missile, and cannot process the volume of data a modern battlefield generates. The autonomous weapon can react at machine speed, coordinate with other autonomous weapons in ways human beings cannot, and therefore defend against threats human beings cannot defend against. The case is compelling, and it is why the major powers are investing heavily in autonomous systems. It is also why they are reluctant to agree to a ban, because a ban would leave them vulnerable to the powers that do not agree to it.

The case against autonomous weapons is about accountability and meaning. When a human being kills, the killing can be attributed to that human being, who can be held responsible, and the responsibility gives the killing a meaning it would not otherwise have. When an autonomous weapon kills, the killing cannot be attributed to anyone in particular; responsibility is diffused among the designers and commanders and politicians who deployed the weapon, and the diffusion makes it possible for the killing to happen without anyone feeling that they have done it. The case against autonomous weapons is therefore a case about the moral experience of killing, continuous with the case against the drone, the bomber, and the crossbow. The objection is always the same: the weapon makes it too easy to kill, and the ease of killing is a moral problem.

The objection has never prevailed. The crossbow was banned by the Second Lateran Council in 1139, and the ban was ignored. The machine gun was denounced as inhuman, and it was adopted by every major army. The bomber was denounced as a violation of the laws of war, and it became the central weapon of the Second World War. The nuclear weapon was denounced as a crime against humanity, and it became the foundation of the postwar order. The pattern suggests the objection will not prevail against autonomous weapons either—that they will be developed and deployed and absorbed into the ordinary conduct of war, that the moral accommodation will happen, and that the world will be changed in ways we cannot now foresee.

But the pattern also suggests that the moral accommodation is not automatic, and that it depends on the choices made at the moment of transition. The nuclear weapon was absorbed into the postwar order, but the absorption was accompanied by the creation of the non-proliferation regime, and the regime was created because statesmen and scientists and citizens made a conscious decision that the spread of the weapon was too dangerous to be allowed. The same kind of conscious decision is possible for autonomous weapons, and it would not require a ban; it would require a set of rules that preserve human control over the decision to kill, and that make the rules binding on the states that develop the weapons. The rules would be difficult to negotiate and difficult to enforce, but the difficulty is not a reason to abandon the attempt, because the alternative is a world in which the decision to kill is made by machines—a world that none of the soldiers and statesmen and citizens who built the weapons of the past would have recognized as the world they were trying to build.

The history of weapons is, in the end, a history of choices. The weapons themselves are inert; they do not choose to be used. The choices are made by the people who design them and build them and deploy them and acquiesce in their deployment. The choices are constrained by the pressures of war and the logic of competition and the fear of the enemy, but the constraints are not absolute, and the history of weapons contains moments when the constraints were overcome and a different choice was made. The decision not to use chemical weapons in the Second World War, despite the fact that every major power had them and every major power had used them in the First World War, is one such moment. The decision not to use nuclear weapons since 1945, despite their availability and despite several close calls, is another. These decisions were not inevitable, and they were not the product of a moral consensus that existed before the weapons were made; they were the product of a moral consensus built after the weapons were made, by people who understood what the weapons could do and chose to restrain themselves.

The building of that consensus is the task that now confronts the world, and it requires a clear understanding of what the history of weapons has taught. The history has taught that weapons change the world, and that the changes are not always the ones the inventors intended. It has taught that moral accommodation to new weapons is possible, but slow and uneven and often incomplete. It has taught that restraint is possible, but requires institutions and norms and a willingness to bear costs. And it has taught that the pace of change is accelerating, that the time available for accommodation and restraint is shrinking, and that the choices made in the next few decades will shape the world for centuries.

The acceleration is the central fact of the modern history of weapons, and it deserves to be examined in its own right, because it distinguishes the present from every previous period. For most of human history, the pace of change was set by the pace of biological and social evolution. A new weapon might be invented in one place and spread to another over centuries. The bow and arrow spread across the world over tens of thousands of years. The sword spread across Eurasia over thousands of years. Gunpowder spread from China to Europe over a few centuries. The pace was slow because the means of communication and production were slow, because the societies that used the weapons were slow to change, and because the weapons themselves changed slowly.

The industrial revolution changed the pace. The rifle was invented in the fifteenth century, but it took four centuries for the rifled musket to become the standard infantry weapon, another half century for the breech-loading rifle, and another half century for the automatic rifle. The pace was still measured in generations, but the generations were becoming shorter and the changes more consequential. The machine gun was invented in 1884, adopted by the major armies within a decade, and transformed the battlefield within a generation. The airplane was invented in 1903, used as a weapon within a decade, and transformed the battlefield within a generation. The tank was invented in 1916, used in mass formations within a generation, and transformed the battlefield within a generation.

The Second World War compressed the pace further. The war began with biplanes and ended with jet aircraft and ballistic missiles and atomic bombs. Its six years saw more technological change than the previous six centuries. The compression was driven by the urgency of the conflict and the scale of the industrial resources devoted to it, and it produced a set of weapons that defined the postwar world. The jet engine, radar, the computer, the rocket, the nuclear weapon—all were developed or perfected during the war, and all shaped the world that followed.

The Cold War maintained the pace but changed its character. The competition between the United States and the Soviet Union was a competition in weapons technology, conducted through increasingly sophisticated systems: intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles, multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles, cruise missiles, stealth aircraft, precision-guided munitions. The competition was driven by the logic of mutual assured destruction, which required each side to maintain a credible second-strike capability, and that requirement drove the development of weapons that were faster and more accurate and more survivable. It was also driven by the logic of proxy war, which required each side to supply its allies with weapons usable in conflicts in the developing world, and that requirement drove the development of weapons that were cheaper and more portable and more usable.

The end of the Cold War did not end the competition; it changed its terms. The United States emerged with a technological advantage unprecedented in the history of warfare, and used it to fight a series of wars in the 1990s and 2000s that demonstrated the power of precision-guided munitions, stealth aircraft, and networked communications. The demonstrations were so successful that they persuaded the rest of the world that the American model of warfare was the model of the future, and the rest of the world began to invest in the technologies that made the model work. The result was a diffusion of precision-guided munitions and drones and networked communications to a much wider set of actors, including middle powers and non-state groups, and the diffusion eroded the American advantage and created a new kind of battlefield in which the technologies developed to give the United States an edge were available to its adversaries.

The diffusion is the second central fact of the modern history of weapons, and it distinguishes the present from the Cold War. During the Cold War, the most advanced weapons were concentrated in the hands of two superpowers, and the rest of the world depended on one or the other for its supply. The concentration made it possible for the superpowers to control the spread of weapons through a system of alliances and export controls, and the control was imperfect but real. The diffusion has undermined that control, because the technologies that make advanced weapons possible are now widely available, and the components that make up the weapons are now commodities that can be bought on the open market. A drone that cost millions of dollars a decade ago can now be built for thousands; a precision-guided munition that required a satellite guidance system a decade ago can now be built with a commercial GPS receiver; a communications network that required a dedicated military satellite a decade ago can now be built with a commercial cellular network. The barriers to entry have fallen, and the fall has changed the balance of power between the states that have advanced weapons and those that do not.

The change is visible in the conflicts of the past decade. The war in Nagorno-Karabakh in 2020 was a war in which Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions to destroy Armenian armor and artillery and air defenses, and the drones were decisive in a way that would have been impossible a decade earlier, because they were cheap enough and reliable enough and numerous enough to be used in mass formations. The war in Ukraine, which began in 2022, has been a war in which both sides have used drones for reconnaissance and strike and artillery spotting, and the drones have changed the character of the battlefield in ways the armies that built them did not anticipate. The war in Gaza, which began in 2023, has been a war in which both sides have used drones and precision munitions and cyber weapons, fought in a dense urban environment in which the distinction between combatant and civilian is almost impossible to maintain. The wars of the past decade have been wars of diffusion, and the diffusion has made them more lethal and more complicated and more morally ambiguous than the wars of the previous decade.

The diffusion is also visible in the proliferation of cyber weapons, the third central fact of the modern history of weapons. Cyber weapons are not weapons in the traditional sense; they are tools that can disable or destroy the systems modern societies depend on, and they can be used without the physical destruction traditional weapons cause. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, was designed to destroy the centrifuges Iran was using to enrich uranium, and it succeeded in destroying a significant number of them without killing anyone. The use of cyber weapons has since become routine, and the routine use has created a new domain of warfare in which the rules are unclear, the attribution of attacks is difficult, and the escalation of attacks is easy. The cyber domain is where the diffusion of weapons technology is most complete, because the tools of cyber warfare are available to anyone with a computer and an internet connection, and that availability has created a situation in which the most powerful states are vulnerable to the least powerful actors.

These three facts—acceleration, diffusion, and the emergence of new domains—define the present, and they are the facts the history of weapons must now address. The history of weapons has always been a history of the relationship between technology and society, and the relationship has always been reciprocal, but the reciprocity has become faster and more complex and more difficult to manage. The weapons being developed now will shape the world in ways we cannot predict, and the choices being made now will determine whether that shaping is done by human beings or by the logic of the technology itself.

The history of weapons is also a history of the institutions that have tried to control them. The institutions have taken many forms: the guilds that regulated weapons production in the medieval period, the state arsenals of the early modern period, the arms manufacturers of the industrial period, the international organizations that have tried to regulate weapons in the modern period. They have always been imperfect, always subject to capture by the interests they were meant to regulate, and always outpaced by the technology they were meant to control. But they have also been the means by which societies have attempted to impose their values on the weapons they make, and the history of the institutions is therefore a history of the attempt to make weapons serve human ends rather than determine them.

The most important of these institutions is the state, because the state has been the primary producer and user of weapons since the early modern period, and the primary source of the norms that govern their use. The state has an interest in controlling weapons, because its monopoly on legitimate violence depends on its ability to control the means of violence, and an interest in limiting their spread, because spread undermines the monopoly. But the state also has an interest in developing weapons, because its survival depends on its ability to defend itself, and the interest in development has often outweighed the interest in control. The tension between the two is the central tension in the history of weapons, and it has never been resolved.

The tension is visible in the history of the arms trade, the mechanism by which weapons spread from the states that produce them to the states and groups that use them. The arms trade has always been a source of wealth and influence for producing states, and a source of danger for receiving states and for the international system as a whole. Producing states have tried to control the trade through export controls and end-use agreements and embargoes, but the controls have always been leaky, and the leaks have always been exploited by the states and groups that want the weapons. The result is a system in which the most advanced weapons are sold to allies and the less advanced to anyone who can pay, and in which the diffusion of weapons is driven by the same commercial logic that drives the diffusion of any other commodity.

The commercial logic is what the history of weapons has always had to contend with, and it has become more powerful as weapons have become more sophisticated and more expensive. The development of a modern combat aircraft costs tens of billions of dollars, a modern nuclear submarine tens of billions more, a modern aircraft carrier tens of billions more, and the costs can only be borne by states with large economies and large tax bases. The states that can bear the costs are few, and the few have an interest in selling the weapons to other states to recoup the costs, and the sales create a cycle in which producing states become dependent on exports and receiving states on imports, and the cycle is difficult to break.

The cycle is why the arms trade has been so resistant to control, and why the history of weapons is not a history of progress in the simple sense. Weapons have become more precise and more powerful and more sophisticated, but the logic that drives their production and spread has not changed, and that logic is the logic of competition and profit and fear. The history of weapons is therefore a history of the interaction between that logic and the values supposed to constrain it, and the interaction has produced a mixed record, with moments of restraint and moments of excess, and no clear trend toward either.

The mixed record is the record the history of weapons must present, and it is the record the preceding fifty-seven parts have tried to present. The history has not been a story of steady progress toward more humane weapons, nor a story of steady decline toward more barbarous ones. It has been a story of oscillation, in which the development of a new weapon is followed by a period of adaptation in which the weapon is absorbed into existing moral and legal frameworks, and in which the absorption has sometimes made the weapon more humane and sometimes more destructive. The oscillation is the pattern, and the pattern is the product of the interaction between technology and society, and that interaction is the subject of the history.

The oscillation is visible in the history of the laws of war, which have evolved in response to the development of weapons. The laws of war are not a single body of law but a collection of treaties and customs and judicial decisions accumulated over centuries, shaped by the weapons with which wars have been fought. The prohibition on the use of poison in war, which dates back to ancient India and Greece, was a response to a weapon considered uniquely treacherous. The prohibition on expanding bullets, codified in the Hague Convention of 1899, was a response to a weapon considered uniquely cruel. The prohibition on chemical and biological weapons, codified in the Geneva Protocol of 1925 and the Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993, was a response to weapons considered uniquely indiscriminate. The prohibition on blinding lasers, codified in the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in 1995, was a response to a weapon considered uniquely inhumane. The pattern is clear: the laws of war have followed the weapons, and tried to constrain them, and the constraint has been partial and uneven.

The unevenness is the product of the fact that the laws of war are made by states, and states are reluctant to constrain their own weapons. The states with the most powerful weapons have the most influence over the laws, and they have used that influence to protect their weapons while restricting those of their adversaries. The result is a body of law more effective at prohibiting the weapons used by the weak than those used by the strong. The prohibition on chemical weapons has been enforced against Iraq and Syria, but not against the states that have large chemical stockpiles. The prohibition on anti-personnel landmines, codified in the Ottawa Treaty of 1997, has been signed by more than one hundred and sixty states, but not by the United States, Russia, and China, the states that produce and use the most landmines. The pattern is the pattern of the history of weapons, and it is the pattern the history must reckon with.

The reckoning is not a counsel of despair. The laws of war have made a difference, even if uneven, and the difference has been greatest where the weapons have been most visible and most horrifying. The prohibition on chemical weapons has prevented their use in most conflicts since the First World War, and the prohibition on biological weapons has prevented their use in almost all. The prohibition on weapons that cause unnecessary suffering has shaped the design of weapons, and the prohibition on indiscriminate weapons has shaped the tactics of armies. The laws of war are not a guarantee of humane warfare, but they are a constraint on inhuman warfare, and the constraint is worth preserving.

The preservation of that constraint is the task the history of weapons now sets for the world, and it requires a clear-eyed understanding of what the history has taught. The history has taught that weapons change the world, and that the changes are not always the ones the inventors intended. It has taught that moral accommodation to new weapons is possible, but slow and uneven and often incomplete. It has taught that restraint is possible, but requires institutions and norms and a willingness to bear costs. It has taught that the pace of change is accelerating, and that the time available for accommodation and restraint is shrinking. And it has taught that the choices made in the next few decades will shape the world for centuries.

Those choices are the subject of the final parts of this book, and they are the choices the history of weapons has been building toward. They are not abstract; they are concrete decisions about specific technologies and institutions and norms. They include whether to develop autonomous weapons, whether to restrict the spread of drones, whether to establish a regime for the control of cyber weapons, whether to strengthen the nuclear non-proliferation regime, and whether to invest in technologies that might make war less likely rather than more lethal. The choices are difficult, and they are made more difficult by the fact that the institutions that would make them are weak and divided and subject to the same pressures that have always shaped the history of weapons.
But the choices are also made more possible by the fact that the history of weapons has given the world a set of precedents and institutions and norms that can be built upon. The nuclear non-pro

paragraphs: The proliferation regime, whatever its flaws, has kept the number of nuclear-armed states to single digits for more than half a century—not by making weapons impossible but by making them costly to acquire and costly to use. The chemical weapons taboo, codified in the 1925 Geneva Protocol and the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention, has not eliminated chemical warfare, but it has made possession and use an international crime and driven the few states that have used such weapons to deny it. The conventions protecting prisoners of war and civilians, from the first Geneva Convention of 1864 to the Additional Protocols of 1977, have not stopped the killing of noncombatants, but they have established a baseline against which that killing can be measured and condemned. The institutions are imperfect, the norms are imperfect, the precedents are imperfect—but they exist, and they are the raw material out of which any future restraint will have to be built.

The history of weapons is, in this sense, a history of the gradual and uneven extension of moral and legal constraint over the means of violence. The constraint has never been complete, never evenly applied, and often honored mainly in the breach. But the long-run direction of travel is unmistakable. When the crossbow appeared in Europe in the tenth and eleventh centuries, the Church tried to ban it at the Second Lateran Council of 1139, declaring its use against Christians an anathema. The ban did not hold—the crossbow was too useful, and the states that adopted it too powerful to be restrained by a council of bishops—but the attempt is the first recorded effort to prohibit a weapon on the grounds that it was inhumane, and it established a precedent that would be invoked again and again. When gunpowder weapons appeared in Europe in the fourteenth century, they were condemned as cowardly and unchivalrous; the knights who condemned them were fighting a rearguard action against a technology that would render their own form of warfare obsolete. But the condemnation was not entirely without effect: it contributed to the laws of war and to the idea that there were limits to what could be done even in war.

The nineteenth century saw the first sustained international efforts to codify the laws of war and regulate weapons development. The Declaration of St. Petersburg of 1868, issued by an international commission convened at the invitation of Tsar Alexander II, declared that the only legitimate object of war was to weaken the enemy's military forces, and that weapons which would "uselessly aggravate the sufferings of disabled men, or render their death inevitable" were contrary to the laws of humanity. Prompted by the invention of the exploding bullet—a projectile designed to explode on contact with the human body—it established the principle that the means of warfare were not unlimited. The Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 codified the principle further, prohibiting poison gas, the dropping of projectiles from balloons, and bullets that expanded or flattened easily in the human body. The conventions were not always honored—poison gas was used on a massive scale in the First World War, and expanding bullets by many armies despite the prohibition—but they established a framework of international law that would be expanded and strengthened in the twentieth century.

The First World War was a turning point in the history of weapons and of efforts to restrain them. The war saw the introduction of poison gas, the tank, the airplane, and the submarine as weapons, and the industrialization of killing on an unprecedented scale. The casualties were catastrophic: roughly 10 million soldiers died and another 20 million were wounded, while civilian populations suffered hunger, disease, and displacement. The war also saw the first sustained efforts to regulate the new weapons. The Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 limited the size and number of battleships and aircraft carriers, and the London Naval Treaties of 1930 and 1936 extended the limits to cruisers and destroyers. The Geneva Protocol of 1925 prohibited the use of poison gas and bacteriological weapons in war and was signed by most major powers, though the United States did not ratify it until 1975. The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 renounced war as an instrument of national policy and was signed by sixty-three states, though it did not prevent the Second World War.

The Second World War was the most destructive in human history, and it saw the development of weapons that would transform the nature of warfare. It introduced the ballistic missile, the jet aircraft, radar, the proximity fuse, and the computer, and it culminated in the development and use of the atomic bomb. The bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 killed roughly 200,000 people and marked the beginning of the nuclear age. The war also saw the systematic bombing of civilian populations, the use of chemical and biological weapons by Japan against China, and the Holocaust, which killed six million Jews and millions of others. It ended with the establishment of the United Nations, whose charter committed its members to international peace and security, and with the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals, which established that individuals could be held accountable for crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The nuclear age transformed the relationship between weapons and strategy. Before 1945, weapons development was driven by the desire to kill more of the enemy more efficiently, and strategy was shaped by the available weapons. After 1945, development was driven by the desire to deter the enemy from using his weapons, and strategy was shaped by the fear of escalation. The doctrine of deterrence—the threat of retaliation would prevent an attack—became the central organizing principle of international security, codified in mutually assured destruction: the United States and the Soviet Union would refrain from attacking each other because each would be destroyed in the retaliation. The doctrine was terrifying and, in a strange way, stabilizing: it created a situation in which the costs of war were so high that war became unthinkable, and it contributed to the long peace of the Cold War—not a peace in the sense of the absence of conflict, but a peace in the sense of the absence of direct war between the major powers.

The Cold War saw a vast array of new weapons and a vast array of new efforts to restrain them. The nuclear arms race produced weapons of staggering power: the hydrogen bomb, tested by the United States in 1952 and the Soviet Union in 1953, had a yield of several megatons, more than a hundred times the bomb that destroyed Hiroshima. The intercontinental ballistic missile, developed by the Soviet Union in 1957 and the United States in 1959, made it possible to deliver a nuclear warhead to any point on the earth's surface in less than an hour. The submarine-launched ballistic missile, developed by the United States in 1960 and the Soviet Union in 1963, made it possible to hide nuclear weapons under the sea, where they could survive a first strike and be used in retaliation. The multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle, developed by the United States in the 1960s and the Soviet Union in the 1970s, made it possible to deliver several warheads to different targets with a single missile—and destabilized the balance of terror by making it possible to destroy the enemy's retaliatory forces in a first strike.

The arms race was accompanied by arms control, and the effort produced a series of treaties limiting the number and kind of nuclear weapons. The Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963 prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space, and under water, and was signed by the United States, the Soviet Union, and the United Kingdom. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968 committed the nuclear powers to pursue negotiations on disarmament and the non-nuclear states to refrain from acquiring nuclear weapons, and established the International Atomic Energy Agency as guardian of the nuclear fuel cycle. The Strategic Arms Limitation Talks of the 1970s produced the SALT I and SALT II treaties, which limited strategic nuclear delivery vehicles, and the Strategic Arms Reduction Talks of the 1980s and 1990s produced the START treaties, which reduced deployed warheads. The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987 eliminated an entire class of nuclear weapons—the first treaty to provide for the actual destruction of nuclear weapons rather than the mere limitation of their numbers.

The arms-control effort was not always successful, nor always honored. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 led to the suspension of SALT II; the United States withdrew from the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty in 2002 and from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in 2019; and New START, which limits deployed strategic warheads, was extended in 2021 but is due to expire in 2026. The effort has also been undermined by new weapons outside the scope of existing treaties: the hypersonic glide vehicle, which can maneuver at speeds above Mach 5 and evade existing missile defenses; the cyber weapon, which can attack the command-and-control systems that control nuclear weapons; and the autonomous weapon, which can select and engage targets without human intervention. Proliferation to states outside the NPT has undermined it further: India, Israel, and Pakistan, which never joined, and North Korea, which announced its withdrawal in 2003 and has since tested nuclear weapons.

Nuclear proliferation is one of the most important developments in the history of weapons and one of the most important challenges to efforts to restrain them. The NPT has 191 states parties and has been remarkably successful in limiting nuclear-armed states to single digits. But it has not prevented determined states from acquiring nuclear weapons, nor non-state actors—though the latter threat has so far been more hypothetical than real. The treaty has also been criticized for the asymmetry it embodies: it divides the world into nuclear haves and have-nots, committing the haves to disarmament while allowing them to keep their weapons in the meantime. The criticism is fair; it has been a source of tension between nuclear and non-nuclear states and has contributed to the failure of the nuclear powers to make progress on disarmament.

The history of efforts to restrain weapons is a history of partial successes and partial failures, shaped by the same forces that have shaped the history of weapons themselves: technological, political, economic, and cultural. The technological forces are the most obvious: a new weapon creates new possibilities and new dangers, and efforts to restrain it are always playing catch-up. The political forces are the most important: states that possess a weapon are reluctant to give it up, states that do not are reluctant to accept a permanent disadvantage, and the international institutions meant to mediate between them are weak and divided. The economic forces are the most pervasive: the defense industry is a major employer and source of profit with a vested interest in new weapons, and it has been able to shape the policies of the states that host it. The cultural forces are the most subtle: the glorification of war and the celebration of military technology are deeply embedded in many cultures, making it difficult to build the public support that serious restraint would require.

The history of weapons is also a history of unintended consequences, which have often been more important than the intended ones. The crossbow was meant to give infantry a weapon that could penetrate armor, and it did—but it also contributed to the decline of the feudal order by making it possible for a common soldier to kill a knight. Gunpowder was meant to give armies a more powerful projectile weapon, and it did—but it also contributed to the rise of the centralized state by making it possible for a monarch to equip and maintain a standing army. The railroad was meant to transport goods and people, and it did—but it also made it possible to mobilize and supply armies on an unprecedented scale, and it contributed to the carnage of the First World War. The airplane was meant to provide faster transport, and it did—but it also made it possible to bomb cities from the air, and it contributed to the doctrine of strategic bombing that killed hundreds of thousands of civilians in the Second World War. The computer was meant to solve mathematical problems, and it did—but it also made possible the guidance and command-and-control systems essential to modern warfare, and the autonomous weapons now on the horizon.

The history of weapons is also a history of the interaction between offense and defense, which has shaped the development of both. The walled city was a response to the siege engine, the cannon a response to the walled city, the star fort a response to the cannon, the explosive shell a response to the star fort. The rifled musket was a response to the smoothbore musket, the trench a response to the rifled musket, the tank a response to the trench, the anti-tank weapon a response to the tank. The bomber was a response to air defense, the missile a response to the bomber, the anti-missile missile a response to the missile, the hypersonic glide vehicle a response to the anti-missile missile. The interaction is a kind of arms race, a constant feature of the history of weapons, and it has driven development in a direction that is increasingly complex and increasingly expensive.

The interaction between offense and defense has also shaped the relationship between weapons and strategy, and that relationship has been transformed in the modern era. In the premodern era, a new weapon could give a state a decisive advantage, which it could use to conquer its neighbors: the Assyrians used iron weapons to conquer the Near East, the Mongols the composite bow to conquer Eurasia, the Spanish gunpowder weapons to conquer the Americas. In the modern era, a new weapon is less likely to confer a decisive advantage, because other states can develop the same weapon or a counter-weapon, and the advantage is likely to be temporary. The tank gave the Germans a decisive advantage in 1939 and 1940, but the Allies developed their own tanks and anti-tank weapons, and the advantage was lost. The atomic bomb gave the United States a decisive advantage in 1945, but the Soviet Union developed its own bomb in 1949, and the advantage was lost. The precision-guided munition gave the United States a decisive advantage in 1991, but other states have developed their own, and the advantage is being eroded.

The erosion of advantage is one of the most important developments in the history of weapons, with implications for the future of warfare. In a world of rapid and widespread diffusion of military technology, the advantage a state can gain from a new weapon is likely to be temporary, while the advantage it can gain from superior organization and training is likely to be more durable. The history of weapons suggests that the states most successful in war have combined technological innovation with organizational innovation and adapted their tactics and strategies to the new weapons. The Romans combined the legion with the road and the fort and held an empire for centuries. The Mongols combined the composite bow with the horse and the discipline of the steppe and conquered the largest contiguous empire in history. The British combined the rifled musket with drill and the discipline of the line and built an empire on which the sun never set. The Germans combined the tank with the radio and the doctrine of blitzkrieg and conquered most of Europe in a few months. The Americans combined the aircraft carrier with radar and the doctrine of the carrier battle group and dominated the Pacific.

The history of weapons is also a history of the relationship between weapons and society, transformed in the modern era. In the premodern era, the weapons of war were often the same as the tools of peace: the bow used to hunt was used to fight, and the knife used to cut was used to kill. In the modern era, the weapons of war have become increasingly specialized and detached from the tools of peace. The tank, the bomber, the missile, and the nuclear weapon have no civilian counterpart and are designed solely for killing. The specialization of weapons has been accompanied by the professionalization of armies and the separation of the military from the rest of society. The soldier is no longer a citizen who takes up arms in time of need but a professional trained and equipped for war, and the gap between military and civilian has grown ever wider.

That gap has been widened further by weapons so complex and expensive that only large organizations can operate them. The aircraft carrier, the nuclear submarine, and the stealth bomber cannot be operated by an individual or a small group; they require the coordinated effort of thousands and the resources of a state. Such weapons have concentrated power in the hands of the states that can afford them and widened the gap between the great powers and the rest of the world—a gap widened further by nuclear weapons, which are so expensive and complex that only a handful of states can afford them, and so powerful that they have transformed the nature of international relations.

The concentration of power in the hands of states that can afford the most advanced weapons is one of the most important developments in the history of weapons, with implications for the future of warfare. Where the most advanced weapons are available only to a few states, those states have a decisive advantage, and the rest are forced to find other ways to compete: asymmetric strategies such as guerrilla warfare and terrorism, and cheaper weapons such as the improvised explosive device and the drone. The history of weapons suggests that the weak have always found ways to challenge the strong, often successfully. The Israelites challenged the Philistines with the sling, the Swiss the Habsburgs with the pike, the Vietnamese the French and Americans with the rifle and the tunnel, and the Afghan mujahideen the Soviets with the Stinger missile.

The development of asymmetric strategies is one of the most important developments in the history of weapons, and it has transformed the nature of warfare. In the premodern era, war was fought between states, and the outcome was determined by the relative strength of armies. In the modern era, war is increasingly fought between states and non-state actors, and the outcome is determined by the combatants' relative ability to adapt to the conditions of the battlefield. The non-state actor has advantages the state does not: it can hide among the civilian population, while the state is constrained by the laws of war and by the need to maintain the support of its own population; it can use cheap, improvised weapons, while the state is constrained by the cost and complexity of its own; it can afford to wait, while the state needs a quick and decisive victory. The history of weapons suggests that the non-state actor has often prevailed against the state, and that the state has often been forced to adapt its tactics and weapons to asymmetric warfare.

The state's adaptation to asymmetric warfare has produced a new generation of weapons designed for the modern battlefield. The precision-guided munition, the drone, the surveillance satellite, and the cyber weapon are all meant to give the state an advantage over the non-state actor, and they have been used with considerable success in the conflicts of the past three decades. Precision-guided munitions make it possible to strike a target with high accuracy and have reduced the collateral damage associated with the bombing campaigns of the Second World War and the Vietnam War. Drones make it possible to conduct surveillance and strike targets without putting pilots at risk, and the United States has used them extensively in Afghanistan, Iraq, and Pakistan. Surveillance satellites make it possible to monitor enemy movements and support the operations of state forces. Cyber weapons make it possible to attack enemy command-and-control systems and disrupt enemy operations.

The new weapons have given the state an advantage over the non-state actor, but not a decisive one, and they have not prevented the non-state actor from continuing to challenge the state. The history of weapons suggests that the state's advantage is likely to be temporary and that the non-state actor will find ways to adapt. It has already adapted to the drone with countermeasures such as camouflage and tunnels, and with its own drones, such as the improvised explosive drone used in Iraq and Syria. It has adapted to the surveillance satellite by hiding its movements, using the civilian population as a shield, and communicating without detection through encrypted messaging apps. It has adapted to the cyber weapon by developing its own cyber capabilities and techniques for defending against cyber attacks.

The non-state actor's adaptation to the new weapons has implications for the future of warfare. Where the non-state actor can adapt, the state's advantage is likely to be temporary, and the state will be forced to develop new weapons and tactics to maintain it. The history of weapons suggests that this competition will continue and will produce new weapons and new forms of warfare we cannot yet imagine—and that it will be shaped by the same technological, political, economic, and cultural forces that have shaped the history of weapons in the past.

The technological forces are likely to be the most important, producing weapons more precise, more autonomous, and more connected than those of today. Artificial intelligence is likely to produce weapons that can select and engage targets without human intervention and learn from experience to adapt to battlefield conditions. The internet of things is likely to produce weapons connected to networks of sensors and controllable remotely, and weapons that can attack the enemy's networks of sensors and controllers. Biotechnology is likely to produce weapons that can target specific individuals or populations, and weapons that can enhance the capabilities of the state's own forces. Nanotechnology is likely to produce weapons too small to be seen, and weapons that can attack the enemy's materials and equipment.

The political forces are likely to shape how the new weapons are used, and they will be shaped by the same tensions that have shaped the history of weapons in the past. The tension between security and liberty is likely to be intensified, producing new debates about the limits of state power. The tension between order and justice is likely to be intensified, producing new debates about the ethics of war. The tension between peace and victory is likely to be intensified, producing new debates about the strategy of war. The history of weapons suggests that these tensions are not likely to be resolved but managed—and that the management is likely to be imperfect.

The economic forces are likely to be the most pervasive, shaping weapons development in ways not always visible. The defense industry will likely remain a major source of profit and employment and will continue to lobby for new weapons. The cost of new weapons will likely keep rising, pressuring the budgets of the states that acquire them and forcing choices about which weapons to acquire and which to forgo. Rising costs will also widen the gap between states that can afford the new weapons and those that cannot, increasing the incentive for the latter to develop asymmetric strategies. The history of weapons suggests that economic forces will be a major driver of new weapons development—and a major obstacle to efforts to restrain it.

The cultural forces are likely to be the most subtle, shaping how the new weapons are perceived and used. The glorification of war and the celebration of military technology will likely remain features of many cultures, continuing to make it difficult to build the public support that serious restraint would require. Fear of the new weapons will also remain a feature of many cultures, continuing to produce demands for regulation and control. The history of weapons suggests that cultural forces will be a major influence on both the development of new weapons and the efforts to restrain them.

The history of weapons is, in the end, a history of human choices—shaped by these forces, but not determined by them. The states that have developed new weapons have always had the option of not developing them; the states that have used them, the option of not using them; the states that have restrained them, the option of restraining them further. The choices have been difficult, often made badly, and often made for the wrong reasons. But they have been made, and they have shaped the world in which we live, and they will continue to shape the world in which our descendants will live.

The most important choice facing the world today is whether to try to restrain the development of autonomous weapons—weapons that can select and engage targets without human intervention, the most significant development in the history of weapons since the atomic bomb. Autonomous weapons have the potential to make war more precise and less costly in human terms, and the potential to make it more likely and more brutal. They have the potential to reduce the risk to the soldiers of the state that possesses them and to increase the risk to civilians caught in the crossfire. They have the potential to be used in ways consistent with the laws of war, and in ways that are not. The choice is a choice about the kind of world we want to live in; it will be made in the next decade, by the states that possess the technology and by the international community trying to regulate it.

The campaign to ban autonomous weapons has been led by a coalition of non-governmental organizations, including Human Rights Watch and the Campaign to Stop Killer Robots, and supported by a number of states, including Austria, Brazil, and the Holy See. The campaign argues that autonomous weapons cross a moral threshold by delegating the decision to kill to a machine, making it possible to kill without human judgment and without human accountability. It also argues that such weapons are likely to lower the threshold for going to war, by reducing the risk to the state that possesses them, and to increase the risk of accidental war, by enabling triggers from malfunction or misinterpretation of data. The campaign has called for a legally binding international treaty prohibiting the development, production, and use of autonomous weapons, arguing that such a treaty is necessary to prevent an arms race in autonomous weapons and to preserve human control over the use of force.

The campaign has been opposed by a number of states, including the United States, Russia, and China, which argue that autonomous weapons are not inherently unethical and can be used consistently with the laws of war. They argue that autonomous weapons can be more precise than human-operated weapons, processing more data and reacting more quickly, and can reduce the risk to civilians by avoiding human error. They also argue that autonomous weapons are necessary to maintain a military advantage, and that a ban would be unverifiable and would be ignored by states determined to develop them. They have called for a non-binding set of guidelines rather than a treaty, developed through the existing Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which operates by consensus and has been slow to act.

The debate over autonomous weapons echoes earlier debates over earlier weapons. When the crossbow was introduced, it was condemned as inhumane, and the Church tried to ban it, and the ban failed. When gunpowder was introduced, it was condemned as cowardly, and the knights tried to ban it, and the ban failed. When the machine gun was introduced, it was condemned as barbaric, and the states tried to limit it, and the limits failed. When the atomic bomb was introduced, it was condemned as a crime against humanity, and the states tried to control it, and the control was only partially successful. The history of weapons suggests that efforts to ban a weapon are often unsuccessful, and that the weapons that are banned are often the ones least useful to the states trying to ban them. But it also suggests that such efforts can have an effect even when they fail, because they establish a norm and shape the way the weapon is used.

The norm against autonomous weapons is already being established—by the statements of states, the reports of non-governmental organizations, and the resolutions of the United Nations. It is not yet codified in a treaty and may never be, but it is shaping state behavior and the development of the technology. States developing autonomous weapons are aware of the norm, careful to describe their weapons as "semi-autonomous" or "human-in-the-loop," and careful to emphasize that a human being retains the authority to make the final decision to kill. The norm is also shaping the technology itself, as developers, aware that their weapons may be judged by it, design them to be more transparent and more accountable.

The norm against autonomous weapons is one of a number of norms being established in response to new weapons, in a world more interconnected and interdependent than ever before. They are being established by a wider range of actors—states, international organizations, non-governmental organizations, and private companies—through a wider range of mechanisms—treaties, guidelines, codes of conduct, and public opinion. The norms are not always effective, consistent, or enforced, but they are a real force in the world, shaping the development and use of weapons in ways that would have been unimaginable to the statesmen who signed the Declaration of St. Petersburg in 1868.

The history of weapons is, in this sense, a history of the gradual and uneven extension of moral and legal constraint over the means of violence, and that extension continues today. The constraint is not complete and may never be, but it is real and growing, and it is the world's best hope for preventing the development of weapons that would make war more likely and more brutal. The history of weapons is also a history of the failure of constraint—failures that have been catastrophic and have cost millions of lives. But those failures have been accompanied by successes that have saved millions of lives, built on the failures and on the precedents, institutions, and norms they produced.

The most important lesson of the history of weapons is that weapons development is not a story of inevitable progress, nor of inevitable doom. It is a story of human choices—shaped by the forces that have shaped the history of weapons, but not determined by them. The states that have developed new weapons have always had the option of not developing them; the states that have used them, the option of not using them; the states that have restrained them, the option of restraining them further. The choices have been difficult, often made badly, and often made for the wrong reasons. But they have been made, and they have shaped the world in which we live, and they will continue to shape the world in which our descendants will live.

The second lesson is that weapons development is a story of unintended consequences, which have often been more important than the intended ones. The crossbow contributed to the decline of the feudal order, gunpowder to the rise of the centralized state, the railroad to the carnage of the First World War, the airplane to the doctrine of strategic bombing, and the computer to the development of autonomous weapons. The lesson is that developing a new weapon is always a gamble—uncertain in outcome and shaped by forces the developers cannot foresee.

The third lesson is that weapons development is a story of the interaction between offense and defense, which has shaped the development of both. The walled city was a response to the siege engine, the cannon to the walled city, the star fort to the cannon, the explosive shell to the star fort. The interaction is a kind of arms race, a constant feature of the history of weapons, and it has driven development in a direction that is increasingly complex and increasingly expensive. The lesson is that a new weapon is always a provocation, the provocation is always answered, and the answer is always a new weapon.

The fourth lesson is that weapons development is a story of the relationship between weapons and society, transformed in the modern era. In the premodern era, the weapons of war were often the same as the tools of peace, and the soldier was often the same as the citizen. In the modern era, the weapons of war have become increasingly specialized and detached from the tools of peace, and the soldier has become increasingly detached from the citizen. The lesson is that a new weapon is always a social transformation, shaped by the forces that shape society and shaping society in turn.

The fifth lesson is that weapons development is a story of the concentration of power in the hands of states that can afford the most advanced weapons, and that concentration has widened the gap between the great powers and the rest of the world. The lesson is that a new weapon is always a political transformation, shaped by the forces that shape the international system and shaping that system in turn.

The sixth lesson is that weapons development is a story of efforts to restrain it, and those efforts have been partially successful and partially unsuccessful. They have produced a body of international law that prohibits the use of certain weapons and limits the development of others, a set of institutions that monitor and enforce the law, and a set of norms that shape the behavior of states.
