paragraphs: The most revealing place to begin the final movement of this history is not with a weapon but with a ledger. On the morning of 6 August 1945, the crew of the B-29 *Enola Gay* carried a gun-type uranium device called Little Boy over Hiroshima. It was 3 meters long, 71 centimeters in diameter, and weighed about 4,400 kilograms. Its yield was roughly 15 kilotons. Three days later, a plutonium implosion device called Fat Man—roughly 3.25 meters long and 1.5 meters in diameter, weighing about 4,600 kilograms—detonated over Nagasaki with a yield of about 21 kilotons. These are small numbers by the standards of what came later and enormous by the standards of everything before. The weapon that ended one war inaugurated a permanent condition. The ledger that mattered was no longer the quartermaster's tally of shells and powder but the accounting of warheads, delivery vehicles, and the minutes of warning time that separated the world from catastrophe.

The Trinity test of 16 July 1945, in the Jornada del Muerto desert of New Mexico, had already announced a new order of power. The plutonium implosion device known as Gadget produced a yield of about 21 kilotons. The scientists who watched understood that they had crossed a threshold that could not be recrossed. The historian of technology will note the engineering: implosion lenses, explosive lenses, the precise timing of detonators, the metallurgy of plutonium. The historian of war will note something else. The weapon was not an incremental improvement in explosives. It was a change in the unit of account. A thousand tons of TNT had been a meaningful measure of a bombing raid. Now a single aircraft could deliver twenty times that, and the next generation would deliver a thousand times more. Weapons development had always been a story of increasing energy delivered at increasing distance. Now both had become effectively unlimited, and the constraint had shifted from physics to politics.

That shift is the central fact of the modern era of weapons, and this final part of the argument must confront it directly. For most of the history traced in these pages, weapons development was driven by the pursuit of advantage in battle. A better bow, a stronger fortress, a faster ship, a more reliable rifle: each answered a tactical or operational problem, and each was tested in the only laboratory that ultimately mattered, the battlefield. The nuclear weapon broke that pattern. It was developed in secrecy, tested in a desert, and used twice. Its subsequent development was driven not by battlefield experience but by the logic of deterrence, by competition between adversaries, and by the effort to make the unthinkable thinkable in a controlled way. The weapon that could not be used in any meaningful sense became the weapon around which the entire structure of international security was organized.

The numbers tell the story of the escalation that followed. The United States, which had held a monopoly in 1945, tested its first thermonuclear device in 1952. The Soviet Union followed with an atomic test in 1949 and a thermonuclear test in 1953. Britain tested in 1952, France in 1960, China in 1964. Each new entrant changed the strategic calculus, and each was met with efforts to restrain the spread. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened for signature in 1968 and in force from 1970, became the central instrument of that restraint. It has 191 states parties. India, Israel, and Pakistan never joined; North Korea announced its withdrawal in 2003. The treaty is the clearest example of the sixth lesson: efforts to restrain weapons development have been partly successful and partly unsuccessful, and the partial success has been purchased at the price of legitimizing the arsenals of those who already held them.

The NPT repays close examination because it reveals the structure of the modern arms-control enterprise. The treaty rests on three pillars: non-proliferation, disarmament, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy. The non-proliferation pillar has been remarkably effective. Since 1970, the number of nuclear-armed states has grown far more slowly than the pessimists of the 1960s predicted. The disarmament pillar has been far less effective. The five recognized nuclear powers have reduced their arsenals from Cold War peaks but have not eliminated them, and several are modernizing. The peaceful-use pillar has been the most ambiguous, because the same technologies that enrich uranium for reactor fuel can enrich it for weapons. The treaty is a bargain, and like all bargains it reflects the interests of those who struck it. The states that had the bomb in 1968 kept it. The states that did not were asked to forgo it, and most did.

The history of arms control is therefore not a story of moral progress in which humanity gradually renounces the instruments of violence. It is a story of managed competition, in which the powerful seek to freeze the distribution of capabilities in their favor, the less powerful seek to change it, and the resulting bargains are unstable because they rest on the interests of the moment rather than on any permanent principle. The same logic runs through the earlier arms-control efforts examined in this book. The medieval Church's attempt to ban the crossbow was an attempt by the powerful to preserve a monopoly on violence, and it failed because the technology was too useful and too easy to copy. Nineteenth-century efforts to ban expanding bullets and poison gas sought to codify the rules of a game the great powers expected to keep playing among themselves. Twentieth-century efforts to ban chemical and biological weapons were more successful, in part because those weapons were less useful to the powerful and in part because the norms they established were genuinely shared.

The development of chemical and biological weapons is a case study in the relationship between technology and restraint. Poison gas was used on a large scale in the First World War, most notoriously at Ypres in 1915, and it caused horrific casualties. Yet it did not become a decisive weapon. The reasons were partly technical—gas is weather-dependent and difficult to control—and partly political, because the revulsion it provoked was genuine and widespread. The Geneva Protocol of 1925 prohibited the use of chemical and biological weapons in war, and although it did not prohibit development or stockpiling, it established a norm that shaped behavior. The Chemical Weapons Convention, in force from 1997, went further, banning development, production, stockpiling, and use, and establishing an inspection regime. The convention has been largely successful, though not entirely: Syria used chemical weapons in its civil war, and the international response was halting. The lesson is that norms can restrain but cannot eliminate, and restraint depends on enforcement.

The same pattern appears in the history of biological weapons. The Biological Weapons Convention of 1972 prohibited the development, production, and stockpiling of biological agents for hostile purposes. Most states have ratified it, but it lacks a verification mechanism, and the history of the Soviet biological weapons program shows how easily a determined state can evade a norm it has formally accepted. Biological weapons development is constrained less by law than by the difficulty of weaponizing pathogens and the fear of blowback. A biological weapon is indiscriminate in a way even a nuclear weapon is not, because it can spread beyond the target and return to the sender. The restraint is therefore partly prudential and partly normative, and the two reinforce each other.

The nuclear case is different because the weapon is so powerful that its use is almost unthinkable, and the restraint is therefore built into the structure of the international system rather than imposed from outside. The doctrine of mutually assured destruction, which dominated strategic thinking during the Cold War, rested on the recognition that a nuclear war could not be won and must not be fought. It was never formally adopted as policy by all parties and was always contested by those who believed nuclear weapons could be used in a limited way or that a defense could be built. But the underlying logic was sound: the more powerful the weapon, the less usable it becomes, and the more weapons development becomes a matter of signaling and deterrence rather than battlefield advantage.

The development of delivery systems tells the same story. The bomber that carried Little Boy was a propeller-driven aircraft with a range of about 3,000 kilometers. The intercontinental ballistic missile that followed had a range of more than 10,000 kilometers and a flight time of about 30 minutes. The submarine-launched ballistic missile added stealth, because a submarine could hide beneath the ocean and launch on short notice. The multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle multiplied the warheads a single missile could deliver. Each development increased speed and reduced warning time, and each made the system more dangerous by putting more pressure on decision-makers who would have to respond in minutes. Weapons development had always compressed the time between the decision to fight and the fight itself. Now it had compressed the time to the point where human judgment was almost excluded.

The paradox of the nuclear age is that the most powerful weapons ever built have not been used in war since 1945. This is not because the world became peaceful. It is because the weapons changed the calculus of war. The great powers fought proxy wars, supported insurgencies, and competed in every domain except direct nuclear confrontation. Conventional weapons continued to develop, becoming more precise, more lethal, and more expensive. The nuclear weapon did not eliminate war. It changed the level at which war was fought and the means by which it was conducted.

The precision revolution is the second great transformation of the modern era, and it most directly affects the battlefield. Precision-guided munitions changed the relationship between weapon and target. For most of the history traced in this book, a weapon was aimed at an area, and the skill of the gunner determined whether the projectile hit. The bomber of the Second World War dropped its bombs on a city, and accuracy was measured in hundreds of meters. The precision-guided munition is aimed at a point, and accuracy is measured in meters or less. The change is not merely quantitative but qualitative, because it changes what a weapon can be used for and against.

The numbers from Desert Storm in 1991 are instructive. Coalition forces dropped about 88,500 tons of bombs. About 6,520 tons were precision-guided, roughly 7.4 percent. Precision munitions were a small share of the total, but they struck high-value targets and reshaped public and military expectations of air power. Images of laser-guided bombs destroying bridges and command bunkers became the defining images of the war, and services that had resisted the expense of precision weapons suddenly found that the public and politicians expected them. Weapons development is always shaped by the expectations of those who pay for it, and those expectations are shaped by the images of war that reach the public.

The precision revolution had deeper roots than the Gulf War. The laser-guided bomb was developed during the Vietnam War and used with some success against bridges and other point targets. The television-guided bomb followed, and the global positioning system made precision available to every aircraft and every artillery battery. The development was incremental, driven by the same logic that had driven rifled muskets and breech-loading rifles: the desire to hit the target with the first shot and use less ammunition to achieve the same effect. The precision revolution continued the long trend toward accuracy but crossed a threshold when accuracy became sufficient to let a single bomb destroy a single building without destroying the neighborhood around it.

The consequences for strategy were profound. If a weapon can hit a target precisely, the number of weapons needed to destroy it falls, and civilian casualties fall with it. The moral case for precision weapons is that they reduce collateral damage; the military case is that they allow a smaller force to achieve a larger effect. But the precision revolution also lowered the political cost of using force, because it reduced the risk of civilian casualties that might provoke domestic opposition. The same weapon that made war more humane in one sense made it more likely in another. Weapons development always has this double character: it solves one problem and creates another.

The drone is the most recent expression of the precision revolution and the weapon that most clearly illustrates the current relationship between technology and war. The armed drone is a precision-guided munition delivered by a remotely piloted aircraft. It combines the accuracy of the precision weapon with the persistence of the aircraft and the safety of the remote pilot. The United States used drones extensively in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Yemen, and Somalia, and their use became a defining feature of the post-9/11 wars. The drone lowered the cost of strike operations by removing the need to put a pilot at risk, and it raised new questions about sovereignty, civilian casualties, and the legal basis for targeted killing.

The drone also changed the geography of war. A pilot sitting in a control station in Nevada could strike a target in Pakistan, and the distance between decision and effect became almost irrelevant. Weapons development had always been a story of extending the warrior's reach, from spear to bow to rifle to missile. The drone extended it to the point where the warrior was no longer physically present in the battlespace at all. The psychological consequences are only beginning to be understood. The pilot who kills from a distance does not see the victim's face, and the moral weight of the act is distributed across a chain of command stretching from the control station to headquarters to policymakers. Weapons development always changes the moral experience of those who use them, and the drone changes it in ways still being worked out.

The Nagorno-Karabakh war of 2020 is the clearest demonstration of how drones have changed the battlefield. In the 44-day war, Azerbaijan used Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones and loitering munitions against Armenian armor, artillery, and air defenses. The drones were not invincible and were vulnerable to well-organized air defenses, but they were effective enough to destroy a significant portion of the Armenian armored force and suppress the air defense systems that might have stopped them. The Royal United Services Institute's 2021 study treated the conflict as a landmark for drone-enabled strike and for the suppression of air defense. Military planners drew the lesson that drones and loitering munitions combined could change the balance of power on the battlefield, and that the traditional advantages of armor and artillery could be eroded by a cheaper, more numerous, and more precise adversary.

The war also illustrated the modern battlefield's vulnerability to surveillance. The drones were effective not only because they could strike but because they could see. Persistent surveillance combined with precision strike created a battlefield where movement was dangerous and concealment difficult. Weapons development had always been a competition between means of attack and means of defense, and the drone shifted the balance toward attack. The defender who could not hide could not survive, and the attacker who could see everything could choose the moment and place of the strike.

The loitering munition is the next step in the same direction. It can cruise over the battlefield, search for a target, and strike when the target is found. It combines the functions of drone and missile and can be used against tanks, radars, and other high-value targets. Development has been rapid, and loitering munitions have been used in Nagorno-Karabakh, Libya, and Ukraine. The most controversial question is whether they can operate autonomously, selecting and striking targets without human intervention. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Libya reported in 2021 that a Kargu-2 loitering munition may have been used in autonomous mode against retreating forces, but the claim remains contested and has not been independently confirmed. The caveat is essential, because the difference between a remote-controlled weapon and an autonomous one is the difference between a tool and an agent, and the moral and legal questions autonomy raises are profound.

The debate over autonomous weapons is the current frontier of the long argument about technology and restraint. The campaign to ban fully autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots," has gathered support from a coalition of states, civil society organizations, and scientists. The argument is that a machine should not be allowed to decide to kill a human being, because that decision requires judgment machines cannot possess and because accountability would be diffused beyond the point where anyone could be held responsible. The counterargument is that autonomous weapons could be more precise and more humane than human soldiers, because they would not act out of fear or anger, and that a ban would be unenforceable because the technology is already spreading. The debate is unresolved and likely to remain so. But its terms are familiar from earlier chapters. Every new weapon has provoked a debate about whether it should be allowed, and the debate has usually ended with the weapon allowed but regulated. The question is whether autonomous weapons will follow the same pattern or be the exception.

Cyber weapons are the other frontier, and in some ways the more disruptive. A cyber weapon is software or a set of techniques used to damage or disrupt an adversary's computer systems. The Stuxnet worm, discovered in 2010, targeted the centrifuges at Iran's Natanz enrichment facility, causing them to spin out of control and destroying a significant number. Stuxnet was a precision weapon in the same sense as a laser-guided bomb: designed to hit a specific target and minimize collateral damage. But it could also spread beyond its target, and it raised questions about attribution and the rules of engagement in cyberspace.

The cyber domain differs from the physical domains in which weapons have traditionally operated. Barriers to entry are low, because a state or non-state actor can develop cyber capabilities with modest resources. Attribution is difficult, because an attacker can hide behind intermediaries and false flags. Effects are difficult to predict, because a cyber weapon can spread in ways the attacker did not intend. And the line between espionage and attack is blurred, because the same techniques used to steal information can be used to damage systems. Cyber weapons development has therefore been accompanied by efforts to establish norms of behavior, and those norms remain weak. The most important norm—that states should not attack each other's critical infrastructure in peacetime—has been violated repeatedly.

The cyber domain also illustrates how weapons development is shaped by the structure of the international system. The great powers have an interest in maintaining cyber stability, because all are vulnerable to cyber attack. But they also have an interest in developing offensive cyber capabilities, because those can gain advantage at lower cost than kinetic weapons. The result is a competition restrained by mutual vulnerability but not eliminated by it. The same logic that produced the nuclear stalemate is at work in cyberspace, but the stakes are lower and the rules less clear.

Hypersonic weapons are the most recent example of competition in conventional and strategic capabilities. A hypersonic weapon is a missile or glide vehicle that travels at more than five times the speed of sound and can maneuver in flight. Speed and maneuverability make it difficult to intercept, and the United States, Russia, and China have all pursued hypersonic weapons. Their strategic significance is that they reduce warning time for a nuclear attack and complicate the calculation of deterrence. If a hypersonic missile can reach its target in minutes, the defender has less time to decide whether the attack is real and how to respond. Hypersonic weapons development is therefore a development in the nuclear balance as well as the conventional balance, and it illustrates how the pursuit of advantage in one domain can destabilize another.

The history of weapons development is not a story of progress in the sense of moral improvement. It is a story of increasing capability, accompanied by increasing efforts at restraint. The two trends are not opposites but two sides of the same coin. The more destructive the weapon, the more urgent the effort to restrain it, and the more successful the restraint, the more the competition shifts to other domains. The nuclear weapon was restrained by the fear of mutual destruction, and competition shifted to conventional precision weapons. The precision weapon was restrained by the laws of war, and competition shifted to drones and cyber. The drone is being restrained by the debate over autonomy, and competition is shifting to hypersonics and artificial intelligence. The pattern is not a cycle, because each new domain is different. But the logic is consistent.

The sixth lesson of this history is that weapons development is a story of efforts to restrain it, and those efforts have been partly successful and partly unsuccessful. The final part of the argument must therefore examine the institutions and norms built to restrain weapons and assess their record. The record is mixed but not negligible. The laws of war, codified in the Geneva Conventions and their additional protocols, prohibit attacks on civilians and require that attacks be proportionate and discriminate. The conventions have been violated repeatedly, but they have also shaped the behavior of states and the expectations of the international community. The prohibition of chemical and biological weapons has been more successful than that of nuclear weapons, because chemical and biological weapons are less useful to the powerful and because the norms against them are more widely shared. The prohibition of anti-personnel landmines, codified in the Ottawa Convention of 1997, has reduced the production and use of landmines, but it has not been universally accepted, and the United States, Russia, and China have not joined.

The institutions that monitor and enforce the law are also mixed in effectiveness. The International Criminal Court can prosecute individuals for war crimes, but it has limited jurisdiction and limited enforcement power. The United Nations Security Council can impose sanctions and authorize the use of force, but it is paralyzed by the veto power of its permanent members. The treaty regimes governing nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons have verification mechanisms, but they are imperfect and the regimes uneven. The lesson is that restraint depends on the convergence of interests among the powerful, and when interests diverge, restraint weakens.

Weapons development has also been shaped by the changing character of the state. The medieval state could not afford a standing army, and weapons development was shaped by the need to equip a militia or levy. The early modern state could afford a standing army, and development was shaped by the need to equip and supply a professional force. The industrial state could afford a mass army, and development was shaped by the need to produce weapons in enormous quantities. The nuclear state could afford a deterrent, and development was shaped by the need to maintain a credible threat. The contemporary state faces a different set of constraints, because the cost of precision weapons and the complexity of the systems that support them have risen to the point where only the wealthiest states can afford a full spectrum of capabilities. The result is a widening gap between the great powers and the rest, and the gap is itself a source of instability.

The economics of weapons development runs through the entire history and deserves a closer look in this final part. Developing a new weapon is expensive, and the expense is borne by the state or by the private firms that contract with it. The expense creates a barrier to entry, and the barrier shapes the distribution of military power. The longbow was cheap to make but expensive to master, requiring years of training. The crossbow was expensive to make but cheap to master, requiring only a few weeks of training. The musket was expensive to make and cheap to master, and the combination made it possible to equip a mass army. The rifle was more expensive than the musket, the machine gun more expensive than the rifle, and the precision-guided munition more expensive than the machine gun. Each step up in cost has been accompanied by a step up in capability, and the states that could afford the step up gained an advantage over those that could not.

The economics of the modern weapons system is dominated by research and development, which is often far greater than the cost of production. Developing a new fighter aircraft can cost tens of billions of dollars, and developing a new nuclear weapon can cost even more. Development is a fixed cost, production a variable cost, and the fixed cost is borne by the state that develops the weapon. The result is that the states with the largest economies have a structural advantage in developing new weapons, and the advantage is cumulative, because states that develop new weapons can sell them and use the revenue to fund further development. The international arms trade is therefore not a side effect of weapons development. It is a central mechanism by which weapons development is funded and diffused.

The arms trade has its own history, which illustrates the relationship between weapons and politics. The great powers have always sold weapons to allies and clients, using the sales to gain influence, support friendly governments, and sustain domestic defense industries. The sales have also been used to restrain the spread of the most sensitive technologies, because sellers can choose their buyers. The result is a system in which the great powers supply the rest of the world with weapons, and the rest of the world uses them in conflicts the great powers may or may not support. The system is stable in that it has persisted for centuries, but unstable in that it constantly generates new conflicts and new demands for weapons.

Weapons development has also been shaped by the changing character of the soldier. The medieval knight was a heavily armored cavalryman who dominated the battlefield because he could afford the armor, the horse, and the training. The longbowman was a commoner who could kill a knight from a distance, and the longbow was therefore a democratization of military power. The musketeer was a commoner who could kill a knight with a single shot, and the musket completed the process. The rifleman could kill from a greater distance, and the machine gunner could kill many at once. The precision-weapons operator is a technician who sits at a console and kills from a distance, and precision weapons have created a new kind of soldier who is more like an engineer than a warrior.

The changing character of the soldier has consequences for the relationship between war and society. The medieval knight was a member of a warrior class with a distinct social status and a code of honor. The longbowman was a commoner paid for his service, with no such status. The musketeer was a soldier in a professional army, and the rifleman a citizen-soldier in a mass army. The precision-weapons operator is a professional in a highly technical military, and the gap between the military and the society it serves has widened. Weapons development has always shaped the relationship between the military and society, and the current phase is shaping it in ways not yet fully understood.

The history of weapons is also a history of the human body. Weapons development has been driven in part by the desire to protect the body from harm, and armor development has been a continuous response to weapons development. The medieval knight wore chain mail and then plate armor, and plate armor was effective against the weapons of the time. Firearms made plate armor obsolete, because a bullet could penetrate armor a sword could not. Modern body armor has been a response to modern firearms, and the armor worn by soldiers in Iraq and Afghanistan has saved many lives. Weapons development has also been driven by the desire to harm the body, and the history of wound ballistics is a history of the effort to make weapons more lethal. The Minié ball, developed in 1849, was a hollow-base bullet that expanded into the rifling of a musket, allowing faster reloading and greater accuracy. It was used in the British Pattern 1853 Enfield and the U.S. Springfield Model 1861, and it contributed to the casualties of the American Civil War by extending the effective range of the rifle and making the battlefield more deadly.

The Minié ball is a good example of how a small technical change can have large consequences. The problem it solved was the difficulty of loading a rifled musket. A rifle has a grooved barrel that spins the bullet, and the spin makes the bullet more accurate. But a bullet that fits tightly enough to engage the rifling is difficult to ram down the barrel, and the difficulty slows the rate of fire. The Minié ball solved the problem by making the bullet smaller than the bore and hollow at the base, so that the expanding gases of the propellant would expand the base into the rifling. The result was a rifle that could be loaded as quickly as a smoothbore musket and was far more accurate. The change was small, but the consequence was large: it made the rifle the standard infantry weapon and extended the range at which infantry could engage.

The machine gun is another example of a small technical change with large consequences. The Maxim gun, demonstrated in 1884, was the first widely adopted self-powered machine gun. It used the recoil of the fired cartridge to operate the mechanism, so the gunner only had to hold the trigger and feed the ammunition. The British Army adopted a .303-caliber Maxim in 1891, and the gun became the template for automatic warfare. The machine gun changed the tactical balance between attack and defense, because a small number of gunners could stop a large number of attackers. The trenches of the First World War were the result, and the tank was the response. The chain of cause and effect runs from the machine gun to the trench to the tank to the anti-tank weapon to the armored vehicle, each step a response to the one before.

Artillery is the third example, and it most clearly illustrates the relationship between industrial production and weapons development. The French 75mm field gun, adopted in 1897, used a hydro-pneumatic recoil system that kept the carriage steady, enabling rapid fire without re-aiming after each shot. The gun could fire roughly 15 rounds per minute and became an icon of the First World War. The Battle of Verdun, which ran from 21 February to 18 December 1916, produced roughly 700,000 casualties, and artillery dominated the battlefield. The battle was fought with shells, the shells were produced by factories, and the factories required coal, steel, and labor. Artillery development was therefore a development in industrial capacity as much as in military technology, and the states that could produce the most shells had an advantage measured in tons rather than tactics.

The First World War is the clearest example of weapons development outrunning tactical development. The weapons of 1914 were far more lethal than those of 1870, but the tactics of 1914 were not much different from those of 1870. The result was a stalemate in which millions of soldiers were killed by weapons their commanders did not understand. The lesson is that weapons development is not enough. Weapons must be integrated into a system of tactics and organization, and integration takes time and costs lives. The same lesson has been learned repeatedly in the history of weapons, and it is being learned again as militaries struggle to integrate drones, cyber, and artificial intelligence into their existing structures.

The Second World War is the clearest example of weapons development accelerated by the demands of total war. The war produced radar, the jet engine, the ballistic missile, the computer, and the nuclear weapon, and each changed the world beyond the battlefield. The Manhattan Project employed more than 100,000 people and cost about 2 billion dollars, a sum worth many times more today. It was a model of state-directed research and development, demonstrating that a government could mobilize the resources of science and industry to solve a problem that had seemed impossible. The model was copied by the Soviet Union, which developed its own nuclear weapon in 1949, and by the other nuclear powers that followed.

The nuclear weapon also changed the relationship between science and the state. The scientists who built the bomb were aware of the moral implications of their work, and many campaigned for international control of nuclear energy after the war. The campaign failed, and the result was a decades-long competition between the United States and the Soviet Union. The lesson is that weapons development is not a neutral activity. It is a political activity, and the scientists who participate in it are political actors whether they intend to be or not. The same lesson applies to the scientists and engineers developing artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons today.

The Cold War is the period in which weapons development became a permanent competition. The United States and the Soviet Union competed in nuclear weapons, delivery systems, conventional forces, and space. The competition was driven by ideology and by fear of the other side, and it produced an arms race that consumed enormous resources and shaped the economies of both countries. It also produced a series of arms-control agreements, beginning with the Partial Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibited nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space, and underwater. The agreements were not a renunciation of weapons. They were a recognition that the competition had become too dangerous to be left unregulated. The same recognition is behind current efforts to regulate artificial intelligence and cyber weapons.

The end of the Cold War did not end weapons development. It changed the context. The United States emerged as the sole superpower and used its advantage to develop a new generation of precision weapons and intervene in conflicts around the world. The interventions in the Balkans, Afghanistan, and Iraq demonstrated the power of precision weapons and the limits of military force. The wars were won quickly and the peace lost slowly, and the lesson was that weapons development could win battles but could not build states. That lesson is being learned again as the great powers compete for influence in a world more multipolar than at any time since the Cold War's end.

The return of great-power competition is the defining feature of the current era, and it is reshaping weapons development. The United States, China, and Russia are competing in every domain, from the seabed to space, and the competition is driving new weapons and new strategies. It is also driving new alliances and institutions, and the result is a world more fragmented and more dangerous than a decade ago. Weapons development is always shaped by the structure of the international system, and the current structure is one of multipolar competition. The weapons being developed today reflect that structure and will shape the structure of the future.

The most important development in the current era may be the integration of artificial intelligence into weapons systems. Artificial intelligence is not a weapon in itself. It is a technology that can make weapons more autonomous, more precise, and more lethal. Its integration into weapons systems is already underway and likely to accelerate. The consequences are difficult to predict, because artificial intelligence is a general-purpose technology applicable to many problems. But the direction is clear: weapons development is moving toward systems that can operate with less human intervention, and the trend raises the same questions as the debate over autonomous weapons. The difference is that the trend is broader than the debate and likely to affect every domain of warfare.

The history of weapons is also a history of the effort to understand the consequences of new technology before it is used. The scientists who built the first nuclear weapon understood that they were creating a weapon of unprecedented power, and they tried to warn the world. The warning was not heeded, and the result was a nuclear arms race. The lesson is that weapons development is always accompanied by an effort to understand its consequences, and the effort is always incomplete. The consequences of a new weapon are never fully known until it is used, and its use changes the world in ways that cannot be predicted. The same is true of artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons, and the effort to understand their consequences is still in its early stages.

Weapons development has also been shaped by the changing character of the battlefield. The medieval battlefield was a field or a castle, and weapons were designed for close combat. The industrial battlefield was a trench or a city, and weapons were designed for mass destruction. The current battlefield is a network of sensors and shooters, and weapons are designed for precision and speed. Changes in the character of the battlefield have changed the character of weapons, and changes in the character of weapons have changed the character of the battlefield. The relationship is circular, driven by the same logic that has driven weapons development throughout history: the desire to gain an advantage over the adversary.

Weapons development has also been shaped by the changing character of the adversary. The medieval adversary was a neighboring lord or rival kingdom, and weapons were designed to defeat a specific enemy. The industrial adversary was a nation-state, and weapons were designed to defeat a mass army. The current adversary is a network of state and non-state actors, and weapons are designed to defeat a diffuse and adaptable enemy. Changes in the character of the adversary have changed the character of weapons, and the change is likely to continue as the international system evolves.

The history of weapons is not a story that can be told without a sense of tragedy. Weapons development has been driven by the desire to protect oneself and one's community, and the result has been the creation of instruments that can destroy entire communities.
